AI is the technology that enables machines to use humanlike intelligence to perform tasks. With AI, computers can learn, plan, and solve problems; they can recognize images and process spoken languages. This takes place through machine learning.

Machine learning teaches computers how to execute specific tasks. To begin, people feed large amounts of data into a computer program. For instance, to create a plant identifier program, photographs of labeled plants are fed into the computer. Its program learns the traits of each species. Then, when a person asks the program to identify an unknown plant, it scans its database for a comparable photograph to determine the answer.

Machine learning also allows AI programs to recognize patterns and make predictions. For instance, streaming services use computers to collect data on the shows their viewers watch. Next, AI programs analyze the data so that they can recommend movies those viewers might enjoy. In a similar way, online companies gather data on purchases and use AI programs to target other items those customers may purchase.

A computer can analyze extensive amounts of unlabeled data from many sources. For instance, self-driving cars rely on deep learning to recognize all the different objects in their surroundings as they navigate.

(1) Medical waste has been a growing concern because of recent incidents of public exposure to discarded blood vials, needles (sharps), empty prescription bottles, and syringes. Medical waste can typically include general refuse, human blood and blood products, cultures and stocks of infectious agents, laboratory animal carcasses, contaminated bedding material, and pathological wastes. (2) Wastes are generally collected by gravity chutes, carts, or pneumatic tubes, each of which has its own advantages and disadvantages. Chutes are limited to vertical transport, and there is some risk of exhausting contaminants into hallways if a door is left open during use. Another disadvantage of gravity chutes is that the waste container may get jammed while dropping, or it may be broken upon hitting the bottom. Carts are primarily for horizontal transport of bagged or containerized wastes. The main risk here is that bags may be broken or torn during transport, potentially exposing the worker to the wastes. Using automated carts can reduce the potential for exposure. Pneumatic tubes offer the best performance for waste transport in a large facility. Advantages include high-speed movement, movement in any direction, and minimal intermediate storage of untreated wastes. However, some objects cannot be conveyed pneumatically.

(3) Off-site disposal of regulated medical wastes remains a viable option for smaller hospitals (those with less than 150 beds). Some preliminary on-site processing, such as compaction or hydropulping, may be necessary prior to sending the waste off site. Compaction reduces the total volume of solid wastes, often reducing transportation and disposal costs, but it does not change the hazardous characteristics of the waste. Compaction may not be economical if transportation and disposal costs are based on weight rather than volume. (4) Hydropulping involves grinding the waste in the presence of an oxidizing fluid, such as hypochlorite solution. The liquid is separated from the pulp and discharged directly into the sewer unless local limits require additional pretreatment prior to discharge. The pulp can often be disposed of at a landfill. One advantage is that waste can be rendered innocuous and reduced in size within the same system. Disadvantages are the added operating burden, difficulty of controlling fugitive emissions, and the difficulty of conducting microbiological tests to determine whether all organic matters and infectious organisms have been destroyed from the waste.

(5) On-site disposal is a feasible alternative for hospitals generating two tons or more per day of total solid waste. Common treatment techniques include steam sterilization and incineration. Although other options are available, incineration is currently the preferred method for on-site treatment of hospital waste. (6) Steam sterilization is limited in the types of medical waste it can treat, but is appropriate for laboratory cultures and/or substances contaminated with infectious organisms. The waste is subjected to steam in a sealed, pressurized chamber. The liquid that may form is drained off to the sewer or sent for processing. The unit is then reopened after a vapor release to the atmosphere, and the solid waste is removed for further processing or disposal. One advantage of steam sterilization is that it has been used for many years in hospitals to sterilize instruments and containers and to treat small quantities of waste. However, since sterilization does not change the appearance of the waste, there could be a problem in gaining acceptance of the waste for landfilling.

(7) A properly designed, maintained, and operated incinerator achieves a relatively high level of organism destruction. Incineration reduces the weight and volume of the waste as much as 95% and is especially appropriate for pathological wastes and sharps. The most common incineration system for medical waste is the controlled-air type. The principal advantage of this type of incinerator is low particulate emissions. Rotary-kiln and grate-type units have been used, but use of grate-type units has been discontinued because of high air emissions. The rotary kiln also puts out high emissions, and the costs have been prohibitive for smaller units.

The School and Society This passage by John Dewey, a philosopher and educational reformer, was first published in 1900.

Some years ago I was looking about the school supply stores in the city, trying to find desks and chairs which seemed thoroughly suitable from all points of view— artistic, hygienic, and educational—to the needs of the children. We had a good deal of difficulty in finding what we needed, and finally one dealer, more intelligent than the rest, made this remark: 'I am afraid we have not what you want. You want something at which the children may work; these are all for listening.' That tells the story of the traditional education. If we put before the mind's eye the ordinary schoolroom, with its rows of ugly desks placed in geometrical order, desks almost all of the same size, with just space enough to hold books, pencils and paper, and add a table, some chairs, the bare walls, and possibly a few pictures, we can reconstruct the only educational activity that can possibly go on in such a place. It is all made 'for listening'—for simply studying lessons out of a book is only another kind of listening; it marks the dependency of one mind upon another. The attitude of listening means, comparatively speaking, passivity.

There is very little place in the traditional schoolroom for the child to work. The workshop, the laboratory, the materials, the tools with which the child may construct, create, and actively inquire, and even the requisite space, have been for the most part lacking. They are what the educational authorities who write editorials in the daily papers generally term 'fads' and 'frills.' We can also examine the uniformity of method and curriculum. If everything is on a 'listening' basis, you can have uniformity of material and method. There is next to no opportunity for adjustment to varying capacities and demands. It is in response to this approach that the curriculum has been developed from the elementary school up through the college. There is just so much desirable knowledge, and there are just so many needed technical accomplishments in the world. Then comes the mathematical problem of dividing this by the six, twelve, or sixteen years of school life. Now give the children every year just the proportionate fraction of the total, and by the time they have finished they will have mastered the whole.

If we take an example from an ideal home, where the parent is intelligent enough to recognize what is best for the child, and is able to supply what is needed, we find the child learning through the activity of the family. Inquiries arise, topics are discussed, and the child continually learns. The child participates in the household occupations, and thereby gets habits of industry, order, and regard for the rights and ideas of others, and the fundamental habit of subordinating his activities to the general interest of the household. Participation in these household tasks becomes an opportunity for gaining knowledge. The ideal home would naturally have a workshop where the child could work out his constructive instincts. The life of the child would extend out of doors to the garden, surrounding fields, and forests. Now, if we generalize all of this, we have the ideal school. There is no mystery about it, no wonderful discovery of pedagogy or educational theory. It is simply a question of doing systematically and in a large, intelligent, and competent way what for various reasons can be done in most households only in a comparatively meagre 45 and haphazard manner. In the first place, the ideal home has to be enlarged. The child must be brought into contact with more adults and more children in order that there may be the freest and richest social life. Moreover, the occupations and relationships of the home environment are not specially selected for the growth of the child. Hence the need of a school. Learning?—certainly, but living primarily, and learning through and in relation to this living. When we take this approach, we do not find that the child is primarily a listening being; quite the contrary. He is already running over, spilling over, with activities of all kinds. He is not a purely latent being whom the adult has to approach with great skill in order gradually to draw out some hidden germ of activity. The child is already intensely active. 61

Option A: idealistic.

Option C: responsive.
Option D: hypocritical.

A friendship bracelet is a fun way to show a friend you care.
You will need:
three pieces of coloured wool, each as long as your arm
sticky tape

1. Tie the three pieces together with a knot at one end.
2. Tape the knot to a table.

4. When it fits around a wrist, tie another knot.
5. Give it to your friend with a big smile.

A friendship bracelet is a fun way to show a friend you care.
You will need:
three pieces of coloured wool, each as long as your arm
sticky tape

1. Tie the three pieces together with a knot at one end.
2. Tape the knot to a table.
3. Plait the wool. Cross the left piece over the middle one, then the right piece over the middle one. Keep going.
4. When it fits around a wrist, tie another knot.
5. Give it to your friend with a big smile.
Tip: Choose your friend's favourite colours. They will know you were thinking of them!

A good campsite can make a camping trip safe and comfortable. Before you put up your tent, take a careful look around.
First, look for flat, even ground. If you sleep on a slope, you may slide to one side of the tent during the night. Clear away sticks and stones so they don't poke you through your sleeping mat.

Finally, think about the wind. A sheltered spot behind a low hill or some bushes will stop your tent flapping all night.
If you choose your spot wisely, you will wake up rested and ready to explore.

Behind the Museum Doors
When you visit a museum, you see only a small part of its collection. Most big museums keep thousands of objects in storerooms that visitors never see. Often only one object in every twenty is on display.
The people who look after these objects are called conservators. Their job is to protect treasures so they last for hundreds of years. They wear gloves, because the oils and salt on our skin can slowly damage old paper, metal and cloth.
Light is another danger. Bright light can make colours fade, so delicate items such as old flags and drawings are kept in dim rooms. Some are shown for only a few months, then rested in the dark.
Conservators also control the air. If a room is too damp, mould can grow. If it is too dry, wood can crack.
So next time you walk through a museum, remember the hidden helpers who keep the past safe for the future.

Option A: The objects are often very dusty.
Option B: Old metal can be sharp to touch.
Option C: Our skin can slowly damage old objects.
Option D: The storerooms are cold and damp.

Up in the canopy, high and wide,
the leaves make a roof where the parrots hide.

the ferns spread wide to let it in.
A cassowary steps, so slow and proud,
with a helmet tall and a boom so loud.

wraps round a tree as the years go by.
It climbs and it hugs, it squeezes tight,
till it stands alone in the pale green light.

So tread softly here, where the old trees grow,
in the dripping dark and the emerald glow.
This forest was here long before me and you.
Let's keep it safe for the young ones too.

Beating Stage Fright
Have you ever felt your knees wobble before a school concert? Many performers feel nervous before they go on stage. This is called stage fright, and even famous singers get it.
When you feel nervous, your body makes a chemical called adrenaline. It can make your heart beat fast and your hands shake. But adrenaline also gives you energy and helps you focus.
Performers use lots of tricks. They practise their piece many times, so their fingers and voice know what to do. Before going on, they take slow, deep breaths. Some picture the audience smiling and clapping. Sam, a drummer in his school band, quietly taps out his rhythm on his knees while he waits backstage.
Remember that the audience wants you to do well. They came to enjoy the show, not to look for mistakes.
So next time your knees wobble, don't panic. Those butterflies in your tummy mean you care about doing a good job. Take a breath, step out and shine!

Before 1872, news from England took about two months to reach Australia by ship. Charles Todd, who was in charge of telegraphs in South Australia, had a plan to change that.
He planned a telegraph line from Adelaide to Darwin. It would stretch about 3,200 kilometres through the middle of the continent. In Darwin, it would join an undersea cable to Java and on to Europe.
Work began in 1870. Teams of workers put up tens of thousands of poles across deserts and scrubland. They faced scorching heat, floods and shortages of food and water.
In August 1872, the final piece of wire was joined. Messages were sent in Morse code, using short and long signals. News that had taken months could now arrive in hours. The thin wire was like a voice that could call across the desert.
Along the way, repeater stations were built to pass messages on. One, near a waterhole named after Todd's wife, Alice, grew into the town of Alice Springs.

Option A: Charles Todd planned the line.
Option B: Workers put up the poles.
Option C: The final wire was joined.
Option D: Alice Springs became a town.

The Toast Mystery
Have you ever dropped a piece of buttered toast? If you have, it probably landed butter side down, making a sticky mess on the floor. Many people think this is just bad luck, but scientists say there is a simple reason.
When toast slides off a plate or the edge of a table, it starts to spin as it falls. A kitchen table is not very high, so the toast only has time to make about half a turn before it hits the floor. The toast started with the butter facing up, so half a turn flips it over and the butter faces down. Splat!
Some people have tested this by dropping toast again and again. It landed butter side down much more often than butter side up.
If tables were much taller, the toast would have time to spin all the way round. But nobody wants a table taller than a grown-up!
So how can you save your snack? The best plan is to hold your plate carefully with both hands. Or you could just eat your toast quickly!

Option A: butter side up
Option B: on its edge
Option C: on the table
Option D: butter side down

When toast slides off a plate or the edge of a table, it starts to spin as it falls. A kitchen table is not very high, so the toast only has time to make about half a turn before it hits the floor. The toast started with the butter facing up, so half a turn flips it over and the butter faces down. Splat!
Some people have tested this by dropping toast again and again. It landed butter side down much more often than butter side up.
If tables were much taller, the toast would have time to spin all the way round. But nobody wants a table taller than a grown-up!
So how can you save your snack? The best plan is to hold your plate carefully with both hands. Or you could just eat your toast quickly!
Question: Why does falling toast usually land butter side down?
Option A: The butter makes one side of the toast heavier.
Option B: People are unlucky when they drop their food.
Option C: It only has time to flip halfway over before landing.
Option D: Toast always spins all the way round as it falls.

Millions of years ago, a dinosaur died beside a muddy river. Over time, its skin and muscles rotted away, leaving only its bones. Layers of mud and sand slowly covered the skeleton like a heavy blanket.
As more layers piled on top, the mud turned into hard rock. Water seeped through the rock and carried tiny bits of minerals into the bones. Bit by bit, the minerals replaced the bone, until the skeleton had turned to stone. This stone copy is called a fossil.
Most dinosaurs never became fossils. Their bodies were eaten by other animals or simply crumbled away before mud could cover them.
Today, scientists called palaeontologists search for fossils in places where wind and rain have worn away old rock. They brush the dirt away gently, using tools as small as toothbrushes. Finding even one fossil tooth can make a palaeontologist's whole year. Each fossil is a clue that helps us learn about the giant animals that lived long ago.

'Can we finish first?' he asked.

Option C: the fire
Option D: two candles

On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, the moon rose big and round over the backyard. Mei and her grandmother, Nai Nai, sat at the table making paper lanterns.
Nai Nai's fingers folded the red paper quickly into a neat rabbit shape. Mei tried to copy her, but her paper kept tearing. When she finished, her rabbit had one long ear and one short ear, and it leaned to the side.
'It looks silly,' Mei grumbled, and pushed it away.
Nai Nai picked it up and turned it in the moonlight. 'It is perfectly imperfect,' she said. 'No one else in the world has a lantern like this one.'
Mei looked at her lantern again. Maybe the floppy ear made it look friendly.
Nai Nai placed a small light inside, and the rabbit began to glow. Then she cut a mooncake into slices, and they shared it while the whole family walked around the garden with their lanterns.
Mei held her rabbit up high. Its crooked ears made the best shadow of all.

Option A: the light of the big round moon
Option B: a candle that Mei held up high
Option C: a small light that Nai Nai put inside
Option D: the lights the family carried outside

Is That Really My Voice?
Have you ever heard yourself on a video and thought, 'Do I really sound like that?' Most people feel a little surprised. There is a simple reason.
When you speak, your voice makes tiny shakes called vibrations. These vibrations travel out through the air and into the ears of the people around you. That is how your friends hear you.
You hear your own voice in two ways at once. Some sound reaches your ears through the air, just like it does for your friends. But some sound also travels through the bones inside your head. Bones carry low sounds well, so this makes your voice seem deeper and fuller to you.
A microphone only picks up the sound that travels through the air. So a recording plays back the voice that everyone else hears every day.
Next time you hear yourself on a video, don't worry. You are hearing your real voice, the same one your friends know.

Option A: bones
Option B: low
Option C: well
Option D: carry

After seeing such a strange creature, they probably told the tale again and again, making the monster bigger each time.
For hundreds of years, nobody saw a living giant squid. Then, in 2004, scientists in Japan finally photographed one deep in the sea. The real 'monster' had been hiding in the dark all along.

Option A: scientists in Japan
Option B: sailors from Norway
Option C: fishermen from Japan
Option D: children in Norway

Dairy Day
The sky is grey, the grass is wet,
The sun has not come up just yet.
Dad hands me my torch at the shed,
And out we go, still half in bed.

The cows plod in along the track
With patient eyes and muddy backs.
They line up for the milking shed
While magpies carol overhead.

By noon the sun is blazing high,
The tractor rumbles, hay bales fly.
I fill the troughs and feed the calves,
I'm hot and dusty. Dad just laughs.

When afternoon turns soft and gold,
We mend the fence, as we've been told.
The kelpie races round the yard
And barks as if she's working hard.

At dusk the cows come plodding back
With swishing tails along the track.
Once more we work the milking shed,
Then stars come out. It's time for bed.

Tomorrow, when the sky is grey
And all the stars have slipped away,
I'll grab my torch and boots, and then
We'll do it all, the same, again.

Option A: a bucket
Option B: some boots
Option C: a hay bale
Option D: a torch

Hooray for Muddy Mangroves
Some people think mangroves are smelly, muddy places that should be cleared away. I think we should protect every mangrove forest we have.
Mangroves are amazing trees that grow where the land meets the sea. Twice a day, the tide covers their roots with salty water. Most trees would die, but mangroves can cope. Some even push extra salt out through their leaves.
Mangroves also guard the coast. Their tangled roots act like a fence. When storms send big waves crashing in, the roots slow the water down, so less sand and soil are washed away.
Best of all, mangroves are a home. Crabs dig burrows in the soft mud, and birds build nests in the branches.
And the smell? It comes from mud full of rotting leaves. That rotting mess is food for tiny creatures, and they are food for bigger animals.
So next time you visit, hold your nose if you must, but please don't wish the mangroves gone. They are working hard for all of us.

Most mountains take millions of years to form. A volcano, however, can grow in a much shorter time.
Deep beneath the ground, it is so hot that rock melts into a thick liquid called magma. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly pushes upward. When it finds a crack, it bursts through the surface. Once magma reaches the air, it is called lava.

Saturday 3 March
Dear Diary,
Today Aunty Rose took me to her art studio by the beach. It smelled of paint and salty air. She gave me a real canvas, not just paper, and three tubes of paint: blue, yellow and white.
'Where's the green?' I asked. 'I want to paint the sea.'
Aunty Rose just smiled and told me to mix it myself. I squeezed out some blue and some yellow and swirled them together with my brush. Like magic, the colour turned green! Adding white made it paler, like the shallow water near the sand.
My first wave looked like a lumpy sausage, so I painted over it. My second try was better. Aunty Rose said the best artists make plenty of mistakes.
By lunchtime my picture was finished. It isn't perfect, but the water really does sparkle. Aunty Rose hung it on her studio wall, right next to her own paintings.
I wonder what colours I could make next time with red!
Leah

Option A: blue, green and white
Option B: blue, yellow and white
Option C: red, yellow and blue
Option D: green, yellow and white

Lights Out at Turtle Beach
When Gran and I walk down at dusk,
we carry one dim, red light,
for baby turtles find the sea
by moonlight in the night.
All summer long the nest has slept
beneath the sand, behind a sign.
Gran checks it every afternoon
and ties a fresh, bright ribbon line.
Tonight the sand begins to stir.
A flipper! Then a tiny head!
A hundred hatchlings tumble out
and scramble from their sandy bed.
A porch light blazes up the hill.
Some hatchlings turn, confused and slow.
I race to knock upon the door.
'Please switch it off!' The light goes low.
Now every hatchling heads for foam.
Gran whispers, 'Only one, I fear,
in every thousand lives to grow
and one day lay her eggs right here.'
I watch the last one reach the waves
and make a promise to the sea:
next year I'll ask our street to dim
their lights, and help them all go free.
Question: Why do Gran and the child carry only one dim light?
Option A: so they can see the moon better
Option B: so the neighbours do not wake up
Option C: so the baby turtles are not confused
Option D: so the nest stays warm at night

Where Unicorns Came From
For thousands of years, people have told stories about unicorns. In most tales, a unicorn looks like a white horse with a single long horn growing from its forehead. But where did the idea come from?
Long ago, travellers returned from faraway lands with stories of strange beasts. Some of them may have seen a rhinoceros and described it to people at home. As the story was told again and again, the heavy grey animal slowly changed into a graceful white one.
Later, traders in Europe sold long, twisty horns. They claimed these were unicorn horns and that they could protect people from poison. Rich kings paid huge amounts of money for them.
In fact, the horns came from narwhals. A narwhal is a whale that lives in icy Arctic seas. The male has a long spiral tooth, called a tusk, that pokes out through its lip.

Most trees begin life on the ground and grow upwards. The strangler fig does the opposite.
Its story starts high in the rainforest canopy. A bird or a bat eats a ripe fig, then leaves a seed in the branches of a tall tree. In the warm, damp air, the seed sprouts. Up there, the tiny plant gets plenty of sunlight.
Next, the fig sends long, thin roots down the trunk of its host tree. When the roots finally reach the soil, they drink in water and food. Now the fig grows quickly. Its roots thicken and wrap around the trunk like a net. Its leaves spread out and shade the host tree.
Over many years, the host tree often dies and rots away. A hollow tower of fig roots is left standing. Animals such as possums, frogs and bats shelter inside.
In north Queensland, one famous strangler fig has roots that hang down like a giant curtain. Visitors come from all over the world to see it.

Option A: high in the branches of another tree
Option B: down on the rainforest floor
Option C: inside a hollow, rotting log
Option D: beside a creek in the shade

Give Kids Pocket Money
Should children get pocket money? I believe every child should, and here is why.
First, pocket money teaches us how to manage money. If I spend all my coins on lollies on Monday, I have nothing left for the rest of the week. That is a lesson I will only need to learn once!
Second, pocket money teaches patience. Last year, I wanted a new soccer ball. I saved two dollars every week for ten weeks. When I finally bought it, I felt so proud. It felt much better than if someone had just handed it to me.
Third, earning pocket money by doing chores helps the whole family. When I feed the dog and set the table, Mum and Dad have more time to relax.
Some adults say children will just waste their money. But how will we ever learn to spend wisely if we never get the chance to try?
Pocket money is not just about money. It is about growing up. Parents, please give it a go!

Option D: a dog lead

Saturday, 3 May
Dear Nonna,
Guess what? Today I played my ukulele at the Riverside Market! Mr Tan, my music teacher, said I was ready, so Mum helped me get a busking permit.
At first, my hands were shaking so much that I dropped my pick twice. I nearly packed up and went home. Then a little boy stopped right in front of me. He started clapping along and wiggling his hips. I couldn't help grinning, and suddenly my fingers remembered every chord.
I played all six songs that you taught me, plus a new one about the sea. People dropped coins into my open case. One lady even asked if I would come back next week.
When I counted the money at home, I had $23.50! I am going to put half in my money box and spend the rest on new strings.
I wish you could have been there. Can we play together when you visit in the holidays?
Love,
Isabella

Option A: Her hands were shaking.
Option B: The pick was too small.
Option C: A little boy bumped her.
Option D: The wind blew it away.

One evening in 1905, an eleven-year-old boy named Frank Epperson was making a drink. He lived in San Francisco, in the United States. Frank stirred some sweet soda powder into a cup of water with a wooden stick.

Soon, that name stuck. Today, people still enjoy icy poles on hot days, all thanks to a forgotten drink.

Firstly, the deep sea is dark, freezing and dangerous. The water presses down with a pressure far too strong for the human body. Robots can be built tough enough to handle it. Nobody needs to be put at risk.

Why Ships Measure Speed in Knots
Cars measure their speed in kilometres per hour. Ships, however, use a different unit called the knot. This strange name comes from a clever trick used by sailors hundreds of years ago.
Back then, there were no engines or speed dials. To find out how fast their ship was going, sailors used a tool called a chip log. It was a flat piece of wood tied to a long rope. Knots were tied in the rope at equal distances apart.
A sailor tossed the wood into the sea behind the ship. As the ship sailed on, the rope hissed and whipped through his fingers. Another sailor turned over a small sand timer. When the sand ran out, they counted how many knots had slipped past. More knots meant a faster ship.
Today, ships use satellites to measure their speed. But sailors still say 'knots'. One knot is a little less than two kilometres per hour.

Option A: a metal weight tied to a chain
Option B: a flat piece of wood tied to a rope
Option C: a sand timer tied to a rope
Option D: a speed dial on a ship's wheel

Roads That Lasted
About two thousand years ago, the ancient Romans built one of the greatest road systems in history. Their roads stretched across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.
Roman roads were built in layers, a bit like a giant sandwich. Workers first dug a deep trench. They filled the bottom with large stones, then added smaller stones and gravel. On top, they fitted flat paving stones tightly together.
The roads were also slightly curved, higher in the middle than at the edges. When it rained, the water ran off into ditches at the sides. This stopped puddles from forming and kept the road strong.
Roman builders liked their roads to be as straight as possible. That way, soldiers, traders and messengers could travel quickly from town to town. Along the way, tall stone markers called milestones showed how far it was to the next town.
Amazingly, some Roman roads are still used today.

Then she frowned. 'But where did I put the cheese?'

Option A: muffled
Option B: brrring
Option C: tapped
Option D: whispered

Digging Under the City
How do you build a railway under a busy city without closing all the streets? You send in a giant tunnel boring machine.
A tunnel boring machine, or TBM, is as long as several train carriages. At its front is a huge round cutter head covered with sharp steel discs. The cutter head turns slowly and grinds through rock and soil. A conveyor belt carries the crushed rock back to the surface, where trucks take it away.
As the machine moves forward, it lines the new tunnel with curved concrete pieces. These fit together to make strong rings, so the tunnel does not collapse.
A TBM is not fast. It may travel only about ten to twenty metres in a whole day. It works day and night, though, with crews of workers taking turns to run it.
By tradition, every TBM is given a name before it starts digging, often a woman's name. Workers believe this brings good luck.
Up above, people walk, shop and drive, with no idea that a machine is quietly chewing its way beneath their feet.

Close your eyes and picture a dinosaur. Did you see a scaly green monster? Many books and films show dinosaurs this way, but it is time we changed our picture.
Over the last thirty years, scientists in China have dug up hundreds of fossils with something surprising pressed into the rock – feathers! Some small meat-eaters, such as Velociraptor, were covered in feathers. Others had fluffy, downy coats like baby chicks.

So next time you draw a dinosaur, grab your coloured pencils and give it feathers. Scientists have done the hard work of digging. Now it is our turn to get the picture right!

Option A: Australia

Option C: Canada
Option D: China

Sea stars are often called starfish, but they are not fish at all. Fish have backbones and gills. Sea stars have neither, which is why many scientists prefer the name sea star.
Most sea stars have five arms, though some kinds have twenty or more. Underneath each arm are hundreds of tiny tube feet. The sea star uses them to creep slowly over rocks and to grip its food.
Sea stars have no brain and no blood. Instead, seawater is pumped through their bodies to help carry food and oxygen. At the tip of each arm is a simple eye that can tell light from dark.
A sea star eats in a very unusual way. When it catches a mussel, it pulls the shell open just a little. Then it pushes its own stomach out of its mouth and into the shell, and digests its meal there.
If a sea star loses an arm, it can grow a new one. This can take months, or even a year.
Next time you visit a rock pool, look closely. You might spot one of these amazing animals.

The Sausage Thief
On Sunday, Ellie's family had a barbecue at the park. Dad sizzled sausages on the hot plate while Ellie set out the bread and sauce.
From a branch above them came a loud cackle. 'Koo-koo-koo-ka-ka-ka!'
'A kookaburra,' said Ellie. 'It's laughing at your cooking, Dad!'
'Nonsense,' said Dad. 'It's admiring my sausages.' He held one up proudly on his fork.
In a flash of brown and white, the kookaburra swooped. Snap! The sausage disappeared from the fork. Dad stared at the empty prongs.
The bird flew back to its branch and whacked the sausage against the bark, again and again, just as it would whack a lizard. Then it gulped it down whole.
Ellie giggled. 'Now it really is laughing at you.'
A ranger walking past smiled. 'They're clever hunters,' she said. 'But please don't let them have sausages. Too much salty food can make them sick.'
For the rest of lunch, Dad cooked with one eye on the hot plate and the other on the tree.
Question: The kookaburra 'gulped it down whole'. Which word means the same as 'gulped'?
Option A: dropped
Option B: swallowed
Option C: chewed
Option D: sniffed

People argue about which season is best. Some say summer, with its beach days. Others love the frosty mornings of winter. But I believe autumn beats them all, and here is why.

How to Bottle-Feed a Poddy Lamb
On farms, a lamb sometimes loses its mother or is not fed by her. This lamb is called a poddy lamb, and it needs a person to feed it. Here is how to do it.
You will need:
- a clean feeding bottle with a rubber teat
- lamb milk powder
- warm water
Steps
1. Mix the milk powder with warm water, following the packet. Do not use cow's milk from the fridge, as it can upset a lamb's tummy.
2. Test a few drops on your wrist. The milk should feel warm, not hot.
3. Stand beside the lamb and hold the bottle tipped up, a little higher than its head, the way a lamb drinks from its mother.
4. Let the lamb suck at its own pace. A happy lamb will wiggle its tail as it drinks.
5. When the bottle is empty, wash it in hot soapy water.
Very young lambs need feeding several times a day, even early in the morning. It is hard work, but a poddy lamb soon learns your voice and will come running to greet you.

Option A: cold, like fridge milk
Option B: warm, not hot
Option C: very hot, like soup
Option D: cool, like tap water

Marjory Stoneman Douglas was born in 1890. In 1915, she moved to Miami, Florida, and became a newspaper writer.
South of Miami lay the Everglades, a huge wetland of sawgrass, birds and alligators. Back then, many people called it a useless swamp. Builders wanted to drain the water away to make farms and towns.
Marjory saw it differently. She studied the Everglades for years and learned that it was really a river – a very wide, shallow one, creeping slowly south through the grass. In 1947, she wrote a book called The Everglades: River of Grass. It helped people understand why the wetland mattered. That same year, part of it became a national park.
Marjory did not stop there. When she was 79, she started a group called Friends of the Everglades to protect it from new building plans. She gave talks wearing a big floppy hat and dark glasses, and people listened.
Marjory lived to the age of 108. She is still remembered as the 'Grandmother of the Glades'.
Question: Where did Marjory move to in 1915?
Option A: New York City
Option B: the Everglades
Option C: Washington
Option D: Miami, Florida

The Sandbar Crossing
When the tide slid out at breakfast time,
a path of sand appeared,
a golden road to Gull Island,
the place we'd always neared.

My sister Jo grabbed both our hats,
I packed an apple each.
We splashed across the shining sand
to reach the island's beach.

We found a cave of dripping rock,
a crab with one big claw,
an old glass float all wrapped in rope,
the best we ever saw.

We climbed the rocks to watch the gulls
that circled round the bay,
and ate our apples on a ledge
and saw the dolphins play.

But then Jo pointed at the path.
'The sea is coming back!'
The water licked across the sand
and filled our winding track.

We ran so fast our chests felt tight,
the waves around our knees.
My heart was thumping like a drum
as loud as stormy seas.

We tumbled on the shore at last,
all puffing, wet and sore,
then laughed and planned to come again,
but check the tide times more.
Question: Why could the children walk to Gull Island?
Option A: the sea had frozen over
Option B: a bridge had been built
Option C: the tide had gone out
Option D: Jo knew a secret tunnel

Wave to the Waste Truck
Every week, a big truck rumbles down your street and empties your bins. Most of us hardly notice. I believe waste collectors are some of the most important helpers in our community, and we should thank them.
Imagine what would happen if they stopped coming. After one week, bins would overflow. After two weeks, rubbish would spill onto footpaths, and the smell would be terrible. Flies and rats would soon arrive.

Tug of war looks simple. Two teams grab opposite ends of a long rope and pull. The team that drags the middle of the rope over its line wins. However, the strongest team does not always win. Teamwork matters just as much.
In a match, each team usually has eight pullers. They stand one behind the other along the same side of the rope. The person at the very back is called the anchor. The anchor is often the heaviest puller and wraps the rope around their body to stop the team sliding forward.
A good team leans back and digs its heels into the ground. Most importantly, everyone pulls at the same moment. If one puller tugs early and another tugs late, their strength is wasted. Many teams have a coach who calls out a steady beat so the pullers move together.
Tug of war was once an Olympic sport, from 1900 to 1920. Today, teams from around the world still compete in big championships.

Option A: the puller at the very back
Option B: the coach who calls the beat
Option C: the middle of the rope
Option D: the line the rope crosses

The Frog That Waits for Rain
Most frogs need ponds, creeks or damp forests. Yet one Australian frog lives in some of the driest places on the continent. It is called the water-holding frog.
When heavy rain finally falls in the desert, these frogs come out of the ground. They eat as many insects as they can and lay their eggs in shallow pools. They also soak up water through their skin until their bodies are round and swollen.
As the pools dry up, each frog digs backwards into the soft mud. Deep underground, it sheds layers of skin, which harden into a cocoon around its body. Only its nostrils stay uncovered so it can breathe. The cocoon is like a raincoat worn inside out, because it stops the stored water from escaping.
Then the frog waits. It may stay buried for months, or even years, until the next big storm. Long ago, some Aboriginal desert people knew how to dig up these frogs and squeeze a drink of water from them.
Question: Why did the writer write this text?
Option A: to inform readers about a desert frog
Option B: to tell a made-up story about a frog
Option C: to teach readers how to dig in mud
Option D: to persuade readers to keep frogs as pets

A Trip Inside a Volcano
Dear Ms Kovac,
Our class has been learning about volcanoes, and I think we should go on an excursion to Tower Hill, near Warrnambool. Here are my reasons.
First, Tower Hill is a real volcano. It erupted many thousands of years ago, and it has been quiet ever since. Today, the giant bowl it left behind, called a crater, holds a lake with islands in the middle. We could stand inside a volcano instead of just reading about one in a book!
Second, it would help with our science work. We could see layers of ash in the rocks and find out how the land changed after the eruption.
Third, Tower Hill is full of wildlife. Emus, koalas and kangaroos live there, and there are walking tracks for every age.
Some people might say the trip is too far. However, the bus ride is only about an hour, and we could learn more in one day than in a week of worksheets.
Please say yes. It would be an adventure none of us would forget.
From Ollie

Option A: next to the school
Option B: on an island
Option C: near Warrnambool
Option D: in a big city

Build a Bug Hotel
A bug hotel gives tiny creatures a safe place to shelter, rest and lay their eggs. Many of these minibeasts help plants grow, so they are great visitors to have in your garden.
You will need:
an empty milk carton, washed and dried
scissors
string
hollow sticks, pine cones, bark and dry leaves
What to do:
1. Ask an adult to cut the top off the milk carton.
2. Pack the carton tightly with the sticks, pine cones, bark and leaves. Make sure the open ends of the hollow sticks face outwards.
3. Tie string firmly around the carton.
4. Hang your hotel from a low branch in a sheltered spot, away from strong wind and rain.
5. Check your hotel each week, but do not poke inside.
Who might move in?
Some native bees lay their eggs inside hollow sticks. Ladybirds and beetles hide in the bark, and spiders love the gaps between pine cones. Each guest chooses the room that suits it best.
Question: In this text, to 'shelter' means to . . .
Option A: go out looking for food
Option B: build a nest out of leaves
Option C: stay safe from weather or danger
Option D: fly a long way from home

The mountain pygmy possum is a tiny animal, about the size of a mouse. It lives only in a few high, rocky places in the Australian Alps of Victoria and New South Wales. Scientists think there are only about two thousand left in the wild.
These possums make their homes in boulder fields, where piles of large rocks are covered by snow in winter. When the cold weather comes, each possum curls up in a gap between the rocks and hibernates. This means it goes into a very deep sleep, sometimes for up to seven months.
In spring, the possums wake up very hungry. They feast on Bogong moths, which fly to the mountains in their millions.
Mountain pygmy possums face many dangers. Warmer winters bring less snow to keep them snug. Fewer moths are arriving, and roads and ski runs have been built across their rocky homes.
At Mount Hotham, workers built a tunnel under a busy road and filled it with rocks. Now possums scurry through it at night.

Why Popcorn Pops
Popcorn is made from a special kind of corn. Each small kernel has a hard, shiny shell. Inside is soft starch and a tiny drop of water.
When the kernels are heated in a pot, the water inside begins to turn into steam. Steam takes up much more space than water, but it cannot escape through the tough shell. The pressure inside the kernel builds and builds, like air being pumped into a bike tyre.
Finally, the shell cannot hold on any longer. With a loud pop, it bursts open. The hot starch puffs out and cools into the white, fluffy shape we love to eat. A popped kernel can be many times bigger than it was before.
Sometimes, a few kernels stay closed at the bottom of the pot. Some people call these 'duds'. Usually, they have a crack in their shell, or they have dried out too much. Without enough water trapped inside, there is not enough steam to make them pop.
Always ask an adult to help when making popcorn, because the pot and the steam get very hot.
Question: What makes the shell of a popcorn kernel burst open?
Option A: the starch cooling down quickly
Option B: steam pressure building up inside
Option C: a crack forming in the pot
Option D: water leaking out of the shell

eleven, twelve, thirteen,
the neatest pattern on a lake
that I had ever seen.

At last they reached the muddy bank
and faded, soft and slow.
I picked another pebble up
and gave it one more throw.

Option B: grey
Option C: brown
Option D: black

Pebble, Plop, Ripple
I found a smooth grey pebble
while walking by the lake.
I tossed it out as far as I could
to see what it would make.

Plop! went the little pebble.
It sank without a trace,
but on the water, rings appeared
and raced to find more space.

The first ring was a tiny one,
a circle, neat and round.
Then out it rolled, and more came too,
without the smallest sound.

They grew and grew, like opening hands,
each wider than the last.
They rocked a leaf, they nudged a duck,
they wobbled reeds they passed.

A water strider skated by
and bobbed upon the rings.
A dragonfly zipped low to look
on shiny, buzzing wings.

I knelt down close and counted them,
eleven, twelve, thirteen,
the neatest pattern on a lake
that I had ever seen.

At last they reached the muddy bank
and faded, soft and slow.
I picked another pebble up
and gave it one more throw.

"Hardly anyone visits now," he told Noah one morning. "If nothing changes, I'll have to close the doors at the end of summer."

My little sister Lily copies everything I do. If I put tomato sauce on my eggs, she wants tomato sauce on her eggs. If I wear my green cap, she digs out her green cap too. It drives me bananas.
On Saturday I decided to test her. At breakfast I slowly tapped my spoon on my head. Tap, tap, tap. Lily grinned and tapped her spoon on her head.
"Mum!" I groaned. "She's doing it again!"
Mum just smiled into her coffee.
Later, when I fell off my scooter and scraped my knee, I tried hard not to cry. I took a deep breath and said, "I'm OK." Lily, who had been watching from the step, didn't say a word.
The next week Lily tripped over in the park. Her bottom lip wobbled. Then she took a big breath, stood up and announced, "I'm OK!"
She looked straight at me, waiting.
I gave her a thumbs-up, and something warm spread through my chest. Maybe having a shadow isn't so bad after all.
Question: What did the narrator tap on their head at breakfast?
Option A: a spoon
Option B: a fork
Option C: a green cap
Option D: a coffee cup

In many Australian schools, one of the busiest places at lunchtime is the tuckshop. In some states it is called the canteen. But have you ever wondered how it all works?
Most tuckshops are run by a manager who plans the menu, orders the food and keeps the kitchen clean and safe. Many managers are helped by parent volunteers, who might butter bread, heat pies or count change.

So next time you buy a sandwich, remember the busy team who made it.

Robots, phones, traffic lights and even washing machines all follow instructions called code. I believe every primary school student should learn how to write code.

Let's give every student the chance to tell a robot what to do!

Robots, phones, traffic lights and even washing machines all follow instructions called code. I believe every primary school student should learn how to write code.

Thirdly, many jobs in the future will use computers. Learning to code now will help us be ready.
Some people say coding is too hard for young children. But simple coding apps use colourful blocks that snap together like puzzle pieces, so even five-year-olds can use them.
Let's give every student the chance to tell a robot what to do!
Question: In coding, what are "bugs"?
Option A: mistakes in the instructions
Option B: insects that get inside robots
Option C: colourful blocks in an app
Option D: games that students design

About 2,500 years ago, the people of ancient Greece loved going to plays. Instead of building theatres with roofs, they carved them into the sides of hills.
The seats rose up the hill in a giant half circle, row after row, like steps. At the bottom was a round, flat space where the actors and a group of singers called the chorus performed. One famous theatre, at Epidaurus, could hold about 14,000 people!
The shape of these theatres was very clever. Sound travelled up the slope, so even people in the back rows could hear the actors. Visitors still test this today by dropping a coin on the stage and listening for the clink from high above.
All the actors were men, and they wore large masks. A smiling mask showed a funny character, and a frowning mask showed a sad one. By swapping masks, one actor could play several different parts.
Plays were held at festivals that lasted for days. Some of these ancient plays are still performed today.
Question: What was the group of singers in a Greek play called?
Option A: the audience
Option B: the chorus
Option C: the orchestra
Option D: the festival

My alarm forgot to ring today,
so I dressed in the dark in a flash.
I gobbled my toast and grabbed my bag
and joined the morning dash.
I raced to school with one shoe snug
and one that flapped and flopped.
It slapped the path like a big wet fish.
Slap, slap! It never stopped.
I didn't stop to check my feet.
I didn't stop to think.
I zoomed past Mrs Kelly's cat
in a flapping, slapping blink.
At line-up, Ava pointed down
and gave a giggle and a hoot.
On one foot sat my own school shoe,
on the other, Dad's brown boot!
My cheeks went hot. My ears went red.
I wanted to hide away.
I tucked that foot beneath my chair
and kept it there all day.
But Ava laughed so hard at lunch
she snorted out her drink,
and soon I couldn't help it.
I was laughing too, I think!
When I got home, I found poor Dad
still searching high and low.
"Has anyone seen my other boot?"
I smiled and said, "I know!"

Option A: loose
Option B: tight
Option C: warm
Option D: small

Jade

Dear Oscar,
Greetings from Lightning Ridge! This outback town is famous for black opals, which are shiny stones full of flashing colours. But guess what? Some opals here used to be bones!
Millions of years ago, this dry land was covered by rivers and a shallow sea. When animals died, their bones were buried in mud and sand. Over a very long time, water carried a substance called silica into the spaces where the bones had been. Slowly, the silica hardened into opal in the exact shape of the bones.
Yesterday at the museum, I saw a dinosaur jawbone that had turned completely into opal. When I tilted my head, it glowed green, blue and orange. It looked like a rainbow was trapped inside!
Tomorrow Mum is taking me fossicking in the piles of rock left by the miners. I'm bringing my magnifying glass. If I find even a tiny chip of opal bone, I'll save it for you.
Your cousin,
Mila

Option C: shallow seas
Option D: gold mines

A report by Class 3K
What we wanted to find out
Many machines use electricity even when they look switched off. This is called standby power. We wanted to find out how many standby sneaks were hiding in our school.
What we did
We worked in pairs with a checklist. After lunch, we walked through every room and looked for small glowing lights on machines that nobody was using. We counted each one.

We found 46 glowing lights! The library had the most, with 12 computer screens left on standby. In the staffroom, a microwave, a coffee machine and a television were all glowing at once.

Every little light wastes electricity, day and night, all year long. That wastes money that could buy new books. Switching off at the wall takes one second. If every class helps, we can catch every sneak!
Our plan
From Monday, two Power Monitors from each class will check the rooms every afternoon.

Option B: electricity used by computers in the library

Option D: electricity used by machines that look switched off

The Footpath Flower
Between two cracked grey squares of path
where hurried shoes go by,
a dandelion, bright as yolk,
is staring at the sky.

No gardener dug a bed for it,
no hose has filled its cup.
It drinks the rain that slips between
the stones, and pushes up.

The trucks go rumbling past at dawn,
the buses huff and wheeze,
but still it lifts its yellow head
and nods in every breeze.

A girl in a red school hat
bends down to say hello.
She steps around it carefully
and lets the brave thing grow.

The council mower roars along
the grassy verge in June,
but blades can't reach inside the crack,
so it will flower soon.

When summer's done, its golden head
turns white and soft as smoke.
The wind blows by, and off they fly,
a hundred tiny folk.

They float above the busy road,
past windows, wires and walls.
Next spring, in cracks all down the street,
small yellow faces call.
Question: Where is the dandelion growing?
Option A: in a garden bed
Option B: in a crack in the footpath
Option C: on the grassy verge
Option D: beside a busy road

Our Straw Pan Pipes Test
By Ava, aged 8
Aim: To find out if the length of a straw changes the sound it makes.
Materials: six paper straws, scissors, a ruler, sticky tape and modelling clay
Method:
1. Cut the straws to different lengths, from 18 cm down to 8 cm.
2. Plug the bottom of each straw with a small ball of clay.
3. Line up the straws from longest to shortest and tape them together.
4. Rest the pipes on your bottom lip and blow gently across the tops.
Results: The longest straw made the lowest note. The shortest straw made the highest, squeakiest note.
Why it happens: Blowing across the top makes the air inside the straw shake, or vibrate. A short straw holds less air, so the air vibrates faster and the note is higher.
Note: My little brother Max couldn't wait to play, so he didn't press his tape down. His pipes fell apart twice! He just laughed, taped them again and played a tune for Nana.
Question: Which word in the report means the same as 'vibrate'?
Option A: blow
Option B: plug
Option C: shake
Option D: squeak

Long ago in ancient Greece, the god Zeus and his son Hermes dressed as tired travellers and walked from village to village. At every house they knocked and asked for food. At every house, the door was slammed in their faces.
At last they came to a tiny hut with a straw roof. Inside lived an old couple named Baucis and Philemon. They were very poor, but they welcomed the strangers warmly. Baucis lit the fire and cooked their last cabbage. Philemon poured drinks from their only jug.

'You shared everything you had,' said Zeus. 'Make a wish.'
Baucis and Philemon looked at each other. 'We only wish to stay together always,' they said.
Their little hut became a fine marble house. When they were very old, they turned into two trees, an oak and a linden, their branches wrapped together.
Question: How were Zeus and Hermes dressed when they visited the villages?
Option A: as poor farmers
Option B: as rich kings
Option C: as old shepherds
Option D: as tired travellers

'She wants to hatch them,' said Dad. 'That's called being broody. Let's leave her be.'
Three weeks later, Tilly heard tiny cheeps from the blackberries. Out marched Pepper, with seven fluffy chicks trotting behind her.
Question: How many eggs did Tilly usually find each morning?
Option A: four
Option B: five
Option C: seven
Option D: three

Walking on Water
On a still pond, you might spot a thin insect skating across the top of the water. This is a water strider, sometimes called a pond skater.
Water striders do not sink because their legs are covered in thousands of tiny hairs. The hairs trap air and keep the water out, so the insect rests on the surface like a leaf.
A water strider has six legs, and each pair has its own job. The short front legs grab food. The long middle legs push against the water like oars. The back legs steer.
Water striders mostly eat small insects that fall onto the pond. When a fly lands in the water, it struggles and makes tiny ripples. The water strider feels these ripples through its legs and races over to catch its meal.
Water striders also make ripples on purpose. By tapping the water, they send messages to other striders nearby.
Next time you visit a pond, sit quietly and watch. You may see these clever skaters at work.

Option A: wings that keep it up
Option B: tiny hairs on its legs
Option C: its very long body
Option D: oil on the water

Max folded his arms. 'Well, the ghost could have borrowed her paws.'
Ruby just laughed and closed the piano lid.

Option B: a cat
Option C: Nana
Option D: a mouse

The giant panda lives in the misty mountain forests of China. With its black and white fur, it is one of the best-known animals in the world. Yet for many years, it was in danger of disappearing.
Pandas eat almost nothing but bamboo. Because bamboo is not very nourishing, a panda must munch for up to 14 hours every day. When people cut down forests to build farms and roads, pandas lost much of their food and their homes.
To help, China created more than 60 nature reserves where the forests are protected. Workers also planted bamboo 'corridors'. These are strips of forest that join one reserve to another, so pandas can travel to find food and mates.
Scientists count wild pandas about every ten years. In the last big count, there were more than 1800. In 2016, experts said the giant panda was no longer endangered, though it is still at risk.
Rangers know the job is not over. But each time they spot a new cub in the wild, they cheer.

Why Pasta Comes in Shapes
Walk down the pasta aisle of a supermarket and you will see tubes, spirals, shells, bows and long ribbons. Pasta is made from just flour and water, sometimes with egg. So why are there hundreds of shapes?
The answer is sauce. Each shape is designed to hold sauce in a different way.
Long, thin spaghetti works well with smooth, oily sauces that coat every strand. Wide, flat ribbons such as fettuccine are good with thick, creamy sauces. Tubes like penne have hollow middles and ridges on the outside, so chunky sauce gets trapped inside and out. Shells act like little cups that scoop up peas and small pieces of meat.
Some shapes are made for soup. Tiny stars and letters fit on a spoon with plenty of broth.
Pasta makers in Italy have invented new shapes for hundreds of years. Some are named after what they look like. Farfalle means 'butterflies' and orecchiette means 'little ears'.
So next time you cook pasta, think about your sauce first.
Question: Chunky sauce gets trapped in penne because penne has . . .
Option A: long, thin strands
Option B: a wide, flat shape
Option C: hollow middles and ridges
Option D: a shape like a cup

Where Surnames Come From
Most people have a first name and a family name, or surname. Long ago, many people had only one name. As villages grew bigger, there might be five men called John! People needed a way to tell them apart, so surnames began.
Some surnames came from jobs. A smith worked with metal, so a man who made horseshoes might be called John Smith. A baker baked bread, and a cooper made wooden barrels.
Other surnames came from places. Someone who lived near a hill might be called Hill, and someone who lived beside a brook, or small stream, might become Brook.
Many surnames simply mean 'son of'. Johnson was once John's son, and Peterson was Peter's son.
Today, children usually share a surname with one or both parents, so the name passes down through the family. Some families join two surnames with a hyphen.
Next time you hear a surname, think about the story it might tell!

Option A: a small stream
Option B: a steep hill
Option C: a wooden barrel
Option D: a small village

One Ting
Leo had the smallest job in the school orchestra. He played the triangle, and in the whole concert piece he had just one note.
'One ting,' his sister teased. 'Don't wear yourself out.'
But Leo knew it mattered. His note came at the very end, after the drums had thundered and the violins had soared. It would be the last sound the audience heard.
On concert night, Leo counted every bar in his head. Forty-one, forty-two . . . His palms were sweaty. Then the violinist beside him sneezed, and Leo lost his place.
Panic rose in his chest. He looked at Mrs Fern, the conductor. She caught his eye and gave the tiniest nod. Leo lifted his beater and struck.
Ting.
The note hung in the silent hall, bright and clear, until it faded away. For a moment nobody moved. Then the clapping began.
Afterwards, his sister hugged him. 'That was the best ting I've ever heard,' she said, and this time she meant it.

Option A: the drums
Option B: the violin
Option C: the recorder
Option D: the triangle

Max stared with his mouth open. 'Can you make one for me?'
Ruby grinned. 'Sure,' she said. 'But first, who's going to pour the milk?'

She spent all of Saturday building. A marble would roll down a ramp of books, knock over a line of dominoes and tip a cup that tugged a string. The string would tilt the cereal box over her bowl.
'It will never work,' said her brother Max, crunching his toast.
Ruby ignored him. She tested it once, and the marble flew off the ramp. She tested it again, and the dominoes fell the wrong way. By lunchtime, the kitchen floor was a sea of cornflakes.
Ruby swept up, moved the ramp and added a wall of pencils. On the tenth try, everything worked. The marble rolled, the dominoes clicked, the cup tipped and the cereal poured perfectly into the bowl.
Max stared with his mouth open. 'Can you make one for me?'
Ruby grinned. 'Sure,' she said. 'But first, who's going to pour the milk?'

Option A: a kind of breakfast cereal
Option B: a machine made of many parts
Option C: a long ramp made of books
Option D: a game played with dominoes

Question: How long do pet rats usually live?
Option A: about six months
Option B: about ten years
Option C: about twenty years
Option D: about two or three years

The Birth of the Ute
In the early 1930s, many Australian farmers had a problem. Cars were comfortable, but they could not carry much. Trucks could carry heavy loads, but they were bumpy and plain.
In 1933, a farmer's wife from Victoria wrote a letter to the Ford car company. She asked for a vehicle that could carry her family in comfort and also take the pigs to market.
A young designer named Lewis Bandt took on the challenge. He joined the front of a car to a strong open tray at the back. In 1934, the first Australian 'coupe utility' rolled out of the factory in Geelong.
Farmers loved it. They could carry hay, tools or animals during the week, then drive to town on the weekend. Soon people shortened the long name to 'ute'.
Today, utes might be seen on farms, building sites and city streets all over Australia. Lewis Bandt must have been proud that one letter led to such a famous Australian car.
Question: Who wrote to the Ford car company asking for a new kind of vehicle?
Option A: a farmer's wife from Victoria
Option B: the designer Lewis Bandt
Option C: a truck driver from Geelong
Option D: a worker at the Ford factory

When Your Foot Falls Asleep
Have you ever sat cross-legged through a long assembly, then stood up and wobbled like a baby giraffe? Your foot has 'fallen asleep'!
Of course, your foot is not really sleeping. Your body is full of nerves. Nerves are like tiny wires that carry messages between your body and your brain. When you sit on your leg or fold it for a long time, you squash some of these nerves. You also squash the blood vessels that bring them food and air.
Squashed nerves cannot send messages properly, so your foot feels numb. You might not even be able to feel the floor!
When you move again, the blood rushes back and the nerves wake up. At first, they send jumbled messages, which feel like prickles. That is why people call it 'pins and needles'.
The feeling is annoying, but it is harmless and fades in a minute or two. Just give your foot a gentle wiggle and wait.

The Secret of the Sleeping Bag
Many campers think a sleeping bag works like a heater. In fact, a sleeping bag does not make any heat at all. Your body is the heater. The bag's job is to stop that warmth from escaping into the cold night air.
Inside the bag is a fluffy filling. This might be duck down or a light, man-made fibre. The filling holds millions of tiny pockets of air. Trapped air is very good at slowing heat down, so your warmth stays close to you. This is also why a squashed, flat bag is less cosy than a puffy one.
The ground is another problem. Cold earth drains heat from your body much faster than air does, and the filling underneath you is pressed flat by your weight. For this reason, experienced campers always sleep on a mat. Even a thin foam mat makes a surprising difference.
Damp is the enemy, too. Wet filling clumps together and loses its air pockets. Smart campers change out of sweaty clothes before bed and air their bags in the sun each morning.
Finally, check the label. Most bags show a temperature rating, such as five degrees. This tells you the coldest night the bag is designed for. Choose the right bag, use a mat and keep everything dry, and you will wake up warm and ready to explore.

Option A: adds to.
Option B: keeps in.
Option C: measures.
Option D: takes away.

Many Chinese families celebrate Lunar New Year, and each year is linked to one of twelve animals. An old legend explains how this order came to be. Like most legends, it has been told in many ways, but one popular version goes like this.

The clever rat knew it was a poor swimmer, so it asked the strong, kind ox for a ride. The ox agreed. Just as they reached the far bank, the rat leapt from the ox's head and landed first. The ox came second, followed by the powerful tiger, who had battled the strong current.
The rabbit hopped across on stepping stones and then clung to a floating log. A gentle breath of wind pushed the log to shore. The rabbit later learnt that the dragon had sent that breeze. The dragon could have flown across first, but it had stopped to bring rain to a village whose crops were dying. It finished fifth.
The horse, goat, monkey, rooster and dog followed. Last of all came the pig, who had stopped for a feast and a nap.
And the cat? It had asked its friend the rat to wake it on race day. The rat said nothing, and the cat slept through the whole race. Some people say that is why cats chase rats to this day.

Option A: the tiger
Option B: the rat
Option C: the ox
Option D: the dragon

The Copycat
My brother Sam is only five
and copies all I do.
If I have honey on my toast,
then Sam wants honey too.

If I wear my stripy beanie,
he finds his stripy hat.
If I sit cross-legged on the rug,
he sits down just like that.

He follows me from room to room
and echoes what I say.
If I say 'Cool!', he shouts out 'Cool!'
a hundred times a day.

One morning I grew grumpy
and snapped at him, 'Go away!
Find someone else to copy, Sam,
just leave me be today!'

That Friday, Sam went off to stay
at Nana's by the sea.
I had the whole house to myself,
as peaceful as could be.

I spread the honey on my toast
and no small voice said, 'Me!'
I sat cross-legged on the rug
with no one by my knee.

I hummed a song while brushing teeth;
no echo filled the air.
I turned to tell a silly joke,
but no one else was there.

The house was hushed. The hall was still.
I wandered room to room.
My toast had somehow lost its taste;
the quiet felt like gloom.

At night I peeked in Sam's small room.
His bed was neat and flat.
The hook beside his door was bare.
I hadn't thought of that.

On Sunday, when the car pulled in,
I raced out to the gate,
my stripy beanie on my head.
I didn't have to wait.

Sam tumbled out in his stripy hat
and grinned from ear to ear.
I grinned right back. It's good to have
my copycat back here.

Option A: The speaker wants to eat toast alone.
Option B: The speaker is tired of being copied.
Option C: Sam is leaving to stay at Nana's.
Option D: Sam has taken the speaker's beanie.

Ella frowned. 'They look fine. And we're painting today, not fiddling with bits.'
'Fine,' muttered Mai, dropping the washers into Ella's toolbox. 'Paint it by yourself, then.' She grabbed her bike and pedalled home.

The next morning she knocked on Mai's door, holding the toolbox. 'You were right,' she said. 'I'm sorry I didn't listen. There's another derby next month. Will you help me fix it?'
Mai looked at the toolbox for a long moment. Then she smiled. 'Only if I get to choose the next paint colour.'

On a hot summer weekend, thousands of Australians head to the beach. Watching over many of them are surf lifesavers in bright red and yellow uniforms. Most lifesavers are volunteers, which means they give up their time without being paid.
Each morning on patrol, lifesavers study the water before they choose where to set up. They look for the safest stretch of beach and mark it with two red and yellow flags. Swimmers should always stay between these flags, because that is the area lifesavers are watching most closely.

If you are ever caught in a rip, stay calm and float. Raise one arm in the air to signal for help. Lifesavers are trained to recognise this signal and will paddle out on a rescue board.
Becoming a lifesaver takes training. Volunteers must pass a swimming test, learn first aid and practise rescues. Many begin as Nippers, in a program where children learn about surf safety and beach skills.
At the end of the day, the flags come down. This tells swimmers that the patrol has finished and nobody is watching over the water.

Option A: are paid to keep beaches safe
Option B: race in surf competitions
Option C: work without being paid
Option D: teach children how to swim

For three nights in a row, clouds had smothered the sky like a grey woollen blanket. Each evening, Zara carried Pop's old telescope onto the back verandah, and each evening she carried it back inside.
'Saturn isn't going anywhere,' Pop said, sipping his tea. 'It's been out there for billions of years. It can wait one more night for you.'

'Look low in the east,' Pop said. 'Find the bright one that isn't twinkling. Stars twinkle, but planets usually shine with a steady light.'

Then she gasped. There it was, tiny and perfect, a little ball wearing a tilted ring like a hat brim.
Zara didn't speak for a long time. She just looked. Finally, she grabbed her sketchbook and began to draw, glancing back at the eyepiece every few seconds to check each line.
Pop smiled into his tea. He had seen Saturn hundreds of times. Tonight, he was happy just watching her see it.

Option A: It was too windy outside.
Option B: Pop wanted to use it.
Option C: Clouds covered the sky.
Option D: It was too late at night.

Not an Empty Land
Many people picture a desert as a hot, empty place where nothing lives. They could not be more wrong. Australia's deserts are bursting with life, and it is time we gave them the respect they deserve.
Take the thorny devil, a small lizard covered in spikes. It does not need to find a pool to drink. Tiny grooves between its scales draw moisture from damp sand or dew towards the corners of its mouth. Then there is the spinifex hopping mouse, which can survive without drinking at all. It gets the water it needs from the seeds and plants it eats.
Deserts can also change in amazing ways. After rare heavy rains, sleeping seeds burst into flower, carpeting red sand with pink, white and yellow. Every few years, water even flows into Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre (Australia's largest lake), and thousands of pelicans fly in to breed.
Yet these places are fragile. Thin crusts on the soil hold the sand in place and help seeds sprout. A single car driving off the track can crush a crust that took many years to form.
So what can we do? When you visit a desert, stay on marked tracks. Take all your rubbish home. Learn about the plants and animals before you go – you will see far more when you know what to look for.
Deserts are not wastelands. They are treasures, and they need us to look after them.
Question: Where does the spinifex hopping mouse get its water from?
Option A: dew that collects on its fur
Option B: pools of water in the sand
Option C: grooves between its scales
Option D: the seeds and plants it eats

On a dairy farm, the working day starts long before most people wake. Many dairy farmers in Australia are out of bed by four o'clock in the morning, because cows need to be milked twice a day, at roughly the same times.
First, the farmer rounds up the herd from the paddock and walks the cows slowly to the milking shed. Cows that are rushed or frightened give less milk.
Inside the shed, where some farmers play soft music on a radio, each cow steps into her own bay. The farmer cleans the cow's teats, then attaches the milking cups, which gently draw out the milk through soft rubber linings.The milk flows through pipes into a large steel vat, where it is quickly chilled.
After milking, the cows head out to fresh pasture. Farmers move the herd to a different paddock every day or two. This gives the grass in the old paddock time to regrow, so the cows always have plenty of good food to eat.
Once a day, a tanker truck arrives to collect the milk from the vat and take it to a factory. There it is tested, packaged and sent to shops.
Dairy farming is hard work in every kind of weather, but it is the most rewarding job in the country. The next time you pour milk on your cereal, remember the early start that brought it to your table.

Giants on the Hill
Drive through parts of South Australia or Victoria and you might spot rows of enormous white towers standing on the hills, their blades turning slowly. These are wind turbines, and they are quietly turning moving air into electricity.
A wind turbine has three main parts: a tall tower, a set of long blades and a box at the top called the nacelle. When the wind blows, it pushes against the blades and makes them spin. The blades are joined to a shaft inside the nacelle. As the shaft turns, it drives a generator, which uses magnets and coils of wire to produce electricity. Cables carry this electricity down the tower and away to the power grid, which delivers it to homes, schools and shops.
Turbines are built tall for a good reason. Winds high above the ground are usually stronger and steadier than winds near the surface. Some towers are taller than a 30-storey building, and a single blade can be longer than an Olympic swimming pool.
Wind power does not burn fuel, so it does not create smoke. However, the wind does not always blow. On calm days, turbines may stand still, so other sources, such as solar panels or batteries, must help fill the gap.
So next time you feel a breeze on your face, imagine it travelling all the way to light up someone's kitchen.

Option A: the generator
Option B: the shaft
Option C: the nacelle
Option D: the grid

Oscar nodded so hard his hair flopped. "Is there a second one?"
Mrs Pham was already reaching for the shelf behind her.

Lena hadn't wanted to visit the museum. Museums, she told Dad, were for people who liked dusty things and being told not to touch.
But Dad had a plan. He led her past the dinosaur bones and the stuffed birds, down a narrow corridor and into a dim room at the very back. Glass cases lined every wall, and inside each one stood a clock. There were tall wooden clocks, tiny silver ones and a brass clock shaped like a ship. In the half-light, their pendulums swung back and forth, and the room was filled with a soft, uneven ticking, like a hundred mice tiptoeing across the floor.
Lena found herself whispering. "Why is it so quiet in here?"
Dad checked his watch. "Wait," he said. "Two more minutes."
Lena pressed her nose close to the ship clock. Its tiny brass sailors stood frozen on the deck. A guard in the corner winked at her.
Then, all at once, the room erupted. Bells clanged, chimes tinkled and a cuckoo burst out of a carved wooden house. On the ship clock, the little sailors spun in a circle while a bell rang out twelve times. Lena laughed out loud, and nobody told her to hush.
When the last chime faded, she tugged Dad's sleeve. "Can we stay until one o'clock?"
Dad grinned. He had been hoping she would ask.
Question: What shape was the brass clock?
Option A: a house
Option B: a ship
Option C: a bird
Option D: a dinosaur

For three weeks, Priya had worked on her painting for the school art show. It showed the beach near her house at sunset, with pink clouds and a long golden strip of sand. Everything was neat and careful. Yet when she stepped back, something bothered her. The painting looked flat, as if the sea had forgotten how to move.
On the morning before the show, Priya reached for her brush and knocked over a jar of dark blue paint. It splashed across the bottom corner of the canvas, spreading over the sand in a wild, splotchy wave.
Priya gasped. Her eyes stung. Three weeks of work, ruined in one second.
Her art teacher, Mr Okafor, came over and studied the canvas for a long time. "Hmm," he said at last. "What does that splash remind you of?"
Priya sniffed and looked again. The blue curled and crashed like water rushing up the sand. She picked up a fine brush and added white flecks along its edge, like foam. Then she dabbed more blue into the waves further out, letting the strokes be loose and messy.
By lunchtime, the sea seemed to roar off the canvas.
At the show, a woman stopped in front of Priya's painting. "The waves look so alive," she said. "How did you do that?"
Priya smiled. "It started with an accident."
Question: What did Priya's painting show?
Option A: a city street late at night
Option B: the beach near her house at sunset
Option C: a forest just after the rain
Option D: a boat on a stormy lake

Mud, Reeds and a Secret
When Aunty Jo said we were going to the wetland, I pictured a smelly swamp full of mosquitoes. I was half right about the mosquitoes.
We arrived just after dawn. Mist hung over the water like a grey blanket, and tall reeds rustled on both sides of the boardwalk. Aunty Jo handed me her binoculars. "Wetlands are like a kidney for the river," she whispered. "They clean the water as it slowly passes through."
I rolled my eyes. All I could see was brown water and mud.
Then Aunty Jo pointed. A long-legged bird stepped carefully through the shallows, one slow foot at a time. "A white-faced heron," she said. "Watch."
The heron froze. Suddenly its beak stabbed down and came up with a wriggling fish. I nearly dropped the binoculars.
After that, I couldn't stop looking. A pair of black swans glided past with three fluffy grey cygnets paddling behind them. Tiny frogs called from the reeds. A dragonfly with see-through wings hovered beside my ear.
By the time the mist lifted, my sneakers were muddy and I had eleven mosquito bites. I had also counted fourteen kinds of birds.
On the way home, I asked Aunty Jo if we could come back next Saturday. She didn't answer. She just smiled, as if she had known all along that I would ask.
