Option A: splashed about noisily.
Option B: flew high into the sky.
Option C: dived under the water.
Option D: moved smoothly and quietly.

One evening, Lily opened her book and felt a warm weight settle onto her lap. Biscuit turned around twice, curled up and began to purr like a tiny engine.
Lily kept reading, very quietly.

Option B: frightened
Option C: sleepy
Option D: playful

Haiku Week at Banksia Primary
Every August, Banksia Primary School holds Haiku Week. For five days, students from every class learn about this short form of poetry, which first became popular in Japan hundreds of years ago.
What is a haiku?
A traditional haiku has just three lines. The first line has five syllables, the second has seven and the third has five again. Many haiku describe a small moment in nature, and the last line often adds a surprise or a new way of seeing things.
How the week works
On Monday, teachers read famous haiku aloud. On Tuesday and Wednesday, students go outside with clipboards to observe the school grounds closely. They might notice a beetle on a leaf or the sound of rain on the roof. On Thursday, everyone drafts and edits their own poems, counting syllables on their fingers. On Friday, the best poems are hung from a string in the library, like washing on a line.
Here is a haiku by Year 4 student Ava:
Magpie on the fence
sings to the empty playground.
The bell rings. We run.
Ava admits she was not excited at first. "I thought poems had to rhyme and be long," she said. "Now I like that a haiku is like a photo made of words."
Teachers say the week helps students slow down and notice the world around them.

Option A: they are questions for readers to answer
Option B: they are headings for each section

Douglas Mawson: Home of the Blizzard
Douglas Mawson was born in England in 1882, but his family moved to Sydney when he was two years old. He grew up to become a geologist, a scientist who studies rocks, and he became fascinated by the frozen continent of Antarctica.
In 1911, Mawson led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition. His team built wooden huts at Cape Denison, which turned out to be one of the windiest places on Earth. The wild, whistling winds often howled at more than 150 kilometres per hour, and the men sometimes had to crawl outside to take their weather readings.

Two Seasons in the Top End
In most of southern Australia, people talk about four seasons: summer, autumn, winter and spring. But in Darwin and much of the tropical north, known as the Top End, many people describe the year in just two parts: the wet and the dry.
The dry season runs from about May to September. Day after day, the sky stays a clear, cloudless blue. The days are warm, the nights are pleasantly cool and the air feels light and dry. Very little rain falls, so creeks shrink and the long grass turns gold.
Between the two seasons comes a time that locals call the build-up. The air grows thick and sticky, and heavy clouds pile up each afternoon without releasing a drop. Many people find these weeks the hardest of the year.
Then the wet season arrives, usually around December. Warm, moist winds blow in from the ocean. Most afternoons, towering storm clouds gather, lightning flickers across the sky and rain hammers down on tin roofs. Darwin receives most of its yearly rain in these months, and some roads flood until the waters go down.
Because the Top End lies much closer to the equator than southern Australia, it is hot for most of the year. That is why the change in rain, rather than the change in temperature, is what people there notice most.

Your teeth have to last a lifetime, so they deserve proper care. Dentists say that most children rush their brushing and miss the hidden places where bits of food hide. Follow these steps every morning and every night.
You will need: a soft toothbrush, a pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste and a timer.
1. Wet the bristles under the tap and squeeze on the toothpaste. Start the timer.
2. Hold the brush at a slight angle against the line where your teeth meet your gums.
3. Move the brush in small, gentle circles. Scrubbing hard from side to side can wear away your gums.
4. Clean the outside, the inside and the chewing surface of every tooth. Count your teeth in your head as you go so that none get skipped.
5. Brush your tongue softly from back to front. Many of the germs that cause bad breath live there.
6. Spit out the toothpaste, but do not rinse your mouth with water. A thin layer of fluoride left behind keeps working to protect your teeth.
Keep brushing until the timer rings after two minutes. Most people stop after only about forty-five seconds without even noticing.
Finally, rinse your brush and stand it upright to dry. You will need a new toothbrush every three months, or sooner if the bristles become frayed and spread out.

Nobody Held the Pen
The bees build rooms with six straight sides
and share each waxy wall,
a golden city, packed so tight
there's not a gap at all.
And nobody held the pen.

The snail's shell is a winding stair
that circles round and in;
it starts out wide, then turns and turns
and tightens to a pin.
And nobody held the pen.

A pebble dropped into the pond
sends rings that ripple out,
each circle wider than the last,
a whisper grown to a shout.
And nobody held the pen.

A snowflake lands upon my glove
with six arms, lacy-white,
each one a copy of the rest,
then melts before my sight.
And nobody held the pen.

A spider spins a silver wheel
of spokes and rings so fine,
each gap the same from hub to edge,
each thread a perfect line.
And nobody held the pen.

The sunflower packs its face with seeds
in spirals, row on row,
some curving left and some curving right,
like whirlpools as they grow.
And nobody held the pen.

The gum leaf has a map of roads
that branch from one thick vein,
like creeks seen from an aeroplane
across a dusty plain.
And nobody held the pen.

The wind combs ridges on the dunes
in long and wavy bands,
as even as the lines I trace
with fingers through the sand.
And nobody held the pen.

I use a ruler for my lines,
a compass for my rounds,
and still I rub out half of them
with grumbling, scratchy sounds.
So who was holding the pen?

Grandpa Theo tapped the little screen beside the wheel. It flickered, showed a grey square, then went dark.
'Well, that's the end of that,' he said cheerfully, as if the boat's map had simply gone to sleep.

'Cape Moss lighthouse,' he said. 'Every lighthouse has its own pattern, so sailors can tell them apart. We're right on track.'
When they tied up at the jetty, Mia's hands were stiff with cold. Grandpa squeezed her shoulder.
'Next time,' he said, 'I might switch that screen off on purpose.'

Sharing the Street with Trams
Melbourne has one of the largest tram networks in the world. Every day, long trams glide along tracks set into busy roads, carrying thousands of people to work, school and the shops.
How does a tram move?
A tram does not carry its own fuel. Instead, a metal arm on its roof, called a pantograph, presses against an electric wire strung above the street. Power flows down the arm to motors under the floor, which turn the wheels. Because there is no engine burning petrol, trams give off no exhaust fumes on the street.
How do trams and cars share the road?
In the city centre, trams run down the middle of many streets. If cars stopped on the tracks to turn right, trams would be stuck behind them. To solve this, drivers at some intersections make a 'hook turn'. They move into the left lane, wait at the far side of the crossing, and turn right only when the lights change. This leaves the tracks clear.
How do trams stay safe?
Trams cannot swerve, so they warn people with a loud clang-clang of the bell. Passengers must take care stepping off, because at some stops they step straight into a traffic lane. Cars must stop behind a tram when its doors open.
Trams are quiet, clean and quick, and they help keep a crowded city moving.

Option A: a trolley rod
Option B: a pantograph
Option C: a power pole
Option D: a track switch

In 1799, a strange skin arrived in England from New South Wales. It had the fur of an otter, the tail of a beaver and a bill like a duck's. Some scientists were sure it was a joke. They searched the skin for stitches, thinking someone had sewn parts of different animals together. They found none. The platypus was real.
Its name comes from two old Greek words: 'platys', meaning flat, and 'pous', meaning foot. Its wide, flat, webbed front feet make it a powerful swimmer.
The platypus is a monotreme, one of only a few mammals in the world that lay eggs. A mother usually lays two tiny, leathery eggs in a burrow dug into a riverbank. When the babies hatch, she feeds them milk, but she has no nipples. Instead, the milk oozes out through patches on her skin, and the babies lap it up.
Underwater, a platypus shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils tight. So how does it find food in the dark mud? Its soft, rubbery bill can sense the tiny electrical signals made by the muscles of moving shrimps, worms and insect larvae.
You would be wise to admire a platypus from a distance. Males have a sharp spur on each back ankle that can deliver a painful venom.
Today the platypus lives in the creeks and rivers of eastern Australia, including Tasmania. Those puzzled scientists would be amazed to learn just how clever it really is.

The Night We Turned Out the Lights
Grandma and I crept down onto the sand,
a dim red torch in her wrinkly hand.
'Keep quiet,' she whispered, 'and watch where you tread.
The loggerhead nest is just there, up ahead.'

Deep in the dune, where the mother had laid
a hundred round eggs in the cool, sandy shade,
the babies were stirring and ready to go
to scramble towards waves that they'd never yet know.

But up on the hill, the new cafe was bright,
its signs flashing pink in the warm summer night.
'They'll head for that glow,' Grandma said with a frown,
'and wander away from the sea into town.'

So I raced up the path, two steps at a time,
my heart thumping hard as I started to climb.
I knocked on the door and I asked, 'Could you please
switch off your lights, so the turtles find the seas?'

The owner looked puzzled, then nodded and smiled.
'For turtles,' she said, 'I'll go dark for a while.'
The hill became shadow. The beach became grey.
The moon on the water now showed them the way.

Out burst the hatchlings, a scurrying stream,
like pebbles on legs in the silvery gleam.
They followed the shine of the moon on the sea
and tumbled through foam, wild and wet and free.

Grandma squeezed my hand as the last one swam out.
'Not many grow up,' she said, 'there's no doubt.
There are fewer each year, so each one counts, you see.'
And I counted them all, from one to ninety-three.

Leaves Built for the Rain
In a tropical rainforest, leaves have a hard life. Rain falls almost every day, the air is hot and steamy, and hungry insects are everywhere. Over millions of years, rainforest plants have developed clever leaves to cope.
Drip tips
Many rainforest leaves end in a long, narrow point called a drip tip. Rainwater runs down the leaf and drips off the point. A leaf that stayed wet would soon be covered in moss, algae and fungus, which block the sunlight the leaf needs to make food.
Waxy coats
Lots of leaves also have a smooth, shiny surface. This waxy coating works like a raincoat, helping water slide away quickly.
Giant leaves near the ground
Only a little sunlight reaches the forest floor, because the tall trees above shade almost everything. Plants that grow down low, such as some palms and wild gingers, often have enormous leaves. A bigger leaf can catch more of the scattered light.
Red new leaves
In some rainforest trees, brand-new leaves hang down limp and red, almost as if they were sick. They turn green only once they become tough. Scientists think the red colour may make young leaves less tasty, or harder for insects to notice.
Each of these features helps a plant survive in one of the wettest, shadiest and busiest places on Earth.

Talking Like the Birds
English is full of expressions that come from watching birds. Each one hides a real piece of bird behaviour.
Pecking order
In a flock of chickens, every hen knows her place. The top hen may peck any bird below her, while the lowest hen gets pecked by everyone and eats last. A scientist first described this in the 1920s. Today, when people talk about the 'pecking order' in a team or a class, they mean who is in charge and who must follow.
Taking someone under your wing
Many mother birds spread their wings over their chicks to keep them warm and dry when it rains. So when an older student takes a new child under her wing, she is looking after them and showing them around.
Ruffled feathers
When a bird is cold, frightened or annoyed, it fluffs up its feathers so that it looks bigger. A person with ruffled feathers is upset, and someone who smooths ruffled feathers calms everyone down.
As the crow flies
People noticed long ago that crows seem to fly straight across fields instead of following the winding roads below. 'As the crow flies' means the shortest distance between two places, in a straight line.
Of course, birds know nothing about these sayings. A magpie simply gets on with its day. But the next time a friend says the walk to the shops is only one kilometre as the crow flies, you might remind them that you cannot fly over the houses!

Option A: to teach them how to fly
Option B: to hide them from the top hen
Option C: to keep them warm and dry
Option D: to make themselves look bigger

The Shadow Show at Nan's
On the last night of the holidays, the power went out at Nan's farmhouse. Ivy and her little cousin Sam sat in the dark lounge room while rain drummed on the roof.
'I'm bored,' Sam moaned. 'There's nothing to do without the TV.'
Ivy switched on the big torch from the kitchen drawer and pointed it at the bare white wall. Then she held up her hands, linked her thumbs and flapped her fingers. A dark bird swooped across the wall.
Sam gasped. 'How did you do that?'
'My hands block the light,' Ivy explained, 'so the wall behind them stays dark. That dark patch is a shadow.'
Sam wanted a turn. He made a dog, but it was tiny. Ivy told him to move his hands closer to the torch. Suddenly the dog grew into a giant that filled half the wall, and Sam squealed with delight.
Soon they were putting on a whole show. Ivy made a rabbit hop, and Sam's giant dog chased it behind the couch. When Ivy wiggled the torch, the shadows trembled as if they were scared. Sam even made up silly voices for the animals, growling and squeaking until his throat was sore. Nan laughed so much that she had to wipe her eyes.
When the lights flickered back on, the wall was plain and white again. Sam looked at the TV, then at Ivy.
'Can we turn the lights off again?' he asked.

Option A: the power had gone out
Option B: they were waiting for Nan
Option C: the torch had stopped working
Option D: it was time for bed

Teeth on the Beach
Dear Max,
You will never guess what I found at Aunty Lou's beach last Sunday. A real fossil shark tooth! It is grey and shiny, about as long as my thumb, and the edges still have tiny jagged points.
Aunty Lou says that millions of years ago this whole area was under the sea. When sharks died, their skeletons rotted away, because they are made of rubbery cartilage, not bone. Their teeth were much harder, so they lasted. Slowly they were buried in mud that turned to rock. Now the waves are wearing the cliffs away, and the teeth are tumbling out onto the sand.
We weren't allowed to keep it, because the fossils there are protected. Instead, we took photos and showed them to a scientist at the museum. She said it came from a shark that lived about five million years ago! She even thanked me for reporting it and said that finds like mine help scientists learn about ancient seas.
Max, you have to come with us in the summer holidays. You are the best spotter I know, and Aunty Lou says the low tides in January are perfect for searching. Just picture it: you, me and a beach full of ancient treasure waiting to be found. Every true fossil hunter needs a partner, and I want it to be you!
Write back soon and say yes.
Your excited cousin,
Ruby

Fix It, Don't Bin It
Every week, our school throws away a mountain of things that could easily be saved. Broken pencil cases, ripped library bags, wobbly chairs and toys with a missing screw all end up in the skip. I believe our school should hold a Fix It Friday once a month, where students, parents and teachers repair broken items instead of throwing them out.
Firstly, repairing things keeps rubbish out of landfill. Even recycling uses energy and water, but a mended bag or chair can simply be used again. Saving one item might seem small, but if every student saved just one item a term, we would rescue hundreds of things each year.
Secondly, Fix It Friday would teach us useful skills. Many of us have never sewn on a button or tightened a screw. Our grandparents grew up mending almost everything they owned. Imagine how much we could learn if they came in to share their know-how.
Finally, repairing saves money. A new school bag can cost forty dollars, but a few stitches cost almost nothing. Families could spend that money on things they really need.
Some people say that fixing things takes too long. However, an hour a month is a tiny price to pay for a cleaner planet. Our skip is hungry, but it is time to put it on a diet. Let's roll up our sleeves and give our broken things a second life!

Option A: the second paragraph
Option B: the fourth paragraph
Option C: the third paragraph
Option D: the fifth paragraph

Running the King's Roads
About 500 years ago, the Inca people ruled a huge empire in the Andes mountains of South America. They had no horses, no wheels for transport and no written alphabet. So how did news travel across their land? The answer was the chasquis, the fastest messengers of their time.
The Inca built a network of roads that stretched for about 40,000 kilometres. Along these roads, small huts were placed every few kilometres. Inside each hut waited two or more young runners, ready to go at a moment's notice.
When a chasqui came near a hut, he blew a shell trumpet to warn the next runner. The new runner jogged beside him while the message was passed on. Then he sprinted off to the next hut, and the first runner rested. Because each person ran only a short distance, every runner stayed fresh, and a message could travel up to 240 kilometres in a single day.
Some messages were spoken and had to be remembered word for word. Others were carried on a quipu, a set of coloured strings tied with knots. The knots recorded numbers, such as how many llamas or bags of corn a village had.
Chasquis were trained from boyhood, and the job was an important duty. Today, some sections of their ancient roads are still used by walkers and travellers.
Question: Which sentence shows that the Inca roads were very long?
Option A: Small huts were placed every few kilometres.
Option B: Some sections are still used by walkers today.
Option C: The empire was in the Andes mountains.
Option D: The roads stretched for about 40,000 kilometres.

On a February afternoon in 1943, a Mexican farmer named Dionisio Pulido was working in his cornfield when he noticed something strange. A crack had opened in the ground, and grey smoke was rising from it. He heard a hissing sound and smelled something like rotten eggs. Frightened, he hurried to the nearby village to tell everyone.

Today, the volcano is still. Visitors hike across the old lava fields, and plants are slowly returning to land that was once a farmer's field.

The next morning, Tom didn't rock the cradle. He chopped wood for the oven instead, whistling as he worked.

Option A: rocking the cradle
Option B: baking the bread
Option C: digging the shaft
Option D: chopping the wood

Priya's little brother Arjun had sprained his ankle and had to stay upstairs. All day he called down to her. 'Priya, can you bring my book? Priya, I need my torch!' Up and down she trudged, until her legs grew grumpy.
One Saturday, she decided to invent a solution.
She found an old wheel from a broken trolley, a long rope and Mum's yellow beach bucket. With Dad's help, she fixed the wheel to a hook high above the stairwell. Then she looped the rope over the wheel and tied the bucket to one end.

Arjun giggled. Priya frowned and tried again. This time she tied the handle with two knots and pulled slowly, steadily, smoothly. The bucket bobbed up the stairwell and landed safely in Arjun's hands.
'It works!' he shouted.
That night, Priya wrote in her notebook: Bucket Lift, Version Two. Problem: wobbling. Solution: slow pulling and double knots. Next, she would add a little bell, so Arjun could ring for his deliveries.
Dad smiled when he read it. 'Every inventor starts with a squeak and a thud,' he said.

Option A: a boy who learns to climb the stairs again
Option B: a girl who invents a way to send things upstairs
Option C: a family who packs a bucket for the beach
Option D: a girl who mends a broken shopping trolley

On the last Wednesday of August, the small town of Buñol in Spain turns bright red. Thousands of visitors crowd into its narrow streets for La Tomatina, the world's biggest tomato fight.

Since 2013, people have needed tickets to join in, because the crowds had grown too large for the small town to hold safely.

Option A: on the first Wednesday of August
Option B: on the last Wednesday of August
Option C: on the last Saturday of August
Option D: on the first Monday of September

Something in the Dark
It was Jai's first night ever in a tent. Dad was snoring softly in his sleeping bag, and the river gurgled somewhere beyond the trees. Jai lay wide awake, staring at the dark green canvas above him.
Then he heard it.
Rustle, rustle. Something was moving through the dry leaves outside. Jai held his breath. Thump! Something heavy landed near the tent. Then came a scratching, scritch-scratch, scritch-scratch, right beside his head.
Jai's heart pounded. He imagined a bear, even though he knew there were no bears in Australia. He imagined a giant lizard with claws like knives. He pulled his sleeping bag up to his nose.
'Dad,' he whispered. 'Dad! Something's out there!'
Dad grunted, rolled over and switched on his torch. Slowly, he unzipped the tent flap and shone the light outside.
Two shiny eyes stared back at them. Sitting on top of the food box was a fluffy grey possum, with a slice of bread clutched in its tiny paws. It blinked in the torchlight, then went on munching as if they weren't there at all.
Jai let out a shaky laugh. 'That's the monster?'
'That's the monster,' Dad chuckled. 'I think we forgot to close the lid properly.'
Jai watched the possum finish its supper and scamper up a gum tree. When he lay down again, the rustles and thumps of the bush didn't seem scary at all. They sounded like neighbours going about their night.
Question: What was Dad doing when Jai first heard the noise?
Option A: sitting beside the river
Option B: fetching the food box
Option C: sleeping in his sleeping bag
Option D: shining his torch outside

Geocaching is a real-life treasure hunt played all over the world. People hide small waterproof containers, called caches, in parks, forests and towns. Then they share each location online so that others can search for it. Here is how to find your first one.
You will need: an adult to come with you, a phone with a geocaching app, a pen, and a small toy or trinket to swap.
Steps
1. Choose a cache marked 'easy' on the app. Check that it is in a safe public place.
2. Follow the arrow on the screen towards the cache. When you are close, put the phone away and use your eyes. The signal can be off by a few metres, so the cache may not be exactly where the arrow points.
3. Look for anything that seems out of place, such as a neat pile of sticks or a hollow log. Never dig, and never climb fences.
4. When you find the cache, open it carefully. Inside, you will find a logbook. Write your name and the date.
5. If there are trinkets inside, you may take one, but you must leave something of equal or greater value.
6. Close the cache tightly and put it back exactly where you found it, hidden in the same way.
7. Record your find on the app.
Tip: Try not to let passers-by see where the cache is hidden, or they might move it by accident.

Option A: a small, cheap ornament or toy
Option B: a large and valuable prize

Option D: a waterproof box with a lid

Your First Geocache Hunt
Geocaching is a real-life treasure hunt played all over the world. People hide small waterproof containers, called caches, in parks, forests and towns. Then they share each location online so that others can search for it. Here is how to find your first one.
You will need: an adult to come with you, a phone with a geocaching app, a pen, and a small toy or trinket to swap.
Steps
1. Choose a cache marked 'easy' on the app. Check that it is in a safe public place.
2. Follow the arrow on the screen towards the cache. When you are close, put the phone away and use your eyes. The signal can be off by a few metres, so the cache may not be exactly where the arrow points.
3. Look for anything that seems out of place, such as a neat pile of sticks or a hollow log. Never dig, and never climb fences.
4. When you find the cache, open it carefully. Inside, you will find a logbook. Write your name and the date.
5. If there are trinkets inside, you may take one, but you must leave something of equal or greater value.
6. Close the cache tightly and put it back exactly where you found it, hidden in the same way.
7. Record your find on the app.
Tip: Try not to let passers-by see where the cache is hidden, or they might move it by accident.

Why Every Class Needs Maui
Our school library has hardly any myths and legends. I believe every class should spend time each week reading the old stories of the world.
Firstly, myths are exciting. In a legend told in Aotearoa New Zealand and on other Pacific islands, the hero Maui decides that the sun races across the sky far too quickly. What student could put down a story like that?
Secondly, myths show us how people long ago made sense of the world. They had no science books, yet they still wondered why the days grow longer or why the moon changes shape. Their answers were imaginative, and they remind us that asking questions is something humans have always done.
Finally, legends connect us to one another. Many families in our community come from places with their own treasured tales. When we read these stories together, classmates can share the versions their grandparents told them.
Some people say myths are just made-up stories and a waste of time. But made-up does not mean useless. Maui's tale also teaches us to be brave, clever and to work as a team.
So, let's fill those empty shelves. Every class deserves a weekly dose of legend.

Option A: The sun was burning his family's crops.
Option B: His family could not finish their work before dark.
Option C: His brothers wanted more time to go fishing.
Option D: The moon had asked him to slow it down.

Keep Cars on the Ground
Every few years, someone promises that flying cars are just around the corner. Videos show shiny machines zooming between skyscrapers. It looks thrilling, but I believe filling our skies with flying cars would be a big mistake.
Imagine it is the year 2075. Ten-year-old Priya steps outside her front door. Above her, hundreds of flying cars buzz like a swarm of angry bees. She cannot hear the birds or even her own thoughts. Her little brother covers his ears and refuses to walk to school. This is the noisy future we could be choosing.
Noise is only the first problem. A car with a flat tyre can pull over to the side of the road. A flying car with a broken engine has nowhere to go but down. Every driver would need far more training than drivers need today, and even skilled pilots make mistakes.
Flying cars would also use huge amounts of energy. Lifting a heavy vehicle into the air takes much more power than rolling it along a road. That means more batteries, more fuel and more harm to our planet.
Supporters say flying cars would end traffic jams. But the sky would soon fill up too, and a jam a hundred metres up is far more dangerous than one on the ground.
Instead of wasting billions on flying cars, let's build better trains, safer bike paths and quieter streets. The future should be calm, clean and safe, not buzzing over our heads.
Question: Which reason does the writer give to show that flying cars would harm the planet?
Option A: Flying cars would be too noisy for birds.
Option B: Drivers would need much more training.
Option C: Lifting a vehicle takes more power than rolling it.
Option D: Engines could break down in the air.

The Last Box
The hallway was full of cardboard boxes, and every one of them had my sister's name on it in thick black marker. Tomorrow Amira was moving to Perth to study, and our house felt like a balloon slowly losing its air.
'Can you pass the tape, Sami?' she asked. I handed it over without a word. My chest felt tight, as if someone had wrapped tape around it too.
Mum kept finding reasons to come upstairs. First she brought sandwiches, then clean towels, then a jar of her famous lime pickle. 'You won't find pickle like this in Perth,' she said, and her voice wobbled.
When Amira went to answer the phone, I slipped into her room. On her desk sat our old walkie-talkies, the ones we whispered through on stormy nights when I was too scared to sleep. I tucked one into the last box, under her jumpers, and hid the other under my pillow.
At dinner, Dad told his silliest jokes. Amira laughed loudly and said she was totally fine, but she hardly touched her rice.
'She's putting on a brave face,' Mum whispered to me.
The next morning, after the car had disappeared around the corner, I flopped onto my bed. Something crackled under my pillow. Taped to my walkie-talkie was a note in Amira's loopy writing.
'Found the other one. They won't reach Perth, but I'm keeping it anyway. Call me every Sunday, little brother.'

Option A: ready for a party
Option B: noisy and crowded
Option C: emptier and sadder
Option D: in need of repairs

Do Animals Have Best Friends?
The word companion comes from two old Latin words: com, meaning 'with', and panis, meaning 'bread'. A companion was someone you shared your bread with. Scientists have discovered that humans are not the only ones who share with their companions.

Inside was a drawing of a green truck with a tiny girl waving from a window. Underneath, Bev had written: Get well soon, Captain Wave.
Nell taped it to the window, facing out, so that every driver could see it.

Bedtime in Orbit
Astronauts on the International Space Station circle Earth about every ninety minutes. That means they see around sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets every day! So getting a good night's sleep takes careful planning.
Where do astronauts sleep?
Each crew member has a tiny private cabin about the size of a phone booth. Inside is a sleeping bag fastened to the wall. Because there is no 'up' or 'down' in space, astronauts can sleep standing up, upside down or sideways. They zip themselves into their bags so they do not drift around. If they forget to tuck in their arms, their arms float out in front of them like a sleepwalker's.
Why are fans so important?
On Earth, warm air rises and moves around, carrying away the air we breathe out. In space, air does not move on its own. Without a fan, the carbon dioxide an astronaut breathes out could gather around their face like an invisible cloud and give them a headache. So the cabins have fans that whirr all night.
Tips for sleeping in space
Astronauts often wear eye masks to block out the sun flashing through the windows. Many use earplugs, because the station's pumps and fans buzz, click and clatter constantly. They also try to sleep at the same times every day.
Sleeping in space may sound strange, but astronauts say that once you get used to floating, it can be surprisingly comfortable.

Rolo was the smallest dung beetle on the farm, but he had the biggest ideas. 'This year,' he told his sister Pip, 'I'm going to roll the biggest dung ball anyone has ever seen.'

Rolo climbed down and began rolling his ball along the bottom of the hill, the long way round.
It took until sunset, but Rolo arrived home with his ball in one piece. Pip was waiting.
'You went around,' she said with a grin.
'I went smart,' said Rolo.

The Crab Who Outgrew His Shell
Beneath the rocks where seaweed sways,
A hermit crab spent all his days
Inside a shell of speckled brown,
The snuggest home in Rock Pool Town.
But crabs keep growing, as crabs do,
And soon his shell would barely do.
His claws stuck out, his legs were pinched,
He shuffled slowly, inch by inch.
'I won't move out!' he told the tide.
'My shell is safe. I'll stay inside.'
The periwinkles shook their heads,
The starfish sighed from sandy beds.
He tried to sleep, he tried to eat,
But bumped his claws and scraped his feet.
Each wave that rolled across the bay
Seemed to whisper, 'Move away.'
Then one bright morning, washed ashore,
He spied a shell not seen before:
A swirl of white with rosy rims,
Wide enough for all his limbs.
He crept up close. He gave a poke.
His heart went thump. He nearly spoke.
For just one breath he'd be out there,
His soft pink body cold and bare.
He thought about the gulls up high,
The hungry fish that drifted by,
Who'd love a snack so soft and small.
He almost didn't move at all.
He counted, 'One... and two... and three!'
And darted, quick as quick could be,
Into the shell of white and rose,
And wriggled in from claws to toes.
Now in the pool where seaweed sways,
He spends his roomy, happy days,
And leaves his old brown shell behind
For some small crab of smaller kind.

Option A: caught sight of
Option B: listened to
Option C: grabbed hold of
Option D: built for himself

When Dad said we were staying with Aunty Jo in Coober Pedy, I pictured a normal house. I did not expect her front door to be cut into the side of a rocky hill.
'Welcome to my dugout,' Aunty Jo said, sweeping her arm wide.

That night, I lay in bed listening. There was no hum of traffic and no rattle of wind. It was the quietest place I had ever been. It felt a bit spooky at first, but soon the stillness wrapped around me and I drifted off.
In the morning, Aunty Jo showed me a small, glittering stone she had found while digging a new cupboard into the wall. It flashed green, blue and red.
'An opal,' she said with a wink. 'In this town, even building a cupboard can be an adventure.'

Option B: twenty-four degrees

Option D: fourteen degrees

When George Washington Carver was a boy in Missouri, USA, in the 1870s, neighbours brought him their sick plants. George would study the drooping leaves, move each plant to a sunnier spot or change its soil, and before long it would be healthy again. People began calling him 'the plant doctor'.

The farmers tried his advice, and their soil began to recover. Soon, though, there was a new problem. They had grown so many peanuts that there were not enough buyers.
George was not worried. He had always believed that a plant could be useful in more ways than people imagined. He headed to his laboratory with a sack of peanuts.

Option A: He studied medicine at college.
Option B: He made sick plants healthy again.
Option C: He sold plants to his neighbours.
Option D: He cured animals on nearby farms.

Clover was a poddy calf with a white patch shaped like a lightning bolt and a stubborn streak as wide as the Murray River. They did not win Champion Calf. That went to a tall black heifer from Coolah. But as Josh led Clover out, the judge called him back and pinned a green ribbon on his shirt. It read: Best Young Handler.
Grandpa winked. 'Told you,' he said. 'A reason to follow.'

Option A: once a day
Option B: twice a day
Option C: three times a day
Option D: every afternoon after school

Michael Faraday was born in London in 1791. His family was poor, and Michael left school at thirteen with only the most basic lessons in reading, writing and arithmetic.
At fourteen, he became an apprentice to a bookbinder. His job was to stitch pages together and fix covers, but Michael did more than bind the books. He read them. Whenever he found a book about science, he studied it late into the night and tried the experiments himself.

Michael once wrote that nothing is too wonderful to be true, if it fits the laws of nature.

At breakfast, Ms Ruiz asked who had slept well. Owen's hand shot up first.
'Like a log,' he said with a big yawn.
Priya caught his eye and smiled, but she didn't say a word. Owen grinned back. Some secrets, he decided, were worth keeping, and Priya was clearly good at keeping them.

Option A: a row of dinosaur bones
Option B: some green exit signs
Option C: the skeleton of a blue whale
Option D: an upside-down wooden boat

Pictures Made of Pieces
A mosaic is a picture made from many small pieces fitted closely together. The pieces are called tesserae, and they can be cut from stone, glass, pottery or tile. When you stand close to a mosaic, you see hundreds of separate bits. When you step back, they blend into one image.
People have made mosaics for thousands of years. The ancient Romans loved them and covered the floors of their homes and bathhouses with scenes of animals, people and the sea. Some of these floors were buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. They have since been dug up in the town of Pompeii, still bright and clear.
Later, artists in the Italian city of Ravenna made mosaics from coloured glass. Some pieces had a thin layer of gold inside them, so the walls glittered in candlelight.
To make a mosaic, an artist first draws a design. Next, the tesserae are pressed into wet cement or glue, leaving tiny gaps. Finally, the gaps are filled with grout, a paste that hardens and holds everything firmly in place.
Because stone and glass do not soak up water, mosaics are still used in swimming pools, fountains and bathrooms. Many towns also have mosaic walls made by local schoolchildren, with each child adding a few pieces to a shared picture.

Option A: grout
Option B: tiles
Option C: designs
Option D: tesserae

People have made mosaics for thousands of years. The ancient Romans loved them and covered the floors of their homes and bathhouses with scenes of animals, people and the sea. Some of these floors were buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. They have since been dug up in the town of Pompeii, still bright and clear.
Later, artists in the Italian city of Ravenna made mosaics from coloured glass. Some pieces had a thin layer of gold inside them, so the walls glittered in candlelight.
To make a mosaic, an artist first draws a design. Next, the tesserae are pressed into wet cement or glue, leaving tiny gaps. Finally, the gaps are filled with grout, a paste that hardens and holds everything firmly in place.
Because stone and glass do not soak up water, mosaics are still used in swimming pools, fountains and bathrooms. Many towns also have mosaic walls made by local schoolchildren, with each child adding a few pieces to a shared picture.

Give the Wolf a Fair Go
Think of the stories you know. Who is the villain? Very often, it is a wolf. In 'Little Red Riding Hood', the wolf tricks a girl and her grandmother. In 'The Three Little Pigs', he huffs and puffs and blows their houses down. In Aesop's fable 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf', the wolf is simply something to fear. I believe it is time we gave wolves a fairer go.
Firstly, storybook wolves are nothing like real ones. Real wolves are shy animals that usually avoid people. They live in family groups called packs, and the parents work together to feed and protect their pups. That sounds more like a loving family than a gang of villains.
Secondly, these stories can make children afraid of animals that need our help. In many countries, wolves were hunted until very few were left. People are less likely to protect an animal they have only ever been taught to fear.
Finally, there are already stories that show wolves in a kinder light. In an old Roman legend, a wolf cared for two baby twins. Some modern picture books tell 'The Three Little Pigs' from the wolf's side, and readers often laugh and change their minds.
Fables and fairy tales will always be loved, and they should be. But next time you read one, ask yourself: is the wolf really so big and bad? Perhaps it is time to retell the tale.

Option A: packs
Option B: herds
Option C: gangs
Option D: litters

Old Juniper
Juniper once raced the wind
from the gate to the old gum tree,
her ears blown inside out with speed,
her tail a flag for me.

She'd chase a ball until the dark
had swallowed up the yard.
She'd leap the creek in one big bound
and never land too hard.

She'd dig for bones beneath the shed,
she'd bark at every bird,
and catch the crinkle of the cheese
before a word was heard.

But now her muzzle's frosted white,
her steps are short and slow.
She stops to sniff at every post
as if there's nowhere to go.

The ball rolls past. She watches it.
She thumps her tail instead,
then finds the patch of sunshine first
and makes the warmth her bed.

At first I tugged her lead and sighed.
I wanted her to run.
I'd grumble, 'Hurry, Juniper!'
and walks were not much fun.

But slowly, as I matched her pace,
I started seeing more:
the beetle on the fence rail,
the moss beside the door,

the magpie feeding her baby,
the way the shadows lie.
Juniper had found these things
while I was hurrying by.

I've learned the scent of rain on stone,
the hum of bees at play,
and how the light turns honey-gold
at the quiet end of day.

So now we stroll, my dog and I,
with nowhere we must be.
She taught me how to run, back then.
Now she's teaching slow to me.
Question: Where did Juniper once race to?
Option A: the creek
Option B: the front gate
Option C: the fence rail
Option D: the old gum tree

Gran's Fifty-Year Postcard
Gran had kept the postcard on her fridge for fifty years. It showed a penguin standing on an iceberg, and on the back, in faded pencil, she had written: One day.
Now, wrapped in a borrowed red jacket, Lily stood beside Gran on the deck of the ship as it slid into a bay in Antarctica. The water was as still as glass. Icebergs drifted past like enormous white sculptures, some streaked with a blue so bright it seemed to glow.
'Look!' Lily pointed. On the shore, hundreds of Adélie penguins waddled and squabbled, their black backs shining.
Small rubber boats carried the passengers to the beach, because the ship was too big to go near the shore. The air was so cold that it stung Lily's nose, and the snow squeaked under her boots. A penguin hopped right past her, carrying a pebble in its beak.
'They build their nests from stones,' said the guide. 'Sometimes they steal them from their neighbours.'
Lily laughed and turned to tell Gran, but Gran wasn't laughing. She was standing quite still, her gloved hands pressed to her mouth, and her eyes were shining.
'Are you all right?' Lily asked.
Gran nodded but didn't speak for a long moment. Then she pulled the old postcard from her pocket and held it up beside the real penguins.
'Not one day any more,' she said softly. 'Today.'

Option A: swam quickly
Option B: slept soundly
Option C: fed their chicks
Option D: argued noisily

Mum sat her down, brought her a cold drink and phoned her daughter, who came straight away. Kai filled Rusty's bowl and led him into the shade.
That evening, a cool change swept through, and the temperature dropped twelve degrees in an hour. Kai never did get to the beach, but when Mrs Lindqvist waved from her garden the next morning, he decided he didn't mind at all.

When the cast finally came off, her right arm looked thin and pale. The doctor explained that muscles shrink when they aren't used, and gave her exercises to make them strong again.

Grandad and I walked onto the beach early, before anyone else had left a footprint. The tide was out, and the wet sand stretched almost to the rocks.
'Look down,' said Grandad.

By the afternoon, the tide had come back in, and the beach ripples were gone.

Option A: tidy
Option B: dirty
Option C: deep
Option D: tiny

Tug Number Nine
The cargo ship comes in at dawn,
a mountain made of steel,
so long she cannot turn alone,
so heavy at the wheel.

Out puffs the tug called Number Nine,
her paint all chipped and red,
no bigger than the giant's bow
that towers overhead.

Her captain grips the little wheel
and squints into the spray;
he knows each sandbar, rock and reef
like streets he walks each day.

She takes a rope and leans her weight,
she nudges, pulls and pushes,
while gulls go wheeling round her mast
and foam goes up in rushes.

The pilot calls from up on deck,
"Hard left! Now slow! Now stay!"
And Number Nine, with chugging heart,
obeys and finds the way.

The wind blows hard across the bay;
the giant starts to swing.
The tug digs in, her engine roars,
the rope pulls tight and sings.

Past buoys that blink their green and red,
past rocks beneath the tide,
she guides the giant to the wharf
and tucks her safe inside.

The giant sighs against the ropes,
her long trip at an end;
the tug gives one last gentle push,
the way you'd help a friend.

The cranes swing down, the workers cheer
the giant at the quay;
nobody turns to thank the tug
that chugs back out to sea.

But Number Nine just toots her horn;
she doesn't mind at all.
Out past the heads another ship
is waiting for her call.
Question: Why does the cargo ship need the tug?
Option A: its engine has broken down out at sea
Option B: it has run out of fuel near the wharf
Option C: it is too long and heavy to turn safely by itself
Option D: its pilot does not know the way into the bay

Build a Tissue-Box Guitar
You don't need an expensive instrument to make music. With a few things from around the house, you can build a guitar that really plays.
You will need: an empty tissue box, four or five rubber bands of different thicknesses, two pencils and some sticky tape.
Steps
1. Take any plastic film off the hole in the box. The hole lets the sound out; without it, your guitar would sound dull and quiet.
2. Stretch the rubber bands lengthwise around the box so that they pass over the hole. Space them about a finger-width apart. Notice how each band gets a little thinner as you stretch it.
3. Slide a pencil under the bands at each end of the hole. These are your bridges: they lift the bands off the box so that they can vibrate freely.
4. Tape the pencils in place so they don't roll away.
5. Pluck each band and listen. Thin bands make high notes; thick bands make low notes.
Troubleshooting
If a band only makes a flat "thwack", it is probably too loose. Swap it for a tighter one. Don't be discouraged if your first song sounds more like a cranky frog than a rock star. Every musician starts out with a few wobbly notes!
Next challenge
Pull one band further around the box to tighten it, then pluck it again. Listen carefully to how the note changes.

Build a Tissue-Box Guitar
You don't need an expensive instrument to make music. With a few things from around the house, you can build a guitar that really plays.
You will need: an empty tissue box, four or five rubber bands of different thicknesses, two pencils and some sticky tape.
Steps
1. Take any plastic film off the hole in the box. The hole lets the sound out; without it, your guitar would sound dull and quiet.
2. Stretch the rubber bands lengthwise around the box so that they pass over the hole. Space them about a finger-width apart. Notice how each band gets a little thinner as you stretch it.
3. Slide a pencil under the bands at each end of the hole. These are your bridges: they lift the bands off the box so that they can vibrate freely.
4. Tape the pencils in place so they don't roll away.
5. Pluck each band and listen. Thin bands make high notes; thick bands make low notes.
Troubleshooting
If a band only makes a flat "thwack", it is probably too loose. Swap it for a tighter one. Don't be discouraged if your first song sounds more like a cranky frog than a rock star. Every musician starts out with a few wobbly notes!

Pull one band further around the box to tighten it, then pluck it again. Listen carefully to how the note changes.

The Train That Hangs
Dear Grandma,
Greetings from Wuppertal in Germany! Today we rode the strangest train I have ever seen. Instead of running on tracks along the ground, it hangs underneath a steel rail, high above a river. Mum says it is called the Schwebebahn, which means "floating railway".
The railway opened in 1901, so it is more than 120 years old. Its rail stretches for about 13 kilometres, and most of it follows the River Wupper. The city is squeezed into a narrow valley, so there was not enough room for a normal railway. The builders put the train above the water instead.
When the carriage came into the station, it swayed gently like a coat on a hook. My stomach did a somersault as we pulled away! Below us the river glittered like spilled sequins, and I could see ducks bobbing between the stones. At every bend the carriage tilted, and I gripped the rail so tightly that my knuckles turned white. Then I looked across at Dad, and he was gripping the rail too!
I think it is the most exciting ride in the whole of Europe. Dad says the old steel frame looks like a giant metal caterpillar stretched across the town.
Tomorrow we are going to ride it again to visit the zoo. I'll bring you home a postcard of it.
Lots of love,
Lena

How to Wrap a Present (and Not Yourself)
Wrapping a present looks easy until the sticky tape attacks. Follow these steps and you might finish with the gift wrapped and your fingers free.
You will need: wrapping paper, scissors, sticky tape and a present with flat sides. (A box is best. A basketball is a very bad idea.)
1. Before you begin, tear off six short pieces of tape and stick them lightly along the edge of the table. Trust me, you will not have a spare hand later.
2. Roll out the paper and place the box upside down in the middle. Cut a piece big enough to wrap all the way round, with a little extra. Too little paper leaves a gap; too much turns your present into a crumpled cabbage.
3. Fold one long side over the box and tape it. Fold the other side over the top so that it overlaps the first, and tape again.
4. At each end, push the sides in to make two triangle flaps. Fold the flaps up and tape them down.
5. Turn the present over. If you see a gap, cover it with a bow. Nobody will ever know.
Common problems
The tape is stuck to itself: give up on that piece and use a new one.
The cat is sitting on the paper: politely ask the cat to move, then wait twenty minutes.
Remember, a lumpy present still holds a gift inside. The person who opens it will care far more about your kindness than your folds.

Option A: tears apart.

Option D: sticks together.

The Lodger Under the Shed
Every afternoon, when the sun warmed the concrete path, a fat grey lizard crawled out from under Ava's garden shed. It had stumpy legs, a striped back and a head like a smooth river stone.
On Saturday, Ava's big brother Sam spotted it. "Ugh! There's a snake with legs out here!" he yelled. "Dad, we need to get rid of it."
The lizard puffed itself up, opened its pink mouth wide and poked out a tongue as blue as a ballpoint pen. Sam jumped back so fast that he tripped over the hose.
Ava knelt down slowly. Her heart was thumping, but she kept her voice calm. "It's a blue-tongue lizard," she said. "That tongue is just a trick to scare off enemies. It doesn't have any venom."
Dad rubbed his chin. "It does look a bit fierce," he said.
"Think about your vegie patch, Dad," said Ava. "Who keeps eating your lettuces?"
"The snails," Dad grumbled.
"And who eats snails? Blue-tongues do! Do you really want to get rid of the best snail-catcher in the street? Lots of gardeners would love to have one."
Dad looked at his holey lettuces. Then he looked at the lizard, which had closed its mouth and was blinking sleepily in the sun.
"All right," he said. "It can stay. But it pays rent in snails."
That evening, Ava placed a flat rock beside the shed while Sam watched from the back step. "Just in case it wants somewhere to sunbake," she explained.

Option A: it ran back under the garden shed
Option B: it puffed up and showed its blue tongue
Option C: it bit Sam on the ankle
Option D: it climbed onto a flat rock

Tears Without Sadness
Have you ever chopped an onion and suddenly found tears rolling down your cheeks? You are not sad. Your eyes are simply protecting themselves.
An onion is made of thousands of tiny cells, each like a little bag. Some of these bags hold special chemicals. As long as the onion is whole, the chemicals stay safely apart. But when a knife slices through the cells, the chemicals spill out, mix together and make a new substance. This substance floats up into the air as an invisible gas.
When the gas reaches your eyes, it stings. Your eyes quickly make tears to wash it away. The more cells you break, the more gas there is, and the more you cry.
Luckily, cooks have found some clever tricks. A sharp knife cuts cleanly through the cells instead of crushing them, so less gas escapes. Putting the onion in the fridge for half an hour before chopping also helps, because the gas does not rise as easily from a cold onion. Some cooks leave the root end until last, as that part holds more of the chemicals.
Once an onion is cooked, it won't make you cry at all. Heat changes the chemicals, which is also why fried onions taste sweet instead of sharp.
So the next time an onion turns on the waterworks, don't worry. Your eyes are just doing their job!

Feet of the Forest Giants
Walk through a tropical rainforest and you may see trees that seem to stand on enormous wooden fins. These are buttress roots. Some are taller than an adult and stretch several metres out from the trunk.
You might expect such huge trees to have roots that dig deep into the ground. In fact, the opposite is true. Rainforest soil is surprisingly thin and poor. Leaves and fallen branches rot quickly in the warm, wet air, and the goodness from them is soaked up almost straight away by roots near the surface. So most rainforest trees keep their roots shallow, where the food is.
Shallow roots, though, do not hold a tree firmly in place. A tall tree catching the wind could easily topple over. That is where the fins help. Like the thick supports built against the walls of some old stone buildings, these wide, flat roots brace the tree on every side. They buttress the trunk, spreading its weight over a larger area of ground.
Buttress roots are useful to animals, too. The narrow spaces between them make shady, sheltered nooks where frogs, insects and small mammals can hide.
Next time you see a picture of a rainforest giant, look down at its feet. Those odd-shaped roots are a clever answer to a tricky problem.

A Birdbath Birds Will Actually Use
Birds need water for drinking and for bathing. A splash keeps their feathers clean, and clean feathers keep birds warm and help them fly. You can help by setting up a birdbath. Follow these steps to make one that birds will visit again and again.
You will need: a wide, shallow dish such as a plant-pot saucer, a few flat stones and a bucket of clean water.
1. Choose a spot that is open but near a tree or tall shrub. Place the bath about two to three metres from the plants, not right underneath them.
2. Put the dish on a stump, a low table or an upturned pot, so that it sits off the ground.
3. Arrange a few flat stones in the dish. Birds like to stand where they can grip, and small birds need somewhere shallow to perch.
4. Fill the dish with water no deeper than about five centimetres.
5. Every two or three days, tip out the old water, scrub the dish and refill it.
Why it works
Birds are cautious when they bathe. Wet feathers make them heavier and slower to take off, so they choose places where they can see danger coming. A nearby tree gives them a quick escape, but thick plants right beside the bath could hide a prowling cat.
Be patient. It may take a week or two before the first visitor decides your bath is safe.
Question: How deep should the water in the birdbath be?
Option A: no deeper than about five centimetres
Option B: about two to three metres
Option C: deep enough to cover the stones
Option D: as deep as the bucket

The Robot Under the Couch
In many homes, a round, flat robot hums across the floor while everyone else is busy. It is a robot vacuum cleaner, and it is smarter than it looks.
A robot vacuum is packed with sensors, which are parts that collect information about the world around it. Bump sensors at the front tell it when it has hit a chair leg or a wall, so it can turn and try a new direction. Cliff sensors underneath shine invisible light at the floor. If the light does not bounce back quickly, the robot knows there is a drop, such as a staircase, and it backs away.
Newer models go one step further. They use cameras or lasers to build a map of each room, so they can clean in neat rows instead of wandering about at random. Some can even remember which rooms get the dirtiest.
When its battery runs low, the robot doesn't need anyone to help. It follows a signal back to its charging dock, plugs itself in and waits. Once it is charged, it can carry on where it left off.
Robot vacuums are not perfect, though. Socks, toys and phone chargers can tangle in their brushes, and a thick rug can stop them in their tracks. Before a robot can do its job, someone usually has to tidy up first!
Still, for many busy families, these little machines are a real help.

Option A: brushes that sweep the floor.
Option B: maps of each room.
Option C: parts that collect information.
Option D: lights that show the way home.

The Hole in Newton's Shutter
In 1666, a young scientist named Isaac Newton wanted to understand light. At that time, most people believed that sunlight was pure white, and that a glass prism somehow added colours to it. Newton was not so sure.
He darkened his room and made a small, round hole in the window shutter, so that only a thin beam of sunlight could enter. He wanted one narrow beam rather than a room full of light, because then he could follow exactly what happened to it. When the beam passed through a prism, it spread out into a band of colours on the far wall: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.
However, this did not yet prove anything. Perhaps the prism really was making the colours. So Newton tried a second test. He let just one colour, such as red, pass through a second prism. If prisms added colour, the red light should have changed. It didn't. It stayed red.
Newton decided that white light is actually a mixture of all the colours. The prism does not create them; it only separates them. Although other people had played with prisms before, Newton's careful tests changed the way scientists thought about light.
Interestingly, Newton chose to name seven colours partly because he liked the idea of matching the seven notes of a musical scale.
Question: "Newton was not so sure" suggests that Newton . . .
Option A: did not know what a prism was.
Option B: believed sunlight was pure white.
Option C: was unsure how to darken his room.
Option D: doubted that the prism added colours to light.

Listening for the Ball
Imagine trying to stop a ball that you cannot see. That is exactly what players do in goalball, a team sport created for people who are blind or have low vision.
Goalball began in the 1940s and is now played at the Paralympic Games. Each team has three players on the court at a time. Because some players can see a little and others cannot see at all, everyone wears dark eyeshades. This makes the game fair for all.
The ball is about the size of a basketball, but it is heavier and has bells inside. Players roll or bounce it hard along the floor, trying to get it past the other team and into a goal that stretches across the whole end of the court. The defenders listen carefully, then throw themselves sideways along the floor to block it with their bodies.
Teamwork is everything in goalball. Since nobody can see, everyone depends on sound. Players call out to one another and tap the floor to show where they are. Raised lines under the tape on the court help them feel their position with their hands and feet.
For the same reason, spectators must stay completely silent while the ball is in play. A cheer at the wrong moment could hide the jingle of the ball. When a goal is scored, though, the crowd is allowed to roar!

Option A: so the crowd knows a goal is scored
Option B: so players can hear where it is
Option C: so the ball is heavier to throw
Option D: so the referee can count the throws

Where Old Tyres Go
Every car, truck and bike eventually wears out its tyres. In Australia, tens of millions of old tyres are thrown away each year. So where do they all go?
For a long time, many were buried in landfill or simply piled up in huge stacks. This caused several problems. Tyres are bulky and take up a lot of space. Buried tyres can trap air and slowly work their way back up to the surface. Rainwater collects inside stacked tyres, making perfect breeding pools for mosquitoes. Worst of all, a tyre pile that catches fire can burn for days, giving off thick, poisonous black smoke.
Today, more and more old tyres are recycled instead. First, machines shred them into small chunks. Strong magnets then pull out the steel wire hidden inside each tyre. The rubber is ground down even further into tiny pieces called crumb rubber.
Crumb rubber can be used in surprising ways. It is spread under swings and slides to make soft playground surfaces that cushion falls. It is mixed into some road surfaces, which can make them last longer and sound quieter. It is also pressed into mats for gyms and stables.
Recycling cannot solve the problem on its own. Keeping your tyres pumped up properly helps them last longer, which means fewer need replacing. The best tyre of all is one that is never thrown away too soon.
Question: What is used to pull the steel wire out of shredded tyres?
Option A: sharp blades
Option B: strong magnets
Option C: large hooks
Option D: hot water

About 4,700 years ago, a clever man named Imhotep lived in ancient Egypt. Nobody knows exactly when he was born, but we do know that he served a king named Djoser. Imhotep was a scribe, an adviser and, most famously, a builder.
In those days, Egyptian kings were buried in flat, low tombs made of mud bricks. Imhotep had a bold idea. Why not build in stone, and why not build upwards? He planned a tomb with six giant steps, each one smaller than the one beneath it, rising high above the desert sand.
The work was enormous. Thousands of workers cut blocks of limestone with copper tools. All day long the quarry rang with the tap, tap, tap of chisels and the scrape of stone on stone. Teams hauled the heavy blocks on wooden sledges, calling out together as they pulled.
At last the Step Pyramid stood finished at Saqqara, about 60 metres tall. It is thought to be the oldest large building made of cut stone. Later pyramids, including the famous ones at Giza, followed the path that Imhotep had paved.
Imhotep was remembered for more than buildings. Over the centuries, Egyptians told stories of his wisdom and his skill as a healer, and statues showed him seated with a scroll across his knees.
Today, more than four thousand years later, his pyramid still stands, weathered and worn, but proud against the bright blue sky.

Option B: Giza
Option C: Saqqara
Option D: Ramses

In those days, Egyptian kings were buried in flat, low tombs made of mud bricks. Imhotep had a bold idea. Why not build in stone, and why not build upwards? He planned a tomb with six giant steps, each one smaller than the one beneath it, rising high above the desert sand.
The work was enormous. Thousands of workers cut blocks of limestone with copper tools. All day long the quarry rang with the tap, tap, tap of chisels and the scrape of stone on stone. Teams hauled the heavy blocks on wooden sledges, calling out together as they pulled.
At last the Step Pyramid stood finished at Saqqara, about 60 metres tall. It is thought to be the oldest large building made of cut stone. Later pyramids, including the famous ones at Giza, followed the path that Imhotep had paved.
Imhotep was remembered for more than buildings. Over the centuries, Egyptians told stories of his wisdom and his skill as a healer, and statues showed him seated with a scroll across his knees.
Today, more than four thousand years later, his pyramid still stands, weathered and worn, but proud against the bright blue sky.

The Newest Land
Out where the ocean was flat and blue,
the fishermen sailed as they'd always done,
till the water began to bubble and stew
and a pillar of steam blotted out the sun.
Deep down below, where no diver goes,
the seafloor had cracked and the rock ran red.
It hissed as it met the cold sea's flow
and hardened to black on the ocean bed.
The fish all fled and the seabirds cried,
the water grew warm and murky and grey;
the fishermen turned their boats aside
and hurried home to the harbour bay.
For weeks it rumbled, for months it grew,
it coughed up ash and it spat out stone,
till one grey morning it pushed right through,
a smoking hill in the sea alone.
The sailors watched from a careful distance;
the scientists came with their charts and pens.
They measured its height with great persistence,
then came back to measure it again.
Some days it roared and some days it slept,
some nights it glowed like a lantern red,
and all the while the island crept
a little higher above its bed.
At last the fires were tired and slow,
the rain came down and the black rock cooled.
Then a seed blew in, and it started to grow,
and a gull came to rest where the lava had ruled.
Now moss creeps green over ash and stone,
and seabirds squabble on cliffs of grey.
The land that was born from fire alone
is learning to live in a gentler way.
Question: What made the water 'bubble and stew'?
Option A: hot rock from a crack in the seafloor
Option B: a strong storm blowing over the sea
Option C: the fishermen's boats speeding past
Option D: a huge whale coming up for air

On Monday morning, Nadia stepped out of the shower and froze. Written across the foggy bathroom mirror were two wobbly letters: HI.
'Who wrote that?' she called. Her little brother, Sam, shook his head. Mum and Dad both said it wasn't them. By the time Nadia had dried her hair, the fog had faded and the letters had vanished.

'So someone wrote it ages ago,' she said slowly, 'and it's been there all along.'
She marched to the kitchen, where Sam was munching cereal. 'Did you draw on the mirror last week?'
Sam's cheeks turned as pink as a strawberry. 'Maybe,' he mumbled. 'I forgot!'
Nadia laughed and handed him a cloth. 'Mystery solved. Now you can polish it off.'

Option A: angry
Option B: sleepy
Option C: puzzled
Option D: pleased

In December 1876, a steamship called the Georgette was in serious trouble off the south-west coast of Western Australia. Water was leaking into the ship, and it had drifted close to the shore near the Bussell family's farm. Huge waves pounded its sides, and the people on board could not get safely to land.

News of the rescue spread around the world. Grace was awarded a silver medal for bravery, and Sam received a bronze medal. Newspapers compared Grace to Grace Darling, a young English woman who had rowed out in a storm to save shipwrecked sailors.
Today, the small coastal town of Gracetown is named in honour of the girl who rode into the sea.

Option A: rough and dangerous
Option B: full of wild animals

Water for Grandmother
Kit had looked forward to visiting his cousins in Chiang Mai for months, but one thing worried him. 'During Songkran, everyone gets soaked,' his cousin Nok had warned on a video call. 'Nobody stays dry.'
Songkran is the Thai New Year. It is held in the middle of April, during the hottest time of the year. When Kit arrived, the streets were already full of laughing people armed with buckets, hoses and brightly coloured water pistols. Kit clutched his bag and tried to hide behind his mum.
'Don't worry,' said Nok, grinning. 'Before the splashing, there's something important we do first.'
She led him into a cool courtyard where their grandmother sat on a low chair. A silver bowl of water stood on a table, with jasmine petals floating on top. One by one, the family knelt and gently poured a little of the fragrant water over Grandmother's hands. Each person whispered a wish for her good health in the new year.
When it was Kit's turn, his hands trembled, but he poured carefully. Grandmother smiled and squeezed his fingers. 'Thank you, little one,' she said softly.
Afterwards, Nok handed him a water pistol. Kit hesitated. Then he took a deep breath, stepped into the sunny street and fired a cheerful spray at his cousin. Nok shrieked with laughter and soaked him right back.
By evening, Kit was dripping from head to toe. To his surprise, he didn't mind one bit.
Question: When is Songkran held?
Option A: at the start of January
Option B: at the end of December
Option C: in the middle of April
Option D: in the middle of June

Three Knots Worth Knowing
A good camper carries a torch, a water bottle and a length of rope. But a rope is only as useful as the knots you can tie in it. Learn these three, and you will be ready for almost anything the bush throws at you.
The reef knot
The reef knot joins two ends of rope together. It is perfect for tying up a bundle of firewood or closing the top of a bag. To tie it, remember 'right over left, then left over right'. A reef knot lies flat and neat, but be careful: it can slip loose if it is pulled very hard, so never use it to hold anything heavy.
The bowline
The bowline (say 'BOH-lin') makes a loop at the end of a rope that will not shrink or slip, no matter how much weight hangs from it. Sailors have trusted it for hundreds of years. Best of all, even after holding a heavy load, a bowline is easy to undo.
The taut-line hitch
This clever knot is a tent's best friend. Tie it where a guy rope loops around a tent peg. It can slide along the rope to tighten or loosen it, yet it grips firmly when the rope is pulled. Ropes often stretch when they get wet, and a sagging tent can collect puddles on its roof overnight. With a taut-line hitch, you simply slide the knot to make the rope tight again.
Why not grab a piece of string tonight and start practising?
Question: In the passage, a 'sagging' tent is one that is . . .
Option A: standing very tall
Option B: drooping loosely
Option C: torn into pieces
Option D: packed away neatly

Three Knots Worth Knowing
A good camper carries a torch, a water bottle and a length of rope. But a rope is only as useful as the knots you can tie in it. Learn these three, and you will be ready for almost anything the bush throws at you.
The reef knot
The reef knot joins two ends of rope together. It is perfect for tying up a bundle of firewood or closing the top of a bag. To tie it, remember 'right over left, then left over right'. A reef knot lies flat and neat, but be careful: it can slip loose if it is pulled very hard, so never use it to hold anything heavy.
The bowline
The bowline (say 'BOH-lin') makes a loop at the end of a rope that will not shrink or slip, no matter how much weight hangs from it. Sailors have trusted it for hundreds of years. Best of all, even after holding a heavy load, a bowline is easy to undo.
The taut-line hitch
This clever knot is a tent's best friend. Tie it where a guy rope loops around a tent peg. It can slide along the rope to tighten or loosen it, yet it grips firmly when the rope is pulled. Ropes often stretch when they get wet, and a sagging tent can collect puddles on its roof overnight. With a taut-line hitch, you simply slide the knot to make the rope tight again.

Could you do me a favour? Next time it rains, please record the sound and send it to me. Nobody here has heard rain for ages.
Love,
Juno

Letters from Coral Station
14 March 2091
Dear Ellie,
Greetings from the bottom of the ocean! Well, nearly the bottom. Coral Station sits forty metres underwater, and our new apartment has a round window the size of a dinner plate. Yesterday a turtle drifted right past it. I bet nobody at our old school has ever seen that at breakfast!
School here is in a dome with only eleven kids. Everyone already has best friends, but that's fine. I'm busy anyway. Mum says I'll settle in soon.
Write back!
Juno
2 April 2091
Dear Ellie,
Thanks for your letter. I can't believe you won the swimming carnival! Here we can only swim in the practice pool, which smells like rubber.
Big news: I've joined the Window Crew. Every Saturday we help the engineers clean algae off the Great Window in the main hall. It's the biggest window on the station, and when the water is clear, real sunlight flickers down through it. The others on the crew are all teenagers, so I'm the youngest, but I don't mind. I'd scrub that glass all day if they let me.
Could you do me a favour? Next time it rains, please record the sound and send it to me. Nobody here has heard rain for ages.
Love,
Juno
P.S. A girl on the crew called Priya asked if I wanted to share her lunch. She knows the name of every fish!
Question: Which best describes Juno as she is shown across both letters?
Option A: excited about everything and without a single worry
Option B: unhappy and unwilling to make any new friends
Option C: cheerful on the surface but quietly missing life on land
Option D: jealous of Ellie's success at the swimming carnival

The Family Meeting
In many homes, big decisions are made in the car, in the kitchen or in a hurry. Some families have found a calmer way. Once a week, everyone sits down together for a family meeting.
A family meeting usually lasts about twenty minutes. It often begins with each person sharing one good thing that happened that week. Then the family looks at a list of topics. Anyone can add a topic to the list during the week. Topics might be planning a holiday, sharing the chores or deciding what to cook on Friday night.
Each meeting has a chairperson, and the job is rotated. The chairperson keeps the meeting on track and makes sure only one person talks at a time. Some families pass around a special object, such as a wooden spoon, and only the person holding it may speak.
Experts who study families say these meetings help children feel that their ideas matter. Even the youngest child gets a week in charge, with a little help. Children practise listening, taking turns and finding solutions that are fair to everyone. Parents often discover problems before they grow bigger.
Of course, a family meeting is not a court case. It should never be a time for blaming or telling off. Most families finish with something fun, like a board game or dessert.
Why not try one in your home this week? Twenty minutes is a small price to pay for a happier, more peaceful household.
Question: How long does a family meeting usually last?
Option A: about ten minutes
Option B: about an hour
Option C: a whole evening
Option D: about twenty minutes

Every Kid Needs a Pen Pal
Imagine opening your letterbox and finding an envelope covered in colourful stamps from a country you have never visited. Inside is a letter written just for you. I believe every primary school student should have a pen pal, and here is why.
First, a pen pal teaches you about the world. My pen pal, Hana, lives in a small town in Japan. From her letters I have learnt that her class cleans the school every afternoon and that she eats rice for breakfast. No textbook ever told me things like that.
Second, writing letters makes you a better writer. When you know a real person will read your words, you take more care with spelling and handwriting. My teacher says my writing has improved more this year than ever before.
Third, a pen pal teaches patience. A letter can take two weeks to arrive, and then you must wait again for a reply. In a world where messages fly back and forth in seconds, learning to wait is a useful skill.
Some people say pen pals are old-fashioned and that video calls are faster. That may be true, but a video call disappears when it ends. A letter can be kept in a shoebox and read again years later. I keep all of Hana's letters, and I have reread the first one so many times that the folds have gone soft.
So grab a pen and some paper. Your new best friend could be waiting on the other side of the world.
Question: In the passage, the word 'old-fashioned' means . . .
Option A: belonging to an earlier time
Option B: costing a lot of money
Option C: hard to understand
Option D: made by hand

Up in the Glass Lantern
Dear Grandma,
Today Dad took me to the airport, but we didn't catch a plane. Instead, we climbed to the top of the control tower! Dad's friend Mei is an air traffic controller, and she let us watch her work for an hour.
The tower is tall so the controllers can see the whole airport. The room at the top has windows on every side, and it felt like standing inside a glass lantern. Below us, planes crawled along the taxiways like slow, shiny beetles.
Mei wore a headset and talked to the pilots by radio. She spoke quickly and clearly, using special words. Instead of saying 'B' she said 'Bravo', and instead of 'yes' she said 'affirm'. She explained that radio voices can crackle, so these words stop pilots mixing up letters that sound alike.
Mei's most important job is keeping planes a safe distance apart. Only one plane may use the runway at a time, so she tells each pilot when to wait and when to go. A small symbol on her screen showed where each plane was, and she watched it like a hawk.
At one point a pilot asked to take off early. Mei glanced at a plane landing in the distance and said, 'Negative, hold short.' The pilot waited, and thirty seconds later the other plane touched down right where he would have been.
I used to think pilots were the bosses of the sky. Now I'm not so sure. I've decided I want to work in the tower when I grow up.
Love,
Olivia
Question: Who is Mei?
Option A: an air traffic controller who is Dad's friend
Option B: a pilot who works with Olivia's dad
Option C: a tour guide who shows people the airport
Option D: Olivia's aunt who works at the airport

The Key Whisperer
The front door clicked shut behind me, and my stomach dropped. My keys were sitting on the kitchen bench, exactly where I'd left them. Mum was at work until six, and it was only half past three.
I rang her from Mrs Patel's phone next door. Mum sighed and said she would call a locksmith.
Twenty minutes later, a battered white van pulled up. A tall man with grey whiskers climbed out, carrying a canvas bag. His name badge said 'Walter'. He didn't smile. He just nodded at me and knelt by the door.
I decided he must be grumpy. I sat on the step and waited for him to tell me off for being careless.
Walter took out two thin metal tools, one bent like a tiny hockey stick. He slid them into the keyhole and closed his eyes. His fingers moved so gently it looked as though he was tickling the lock.
'Locks have little pins inside,' he murmured without opening his eyes. 'Each one has to be lifted to just the right height. You can't force them. You have to listen with your fingers.'
After a minute there was a soft click, and the door swung open.

I am a comet, a snowball of dust,
far out where the cold planets roam.
I drift through the dark for a hundred long years,
