my tail drifting after like smoke.
Remember my face, little planet of blue,
and the night that I passed and you woke.

The children who wave at me now will be old
when I come back this way once again,
so tell all their grandchildren, 'Look to the sky!'
for I promise that I'll see them then.

Summer's Loudest Singers
On a hot summer afternoon in Australia, the air can fill with a buzzing so loud that it drowns out conversation. This noise comes from cicadas, insects with clear wings and bulging eyes.
Only male cicadas sing. They make their sound with tymbals - special drum-like parts on the sides of their bodies. Muscles pull the tymbals in and out very quickly, making a clicking noise. The cicada's mostly hollow body works like a speaker and makes the sound much louder. Each kind of cicada has its own song, which helps females find males of the right kind.
A cicada's life begins as a tiny egg laid inside a tree branch. When the young cicada (called a nymph) hatches, it drops to the ground and burrows into the soil. There it feeds on sap from tree roots. Some kinds stay underground for several years.
At last, usually on a warm evening, the nymph digs its way up and climbs a tree trunk. Its back splits open, and the adult slowly pulls itself out. Its crumpled wings unfold and harden. The empty brown shell is left clinging to the bark, where children often find it the next morning.
The adult's life above ground is short: only a few weeks. In that time it must sing, find a mate and lay eggs.
Australian children have given cicadas wonderful nicknames. The Green Grocer is bright green, the Black Prince is dark brown and black, and the Yellow Monday is golden yellow.

Three Cheers for Sea Cucumbers
When people think of amazing ocean animals, they picture dolphins, whales or colourful fish. Hardly anyone thinks of the sea cucumber. This lumpy, slow creature looks like a giant pickle lying on the sea floor. But I believe sea cucumbers are some of the most underrated animals in the ocean, and they deserve our protection.
First, sea cucumbers are the vacuum cleaners of the sea. They creep along, swallowing sand and mud. They digest the tiny scraps of dead plants and animals mixed in with it, then push out clean sand behind them. One sea cucumber can clean many kilograms of sand every year.
Second, they help coral reefs. As they digest their food, sea cucumbers release substances that coral can use to build its hard skeleton. A reef with plenty of sea cucumbers is a healthier reef.
Sadly, in some parts of the world, so many sea cucumbers have been caught and sold as food that they have almost disappeared. When they are gone, the sand around the reef becomes dirty and the coral suffers.

Nell unzipped the tent and crawled out into the cold desert dawn. The red dunes were glowing pink, and the air smelt of dust and saltbush.

'Something that hops,' Nell whispered. 'Something small.'

Most plants are eaten by animals, but a few plants turn the tables. The Venus flytrap is one of them. It catches and digests insects and spiders.
In the wild, Venus flytraps grow in only one small area of the United States, in wet, boggy ground. The soil there is very poor. It does not contain enough nutrients, which are the substances plants need to grow strong. Like other plants, the flytrap makes its food from sunlight, but it gets extra nutrients from its prey.
Each trap is made of two leaf halves joined like a hinge. The edges are lined with stiff bristles, and inside are tiny trigger hairs. When an insect brushes against one hair, nothing happens. But if a second hair is touched within about twenty seconds, the trap snaps shut in less than a second.
Why does the flytrap wait for two touches? Closing takes a lot of energy, and a falling raindrop or a speck of dust might touch a hair by accident. Waiting for a second touch makes it more likely that the trap has caught something alive and moving.
Once the trap is closed, it fills with juices that slowly break down the insect's soft body. This takes about a week. Then the trap opens again, leaving behind only the hard outer shell.
People who grow flytraps are told never to poke the traps just for fun. Each trap can only close a limited number of times before it turns black and dies.

Shearing Time
On many Australian sheep farms, the quiet of the paddocks is broken once a year by the buzz and clatter of the shearing shed.
Shearing often happens in spring, before the hottest weather. A Merino sheep's woolly fleece keeps growing and never falls out by itself. If a sheep went years without being shorn, its fleece would become so heavy and hot that the animal could become sick.
Before shearing begins, the farmer and the dogs muster the sheep into pens beside the shed. If rain is likely, the farmer keeps them under cover the night before. Wet wool cannot be shorn or packed.
Inside, each shearer drags a sheep from the pen and holds it in a sitting position. With electric clippers, the shearer peels the fleece off in one big piece, like taking off a woolly overcoat. A skilled shearer can shear a sheep in about two minutes and may shear more than two hundred sheep in a day.
The shearer is not the only worker. A shed hand, sometimes called a rouseabout, gathers each fleece and throws it onto a slatted table. There, the wool classer checks how fine, long and clean the wool is, and sorts it into groups. The wool is then pressed into huge bales to be sold.
Shearing is hot, hard work. Workers stop for 'smoko', a short break for tea and something to eat. By evening, the pens are full of pale, skinny-looking sheep, and the bales are stacked high.

Before shearing begins, the farmer and the dogs muster the sheep into pens beside the shed. If rain is likely, the farmer keeps them under cover the night before. Wet wool cannot be shorn or packed.
Inside, each shearer drags a sheep from the pen and holds it in a sitting position. With electric clippers, the shearer peels the fleece off in one big piece, like taking off a woolly overcoat. A skilled shearer can shear a sheep in about two minutes and may shear more than two hundred sheep in a day.
The shearer is not the only worker. A shed hand, sometimes called a rouseabout, gathers each fleece and throws it onto a slatted table. There, the wool classer checks how fine, long and clean the wool is, and sorts it into groups. The wool is then pressed into huge bales to be sold.
Shearing is hot, hard work. Workers stop for 'smoko', a short break for tea and something to eat. By evening, the pens are full of pale, skinny-looking sheep, and the bales are stacked high.

The Living Battery
In the muddy rivers of South America lives a fish that can make its own electricity. It is called the electric eel, although it is not a true eel at all. It is actually a kind of knifefish.
An electric eel can grow longer than two metres. Most of its body is packed with thousands of special cells that work like tiny batteries. Each cell makes only a small amount of electricity. But when they all fire together, they can produce a shock of more than 600 volts. That is about fifty times stronger than a car battery!
The eel uses its electricity in different ways. Its rivers are often murky, and its eyesight is poor, so it gives off weak pulses to sense what is around it. When it finds a fish to eat, it switches to strong bursts. The shock makes the prey's muscles twitch and freeze for a moment, and the eel gulps it down.
Because its water contains little oxygen, the electric eel has an unusual habit. Every ten minutes or so, it swims to the surface to gulp air. Most of its oxygen comes from the air it gulps.
Some scientists are studying its cells to help design new kinds of soft batteries. Others simply marvel that a creature living quietly in the mud carries a power station inside its body.
If you ever visit a river in the Amazon, there is no need to panic. Electric eels use shocks to hunt or defend themselves, not to bother swimmers who leave them alone.

Letters Made of Metal
Six hundred years ago in Europe, books were rare treasures. Each one was a manuscript, copied out by hand with pen and ink. Making a single book could take a scribe many months, so only churches, universities and very rich people owned them.
Johannes Gutenberg was born in the German city of Mainz around the year 1400. As a young man, he learnt to work with metal, a skill that would later change the world.
Gutenberg had an idea. What if every letter of the alphabet were made as a separate small block of metal? The blocks could be arranged into words and lines, inked, and pressed onto paper. Afterwards they could be taken apart and used again for a new page. This system is called movable type.
For years, Gutenberg worked in his workshop, testing metals and mixing a sticky ink that would cling to the letters. He built a press based on the machines used to squeeze grapes for wine. He borrowed large sums of money to pay for it all.
Around 1455, his workshop finished printing a Bible. About 180 copies were made, far more than a scribe could copy in a lifetime.
Sadly, Gutenberg did not grow rich. A man who had lent him money took him to court, and he lost much of his workshop. He died in 1468.
But his invention spread like wildfire across Europe. Within fifty years, millions of books had been printed, and reading was no longer only for the wealthy.

Option A: Gutenberg learnt to work with metal.
Option B: Gutenberg printed a Bible.
Option C: Gutenberg was taken to court.
Option D: Gutenberg built his press.

Thimble Forty-Seven
Every Saturday, Lina helped Mrs Okafor at the Wattleby History House. Lina liked things in order. At home, her pencils were lined up by colour and her books by height, so her favourite job was dusting the thimble cabinet. It held one hundred tiny thimbles, each in its own numbered hole in a velvet tray.
This morning, as Lina lifted the glass lid, her heart sank. Hole forty-seven was empty.
Lina knew that thimble well. It was silver, with a band of tiny blue flowers, and it had belonged to the town's first schoolteacher. Mrs Okafor called it the jewel of the collection.
Mrs Okafor had been unwell all week, and Lina did not want to worry her. She decided to search on her own first. She checked under the cabinet. She peered behind the potted fern. Nothing.
Then she remembered the drawer under the tray. It always stuck, and last Saturday Mrs Okafor had slammed it shut with a loud clunk. Lina tugged it open, slid her fingers into the narrow gap at the back, and felt something cool and round.
Out came thimble forty-seven, its blue flowers winking in the light.
'Found it!' Lina cried, just as Mrs Okafor shuffled in with two cups of tea.
Mrs Okafor smiled and pulled a small card from her bag.
'That drawer needs a carpenter,' she said, 'and this cabinet needs a proper keeper.'
The card read: Lina Haddad, Assistant Collections Keeper.

Option A: reached quickly
Option B: looked closely
Option C: walked slowly
Option D: called loudly

Stairs for Fish
Many Australian rivers have weirs. A weir is a low wall built across a river to hold back water for towns and farms. But weirs cause a big problem for fish.
Fish such as golden perch and Murray cod need to move up and down a river during their lives. Some travel hundreds of kilometres to find food or to breed. When a fish swimming upstream meets a weir, the wall blocks its path.
To solve this problem, engineers build fishways. A fishway is like a staircase made of water. It is a channel beside the weir, divided into small pools. Each pool sits a little higher than the one below it.
A fish moving upstream first finds the entrance at the bottom of the fishway. It swims through a narrow gap into the first pool. There, the water is calm, so the fish can rest. Then it pushes through the next gap into the next pool. Pool by pool, it climbs until it reaches the river above the weir.
Engineers shape the pools so that the water inside them moves slowly. If the current were too strong, small fish would tire out and could not finish the climb.
Fishways have been built at many weirs along the Murray River. At some of them, scientists have trapped and counted the fish coming out of the top. They have found many kinds of native fish, including tiny fish only a few centimetres long.
In my opinion, fishways are one of the cleverest ideas ever used to help rivers.

Option A: Fishways are one of the cleverest ideas ever used to help rivers.
Option B: Fishways have been built at many weirs along the Murray River.
Option C: A weir is a low wall built across a river to hold back water.
Option D: Each pool sits a little higher than the one below it.

Five Books of Clever Animals
Long ago in India, a king had a problem. His three sons were lazy and did not want to learn. Teacher after teacher had tried, but the princes refused to study.
According to an old legend, a wise man named Vishnu Sharma promised the king that he could make the princes wise in just six months. Instead of long lessons, he told them stories about animals. The princes were so eager to hear what happened next that they listened closely, and they learnt without even noticing.
These stories became the Panchatantra. The name means 'five books' or 'five lessons'. The tales are more than two thousand years old, and they were first written in Sanskrit, an ancient language of India.
In one famous tale, a monkey shares sweet fruit with a crocodile. But the crocodile's greedy wife wants to eat the monkey's heart. The crocodile slides silently up to the bank, smiling a sly, sneaky smile, and offers the monkey a ride on his back. In the middle of the river, he reveals his plan. Thinking quickly, the monkey says he has left his heart up in his tree. The silly crocodile swims back, and the monkey scrambles safely up the trunk.
Many Panchatantra tales hide stories inside other stories, like boxes inside boxes. Over the centuries, they were translated into dozens of languages. Some fables you know today may have come from these clever old books.

Option A: keen
Option B: bored
Option C: afraid
Option D: sleepy

Sam thought for a moment. 'A bigger tank,' he said, 'so Floss has more room.'

Lunchtime at Hillgrove Primary is loud. Balls thump against walls, whistles blow, and hundreds of voices shout across the playground. Many students love it. But not everyone does, and I believe our school should open a quiet room every lunchtime.
Firstly, some students need a break from noise. A classroom full of chatter can be tiring. A quiet room would give these students a calm place to rest, so they feel ready to learn in the afternoon.
Secondly, a quiet room would give students more choices. If you don't want to play sport or run around, there is very little to do. In a quiet room, students could read, draw, play chess or work on a jigsaw puzzle.

Our school says it wants every student to feel welcome. A quiet room would help make that true for students who like peace as well as those who like noise.
Please vote for the quiet room at the next school council meeting.
Amira, Year 4

Bolt and the Bent Tomato
When Mrs Lin went north to stay
with her sister for a month away,
she asked if I would mind her yard.
'Just water daily. It isn't hard.'

But I had built from tins and wire
a robot, Bolt, who'd never tire.
I gave him code: 'Roll down each row.
Stop every step. Spray low. Then go.'

On Monday Bolt rolled out at eight.
He sprayed each bed and shut the gate.
On Tuesday, Wednesday, just the same,
he sprayed and rolled, and home he came.

I watched him from the kitchen chair
and thought, 'I'm hardly needed there.'
I read my comics, ate my toast,
and bragged to friends about him most.

But by the Friday I could see
one tomato drooping by the tree.
Its leaves were curled, its stem was bent;
it leaned away from where Bolt went.

Bolt sprayed the spot it used to be,
exactly where the code said he
should spray. The plant had moved aside,
so Bolt's spray missed it, though he tried.

He couldn't see; he only knew
the steps I'd told him he should do.
So on the Saturday I knelt
and checked how dry the garden felt.

The soil beneath it, cracked and pale,
was dry as dust. I'd let it fail.
I'd trusted Bolt to do it all;
he wasn't built to see things fall.

I tied the stem up to a stake
and gave it water for its sake,
then wrote a new line in Bolt's code:
'Each evening, wait for Priya's load:

a list of plants that need a look.'
And every night I wrote a book
of notes for Bolt: 'The beans are dry.'
'The basil's sad.' 'The mint is high.'

Bolt reads my list at half past five,
then rolls out, humming, half alive,
and sprays the beans, the basil bed,
the very plants my notes have said.

Now Mrs Lin comes home next week.
The tomato's standing, red of cheek.
Bolt hums along. He's quite a sight,
but I'm the one who checks it's right.
Question: Why did Priya need to look after Mrs Lin's garden?
Option A: Mrs Lin was too busy at work
Option B: Mrs Lin was staying with her sister
Option C: Mrs Lin had moved to a new house
Option D: Mrs Lin wanted to test Priya's robot

Four Legs, One Whistle
On a large sheep station, a farmer may need to move hundreds of sheep from one paddock to another. Doing this alone on foot would take all day. That is why many Australian farmers rely on a partner with four legs: the working dog.
The most famous of these is the Australian kelpie. Kelpies were developed in Australia in the late 1800s from collie-type dogs brought over from Scotland. Farmers wanted a dog that could cope with long distances, rough ground and scorching heat, and the kelpie was the result.
A good kelpie moves sheep by using its body and its eyes. It circles wide around a mob, then crouches low and stares. This steady gaze, which farmers call 'eye', makes the sheep bunch together and walk away from the dog. In crowded yards, a kelpie may even run across the backs of the sheep to reach the front of the mob. Farmers call this 'backing'.
Kelpies are not born knowing all these skills. A young dog, or pup, learns through months of patient training. The farmer uses whistles and short spoken commands. One whistle might mean 'go left', while another means 'stop'. Some farmers say a well-trained dog can do the work of several people on horseback or motorbikes.
However, a working dog is not a machine. It needs rest in the shade, plenty of water and a proper diet, especially in summer. Many farmers say that the bond between dog and handler matters as much as any whistle. A dog that trusts its owner will keep listening even when the sheep are stubborn and the day is long.
So the next time you see a kelpie riding on the back of a farm ute, remember that it is not just a pet along for the ride. It is a skilled worker, and one of the most important members of the team.

Flash, Then Boom
The power went out at Grandpa's house just after dinner. One moment the kitchen was bright and the radio was playing; the next, everything was black and silent. Then the window flashed white, and Leo grabbed Mia's arm.
'It's only lightning,' Mia said, though her own heart was thumping.
Grandpa struck a match and lit the old lantern he kept on top of the fridge. Its yellow glow made their shadows stretch up the walls like giants. A long, low rumble rolled across the roof.
'Want to know a trick?' Grandpa asked, sitting down beside them. 'Next time you see a flash, start counting slowly. Stop when you hear the thunder.'
The window lit up again. 'One, two, three,' they counted together, and then a boom shook the glass.
'Light travels much faster than sound,' Grandpa explained. 'You see the flash almost straight away, but the sound takes about three seconds to cover each kilometre. So three seconds means the storm is roughly one kilometre away.'
Leo stared at him, thunderstruck. Then a slow grin spread across his face. 'So we can measure it? Without even going outside?'
'Exactly,' said Grandpa.
For the next half hour, Leo would not stop counting. At first the numbers stayed small, and he squeezed Mia's hand at every crash. Then something changed. This time Mia reached nine before the rumble came, and it sounded softer, like furniture being dragged in a faraway room.
'Nine seconds,' Leo whispered. 'That's three kilometres.'
The rain eased to a gentle patter. The next count reached twelve. Leo yawned so widely that his jaw clicked.
'Grandpa,' he mumbled, curling up on the couch, 'wake me up if the numbers get small again.'
Grandpa tucked a blanket around him and winked at Mia over the lantern's flickering flame.

Option A: a torch from a drawer
Option B: a row of candles
Option C: the light on his phone
Option D: an old lantern

Leave Only Footprints? Not Even Those
Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent on Earth. For millions of years, it had no human visitors at all. Today, more than one hundred thousand tourists travel there in a single summer season. I believe that we must limit how many people visit, before it is too late.
Some people say that tourists do no harm because they only stay for a few hours. However, even a short visit leaves a mark. Antarctic mosses grow incredibly slowly, sometimes less than a centimetre in a whole year. A single careless step can crush plants that took decades to grow.
There is a hidden danger too. Scientists have found seeds from other continents stuck to visitors' clothing, bags and boots. If those seeds take root, they could spread and crowd out the few plants that belong there.
To be fair, tour companies already have rules. Before going ashore, visitors must vacuum their pockets and scrub their boots. Once on land, they are told to stay at least five metres from penguins and seals. After returning to the ship, they scrub their boots again. These rules help, but rules cannot fix the problem of sheer numbers. A hundred careful visitors still make a hundred sets of footprints.
You might think that one more visitor cannot make a difference. But every visitor thinks the same thing. That is exactly how small harms add up to large ones.
I am not saying that no one should ever see Antarctica. I am saying that we should share it wisely. Fewer landings, smaller groups and strict yearly limits would let people experience this wild place while protecting it for the wildlife that depends on it.
Antarctica has looked after itself for millions of years. Now it is our turn to look after it.

Option A: about five centimetres
Option B: nearly a metre
Option C: several metres
Option D: less than a centimetre

What We Didn't Bring
The first night out, I made a list
of everything I knew I'd missed:
no screen, no fridge, no bedroom light,
no pillow plumped up soft and right.

Dad pitched the tent beside the creek.
The poles were bent; the zip would squeak.
Mum lit the stove. The billy steamed.
I sat apart from them and dreamed

of home, where taps ran hot on cue
and no one ever asked me to
'Go fetch the water from the creek'
or 'Find some sticks that aren't too weak.'

But dusk crept in, a purple hush,
and something rustled in the brush.
A possum peered from up a gum,
then scampered off to find a crumb.

The fire popped. The stars came out,
so many that I had no doubt
someone had spilt them, pale and wide,
like sugar flung from side to side.

Mum showed me how the Southern Cross
could point the way if we were lost,
and Dad, who never sings at all,
hummed softly as the dew would fall.

I fell asleep to frogs and wind,
the fire low, the lantern dimmed,
and woke to magpies, sharp and clear,
announcing that the day was here.

For breakfast, damper on the coals,
a little burnt, with blackened holes,
but drizzled thick with syrup gold,
it beat my toast at home, all told.

I fetched the water. No one asked.
I gathered sticks. I liked the task.
I raced Dad down the bank to see
who'd skip a stone the furthest. Me!

That afternoon, a shower came.
We huddled close and played a game
of I-spy in the dripping tent
and laughed until the rain was spent.

The second night, I made a list
of everything I would have missed:
the possum's eyes, the creek's low sound,
the sugar stars spilt all around,

the smoky air, the magpies' tune,
the stone that skipped six times at noon.
Then I turned back to that first list
and crossed out all the things I'd missed.

Option A: under a gum tree
Option B: at the top of a hill
Option C: next to the car
Option D: beside the creek

Annie and the Bicycle Bet
In June 1894, a young woman wheeled a heavy bicycle out of Boston, in the United States, while a crowd cheered. Her name was Annie Kopchovsky, and she announced that she was going to ride around the world.
Annie was hardly a keen cyclist. In fact, she had barely ridden a bicycle before. According to the story she liked to tell, two wealthy men had bet each other that no woman could cycle around the world in fifteen months. Annie was happy to prove them wrong. She also needed money, because she had a husband and three young children at home.
Before she set off, a spring-water company called Londonderry paid her one hundred dollars to carry its sign on her bicycle. Annie went one step further and called herself 'Annie Londonderry' for the whole trip. Along the way, she sold space on her bike and clothes to other businesses, and she charged people to hear her give talks.
Her first bicycle weighed about 19 kilograms, and Annie rode it in a long skirt. By the time she reached Chicago, she had swapped it for a much lighter man's bike and changed into loose trousers called bloomers. Both changes made riding far easier.
After cycling across France, Annie sailed on to Asia, stopping at ports such as Colombo, Singapore and Hong Kong. However, she did not pedal every kilometre. She crossed the oceans by steamship and sometimes rode on trains. Her talks were full of thrilling tales of danger and narrow escapes, and some of them were probably made up.
In September 1895, Annie rolled into Chicago, fifteen months after leaving Boston. One newspaper called her trip the most extraordinary journey ever made by a woman. Whether or not she rode every road, Annie showed the world that a woman on a bicycle could go almost anywhere.

Oonagh and the Giant Baby
Long ago, on the northern coast of Ireland, there lived a giant named Finn McCool. Finn was strong and good-natured, but he had a habit of shouting insults across the sea at a giant in Scotland called Benandonner. One day, to settle their quarrel, Finn tore great columns of rock from the cliffs and hammered them into the seabed, building a stone road all the way to Scotland.
But when Finn strode along his causeway and caught sight of Benandonner, his knees began to wobble. The Scottish giant was enormous, as tall as a mountain, with fists like boulders. Finn turned and ran home as fast as his legs could carry him.
'Oonagh!' he panted to his wife. 'He's coming, and he's twice my size!'
Oonagh did not panic. She was known across the land for her quick thinking. She dressed Finn in a nightgown and a frilly bonnet, then squeezed him into an enormous cradle by the fire. Next, she baked a batch of griddle cakes, hiding a flat iron pan inside every one except one.
Soon the ground shook. Benandonner's footsteps boomed like thunder rolling down a valley, and his shadow swallowed the whole cottage.
'Where is Finn McCool?' he roared.
'Out hunting,' said Oonagh sweetly. 'Do sit down and have a griddle cake while you wait.'
Benandonner bit into a cake and howled. Two of his teeth had cracked on the iron. 'Goodness,' said Oonagh, 'Finn eats those every morning. Even the baby can manage them.' She handed the one plain cake to Finn, who gobbled it happily.
Benandonner peered into the cradle at the huge baby and turned pale. If Finn's baby was this big, how gigantic must Finn himself be?
Without a word, the Scottish giant fled back across the causeway, ripping up the stones behind him so that Finn could never follow. Only the ends remain today, one on each coast, still standing where the giants left them.
Question: What did Finn build to reach Scotland?
Option A: a stone road across the sea
Option B: a wooden bridge over a river
Option C: a stone wall along the cliffs
Option D: a large boat made of rock

The Bird Behind the Mud Wall
In the forests of Asia and Africa lives a bird with one of the strangest nesting habits on Earth. Hornbills are large birds with huge curved beaks, and many species have a hollow helmet called a casque on top. But it is what happens inside their nests that truly amazes scientists.
When it is time to lay her eggs, a female hornbill chooses a hollow in a tall tree. She climbs inside, and then she does something remarkable: she seals herself in. Using mud, chewed fruit and her own droppings, she plasters the entrance until only a narrow slit remains. In some species, her mate brings mud to help.
For the next few weeks, sometimes for several months, the female stays shut inside. In many species she sheds her flight feathers while she is there. She lays her eggs, keeps them warm and cares for the chicks when they hatch.
The wall works like a fortress. Snakes, monkeys and other hungry animals cannot reach the eggs through such a tiny gap. But it also means the female depends completely on her partner.
The male's task is exhausting. Day after day, he flies back and forth through the forest, collecting fruit, insects and small animals. He swallows the food, carries it to the nest, then brings it back up and passes it, piece by piece, through the slit to the female's waiting beak. A male may make dozens of trips in a single day. If something happened to him, his family would be in serious trouble.
When the chicks are larger and the nest is crowded, the female breaks out through the wall. In some species, the chicks then rebuild the seal by themselves and stay safely inside until they are ready to fly.
Sadly, many hornbills are now threatened because the giant trees they need are being cut down. Without old trees with big hollows, there is nowhere to build these remarkable mud-walled nurseries.

Lunch Run
On the first Monday of the holidays, Leo's grandmother handed him a cooler bag. 'You're my offsider today,' Nonna said. 'Twelve lunches, twelve doors. Don't drop the custard.'
Leo had hoped to spend the morning on his tablet. Instead, he sat in Nonna's little hatchback with a list of names on his knee while she drove from street to street. Nonna had volunteered for Meals on Wheels for nine years, delivering hot meals to older people who found it hard to cook for themselves.
At the first house, Mr Abara opened the door before they even knocked. He wanted to know the cricket score. At the third, Mrs Lindqvist showed Leo a photo of her new great-grandson. At the fifth, a lady with a walking frame asked Nonna to read a letter because her glasses had broken. Nonna read it twice, slowly.
'We're behind schedule,' Leo whispered.
'The meals are only half the job,' Nonna whispered back.
The eighth name on the list was Mr Doyle. Nonna frowned as they pulled up. 'His blind is still down,' she said. 'He always has it up by eight.'
She knocked. No answer. She knocked again and called his name. At last, they heard a faint voice from inside. Mr Doyle had slipped in the hallway and couldn't get up. Nonna phoned for an ambulance, then opened the key safe beside the door. Leo sat on the floor with Mr Doyle and held his hand until the paramedics came. The old man's hand was cold and trembling, so Leo kept talking about anything he could think of, even the cricket.
Later, back in the car, Leo was quiet for a long time. He looked down at the list on his knee. Four names still had no ticks beside them.
'Nonna,' he said finally, 'can I come again on Thursday?'
Nonna smiled and started the engine. 'Grab the next bag,' she said. 'Mrs Nguyen likes a chat.'

Option B: A boy and his grandmother race to finish their deliveries before lunch.
Option C: An old man teaches a boy about cricket while they wait for help.
Option D: A grandmother teaches her grandson how to cook meals for neighbours.

Joanne Simpson and the Hot Towers
Joanne Simpson was born in Boston, in the United States, in 1923. From an early age she was curious about the sky. Why did some clouds stay small and fluffy, while others swelled into towering storms? Years later, she would become one of the world's leading experts on exactly that question.
During the Second World War, Joanne studied weather at the University of Chicago so that she could teach it to the people forecasting for pilots, who needed to understand the skies they flew through. She was fascinated, and after the war she decided to keep studying. Her professors were not encouraging. Clouds, many of them said, were too messy and unpredictable to study seriously, and women did not belong in the field. One professor is said to have told her that no woman had ever earned a doctorate in meteorology and none ever would.
Joanne refused to be put off. In 1949, she became the first woman in the United States to earn a doctorate in meteorology. Even then, finding work was a struggle.
Her greatest idea came from studying clouds over warm tropical oceans. Working with another scientist, Herbert Riehl, she showed that giant thunderclouds act like chimneys, carrying heat from the ocean high into the sky. These 'hot towers', as they called them, help drive the winds that move warm air around the planet. Later research showed that hot towers can also help to power hurricanes.
At the American space agency NASA, Joanne led the science team for a satellite that measured rainfall across the tropics from space. It was launched in 1997 and sent back information for seventeen years.
Joanne Simpson died in 2010, having opened a door that had once been firmly shut. Today, many women study the weather, and the clouds that once puzzled a curious girl are far better understood.

Windows into the Wild
Walk into many natural history museums and you will find glass cases that seem to open onto another world: a misty rainforest, a snowy mountain slope or a billabong at sunset. These scenes are called dioramas. Although each one looks like a window, it is really a clever illusion built by a team of artists and scientists.
Creating a diorama usually happens in several stages.
First, the team studies the real place. Artists visit the location, take photographs, make sketches and collect samples of soil, leaves and rocks. Scientists check which animals and plants really belong together, and at what time of year.
Next, a painter creates the background on a curved wall at the back of the case. Because the wall curves, there are no corners to give the trick away. Distant hills and sky are painted in soft, pale colours, since faraway things look hazy to our eyes.
Then the foreground is built. This is the part closest to the glass. It holds real or carefully copied rocks, logs and soil, along with model leaves made one by one from wax, paper or plastic. Some dioramas contain thousands of handmade leaves.
The hardest job is joining the two parts. Where the real ground meets the painted wall, the colours and shapes must match exactly. If they do, visitors cannot tell where the solid ground ends and the painting begins.
Finally, preserved animals or lifelike models are put in place, and the lighting is set. Lights hidden above the case can make a scene look like early morning or late afternoon.
Some visitors today prefer screens and touch displays, and a few museums have removed their older dioramas. Yet many people still stand at the glass for minutes at a time. A good diorama lets you see an animal in its home, all in a single glance, in a way that a label or a photograph never could.

Option A: so the lights can be hidden behind it
Option B: so more animals can fit inside the case
Option C: so there are no corners to give the trick away
Option D: so visitors can see it from both sides

In 1826, in a stone house on the edge of the wild Yorkshire moors in England, four children received a present that would change their lives. Their father brought home a box of twelve wooden toy soldiers for Branwell, the only boy. Before long, his sisters Charlotte, Emily and Anne had each claimed a soldier of their own.
The Bronte children had already known sadness. Their mother had died when they were very young, and two older sisters had died too. Their aunt had moved in to help run the household, but the children spent many hours entertaining themselves. They had few friends nearby, so they turned to each other.

The Gap in the Arch
All through the winter of 1930, Molly Fraser walked to the end of her street in North Sydney every afternoon to look at the bridge. For years it had been growing out from both sides of the harbour, two great steel arms reaching towards each other across the water. Each day the gap between them looked a little smaller.
Molly's father was a rigger on the bridge. He left before dawn and came home with grease on his hands and stories in his head. He told her about the creeper cranes that crawled along the top of each half-arch, lifting steel into place. He told her about the riveting gangs, too: one worker heated the rivets in a little furnace until they glowed, then tossed them through the air to a catcher who snatched them in a metal cup.
'What stops the two halves from falling into the harbour?' Molly asked one night.
'Cables,' said Dad. 'Huge steel cables anchored in tunnels in the rock. They hold each half back, like a hand on a dog's collar.'
In August, the workers began to let the cables out, slowly, a little each day. The two half-arches tilted forward, inch by careful inch. Half of Sydney seemed to be watching.
Then, late on the night of the nineteenth, the two halves touched. Molly heard the news from a neighbour running down the street, shouting. The next morning she raced to the corner. The ragged gap had gone. Instead, one enormous arch curved across the sky, steel grey against the blue, as if it had always been there.
That evening, Dad came home tired but smiling. Molly could hear the ships in the harbour hooting, and the clatter, clang and rattle of the riveters still working in the distance.
'Is it finished?' she asked.
'Not yet,' said Dad, ruffling her hair. 'But the hardest part is done. Now they can hang the road.'

Option A: He was a crane driver.
Option B: He was a rivet catcher.
Option C: He was a rigger.
Option D: He was a ship's captain.

The Snail Who Bought a Clock
In a garden where the pumpkins grew as large as houses, there lived a snail named Pell. Every morning the other creatures hurried past him. The ants marched, the beetles bustled and the bees zipped from flower to flower. 'Slow old Pell,' they laughed. 'By the time you get anywhere, the day is over!'
Pell pretended not to mind, but each time they laughed, he tucked himself a little further into his shell.
One day a magpie named Glint landed on the garden wall with a cart full of shiny objects. 'Clocks!' she called. 'Magic clocks! Wind one up, and time itself will speed along for you.'
Pell's eyes stretched out on their stalks. 'Would I be fast, then?'
'Faster than you can imagine,' said Glint. 'It costs only your finest possession.'
Now, Pell's finest possession was a dewdrop he had kept on a leaf all summer. It sparkled like a tiny moon. He had been saving it to give to the night-blooming flower at the end of the garden, which opened only once a year. Still, he handed it to Glint, took a clock and wound it tight.
The hands spun wildly. Pell stared at them, waiting to feel fast. He stared all morning and all afternoon. He did not see the ants pass by, or the bees, or the evening shadows creeping across the lawn. He only watched the clock.
When the moon rose, Pell finally looked up. At the end of the garden, the flower was closing its petals. It had bloomed and faded while he stared at the spinning hands.
Pell wept. The clock had not made him faster. It had only made him forget to look.
The next morning, the ants laughed again. This time, Pell simply smiled and kept moving, slowly, with his eyes open to everything along the way.
And high on the garden wall, a magpie admired the newest jewel in her nest.

The ants marched, the beetles bustled and the bees zipped from flower to flower. 'Slow old Pell,' they laughed. 'By the time you get anywhere, the day is over!'
Pell pretended not to mind, but each time they laughed, he tucked himself a little further into his shell.
One day a magpie named Glint landed on the garden wall with a cart full of shiny objects. 'Clocks!' she called. 'Magic clocks! Wind one up, and time itself will speed along for you.'
Pell's eyes stretched out on their stalks. 'Would I be fast, then?'
'Faster than you can imagine,' said Glint. 'It costs only your finest possession.'
Now, Pell's finest possession was a dewdrop he had kept on a leaf all summer. It sparkled like a tiny moon. He had been saving it to give to the night-blooming flower at the end of the garden, which opened only once a year. Still, he handed it to Glint, took a clock and wound it tight.
The hands spun wildly. Pell stared at them, waiting to feel fast. He stared all morning and all afternoon. He did not see the ants pass by, or the bees, or the evening shadows creeping across the lawn. He only watched the clock.
When the moon rose, Pell finally looked up. At the end of the garden, the flower was closing its petals. It had bloomed and faded while he stared at the spinning hands.
Pell wept. The clock had not made him faster. It had only made him forget to look.
The next morning, the ants laughed again. This time, Pell simply smiled and kept moving, slowly, with his eyes open to everything along the way.
And high on the garden wall, a magpie admired the newest jewel in her nest.

Option B: Being laughed at hurt so much that becoming fast mattered more to him.
Option C: He thought the magpie needed the dewdrop more than he did.
Option D: He wanted to beat the ants in a race across the garden.

Wednesday, 9 April

You know how I always said Mum's job sounded boring? Well, I take it back. Yesterday she took me to work with her at the airport, and it was the best day of the holidays so far.

Although my feet ached by the end, I didn't want to leave. Mum says I'm a chip off the old block, because I asked about a hundred questions.

The Unsung Hero in Your Mouth
Most people never give it a second thought, and some think it is a bit disgusting. Yet saliva, or spit, is one of the hardest-working liquids in the human body. Without it, eating a single biscuit would be a dry, difficult and tasteless job.
Saliva is made by small organs called salivary glands. You have three main pairs: one in front of each ear, one under the jaw and one under the tongue. Together they produce between half a litre and one and a half litres of saliva every day.
Saliva's first job is to make food soft and slippery. As you chew, it mixes with each mouthful and turns it into a soft lump that slides easily down your throat. Saliva also starts digestion before food even reaches your stomach. It contains a chemical that begins breaking down starch, the main ingredient in bread, rice and pasta. If you chew a plain cracker for a long time, it starts to taste slightly sweet, because some of the starch has been turned into sugar.
Saliva helps you taste, too. Your taste buds can only detect flavours that have dissolved in liquid. If you dab your tongue dry with a tissue and place a few grains of sugar on it, you will hardly taste them until saliva washes back in.
Saliva also protects your teeth. It rinses away scraps of food and weakens the acids that cause tooth decay. That is one reason a dry mouth, which can happen when people are nervous or unwell, is bad news for teeth.
Your body even makes saliva before you take a bite. Just smelling a sizzling sausage or thinking about a juicy lemon can make your mouth water, as your glands get ready for the meal they expect is coming.
So next time you lick your lips, spare a thought for the small but mighty liquid that makes every meal possible.

Option B: about three litres
Option C: enough to fill a bucket
Option D: between half a litre and one and a half litres

The Messiest Hour on Earth
Imagine twenty thousand people packed shoulder to shoulder in a narrow street, all wearing old white T-shirts and swimming goggles. Suddenly a signal sounds, trucks rumble in, and the air fills with flying tomatoes. This is La Tomatina, held every August in the small Spanish town of Buñol, and I believe everyone should experience it at least once.
Some people say the festival is a terrible waste of food. However, the tomatoes used are not the kind you would ever find in a salad. They are grown cheaply especially for the event and are too sour and soft to sell in shops. In other words, they would never have reached anyone's dinner plate anyway.
Others worry that the festival is dangerous. In fact, it has clear rules that keep everyone safe. Every tomato must be squashed in your hand before you throw it, so it lands with a harmless splat rather than a thud. You must not tear anyone's clothes, and you must step aside when the trucks come through. Best of all, the throwing lasts for exactly one hour. When a second signal sounds, everybody stops.
What happens next is the most surprising part. Fire trucks hose down the streets, and because tomatoes are slightly acidic, many say the cobblestones end up cleaner than they were before the festival began. Local people even open their gardens so visitors can rinse off under garden hoses. Where else could a food fight leave a town sparkling?
La Tomatina is not about winning or losing. Nobody keeps score, and strangers from dozens of countries end up laughing together, dripping in red pulp. Since 2013 the town has sold a limited number of tickets, so if you want to join in, you will need to plan ahead. Pack clothes you never want to see again, and get ready for the juiciest hour of your life.

Option B: in a small fishing town in Mexico
Option C: in the small town of Buñol in Spain

The Same Shape Twice
Lena's art teacher had asked the class to draw 'a pattern found in nature', and by Saturday morning Lena still had a blank page. Half the class had already done zebra stripes. Spider webs were too fiddly.
'Come up Tawny Hill with me,' said Grandpa, lacing his boots. 'Patterns are easier to find when you stop looking so hard.'
The track was steep and dusty. Halfway up, Lena picked up a fallen gum leaf. A pale line ran down its middle, and thinner lines branched off it, then split again and again until they were as fine as hairs. She tucked it into her sketchbook without thinking much about it.
At the top, they sat on a flat rock. Far below, the creek wound across the flats towards the sea. Near the coast it split into two channels, then four, then a dozen silver threads that spread out like the fingers of a hand dipping into the water.
Lena frowned. Something about it tickled her memory. She opened her sketchbook, and the gum leaf slid out onto the rock. She held it up against the view. The thick middle vein, the branches, the tiny threads at the edges: the creek was drawing the very same shape across the land.
'Grandpa,' she whispered, 'the river copied the leaf.'
Grandpa chuckled. 'Or the leaf copied the river. Look behind you.'
Lena turned. A dead tree stood at the edge of the hilltop, its bare branches black against the sky. Trunk, branches, twigs, smaller twigs. The same shape again, this time reaching up instead of out.
All the way home, Lena kept finding it. In the cracks of a dried-up puddle. In the blue veins on the back of Grandpa's wrist. That night a summer storm rolled in, and as lightning forked across the clouds, she pressed her nose to the window and laughed out loud.
On Monday, Lena handed in a page divided into five boxes: a leaf, a river, a tree, a wrist and a flash of lightning. Underneath, in her neatest writing, was one word: Branches.

Option A: She picked it up from the dusty track.
Option B: She turned around to look at the dead tree.
Option C: She tucked it back into her sketchbook.
Option D: She held it up against the view.

Comics Count Too
Every afternoon at our school, there is twenty minutes of silent reading time. It is a great idea, except for one rule: comics and graphic novels are not allowed. I believe this rule should be dropped, and here is why.
First, reading a comic is real reading. A graphic novel has characters, a setting, a problem and a solution, just like any other story. Many contain words such as 'treacherous' and 'catastrophe' that readers might never meet in a simple chapter book. The pictures do not do the work for you, either. Readers must link what they see with what they read, noticing a worried face or a shadow in a corner that the words never mention. That is a skill, not a shortcut.
Second, comics can turn reluctant readers into keen ones. My friend Sam used to stare at the same page for the whole twenty minutes. Then his aunt gave him a graphic novel about a lighthouse keeper's daughter. He finished it in two days and went straight to the library to borrow the next one in the series. Now he reads chapter books as well. Surely a book that can do that deserves a place in our classroom.
Some teachers argue that comics are too easy. Yet many graphic novels have won major book awards, and our own school library has a whole shelf of them. It seems strange to buy books for the library and then ban them from reading time.
Finally, silent reading should be enjoyable. If students can choose stories they love, they will look forward to reading time instead of watching the clock. A good read is a good read, with or without pictures.
I am not asking for chapter books to be thrown out. I am simply asking for comics to be given a fair go. Please let us bring them back to silent reading time.
Question: How long is silent reading time at the writer's school?
Option A: ten minutes
Option B: twenty minutes
Option C: half an hour
Option D: a whole lesson

First, reading a comic is real reading. A graphic novel has characters, a setting, a problem and a solution, just like any other story. Many contain words such as 'treacherous' and 'catastrophe' that readers might never meet in a simple chapter book. The pictures do not do the work for you, either. Readers must link what they see with what they read, noticing a worried face or a shadow in a corner that the words never mention. That is a skill, not a shortcut.
Second, comics can turn reluctant readers into keen ones. My friend Sam used to stare at the same page for the whole twenty minutes. Then his aunt gave him a graphic novel about a lighthouse keeper's daughter. He finished it in two days and went straight to the library to borrow the next one in the series. Now he reads chapter books as well. Surely a book that can do that deserves a place in our classroom.
Some teachers argue that comics are too easy. Yet many graphic novels have won major book awards, and our own school library has a whole shelf of them. It seems strange to buy books for the library and then ban them from reading time.
Finally, silent reading should be enjoyable. If students can choose stories they love, they will look forward to reading time instead of watching the clock. A good read is a good read, with or without pictures.
I am not asking for chapter books to be thrown out. I am simply asking for comics to be given a fair go. Please let us bring them back to silent reading time.

Option B: reasonable, as if the request is only a small one

The Smiling Salamander
With its wide, wobbly grin and feathery frills, the axolotl (say 'ax-oh-lot-ul') looks more like a cartoon character than a real animal. Yet these unusual creatures have become popular pets in Australian homes. Before you rush out to buy one, it helps to know what makes them special and what they need.
An axolotl is a type of salamander, which is a kind of amphibian. Most amphibians, such as frogs, begin life in water and then change so they can live on land. The axolotl never makes this change. It keeps its gills, the pink, feathery frills on each side of its head, for its whole life and stays underwater. In the wild, axolotls are found only in a few lakes and canals near Mexico City, where they are now endangered. Pet axolotls are bred in captivity.
Axolotls are also famous for an amazing ability. If one loses a leg, a toe or even part of its tail, it can grow the missing part back. Scientists study axolotls to learn how this works.
Looking after an axolotl takes care. They need a large tank of clean, cool water, ideally between 16 and 18 degrees Celsius. Warm water stresses them, so many owners in hot parts of Australia use a fan or a water chiller in summer. The bottom of the tank should be bare or covered with fine sand, because axolotls gulp their food and may swallow gravel by accident. They eat worms, small pieces of fish and special pellets.
Axolotls have soft, delicate skin and should not be handled. They are best enjoyed by watching. Many owners say their axolotls seem to recognise them, swimming to the front of the tank at feeding time.
With the right care, an axolotl can live for ten to fifteen years. That is a long time, so anyone thinking of getting one should be ready for a slow, steady, splash-free friendship.

Kettles Under Iceland
Beneath the snow the rocks are hot,
They warm the earth like a cooking pot.
The steam comes up, the turbines turn,
And not a scrap of coal we burn.
Iceland is a small island country near the Arctic Circle, famous for glaciers, long winters and dark skies. It is also one of the best places in the world to make electricity from the heat inside the Earth. This kind of energy is called geothermal energy. The word comes from two Greek words: 'geo', meaning earth, and 'therme', meaning heat.
Deep underground, the Earth is extremely hot. In most places this heat lies many kilometres below the surface, far out of reach. Iceland, however, sits on a crack between two huge plates of the Earth's crust, where hot rock is much closer to the surface. Rainwater and melted snow trickle down through the ground, are heated by the rock and sometimes burst out as steaming hot springs and geysers.
To make electricity, engineers drill wells up to two kilometres deep. Steam and hot water rush up the pipes and are used to spin turbines. The turbines are connected to generators, which turn the spinning movement into electricity. After the heat has been used, much of the water is pumped back underground so it can be heated again.
About a quarter of Iceland's electricity comes from geothermal power stations, and almost all of the rest comes from rivers flowing through hydro-electric stations. Hot water is also piped straight into homes. Around nine out of ten houses are heated this way, and some towns even run hot pipes under footpaths so snow melts without anyone needing a shovel.
Geothermal energy does not run out the way coal does, and it causes very little pollution. Still, it cannot be used easily everywhere. Iceland is lucky to have its giant kettle so close to the surface.

Option A: earth and heat
Option B: rock and steam
Option C: water and fire
Option D: ground and power

Ten Minutes Before Maths
A report by the Year 5 Student Council, Kurrajong Primary School
Purpose
In Term 2, the Student Council suggested a ten-minute fitness break before maths each morning. We believed that moving our bodies would help students concentrate. The principal agreed to a four-week trial in the three Year 5 classes. This report describes what happened.
What we did
Each morning at 9.50, classes went to the basketball court. Student leaders took turns running the session, which included star jumps, skipping, a short jog and a stretching cool-down. On wet days, classes did seated stretches inside instead.
What we found
At the end of the trial, we surveyed all 72 Year 5 students. Fifty-one said they enjoyed the breaks, twelve said they did not mind them, and nine said they would rather stay inside. Teachers noticed that students settled into maths more quickly on most days.
Many students wrote comments. 'I used to feel sleepy by the time maths started, but now I'm wide awake and ready to go,' wrote Priya from 5B. Jonah from 5C wrote, 'The jog made me so puffed that my hand shook when I tried to write.'
We also noticed some problems. On cold mornings, frost glittered on the court and the icy air nipped at our fingers, so some students were slow to warm up. The trial also took ten minutes from each maths lesson, and one teacher said her class did not finish its work on two days.
Recommendation
The Student Council strongly recommends that the fitness break continue for all classes from Year 3 to Year 6. We believe the benefits clearly outweigh the small problems. On very cold days, we suggest moving the break into the hall.
Question: Which piece of evidence shows that most students enjoyed the fitness breaks?
Option A: Nine students said they would rather stay inside.
Option B: Student leaders took turns running the sessions.
Option C: Fifty-one of the 72 students said they enjoyed them.
Option D: Classes did seated stretches inside on wet days.

Riddles in the Letterbox
The first envelope arrived on a Monday. It was small and pale blue, with Theo's name written across the front in curly, old-fashioned letters. There was no stamp and no return address. Inside was a single card.
I have keys but open no locks. I have space but no room. What am I?
Theo stared at it all through breakfast. Then, halfway through brushing his teeth, he gasped. 'A keyboard!' he spluttered, spraying toothpaste across the mirror.
The next morning, another blue envelope was waiting. This riddle was harder, and it took Theo until lunchtime. By the end of the week he had solved five and pinned every card to the wall above his desk.
'Who's sending them?' he asked his mum.

He also noticed a faint smell of lavender on the paper. The only lavender bushes in the street grew in front of number 14, where old Mrs Abara lived on her own. Since she had retired and her family had moved interstate, Theo had hardly seen her outside.
On Saturday, Theo wrote his own riddle, slipped it into an envelope and pushed it under the door of number 14. What gets bigger the more you take away?

'I do,' said Theo, and he pulled out a notebook full of new ones.

Option B: plain white
Option C: pale blue
Option D: bright yellow

On the Tip of My Tongue
A quiz kid called Lachlan McRae
Knew the answer but just couldn't say.
It was there on his tongue,
Like a bell left unrung,
And it came to him later that day.
You know the feeling. You are trying to remember the name of a film, a song or the kid who sat next to you in Year 2. You might even know that it starts with 'M' or has three syllables, but the word itself refuses to come out. Scientists have a name for this everyday mishap. They call it a tip-of-the-tongue moment.
In 1966, two researchers at Harvard University decided to study it. They read out dictionary definitions of rare words, such as 'sampan', and asked students to name each word. Many students got stuck partway. Often they could guess the first letter, or they came up with words that sounded similar, like 'Siam' and 'sarong'. This showed that the brain had found part of the word, but not all of it.
Since then, studies have found that most people have a tip-of-the-tongue moment about once a week. These moments become more common as people get older, and they happen most often with names.
So what should you do when a word gets stuck? Strangely, trying harder can make things worse, because your brain keeps landing on the wrong word. Many experts suggest thinking about something else. The missing word often pops up on its own, sometimes hours later, usually at a moment when it is no help at all.
My uncle Dev learned this the hard way. At a trivia night, his team needed one last answer: the name of the longest river in Australia. Dev was sure he knew it. He scrunched up his face, drummed on the table and muttered 'Mur... Mur...' until the time ran out. His team lost by one point. Halfway home in the car, he suddenly shouted 'The Murray!' so loudly that Aunty Mel nearly dropped her phone. He still blames the trivia host.
Question: Which words best describe the tone of the text?
Option A: serious and worried
Option B: light-hearted and informative
Option C: angry and complaining
Option D: sad and thoughtful

The Staircase That Changes Its Mind
On her first morning in Hong Kong, Ruby stood at the bottom of a street so steep it seemed to lean against the sky. Her cousin Wing lived somewhere near the top.
'We have to climb that?' she groaned.
'Nobody climbs it,' said Wing. 'We ride it.'
He led her to a covered escalator that rose from the street and disappeared between tall buildings. Wing explained that it was not one escalator but a chain of about twenty, stretching around 800 metres up the hillside.
There was just one problem. It was moving down.
A river of office workers in neat shirts glided towards them, sipping coffee and checking phones. 'In the morning, everyone is heading down to work,' Wing said, 'so the escalator runs downhill until ten o'clock. Then it changes direction.'
Ruby checked her watch. It was twenty to ten. 'Let's just walk,' she said.
Wing shook his head. 'Why would you climb a mountain when, in twenty minutes, the mountain will carry you? Besides, the best egg tarts in the city are right here.'
So they waited, eating warm, wobbly tarts from a paper bag. At exactly ten o'clock, the escalator slowed and stopped. A worker turned a key, and with a soft hum the steps began rolling the other way.
The ride up was like flicking through a picture book. Ruby glided past a tiny shop selling dried mushrooms, a balcony hung with washing, a cafe where an old man was reading the newspaper and a window full of steaming dumplings. Each time she wanted to look more closely, the escalator smoothly carried her away.
That night, Ruby asked Wing a question that surprised him.
'Can we get up early tomorrow and walk down the steps beside the escalator?'
'Walk? Why?'
Ruby grinned. 'I want to buy some of those dumplings. And I'd like to see if that old man ever finishes his newspaper.'
Question: The writer's main purpose in this text is to
Option A: entertain readers with a story about an unusual escalator
Option B: persuade readers to move to the city of Hong Kong
Option C: explain to readers how escalators are built and repaired
Option D: instruct readers on how to bake their own egg tarts

The Light at Cape Morrow
Grandpa Theo tapped the screen twice, then a third time, as though it might wake up if he were firm enough. The chart plotter stayed blank and grey.
'Well, Mia,' he said, 'it seems we're sailing the old way this afternoon.'
Mia looked past the mast. An hour ago the bay had sparkled. Now a wall of fog had rolled in from the south, swallowing the headland, the beach huts and finally the water itself, until the little ketch Wren floated in a soft white room with no walls. Somewhere to the west, swell slapped against rocks she could hear but not see.
Grandpa pulled a battered tin box from under the bench. Inside lay a folded paper chart, a pencil, a ruler and a stopwatch. He spread the chart across his knees and weighed down the corners with their sandwiches.
'We passed the channel marker at two o'clock,' he said. 'We've been heading north-east at about four knots since then. So where are we?'
Mia frowned. It felt like a maths test on a rocking floor. But she measured along the line he had drawn, checked the minutes on the stopwatch and made a small pencil cross.
'Here,' she said. 'Just past the reef.'
'Good. Now steer three-two-zero by the compass and keep her there.'
The compass swung in its bowl like a nervous fish. At first Mia chased it, pushing the tiller too far one way and then the other. Grandpa said nothing. Slowly she learnt to make tiny movements and to wait for the needle to settle before she corrected again.
Twenty minutes crept by, with no sound but the creak of the rigging. Mia's hands were cold and her neck ached from staring. She began to wonder whether her cross had been in the wrong place all along.
Then, ahead and slightly to the left, the fog blinked.
One flash. Darkness. One flash. Darkness. Two flashes close together.
'Count it,' said Grandpa.
Mia checked the list printed on the edge of the chart. 'One, one, two. That's Cape Morrow!'
Grandpa grinned and finally put the sandwiches back in their bag. 'Then your cross was right, navigator. Bring her round, and we'll follow the light home.'
Mia eased the tiller over. She had sailed with Grandpa every summer since she was six, but this was the first time she felt the boat was truly listening to her.
Question: What did Grandpa use to hold down the corners of the chart?
Option A: the tin box
Option B: the sandwiches
Option C: the stopwatch
Option D: the ruler

Putting the Logs Back
For more than a hundred years, people worked hard to pull dead trees out of the Murray River. Today, people are working just as hard to put them back in.
In the 1800s, paddle steamers carried wool, wheat and passengers along the Murray. Fallen river red gums lay in the water, and these 'snags' could rip a hole in a wooden hull. So snag boats fitted with winches and saws were sent out to clear the channel. Over the following decades, crews removed enormous numbers of logs from the Murray and the rivers that flow into it. It seemed like common sense: a clear river was a safe river.
What nobody understood then was that the snags were not rubbish. They were homes. River red gum wood is so hard and dense that a fallen trunk can lie underwater for hundreds of years. Over that time, it becomes the centre of a busy community. Slimy films of algae grow on its surface and feed tiny insects and shrimps. Small fish shelter among the branches. And in the shadows waits the river's most famous resident, the Murray cod.
Murray cod are ambush hunters. They lurk beside a snag and lunge at passing prey. They also lay their eggs on hard surfaces, such as the inside of hollow logs, and the male guards the eggs until they hatch. As the snags disappeared, so did many of the cod.
Fish ecologist Mara Quinn has spent fifteen years helping to return logs to rivers. "People expect me to say I love fish," she laughs, "and I do. But mostly I love logs." On a typical day she might be waist-deep in brown water at dawn, then arguing politely with an engineer about the exact angle of a three-tonne trunk. She admits she is impatient with slow paperwork but endlessly patient with the river. "A log might take a year to grow a good coat of algae," she says. "You can't hurry that, so you don't try."
Resnagging crews now use cranes and barges to lower logs into carefully chosen spots. The logs are anchored so that floods cannot wash them downstream into weirs or bridges. Years later, divers and survey teams return to count the fish.
The results have been encouraging, with fish often moving into new snags within months. It turns out that the river looked "messy" for a reason, and that sometimes the best way to help nature is to give back what was taken away.

Option A: They were blocking the flow of floodwater.
Option B: They could damage the hulls of paddle steamers.
Option C: They were needed as timber to build bridges.
Option D: They were spoiling the water for the cod.

The Lot on Mercer Street
The lot on Mercer Street was bare:
just broken bricks and bottle caps,
a rusty trolley parked out there,
and weeds that pushed through all the gaps.
Then Mrs Okafor came by
one Saturday in autumn rain,
with seedlings in an old esky
and gumboots muddy from the lane.
She didn't ask, she didn't wait;
she knelt and cleared a little square.
We watched her from behind the gate
and wondered what was growing there.
By winter, broad beans grew up tall,
their flowers black and white like eyes,
and silverbeet along the wall
held up red stems to cloudy skies.
Then Mr Tran brought round his spade,
the twins from Number Nine brought seed,
I brought a jug of lemonade
and learnt to tell a plant from weed.
Then Grandma Rossi brought a hose,
and Sanjay built a wooden bench,
and Mrs Kim, who loved a rose,
grew three of them against the fence.
We fed the compost kitchen scraps,
we taught the peas to climb a wire,
we caught the snails in saucer traps
and watched the sunflowers stretching higher.
When summer baked the garden brown,
we formed a line from tap to bed
and passed the buckets up and down
till every thirsty root was fed.
One night a windstorm, wild and loud,
knocked flat the sunflowers in their row;
by breakfast we had formed a crowd
to stake them up and help them grow.
At Number Two lived Mr Lee,
whose curtains always stayed shut tight.
Some mornings, though, we'd turn and see
a gap, a face, then gone from sight.
One day he shuffled out alone
and, though he hardly said a word,
he showed us how pumpkins should be grown
and named for us each passing bird.
By autumn we had picked so much
we set a table in the lot
with pumpkin soup and bread and such,
and everybody brought a pot.
We ate until the light grew thin.
The twins sang songs. The dogs ran free.
Then someone laughed out loud, and when
we turned, we saw it was Mr Lee.
The lot on Mercer Street is green.
The trolley holds a strawberry bed.
The broken bricks, scrubbed bright and clean,
now make a path where gumboots tread.
And Mrs Okafor still kneels
each Saturday, in rain or sun,
but now she knows just how it feels
to share the work with everyone.

Option A: a rusty trolley
Option B: an old esky
Option C: a pair of gumboots
Option D: a wooden bucket

Seven on the Court
Ten minutes left. We trailed by three.
The crowd was loud, the air was thick,
and Jada, clutching at her knee,
limped off the court. I felt quite sick.
She was our shooter, calm and tall,
who almost never seemed to miss.
Coach scanned the bench along the wall
and pointed: me. It came to this.
They used to call me 'Butterfingers'
in Year Four, when I joined the side,
and though I've grown, that old name lingers,
a pebble that I keep inside.
I tugged the bib on: GS, bright.
The letters seemed too big for me.
I told myself I'd be all right,
but my knees knocked for all to see.
The first pass came. I grabbed. I dropped.
Their keeper flicked the ball away.
A groan rolled down. My stomach flopped.
I wished I'd stayed at home that day.
Then Mei-Lin, our Goal Attack, came near.
She didn't sigh or shake her head.
'Just stand beneath the ring, right here,
and we will bring it in,' she said.
I'd thought she'd tell me, 'Don't you dare
go dropping it again, okay?'
Instead she squeezed my arm right there
and jogged back to her spot to play.
At time-out, Coach told us to keep
our passes short and quick and low:
no lobs, no hopeful, floating leaps,
just hand to hand, the way we know.
I wiped my palms and found my place
right underneath the ring, quite still,
and tried to wear a brave, calm face,
though half of me was feeling ill.
So that is what we did. The ball
went Ana, Kiri, Mei-Lin, me,
so close beneath the ring that all
I had to do was lift it free.
It dropped right through. And then once more.
And then again. Our bench went wild.
The crowd began to stamp and roar,
and Jada, with her ice pack, smiled.
With seconds left, they had the ball.
Their shooter steadied, aimed it true,
but Tess, our keeper, stretched up tall
and tipped it out. The siren blew.
We won by one. Nobody claimed
I'd saved the game all on my own,
and that felt right. Each goal I aimed
was built by seven, not by one.
That night my brother tried, for fun,
the old name: 'Butterfingers! Hey!'
I laughed. The sting of it was gone.
Some names, I guess, just fade away.

Option A: were ahead in the score.
Option B: were behind in the score.
Option C: had drawn level in the score.
Option D: were following the other team.

Stop Saying 'I Can't Draw'
Walk into a kindergarten classroom and ask who can draw. Every hand will shoot up. Ask the same question in a Year 6 classroom and only a few hands will rise, slowly. What happened in between? Those students did not lose their hands or their eyes. They lost their confidence. I believe that drawing is a skill anyone can learn, and it is time we started treating it that way.
Firstly, drawing is learned, just like reading. Nobody expects a child to read a novel without years of practice, yet we expect people to draw well straight away, and we decide they are 'not artistic' when they don't. Even famous artists had to practise. Leonardo da Vinci filled thousands of notebook pages with sketches of hands, faces, plants and machines, many of them rough attempts that he drew again and again.
Secondly, drawing helps us think. Scientists sketch what they see through microscopes. Engineers and architects draw plans long before anything is built. Researchers have even found that people tend to remember a word better if they draw it than if they write it out several times. Drawing is not only for artists; it is a tool for everyone.
Some people argue that schools are too busy for drawing, because students need to focus on literacy and numeracy. But drawing supports those subjects. A diagram can make a maths problem clear. A story map can help a writer plan. Time spent drawing is not time stolen from learning; it is part of learning.

Tree Keeper
Ares Dome, Mars. Sol 412 (that's a Tuesday, for anyone reading this on Earth)
Dear Diary,
Today started as the most boring day in the history of Mars. The dust storm has been blowing for nine sols, so outdoor walks are cancelled, the windows are brown, and the only thing on the learning screen was a lesson about air filters. AIR FILTERS. I live in a dome where the air is filtered every second of every day. I think I know about air filters.
Then, after lunch, Commander Osei made an announcement. The cargo lander that touched down before the storm had brought something special, and everyone was to meet in the Green Bay at fifteen hundred hours.
The Green Bay is where we grow lettuce, tomatoes and beans under pink lights. It always smells damp and a bit like socks. Today it was packed. Right in the middle, in a big pot, stood a tree.
Okay, it was not a big tree. It was about as tall as me, with a thin grey trunk and maybe forty leaves. The label said Eucalyptus, which Dad says is from Australia, where he grew up. But it was a TREE, Diary. A real one, not a picture or a hologram.
Here's the strange part. The adults who were born on Earth went very quiet. Mrs Petrova put her hand over her mouth. Dad crouched down, crushed a leaf between his fingers and breathed in, and his eyes went shiny. He said it smelt like a summer holiday he had when he was nine.
When it was my turn, I touched the trunk. It was smooth in some places and peeling in others, as if it were taking off an old jacket. I crushed a leaf too. It smelt sharp and clean, like medicine, but alive. It didn't remind me of anything, because I don't have any summer holidays on Earth to remember. Still, my chest felt tight, in a good way.
The botanists say that if the tree survives, its seeds could one day grow a whole grove inside the new dome. I asked if I could help look after it. Dr Ahmed said yes, on Thursdays.
So now I have a job. Tree Keeper, Ares Dome. The storm is still blowing, but I don't mind so much any more.
Leo

Goldfish Are Smarter Than You Think
You may have heard that a goldfish has a memory of only three seconds. According to this popular story, a goldfish swimming around its bowl finds every lap a brand-new adventure. It is a charming idea. It is also completely wrong.
Scientists have tested goldfish memory many times. In one kind of experiment, fish are fed just after a particular sound is played. Within days, the fish begin to gather at the feeding spot as soon as they hear the sound, even before any food appears. Some studies have found that goldfish still respond to such a sound months later. Other researchers have trained goldfish to push levers, swim through simple mazes and tell the difference between certain colours and shapes.
Many pet owners notice this cleverness too. They report that their goldfish rush to the front of the tank when the person who usually feeds them walks into the room, but take little notice of visitors.
So why does the three-second myth survive? Perhaps it makes people feel better about keeping a fish in a tiny, empty bowl. If the fish forgets everything instantly, the thinking goes, it cannot possibly be bored.
Unfortunately, the classic round bowl is one of the worst homes for a goldfish. Goldfish produce a lot of waste, and in a small amount of water this quickly builds up to harmful levels. Bowls rarely have room for a filter, and their narrow tops let in very little oxygen. Goldfish also grow far larger than most people expect. A common goldfish can reach more than twenty centimetres in length if it is given enough space.
Experts recommend a large tank with a filter, regular partial water changes and some plants or decorations to explore. In good conditions, goldfish often live for more than ten years. One famous goldfish in England, named Tish, lived to the age of 43.
None of this means that goldfish are geniuses. But it does mean they are living creatures that learn, remember and respond to the world around them. The next time someone jokes about a goldfish's memory, you might gently set them straight, and perhaps suggest that the fish deserves a bigger home.

Option A: 10 years old
Option B: 20 years old
Option C: 43 years old
Option D: 3 years old

Long ago, before there were clocks or calendars, the Sun never left the sky. It blazed from one horizon to the other without rest, and the world below grew weary. The rivers shrank to trickles.
