The Ship That the Ice Swallowed
In August 1914, the ship Endurance sailed from England carrying 28 men led by the explorer Ernest Shackleton. Their goal was bold: to land on Antarctica and become the first expedition to cross the entire frozen continent on foot.
They never set foot on it. In January 1915, as Endurance pushed through the Weddell Sea, the pack ice closed around her like a fist. For ten months the crew lived aboard, drifting slowly with the ice, playing football on the frozen sea and training their sled dogs. Then the pressure of the ice began to crack the ship's timbers. In November 1915, Endurance sank.
The men camped on the drifting floes with three small lifeboats they had dragged from the ship. When the ice broke up in April 1916, they launched the boats into freezing seas and, after several exhausting days, reached Elephant Island. It was the first solid ground they had stood on in well over a year. But the island was bare and rocky, far from any shipping route, and nobody knew they were there.
Shackleton made a daring decision. He and five companions would sail one lifeboat, the James Caird, about 1300 kilometres to the island of South Georgia, where there was a whaling station. The remaining men would wait on Elephant Island, sheltering beneath the other two boats turned upside down.
The voyage took about sixteen days through some of the stormiest seas on Earth. Waves towered over the tiny boat, and ice coated it so thickly that the men had to chip it off to stop it from capsizing. Navigator Frank Worsley, using a sextant on the few occasions he glimpsed the sun, guided them to South Georgia.
Even then, they had landed on the wrong side of the island. Shackleton, Worsley and Tom Crean had to cross its unmapped, icy mountains on foot, with screws from the boat pushed into their boots for grip. After about 36 hours, they stumbled into the whaling station at Stromness.
It took four attempts, but in August 1916 Shackleton returned to Elephant Island aboard a Chilean ship, the Yelcho. Every one of the men he had left behind was alive.
In 2022, searchers finally found the wreck of Endurance on the sea floor, about three kilometres down and remarkably well preserved.

Wire Across the Red
(A linesman writes home, 1872)
You ask me, Kate, in every letter
why I won't come home this year,
and why a desk in town's not better
than the flies and heat out here.
So here's my answer, plain and true,
by lamplight, short and clear:
the thing we're building's something new,
and that is why I'm here.
First, think how long a letter takes
from here to London town:
two months by ship, for goodness' sake,
with storms to slow it down.
But once this line is joined up north
to cables on the ocean floor,
our words will flash out, back and forth,
in hours, not months, from shore to shore.
At every station, built of stone,
a man will sit all day
and tap the clicks out, on his own,
to send them on their way.
Second, the work is hard but good.
We dig each hole by hand
and stand the poles of sawn hardwood
across the red, flat land.
The summer sun beats like a drum
upon my battered hat,
and flies, a thousand, buzz and hum
and laugh at every swat.
The white ants chewed the timber through
(they think we've brought them lunch!),
so now we're hauling iron, too,
that no white ant can munch.
We haul the wire by bullock dray
and camels, nose to tail,
and string it on, from day to day,
mile after dusty mile.
We've crossed the ranges, red and steep,
and plains as bare as bone;
the stars hang low above our sleep
like lamps we've never known.
And third, I've mates who share my tent,
my damper and my tea,
and when one man is sick or spent,
the rest pitch in, you see.
On Sundays, when the work is still,
we wash our shirts and sing,
and Paddy plays his fiddle till
the gum trees seem to ring.
But since you've asked me, Kate, I'll say
the rest, and tell it true:
the nights are long, and far away
is very far from you.
I keep your letters in my coat
and read them by the fire;
I've learnt by heart the last you wrote.
It travels with the wire.
Each pole we raise, I count as one
more day gone by, and then
I think: when all these poles are done,
I'll see your face again.
So wait for me one season more.
When this long line is done,
a telegram will reach your door:
'Your Dad is coming home.'

Option A: a daughter's long journey to visit her father in the outback
Option B: the trouble caused by white ants in the Australian bush

Option D: the invention of the telegraph by engineers in England

Four Floors of the Forest
A tropical rainforest can look like a tangle of green, but scientists who study it see something more organised: a building with four floors. Each layer receives a different amount of light and rain, and each is home to different plants and animals.
The emergent layer
The tallest trees push up above everything else, sometimes more than 50 metres high. Up here, they are blasted by sun, wind and heavy rain. Their leaves are often small and waxy, which helps stop them drying out. Birds of prey perch on the highest branches to scan for food.
The canopy
Below the emergents lies the canopy, a thick roof of leaves and branches. It catches most of the sunlight, so it is the busiest layer of all. Fruit, flowers and insects attract birds, possums, tree frogs and flying-foxes, and many canopy animals rarely, if ever, come down to the ground. Lots of canopy leaves have pointed 'drip tips' that let rainwater run off quickly, so moss and algae cannot easily grow on them.
The understorey
Beneath the canopy, the air is still, warm and damp. Only a little sunlight filters through, so understorey plants such as palms and ferns often have very large leaves to catch whatever light they can. Young trees wait here, sometimes for years, until an old giant falls and opens a gap of sunlight above them.
The forest floor
As little as two per cent of the sunlight that reaches the top of the forest makes it all the way to the floor. It is dark, and few plants grow. However, the floor is far from lifeless. Fallen leaves, fruit and branches are broken down rapidly by fungi, termites and other decomposers, returning nutrients to the soil. Because rainforest soil is often thin, many trees have shallow roots, and some grow wide, flat buttress roots that act like props to stop them toppling over.
In the rainforests of northern Queensland, the southern cassowary walks the forest floor eating fallen fruit. The seeds pass through its body and are dropped, often far from the parent tree, ready to sprout. Because some plants with large seeds rely heavily on cassowaries to spread them, the bird is sometimes called a 'rainforest gardener'.
The layers are not separate worlds. Rain, light, animals and nutrients move constantly between them, and a change on one floor can affect every other.

Option A: to stop rainwater from reaching the forest floor
Option B: to protect their leaves from strong winds
Option C: to catch as much of the dim light as they can
Option D: to hide young trees from hungry animals

Mending a Friendship: A Step-by-Step Guide
Even the best of friends fall out sometimes. Arguments are a normal part of any friendship; what matters most is what happens next. If you have had a falling-out with a friend, these steps can help you patch things up.
You will need: some time, a quiet place to talk and an open mind.
Step 1: Cool off first
Strong feelings make it hard to think clearly. Before you try to fix anything, give yourself time to calm down. Go for a walk, shoot some hoops or write down how you feel. A few hours, or even a day, is usually enough. Trying to talk while you are still furious often makes things worse.
Step 2: Work out your part
Ask yourself honestly: what did I do or say that might have hurt my friend? It is rare for an argument to be one hundred per cent one person's fault. You do not have to decide that everything was your fault, but noticing your own part will make Step 4 much easier.
Step 3: Choose the right moment
Find a time when you can talk privately, without an audience. Trying to sort things out in front of the whole class can make your friend feel embarrassed or cornered.
Step 4: Apologise for your part
Keep your apology clear and specific, for example: 'I'm sorry I laughed when you dropped the ball.' Avoid saying 'I'm sorry, but . . .', because the word 'but' tends to cancel out everything that came before it.
Step 5: Listen
Now let your friend explain how they felt. Try not to interrupt or argue back, even if you see things differently. Nod, and repeat back what you heard: 'So you felt left out when I picked Sam first.' Feeling understood often matters more to people than being proved right.
Step 6: Agree on what happens next
Decide together how you might handle a similar problem in future. Then do something ordinary together, such as walking to the canteen or playing a game, to show that the friendship is back on track.
Remember: not every friendship can be mended straight away. If your friend is not ready to talk, give them time and space, and try again later. You have done your part, and that is something to be proud of.

Tilted Towards Summer
Ask people why summer is hot and many will say that Earth must be closer to the Sun. It sounds sensible, but it is not true. In fact, Earth is at its closest to the Sun in early January, which is summer in Australia but winter in Europe and North America. If distance caused the seasons, both halves of the planet would have summer at the same time.
The real cause is a tilt. Earth spins on an imaginary line called its axis, which runs through the North and South Poles. This axis is not straight up and down but leans at an angle of about 23.5 degrees. As Earth travels around the Sun over a year, the tilt stays pointing in the same direction in space.
For part of the year, the Southern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun. Sunlight strikes it more directly, concentrating its energy on a smaller area, and days are longer than nights. The land and sea have more time to warm up. That is our summer. Six months later, when Earth is on the other side of its orbit, the Southern Hemisphere leans away. The Sun sits lower in the sky, its rays are spread over a larger area, and the nights are long. That is our winter.
You can see this with a torch. Shine it straight down at a table and you get a small, bright circle. Tilt the torch, and the light spreads into a larger, dimmer oval. The same amount of light is being shared over more surface.
Places near the equator receive fairly direct sunlight all year, so they do not have a cold winter. Instead, many tropical regions have a wet season and a dry season. Near the poles, the effect is extreme: in midsummer the Sun may not set at all, while in midwinter it may not rise for weeks.
The four seasons on Australian calendars came from Europe. However, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have long observed seasons that suit their own country. In the Kakadu region, for example, some groups recognise six seasons, each marked by changes in weather, plants and animals. Calendars like these show that seasons are not only about temperature; they are about reading the patterns of the land.

Option A: in early July
Option B: in early January
Option C: in late December
Option D: in the middle of winter in Australia

Second in Everything
More than two thousand years ago, a boy named Eratosthenes was born in Cyrene, a Greek city on the coast of North Africa, in what is now Libya. As a young man he travelled to Athens to study, and he soon became known for his poetry, his mathematics and his writing about history. Although he was talented in many subjects, he was rarely called the very best at any single one.
Around 245 BC, the ruler of Egypt invited Eratosthenes to Alexandria to work at its famous library, which he later ran. The Library of Alexandria held one of the greatest collections of knowledge in the ancient world. Scholars came from far and wide to read its scrolls, and copies of books from passing ships were added to its shelves. For a curious mind, it was like being handed the keys to a treasure house.
Some of his fellow scholars gave Eratosthenes a teasing nickname: 'Beta', the second letter of the Greek alphabet. They meant that he was second-best in every field. Yet the list of fields was remarkably long. He drew a map of the known world with lines running across it to help locate places. He invented a clever method for finding prime numbers, now called the Sieve of Eratosthenes. He is even credited with creating the word 'geography'.
His most famous achievement, however, began with a simple report. Eratosthenes had read that in the town of Syene, far to the south, the sun shone straight down a deep well at noon on the longest day of the year, so that no shadow fell. In Alexandria on the same day, he noticed, an upright pole still cast a short shadow.
Eratosthenes reasoned that this could only happen if the Earth's surface was curved. By measuring the angle of the shadow in Alexandria, he found it was about one-fiftieth of a full circle. He knew the distance between the two towns, so he multiplied it by fifty. His answer for the distance around the Earth was remarkably close to the figure scientists use today.
Eratosthenes never sailed around the globe. He used a stick, a shadow, a written report and careful thinking. 'Beta' may have been second in many things, but in this he was first.

Let the Sun Pay the Bills
Every summer afternoon, the sun beats down on the wide, flat roofs of our school buildings. All that sunshine lands on bare metal and simply turns into heat. Meanwhile, the school pays thousands of dollars each year for electricity, much of it made by burning coal. I believe our school should cover those roofs with solar panels, and I think the reasons are clear.
First, solar panels would save money. Once the panels are installed, sunlight is free. Australia is one of the sunniest countries on Earth, so our panels would produce power on most days of the year. Schools use most of their electricity during the day, exactly when the panels are working hardest. The money saved could be spent on things students actually notice, such as new library books, sports equipment or shade sails for the playground.
Second, solar power is cleaner. Burning coal releases carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere. Every unit of electricity our panels make is a unit that does not need to come from a coal-fired power station. Over the twenty-five years or more that panels usually last, that adds up to a huge difference.
Third, the panels would be a lesson in themselves. Many solar systems come with a screen showing how much power is being produced. Imagine a display in the front office where students could watch the numbers climb on a sunny morning and drop when a cloud drifts past. We could use real data in maths, science and even persuasive writing like this.
Some people argue that solar panels cost too much to install. It is true that the starting price is high. However, grants are often available to help schools, and many systems pay for themselves within several years. After that, the savings just keep adding up.
Others say that panels do not work at night. That is correct, but our school is empty at night anyway! Any extra power made on weekends and during the holidays can be sent back into the grid for other households to use.
I get frustrated every time I walk past those empty, shimmering roofs. They are not just roofs; they are wasted opportunities. Let's put the sun to work.
Question: According to the writer, what is one thing the money saved could be spent on?
Option A: new computers
Option B: a school bus
Option C: new library books
Option D: more solar panels

The Man Behind Mother Goose
Most people know the stories of Cinderella, Puss in Boots and Sleeping Beauty. Far fewer know the name of the man who first wrote them down in the form we recognise today. His name was Charles Perrault, and for most of his long life, fairy tales were the last thing anyone expected from him.
Perrault was born in Paris in 1628, the youngest son of a well-off family. He was a clever, confident student who once walked out of school after arguing with his teacher, and then taught himself by reading at home with a friend. Later he trained as a lawyer, although he did not stay in that work for long.
In his thirties, Perrault became an assistant to Jean-Baptiste Colbert, one of the most powerful ministers serving King Louis XIV of France. For twenty years he helped to organise the king's building projects and the arts. He even suggested a maze for the gardens of the Palace of Versailles, filled with fountains showing scenes from Aesop's fables.
Perrault also held an opinion that annoyed many scholars of his time. Most of them believed that the writers of ancient Greece and Rome could never be equalled. Perrault disagreed. He argued that modern writers could be just as good, and he was not afraid to say so in public.
When Colbert died, Perrault lost his position. His wife had died some years earlier, and he now had more time to spend with his children. Perhaps it was during those years, sitting by the fire, that he began to think seriously about the old stories told to children by nurses and servants.
In 1697, when he was almost seventy, a small book appeared called Stories or Tales from Times Past. It contained eight tales, including Little Red Riding Hood and Cinderella, and each one ended with a short rhyming moral. Curiously, the book was published under the name of his teenage son, Pierre. Historians still argue about why.
Perrault did not invent these tales. Versions of them had been passed down by word of mouth for centuries. But he gave them a lively, polished style that delighted readers, and he showed that simple folk stories were worthy of a printed book. In a way, it was the perfect proof of his old argument: a modern storyteller had created something that would outlast almost everything else he wrote.
Question: When and where was Charles Perrault born?
Option A: in Versailles in 1697
Option B: in Paris in 1628
Option C: in Rome in 1628
Option D: in Paris in 1697

He was a clever, confident student who once walked out of school after arguing with his teacher, and then taught himself by reading at home with a friend. Later he trained as a lawyer, although he did not stay in that work for long.
In his thirties, Perrault became an assistant to Jean-Baptiste Colbert, one of the most powerful ministers serving King Louis XIV of France. For twenty years he helped to organise the king's building projects and the arts. He even suggested a maze for the gardens of the Palace of Versailles, filled with fountains showing scenes from Aesop's fables.

In a way, it was the perfect proof of his old argument: a modern storyteller had created something that would outlast almost everything else he wrote.

Option B: He did not enjoy reading and preferred to spend time with friends.

Option D: He was shy and found it hard to speak up in front of a class.

Let the Mall Sing
Walk through our town mall on a Saturday morning and what do you hear? The beep of a pedestrian crossing, the rumble of delivery trucks and perhaps a crying toddler. What you will not hear is music. Since the council introduced strict new rules last year, buskers have almost vanished from our streets. I believe these rules should be relaxed, and street performers welcomed back.
Under the current rules, buskers must buy a permit costing one hundred dollars, perform only in two small marked squares beside the car park and finish by eleven o'clock in the morning. For a teenager hoping to earn a little pocket money with a guitar, that is a steep price for a spot that hardly anyone walks past.
Street music brings life to a town. A violinist playing outside the bakery makes people slow down, smile and linger. When shoppers linger, they spend. Shop owners in many other towns have found that a lively street draws more customers, not fewer. Music is an invitation; silence is a shrug.
Busking also gives young performers a stage. Not every talented musician can book a concert hall. Some of Australia's best-known performers began by playing on footpaths, learning to win over people who had not come to hear them. That is a tough audience, and it builds skill and confidence quickly.
Finally, buskers make music free for everyone. A concert ticket can cost more than many families can afford. On the street, a child can stop and watch a juggling drummer for as long as they like, and pay nothing more than a clap.
Of course, the council has reasons for its rules. Some shopkeepers complained about performers who were too loud or who played the same three songs all day. These concerns are fair. But the answer is not to drive buskers away; it is to set sensible limits. A cheap permit, a volume limit and a rule that performers move spots every two hours would solve most problems without silencing anyone.
Our mall was built for people, and people have always gathered around music. Let's change the rules, unpack the guitar cases and let the mall sing again.
Question: 'A violinist playing outside the bakery makes people slow down, smile and linger.' What does 'linger' mean?
Option A: hurry away
Option B: sing along
Option C: stay for longer
Option D: complain loudly

Sleeping, Not Dead
Ask most Australians where to find a volcano and they will point to Hawaii, Iceland or Indonesia. Few would point to their own backyard. Yet across western Victoria and south-eastern South Australia lies a region scattered with around four hundred old volcanoes. It is time we stopped ignoring them.
Let me be clear: I am not suggesting that anyone panic. An eruption in Australia is unlikely in our lifetimes. But 'unlikely' is not the same as 'impossible', and that difference matters.
Consider Mount Gambier, a city of more than twenty-five thousand people. It is built around a volcano that erupted only about five thousand years ago. In the long history of the Earth, five thousand years is the blink of an eye. Scientists describe this region as dormant, meaning sleeping, rather than extinct. A sleeping volcano can wake up.
At present, however, there is very little equipment here watching for volcanic warning signs. In countries such as New Zealand and Japan, instruments constantly measure tiny earthquakes and changes in the ground that might signal rising magma. Networks like these have given communities days or even weeks of warning before eruptions. Australia should install similar instruments. They are not expensive compared with the cost of being caught unprepared.
Second, we should teach students about the volcanoes on their doorstep. Many children in Victoria walk past old stone walls, picnic beside crater lakes and play on grassy hills without realising they are volcanic. Learning about these landforms would make geography lessons come alive and help the next generation understand the land they live on.
Finally, our volcanoes are a treasure that could attract visitors. The Undara lava tubes in Queensland, formed about 190 000 years ago, already draw tourists from around the world. The crater lakes and cones of Victoria could do the same if they were better known, bringing jobs to country towns.
Some people will say that spending money on something that may not happen for thousands of years is wasteful. But we buy smoke alarms hoping never to hear them. Monitoring is simply a smoke alarm for the land.
Australia's volcanoes are sleeping, not dead. We should get to know them, watch over them and be proud of them, before they decide to remind us that they are there.
Question: In the third paragraph, what does 'dormant' mean?
Option A: dead and never able to erupt again
Option B: sleeping, but able to become active again
Option C: erupting regularly every few years
Option D: hidden deep under the ocean floor

The City That Kept Its Trams
If you stand on a Melbourne street corner for a few minutes, you will probably hear a cheerful 'ding ding' before a tram glides past. Trams are so much a part of the city that it is hard to imagine it without them. Yet Melbourne's trams very nearly disappeared, and the story of how they survived says a lot about how cities change.
In the 1880s, Melbourne was booming. To move its growing population, the city built a network of cable trams. These had no engines of their own. Instead, a steel cable ran in a channel beneath the road, pulled along by giant steam engines in powerhouses. The driver used a grip to clamp onto the moving cable to go, and released it to stop. For a time, Melbourne had one of the largest cable tram systems in the world.
Electric trams, powered by overhead wires, soon proved faster and cheaper to run. Gradually they replaced the cable trams, and the last cable tram rattled through Melbourne's streets in 1940.
By the 1950s, a new challenge had arrived: the family car. Many people believed that trams were old-fashioned and simply got in the way of traffic. One by one, other Australian cities pulled up their tram tracks and replaced them with buses. Sydney's last tram ran in 1961, and Brisbane's followed in 1969.
Melbourne went a different way. Its wide, straight streets had plenty of room for both cars and trams, and the people who ran the tramways argued strongly that trams could carry large crowds more efficiently than buses. The trams stayed. Today Melbourne has the largest tram network in the world, with around 250 kilometres of track.
Interestingly, some of the cities that removed their trams have begun to change their minds. The Gold Coast opened a light rail line in 2014, and both Sydney and Canberra opened new lines in 2019. Modern light rail vehicles are sleeker and quieter than the old trams, but the idea is much the same: carrying many people along busy streets on steel rails, using electricity rather than petrol.
Planners now point out that one full tram can replace dozens of cars, easing traffic jams and reducing pollution. What once seemed outdated has started to look like the future. Sometimes the best way forward is to hold on to a good idea long enough for everyone else to catch up.

Option A: The driver gripped a moving cable under the road.
Option B: An engine inside the tram turned its wheels.
Option C: Electricity flowed to it from overhead wires.
Option D: Horses pulled it along a set of steel rails.

Pim's List
The robot opened the front door before Tavi could even knock. It was about as tall as his shoulder, with a smooth white body, two soft grey arms and a round screen for a face. Two blue dots blinked at him.
'Good afternoon, Tavi,' it said. 'I am Pim. Your grandmother is in the garden.'
Tavi frowned. Mum had told him about the robot in the car. It could remind Nana to take her tablets, carry the shopping and call for help if she fell. 'It means she can keep living in her own house,' Mum had said. Tavi understood that. He just didn't like it. Last summer he had stayed with Nana for two whole weeks, and carrying the shopping had been his job.
In the garden, Nana hugged him so tightly that his glasses slid sideways. Pim rolled out behind them with a tray holding two glasses of lemon cordial and a plate of ginger biscuits.
Tavi stared. Ginger biscuits were his favourite. Nobody else in the family even liked them.
'How did it know?' he asked.
Nana just smiled and sipped her cordial.
Later, while Nana dozed in her armchair, Tavi followed Pim into the kitchen. 'Are you going to do everything for her now?' he asked quietly.
Pim's blue dots tilted, as if it were thinking. 'I can do many tasks,' it said. 'But some things are not on my list.'
'What list?'
The screen changed. Tavi read the words slowly. Things Tavi likes: ginger biscuits. Card games, especially Snap. The blue wren that visits the birdbath. Stories about Grandad's boat.
The list went on and on, far longer than he could have guessed. Underneath, a single line glowed in small letters: Information supplied by Mrs Ana Rua, most days.
Tavi swallowed hard. He looked at the kitchen table, set with one placemat, and at the calendar on the wall, where only a few squares had anything written in them.
He went back to the lounge room and found the old pack of cards in the drawer where it had always been. When Nana opened her eyes, he was dealing them out on the coffee table.
'Snap?' he said.
Her face lit up. Behind them, Pim rolled quietly to the doorway and, as far as a robot can, seemed to watch with approval.
'Pim,' Tavi said, without looking up, 'you can add something to your list. Tavi visits on Saturdays.'
Question: Which of these is one of the jobs Pim can do?
Option A: drive Nana to the shops
Option B: remind Nana to take her tablets
Option C: cook Nana's evening meals
Option D: teach Nana new card games

Our Kitchen Table
At seven, our table is buried in toast,
In lunchboxes, homework and yesterday's post.
Dad hunts for his keys while the kettle complains,
And Mum checks the weather and sighs at the rains.
At four, it's a desk for my sister and me,
With fractions and spelling and biscuits and tea.
She chews on her ruler; I tap with my pen;
We argue, we giggle, we argue again.
At six, it's a stage for the stories we share:
The goal that I scored and the dog's chewed-up chair,
The news from Nan's phone call, the fuss at Dad's work,
And who left the milk out (Dad blames me, with a smirk).
On Saturdays, Mum sorts the bills into piles,
With her glasses pushed up and a sigh between smiles.
Dad brings her a coffee and leans on her chair,
And says, 'We'll be right,' as he ruffles her hair.
On birthdays it shines with a cloth and a cake,
And candles that flicker, and wishes we make.
My sister once wished for a pony; instead
She got a stuffed horse that still sleeps on her bed.
On Sundays the table belongs to my brother,
Who flips golden pancakes, one after another.
He tosses them high and he catches them neat,
Then bows like a waiter and offers a seat.
When Jai was just small, Mum says, he sat right here,
On two fat phone books, so his chin would appear.
He spilled his first milkshake. He carved his first 'J'
In the wood by the window. It's still there today.
But Jai got a letter that came in July:
A job up in Darwin. He's packing. 'Goodbye'
Is a word he keeps saying as if it's a joke,
But Mum went quite quiet, and Dad hardly spoke.
Last Sunday I stood by his elbow and stared
At every small step and the way he prepared:
A cup and a half, and the pan must be hot,
Then wait for the bubbles, then flip on the spot.
At night, when the house has gone sleepy and still,
The table keeps watch by the dark windowsill.
It holds all our crumbs and our scratches and rings,
The marks that we leave with our ordinary things.
Next month there'll be one empty chair at our meal,
A gap in the stories. I know how that will feel.
But I've copied his secrets in pen on a card:
A cup and a half. Wait for bubbles. Not hard.

Option C: He is moving to a house next door.
Option D: He is going on a holiday in July.

The Woman Who Changed Dinner
In the 1950s, a typical Australian family dinner looked much the same in almost every house: grilled chops or roast meat, boiled potatoes and vegetables cooked until they were soft. Garlic was rare, spaghetti usually came out of a tin, and few people had ever tasted a curry. Within a generation, that had changed dramatically, and one woman had a great deal to do with it.
Margaret Fulton was born in Scotland in 1924. When she was three, her family sailed to Australia and settled in Glen Innes, a country town in New South Wales. Margaret grew up watching the women in her family bake scones and shortbread in the kitchen.
As a young woman, Margaret tried a range of jobs. One of them was demonstrating cooking, which meant standing in front of crowds and showing them how to make dishes step by step. She discovered that she loved explaining food clearly and making it seem possible for anyone.
Margaret was also curious about the foods that new migrants were bringing to Australia from Italy, Greece, China and many other places. Rather than turning up her nose at unfamiliar flavours, she sought them out, asked questions and tested recipes in her own kitchen. She believed ordinary families deserved to enjoy this food too.
In 1968 she published The Margaret Fulton Cookbook. It was full of bright colour photographs and clear instructions, and it included dishes such as spaghetti bolognese, stir-fries and curries alongside the traditional roasts. The book was a huge success, selling more than a million copies. For many families, it was the first cookbook that showed them how to cook something new.
Over the following decades Margaret wrote many more books, appeared on television and travelled widely to learn about food. She encouraged people to cook with fresh ingredients and to sit down and eat together. Even in her eighties, she was still writing and cooking.
Margaret Fulton died in 2019 at the age of ninety-four. Today, Australians eat dishes from all over the world without a second thought. Many of the dinners that seem completely ordinary to us now were once exciting and strange, and for millions of home cooks, Margaret Fulton was the person who first showed them the way.

Option A: Sydney, in New South Wales
Option B: Glen Innes, in New South Wales
Option C: a town in Scotland
Option D: a farm in Victoria

For three whole evenings, the lounge room floor had been covered in paper aeroplanes. Some had pointed noses, some had blunt ones, and one had wings so wide that Mia's little brother called it the Flying Pancake. None of them flew far.
The school's Great Paper Plane Challenge was on Friday. The rules were simple: one sheet of A4 paper, no tape, no glue and no more than one paperclip. The plane that glided furthest across the hall would win.
'Mine all do the same thing,' Mia complained to Grandpa Joe, who had spent forty years fixing real aircraft. She launched her favourite dart-shaped design. It shot upwards, slowed, hung in the air for a moment, then tipped backwards and dropped onto the carpet.
'Ah,' said Grandpa Joe. 'It's stalling.' He explained that when a plane's nose points up too steeply, the air stops flowing smoothly over the wings and the plane loses its lift. 'Your plane is too light at the front, so the nose keeps rising. Real aircraft have to be balanced too. If the weight is in the wrong place, they won't fly properly.'
'So how do I fix it?'
Grandpa Joe smiled and held up a single paperclip.
Mia slid the clip right onto the tip of the dart and threw it again. This time it dived straight into the leg of the coffee table.
'Too much,' said Grandpa Joe. 'Try moving it back a little. And only change one thing at a time, or you'll never know what worked.'
Mia moved the clip back a few millimetres and threw the plane again before she touched anything else. Later, she folded the back edges of the wings up very slightly. She wrote every change in a notebook and measured each flight with Dad's tape measure. Slowly, the numbers grew: four metres, six metres, nearly eight.
On Friday, the school hall was noisy and crowded. When her turn came, Mia's hands were trembling. She took a breath, remembered to throw gently and level rather than hard and high, and let go.
The plane slid through the air in a long, smooth line, past the six-metre mark, past the eight, and settled softly on the polished floor at nine metres and forty centimetres.
She didn't win. A Year 5 boy's plane flew just over ten metres. But when Mia got home, she opened her notebook to a fresh page and drew a careful diagram of his wings.
Grandpa Joe looked over her shoulder and chuckled.

Look closely at a honeycomb and you will see row upon row of neat six-sided cells, fitted together without a single gap. Making wax takes a lot of energy; a colony must eat a large amount of honey to produce even a small amount of wax. By building hexagons, bees create the most storage space while using the least wax. Open Wide at the Reef Clinic
On a coral reef, a large fish hangs perfectly still in the water, its mouth wide open and its gills flared. A tiny striped fish darts straight inside, nibbling between the big fish's teeth. You might expect the big fish to snap its jaws shut. It doesn't. Instead, it waits patiently until the little fish swims out again.
The small fish is a bluestreak cleaner wrasse, and it is doing its job. Cleaner wrasse feed on parasites, dead skin and scraps of food that cling to larger fish. A wrasse, or a small group of them, sets up a 'cleaning station' at a particular spot on the reef, such as a bommie or a coral ledge. Other fish, known as clients, visit to be cleaned, sometimes waiting their turn.
To advertise its services, a cleaner wrasse performs a bobbing, up-and-down swimming display. Clients signal that they are ready by holding still, opening their mouths or changing colour. Even large predators that would normally eat a fish this size, such as groupers, usually leave the cleaners alone. A busy wrasse may inspect well over a thousand clients in a single day.
The arrangement benefits both sides. The cleaner gets a steady supply of food, and the client gets rid of parasites that could make it sick. In experiments where cleaner wrasse were removed from small patches of reef, scientists later found fewer kinds of fish living there.
However, the relationship is not always perfectly honest. What cleaner wrasse really prefer to eat is the slimy mucus that protects a client's skin. Taking a bite of mucus hurts the client, which often jolts and swims away. Researchers have noticed something remarkable: cleaners tend to behave much better when other clients are waiting nearby and watching. Could a fish really care about its reputation?
There is also an impostor on the reef. The false cleaner blenny looks almost exactly like a cleaner wrasse, with the same stripes and colours. It even copies the bobbing dance. But when a client fish relaxes and waits to be cleaned, the blenny darts in and bites off a piece of fin before racing away.
Scientists are still trying to understand exactly how client fish tell a true cleaner from a fake one. What is clear is that, on a busy reef, the cleaning station is one of the most important places of all.
Question: What do cleaner wrasse feed on?
Option A: parasites, dead skin and scraps of food
Option B: coral, seaweed and tiny shellfish
Option C: the eggs of larger reef fish
Option D: small fish that live near the bommie

You might expect the big fish to snap its jaws shut. It doesn't. Instead, it waits patiently until the little fish swims out again.
The small fish is a bluestreak cleaner wrasse, and it is doing its job. Cleaner wrasse feed on parasites, dead skin and scraps of food that cling to larger fish. A wrasse, or a small group of them, sets up a 'cleaning station' at a particular spot on the reef, such as a bommie or a coral ledge. Other fish, known as clients, visit to be cleaned, sometimes waiting their turn.
To advertise its services, a cleaner wrasse performs a bobbing, up-and-down swimming display. Clients signal that they are ready by holding still, opening their mouths or changing colour. Even large predators that would normally eat a fish this size, such as groupers, usually leave the cleaners alone. A busy wrasse may inspect well over a thousand clients in a single day.
The arrangement benefits both sides. The cleaner gets a steady supply of food, and the client gets rid of parasites that could make it sick. In experiments where cleaner wrasse were removed from small patches of reef, scientists later found fewer kinds of fish living there.
However, the relationship is not always perfectly honest. What cleaner wrasse really prefer to eat is the slimy mucus that protects a client's skin. Taking a bite of mucus hurts the client, which often jolts and swims away. Researchers have noticed something remarkable: cleaners tend to behave much better when other clients are waiting nearby and watching. Could a fish really care about its reputation?
There is also an impostor on the reef. The false cleaner blenny looks almost exactly like a cleaner wrasse, with the same stripes and colours. It even copies the bobbing dance. But when a client fish relaxes and waits to be cleaned, the blenny darts in and bites off a piece of fin before racing away.
Scientists are still trying to understand exactly how client fish tell a true cleaner from a fake one. What is clear is that, on a busy reef, the cleaning station is one of the most important places of all.

Time Capsules Made of Ice
Every winter, snow falls on the vast ice sheet that covers Antarctica. In the coldest parts of the continent, that snow almost never melts. Instead, each new layer presses down on the layers beneath it, squeezing them slowly into solid ice. Over hundreds of thousands of years, this process has built ice more than three kilometres thick. To scientists, this ice is far more than frozen water. It is a record of Earth's past, stacked layer upon layer like the pages of a book.
To read this record, scientists drill an ice core. A hollow drill bores down into the ice and brings up a long cylinder, usually about ten centimetres across. The core is cut into sections about a metre long, labelled carefully and kept frozen at all times, both on the ice and on the long journey back to laboratories. A single deep drilling project can take several summers to complete.
What makes ice cores so valuable is what is trapped inside them. As snow turns to ice, tiny bubbles of air are sealed in. These bubbles are samples of the atmosphere as it was when the ice formed. By measuring the gases in them, scientists can find out how much carbon dioxide was in the air thousands of years ago, long before anyone was able to measure it directly. The ice itself also holds clues about past temperatures, while thin bands of ash reveal when distant volcanoes erupted.
The oldest continuous ice core yet drilled, from a site called Dome C, reaches back about 800 000 years. It shows that Earth's climate has swung between long ice ages and warmer periods many times. It also shows that carbon dioxide levels rose and fell along with temperature. Today's carbon dioxide levels are higher than at any point in that entire record.
Scientists are not finished yet. Teams are now searching for ice that is more than a million years old, hoping to understand why the rhythm of the ice ages changed long ago. Finding the right spot is difficult. The ice must be very old, undisturbed and not melted at its base by heat from the rock below.
It may seem strange that some of the most important clues about our climate are hidden in the emptiest place on Earth. Yet in Antarctica, the past has been waiting quietly, frozen in place, for anyone patient enough to dig it up.

Lessons Over the Airwaves
Imagine starting the school day by switching on a radio instead of walking through a classroom door. For thousands of children growing up on remote cattle stations in outback Australia, that was exactly how school worked.
In the early twentieth century, families living hundreds of kilometres from the nearest town had very few ways to contact the outside world. In 1929, an engineer named Alfred Traeger invented a pedal-powered radio. By pumping two pedals with their feet, people could generate enough electricity to send messages, so homesteads without mains power could call the Flying Doctor Service in an emergency. The radio network soon became a lifeline for outback families.
Adelaide Miethke, an educator who had worked as a school inspector, noticed something about the way children used these radios. They loved chatting over the airwaves, yet many of them were taught at home by busy parents, and some had almost no contact with other children their age. Miethke believed the radio network could offer them something more: a real teacher and a class to belong to. She campaigned for the idea, and in 1951 the first School of the Air lessons were broadcast from the Flying Doctor base in Alice Springs.
Lessons were short and lively. A teacher in the studio would speak to a group of students scattered across an area larger than many countries. Children answered questions, sang songs and read aloud, waiting for their turn to speak because only one person could talk at a time. Between lessons, they completed written work, which was sent back and forth by mail plane or truck. Parents or hired tutors, often called home supervisors, sat beside the children and helped them with their daily work.
The technology has changed greatly since then. Today's students use satellite internet and video lessons, so they can see their teachers and classmates on screen. Many schools also hold gatherings once or twice a year, when families travel long distances so that students can finally meet their classmates face to face. For children who have shared lessons for months without ever standing in the same room, these meetings are often the highlight of the year.
School of the Air proved that distance did not have to mean missing out. It remains a uniquely Australian solution to the challenge of educating children in some of the loneliest places on Earth.

Option A: persuade families to move to remote cattle stations.
Option B: explain how to build and use a pedal-powered radio.
Option C: inform readers about how School of the Air began and changed.
Option D: entertain readers with a story about one outback child.

Rooms Full of Wonders
Walk into a modern museum and you will usually find neat glass cases, clear labels and objects arranged by type or age. Museums were not always so orderly. Four hundred years ago, many of them began as a single crowded room in a wealthy person's home, packed from floor to ceiling with anything its owner found strange or marvellous.
These rooms were called cabinets of curiosities. A collector might display a crocodile hanging from the ceiling beside seashells, rare coins, carved ivory, dried plants, ancient tools and the bones of creatures nobody could identify. Some objects were real treasures. Others were mistakes or even fakes. Visitors were sometimes shown 'dragon' skeletons and 'mermaid' remains that had been stitched together from parts of different animals.
Why would anyone collect such a jumble? In the 1500s and 1600s, European travellers were returning from voyages with plants, animals and objects that most people had never seen before. Collectors wanted to gather the whole world into one room, so that they could study it, compare things and, of course, impress their guests.
One famous collector was Ole Worm, a Danish doctor who lived from 1588 to 1654. His museum in Copenhagen held thousands of items. At the time, many Europeans believed that long, spiralled tusks came from unicorns and had magical healing powers. Worm examined these tusks carefully and showed that they actually came from the narwhal, a small whale of the Arctic seas. His collection was a place for testing ideas, not just for admiring objects.
Over time, some private collections grew into public institutions. In England, a collection gathered by a father and son, both named John Tradescant, passed to a man named Elias Ashmole. In 1683 it went on display at the University of Oxford as the Ashmolean Museum, one of the first museums in the world open to the public.
So the next time you wander past a display of fossils or ancient pottery, spare a thought for those cluttered old rooms. Their owners did not always get things right. Yet their curiosity, and their urge to collect, sort and share, laid the foundations for the museums we enjoy today.

Option B: Most objects in the cabinets were valuable coins and carved ivory.
Option C: Cabinets of curiosities held a mix of real, mistaken and fake objects.
Option D: Dragons and mermaids were common creatures in the 1600s.

The Slowest Job in the World
The bone was smaller than my hand, and I had been working on it for three days.
'Patience, Mia,' said Aunt Leonie, without looking up from her own workbench. 'That rock has been sitting there for a hundred million years. It can wait another afternoon.'
I adjusted my magnifying lamp and went back to scraping. The tool I was using looked like a dentist's pick. Each stroke removed a crumb of grey stone no bigger than a grain of sugar. Around me, the fossil laboratory hummed with the sound of fans and the quiet tapping of volunteers bent over their own blocks of rock.
It had all started two weeks earlier, at the dig site on a sheep station west of town. The ground there was cracked and bare, and heat shimmered off it in waves. We had spent most of the morning finding nothing but pebbles. Then, just before lunch, I noticed a dark, glossy edge poking out of the dirt near my boot. I almost walked past it. When Aunt Leonie saw it, she went very still, then knelt and brushed away the soil with her fingers.
'Well done,' she said softly. 'That's bone.'
The block of rock was wrapped in plaster, like a broken arm, and carried back to the laboratory on the back of a truck. I had imagined that we would simply crack it open and pull out a skeleton. Instead, Aunt Leonie handed me the pick and showed me how to remove the rock one tiny flake at a time.
Now, on the third afternoon, something changed. As I brushed away the dust, a smooth curve appeared, then a ridge, then a row of tiny pits along the surface. I held my breath.
'Aunt Leonie,' I whispered. 'I think it's a joint.'
She came over and leaned in close to the lamp. For a long moment she said nothing. Then she smiled, wider than I had ever seen her smile.
'It's the end of a toe bone,' she said. 'Do you know what that means? Where there's one toe, there might be a foot. And where there's a foot . . .'
She didn't need to finish. I looked down at the little grey bone, and suddenly three days didn't seem slow at all. It seemed like the beginning of something.
I picked up my tool and leaned closer to the lamp.

Option A: The laboratory was about to close for the day.
Option B: The work of uncovering the bone could not be rushed.
Option C: Mia was making too much noise with her tool.

Pack a Beanie: The Case for Winter Camping
Ask most Australian families when they go camping, and they will say the summer holidays. It makes sense. The days are long, the weather is warm and school is out. But I believe that families who pack away their tents when the weather cools are missing out on the best camping of the year. It is time to give winter camping a chance.
First, consider the crowds, or rather the lack of them. In January, popular campgrounds are booked out months ahead. Tents are squeezed together so tightly that you can hear your neighbours snoring. In June or July, many of those same campgrounds are almost empty. You can choose the best site, wander along quiet tracks and hear nothing at night but the wind in the trees.
Second, winter is often more comfortable than summer. Anyone who has tried to sleep in a tent on a 35-degree night knows how miserable it can be. In many parts of Australia, winter days are mild and sunny, perfect for long walks without the risk of heatstroke. There are fewer flies and mosquitoes to battle, too. When the temperature drops after dark, a good sleeping bag and a woolly beanie will keep you snug.
Third, winter brings experiences that summer simply cannot offer. With fire restrictions often eased in the cooler months, many campgrounds allow campfires, where families can gather to talk, cook and toast marshmallows. Long, dark nights mean you can see the stars well before bedtime. On a clear winter night, away from city lights, the Milky Way spills across the sky like a river of sugar.
Some people will argue that winter camping is too cold and too wet. It is true that you need to be prepared. Pack warm layers, a waterproof jacket and a tent that can handle rain, and always check the weather forecast before you leave. But a little preparation is a small price to pay. After all, as the saying goes, there is no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong clothes.
So this winter, don't let your tent gather dust in the garage. Pack your beanie, grab your thermos and head outdoors. You may find that the coldest season gives you the warmest memories.

Option A: The days are too short for long walks.
Option B: Most walking tracks are closed to visitors.
Option C: Tents often leak during summer storms.
Option D: Campgrounds are crowded and booked out early.

Seven Down
Grandpa Ray loved puzzles more than anyone I knew. Every morning he did the crossword in the newspaper with a blue pen, never a pencil, and he refused to check the answers until the next day. So when he announced that he had hidden my birthday present, I should have known it would not be easy to find.
'It's somewhere in this house,' he said, handing me a folded square of paper. 'Solve this, and you'll know where to look.'
It was a small, home-made crossword. Every answer had already been filled in with his neat capital letters except one: Seven Down. The clue read: It has plenty of keys but opens no doors (5).
'Keys,' I said at once. 'Easy.' I raced to the hook by the back door where Mum kept the house keys and the car keys. Nothing was hanging there except keys. I checked the drawer underneath. Batteries, string, a broken torch. No present.
Grandpa watched me from his armchair, sipping his tea. 'Did you count the letters?' he asked mildly.
I hadn't. I went back to the grid. Five letters. The second letter had to be an I, because it crossed Four Across, and the last letter had to be an O, because it crossed Nine Across.
I said every word I could think of that ended in O. Radio. Hello. Patio. None of them had keys. I lay on the rug and stared at the ceiling, completely stuck, while Grandpa hummed a tune and tapped his fingers on the arm of his chair as if he were playing something.
Then I sat up.
He was playing something. Not on the chair, of course, but in his head. And in the corner of the lounge room, covered in photo frames and Grandma's lace cloth, stood the one thing in the house that had eighty-eight keys and had never opened a single door.
'Piano!' I shouted. P, I, A, N, O. It fitted perfectly.
I lifted the lid of the old piano stool. Inside, on top of a pile of yellowed music books, lay a small parcel wrapped in newspaper. Of course it was newspaper. On the front, in blue pen, Grandpa had written one word: Congratulations.
'You took eleven minutes,' he said, checking his watch. 'Not bad. I took eight to write it.'
Inside the parcel was a thick book of crosswords, and a brand-new blue pen.

Option A: in an angry voice.
Option B: in a calm, gentle way.
Option C: very loudly.
Option D: in a worried way.

Helmet Season
Every spring, the magpie in the big gum tree on Wattle Lane went to war with Leo Fischer.
At least, that was how Leo saw it. For three weeks each September, he could not ride to school without hearing the snap of a beak and the whoosh of black-and-white wings just above his head. He had tried everything. He had stuck cable ties to his helmet so they stood up like spikes. He had ridden the long way round. He had even pedalled past at top speed, yelling, which only seemed to make things worse.
'He's got it in for me,' Leo told his neighbour, Mrs Okafor, one afternoon. She was weeding her front garden, right beneath the gum tree.
Mrs Okafor sat back on her heels. 'He doesn't hate you, love. He's a dad. See up there?' She pointed with her trowel. High in a fork of the tree, Leo could just make out a messy bowl of sticks. Something inside it was squawking. 'Three chicks. He's just making sure nobody gets too close.'
'But I'm not trying to hurt them.'
'He doesn't know that. To him, you're a big, fast stranger who rushes past twice a day.' She smiled. 'Magpies remember faces, you know. If you give him a reason to trust you, he might leave you alone.'
Leo was doubtful, but over the next week he tried something different. Instead of racing past, he walked his bike slowly beneath the tree. He kept his eyes down and didn't wave his arms. Sometimes he stopped to chat with Mrs Okafor, and the magpie watched from a low branch, head tilted.
On the eighth day, Leo realised he had walked all the way under the tree without a single swoop.
By October, the chicks had left the nest. Leo would see them hopping about the park with their father, making wobbly, gargling attempts at a song. One afternoon, as he sat on the kerb fixing his bike chain, the magpie landed a few metres away and stood there, watching him with one bright reddish-brown eye.
Leo looked back. Neither of them moved.
'Truce?' Leo said quietly.
The magpie warbled a long, rolling note, then flew back to its tree. Leo decided to take that as a yes.
The next spring, he left the cable ties in the garage.
Question: What had Leo stuck to his helmet?
Option A: plastic spikes
Option B: black feathers
Option C: reflective stickers
Option D: cable ties

The Red Wall
The Year 6 relay was supposed to be the highlight of the Coober Creek sports carnival. Tasha had been practising her baton change for weeks, and as she stood at the edge of the dusty oval, she could feel her heart thumping.
It was the hottest day of the term. There had been no rain for months, and the paddocks beyond the school fence were bare and cracked. A hot wind had been blowing from the north since breakfast, flicking grit into everyone's eyes.
'Runners, take your places!' called Mr Hassan through his megaphone.
Tasha crouched at the start line. Then she noticed that the sky to the west looked strange. The horizon had turned a deep, rusty orange, and above it rose a dark, rolling cloud that seemed to stretch from one end of the earth to the other.
'Sir?' she called. 'What's that?'
Mr Hassan lowered his megaphone. For a moment he just stared. Then he blew three short blasts on his whistle, the signal everyone at Coober Creek knew by heart.
'Dust storm! Everyone inside, now. Walk, don't run!'
There was a scramble of hats, drink bottles and folding chairs. Teachers herded the younger children towards the hall while parents grabbed picnic rugs. Tasha helped a kindergarten boy who had dropped his sandwich and was crying about it. By the time the hall doors closed behind them, the light outside had turned the colour of a ripe mandarin.
Then the storm hit. Wind hammered the windows, and the world outside disappeared into a swirling red haze. Dust crept in under the doors and settled on the floor like fine paprika. Somebody's mum handed out damp paper towels so people could breathe through them.
It lasted nearly an hour. When the wind finally dropped and the doors opened again, the town looked as if it had been painted red. Cars, roofs and the finish-line tape were all coated in a thick layer of dust. The oval was covered in small red drifts.
'Well,' said Mr Hassan, brushing off his hat, 'I suppose the relay will have to wait until next week.'
Tasha looked at the red drifts and grinned. She had spent so much time worrying about dropping the baton. Compared with a wall of dust as tall as the sky, a baton change didn't seem so frightening any more.
Question: What signal did Mr Hassan give to warn everyone about the storm?
Option A: one long blast on his whistle
Option B: a warning through his megaphone
Option C: three rings of the school bell
Option D: three short blasts on his whistle

The Year 6 relay was supposed to be the highlight of the Coober Creek sports carnival. Tasha had been practising her baton change for weeks, and as she stood at the edge of the dusty oval, she could feel her heart thumping.
It was the hottest day of the term. There had been no rain for months, and the paddocks beyond the school fence were bare and cracked. A hot wind had been blowing from the north since breakfast, flicking grit into everyone's eyes.
'Runners, take your places!' called Mr Hassan through his megaphone.
Tasha crouched at the start line. Then she noticed that the sky to the west looked strange. The horizon had turned a deep, rusty orange, and above it rose a dark, rolling cloud that seemed to stretch from one end of the earth to the other.
'Sir?' she called. 'What's that?'
Mr Hassan lowered his megaphone. For a moment he just stared. Then he blew three short blasts on his whistle, the signal everyone at Coober Creek knew by heart.
'Dust storm! Everyone inside, now. Walk, don't run!'
There was a scramble of hats, drink bottles and folding chairs. Teachers herded the younger children towards the hall while parents grabbed picnic rugs. Tasha helped a kindergarten boy who had dropped his sandwich and was crying about it. By the time the hall doors closed behind them, the light outside had turned the colour of a ripe mandarin.
Then the storm hit. Wind hammered the windows, and the world outside disappeared into a swirling red haze. Dust crept in under the doors and settled on the floor like fine paprika. Somebody's mum handed out damp paper towels so people could breathe through them.
It lasted nearly an hour. When the wind finally dropped and the doors opened again, the town looked as if it had been painted red. Cars, roofs and the finish-line tape were all coated in a thick layer of dust. The oval was covered in small red drifts.
'Well,' said Mr Hassan, brushing off his hat, 'I suppose the relay will have to wait until next week.'
Tasha looked at the red drifts and grinned. She had spent so much time worrying about dropping the baton. Compared with a wall of dust as tall as the sky, a baton change didn't seem so frightening any more.
Question: What is the main idea of the paragraph that begins 'Then the storm hit'?
Option A: A parent handed out damp paper towels to everyone.
Option B: The strong wind broke the windows of the school hall.
Option C: The storm was fierce and filled the air with dust.
Option D: The hall was a fun place for children to play.

Every Single Leaf
For as long as Amira could remember, trees had been soft green clouds. She had never thought about it. Trees were simply blurry at the top, the same way the whiteboard was blurry from the back row and faces were blurry across the playground. That was just how the world looked.
It was Mr Delaney who first noticed something was wrong. He saw Amira squinting at the board during maths and asked her to read out a sum. She guessed, and got it wrong. Later he asked her to move closer, and she read it perfectly.
'I think Amira should get her eyes tested,' he told her mum that afternoon.
At the optometrist, Amira sat in a big chair while a friendly woman named Dr Shah asked her to read rows of letters on a chart. The top row was easy. By the fourth row, the letters had melted into grey smudges. Dr Shah clicked different lenses in front of her eyes. 'Better like this, or like this?' she asked again and again, until suddenly the bottom rows sharpened into crisp black letters.
'You're short-sighted,' Dr Shah explained. 'Your eyes focus well on things that are close, but things far away look fuzzy. Glasses will bend the light so that it focuses properly.'
A week later, Amira's new glasses were ready. They had red frames, which she had chosen herself. She put them on in the shop and blinked. Then she walked outside.
The world exploded into detail.
The car parked across the road had a number plate she could actually read. A woman at the bus stop had freckles. And the tree on the corner, the same tree she had walked past a hundred times, was not a cloud at all. It was made of leaves, thousands and thousands of separate leaves, each one trembling on its own tiny stem. Some were bright green, some were dark, and a few at the edges had turned yellow.
Amira stood on the footpath with her mouth open.
'Are you all right?' Mum asked.
'The tree,' Amira whispered. 'It has leaves. Every single one.'
Mum laughed, then stopped, her eyes suddenly shiny. She seemed to realise how much Amira had been missing without anyone knowing.
That night, Amira wrote in her diary: Today I saw a tree for the first time. It was much better than I expected.
Question: Who first noticed that Amira might have trouble seeing?
Option A: her mum
Option B: Dr Shah, the optometrist
Option C: Amira herself
Option D: her teacher, Mr Delaney

Twenty-Two Yards of Grass
Before the first ball of a cricket match is bowled, someone has already spent weeks getting the pitch ready. That person is the curator, and the strip of ground they care for is only about 20 metres long and 3 metres wide. Yet it may be the most closely watched patch of grass in any sport.
What a curator does
A curator looks after the whole ground, from the outfield to the practice nets, but the centre pitch is the most important part of the job. The ball usually bounces off the pitch before it reaches the batter, so the pitch affects every delivery. If it is too soft, the ball barely bounces. If it is too hard and cracked, the bounce can become uneven and dangerous.
Preparing a pitch
Work on a match pitch often begins two to three weeks before the game. The curator first waters the strip deeply so that moisture soaks well down into the clay soil. Next comes rolling. A heavy roller moves slowly up and down the strip, again and again, squeezing out air and packing the soil tightly together. As the days pass, the curator waters less and rolls more, so the surface gradually becomes firm.
The grass is mown shorter and shorter until only a few millimetres remain, but its roots still help to hold the soil together. Leaving a little extra grass usually helps fast bowlers, because the ball can grip and move sideways. A drier, barer pitch tends to help spin bowlers, especially late in a long match when the surface begins to crumble.
Watching the weather
Rain is a curator's biggest worry. If a storm is forecast, covers are rolled out over the pitch. A soaked pitch can delay play for hours, while a sudden heatwave can dry the surface out too quickly. Many curators check the forecast several times a day in the week before a big match.
Becoming a curator
Most curators complete a turf management course and spend years working under an experienced head curator. The hours are long, the work starts early, and much of it happens alone on an empty ground.
"Nobody claps for the pitch," says Dave, who has looked after a country ground for eighteen years. "If the game goes well, nobody mentions me. If the ball keeps low, everyone knows my name by lunchtime." He admits that the first morning of a match still makes his stomach flutter. "Once the first over is bowled and the ball carries nicely through to the keeper, I can finally have my breakfast."
Question: About how long is the pitch a curator prepares?
Option A: 20 metres
Option B: 3 metres
Option C: 22 metres
Option D: 200 metres

Before the first ball of a cricket match is bowled, someone has already spent weeks getting the pitch ready. That person is the curator, and the strip of ground they care for is only about 20 metres long and 3 metres wide. Yet it may be the most closely watched patch of grass in any sport.

Preparing a pitch
Work on a match pitch often begins two to three weeks before the game. The curator first waters the strip deeply so that moisture soaks well down into the clay soil. Next comes rolling. A heavy roller moves slowly up and down the strip, again and again, squeezing out air and packing the soil tightly together. As the days pass, the curator waters less and rolls more, so the surface gradually becomes firm.
The grass is mown shorter and shorter until only a few millimetres remain, but its roots still help to hold the soil together. Leaving a little extra grass usually helps fast bowlers, because the ball can grip and move sideways. A drier, barer pitch tends to help spin bowlers, especially late in a long match when the surface begins to crumble.
Watching the weather
Rain is a curator's biggest worry. If a storm is forecast, covers are rolled out over the pitch. A soaked pitch can delay play for hours, while a sudden heatwave can dry the surface out too quickly. Many curators check the forecast several times a day in the week before a big match.

Four-Winged Hunters
If you have ever sat beside a pond on a summer afternoon, you have probably seen a dragonfly zipping over the water like a tiny jet. It is easy to admire their shimmering wings and bright colours. But do not be fooled by their beauty. Dragonflies are among the most successful hunters in the animal kingdom.
Ancient flyers
Dragonflies have been around for an astonishingly long time. Their ancestors were flying through forests about 300 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs appeared. Some of those early relatives were giants, with wings that stretched about 70 centimetres from tip to tip. Scientists think the air at that time held more oxygen than it does today, which may have helped insects grow so large.
Masters of the air
A dragonfly has four wings, and each one is powered by its own set of muscles, so it can move each wing separately. As a result, a dragonfly can hover, fly backwards and change direction in an instant.
Its eyes are just as impressive. Each huge compound eye is made up of thousands of tiny lenses, and together the two eyes wrap almost all the way around its head. A dragonfly can see in nearly every direction at once, tracking a small fly as it darts through the air.
Put these skills together and you have a remarkable predator. In some studies, dragonflies caught their prey in more than nine out of every ten attempts. Lions, by comparison, succeed only about a quarter of the time.
A secret life underwater
Most people never see the longest part of a dragonfly's life. Dragonflies lay their eggs in or near water, and the young, called nymphs, live beneath the surface for months or even years. A nymph is a fierce hunter too. It has a hinged lower lip that shoots forward in a fraction of a second to grab tadpoles, small fish and insect larvae.
When it is fully grown, the nymph climbs up a reed, splits its skin and slowly pulls out its new body and crumpled wings. Within hours, a new adult takes to the sky.
So the next time a dragonfly flashes past you, take a moment to watch. You are looking at one of nature's most ancient and skilful hunters, and I think that is something worth stopping for.

The Devil That Drinks Through Its Skin
With its body covered in sharp spikes and a strange lump on the back of its neck, the thorny devil looks like a creature from a fantasy film. Yet this small lizard, which grows to only about 20 centimetres long, is completely harmless to people. It lives in the sandy deserts and dry scrublands of western and central Australia, and its unusual features are all about one thing: surviving in a harsh land.
Spikes and a false head
Thorny devils move slowly, so they cannot easily run from predators such as birds of prey and goannas. Instead, they rely on defence. Their spikes make them difficult and painful to swallow. When threatened, a thorny devil tucks its real head down between its front legs. This leaves the knobbly lump on its neck sticking up, where it looks like a head. A predator that bites this 'false head' may get a mouthful of spikes instead.
Colour helps too. A thorny devil can change its colouring, becoming paler in the heat and darker in cooler weather. Its patterns of brown, red and yellow help it blend into the sand.
A diet of ants
The thorny devil eats almost nothing but small black ants. It sits beside an ant trail and flicks them up with its tongue, one at a time. Because each ant is so tiny, a thorny devil may eat thousands of them in a single day.
Drinking with its skin
The most remarkable thing about the thorny devil is the way it collects water. Rain is rare in its habitat, and there are few pools to drink from. However, between the scales on its skin are tiny grooves. When the lizard touches damp sand or dew, water is drawn into these grooves and travels along them without any effort from the lizard. The grooves lead to the corners of its mouth, where the lizard gulps the water down.
Scientists have studied the thorny devil's skin closely. Some are exploring whether surfaces inspired by its grooves could one day help collect and move water for people in dry places.
The thorny devil may look fierce, but it is a gentle, patient animal. Every feature of its prickly body tells a story about life in one of the driest places on Earth.

Option A: small black ants
Option B: beetles and spiders
Option C: desert plants and seeds
Option D: smaller lizards

Mia had pictured wombats waddling about in the sunshine, but on her first afternoon at Epping Forest National Park, she didn't see a single one.
'They're asleep,' said her mum, who was one of the rangers. 'Northern hairy-nosed wombats spend the day underground. They come out at night to graze, and they're very shy.'
The park was a stretch of dry, open woodland in central Queensland, surrounded by a tall wire fence. Mum explained that the fence had been built to keep out wild dogs. In the early 1980s, only about thirty-five of these wombats were left on Earth, all of them here. Now there were more than three hundred, and a second group had been started far away in case something went wrong in this one.
'So how do you count them,' Mia asked, 'if they're always hiding?'
Mum held up a roll of double-sided sticky tape. 'With this.'
Late that afternoon, they walked from burrow to burrow, stretching a strip of tape across each entrance, a little above the ground, between two small wooden pegs. Mia's job was to write the burrow number in the notebook and check that each strip was tight.
'When a wombat comes out tonight,' Mum said, 'it'll brush under the tape, and a few hairs will stick. We don't need to catch it or even see it.'
At sunrise, they went back. Some strips were empty. Others held small grey tufts, as soft as cotton wool. Mia used tweezers to drop each tuft into a paper envelope, then wrote the burrow number and the date on the front.
'The hairs go to a laboratory,' Mum explained. 'Scientists can read the DNA in them, and every wombat's DNA is different. That tells us which wombat used which burrow, and how many there are altogether.'
By the end of the week, Mia had filled forty-two envelopes. She had still not seen a wombat.
On the last night, as they drove slowly towards the gate, Mum suddenly stopped the car. In the headlights, a broad, furry shape was munching grass beside the track. It lifted its square nose, blinked at them, and trundled calmly into the dark.
Mia let out her breath. 'Hello, number forty-two,' she whispered.
Mum laughed. 'You can't know that.'
'No,' said Mia, smiling. 'But the laboratory will.'
Question: Which of these events happened first?
Option A: Mia dropped grey tufts of hair into paper envelopes
Option B: Mia and Mum stretched tape across the burrow entrances
Option C: a wombat appeared in the headlights beside the track
Option D: Mia finished filling her forty-second envelope

The park was a stretch of dry, open woodland in central Queensland, surrounded by a tall wire fence. Mum explained that the fence had been built to keep out wild dogs. In the early 1980s, only about thirty-five of these wombats were left on Earth, all of them here. Now there were more than three hundred, and a second group had been started far away in case something went wrong in this one.
'So how do you count them,' Mia asked, 'if they're always hiding?'
Mum held up a roll of double-sided sticky tape. 'With this.'
Late that afternoon, they walked from burrow to burrow, stretching a strip of tape across each entrance, a little above the ground, between two small wooden pegs. Mia's job was to write the burrow number in the notebook and check that each strip was tight.
'When a wombat comes out tonight,' Mum said, 'it'll brush under the tape, and a few hairs will stick. We don't need to catch it or even see it.'

A Whisper Across the Water
Dear Callum,
You will never guess what I heard on Saturday. Actually, you might, because it was a voice I know very well, but it came from about a hundred and forty metres away.
Mum, Dad and I drove out to the Barossa Reservoir, which is a big lake in the hills north-east of Adelaide. The lake is held back by a dam wall that was finished in 1902. From the top, the wall doesn't look special. It's just a long, curved concrete wall with a path along it. But everyone calls it the Whispering Wall, and now I know why.
Dad stayed at one end of the wall while Mum and I walked all the way to the other end. When we got there, Dad looked tiny, like a toy figure. Then I heard his voice, right next to my ear, saying, 'Can you hear me, Isla? Don't look so surprised.' I actually spun around, because I thought someone was standing behind me. Nobody was there.
Mum explained it on the way home. The wall is curved like a giant bowl turned on its side. When you speak quietly close to the wall at one end, the sound waves don't just spread out and fade away. They hug the curve of the wall, bouncing along it again and again, until they arrive at the other end. Because the sound stays close to the wall, it doesn't get spread thin across the open air, so it is still loud enough to hear clearly. The engineers who built the dam weren't trying to make it do this, though. They chose the curved shape because it made the wall strong enough to hold back all that water.
The funny part was that I could only hear Dad properly if I stood right against the concrete. When I stepped back just two big steps, his voice disappeared into the wind. A boy near us kept shouting from the middle of the path and getting cross that his sister, at the far end, couldn't hear a word. I wanted to explain, but he didn't look like he wanted advice.
I've attached a photo of Dad at the far end. He's the little dot on the left. Next time you visit, we'll go together, and you can whisper a secret to me from across the lake.
Your cousin,
Isla

Instead of staying in one classroom, secondary students move between rooms for different subjects, such as science in a laboratory, art in a studio and physical education in the gym. A bell, or sometimes a recorded tone, marks the end of each lesson. Students might see five or six teachers in a single day, and each teacher has their own expectations about homework and equipment.
Many schools give new students a locker. This sounds simple, but learning to pack the right books for each part of the day takes practice. 'In my first week I carried every single book in my bag because I was scared of forgetting something,' remembers Amira, now in Year 8. 'My shoulders were sore by Wednesday. Then I started checking my timetable each morning, and it was fine.'
Secondary schools are also usually much bigger. A Year 7 group alone might have more students than an entire primary school. Some students find this exciting, while others feel lost. Ben, who started Year 7 last year, admits he spent his first lunchtimes alone in the library. 'I didn't know anyone, and the playground felt enormous. Then I joined the chess club, and suddenly I had people to sit with. I wish I'd done it in the first week instead of the fifth.'
To help, many schools run transition days near the end of Year 6, when students tour the buildings, meet teachers and practise reading a timetable. Some also give each Year 7 student an older buddy who can answer questions such as where the canteen is or what to do if they get lost.
Teachers say the most useful thing new students can do is ask for help early. Nobody expects a Year 7 student to know everything on the first day. Every student in the senior years once stood in the same corridor, holding a crumpled map and wondering which way to go.
