Option A: an important stage or event
Option B: a very long distance
Option C: a difficult final test
Option D: a heavy responsibility

The Southern Wren Logbook
Monday
Day one on the Southern Wren, and I have already been seasick twice. Our sail training ship is a two-masted brigantine with eighteen young crew, all aged between twelve and sixteen, plus six adults who actually know what they are doing. We sailed out of Port Phillip Heads this afternoon, and the water turned from calm green to big grey swells almost straight away. Captain Rhee says my stomach will get used to it. My stomach disagrees.
Tuesday
Today I took my first turn at the helm. Steering a ship is nothing like steering a bike. You turn the wheel, and for a long, worrying moment nothing happens. Then the bow swings much further than you wanted. The trick is to make tiny corrections early and to keep your eyes on the compass rather than the waves. Our course was 095, which means just south of due east. I kept drifting to 100, and the watch leader kept saying, 'Gently, Lena, gently.'
Wednesday
No land in sight all day. The first mate, Sione, showed us how sailors worked out their position before satellites. It is called dead reckoning. You start from a known position, then use your speed, your direction and the time that has passed to calculate where you must be now. Every hour we wrote our speed and heading in the logbook and marked a small cross on the chart. 'If you don't write it down,' Sione said, 'you might as well be lost.' He made it sound like a joke, but nobody laughed.
Thursday
At dawn, a dark smudge appeared exactly where our crosses on the chart said it would be. It was Wilsons Promontory. I felt as proud as if I had built it myself. Sione pointed out that the GPS had known where we were the whole time, but he also said that screens can fail and pencils almost never do.
Friday
We are anchored in a calm bay tonight, and I haven't been sick since Tuesday. This afternoon I steered for a whole hour without a single 'gently'. I keep thinking about the sailors long ago who crossed entire oceans with only a compass, a clock and a pencil. Before this week, I thought that sounded simple. Now I think it sounds brave.
Question: What is the diary mainly about?
Option A: the history of sailing ships in Bass Strait
Option B: the best ways to cure seasickness at sea
Option C: Lena's week learning to sail and navigate a ship
Option D: the reasons GPS is better than a compass

What the Waterbugs Told Us
A report by Class 6K, Millbrook Primary School
Aim
Our aim was to find out whether Millbrook Creek is healthier above the town or below it. Instead of testing the water with chemicals, we studied the small animals living in it, called macroinvertebrates, or waterbugs.
Why waterbugs?
Different waterbugs can survive different amounts of pollution. Mayfly and stonefly nymphs need clean water with plenty of oxygen, so finding them is a good sign. Worms and midge larvae can live in dirtier water. By seeing which bugs live in a creek, scientists can judge how healthy it has been over many weeks, not just on the day of the test.
Method
1. We chose two sites: Site A, upstream of the town near the walking track, and Site B, downstream beside the drain from the shopping centre car park.
2. At each site, one person held a fine net on the creek bed while another gently kicked the stones just upstream for one minute, so that bugs were washed into the net.
3. We emptied the net into a white tray with a little creek water. The white background made small bugs easier to see.
4. Using magnifying glasses and an identification chart, we sorted and counted the bugs.
5. We returned every bug to the creek where we found it.
Results
At Site A we found 14 mayfly nymphs, 6 stonefly nymphs, 9 caddisfly larvae and 3 worms. At Site B we found no stoneflies, 2 mayfly nymphs, 21 midge larvae and 17 worms.
Discussion
Site A had many pollution-sensitive bugs, which suggests clean water. Site B had mostly tolerant bugs, which suggests the water there is affected by something. After a storm, we noticed oily rainbows on the water near the drain, which may be part of the cause.
Mr Kelly reminded us that one sample is not enough to be certain. Hamish suggested adding a third site halfway between the two, so we could see where the change begins. Grace asked if we could test in every season, because her uncle had told her that waterbug numbers change through the year.
Conclusion
Our results suggest that Millbrook Creek is healthier above the town than below it. We plan to share our report with the local council and ask whether the car park drain could be fitted with a filter.
Question: Why did the class use a white tray?
Option A: The white plastic kept the creek water cool.
Option B: The tray matched the colours on the chart.
Option C: The bugs were less likely to escape from it.
Option D: The white background made small bugs easier to see.

Our aim was to find out whether Millbrook Creek is healthier above the town or below it. Instead of testing the water with chemicals, we studied the small animals living in it, called macroinvertebrates, or waterbugs.
Why waterbugs?
Different waterbugs can survive different amounts of pollution. Mayfly and stonefly nymphs need clean water with plenty of oxygen, so finding them is a good sign. Worms and midge larvae can live in dirtier water. By seeing which bugs live in a creek, scientists can judge how healthy it has been over many weeks, not just on the day of the test.
Method
1. We chose two sites: Site A, upstream of the town near the walking track, and Site B, downstream beside the drain from the shopping centre car park.
2. At each site, one person held a fine net on the creek bed while another gently kicked the stones just upstream for one minute, so that bugs were washed into the net.
3. We emptied the net into a white tray with a little creek water. The white background made small bugs easier to see.
4. Using magnifying glasses and an identification chart, we sorted and counted the bugs.
5. We returned every bug to the creek where we found it.
Results
At Site A we found 14 mayfly nymphs, 6 stonefly nymphs, 9 caddisfly larvae and 3 worms. At Site B we found no stoneflies, 2 mayfly nymphs, 21 midge larvae and 17 worms.
Discussion
Site A had many pollution-sensitive bugs, which suggests clean water. Site B had mostly tolerant bugs, which suggests the water there is affected by something. After a storm, we noticed oily rainbows on the water near the drain, which may be part of the cause.
Mr Kelly reminded us that one sample is not enough to be certain. Hamish suggested adding a third site halfway between the two, so we could see where the change begins. Grace asked if we could test in every season, because her uncle had told her that waterbug numbers change through the year.
Conclusion
Our results suggest that Millbrook Creek is healthier above the town than below it. We plan to share our report with the local council and ask whether the car park drain could be fitted with a filter.

Three Plants, One Patch
Most vegetable gardens keep each crop in its own neat row. For centuries, however, many Indigenous peoples of North America grew three crops together in the same small mound: corn, climbing beans and squash. The Haudenosaunee people, among others, call these plants the Three Sisters, and the way they help each other is a clever lesson in gardening.
The planting happens in stages. First, corn seeds are planted in a low mound of soil. When the corn seedlings are about a hand's width tall, beans are planted around them. A little later, squash seeds go in around the edge of the mound.
Each sister has a job. The corn grows tall and straight, so it acts as a living pole for the beans to climb. Without the corn, the bean vines would sprawl across the ground, where their pods could rot or be eaten. The beans, meanwhile, help to feed the soil. Tiny bacteria living in lumps on bean roots can take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use. Corn is a hungry plant that needs plenty of nitrogen, so having beans nearby helps to keep the soil fertile.
The squash has the lowest job but an important one. Its broad, prickly leaves spread across the ground like umbrellas. They shade the soil, which keeps it moist and makes it harder for weeds to grow. The prickles on the stems also discourage some animals from wandering through the patch.
The three crops work together in the kitchen as well as the garden. Corn, beans and squash together provide a more balanced diet than any one of them alone, and all three can be dried and stored for winter.
Gardeners today still try the Three Sisters method, although results vary. If the beans are planted too early, their vines can pull young corn plants over before the stalks are strong. In dry climates, gardeners sometimes plant in a shallow hollow instead of a mound, so that rainwater collects around the roots.
The Three Sisters show that a garden does not have to be a collection of plants competing for space. With careful planning, it can be a team.

Option A: Corn is the most important crop in any vegetable garden.
Option B: Corn, beans and squash grown together help each other to grow.
Option C: Squash leaves protect a garden from every kind of animal.
Option D: Beans should always be planted before corn in a mound.

No Whistle
The score was nine-all, and the next point would decide the grand final.
Mei crouched at the end line with the rest of the Kookaburras, her heart thumping. Across the field, the Harbour Hawks were huddled together, arms around each other's shoulders. There was no referee waiting to blow a whistle. In Ultimate, there never was. The players made every call themselves, and after each game, both teams gave each other a score for fairness and good spirit as well as for skill.
Mei had always liked that rule. Today, it made her nervous.
The Hawks threw off, and the disc floated high and slow towards her. She caught it cleanly and pivoted, looking for a teammate. Raff was cutting hard down the left side. Mei flicked the disc low and fast, and it curved past a defender's fingertips into his hands.
They worked it up the field, pass after pass, nobody holding the disc for more than a few seconds. Then Mei found herself sprinting towards the end zone, with the disc spinning towards her and a tall Hawks player named Jonah racing beside her.
They both leapt. Mei felt Jonah's arm bump hers just as the disc reached her fingers, and it bounced off her hand onto the grass.
'Foul,' she called, almost without thinking.
Jonah stopped. For a long moment, everyone waited. Mei's teammates were already shouting that it was obvious. A Hawks parent on the sideline groaned loudly.
Then Jonah nodded. 'Yeah. I hit your arm. Fair call.'
The disc went back to Mei. On the next throw, she caught it in the end zone. The Kookaburras exploded off the line, cheering, and Mei disappeared under a pile of teammates.
Later, after the medals were handed out, the two teams sat together in a circle on the grass, as they always did. The Hawks captain stood up first. 'Our spirit award goes to Mei,' she said, 'for making a tough call calmly and honestly.'
Then Raff stood. 'And ours goes to Jonah,' he said, 'for owning up when it mattered most.'
Mei looked across the circle. Jonah grinned and gave her a small wave. She realised that she would remember that moment longer than the winning catch.
Question: In Ultimate, who makes the calls during a game?
Option A: a referee with a whistle
Option B: the players themselves
Option C: the team captains only
Option D: the parents on the sideline

The Plate Path
The path to Aunty Vi's front door is made of broken plates. If you walk along it slowly, you can see blue willow patterns, pieces of a yellow teapot, half a cartoon rabbit from my old breakfast bowl and, near the step, a white fragment with a gold edge. That piece is mine. I mean, it is my fault.
Two summers ago, I was helping Aunty Vi carry her good dinner set out to the verandah for Nana's birthday. It was the set with the thin gold rim that had belonged to her own mother. I was carrying four plates at once, to show I could, and I missed the step. The noise was terrible. I remember standing among the white pieces, waiting to be yelled at.
Aunty Vi didn't yell. She looked at the pieces for a long time. Then she went to the shed and came back with a bucket.
'Pick up every bit,' she said. 'Even the tiny ones.'
I thought it was a punishment. It wasn't. That afternoon she showed me how she made mosaics. She laid the pieces on an old towel, folded it over and tapped them with a hammer until they were the size of coins. She spread cement on a square of concrete beside the path, and then let me press each piece in, leaving small gaps between them. I put the gold edges facing outwards, so that they made a wobbly ring around the middle, like the rim of a giant plate. Afterwards we rubbed grout into the gaps and polished the surface with a rag until the gold edges shone.
'A plate can only be a plate,' she told me, wiping her hands. 'But broken, it can be anything.'
Since then, the path has grown. Neighbours drop off chipped mugs. My cousins brought a cracked vase. Every time I visit, there are new squares, and Aunty Vi lets me choose where the next pieces go.
Last week I knocked a glass off the bench at home, and Dad sighed the way grown-ups do. I didn't get the hot, sick feeling I used to get. I just asked if I could keep the pieces.
'Glass is too sharp for a path,' Dad said.
'Not for a window,' I told him. 'Aunty Vi says you can make a window out of anything.'
He looked at me as if I'd turned into someone else. Maybe I have.

Option A: near the step
Option B: in the middle of the path
Option C: beside the cartoon rabbit
Option D: next to the front gate

Keep Our Skies Quiet
For as long as people have imagined the future, they have imagined flying cars. Cartoons, films and comics are full of them, zipping between shining towers. Now several companies are building real ones, and some promise they will be carrying passengers within a few years. I believe that would be a mistake. Flying cars may look exciting on a movie screen, but in our real cities they would cause more problems than they solve.
The first problem is noise. A flying car cannot glide silently like a bird. To lift a heavy cabin off the ground, it needs powerful spinning rotors, and spinning rotors are loud. Picture your backyard on a Sunday afternoon: the birds singing, the neighbours chatting, and then, overhead, the whirr and thrum of one aircraft after another. Roads at least stay in one place. The sky is above every home, school and park.
The second problem is safety. When a car breaks down on a road, it rolls to a stop. When a flying car breaks down, it falls. Even a small mistake by a pilot or a computer could put the people underneath in danger, not just the passengers inside.
Third, flying cars would serve only a lucky few. Early models are expected to cost far more than ordinary cars, and rides will be priced to match. While a handful of people float above the traffic, everyone else will still be stuck in it, only now with buzzing machines above their heads as well.
Supporters say flying cars will end traffic jams. But a jam in the sky would be far more dangerous than a jam on the ground, and every flying car would still need somewhere to take off and land. Imagine every rooftop turned into a crowded landing pad.
There is a better way to the future, and it is already here. Fast trains, safe bike paths and frequent buses can move thousands of people at once, quietly and cheaply. Instead of spending billions on a dream from old cartoons, we should spend it on transport that works for everyone.
Let the birds keep the sky. We have plenty of work to do down here on the ground.

Option A: to explain how the rotors of a flying car work
Option B: to describe the flying cars seen in old cartoons
Option C: to persuade readers that flying cars should not fill our cities
Option D: to entertain readers with a story about the future

Now several companies are building real ones, and some promise they will be carrying passengers within a few years. I believe that would be a mistake. Flying cars may look exciting on a movie screen, but in our real cities they would cause more problems than they solve.
The first problem is noise. A flying car cannot glide silently like a bird. To lift a heavy cabin off the ground, it needs powerful spinning rotors, and spinning rotors are loud. Picture your backyard on a Sunday afternoon: the birds singing, the neighbours chatting, and then, overhead, the whirr and thrum of one aircraft after another. Roads at least stay in one place. The sky is above every home, school and park.
The second problem is safety. When a car breaks down on a road, it rolls to a stop. When a flying car breaks down, it falls. Even a small mistake by a pilot or a computer could put the people underneath in danger, not just the passengers inside.

There is a better way to the future, and it is already here. Fast trains, safe bike paths and frequent buses can move thousands of people at once, quietly and cheaply. Instead of spending billions on a dream from old cartoons, we should spend it on transport that works for everyone.
Let the birds keep the sky. We have plenty of work to do down here on the ground.

The Brothers Who Gathered Stories
Almost everyone knows the stories of Hansel and Gretel, Rapunzel and Snow White. Fewer people know the names of the two brothers who wrote them down: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm.
Jacob was born in 1785 and Wilhelm in 1786, in the German town of Hanau. They were the eldest of a large family, and when their father died suddenly, money became very tight. The two boys were sent away to school together, and they stayed close for the rest of their lives, studying at the same university, sharing a home and even working at desks side by side.
Neither brother set out to entertain children. They were scholars who loved old languages and believed that the folk tales told by ordinary people were a precious part of their country's history. They feared these stories would disappear as towns grew and people stopped telling them aloud. So they began to collect them.
Some tales came from books, but many came from storytellers. One of the most famous was Dorothea Viehmann, a tailor's wife who sold vegetables and visited the brothers to share stories she had learned as a girl. She remembered tales so exactly that she could repeat them almost word for word, and Wilhelm wrote them down as she spoke.
In 1812 the brothers published their first collection, called Children's and Household Tales. It was not an instant success. Some readers complained that the stories were too frightening and too rough for young people. Over the next forty years, Wilhelm in particular kept revising the book, smoothing the language and softening some of the harsher parts. By the seventh edition in 1857, it held more than two hundred tales and had become one of the most loved books in Germany.
In later life, the brothers began an enormous dictionary of the German language. It was so ambitious that neither lived to see it finished. Wilhelm died in 1859, and Jacob died in 1863 while working on the letter F. Other scholars completed it about a century later.
Today their collection has been translated into more than a hundred languages. The brothers who wanted only to save old stories had, without meaning to, given them to the whole world.

Option A: Dorothea Viehmann
Option B: the brothers' mother
Option C: the brothers' sister
Option D: Rapunzel

Please Let Me Go Underground
Dear Mum and Dad,
I know you said you would think about the Year 6 caving trip, and I know 'think about it' usually means 'no'. So before you decide, I have written down my reasons. Please read all of them before you say anything.
The trip is to Jenolan Caves in the Blue Mountains. On the second day, our group will do an adventure caving tour, where we wear helmets with lamps and crawl through passages that are not part of the normal walking tours. I know that sounds scary to you, but I have found out some facts.
First, it is safe. Every group is led by trained guides who take the same route many times a year. We get helmets, lights, overalls and gloves, and the guide checks everyone's equipment before we go in. The tour is designed for beginners as young as ten.
Second, it is not as tight as you imagine. Ms Patel showed us photos. Yes, there is one squeeze where you slide through on your stomach, but it only takes about ten seconds, and anyone can turn back at the start if they change their mind.
Third, I would learn things I can't learn in a classroom. The caves are hundreds of millions of years old, and every column and straw inside them was made by water dripping through limestone, one tiny drop at a time. Our science unit next term is about rocks and erosion, so the trip would help me with my assignment.
I know what you will say next: 'What about when you got scared on the Ghost Train at the Show?' That was when I was seven. Since then I have done swimming carnivals, a night walk at camp and the high ropes course, and I didn't cry once (well, only a tiny bit on the high ropes, and I still finished).
Finally, almost everyone in my class is going. If I stay home, I will be the only one who doesn't know what a cave straw looks like in real life.
I will do extra jobs to help pay for it, and I promise to listen to the guide every second.
Love from your bravest child (who also does the dishes without being asked),
Ruby

Thirty Languages in Cooma
Anna's first word of English was 'snow', and she learned it the week her family arrived in Cooma in the winter of 1952.
Her father had come from Norway six months earlier to work on the Snowy Mountains Scheme, the enormous project to build dams, tunnels and power stations in the mountains of New South Wales. Now Anna, her mother and her baby brother had followed him across the world. From the bus window, Cooma looked small and wind-swept, with rows of new houses and muddy streets. But on the main street, Anna heard more languages in five minutes than she had heard in her whole life: Italian, German, Polish, Greek, Dutch and others she couldn't name.
'Men from more than thirty countries,' her father told her. 'All here to bring water and electricity to Australia.'
School was the hardest part. On her first morning, the teacher, Mrs Hartley, wrote 'Welcome Anna' on the blackboard and pointed to a seat next to a girl with dark plaits. The girl was called Lucia, and she was from Italy. She knew only a few more English words than Anna, but she smiled and pushed half of her pencils across the desk.
For weeks the two girls spoke in a mixture of English, pointing and drawings. Lucia taught Anna 'playground' and 'lunch'. Anna taught Lucia how to make a snow angel. When Mrs Hartley asked the class to draw where their fathers worked, the girls discovered that their fathers were digging the same tunnel, one from each end.
In the evenings, Anna's father came home grey with rock dust, so tired he sometimes fell asleep at the table. Anna's mother worried, but her father always said the same thing: 'One day you will switch on a light, and some of that power will come from our mountain.'
By spring, Anna could read simple books in English. She still spoke Norwegian at home, but at school she sometimes forgot which language she was using until she saw Lucia laughing.
Years later, when the tunnel was finished, the two families stood together at the opening ceremony. Anna and Lucia, now taller than their mothers, held hands as the water rushed through the mountain their fathers had joined.

Option A: covered in deep snow
Option B: exposed to strong winds
Option C: freshly swept and clean
Option D: crowded with people

The Backwards Hour
Great-Aunt Vera never simply gave presents. On the first morning of the holidays, Priya found an envelope propped against her cereal bowl. Inside, in Vera's looping handwriting, was a single line: Where the hours run backwards, the key is waiting.
“There's a tin in this house that's been locked for fifty years,” Vera said, sipping her tea. “Find the key by Sunday and whatever is inside is yours.”
Priya began with the obvious. The grandfather clock in the sitting room (which Vera wound every Sunday without fail) ticked steadily forwards. Priya checked behind it, beneath it and even inside the tall wooden case where the pendulum swung. Nothing. Next she tried the sundial in the garden. She scraped the moss from its base and found only a startled slater.
On Wednesday she tried questioning Vera instead. “Is it in the kitchen? The shed? Is it even inside the house?” Vera only buttered her toast. “A good puzzle,” she said, “usually hides in plain sight. You just have to look at it properly.” That night Priya lay awake, listening to the clock chime eleven through the wall, turning the clue over and over in her mind.
On Thursday it rained. Priya wandered the house, listening to the drip, drip, drip of the gutters and the clock's patient tick-tock. She stopped at the old mirror in the hallway, which hung opposite the sitting-room door. In the glass she could see the grandfather clock behind her – and something was wrong. Its hands seemed to be sweeping the wrong way.
Of course, she thought. A mirror flips everything. In the reflection, the hours really did run backwards.
She ran her fingers around the heavy frame. Nothing. Then she knelt. Directly beneath the mirror, one strip of skirting board stuck out slightly from the wall. She pressed it, and it swung open on a hidden hinge. Inside lay a tiny brass key, furred with dust.
The tin sat on top of the wardrobe in Vera's room, its lid painted with faded roses. The key turned stiffly, then gave with a soft click.
Inside was a photograph of a grinning girl about Priya's age, kneeling beside the very same mirror. On the back, someone had written: Vera, 1974. Clever girl. Your turn to hide it next. Beneath the photo lay a second envelope, blank and unsealed.
Priya looked up. Vera was standing in the doorway, her eyes bright.
“My grandmother set that puzzle for me,” she said quietly. “I've waited a long time to see someone else solve it.”
Priya turned the empty envelope over in her hands. Already she was wondering where a person might hide a key so that it could only be found by looking at the world the other way around.
Question: Where did Priya search straight after checking the grandfather clock?
Option A: the mirror in the hallway
Option B: the skirting board in the hall
Option C: the wardrobe in Vera's room
Option D: the sundial in the garden

Reading the Mountain's Mood
A volcano rarely erupts without warning. Long before lava or ash appears, molten rock called magma begins to rise from deep underground, and as it moves it leaves clues. The scientists who study volcanoes, known as volcanologists, have learnt to read these clues in much the same way a doctor reads a patient's pulse.
The first clue is often shaking. As magma forces its way upwards, it cracks the rock around it, triggering swarms of small earthquakes. Most are too weak for people to feel, but sensitive instruments called seismometers record every tremor. When the number of tiny quakes climbs sharply, or when they begin to occur closer to the surface, scientists take notice.
The second clue is swelling. Rising magma pushes the ground upwards, sometimes by only a few centimetres. Satellites and GPS stations can detect these small bulges, and instruments called tiltmeters measure even slight changes in the slope of a volcano's sides.
The third clue is gas. Magma contains dissolved gases, including sulfur dioxide. As it nears the surface, these gases escape through cracks and vents. A sudden rise in sulfur dioxide can signal that fresh magma is on its way.
None of these signs proves on its own that an eruption is coming. However, when several appear together, the warning becomes much harder to ignore. That is why volcanologists measure all three over long periods, comparing new readings with old ones.
That is exactly what happened at Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines in 1991. The volcano had been quiet for around 500 years, and many people living on its slopes did not realise it was a volcano at all. Then, in the months before the eruption, steam explosions, earthquake swarms and rising gas levels alerted scientists. Working with local officials, they raised the alert level step by step and urged tens of thousands of people to leave.
On 15 June 1991, Pinatubo produced one of the largest eruptions of the twentieth century. Ash fell across a vast area, and so much gas reached the upper atmosphere that average temperatures around the world dropped by about half a degree Celsius over the following year. Yet because of the evacuations, thousands of lives were saved.
Even so, volcanologists are careful about what they promise. They can often say that an eruption is likely, but not the exact day or hour. Some volcanoes show warning signs for years and then settle down again. For this reason, scientists keep watching, measuring and comparing, knowing that a mountain's mood can change.
Question: According to the passage, what causes swarms of small earthquakes before an eruption?
Option A: sulfur dioxide escaping through cracks and vents
Option B: ash falling heavily across the land
Option C: the ground cooling after an eruption ends
Option D: magma cracking the rock as it forces its way upwards

The Hotel Diary
Saturday 3 February
Mr Okafor says our science project is due in three weeks, and the best one goes in the library display case. I am going to win. My plan is an insect hotel: a wooden box stuffed with bamboo tubes, pinecones and blocks of wood with holes drilled in them. Dad helped me with the drill. I painted HOTEL on the roof in gold letters, mostly so it looks impressive in photos.
Tuesday 6 February
Nothing has checked in. I've hung the hotel on the back fence, facing the morning sun like the website said, but the only visitor so far is a slater, and I'm not sure slaters count. My brother Tom asked if I'd put up a 'No Vacancies' sign. Hilarious.
Saturday 10 February
Finally! This morning a small dark bee kept landing on the wooden block. Each time, it carried something green. It was a piece of leaf, cut into an almost perfect circle! It's a leafcutter bee. The female snips neat pieces from leaves and uses them to line little rooms inside a hole, then lays an egg in each room with a store of pollen and nectar. Sure enough, several of Mum's rose leaves have round bites missing from their edges. Mum was not thrilled, until I explained.
Wednesday 14 February
Three holes are now sealed with leaf plugs. I spent my whole lunchtime drawing them, which is not normal behaviour for me. I've started a chart: the time each bee arrives, the weather, and how long she stays inside. Today one bee made eleven trips in twenty minutes. I don't know how something that small can work that hard.
Sunday 18 February
Hot day, nearly 38 degrees. I worried the hotel would cook, so I tied an old beach umbrella to the fence above it and put out a saucer of water with pebbles in it, so the bees could drink without drowning. Mum, who has now forgiven the bees for her roses, found me the saucer.
Monday 19 February
Problem. The project is due Friday, and the plan was always to carry the hotel to school. But if I unhook it and bump it around in the car, what happens to the eggs? The website says the young bees might not come out until spring, or even next summer. That's months.
Thursday 22 February
I've decided. The hotel stays on the fence. Instead, I'm bringing my chart, my drawings and a photo of the sealed holes. Tom says I've thrown away my chance to win. Maybe. But I'd rather have bees than a spot in a glass case.
Friday 23 February
Mr Okafor read my chart twice and asked if he could borrow the idea for his Year 5 class. I didn't get the display case. I don't really mind. When I got home, I went straight to the fence to check on my guests.

Option A: a complete sentence with a subject and a verb
Option B: a question that is missing its question mark
Option C: two sentences joined by a conjunction
Option D: a one-word sentence used to grab attention

Four Blades, One Boat
Sam Nguyen was the strongest rower in the Year 7 squad, and everyone knew it, including Sam. On the rowing machine at training, his scores were always at the top of the whiteboard, usually by a long way.
So he couldn't understand why their boat kept losing.
“You're pulling too hard,” said Coach Daly after another wobbly practice on the river. She was a small woman with a big voice and a whistle she rarely needed.
“Isn't that the point?” Sam asked.
“Not if you're pulling harder than everyone else. When one oar goes in early and comes out late, the boat rolls. Every roll slows us down.” She pointed to the girl in the seat nearest the stern. “Ellie sets the rhythm. Your job is to follow her.”
Sam glanced at Ellie. She was the smallest in the crew, quiet and freckled, and her score on the machine was the lowest of the four. Following her felt like being told to walk at a toddler's pace.
At the next session, Sam tried. He lasted about four strokes. Then the boat began to feel heavy and slow, and without meaning to he dug his oar in harder. The hull lurched sideways. Ellie didn't turn around. She simply kept the same steady beat, as if nothing had happened, and Sam felt his face burn.
For the next week, Coach Daly made them row with their eyes almost closed, listening instead of looking. Sam learnt to hear the soft clunk of four oars turning at the same moment, and the hiss of the hull sliding forward between strokes. When he rushed, the sounds broke apart into a messy clatter. When he waited, they joined into one.
It was harder than pulling hard. It meant holding back when every muscle wanted to charge.
On race day, the river was flat and grey. As the starter called “Go!”, Sam felt the old urge surge through his arms. He fixed his eyes on the back of Ellie's neck and matched her, stroke for stroke.
At the halfway buoy they were third. Then, slowly, the boat began to run. It no longer rocked. It felt light, almost as if it were gliding on its own. They passed one crew, then edged up beside the leaders. With two hundred metres left, Ellie called for a push, and four blades bit the water together.
They lost by less than a second.
Sam slumped over his oar, chest heaving. He waited to feel the familiar sting of losing. Instead, he felt something he couldn't name.
Back on the bank, Coach Daly handed him his drink bottle. “Best you've ever rowed,” she said.
“We didn't win.”
“No,” she agreed. “But for the first time, you rowed in a crew, not just in a boat.”
Sam looked over at Ellie, who was laughing with the others as they carried the boat up the ramp. He hurried to take his share of the weight.
Question: Which detail shows that Sam was the strongest rower in the squad?
Option A: Sam felt the old urge surge through his arms.
Option B: Sam slumped over his oar, chest heaving.
Option C: His scores were always at the top of the whiteboard.
Option D: He hurried to take his share of the weight.

The Mimic of Sherbrooke
Noah had not known that a morning could be this cold. At six o'clock, the car park in Sherbrooke Forest was still grey, and his breath hung in front of him like smoke.
“Remind me why we're here?” he muttered, thumbs moving across his phone.
“Lyrebirds,” said Gran, tugging her beanie lower over her hearing aids. “Winter is when the males sing their hearts out. Your Pop and I came every June for forty years.”
They walked along a track lined with tree ferns, their boots squelching through the mud. Somewhere above them, a bird let out a long whistle that snapped into a sharp crack, like a whip.
“Whipbird,” Gran said, though she was frowning slightly, tilting her head. “Was that one or two?”
“Just one,” Noah said. He hadn't realised you could count birds by their calls.
As they walked, Gran told him how Pop used to stand perfectly still for an hour, so still that once a lyrebird scratched up leaves right beside his boots. “He always said you can't go and find a lyrebird,” she said. “You have to let it find you.”

Mrs Lang's Fairy Books
In 1889, a book with a bright blue cover appeared in London bookshops. The Blue Fairy Book gathered old tales such as "Cinderella", "Rumpelstiltskin" and "Beauty and the Beast", and it sold so well that a Red Fairy Book followed the next year. By 1910 there were twelve volumes, each named after a different colour. Every one carried the same name: Andrew Lang. Yet the person who did most of the writing was barely mentioned.
Leonora Blanche Alleyne was born in 1851 and in 1875 married Andrew Lang, a Scottish scholar and journalist. Andrew was fascinated by folklore and believed fairy tales deserved serious study, not merely a place in the nursery. He was also extraordinarily busy, turning out poems, essays, histories and newspaper columns at a startling pace.
Leonora had a gift for languages. As the fairy book project grew, she took on the task of turning stories from French, German, Spanish, Italian and other languages into lively English. She did not simply translate word for word. She reshaped each tale for young readers, trimming slow passages and softening details that seemed too gruesome for a Victorian nursery. In time she oversaw a small team of translators, most of them women, and polished their work into one consistent voice.
Andrew's role was mainly to choose the stories' themes, write the prefaces and lend his famous name, which helped the books sell. He never pretended to have done everything. In the preface to The Lilac Fairy Book, the final volume, he stated plainly that the books had been almost wholly the work of Mrs Lang. Few readers noticed. The covers did not change, and for generations, children and librarians spoke of "Andrew Lang's fairy books".
Leonora also published books under her own name, including The Red Book of Heroes and The Book of Princes and Princesses. These attracted far less attention than the coloured series.
Why did she stay in the background? Part of the answer lies in the customs of the time. Victorian publishers believed a well-known male author would attract buyers, and many women writers accepted that their work would be credited to someone else. How Leonora herself felt about this is not well recorded.
Today, historians of children's literature are giving her more credit. The coloured fairy books helped decide which tales English-speaking children grew up with, and Leonora's choices about what to keep, what to soften and what to cut still echo through countless picture books and films. She was, in a sense, the invisible gatekeeper of the fairy-tale kingdom.
Question: According to the passage, why did publishers want a well-known man's name on the books?
Option A: They believed men were better translators.
Option B: They wanted to hide that the tales were old.
Option C: They wanted to keep Leonora's name private.
Option D: They believed it would attract more buyers.

Painting the Same Thing Twice
Most artists, once they have finished a painting, move on to a new subject. Claude Monet did the opposite. Again and again, the French painter returned to the very same scene: a stack of wheat in a field, the front of a cathedral, a pond full of water lilies. To some people this looked like a lack of imagination. To Monet, it was the whole point.
Monet was one of the founders of Impressionism, a style that began in France in the 1870s. Impressionists often worked outdoors, using quick, visible brushstrokes to capture a moment as it actually appeared. In fact, the movement's name came from a critic who mocked Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, suggesting it was no more than an unfinished sketch. The artists happily adopted the label.
For Monet, the real subject of a painting was not the object in front of him but the light falling on it. A haystack at dawn, he realised, was a completely different sight from the same haystack at noon or under winter frost. Its shadows changed colour; its edges softened or sharpened. So in 1890 and 1891 he painted the stacks near his home in Giverny about twenty-five times.
Capturing light was frustrating work, because light never stays still. Monet complained in letters that the sun moved too quickly for him to keep up. To solve this, he worked on several canvases at once. When the light shifted, he would put one painting aside and pick up another that matched the new conditions, returning to the first at the same time the next day.
His longest series grew from his own garden. At Giverny, Monet dug a pond, planted water lilies and built a small Japanese-style bridge. For almost thirty years, until his death in 1926, he painted that pond around 250 times, sometimes on canvases taller than a person. He was a harsh judge of his own work and sometimes destroyed paintings he felt had failed.
In his later years, Monet developed cataracts, a condition that clouds the lens of the eye. Colours appeared muddy and yellowish to him, and the paintings from this period are full of heavy reds and browns. After surgery in 1923 improved his sight, he reworked some of these canvases.
Today, Monet's series are often displayed side by side in galleries, and that is when their purpose becomes clear. Viewed together, they show something no single painting could: that the world we think we know is constantly changing, hour by hour and season by season.

Option A: relaxed
Option B: proud
Option C: frustrated
Option D: bored

A haystack at dawn, he realised, was a completely different sight from the same haystack at noon or under winter frost. Its shadows changed colour; its edges softened or sharpened. So in 1890 and 1891 he painted the stacks near his home in Giverny about twenty-five times.

When the light shifted, he would put one painting aside and pick up another that matched the new conditions, returning to the first at the same time the next day.

Nine Logs and an Ocean
In April 1947, six men pushed off from the coast of Peru on a raft that many experts were sure would sink. It had no engine and no modern hull, just nine logs of balsa wood lashed together with rope, a small bamboo cabin and a square sail. Its name was Kon-Tiki, and its leader was a Norwegian explorer named Thor Heyerdahl.
Heyerdahl had a bold idea. He believed that people from South America might have sailed west across the Pacific long ago and settled the islands of Polynesia. Most scientists disagreed. They argued that ancient South Americans had no boats capable of such a journey. Heyerdahl decided there was only one way to answer them: build a raft from materials those people could have used, and sail it himself.
Before they left, the doubters were loud. Balsa, they warned, would soak up water and become too heavy to float. The ropes would rub through. The crew would be lucky to last a fortnight.
The ocean had other plans. Carried by the trade winds and a strong current, the raft drifted steadily westward. The logs did absorb some water, but they stayed afloat. The ropes sank into the soft balsa instead of fraying against it. The men fished, collected rainwater and woke most mornings to find flying fish that had landed on the deck overnight. One day a whale shark, the largest fish in the sea, circled the raft, its spotted back sliding beneath the logs while the crew watched nervously.
After 101 days and nearly 7,000 kilometres, the voyage ended with a crash. Waves drove the raft onto a coral reef near the island of Raroia, and the crew scrambled through the surf to the shore. Battered but unhurt, they had crossed a large part of the Pacific Ocean.
Heyerdahl's book about the expedition was translated into dozens of languages, and a film of the journey won an Academy Award. Around the world, readers were thrilled by the story of a few determined people taking on the ocean with an ancient design.
Yet the voyage did not settle the scientific question. It proved that such a trip was possible, not that it had actually happened. Later studies of language, objects and DNA suggest that Polynesians came mainly from the west, from islands closer to Asia, although some evidence hints at contact with South Americans many centuries ago.
Even so, Kon-Tiki showed something valuable. Sometimes the best way to test an idea is to step off the shore and try it.

Option A: wooden planks nailed onto a modern hull
Option B: bundles of reeds tied with vines
Option C: nine balsa logs tied together with rope
Option D: bamboo poles joined with metal bolts

Footprints at Lark Quarry
About 95 million years ago, in what is now central-western Queensland, the ground beside a river was soft, sticky mud. Dinosaurs walked, ran and perhaps even swam through it, leaving thousands of footprints behind. Before the mud could be washed smooth, it was covered by layers of sand and silt. Over millions of years, these layers hardened into rock, preserving the prints like a message sealed in an envelope.
Today, the site is called Lark Quarry, near the town of Winton. More than 3,300 footprints have been uncovered there, and they are now protected inside a building so that wind and rain cannot wear them away.
Footprints are a special kind of fossil. Bones tell scientists what an animal looked like, but tracks reveal how it behaved. The size of a print, the distance between steps and the depth of each toe mark can suggest how big an animal was, how fast it was moving and even whether it was alone or in a group. Such clues are known as trace fossils, because they record an animal's activity rather than its body.
When scientists studied Lark Quarry in the late 1970s and early 1980s, they came up with a dramatic explanation. Most of the prints were small, made by dinosaurs no bigger than chickens or emus. A few were much larger, with three long toes. The researchers concluded that a large meat-eating dinosaur had approached a mixed group of small dinosaurs gathered by the water, and that the small animals had fled in panic. The site became famous as the only known record of a dinosaur stampede.
More recent research has challenged this story. In 2011, scientists re-examining the large prints argued that their shape better matched a plant-eating dinosaur, possibly similar to Muttaburrasaurus, which lived in Queensland at about the same time. Then, in 2013, the same team suggested that many of the small prints were not running steps at all. A large number show only the tips of claws scraping the mud, with no clear heel or pad. This, they argued, is what you would expect if the dinosaurs were floating in shallow water and pushing themselves along with their toes.
Not everyone agrees with the new ideas, and the debate continues. That is not a failure of science; it is science working as it should. Each time researchers look again, with new methods and fresh eyes, they test old conclusions and sometimes replace them.
The footprints themselves have not changed in 95 million years. What has changed is how carefully we have learnt to read them.

Option A: protecting
Option B: covering
Option C: destroying
Option D: keeping

Today, the site is called Lark Quarry, near the town of Winton. More than 3,300 footprints have been uncovered there, and they are now protected inside a building so that wind and rain cannot wear them away.
Footprints are a special kind of fossil. Bones tell scientists what an animal looked like, but tracks reveal how it behaved. The size of a print, the distance between steps and the depth of each toe mark can suggest how big an animal was, how fast it was moving and even whether it was alone or in a group. Such clues are known as trace fossils, because they record an animal's activity rather than its body.
When scientists studied Lark Quarry in the late 1970s and early 1980s, they came up with a dramatic explanation. Most of the prints were small, made by dinosaurs no bigger than chickens or emus. A few were much larger, with three long toes. The researchers concluded that a large meat-eating dinosaur had approached a mixed group of small dinosaurs gathered by the water, and that the small animals had fled in panic. The site became famous as the only known record of a dinosaur stampede.
More recent research has challenged this story. In 2011, scientists re-examining the large prints argued that their shape better matched a plant-eating dinosaur, possibly similar to Muttaburrasaurus, which lived in Queensland at about the same time. Then, in 2013, the same team suggested that many of the small prints were not running steps at all. A large number show only the tips of claws scraping the mud, with no clear heel or pad. This, they argued, is what you would expect if the dinosaurs were floating in shallow water and pushing themselves along with their toes.
Not everyone agrees with the new ideas, and the debate continues. That is not a failure of science; it is science working as it should. Each time researchers look again, with new methods and fresh eyes, they test old conclusions and sometimes replace them.

Hand Over the Wooden Spoon
In many Australian homes, the evening meal is cooked by the same tired adult night after night, while the children wait to be called to the table. I believe this should change. Every child aged ten or older should be responsible for cooking one family dinner each week.
The first reason is simple: cooking is a life skill. Sooner or later, every young person will leave home. Those who have never chopped an onion or boiled an egg will survive on takeaway food and bowls of cereal. A teenager who has cooked once a week since the age of ten will have prepared more than three hundred dinners by the time they finish school. That is real experience, and it cannot be gained from watching cooking shows.
Second, a weekly cooking night shares the load fairly. Parents and carers work hard, and planning, shopping and cooking take hours every week. When children take a turn, adults get a well-earned break, and children begin to understand how much effort goes into the meals they usually take for granted. After you have spent an hour making a lasagne, you are far less likely to complain that dinner is 'boring'.
Some people argue that children are too young to handle sharp knives and hot stoves. This concern is understandable, but it is easily managed. Younger cooks can begin with simple dishes such as salads, wraps or scrambled eggs, with an adult nearby. As their confidence grows, so can the challenge. Nobody expects a ten-year-old to roast a turkey on their first night.
Others worry that the food will not be very good. They are probably right, at least at first. The rice may stick to the pot and the pasta may be a little soft. But families who eat a less-than-perfect meal together, and laugh about it, are learning something more important than a recipe. They are learning patience and encouragement. My own brother's first attempt at fried rice was so salty that we each drank three glasses of water, yet he still talks proudly about it. Last month he made a curry that my grandmother has asked him to cook again.
Finally, cooking gives children a voice in the family. The person who cooks chooses the menu, and that choice can be a chance to share a favourite dish, try a recipe from a friend's culture or recreate a meal from a holiday.
It is time to hand over the wooden spoon. A child who cooks once a week becomes more capable, more grateful and more involved in family life. The cost is a few burnt saucepans. The reward is a family that works as a team.

Option A: Parents and carers should stop cooking dinner altogether.
Option B: Families should eat takeaway food less often each week.
Option C: Children aged ten or older should cook one family dinner a week.
Option D: Children should learn to cook by watching cooking shows.

In many Australian homes, the evening meal is cooked by the same tired adult night after night, while the children wait to be called to the table. I believe this should change. Every child aged ten or older should be responsible for cooking one family dinner each week.
The first reason is simple: cooking is a life skill. Sooner or later, every young person will leave home. Those who have never chopped an onion or boiled an egg will survive on takeaway food and bowls of cereal. A teenager who has cooked once a week since the age of ten will have prepared more than three hundred dinners by the time they finish school. That is real experience, and it cannot be gained from watching cooking shows.
Second, a weekly cooking night shares the load fairly. Parents and carers work hard, and planning, shopping and cooking take hours every week. When children take a turn, adults get a well-earned break, and children begin to understand how much effort goes into the meals they usually take for granted. After you have spent an hour making a lasagne, you are far less likely to complain that dinner is 'boring'.
Some people argue that children are too young to handle sharp knives and hot stoves. This concern is understandable, but it is easily managed. Younger cooks can begin with simple dishes such as salads, wraps or scrambled eggs, with an adult nearby. As their confidence grows, so can the challenge. Nobody expects a ten-year-old to roast a turkey on their first night.
Others worry that the food will not be very good. They are probably right, at least at first. The rice may stick to the pot and the pasta may be a little soft. But families who eat a less-than-perfect meal together, and laugh about it, are learning something more important than a recipe. They are learning patience and encouragement. My own brother's first attempt at fried rice was so salty that we each drank three glasses of water, yet he still talks proudly about it. Last month he made a curry that my grandmother has asked him to cook again.
Finally, cooking gives children a voice in the family. The person who cooks chooses the menu, and that choice can be a chance to share a favourite dish, try a recipe from a friend's culture or recreate a meal from a holiday.
It is time to hand over the wooden spoon. A child who cooks once a week becomes more capable, more grateful and more involved in family life. The cost is a few burnt saucepans. The reward is a family that works as a team.

Switching On the Bush
Today, most Australians expect light to appear the moment they press a switch. Yet for many families living on farms, mains electricity is a surprisingly recent arrival. While people in the cities had electric lights by the early twentieth century, large parts of the countryside were not connected until the 1950s and 1960s, and some remote properties waited even longer.
The main reason was distance. In a city street, a single power line can supply hundreds of houses. Building those lines was expensive, and electricity suppliers were slow to pay for them when so few people would be using the power.
Before the lines arrived, daily life on a farm was laborious. Houses were lit by kerosene lamps, which had to be filled and trimmed every evening. Food was kept cool in an ice chest, or in a Coolgardie safe, a cabinet covered in wet hessian that cooled by evaporation. Clothes were boiled in a copper over a fire, and irons were heated on the wood stove, so washing and ironing could take up two full days of every week. A few wealthier families owned a petrol-driven generator, but it was noisy, costly to run and usually powered only a handful of lights.
When the poles finally marched across the paddocks, the change was dramatic. Children raced from room to room flicking switches on and off. Electric washing machines, refrigerators and irons began to replace the copper, the ice chest and the stove-heated iron. Dairy farmers could use electric milking machines, which saved hours of work each day, and water could be pumped by electric motors instead of by windmill alone.
However, not everyone was won over at once. Early country supply was not always reliable. Storms brought down lines, and repairs to a distant property could take days. Some older farmers also worried about the size of their first electricity bills and only switched on the light in the room they were using. Many families kept their kerosene lamps polished and filled on a high shelf for years afterwards, even though they rarely lit them.
Within a generation, those lamps had become ornaments. Most country children grew up unable to imagine life without power, and the stories of their parents and grandparents began to sound like tales from another century. Yet those stories remind us that something we now take for granted was once a hard-won luxury.

The Counting Book
The canoe slid away from the bank with barely a sound. Mist hung over Wattle Lagoon in pale ribbons, and somewhere in the reeds a frog was clicking like a wind-up toy. Kira sat in the front, paddle across her knees, trying not to yawn.
'Five o'clock,' she muttered. 'Normal people are asleep.'
'Normal people miss the best part of the day,' said Pop from the back of the canoe. He handed her a battered notebook wrapped in a plastic bag. 'You're in charge of this.'
Kira knew the book well. For forty years, Pop had come to the lagoon each spring to count the waterbirds, writing every number in the same neat capitals. Then the drought came. For three summers the lagoon shrank to a cracked plate of mud, and the pages for those years held only one word: DRY. Kira remembered standing on that mud with him, the dead reeds rattling, and Pop saying nothing at all the whole way home.
But this winter the rain had come at last. Storms in the hills had swollen the river until it burst its banks and poured into the lagoon, filling it in a single week. Now the water stretched further than Kira had ever seen it.
'Ibis on the left,' said Pop. 'How many?'
Kira counted the white birds picking through the shallows. 'Twelve. No, fourteen.'
'Write it down.' He paused. 'And that dark one on the dead tree. Darter or cormorant? Tell me what you see.'
Kira squinted. 'Long skinny neck, sort of like a snake. Wings spread out to dry.'
'Darter,' said Pop with satisfaction. 'Good eyes.'
They went on like that for an hour, Pop steering and asking questions, Kira peering, counting and writing. Spoonbills sweeping their flat bills from side to side. A pair of black swans with four grey cygnets. Each time, Pop asked her to describe the bird before he named it, and twice he held the notebook out at arm's length, frowning, before handing it straight back.
By the time the sun had burned off the mist, the page was full. Kira noticed that every entry was in her round, sprawling handwriting, not Pop's capitals.
'You didn't write anything,' she said.
Pop rested his paddle and looked out over the water. 'I've written enough,' he said. 'Forty years is a good run. The book needs a new counter.'
Kira looked down at the page. Fourteen ibis. One darter. Two swans, four cygnets. It didn't look like much, but she suddenly understood that it was the most important thing she had written all year.
'Same time next spring?' she asked.
Pop smiled. 'Five o'clock,' he said. 'Bring a pencil.'
Question: Why was Wattle Lagoon full of water again?
Option A: Storms in the hills made the river overflow into it.
Option B: Pop had pumped water into it from the river.
Option C: Rain had slowly filled it over three summers.
Option D: Water had been released from a dam upstream.

Lanterns for the Full Moon
The Mid-Autumn Festival is celebrated in China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore and many other places, including by Chinese and Vietnamese communities across Australia. It falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar – usually in September or early October – when the moon is said to be at its fullest and brightest. Families gather outdoors to admire the moon, share round mooncakes and carry glowing lanterns through the evening. Mooncakes are rich pastries, often filled with sweet lotus-seed paste. Because the full moon is round and complete, it has become a symbol of families being together.
Making your own lantern is a simple way to join in. This one takes about forty minutes.
You will need:
two sheets of coloured card (A4 size)
a ruler and a pencil
scissors
a glue stick and sticky tape
a strip of card for the handle (about 20 cm long)
a battery-operated tea light (never a real candle)
Steps
1. Fold one sheet of card in half lengthways; the fold should run along the long side.
2. Using the ruler, draw lines across the folded card about 2 cm apart. Stop each line 3 cm from the open edges.
3. Cut along each line, starting from the fold. Be careful not to cut all the way through.
4. Unfold the card and roll it into a tube, with the cuts running up and down. Glue the short edges together.
5. Press down gently on the top of the tube so that the cut strips bulge outwards. This gives the lantern its round, moon-like shape.
6. Roll the second sheet of card into a slightly narrower tube and slide it inside the first. This inner tube softens the light and makes the colours glow.
7. Tape the handle across the top.
8. Switch on the tea light and place it carefully at the bottom of the lantern.
Tips
Choose warm colours such as red, gold and orange; these are traditional festival colours. You can decorate the outside with paper cut-outs of rabbits, stars or the moon. Rabbits are a popular choice because, in Chinese folk tales, a jade rabbit is said to live on the moon. In Vietnam, star-shaped lanterns are especially popular, and children parade through the streets with them.
Most importantly, do not make your lantern alone. In many families, older relatives show younger ones how to fold and cut, and the finished lanterns are carried together on the night of the full moon. The lantern itself may be made of paper, but the time spent making it – and the people you share it with – are what the festival is really about.

Option A: show that some words have been left out

The Planet Behind the Veil
Just after sunset or just before dawn, you may notice a dazzling point of light low in the sky. It shines more brightly than any star, and for thousands of years people called it the 'evening star' or the 'morning star'. In fact, it is not a star at all. It is Venus, the second planet from the Sun and our closest planetary neighbour.
Venus has often been called Earth's twin. The two planets are almost the same size, and they are made of similar rocky material. Early astronomers could not see its surface, because it is hidden beneath a thick blanket of cloud. Some imagined that, under those clouds, there might be warm swamps or steamy jungles full of life.
The truth turned out to be very different. When space probes finally reached Venus in the 1960s and 1970s, they revealed one of the most hostile places in the solar system. The surface temperature is about 465 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt lead. Surprisingly, this makes Venus hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is much closer to the Sun.
The reason lies in the air. Venus's atmosphere is made almost entirely of carbon dioxide, and it is extremely dense. Sunlight passes through the clouds and warms the ground, but the heat cannot easily escape back into space. Instead, it is trapped by the thick atmosphere, a process known as the greenhouse effect. Mercury, by contrast, has almost no atmosphere, so heat escapes from its surface and the side facing away from the Sun becomes bitterly cold.
The atmosphere of Venus also presses down with tremendous force. Standing on its surface would feel like being nearly a kilometre deep in the ocean. The clouds themselves contain droplets of sulfuric acid, a chemical that can eat away at metal.
Venus is strange in other ways, too. It spins very slowly, and in the opposite direction to most planets. One full turn takes about 243 Earth days, which is longer than the 225 days it takes to travel around the Sun. In other words, a day on Venus is longer than its year.
Several landers sent by the Soviet Union reached the surface between 1970 and 1985. They were built as tough as armoured tanks, yet the heat and pressure silenced each of them within about two hours. The photographs they sent back show a flat, orange-tinted landscape of broken rock.
Scientists are now planning new missions to Venus. They hope to learn how a planet so similar to Earth in size became so different. Understanding what happened to our twin may help us appreciate how fortunate we are to live on a world with mild temperatures and air we can breathe.

Option A: very distant and hard to reach
Option B: beautiful but very strange
Option C: harsh and unfriendly to life
Option D: busy and full of activity

The Last Garden on Kepler Ridge
In the year 2163, almost nobody on Kepler Ridge Station had eaten food grown in soil. Meals arrived in neat foil packets from the nutrition printers: protein squares, vitamin gel and a beige paste that was supposed to taste like banana. They were safe, efficient and completely forgettable.
The exception was Ana Okafor's great-grandmother, who still tended the old garden dome on the edge of the station. It was a cramped, steamy bubble of glass full of tomato vines, herbs and one stubborn strawberry patch. Most people had forgotten it existed. Ana went there every afternoon after lessons, because it was the only place on the station that smelled of something other than metal.
Then the notice appeared on every screen: the Station Council planned to clear the garden dome and turn it into a storage bay for printer cartridges. The vote would take place in three days.
Ana's great-grandmother simply shrugged. 'I'm a hundred and four,' she said. 'The garden will outlive me or it won't.'
But Ana could not bear it. Citizens were allowed two minutes to speak before any vote, so on the third day she stood in front of the council with her hands shaking and a small covered tray balanced on her arm.
'Councillors,' she began, 'you are about to vote on a room. But it isn't really a room. It's the only place on Kepler Ridge where something is alive that isn't us.' She took a breath. 'Our printers make every meal we eat. What happens if they break? What happens if the cartridges stop arriving? Do any of us know how to grow a single bean?'
A few councillors shifted in their seats. One glanced at the clock.
'I'm not asking you to give up the printers,' Ana went on. 'I'm asking you to keep one small garden, so that our children will know what real food is. Before you vote, I'd like you to try something.'
She lifted the cloth. On the tray sat seven small red strawberries, one for each member of the council.
There was an awkward pause. Then the oldest councillor, a stern woman named Director Hale, picked one up, studied it and bit into it. Her eyes widened. For a long moment she said nothing at all.
'My mother used to talk about these,' she said quietly. 'I thought she was exaggerating.'
One by one, the others tasted theirs. Someone laughed in surprise. Someone else asked whether there were any more.
When the vote was taken, the garden dome was saved, six votes to one. By the end of the month the council had approved two new garden domes, and a list of volunteers stretched across the noticeboard.
Ana's great-grandmother pretended not to be pleased. But that evening, Ana found her teaching three small children how to plant tomato seeds, and she was humming.

Option A: tasting rich, sweet and very filling
Option B: old-fashioned and rarely used any more
Option C: costing a great deal of money to make
Option D: working well without wasting time or effort

In the year 2163, almost nobody on Kepler Ridge Station had eaten food grown in soil. Meals arrived in neat foil packets from the nutrition printers: protein squares, vitamin gel and a beige paste that was supposed to taste like banana. They were safe, efficient and completely forgettable.

A few councillors shifted in their seats. One glanced at the clock.
'I'm not asking you to give up the printers,' Ana went on. 'I'm asking you to keep one small garden, so that our children will know what real food is. Before you vote, I'd like you to try something.'
She lifted the cloth. On the tray sat seven small red strawberries, one for each member of the council.

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
The Borrowed House
Beneath the ledge where the brown kelp sways,
in a rock pool warmed by the morning's rays,
a hermit crab in a borrowed shell
has found his house no longer fits him well.

He chose it small when he too was small,
a spiral of cream with a speckled wall;
it sat on his back like a well-made hat,
and he never dreamed he'd grow out of that.

All summer long he would trundle about
with his roof on his back and his feelers out,
nibbling the scraps that the currents brought,
as safe as a sailor tied up in port.

He watched the periwinkles grazing slow,
and the shrimp flick past in the light below,
and he tucked himself in when the waves rolled high
and waited in darkness till storms went by.

But crabs keep growing, as all crabs do,
and the speckled spiral pinched, and grew
too tight to tuck his soft tail inside
when a gull's grey shadow skimmed the tide.

So out he must creep, though he dreads to go
from the only walls he has come to know,
for a crab without armour is soft as bread,
and the open sand is a place of dread.

He measures a cockle: too flat, too wide.
He measures a whelk with a crack in its side.
He measures a cone, but it's heavy as stone,
and each time he scuttles away alone.

He pokes at a bottle cap, shiny and red,
but it's far too shallow to cover his head.
The water darkens; the tide turns round;
a gull cries once with a hungry sound.

Should he creep back now to the cramped old shell,
and squeeze himself in, and pretend all's well?
He pauses a moment, then turns his head
and scuttles on through the weed instead.

Past starfish sprawled like a dropped red glove,
past the darting wrasse in the swell above,
through ribbons of weed and a forest of stalks,
he hurries along on his sideways walks.

Then, wedged in a crevice where anemones cling,
he spies it at last: a turban, a thing
of pearl and ridges, empty and clean,
the finest house he has ever seen.

He tests it twice with a careful claw,
he peers inside for a crack or a flaw,
then quick as a flicker, as swift as a wave,
he slips from the old to the new, and is safe.

He shuffles and wriggles to make it fit,
he turns himself round in it, bit by bit,
till his tail is curled in the pearly deep
and the whole rock pool seems to whisper, 'Sleep.'

Now snug in his turban he settles down
like a king who has found a much finer crown,
and the speckled spiral he left behind
lies on the sand for the next crab to find.

For nothing he owns has ever been his:
each house is a loan, and that's how it is.
He'll wear this one till it pinches too,
then he'll go out searching, as all crabs do.
Question: Why does the crab reject the whelk shell?
Option A: It is too flat and too wide.
Option B: It is as heavy as a stone.
Option C: It is far too shallow.
Option D: It has a crack in its side.

Out of Tune
My cello and I arrived at Riverside Hall forty minutes early, which turned out to be thirty-nine minutes too many. There is only so long you can sit in a cramped backstage room, listening to other people warm up, before your stomach starts turning cartwheels.
I was playing 'The Swan', a slow, gentle piece I had practised every day for two months. Ms Varga, my teacher, had made me play it so many times that I could hear it in my sleep. At our last lesson, she had given me one piece of advice. 'If something goes wrong, don't stop,' she said. 'An audience follows the music, not the mistakes. If you keep going, most of them will never know.'
I nodded, but privately I thought nothing would go wrong. I knew every note.
Backstage, the only free chair was beside an old electric heater that clanked and hissed in the corner. I propped my cello against the wall next to it and spent the next half-hour reading the program over and over, as if my name might vanish from it.
At last the stage manager called, 'Sam Taylor, you're on.'
The lights were brighter than I had expected, and the hall was full. Somewhere in the third row sat my grandfather, who had driven two hours to be there. I placed my bow on the strings and began.
The first few lines went beautifully. The notes floated out over the audience exactly the way Ms Varga had taught me. Then, halfway through, I reached for a high note on the A string, and something was badly wrong. The note came out flat, sour and wobbly, like a singer who has forgotten the tune. I tried the next note. That was flat too. My string had slipped out of tune.
For one terrible second my bow froze. I could feel hundreds of eyes on me. My hand wanted to stop, put the cello down and run.
Then I heard Ms Varga's voice in my head: don't stop.
So I didn't. I kept the bow moving and listened harder than I had ever listened in my life. If the string was low, I would have to place my fingers a little higher to find the right sound. It felt strange and awkward, like writing with the wrong hand, but slowly the notes began to sound right again. I reached the final long note, let it fade into silence and lifted my bow.
The applause was loud and warm. My grandfather was clapping above his head.
Afterwards, Ms Varga found me in the corridor. She tapped the cello's tuning peg and raised an eyebrow. 'You left it next to the heater, didn't you?' Then she smiled. 'Nicely rescued.'
My grandfather told me it was the best thing he had heard all year. He hadn't noticed a thing.
Question: The story is told from the point of view of
Option A: Ms Varga, the teacher
Option B: Sam, the young cellist
Option C: Sam's proud grandfather
Option D: the stage manager

Under the Green Ceiling
Monday, 8 July
Aunt Rosa warned me that the rainforest would be wet, but I didn't expect it to be this wet. We arrived at the research station near Cape Tribulation just after lunch, and within ten minutes my socks were soaked through. The air feels thick, as if you could wring it out like a towel. Aunt Rosa says this is normal for the Wet Tropics, even in winter, which is the dry season here. I asked what the wet season is like and she just laughed.
The station is a cluster of timber huts on stilts, joined by boardwalks. My room has a fan, a bunk and a gecko that lives behind the mirror. I've named him Clive.
Tuesday, 9 July
This morning we walked to the canopy crane, a tall tower with an arm that lifts scientists into the treetops in a sort of cage. I wasn't allowed to go up, which was disappointing, but Aunt Rosa explained that the canopy is where most of the action is. Up there, leaves catch the sunlight, and flowers, fruit, insects and birds crowd together. Down on the forest floor it is dim and surprisingly quiet. Hardly any light reaches the ground, so only a few plants grow there, mostly ferns and seedlings waiting for their chance.
'Waiting for what?' I asked.
'For a tree to fall,' she said. When an old giant comes down in a storm, it opens a gap in the canopy and sunlight floods in. Then all the seedlings race upwards, and whichever grows fastest wins the gap. I thought that sounded harsh, but she said a fallen tree isn't really a loss. Fungi and termites break down the trunk, and its nutrients go back into the soil.
Wednesday, 10 July
Today I saw a cassowary! We were on the track to the creek when Aunt Rosa grabbed my arm and pointed. It was taller than me, with glossy black feathers, a bright blue neck and a hard helmet on its head called a casque. We stood very still and it ignored us completely, pecking at fallen fruit before strolling off into the ferns. My heart was hammering the whole time.
Aunt Rosa told me cassowaries swallow fruit whole and drop the seeds, sometimes kilometres away, in their droppings. Some rainforest trees have fruit so large that almost no other animal can spread them. If the cassowaries disappeared, those trees might slowly disappear too.
Thursday, 11 July
Last day. I spent the afternoon helping Aunt Rosa count seedlings in a gap where a huge fig fell during a storm last summer. There were dozens, some already up to my knees. A few had sprouted from a pile of cassowary droppings, which Aunt Rosa found far more exciting than I did.
I used to think a rainforest was just a lot of trees. Now I think it's more like a giant machine where every part depends on another. I'm going to miss Clive.

Option C: shake something hard to clean it
Option D: squeeze the water out of something

Ari's group was Ari, Mei and Tom. Mei was the kind of person who coloured in her diagrams and labelled them in neat capitals. Tom was the kind of person nobody really noticed. In the first week he had shyly pushed his notebook across the desk, showing a sketch covered in little triangles.
