Thirty-Two Millimetres
Every morning at seven, Nan walked down to the fence post by the gate, tipped the rain gauge towards the light and squinted at it. Then she wrote a number in the battered green notebook she kept in her apron pocket. For the whole of that summer, the number was zero.
I had come to stay on her farm outside Dubbo for the school holidays. Mum said Nan needed company, but I think Mum really wanted me off my phone. The paddocks were the colour of toast. The dam had shrunk to a brown puddle ringed with cracked mud, and the sheep stood in the shade of the one big gum tree as if they were waiting for something.
They were. So was Nan. 'It'll come,' she said, every single morning.
I wasn't so sure. I checked the weather app ten times a day. It showed a little sun, over and over, with the words '10% chance of rain'.
Nan didn't trust the app. She trusted the ants. 'See them carrying their eggs up the step?' she said one afternoon. 'They're moving uphill. They know.' She trusted the galahs, too, which had started screeching more than usual, and the smell of the evening air, which she said was 'getting heavy'. I thought it was all superstition, but I didn't say so.
A week later, the clouds came. They piled up over the western ridge like grey cauliflowers, and thunder grumbled in the distance. Nan and I stood on the veranda, holding our breath. Fat drops smacked into the dust, one, two, ten, and I smelled wet earth for the first time in months. Then the wind changed. The clouds slid away to the south, and the sun came out as if nothing had happened.
I went inside and cried. It felt worse than no storm at all.
Nan sat beside me on the couch. 'The land has waited a lot longer than you have, love,' she said. 'It doesn't give up because of one bad afternoon.'
For five more mornings she wrote zero in the green notebook. On the sixth night I woke to a sound I didn't recognise at first: a soft, steady drumming on the iron roof. It wasn't a storm. It was gentle rain that went on and on, the kind Nan called 'a proper soaking'. I lay listening until I fell asleep smiling.
In the morning I was out of bed before Nan. I ran barefoot through the puddles to the fence post, tipped the gauge towards the light and squinted at it, the way I had watched her do all summer. Thirty-two millimetres.
Nan came down the path behind me and held out the green notebook and pencil without a word. Underneath her long column of zeros, in my own wobbly handwriting, I wrote the number 32.
Question: Where did Nan record the rainfall each morning?
Option A: on a calendar hanging in the kitchen
Option B: in a green notebook from her apron pocket
Option C: in a weather app on her phone
Option D: on a card pinned to the fence post

In March 1887, a twenty-year-old woman arrived in the small town of Tuscumbia, Alabama, to meet the child who would shape the rest of her life. The woman was Anne Sullivan. The child was Helen Keller, who was almost seven and had been unable to see or hear since a severe illness as a baby.
Anne understood more about darkness than most people. She had grown up in poverty, and an eye disease had left her nearly blind as a girl. At fourteen she entered the Perkins Institution for the Blind in Boston, where operations partly restored her sight. She worked hard, graduated at the top of her class, and soon afterwards accepted a job teaching a deafblind girl in the South.
The Helen she met was frustrated and often wild. Cut off from language, she could not explain what she wanted, so she kicked, screamed and grabbed food from other people's plates. Many people thought she could not be taught. Anne refused to believe it. She began spelling words into Helen's palm using a finger alphabet: d-o-l-l for a doll, c-a-k-e for cake. Helen copied the finger movements, but to her they were just a game. She had no idea that the shapes stood for things.
The breakthrough came in April, at the water pump outside the house. Anne held one of Helen's hands under the cold, gushing water and spelled w-a-t-e-r into the other, again and again. Suddenly, Helen went still. It was as if a door had swung open. Everything had a name, and every name was a key. By nightfall she had learnt many new words.
From then on, the two were rarely apart. When Helen went to Radcliffe College, Anne sat beside her in lectures, spelling the professors' words into her hand hour after hour. Reading so many textbooks for Helen strained Anne's weak eyes badly, but she kept going. In 1904 Helen graduated, becoming the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree.
Helen went on to become a famous author and speaker who campaigned for people with disabilities around the world. Anne travelled with her almost everywhere. Their friendship was not always easy. Anne could be stubborn and quick-tempered, and Helen sometimes longed for more independence. Still, neither could imagine life without the other.
Anne Sullivan died in 1936, after almost fifty years at Helen's side. Helen never stopped calling her by the name she had used since childhood. To the world, Anne was a famous teacher. To Helen, she was simply 'Teacher', and the dearest friend she ever had.

Option A: a broken piece of equipment
Option B: a sudden important step forward
Option C: an escape from a locked room
Option D: a short rest from hard work

Two Stories at Once
Spin around on the spot ten times, then stop. The room seems to keep turning, your legs wobble and you may need to grab something to stay upright. That strange feeling is a clue to one of the body's cleverest systems, one that most people never think about until it is fooled.
Staying balanced is a team effort. Your brain constantly gathers information from three main sources: your eyes, the muscles and joints of your body, and a tiny structure hidden deep inside each ear. By comparing these messages many times every second, the brain works out which way is up, whether you are moving and how to stop you from toppling over.
The inner ear's part of the job is done by the vestibular system. It includes three small, looping tubes called semicircular canals, set at roughly right angles to one another, like the edges meeting at the corner of a box. Each canal is filled with fluid. When you turn your head, the fluid lags behind for a moment and swirls, bending tiny hair cells that line the canals. The hair cells send signals to the brain describing which way, and how fast, your head is turning. Nearby, two small chambers contain even tinier crystals that shift with gravity, telling the brain whether your head is tilted and whether you are speeding up or slowing down.
This explains the spinning trick. When you twirl steadily, the fluid in your canals eventually catches up and moves along with them. When you stop suddenly, the fluid keeps swirling for a few seconds. Your inner ears report that you are still turning, while your eyes report that the room is still. The brain receives two different stories at once, and the result is dizziness.
The same kind of mix-up causes car sickness. If you read a book in the back seat, your inner ears feel every bump and corner, but your eyes, fixed on a still page, report no movement at all. Many people feel queasy as a result. Looking out of the window at the horizon usually helps, because it lets the eyes and ears agree again.
The third source, your muscles and joints, is easy to overlook. Sensors inside them tell your brain where each part of your body is, even when you cannot see it. That is why you can touch your nose with your eyes closed.
So the next time the room spins after a ride at the show, don't blame your ears for getting it wrong. They are doing exactly what they were built to do. It's just that, for a few seconds, your brain has been handed two stories and cannot decide which one to believe.
Question: What are the three looping, fluid-filled tubes in the inner ear called?
Option A: semicircular canals
Option B: hair cells
Option C: vestibular crystals
Option D: sensor chambers

Build a Robot That Follows a Line
A line-following robot is one of the simplest robots you can build, yet it uses the same basic ideas as some of the machines that carry goods around modern warehouses. This guide explains how to build one using a beginner's robotics kit.
What you need
You will need a robot chassis with two motors and wheels, a small microcontroller board, two infrared (IR) sensors, a battery pack, a large sheet of white cardboard, a roll of black electrical tape, and a computer to write and upload your program.
How it works
Before you start, it helps to understand how your robot will 'see'. Each IR sensor has two parts: a tiny light that shines invisible infrared light downwards, and a detector that measures how much of that light bounces back. White surfaces reflect most of the light. Black surfaces absorb most of it. So when a sensor is over white card, it receives a strong signal, and when it is over black tape, the signal is weak.
The microcontroller is the brain of the robot. It reads the signals from both sensors many times every second and decides what the motors should do.
Steps
1. Use the black tape to make a track on the white card. Start with a large oval, and avoid sharp corners until your robot is working well.
2. Attach the two sensors to the front of the chassis, facing down, about two centimetres apart. They should sit on either side of the tape, not on top of it.
3. Connect the sensors and motors to the microcontroller, following the diagram in your kit.
4. Write a program with three simple rules. If both sensors see white, drive both motors forward. If the left sensor sees black, the robot has drifted right, so slow the left motor to turn left. If the right sensor sees black, slow the right motor to turn right.
5. Upload the program, place the robot on the track with the tape between its sensors, and switch it on.
Troubleshooting
Don't be discouraged if your robot does something strange the first time. Finding and fixing problems, called debugging, is a normal part of robotics. Think of your robot as a very obedient assistant with no common sense. It will do exactly what your program says, even if what you said is not what you meant.
If your robot swerves away from the line instead of following it, you have probably swapped the left and right motor connections, so every correction sends it the wrong way. If it wobbles wildly from side to side, try reducing its speed. If it ignores the line completely, check that the sensors are close enough to the card to pick up the reflected light.
Once your robot can complete the oval, try a figure eight, or add a sharp bend and see whether your program can handle it.
Question: How far apart should the two sensors be placed?
Option A: about five centimetres
Option B: about one centimetre
Option C: about two centimetres
Option D: about ten centimetres

You will need a robot chassis with two motors and wheels, a small microcontroller board, two infrared (IR) sensors, a battery pack, a large sheet of white cardboard, a roll of black electrical tape, and a computer to write and upload your program.
How it works
Before you start, it helps to understand how your robot will 'see'. Each IR sensor has two parts: a tiny light that shines invisible infrared light downwards, and a detector that measures how much of that light bounces back. White surfaces reflect most of the light. Black surfaces absorb most of it. So when a sensor is over white card, it receives a strong signal, and when it is over black tape, the signal is weak.
The microcontroller is the brain of the robot. It reads the signals from both sensors many times every second and decides what the motors should do.
Steps
1. Use the black tape to make a track on the white card. Start with a large oval, and avoid sharp corners until your robot is working well.
2. Attach the two sensors to the front of the chassis, facing down, about two centimetres apart. They should sit on either side of the tape, not on top of it.
3. Connect the sensors and motors to the microcontroller, following the diagram in your kit.
4. Write a program with three simple rules. If both sensors see white, drive both motors forward. If the left sensor sees black, the robot has drifted right, so slow the left motor to turn left. If the right sensor sees black, slow the right motor to turn right.
5. Upload the program, place the robot on the track with the tape between its sensors, and switch it on.
Troubleshooting
Don't be discouraged if your robot does something strange the first time. Finding and fixing problems, called debugging, is a normal part of robotics. Think of your robot as a very obedient assistant with no common sense. It will do exactly what your program says, even if what you said is not what you meant.
If your robot swerves away from the line instead of following it, you have probably swapped the left and right motor connections, so every correction sends it the wrong way. If it wobbles wildly from side to side, try reducing its speed. If it ignores the line completely, check that the sensors are close enough to the card to pick up the reflected light.

The Weaver Who Lit the Sky
Long ago, in a village near the top of the world, winter was a time of endless dark. For two whole months the sun did not rise at all, and the people lived by the glow of their fires and the cold light of the stars. The old ones said that the North Wind sometimes walked among people in disguise, testing whether their hearts were warm or cold.

Every summer, while the sun circled the sky day and night, she wandered the hills gathering flowers, berries, lichen and roots. She boiled them in great pots to make her dyes: crimson from cranberries, gold from birch leaves, deep green from moss and a violet that no one else could match. She dipped her wool in them and hung the skeins to dry in the long summer light. Each thread was a summer she had saved.
That year, Ylva wove a cloak from her brightest threads. It shimmered like the sea at sunset, and she meant to wear it to the midwinter gathering, where every eye would turn to her.
Three nights before the gathering, there was a knock at her door. Outside stood a gaunt old man in a grey coat. His beard was white with frost, and when he spoke, his breath turned to ice crystals even in the warmth of her doorway.
'I have travelled far, and the dark has worn me thin,' he said. 'Do you have a scrap of colour to spare?'
Ylva hesitated. Her baskets of thread were nearly empty. All that remained of her summer was the cloak. She thought of the gathering and of everyone admiring her. Then she looked at the old man's tired face, and at the darkness pressing against the windows, and she took the cloak from its hook and placed it in his hands.

Speaking With Your Hands
At an emergency briefing during a bushfire or flood, you may notice someone standing beside the speaker, hands moving quickly, face full of expression. That person is an Auslan interpreter, and for thousands of Deaf Australians, they are the link to information that could keep them safe.
Auslan is Australian Sign Language, the language of the Deaf community in Australia. Many people assume it is simply English spelt out on the hands, but it is a complete language with its own vocabulary and grammar. Word order can differ from English, and facial expressions are not just decoration. Raised eyebrows can turn a statement into a question, and the shape of the mouth can show whether something is tiny or enormous. A good interpreter must be fluent in both Auslan and English and able to switch between them almost instantly.
Interpreters work in many places besides television. They help at doctors' appointments, university lectures, job interviews, courts, weddings and school assemblies. Wherever a Deaf person and a hearing person need to understand each other, an interpreter may be needed.
The work is far more tiring than it looks. An interpreter must listen to one language, understand its meaning and express that meaning in another, all while the speaker keeps talking. For this reason, interpreters often work in pairs on long jobs, swapping roles about every twenty minutes. The one who is resting watches closely and quietly feeds in any missed number or name.
In Australia, professional interpreters are usually certified by a national body called NAATI. Most study Auslan for several years and complete a qualification before they sit the certification test. They also follow a strict code of ethics: they must keep everything they hear private and interpret faithfully, without adding their own opinions.
Mira Santos has worked as an interpreter for eleven years. Both of her parents are Deaf, and Auslan was the first language she learned. 'By the time I was eight, I was interpreting for Mum and Dad at the bank and the doctor's,' she says. 'I was proud to help, but it wasn't really fair on any of us. A kid shouldn't have to explain a medical test result to her own father.'
Today Mira works mostly in hospitals. She says the best moments are the quiet ones: a patient nodding because they finally understand what will happen during their operation, or a parent asking the doctor questions directly, in their own words.
'My job is to disappear,' she says. 'If I've done it well, the two people feel as if they've been talking to each other the whole time.'
Question: According to the text, what is Auslan?
Option A: a way of spelling out English words on the hands
Option B: the language of the Deaf community in Australia
Option C: the national body that certifies interpreters
Option D: a code of ethics that all interpreters follow

Building and Trimming a Paper Glider
A paper glider is more than a toy. Every time it floats across a room, it relies on the same four forces that keep a passenger jet in the air. This report explains those forces and then shows you how to build and test a glider of your own.
The four forces
Any aircraft in flight is affected by four forces. Weight is the pull of gravity, dragging the aircraft down. Lift is the upward push created as air flows over and under the wings. Thrust moves the aircraft forward, and drag is the resistance of the air pushing back against it. A jet's engines provide thrust, but a glider has no engine. Its only thrust comes from your throw. After that, it trades height for distance, sliding gently downwards through the air.
Making the glider
You will need a sheet of A4 paper and a paper clip.
1. Fold the paper in half lengthways, crease it firmly, and open it out again.
2. Fold the two top corners in to meet the centre crease, forming a point.
3. Fold the new slanted edges in to the centre crease again, making the point narrower.
4. Fold the whole plane in half along the centre crease, with the folds on the outside.
5. Fold each side down to make the wings, so that the top edge of each wing lines up with the bottom of the body.
6. Open the wings so that they form a slight V shape when viewed from the front.
Testing and trimming
Find a large indoor space, so that wind will not affect your results. Hold the glider under the wings and launch it gently forward and level. Do not throw it hard; a glider flies best at a smooth, steady speed.
Watch carefully how it flies. Pilots and engineers call the small adjustments that follow 'trimming'.
If the glider climbs steeply, slows, then drops suddenly, it is stalling. Its nose is pointing too high, so the wings can no longer produce enough lift. Slide a paper clip onto the nose. The extra weight at the front will help keep the nose down.
If the glider dives straight into the floor, its nose is pointing too low. Bend the back edges of both wings up very slightly, by about two millimetres. Air hitting these raised edges will push the tail down and lift the nose.
If the glider turns sharply to one side, check that both wings are the same shape. Small differences can make a big difference.
Change only one thing at a time, and test it several times before making another change. That way, you will know exactly which adjustment made the difference. Real aircraft designers work in much the same way: testing, adjusting and testing again. Very few planes, paper or otherwise, fly perfectly on the first try.
Question: Where does a paper glider's thrust come from?
Option A: the person's throw
Option B: the air under the wings
Option C: the paper clip on the nose
Option D: the pull of gravity

March, Above the Den
For five dark months she has not eaten.
Under a drift on the hillside she lay
while the long night pressed on the roof of snow
and the wind came hunting and wandered away.

In the deepest cold she gave birth to two,
blind, and no bigger than rabbits then,
and she fed them warm from her own thin store
in the blue-white hollow she'd dug for a den.

Through the weeks of the dark they grew round on her milk
while she curled her great body about them, a wall,
and she shifted in sleep so they never felt cold,
and she gave, and she gave, and took nothing at all.

Now the sun has come back to the rim of the world,
low and pale as a lamp turned down,
and she breaks through the crust with a single paw
and squints at the brightness, and looks around.

The cubs tumble after, all elbows and fluff,
and they roll down the slope as if snow were a game.
She lets them. For days she stays close by the door
while their small legs learn the cold by name.

They chase their own shadows, they wrestle and squeal,
they bat at the flakes that blow down from the hill,
while she lies at the mouth of the den and watches,
her great head heavy, her great paws still.

She is thinner by far than the bear who dug in;
you could count her ribs through the fur on her side.
Out past the shore lies the frozen sea
where the seals breathe up through the holes they hide.

Each hour that she waits, her hunger grows louder.
Each hour that she waits, the cubs grow more strong.
She lifts her nose to the wind from the coast,
and she knows that the ice will not last for long.

So one grey morning she turns for the sea
and walks without stopping, and they must keep pace;
when the smaller one stumbles and cries in the snow,
she goes back, and she touches her nose to its face.

Over the ridges and pressure-cracked floes,
with a white fox trailing for scraps behind,
she leads them out on the creaking plain
where the wind is sharp and the light unkind.

Once the ice groans and splits at their feet
and a black lane of water opens wide;
she slides in first, and they follow her close,
and she noses them up on the farther side.

She does not hurry, though every bone aches.
She does not stir when the cubs grow bold.
She has waited all winter; she can wait an hour
with her belly pressed flat to the bitter cold.

By a hole in the ice she lies flat as a shadow.
The cubs at her back try hard not to shift.
An hour goes by, and another, and more,
till a whiskered head rises, grey and swift.

She eats, and they watch her. Next year they will try
the same long stillness, the same sudden spring.
But tonight, as they curl in the lee of a ridge,
she is full, and she sleeps, and she wants for nothing.
Question: How long has the mother bear gone without eating when the poem begins?
Option A: five months
Option B: one winter night
Option C: two weeks
Option D: a whole year

Before the sun had cleared the city wall, Dhara was already sweeping the workshop floor. Her uncle Kavi carved seals for the merchants of the city, and for a whole year she had been allowed to do nothing but sweep, fetch water and watch.
The seals were small squares of soft grey stone, about as wide as her thumb was long. On each one her uncle cut a tiny animal, a short row of signs above it, and a knob on the back with a hole for a cord. A merchant pressed his seal into damp clay to mark his bundles of cotton or jars of grain, so that anyone, even in a distant port, would know whose goods they were. Once the carving was done, each seal was baked until it turned hard and pale.
'Today,' said Kavi, setting a blank square in front of her, 'you will cut your own.'
Dhara's heart jumped. She had practised on scraps for months, scratching clumsy bulls and lopsided elephants that she quickly rubbed away. But this was a real seal, ordered by the cloth merchant Ilan.
She chose a bull, because it was the animal she had practised most. Her uncle showed her again how to hold the copper tool low and at an angle. 'Remember,' he said, 'everything must be backwards. What you cut on the left will print on the right.'
All morning she worked in the doorway, where the light was best. Outside, carts rattled over the baked-brick street and water gurgled through the covered drains beneath it. She hardly noticed. The bull's horns came first, then its broad shoulders, then the folds of skin at its neck. By midday her eyes ached.
Then she reached the signs. Kavi had scratched them for her on a piece of broken pottery: five marks that stood for the merchant's name, though Dhara could not read them. She copied them carefully, one by one, and when she had finished she sat back and smiled.
Her uncle pressed the seal into a lump of clay and held the clay to the light. He was quiet for a long time.
'The bull is fine work,' he said at last. 'But look at your signs.'
Dhara looked. The bull faced the right way. The signs did not. She had remembered to reverse the animal she had drawn a hundred times, but she had copied the signs exactly as they appeared on the pottery, and now on the clay they ran the wrong way.
Her face burned. Kavi did not scold her. He took another blank square from the shelf and placed it before her. 'Ilan's ship does not sail until tomorrow,' he said. 'As for that one, keep it, and look at it whenever you are tempted to hurry.'
That night, by the light of an oil lamp, Dhara cut a second bull. This time, before she began the signs, she pressed the pottery scrap into clay and copied them from the print.

Option A: a simple sentence with only one verb

The car stopped with its nose pointing at the sky and its back wheels spinning in the sand. Ahead of us, beyond the crest, I could see nothing but the next dune, and the one after that, red ridges lined up to the horizon like waves that had forgotten how to move.
'Number twenty-seven,' I said, writing it in my notebook. 'Twenty-seven and stuck.'
Dad didn't answer. He climbed out, walked around to the back and stared at the two deep trenches the tyres had dug.
That morning, at the camping ground on the western edge of the desert, an old man with a sun-cracked face had wandered over while we packed. He'd looked at our tyres and shaken his head. 'Let them down,' he'd said. 'Eighteen, maybe twenty. Hard tyres just dig. Soft ones spread out and float.' Dad had thanked him politely, and then, when the man had gone, said that our car had crossed plenty of rough country before and he didn't want to waste the morning fiddling with gauges. I had written that down too: Old man says 18. Dad says no.
Now the sun was high and the sand was hot enough to sting through my sneakers. Dad reversed down the slope and took another run. The engine roared, the car lurched forward three metres, and the wheels sank deeper. He tried again. This time we didn't move at all.
He sat on the sand with his hat pulled low. I sat beside him. A small lizard ran across the crest, stopped, and lifted two of its feet off the scorching ground, then swapped them for the other two, as if it were dancing. Somewhere behind us a crow called, and the sound seemed to hang in the heat.

The Gold in the Kitchen Drawer
Somewhere in most Australian homes there is a drawer full of forgotten technology: a cracked phone, a tangle of chargers, a music player that no one has switched on for years. It is easy to think of these things as junk. Recyclers see them very differently. To them, that drawer is a small mine.
A mobile phone is built from dozens of materials. Its circuit board contains tiny amounts of gold, silver and copper, because these metals carry electricity extremely well. Its battery holds lithium and cobalt. Getting these materials out of the ground is expensive and damaging. Mines clear land, use enormous amounts of water and energy, and leave behind mountains of waste rock.
This is where the idea of 'urban mining' comes in. Instead of digging up new ore, recyclers recover metals from old devices. The numbers are surprising. A tonne of discarded phones can contain many times more gold than a tonne of rock from a typical gold mine. In other words, some of the richest gold deposits on Earth may now be sitting in kitchen drawers.
Recovering these metals takes several stages. First, devices are collected at drop-off points such as libraries, council depots and some shops. Next, workers remove the batteries by hand, because batteries can catch fire if they are crushed. The remaining parts are then shredded, and magnets, air currents and other methods are used to separate the plastic, glass and different metals. Finally, the metal-rich material is sent to specialist refineries, where the precious metals are extracted and purified so they can be used again.
Unfortunately, much of our electronic waste never reaches a recycler. Some of it is thrown into ordinary household bins and buried in landfill, where valuable metals are lost forever and harmful substances such as lead and mercury can leak into soil and water. Batteries hidden in rubbish have also caused fires in garbage trucks and at waste centres.
Australians are among the world's biggest users of electronic devices per person, which means we also produce a great deal of e-waste. Several states, including South Australia and Victoria, have now banned it from landfill altogether. Bans help, but they work only if people know where to take their old devices and bother to do so.
So the next time you open that drawer, think twice before tipping its contents into the bin. That old phone is not rubbish. It is a tiny treasure chest, and with a short trip to a collection point, its gold can shine again.

Option A: gold stops the phone from overheating
Option B: gold makes the phone last much longer
Option C: gold carries electricity extremely well
Option D: gold is cheaper than other metals

Tunnels Under the Snowy
In the years after the Second World War, Australia faced two problems at once. Much of the inland was dry, and farmers along the Murray and Murrumbidgee rivers needed more reliable water. At the same time, the growing cities of the south-east needed more electricity. In 1949, the federal government announced a bold answer to both: the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Scheme.
The idea was simple to describe but enormously difficult to build. Each spring, melting snow in the Australian Alps poured into the Snowy River, which flowed south to the sea. Engineers planned to capture this water behind dams and send it west through tunnels under the mountains, into the inland rivers. On the way, the falling water would spin turbines in power stations and generate electricity.
Over the next twenty-five years, workers built sixteen major dams, seven power stations, about 145 kilometres of tunnels and 80 kilometres of aqueducts. Much of this work took place in remote country, through freezing winters, with tunnels blasted through solid rock. New towns, such as Cabramurra, were built to house workers, and old towns, including Adaminaby and Jindabyne, were moved to make way for new lakes.
Remarkable as the engineering was, the people who did it are just as much a part of the story. More than 100,000 people worked on the Scheme, and around two-thirds of them came from overseas, from more than thirty countries. Many had left a Europe shattered by war. The Gardener of the Mallee
In the low, dry scrubland of southern Australia lives a bird that never sits on its eggs. Instead, the malleefowl builds an enormous compost heap, buries its eggs inside, and lets the heat of rotting leaves do the work. Then it spends most of the year adjusting the heap, like a cook who refuses to leave the kitchen.
The malleefowl is about the size of a domestic chicken, with feathers patterned in grey, brown and cream that blend into the leaf litter. It belongs to a family called megapodes, which means 'large feet', and those big, strong feet are its most important tools. Malleefowl usually live in pairs, and a pair may return to the same mound year after year.
Work on the mound begins in winter. The male, sometimes helped by the female, scratches out a pit that can be several metres across. He rakes leaves, twigs and bark into it, and once winter rain has soaked this material, he covers it with a thick layer of sandy soil. As the wet leaves rot, they give off heat, just as a garden compost heap does. The finished mound may be a metre high and contain several tonnes of material, all shifted by one bird's feet.
From spring onwards the female lays her eggs in a chamber inside the mound, one every few days, sometimes more than twenty in a season. The eggs need to stay at about 33 degrees Celsius to develop. This is where the male's real labour begins. Many times a day he pushes his beak into the mound, and scientists believe he uses it to judge the temperature. If the mound is too hot, he opens it up to let heat escape. If it is too cool, he heaps on more soil. By summer, the sun has become the main source of heat, so he may spread the soil out in the cool of the morning and pile it back on before the afternoon. He keeps up this careful work for up to eleven months of the year.
The chicks receive no care at all. Each one digs its own way up through the soil, which can take many hours, and walks off alone into the scrub. Within a day it can fly. It will never meet its parents. Many chicks are taken by foxes, cats or birds of prey in their first weeks.
Sadly, malleefowl numbers have fallen across much of their range. Land clearing has removed their habitat, foxes take eggs and chicks, and bushfires can destroy huge areas of mallee at once. The species is now listed as vulnerable. Volunteers in several states count active mounds each year, and their records show where the birds are holding on and where they are vanishing.
A bird so devoted to its mound deserves the same devotion from us.

Pictures Made of Sound
Ernst Chladni was born in 1756 in Wittenberg, in what is now Germany. His father, a strict lawyer, was determined that his son would follow him into the law. Young Ernst was kept close to home, and he studied hard and earned a law degree. But when his father died, Chladni put the law aside and turned to the subjects that had always fascinated him: science and music.
Chladni was an amateur musician, and he wanted to understand exactly how objects make sound. Scientists already knew that sound is caused by vibration, but vibration is usually too fast to see. A violin string or a metal bell shivers hundreds of times a second, and the eye sees only a blur, if it sees anything at all. Chladni wanted a way to make those invisible movements show themselves.
His solution was beautifully simple. He took a thin, flat plate of metal or glass, held it firmly at the centre, and scattered fine sand over its surface. Then he drew a violin bow along the edge. As the plate began to ring, the sand jumped and danced, then gathered into lines and curves. Some parts of the plate were vibrating strongly, throwing the sand away. Other parts, called nodes, stayed almost perfectly still, and that is where the sand came to rest. The result was a delicate pattern of stars, rings and crosses. When Chladni changed the note, by bowing at a different spot or touching the edge with a finger, the sand scattered and a completely new pattern formed.
Chladni published his findings in 1787 and then spent years travelling across Europe, demonstrating his 'sound figures' to amazed audiences. In 1809 he performed for the French emperor Napoleon, who was so impressed that he gave Chladni 6,000 francs to translate his work into French. The Man Who Asked Why Shapes Grow
Why is a soap bubble round? Why does a snail's shell coil in a spiral that widens as it grows? Why are the bones of a bird's wing hollow? For most of history, people admired the shapes of nature without asking why they took the form they did. D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson spent his life asking.
Thompson was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1860. His mother died shortly after his birth, and he was raised partly by his grandfather, who encouraged his love of natural history, and partly by his father, a teacher of Greek and Latin. As a result, the boy grew up equally at home with ancient languages and with beetles. At university he studied medicine and then zoology, the science of animals, and at just twenty-four he became a professor at a small new college in Dundee.
Thompson was a remarkable teacher. He was tall, bearded and full of energy, and he filled his museum with specimens of every kind: shells, skeletons, sponges and stuffed birds. Students remembered his lectures for their sense of wonder, and visitors remembered the parrot that sometimes kept him company in his office.
But it was a book that made him famous. In 1917, during the First World War, he published On Growth and Form. In it, Thompson argued that living things are shaped not only by the slow changes of evolution but also by the ordinary laws of physics and mathematics. A bubble is round because a sphere holds the most air inside the smallest surface. A bird's hollow bones are light yet strong, like the frame of a well-built bridge. A snail's shell keeps its shape as it grows because new material is added in a regular spiral.
The most striking part of the book showed drawings of fish on a background of squares, like graph paper. Thompson then stretched, squashed or slanted the squares, and showed that the outline of one kind of fish could be turned smoothly into the outline of a quite different kind. It was as if nature had drawn one design and then simply bent the paper.
Not every scientist agreed with him, and some of his ideas have since proved incomplete. Thompson knew little about genes, which were only beginning to be understood. Yet his book was written so clearly, and with such delight, that it has never gone out of print. Artists, architects and engineers have read it as eagerly as biologists.
Thompson taught for more than sixty years and was knighted in 1937. He died in 1948, still working. His great question, why living things take the shapes they do, is one that scientists are still trying to answer today.

By the Mark
The fog came down at the turn of the tide
like a grey sheet over the bay;
it swallowed the headland, it swallowed the stars,
it swallowed the lamp on the quay.

The captain stood still with his hand on the rail
and listened, as if he could hear
the rocks that he knew lay under the swell
somewhere unseen, and near.

'Fetch out the lead,' was all that he said,
'and Tom, you'll be calling tonight.'
So I took up the line with its weight of grey lead
and its rags and its leathers tied tight.

I was twelve and a half, the youngest aboard,
and I'd practised by day at the dock,
but never by night, with the ship in my hands
and the sea full of hidden rock.

Two strips of leather for two fathoms down,
and three strips for three; and then
a white rag for five, and a red rag for seven,
and leather with a hole for ten.

I had learned them by feel, for at night in the fog
there is nothing a sailor can see;
you read the wet line with your fingers alone,
and your fingers must tell it true.

I swung it and flung it out over the bow
and felt it sink down through the black;
I found the right mark as the line came straight
and sang out, 'By the mark, ten!' and hauled it back.

The men on the deck stood as still as the masts;
not a boot on the planking stirred.
The only sounds were the drip of the line
and my voice, and the captain's word.

Again and again, and the numbers grew small:
'By the mark, seven!' 'And a half, five!'
The captain said nothing. He eased the wheel
as though the ship were alive.

He swung her away from the sound of the shore,
he brought her round slow on the swell,
and I flung the lead and I flung it again
and I called every mark as it fell.

'By the mark, three!' My voice cracked on the word,
and close by I heard the surf roar.
'Let go the anchor!' the captain cried,
and it plunged to the sandy floor.

We swung on the chain through the rest of the night
and nobody slept or spoke;

Racing the Weather
For most of the year, a wheat farm in the Wimmera region of Victoria is a quiet place. But for a few weeks in late spring and early summer, it becomes a round-the-clock operation. Harvest has arrived, and every farmer knows that a whole year's income depends on getting the crop off the paddock safely.
The story of a harvest really begins months earlier. In autumn, after the first good rains, farmers sow the seed with machines that drop it into narrow rows. Through winter the crop grows green and thick, while farmers check their paddocks for weeds, pests and disease. By spring the plants have formed heads of grain, and as the weather warms, the paddocks slowly turn from green to the colour of honey.
Before harvest can start, the grain must be dry enough. Farmers rub a few heads between their palms, chew a grain or two, and test samples with a moisture meter. Grain that is harvested too wet can go mouldy in storage. But waiting too long is risky as well. A single hailstorm can flatten a crop in minutes, and heavy rain can cause the ripe grain to sprout or lose quality.
Once the grain is ready, the header rolls in. This huge machine, also called a combine harvester, cuts the plants, shakes the grain from the heads and blows away the light straw and husks, which spill out behind it. The clean grain fills a tank inside the header. A tractor pulling a chaser bin drives alongside, and the header empties its tank into the bin without stopping. The chaser bin then carries the grain to trucks waiting at the edge of the paddock, and the trucks take it to a silo or a large receival site. On a good day, a modern header can harvest dozens of hectares.
During harvest, the whole family and often hired workers pitch in. Headers may run late into the night under bright lights, while someone else drives meals out to the paddock. Fire is a constant worry. A spark from a machine can set dry stubble alight, so farmers keep fire-fighting water units close by, and on days of extreme heat and wind, harvesting is banned.
When the last paddock is stripped and the final truck leaves for the silo, there is a sense of relief that every farming family understands. Neighbours ring one another to compare yields, and talk at the local store turns to how much grain the district has brought in. The paddocks lie bare and golden in the summer sun. Then, before long, the cycle begins again, with farmers watching the autumn sky and waiting for the rain.

Option A: it is emptied into a chaser bin
Option B: it is taken to the silo by truck
Option C: it is tested with a moisture meter
Option D: it is left at the edge of the paddock

a rowboat heading for home,

that same orange cat, rowing hard.

I noted the colours, the time that I found them,
and wrote what I learned in a book:

Drawn before seven. Drawn by small hands;
the lines never reach very far.

Always that orange cat.

I asked at the shop and I asked at the school
if anyone knew of a cat
that was orange and small with a white-tipped tail.

I saw what I'd passed every day:
on the fence of the house where the removal truck
had stopped the Sunday before,

a stub of blue chalk worn down to a pebble,
dropped, or perhaps left behind.

and a girl in a dressing gown crept out.

a whale with two children riding its back
and an orange cat steering. And waited.

and she didn't run back inside.

and rockets and cats, end to end,
and by lunchtime the mystery had a name,

Old Bricks, New Risks
Walk down the main street of almost any Australian country town or older suburb and you will see them: handsome brick shops and hotels built a century or more ago, with decorative parapets along their rooftops and verandahs stretching over the footpath. They are part of our history, and we are right to treasure them. But many of them share a hidden weakness, and it is time we did something about it.
Most of these buildings are made of what engineers call unreinforced masonry. That means bricks or stones held together only by mortar, with no steel inside to stop the walls pulling apart when they are shaken. In normal conditions, such buildings can stand for generations. In an earthquake, their walls can crack, and their heavy parapets can topple straight onto the street below.
Many Australians believe that earthquakes happen only in other countries. They are mistaken. Geoscience Australia records many earthquakes across the continent every year, and every so often a damaging one strikes. On 28 December 1989, a magnitude 5.6 earthquake hit Newcastle in New South Wales. By world standards it was only a moderate quake, yet thirteen people died and more than 160 were injured, and much of the worst damage was to older brick buildings. In September 2021, an earthquake near Mansfield in Victoria shook Melbourne, and part of a brick shopfront on Chapel Street crashed onto the footpath. If that wall had collapsed on a busy Saturday afternoon, the result might have been tragic.
The good news is that this problem can be fixed. Engineers can tie parapets back to the roof with steel brackets, brace weak walls and add anchors that hold floors and walls together. These methods are well understood and far cheaper than rebuilding after a disaster. Across the Tasman, New Zealand has passed laws requiring owners of earthquake-prone buildings to strengthen them within set time limits, and the work is steadily being done.
Some people argue that strengthening is too expensive, or that it will spoil the character of our heritage streets. Both concerns deserve a fair hearing, but neither stands up for long. Councils and governments can offer grants to help owners meet the cost, and careful work can be almost invisible from the street. In any case, a building that has fallen down has no heritage value at all.
So I am asking our councils to act. Every council should list the old brick buildings in its area, offer owners practical help, and set a reasonable deadline for the work to be done. We cannot stop earthquakes. We can make sure that when the next one comes, our beautiful old streets are still standing, and so is everyone walking along them.
Question: What is 'unreinforced masonry'?
Option A: walls made of steel covered with bricks
Option B: buildings that have been strengthened
Option C: bricks or stones held together only by mortar
Option D: bricks that have been made by hand

Living Pantries
In the red sand country of central Australia, rain can stay away for months. Plants wilt, flowers vanish and food for small creatures becomes scarce. Yet deep beneath the mulga scrub, colonies of honeypot ants have a clever way to survive the lean times. They store their food inside the bodies of their own sisters.

A fully loaded replete can be as large as a grape, its body so swollen that the thin skin between its hard plates becomes almost see-through and glows amber, like a drop of honey. Too heavy to walk, the repletes hang from the ceilings of chambers that may lie more than a metre below the surface, where the soil stays cool and damp.

In response, it brings up a droplet of stored food and passes it mouth to mouth. In this way a few hundred living storage jars can keep an entire colony alive until the rains return. Scientists believe the repletes may store water as well, which would be just as precious in the desert.

Give Every Kid a Turn
Walk past any junior soccer field on a Saturday morning and you will probably see the same thing. The fastest child is up front, scoring. The tallest child is in goal. And somewhere out on the wing, a quieter player has not touched the ball for twenty minutes. I believe this needs to change. In junior sport, every player should rotate through every position.
The first reason is simple: children are still growing. A ten-year-old who is short and slow this season may be tall and quick in two years' time. If coaches lock players into positions too early, they are judging them on who they are now, not on who they might become.
Second, playing different positions makes players smarter. A striker who has spent a few games in defence understands what defenders fear. A goalkeeper who has played in the midfield knows how hard it is to find space. When every player has seen the game from several angles, the whole team reads play better. As one under-12 coach at my club puts it, "When my kids have stood in each other's boots, they stop blaming and start helping."
Some parents argue that rotating positions means losing more games. They may be right, at least at first. But junior sport is not meant to be a miniature version of the professional leagues. Its purpose is to build skills, fitness and friendships, and a scoreboard is a poor measure of those things. Surveys have repeatedly found that one of the most common reasons children give for quitting sport is that it has stopped being fun. Spending a whole season stuck in one spot, never getting near the action, is a sure way to drain the fun away.
Rotation also builds a kind of teamwork that a winning-at-all-costs approach cannot. When the star striker takes a turn in defence, she learns to trust her teammates to score. When the shy winger finally gets a turn up front, the others learn to pass to him. A team is not a machine made of fixed parts; it is a group of people who need to understand one another.
Of course, there is a place for specialist positions. Older teenagers who choose to play competitively will naturally settle into the roles that suit them best. But for children under thirteen, the aim should be to give everyone a taste of everything.
So, coaches, next Saturday, try it. Put your tallest player on the wing and your fastest in goal. You might lose a match. But you will win something more valuable: a team in which every player feels they belong.

Option A: the fastest players should always be strikers
Option B: junior sport should not keep any scores at all
Option C: coaches should choose players by their height
Option D: junior players should take turns in every position

Every September, Nell's walk to school became a battle. Halfway down Wattle Street, a magpie would launch from the old gum outside number fourteen, and Nell would hear the whoosh of wings a split second before a beak clacked beside her ear.

"So what am I supposed to do?"
"Go around. Six weeks, maybe less, and the babies will be flying."

The Finder's Lamp
Tobin stood on the doorstep of the mill house with a lamp in his hand that would not stop pointing, and wondered how a lost marble had led him here.
It had begun that morning, in the market square of Little Harrow. Tobin had lost his best marble, a blue glass one with a silver swirl at its heart, somewhere near the well. He had searched every crack in the cobblestones until his knees ached, while the baker's cat watched him from a windowsill as if it knew exactly where the marble was and had no intention of saying.
That was when he noticed the stall. It had not been there yesterday, and the woman behind it was so old and so still that she might have been carved from the same wood as her table. On the table sat a single brass lamp, dented and dull, with a wick that looked as if it had never been lit.
"A finder's lamp," she said, before Tobin could ask. "Light it, and its flame leans towards whatever you have truly lost. One copper to borrow it until sunset."
Tobin paid. The flame flickered, then bent sharply, like a dog pulling on a lead, towards the eastern road.
"But the well is that way," Tobin said, pointing west.
The woman only smiled. "The lamp knows what it knows."
So Tobin followed. The flame led him out of the square and down the eastern road beside the river. It led him across the stone bridge where he and Pell had once raced paper boats, past the willow they had climbed every summer until last spring, and up the lane to the mill, where Pell's family lived.
Tobin had not spoken to Pell since the quarrel. He could hardly remember now what it had been about - something to do with a broken kite and who was to blame. He remembered only the words they had shouted, and the long silence that followed, which had grown harder to break with every passing week.
Now he stood on the doorstep, and the flame pointed straight at the door, steady as a compass needle. His heart was thumping. He thought about turning round and going home, and pretending none of this had happened.
Tobin knocked.
The door opened. Pell stood there, taller than Tobin remembered, holding something in his open palm: a blue glass marble with a silver swirl.
"I found it by the well this morning," Pell said. "I knew it was yours. I've been standing here for ages, trying to decide whether to bring it over."
Tobin looked down at the lamp. The flame had gone out.
That evening, when Tobin ran back to the market to return the lamp, the stall was gone. There was nothing in its place but a few curls of wood shavings and a single copper coin, shining on the cobblestones.
Question: What did Tobin's lost marble look like?
Option A: green glass with a gold stripe
Option B: blue glass with a silver swirl
Option C: clear glass with a blue swirl
Option D: silver metal with a blue spot

Mapping the House for Pudding
Pudding had been my cat for as long as I could remember. She was older than my little sister and almost as old as me, a round grey tabby who spent her days following the sunlight from room to room.
The first sign was small. One evening she walked straight into the leg of the kitchen table, stopped, and sat down as if she had meant to do it. A week later she missed the jump onto my bed and slid back to the floor with a soft thump. When she started crying at night in the hallway, Mum took her to the vet.
Dr Amara shone a tiny torch into Pudding's eyes and frowned. "Her eyesight is fading," she said gently. "It's common in older cats. It won't hurt her, but she'll need some help to adjust."
I wanted to know exactly what kind of help, so Dr Amara gave me a list. Keep the furniture where it is. Keep her food and water bowls in the same place, always. Talk to her before you touch her, so she isn't startled. And give her ways to find her way around that don't depend on her eyes.
That weekend, I became the house's chief engineer. I pushed the footstool back against the wall where it had always lived and banned my sister from leaving her school bag in the hallway. I put a strip of soft carpet at the bottom of the stairs and a rough doormat at the top, so Pudding could feel with her paws where the steps began and ended. Dad helped me build a ramp of sturdy boxes up to my bed, and we dabbed a drop of vanilla on each table leg so her nose could warn her before her whiskers did.
For the first few days, Pudding moved slowly, her nose low, her whiskers fanned forward like antennae. She stopped often, listening. I worried that we had made things worse. Then one morning I heard a steady pad-pad-pad down the hallway, a soft scrabble up the ramp, and a warm weight settling on my feet. She had charted the whole route on her own.
Now, a few months later, Pudding moves around the house almost as confidently as she used to. Visitors don't even notice that she can't see. The only clue is that she still pauses in each doorway, head tilted, as though she is reading a map only she can see.
My sister asked me once whether Pudding was sad about losing her sight. I thought about it for a long time. "I don't think she misses it the way we would," I said. "She's still finding the sun."
And she is. Every afternoon, she follows its warmth across the floorboards, from the kitchen to the lounge to the patch by the back door, exactly as she always has.

Option A: at the bottom of the stairs
Option B: beside the kitchen table
Option C: at the foot of the bed
Option D: at the top of the stairs

Flowers Carved in Wood
In the early twentieth century, many Australian artists believed that real art came from Europe. They painted gentle landscapes in soft European light and dreamed of exhibiting in London or Paris. Margaret Preston thought differently. She believed Australia deserved an art of its own, and she spent much of her long career trying to create one.
Preston was born Margaret Rose McPherson in Port Adelaide in 1875. As a girl she visited galleries and decided early that she would be an artist, at a time when few women were able to make a living that way. She studied art in Melbourne and Adelaide and then, like many artists of her day, travelled to Europe to learn more. There she saw the bold, flat colours of modern French painting and the simple, strong lines of Japanese woodblock prints. Both would shape her work for the rest of her life.
After she married William Preston in 1919, the couple settled in Sydney. It was there that Margaret produced the works for which she is best remembered: still-life paintings and woodcut prints of Australian native flowers. Instead of roses and violets, she chose banksias, waratahs, gum blossoms and flannel flowers. She carved her designs into blocks of wood, printed them in black ink and then often coloured each print by hand. The results were striking. The flowers were shown with heavy outlines and bright, flat areas of colour, almost like patterns.
Not everyone approved. Some critics found her work too harsh and too modern. Preston was not discouraged. She wrote articles and gave talks arguing that Australian artists should look closely at their own surroundings instead of copying overseas styles. She also believed that art should not be kept only in galleries. Because woodcuts could be printed many times, her images could be sold cheaply and hung in ordinary homes, and some of her designs appeared on magazine covers.
Preston kept experimenting until late in life, trying new techniques such as stencils and monotypes. She was always restless, always asking what Australian art could become. She died in 1963, aged eighty-eight.
Today her prints hang in major galleries across the country, and her bold banksias and waratahs are instantly recognisable. Yet perhaps her greatest achievement was not any single picture. It was helping Australians to see that the plants growing outside their own back doors were worthy subjects for art.

Option A: the history of woodblock printing in Japan and France
Option B: the reasons critics disliked modern Australian art
Option C: Margaret Preston's work to create a truly Australian art
Option D: the native flowers that grow around Sydney

Margaret Preston thought differently. She believed Australia deserved an art of its own, and she spent much of her long career trying to create one.
Preston was born Margaret Rose McPherson in Port Adelaide in 1875. As a girl she visited galleries and decided early that she would be an artist, at a time when few women were able to make a living that way. She studied art in Melbourne and Adelaide and then, like many artists of her day, travelled to Europe to learn more. There she saw the bold, flat colours of modern French painting and the simple, strong lines of Japanese woodblock prints. Both would shape her work for the rest of her life.
After she married William Preston in 1919, the couple settled in Sydney. It was there that Margaret produced the works for which she is best remembered: still-life paintings and woodcut prints of Australian native flowers. Instead of roses and violets, she chose banksias, waratahs, gum blossoms and flannel flowers. She carved her designs into blocks of wood, printed them in black ink and then often coloured each print by hand. The results were striking. The flowers were shown with heavy outlines and bright, flat areas of colour, almost like patterns.
Not everyone approved. Some critics found her work too harsh and too modern. Preston was not discouraged. She wrote articles and gave talks arguing that Australian artists should look closely at their own surroundings instead of copying overseas styles. She also believed that art should not be kept only in galleries. Because woodcuts could be printed many times, her images could be sold cheaply and hung in ordinary homes, and some of her designs appeared on magazine covers.
Preston kept experimenting until late in life, trying new techniques such as stencils and monotypes. She was always restless, always asking what Australian art could become. She died in 1963, aged eighty-eight.
Today her prints hang in major galleries across the country, and her bold banksias and waratahs are instantly recognisable. Yet perhaps her greatest achievement was not any single picture. It was helping Australians to see that the plants growing outside their own back doors were worthy subjects for art.

Letters from the Ironbark Country
Dear Sam,
Greetings from the box-ironbark forest in north-east Victoria! I promised I would write and tell you about this volunteer trip, so here it is: I'm spending a week helping to look for one of Australia's rarest birds, the regent honeyeater.
You've probably never seen one, and that's the problem. Scientists think there may be only a few hundred left in the wild. Regent honeyeaters are gorgeous - black heads, wings edged with bright yellow, and a patch of bumpy pale skin around each eye. They feed mostly on nectar from flowering eucalypts such as mugga ironbark and yellow box. Over the last two centuries, though, most of those woodlands were cleared for farms and towns, so the birds have far fewer places to feed and nest.
Our job is to help track honeyeaters that were bred at Taronga Zoo and released here last spring. Some wear tiny radio transmitters, which beep in our headsets when we point the antenna the right way. Yesterday I stood under a flowering ironbark for nearly two hours and finally saw one! It darted between the blossoms and even chased off a much bigger wattlebird. I was so excited I nearly dropped the antenna.
But the most surprising thing I've learned is about their song. Young males learn to sing by listening to older males. With so few birds left, many young males never hear a proper regent honeyeater song, and researchers have recorded wild males singing tunes that sound more like other species. Our team leader, Dr Hollis, says this could matter, because females may not choose a male that sings the "wrong" song. So at the zoo, keepers now play recordings of wild regent honeyeaters to young birds before they are released, a bit like music lessons.
I asked Dr Hollis whether all this effort was worth it. She pointed at the trees around us. "Every tree we protect here helps the gliders, the bats and a hundred other species too," she said. "The honeyeater just tells us how the whole forest is doing."
Tomorrow we're planting seedlings in a paddock that a farmer has offered to fence off and give back to the bush. It will be many years before those trees are big enough to flower well, but I like knowing that a regent honeyeater might feed there one day.
I'll show you my photos when I get home. They are mostly of leaves, because the birds move so fast, but there's one blurry yellow wing I'm very proud of.
Your cousin,
Ruby
Question: Where were the released honeyeaters bred?
Option A: in a farmer's paddock
Option B: at Taronga Zoo
Option C: in Dr Hollis's garden
Option D: in the ironbark forest

Seven Miles Down
On the morning of 23 January 1960, two men squeezed through a narrow hatch into a steel ball barely two metres wide. Above them bobbed a strange vessel that looked more like a floating fuel tank than a submarine. Beneath them lay the deepest known place in the ocean: the Challenger Deep, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, almost eleven kilometres down.
The men were Jacques Piccard, a Swiss engineer, and Don Walsh, a lieutenant in the United States Navy. Their vessel, the Trieste, was a bathyscaphe, a name meaning "deep boat". It had been designed by Jacques's father, Auguste Piccard, who had earlier used a sealed cabin to ride a balloon high into the sky. Now the family's ideas were heading in the opposite direction. The steel walls of the cabin were about thirteen centimetres thick, and the only link with the support ship above was an underwater telephone.
A bathyscaphe works rather like a balloon in reverse. The Trieste's huge upper hull was filled with petrol, which is lighter than water and hardly squashes under pressure, so it stopped the craft from sinking too fast. Tonnes of iron pellets acted as ballast, dragging it down. To come back up, the crew would release the pellets and let the petrol lift them.
The descent took almost five hours. The water outside turned from blue to black, and the cabin grew so cold that the men shivered. Then, at a depth of about nine thousand metres, the cabin shook with a loud crack. One of the outer windows had split. The water pressure outside was by then hundreds of times greater than at the surface.
Piccard and Walsh checked their instruments and looked carefully at the cabin walls. No water was leaking in, and the craft was still sinking smoothly. They decided to keep going.
At 1.06 in the afternoon, the Trieste settled gently onto the seabed. The craft stirred up a cloud of fine silt that drifted across the window like milk, making it hard to see. Piccard later reported glimpsing a flat, fish-like creature, although some scientists now doubt that a fish could live so deep. The men stayed only about twenty minutes before dropping ballast and beginning the three-hour climb back to the sunlight.
For more than fifty years, no one returned to the Challenger Deep with a crew. Yet the dive had proven something important: that people could build a machine strong enough to reach the deepest part of the sea and bring its passengers safely home.

Option A: petrol
Option B: iron pellets
Option C: fresh air
Option D: sea water

When Words Swap Places
Have you ever meant to say "a crushing blow" and heard yourself say "a blushing crow" instead? If so, you have made a spoonerism: a slip of the tongue in which the first sounds of two words swap places. The result is often nonsense, sometimes oddly poetic, and nearly always funny.
Spoonerisms are named after William Archibald Spooner, a kindly, white-haired teacher at Oxford University in England more than a hundred years ago. Spooner was said to mix up his words so often that his students began collecting his mistakes. He supposedly scolded one lazy student for having "hissed all my mystery lectures", and is said to have told another that he had "tasted a whole worm" when he meant "wasted a whole term". Before long, any such slip was simply called a "spoonerism".
There is just one problem with these famous stories: most of them are probably not true. Spooner admitted to only a few slips, and historians suspect that his students invented many of the best ones, polishing them for laughs and passing them on. Spooner reportedly found his fame rather tiresome. Even so, the name stuck.
Whether Spooner said them or not, slips like these are real, and scientists who study language find them fascinating. When you speak, your brain does not choose one word at a time. It plans several words ahead, lining up the sounds before you say them. Occasionally, a sound from a word that is coming up jumps the queue and lands in the wrong place. That is why spoonerisms almost always swap sounds in matching positions, such as the beginnings of two words, and why the mixed-up result usually still sounds as if it could be English. Even when we make mistakes, our brains follow the rules. Researchers have even caused spoonerisms on purpose in experiments, by flashing pairs of words on a screen and asking volunteers to read them aloud as quickly as possible.
In other words, a spoonerism is not a sign of a careless mind. It is a tiny window into how busy and organised our brains are while we talk.
Spoonerisms have also become a favourite toy for writers and comedians, who make them up on purpose. Here is a limerick built around one:
An usher, with manners so neat,
Met a lady who'd come off the street.
With a bow and a smile
He led her down the aisle,
And said, "Let me sew you to your sheet!"
So if you ever make a spoonerism yourself, there is no need to feel embarrassed. You are in good company. Just smile, correct yourself and carry on. After all, a brain that can swap sounds so neatly is running like a well-boiled icicle.

Wrapping a Giant: How to Jacket a Fossil
When palaeontologists find a large fossil bone in the field, they cannot simply pick it up and carry it home. Bones that have spent millions of years in rock are often cracked and fragile, and many would crumble the moment they were lifted. Instead, field crews wrap them in a protective plaster jacket, much like the cast a doctor puts on a broken arm. Here is how it is done.
You will need: brushes and small picks, a shovel, a hardening glue called a consolidant, damp paper towel or aluminium foil, strips of hessian cloth, plaster of Paris, a bucket of water and a permanent marker.
Step 1: Expose the top of the fossil. Using brushes and picks, carefully remove the rock and soil from the upper surface of the bone. Do not try to dig it out completely. The rock underneath is supporting it.
Step 2: Strengthen the bone. Paint any cracks with consolidant. It soaks into the fossil and hardens, binding loose pieces together.
Step 3: Dig a trench. Use the shovel to dig a trench all the way around the fossil, leaving it sitting on a raised column of rock called a pedestal. Leave a generous margin of rock around the bone itself - at least a hand's width.
Step 4: Add a separating layer. Cover the exposed bone with damp paper towel or foil. This step is vital. Without it, the plaster would stick directly to the fossil, and removing the jacket later could tear away pieces of bone.
Step 5: Apply the plaster. Mix the plaster with water until it is like thick cream. Dip the hessian strips into it, then lay them over the fossil and down the sides of the pedestal, overlapping each strip with the last. Smooth each layer with your hands. Work quickly: plaster begins to set within minutes.
Step 6: Wait, then flip. Once the jacket has hardened, dig beneath the pedestal until the fossil and its rock base are balanced on a narrow stem. Then, with several people working together, snap the stem and roll the jacket over. Plaster the newly exposed underside so the fossil is completely enclosed.
Step 7: Label it. Write the field number, date and location on the jacket. A fossil with no record of where it came from loses much of its scientific value.
Back at the museum, preparators cut the jacket open with saws and spend weeks, sometimes months, freeing the bone from its rock. It is slow, painstaking work. But thanks to a few strips of wet cloth and a bucket of plaster, a bone that survived millions of years underground can survive the bumpy trip to the laboratory as well.

Gardens That Belonged to the Land
When Edna Walling arrived in Melbourne as a teenager in 1914, few people would have guessed that she would change the way Australians thought about their gardens. Born in England in 1895, she had spent her childhood roaming the countryside with her father, learning the names of wildflowers and noticing how old stone walls followed the shape of the land. Her family moved to New Zealand and then to Australia, and Edna, restless and practical, soon decided she wanted to work outdoors.
She enrolled at Burnley Horticultural College in Melbourne, one of the few places where women could then study gardening. After earning her certificate, she found work as a jobbing gardener, digging and planting in other people's yards. It was hard physical labour, but it taught her how plants really grew, not just how they looked in books.
In the 1920s, Walling began designing gardens of her own. Many wealthy Melbourne families at the time preferred neat lawns, clipped hedges and rows of brightly coloured flowers. Walling's gardens were different. She liked curving paths, low walls of local stone, and plants allowed to spill over edges and soften hard lines. To her, a garden should feel like part of the landscape around it, not a picture placed on top of it.
She also put her ideas into practice in her own life. On land at Mooroolbark, east of Melbourne, she built herself a stone cottage called Sonning, and later planned a small village of cottages and gardens named Bickleigh Vale. Rather than sell the land to just anyone, she chose buyers who agreed to build homes she had designed and to keep the gardens in her style.
Over her long career, Walling designed hundreds of gardens and wrote books and magazine columns that were read by gardeners across the country. As the years passed, her interest turned more and more to Australian native plants. She grew alarmed at how quickly bushland along country roads was being cleared or overrun by weeds, and in the 1950s she wrote a book urging people to protect roadside plants.
Walling spent her final years in Queensland, where she died in 1973. Today, several of her gardens are protected for their heritage value, and designers still study her work. Her beliefs about letting gardens belong to their landscapes, and about valuing the plants that grow naturally around us, are now widely shared. In her own time, though, they were unusual ideas, and she held onto them firmly.

Option A: at Burnley Horticultural College

The Shelf Above My Bed
Mum announced the garage sale on a Sunday night, in the same voice she used for dentist appointments. "We're moving in six weeks," she said. "The new place is half the size. Everything we don't need goes on the front lawn on Saturday."
My brother Theo, who is eight, cheered. He had already decided the money would buy him a skateboard. I said nothing. I was thinking about the shelf above my bed.
That shelf was a museum of me. A clay owl I made in Year 2, with one ear bigger than the other. A jar of shells from every beach holiday. A battered toy rabbit called Admiral, who had lost his whiskers and most of his dignity years ago. None of it was useful. All of it was mine.
All week the house hummed with sorting. Boxes thudded onto the floor. Tape screeched off rolls. Dad found a crate of his old records and played every single one, which slowed things down considerably. Even Grandma sorted her sewing tin, though as far as I could tell she put everything back in.
By Friday night, my shelf was the only thing in the house still untouched. Mum came in and sat on the end of my bed.
"You don't have to sell all of it, Lily," she said. "But the new room is small. Choose what matters."
I lay awake for a long time, looking at the shapes of things in the dark. The owl's lopsided ears. The jar, faintly shining. Admiral, slumped against the wall like a tired old sailor.
Saturday arrived bright and noisy. Neighbours drifted up the driveway clutching coffee cups. Theo sold his old scooter and immediately spent part of the money on a lemonade from his own sister's stall, which I thought showed a poor head for business.
I had put my shells on a table at twenty cents a bag. A little girl in gumboots stood in front of them for ages, turning a spiral shell over and over in her fingers. Her father tried to hurry her along. She would not be hurried.
"You can have it," I said. "Free."
She smiled as if I had handed her the moon.
Something shifted in me then. I had been holding on so tightly, as if letting go of my things meant letting go of the memories. But the memories weren't in the shells. They were in me, and they were coming to the new house whether I packed them or not.
By the afternoon, the shells were gone, and so was the clay owl, bought by an old man who said it looked like his wife's cooking. I laughed until my eyes watered.
Admiral, though, went into a box marked LILY - KEEP. Some things you don't sell. Some things just come with you.

Option A: a family earning money for a new skateboard
Option B: a girl learning to part with her things before a move
Option C: a girl who refuses to move to a new house
Option D: a brother and sister running a lemonade stall

Four per cent. Tess watched the number on her phone as if staring at it might stop it shrinking. The storm had torn through the valley overnight, and since dawn the farmhouse had been silent: no fridge hum, no lights, no internet. "More junk?" Tess asked.
"A radio," said Pop. "Or it will be, once we build it."

The River That Cut Its Own Corner
Fly over the plains of inland Australia and you may notice something strange beside the big rivers. Here and there, curved ponds lie on the land like dropped horseshoes, close to the river but no longer part of it. In Australia many of these are called billabongs. Geographers call them oxbow lakes, and each one is the leftover piece of a river that changed its course.
Rivers on flat land rarely run straight. Even a small bend tends to grow, because water does not flow at the same speed all the way across a channel. On the outside of a bend, the current is fastest and strongest. It scrapes at the bank, carrying away soil and undercutting the edge until chunks collapse into the water. On the inside of the bend, the water slows down, and as it slows it drops the sand and silt it was carrying. Over many years the outer bank wears away while the inner bank builds up, and the bend swings wider and wider. These looping curves are called meanders.
Eventually a meander can loop around so far that only a narrow neck of land separates one part of the river from the next. Then a flood arrives. Floodwater does not need to follow the long way round; it pours straight across the neck, cutting a new, shorter channel. Once the river has found this shortcut, most of its water takes the easier path. Mud and sand settle at the ends of the old loop, sealing it off, and the abandoned bend becomes a lake of its own.
An oxbow lake does not last forever. With no current flowing through it, it slowly fills with silt and dead plants. Some dry out in summer and refill only when floods return. Over hundreds of years many become swamps, then meadows, leaving only a faint curve that can be traced from the air.
While it lasts, however, an oxbow lake is extremely valuable. Its still, shallow water warms quickly, which suits frogs, turtles and the tiny animals that fish feed on. Waterbirds such as egrets and spoonbills nest in the river red gums along its edge. When floods reconnect the lake to the river, young fish that hatched in its calm water can swim out into the main channel.
Because these wetlands depend on floods, they suffer when rivers are dammed or when water is taken for farms and towns. Without regular flooding, a billabong may stay dry for years. Scientists and landholders now work together to release "environmental water" at the right times, so that these curved lakes, carved by the river itself, can keep doing their job.
Question: Where is the current of a river fastest?
Option A: on the inside of a bend
Option B: across the narrow neck of land
Option C: at the ends of an oxbow lake
Option D: on the outside of a bend
