The Cold Machine of Geelong
In the 1850s, summer in the colony of Victoria could be brutal. Meat spoiled within a day, milk soured, and the only ice available was shipped from frozen lakes in North America, arriving months later at a price few people could afford. A Scottish-born newspaper man named James Harrison believed there had to be a better way.
Harrison ran a newspaper in Geelong, and the story is often told that he noticed something while cleaning metal printing type with ether, a liquid that evaporates very quickly. As the ether dried, the metal became noticeably cold. Harrison understood why: when a liquid evaporates, it takes heat from whatever it touches. If that effect could be controlled and repeated, it could be used to make cold on demand.
He spent years experimenting. His machine turned ether into vapour, squeezed the vapour back into a liquid, and let it evaporate again in a continuous cycle, drawing heat out of the water around the pipes until the water froze. In the mid-1850s he patented his design, and soon his machines were producing tonnes of ice. Businesses that needed to keep their products cool were eager to buy them.
Harrison's greatest dream, however, was bigger than ice. Australia had millions of sheep and cattle but only a small population to eat the meat. Britain, on the other side of the world, had many people who could not afford enough of it. If meat could be kept frozen during the long voyage, both countries would benefit.
In 1873 he displayed meat in Melbourne that had stayed frozen and fresh for months, and crowds came to see it. Confident, he loaded a ship called the Norfolk with frozen beef and mutton and sent it to London. Partway through the voyage, the cooling system failed. By the time the ship reached Britain the meat had spoiled and had to be thrown away. Harrison had invested so heavily in the venture that the loss ruined him financially.
He returned to journalism, writing about farming and science. He never abandoned the idea, but he never again had the money to test it on a grand scale.
Seven years later, in 1880, a ship called the Strathleven arrived in London from Australia carrying frozen meat in excellent condition. It used a different cooling system, but it proved that Harrison's dream had been possible all along. Within a few decades, refrigerated ships were carrying meat, butter and fruit from Australia around the globe.
Harrison died in 1893. Today he is remembered as a pioneer of refrigeration, and the principle he used, evaporation drawing heat away, still keeps food cold in almost every kitchen.
Question: What did Harrison notice when he cleaned printing type with ether?
Option A: the ink turned to ice
Option B: the metal became cold
Option C: the ether caught fire
Option D: the metal began to rust

Two weeks before Nowruz, my grandmother handed me a saucer, a damp cloth and a handful of wheat grains. "This year, Leila, the sabzeh is yours," she said, as if she were giving me the keys to a palace.
Nowruz is the Persian New Year, and it begins on the first day of spring. Here in Adelaide it falls in autumn, but Maman Bozorg says the calendar on the wall is not the boss of her. Every year our family sets a special table with seven items whose Persian names begin with the letter "s": sprouts, apples, garlic, vinegar, sumac, a sweet wheat pudding and dried oleaster fruit. Each one stands for a wish for the coming year. The sabzeh, the sprouts, stands for new life, and it sits right in the middle.
For three days my grains did nothing at all. Then a few pale shoots appeared, leaning sideways like tired passengers on a bus. I had put the saucer on the laundry shelf, where it was dark, and I forgot to water it on the weekend we went camping. When I remembered, I watered it three times a day to make up for it, but it was too late.By the day before Nowruz, my sabzeh looked like a bald man's comb-over.
My cousin Darius, of course, arrived with a sabzeh so thick and tall it could have hosted a cricket match. A red ribbon was tied around it. He set it down near the end of the table and said nothing, which I decided was his way of showing off. I was sure his mum had bought it from the Persian grocery on Prospect Road.
On the morning of Nowruz the house smelled of saffron rice and fried herbs, and the table glowed with candles, a mirror and a bowl holding a single goldfish. Maman Bozorg picked up both dishes. Then she placed mine in the very centre of the table.
"When I was nine, in Tehran," she said, "my first sabzeh grew a coat of grey mould. My mother put it on the table anyway. Do you know why? Because it was the first one I grew."
Later, while the adults were busy with tea, Darius sat down next to me. "Mine died the first time too," he muttered. "Mum and I started again. I watered it twice a day so I wouldn't stuff it up." He shrugged. "Yours has more character."
I looked at my lopsided shoots and felt my face go hot, though not for the reason I had expected.
Thirteen days after the new year, our whole family went to a picnic beside the River Torrens, as Persian families do on that day. Darius and I carried our sabzehs down to the water together. We tossed them in, his thick green mat and my scraggly little tuft, and watched them float away side by side, carrying the old year with them.

Option B: on a dark shelf in the laundry
Option C: in the tent on the camping trip
Option D: at the end of the Nowruz table

Reading a Train Map Without Getting Lost
The first time you stand in front of a big city's train map, it can look like a bowl of coloured spaghetti. Don't panic. Those tangled lines follow a few simple rules, and once you know them you can travel almost anywhere. Follow these steps.
Step 1: Understand what the map is (and isn't)
Most train maps are diagrams, not true maps. In 1931 an engineering draughtsman named Harry Beck designed a map of the London Underground that ignored real distances and drew every line as straight, running horizontally, vertically or diagonally. Stations were spaced evenly so the map was easy to read. Passengers loved it, and cities around the world copied his idea. The catch is that two stations that look close together on the map might be several kilometres apart, while others that look far apart could be a short walk. If distance matters, check a street map as well.
Step 2: Find yourself
Look for a "You are here" marker, or find the name of your station. Then find the station you want to reach. It helps to put a finger on each.
Step 3: Follow the colours
Every line has its own colour, and often a name or number too. Trace the line that passes through your station. If your destination is on the same line, you're nearly done. If not, look for an interchange: a station, usually shown with a larger circle or a special symbol, where two or more lines meet and you can change trains.
Step 4: Work out your direction
This is where many travellers go wrong. Trains are usually labelled with the last station on the line, not with a compass direction. So if you need to travel towards the end of the line called Riverside, you must catch a train marked "Riverside", even if you are only going two stops.
Step 5: Count the stops
Count how many stations lie between you and your destination. Keep that number in your head and tick off each stop as the train pulls in. Most trains also announce the next station, but announcements can be hard to hear in a crowded carriage.
Step 6: Check before you go
Before setting off, look for notices about trackwork or closed stations, especially on weekends. A quick check can save you an hour on a replacement bus.
A final tip: if you do catch a train going the wrong way, relax. Get off at the next station, cross to the other platform and travel back. Everyone does it at least once, and the map will make sense a little sooner each time you use it.
Question: Who designed the London Underground map described in the passage?
Option A: a London station master
Option B: an engineering draughtsman
Option C: a team of city builders
Option D: a group of passengers

The Moon That Never Stops Erupting
Of all the worlds in our solar system, the most restless may not be a planet at all. It is Io, one of the four large moons of Jupiter. Slightly larger than our own Moon, Io looks like nothing else in space. Its patchy, pizza-like surface is painted yellow, orange, red and black by sulphur from more than four hundred active volcanoes, making Io the most volcanically active body known.
Before 1979, nobody knew this. Scientists expected Io to be a cold, dead ball of rock, much like Earth's Moon, scarred by ancient craters. Then, in March 1979, the Voyager 1 spacecraft flew past Jupiter and sent back thousands of images. A few days later, a young engineer named Linda Morabito was studying one of them. Her job was not to hunt for discoveries. She was using pictures of moons against background stars to work out exactly where the spacecraft was, so that it could be steered accurately. To see the faint stars, she boosted the brightness of an image of Io. Beside the moon's edge, she noticed a strange umbrella-shaped cloud rising hundreds of kilometres into space.
Morabito checked carefully that it was not a fault in the camera or another moon peeping out from behind Io. It was neither. She had found a volcanic plume erupting on another world, the first active volcano ever seen beyond Earth.
Remarkably, a team of scientists had predicted this only days earlier. They had published a paper arguing that Io must be heated from the inside, not by the Sun, but by Jupiter itself.
Here is how it works. Io's orbit around Jupiter is not quite a circle, so its distance from the giant planet keeps changing. Jupiter's enormous gravity squeezes Io harder when it is close and less when it is further away. Io's neighbours, the moons Europa and Ganymede, keep tugging on it so that its orbit never settles into a neat circle. On every orbit, which takes about forty-two hours, Io is stretched and relaxed, and its solid ground rises and falls by as much as a hundred metres. All that flexing creates heat deep inside, just as a paperclip grows warm when you bend it back and forth. The heat melts rock, and the molten rock bursts out through the surface.
Io's volcanoes change its face constantly. Spacecraft visiting years apart have found new lava flows, fresh dark spots and coloured rings where plumes have rained down. No map of Io stays accurate for long.
Studying Io helps scientists understand how gravity can heat a world. That matters, because the same kind of squeezing may keep an ocean of liquid water hidden beneath the ice of Io's neighbour Europa.

Option A: alliteration
Option B: onomatopoeia
Option C: rhyme
Option D: personification

Sixpence on the Platform
In 1934 a young London publisher named Allen Lane was waiting for a train at Exeter station after spending the weekend with the crime writer Agatha Christie. He wanted something good to read on the journey home. The station bookstall offered glossy magazines and dusty reprints of old novels, but nothing he actually wanted. Good new books existed, of course, but they were hardbacks, heavy and expensive, sold in quiet bookshops rather than on busy railway platforms.
Lane began to wonder. What if excellent books could be sold as cheaply as a magazine, small enough to slip into a coat pocket and available wherever people waited and travelled?
In July 1935 he launched Penguin Books with ten paperback titles, including novels, a biography and a detective story. Each cost sixpence. The covers were bold and simple: horizontal bands of colour with the title in clear lettering, orange for fiction, green for crime and dark blue for biography. A young office worker, Edward Young, was sent to London Zoo to sketch the penguin that would appear on every spine.
Many people in the book trade thought Lane had lost his mind. Booksellers feared that cheap books would drive down the price of all books, and some authors worried that they would earn almost nothing from each copy. Even the writer George Orwell, who praised the books as splendid value, warned that they might be bad for the trade. Lane needed to sell around 17,000 copies of each title just to cover his costs.
Then came a stroke of luck. The buyer for the Woolworths chain of shops ordered 63,500 copies, reportedly after his wife liked the look of them. Suddenly Penguins were stacked in high-street stores, where people who had never set foot in a bookshop could pick one up along with their soap and string. Within a year, Penguin had sold millions of books.
Soon the orange-and-white paperbacks seemed to be everywhere. They were crammed into soldiers' kitbags, tucked into students' satchels and bulging from the pockets of factory workers on their lunch breaks. Readers who could never have afforded a hardback could now build their own small libraries, one sixpence at a time.
Other publishers soon followed, and before long the paperback had become ordinary. Today most of us cannot imagine a world in which a good book was a luxury. Yet it was a dull wait on a railway platform, and one man's frustration, that helped put reading within everyone's reach.

Option B: threepence
Option C: sixpence
Option D: a pound

The Man Who Parked Satellites in the Sky
Every time you watch a live sports match broadcast from the other side of the world, you are relying on an idea that a young man wrote down in 1945. His name was Arthur C. Clarke, and for most of his life he imagined the future so clearly that the future kept catching up with him.
Clarke was born in 1917 in the seaside town of Minehead, England, and grew up on a farm. As a boy he mapped the Moon with a homemade telescope built from a cardboard tube and old lenses, and he devoured cheap American science fiction magazines with lurid covers. As a teenager he joined the British Interplanetary Society, a small group of enthusiasts who believed, when most people laughed at the idea, that humans would one day travel into space.
During the Second World War, Clarke worked as a radar instructor with the Royal Air Force. Radar taught him about radio waves, and in 1945 he wrote an article for a magazine called Wireless World. In it, he pointed out that a satellite placed about 36,000 kilometres above the equator would circle the Earth exactly once a day. Seen from the ground, it would seem to hang motionless in the sky. Three such satellites, spaced evenly, could relay radio and television signals to almost the entire planet. At the time no rocket was powerful enough to put anything into orbit. Twenty years later, the first commercial communications satellite did exactly what he had described. That orbit is now often called the Clarke Orbit.
Clarke never patented the idea and later joked that it had cost him a fortune. He did not seem to mind much. After the war he studied physics and mathematics at university, then turned to writing full-time. His stories were famous for their careful science and their sense of wonder. In the 1960s he worked with the film director Stanley Kubrick to create 2001: A Space Odyssey, a film whose realistic scenes of spaceflight amazed audiences a year before astronauts first walked on the Moon.
In 1956 Clarke moved to Sri Lanka, drawn by its warm seas. He became a keen scuba diver, explored shipwrecks and wrote books about the ocean as well as space. He also became known for his "laws" about the future. The most quoted says that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
Clarke died in 2008 at the age of ninety. By then, satellites in his orbit were carrying phone calls, weather pictures and television to billions of people. Few writers have seen their imagination turn so completely into everyday life, and fewer still have watched it happen from the comfort of their own armchair.

Option A: Clarke joined the British Interplanetary Society
Option B: Clarke worked as a radar instructor
Option C: Clarke moved to Sri Lanka
Option D: Clarke wrote his article for Wireless World

Snow That Falls Upward
All year the reef keeps still and quiet,
a city built of patient stone,
where every polyp shapes its sliver
of limestone house and lives alone.

It feeds by night with tiny fingers,
it rests by day in sun-warmed seas,
and no one guesses what it's saving
beneath its slow and stony ease.

For months it builds a hidden treasure,
a bundle tucked within its wall,
and holds it close through autumn, winter,
and keeps it secret from them all.

But as the spring days stretch and lengthen,
the water warms, degree by degree,
and something deep inside the coral
begins to count, and wait, and see.

The moon swells round and silver-heavy,
then thins a little, night by night,
until, one dusk, a silent signal
says: Now. Tonight. The time is right.

Then up it comes, a pink-white blizzard,
ten million beads released as one,
each bundle bobbing to the surface
as if the reef had learned to run.

From brain and staghorn, plate and table,
from boulder coral, old and wide,
the beads float up like snow in reverse
and spread across the turning tide.

For if one coral spawned in secret,
its eggs would drift too far apart;
so all of them must choose one moment,
as if they shared a single heart.

The eggs and sperm drift up and mingle
where wave and wind will stir the sea,
and there, among the floating millions,
the next young corals start to be.

The divers hover, torches glowing,
and gasp into their bubbling air;
they've waited weeks to guess the evening,
and now can only float and stare.

Their torchlight catches every bundle
like dust that dances in a beam,
and for an hour the whole dark ocean
is stranger than the strangest dream.

The fish arrive to snap and gobble,
the drifting jellies take their fill,
yet from that crowd of tiny bundles
uncounted thousands float on still.

By dawn a pink slick paints the water,
a ribbon kilometres in length;
the reef has spent its year of saving
and poured it out with all its strength.

The seabirds circle, sharp and hungry,
the morning breezes start to blow,
and bit by bit the ribbon scatters
to waters none of us will know.

The few that last, as drifting larvae,
will ride the currents, far and blind,
then settle on some bare grey boulder
to build the reef they left behind.

So if you dive one night in springtime
and see the upward snowfall climb,
be still, and watch an ancient city
keep its appointment, right on time.

Note: Each year, a few nights after a full moon in late spring, many corals on the Great Barrier Reef release tiny bundles of eggs and sperm into the sea at the same time.
Question: According to the poem, what helps to signal the corals that it is time to spawn?
Option A: the arrival of hungry fish and jellies
Option B: warming water and the changing moon
Option C: the glowing torches of the divers
Option D: strong storms and high tides in spring

The Instrument You Never Touch
Imagine walking on stage, standing in front of a wooden box with two metal rods sticking out of it, and raising your hands into empty air. You haven't touched anything, yet a voice-like note begins to float through the hall, rising and falling as your fingers move. You are playing a theremin, the only well-known musical instrument that is played without being touched.
The theremin was invented around 1920 by a young Russian scientist named Lev Termen, who later became known as Leon Theremin. He was not trying to create music at all. He was building a device to measure gases, and he noticed that when his hand came near the equipment, the whistling sound it made changed pitch. Being a trained cellist as well as a physicist, he realised he had stumbled onto a new kind of instrument.
Here is the secret. Each metal rod, called an antenna, creates an invisible electrical field around itself. Your body, which conducts electricity, disturbs that field. The upright antenna controls pitch: move your hand closer and the note goes higher; draw it away and the note drops. The looped antenna, which sticks out sideways, controls volume. Lower your other hand towards it and the sound fades; lift it away and the sound swells.
This sounds simple, and that's the trap. A piano has keys and a guitar has frets, so you always know where the notes are. A theremin has nothing to guide you. Move your finger a centimetre too far and you are out of tune. Even shifting your weight from one foot to the other, or tilting your head, can bend the note, because your whole body affects the field. Players must stand almost perfectly still and rely entirely on their ears.
Theremin toured Europe and the United States in the 1920s, and audiences were astonished. The Long Way Down
When the storm breaks over the rainforest,
drumming on a million leaves at once,
the rain does not reach the ground.
Not at first.

It lands on the roof of the forest,
a hundred thousand leaves held open like hands,
and the canopy drinks
before anything below
is offered a single drop.

Up here the storm is loud:
a roar like a crowd in a stadium,
every leaf a drumskin,
every branch shaking with it.

Leaves here are built for rain.
Each one narrows to a slender point,
a drip tip, where water gathers, swells
and lets go,
so that no leaf stays wet long enough for mould to grow.

From leaf to lower leaf the water travels,
a slow staircase, step by green step,
pausing on a palm frond,
sliding off a fern,
resting in the cupped heart of a bird's nest fern
where a tiny frog sits in its private pool.

Some of it chooses the trunks instead,
running in thin silver streams down the bark,
soaking the moss until it hangs heavy as a sponge,
following the vines like ropes let down
from the deck of a ship to the shore.

Orchids clinging high on the branches
sip what passes, and let the rest go by.
Nothing grabs more than it needs.

A leech lifts its head from a leaf and waits.
A beetle shelters under a mushroom's cap.
Somewhere a cassowary shakes out its feathers
and walks on, unbothered.

Above, the thunder has already rolled away.
The clouds have moved on towards the mountains.
The sun is out again on the canopy,
steaming the top leaves dry.

But down here, in the green half-light,
it is still raining.
Drops fall from every edge,
slow and steady, tick, tick, tick,
as the forest lets go of the storm a little at a time,
the way a towel keeps dripping
long after the swim is over.

When at last the water reaches the floor,
it does not rush.
It sinks into the leaf litter,
into the soft dark soil,
down to the roots that have been waiting, patiently,
all along.

Hours later, the creek at the bottom of the gully
is still rising,
brown and swollen,
fed by a storm
that nobody up in the sunlight remembers.

And nothing is wasted.
The trees will draw the water up again,
through trunk and branch to the highest leaf,
and breathe it out as mist
that gathers above the canopy at dawn,
white and quiet,
ready to become the next storm.

So if you walk here after rain
and feel drops on your face beneath a clear blue sky,
don't look up for a cloud.
The forest is simply remembering
the weather it has already had.
Question: Where does the rain land first?
Option A: on the leaves of the canopy
Option B: on the soft forest floor
Option C: in the bird's nest fern
Option D: on the distant mountains

Somewhere a cassowary shakes out its feathers
and walks on, unbothered.

Above, the thunder has already rolled away.
The clouds have moved on towards the mountains.
The sun is out again on the canopy,
steaming the top leaves dry.

But down here, in the green half-light,
it is still raining.
Drops fall from every edge,
slow and steady, tick, tick, tick,
as the forest lets go of the storm a little at a time,
the way a towel keeps dripping
long after the swim is over.

When at last the water reaches the floor,
it does not rush.
It sinks into the leaf litter,
into the soft dark soil,
down to the roots that have been waiting, patiently,
all along.

Hours later, the creek at the bottom of the gully
is still rising,
brown and swollen,
fed by a storm
that nobody up in the sunlight remembers.

And nothing is wasted.
The trees will draw the water up again,
through trunk and branch to the highest leaf,
and breathe it out as mist
that gathers above the canopy at dawn,
white and quiet,
ready to become the next storm.

So if you walk here after rain
and feel drops on your face beneath a clear blue sky,
don't look up for a cloud.
The forest is simply remembering
the weather it has already had.

Let Students Run the Meeting
Picture a typical parent-teacher interview. A parent perches on a plastic chair built for a twelve-year-old. A teacher, who has already seen twenty families that evening, sums up a whole term of work in ten minutes. And the person being discussed? Usually at home, waiting nervously to hear what was said. It is time for a change. Our school should replace traditional parent-teacher interviews with student-led conferences, in which students explain their own learning to their families while the teacher is there to support them.
The first reason is simple: students know their own learning best. A teacher can tell a parent that a student's writing has improved, but only the student can explain which feedback helped, which piece they are proudest of and where they still get stuck. When my old primary school trialled student-led conferences, I showed my dad three drafts of a single story. He saw for himself how a messy first version had grown into something I was proud of. No report comment could have done that.
Secondly, student-led conferences teach responsibility. To prepare, students must look back over their work, choose examples and set goals for the next term. That is exactly the kind of thinking that helps in high school and beyond. Schools that use this approach report that students take more ownership of their results, because they cannot simply blame a report they had no part in.
Some people argue that students will hide their weaknesses and show only their best work. This is a fair concern, but it has an easy answer. The teacher stays in the room. Every student must present at least one goal they are still working towards, and the teacher can add anything important that the student leaves out. Honesty becomes part of the task rather than something to avoid.
Others worry that students will be too nervous. Certainly, speaking in front of a parent and a teacher can be daunting at first. Yet we are asked to give speeches, present projects and perform at assemblies all the time. Explaining your own work to people who care about you is surely one of the gentlest ways to build that confidence.
Finally, the change would bring families into the conversation. Too often, a parent comes home from an interview and asks, "Why didn't you tell me about this?" When students lead the meeting, there are no surprises, and everyone leaves knowing the plan for next term.
Parent-teacher interviews have barely changed in fifty years. Our learning has. Let's give students a seat at the table, a proper chair this time, and let them do the talking.

Option A: three drafts of a single story
Option B: a report card from the term
Option C: a speech from a school assembly
Option D: a list of goals for high school

Ice from a Summer Sky
On a hot November afternoon, it can seem impossible that lumps of ice might soon be bouncing off car roofs. Yet in many parts of eastern Australia, late spring and summer are exactly when hail is most likely. The reason lies high above the ground, inside a towering storm cloud called a cumulonimbus.
A cumulonimbus forms when warm, moist air rises quickly. On a hot day the ground heats the air just above it, and that air begins to climb. As it rises, it cools, and its water vapour condenses into droplets. In a strong storm, the rising currents of air, known as updrafts, can travel faster than 100 kilometres per hour. They carry the droplets many kilometres upward, far above the level where the temperature drops below freezing.
Surprisingly, many of these droplets do not freeze straight away. Very small, pure droplets can stay liquid well below zero degrees. Scientists call this supercooled water. When a supercooled droplet touches a tiny particle, such as a speck of dust or a frozen raindrop, it freezes onto it almost instantly. That frozen centre is the beginning of a hailstone.
As the young hailstone is tossed around inside the cloud, it collects more and more ice. If it passes through a region crowded with supercooled droplets, the water spreads over its surface and freezes slowly, forming a clear layer. If it passes through drier air, the droplets freeze the moment they strike, trapping tiny bubbles and forming a cloudy, white layer. Cut a large hailstone in half and you may see rings of clear and cloudy ice, rather like the layers of an onion. Each ring is a record of the stone's journey.
A hailstone keeps growing for as long as the updraft can hold it up. Once it becomes too heavy, it falls. Only a very powerful updraft can support a stone the size of a cricket ball. The largest hailstone ever officially measured fell in South Dakota, in the United States, in 2010. It was about 20 centimetres across.
Hail is less common in the tropics than many people expect, even though tropical storms are frequent and fierce. There, the freezing level sits very high in the sky, so hailstones must fall through a long stretch of warm air before they reach the ground. Most of them melt on the way down and arrive as heavy rain.
For forecasters, hail is a serious concern. Large stones can smash windows, dent cars and flatten crops in minutes. By studying the height of the freezing level and the strength of the rising air, experts can warn communities when a storm is likely to carry ice. Even an hour's warning gives people time to move cars under cover and bring pets inside.

Option A: because ice seems out of place on such a hot day
Option B: because hail never falls in eastern Australia
Option C: because hail only forms in the middle of winter
Option D: because November storms rarely produce any rain

They carry the droplets many kilometres upward, far above the level where the temperature drops below freezing.
Surprisingly, many of these droplets do not freeze straight away. Very small, pure droplets can stay liquid well below zero degrees. Scientists call this supercooled water. When a supercooled droplet touches a tiny particle, such as a speck of dust or a frozen raindrop, it freezes onto it almost instantly. That frozen centre is the beginning of a hailstone.
As the young hailstone is tossed around inside the cloud, it collects more and more ice. If it passes through a region crowded with supercooled droplets, the water spreads over its surface and freezes slowly, forming a clear layer. If it passes through drier air, the droplets freeze the moment they strike, trapping tiny bubbles and forming a cloudy, white layer. Cut a large hailstone in half and you may see rings of clear and cloudy ice, rather like the layers of an onion. Each ring is a record of the stone's journey.
A hailstone keeps growing for as long as the updraft can hold it up. Once it becomes too heavy, it falls. Only a very powerful updraft can support a stone the size of a cricket ball. The largest hailstone ever officially measured fell in South Dakota, in the United States, in 2010. It was about 20 centimetres across.
Hail is less common in the tropics than many people expect, even though tropical storms are frequent and fierce. There, the freezing level sits very high in the sky, so hailstones must fall through a long stretch of warm air before they reach the ground. Most of them melt on the way down and arrive as heavy rain.
For forecasters, hail is a serious concern. Large stones can smash windows, dent cars and flatten crops in minutes. By studying the height of the freezing level and the strength of the rising air, experts can warn communities when a storm is likely to carry ice. Even an hour's warning gives people time to move cars under cover and bring pets inside.

Miles Apart: Keeping a Friendship Going After a Move
When a close friend moves to another town, state or country, it can feel as though the friendship has been packed into a removal truck and driven away. It does not have to be that way. Friendships at a distance are common, and many of them last for years. Like a garden, though, a long-distance friendship needs tending. The steps below can help.
Step 1: Talk before the move. In the weeks before your friend leaves, sit down together and agree on how you will stay in touch. Will you message, call or write letters? How often? Swap addresses and usernames, and write them down somewhere safe. Making a plan while you are still together means neither of you has to wonder later who should make the first move.
Step 2: Choose a regular time. A video call at the same time each Sunday is easier to keep than a vague promise to 'chat soon'. If your friend is in a different time zone, check the clock carefully. During daylight saving, a call at seven in the evening in Perth is ten o'clock at night in Sydney.
Step 3: Share the small things. It is tempting to save up news for something big, but friendships are built from everyday details. Send a photo of the strange sandwich at the canteen, or a voice message about the dog chasing its tail. Small, frequent messages remind your friend that they are still part of your ordinary life.
Step 4: Do something together, apart. Watch the same film at the same time, read the same book and compare notes, or play an online game. Shared activities give you something to talk about besides 'What's new?' They also make the distance feel smaller, because for an hour or two you are sharing the same experience.
Step 5: Make room for new friends. Your friend will meet new people, and so will you. This is healthy, not a betrayal. A friendship that lets both people grow is far stronger than one that demands to be the only one.
Step 6: Accept the quiet patches. There will be weeks when one of you is busy with exams, sport or family events, and messages slow down. Do not panic. A short note such as 'Thinking of you, talk soon' keeps the door open until life calms down.
Step 7: Plan a visit if you can. A date to look forward to, even one many months away, gives you both something to count down to. If a visit is not possible, a letter or small parcel in the post can feel almost as special, because it is something your friend can actually hold.
A friendship that survives a move is often stronger for it. It has been tested, and it has shown that it does not depend on sitting side by side in class.

Beetles, spiders, skinks and small marsupials shelter in and under them, while fungi slowly break them down, returning goodness to the soil. The Clatter Room
The Hartwell Typewriter Museum occupied two rooms above the bakery, and on Saturdays it smelt faintly of cinnamon. Ivy had been volunteering there for three weeks. Mostly, she dusted the glass cases and handed out leaflets while Mr Okafor, who had collected the machines for forty years, talked to visitors about ribbons, carriage returns and keys that stuck.
Today was different. Today was Letter Day, when visitors could sit at the six machines in the back room and type a real letter on real paper. Mr Okafor called it the Clatter Room, and as soon as the doors opened, Ivy understood why. Clack, clack, clack-clack went the keys as a dozen fingers hammered at once, and every few seconds a bright little bell rang out, ding, warning a typist that the line was nearly full.
Ivy's job was to help. She showed a small boy how to feed a sheet of paper behind the roller, and how to push the lever at the end of each line so that the carriage slid back with a satisfying clunk. She showed a teenager that there was no delete key, and that a mistake meant either starting again or living with it. The teenager groaned, then laughed, then typed very slowly. Mr Okafor moved between the tables, beaming, as if every clack were music.
Late in the morning, an elderly woman came in leaning on a walking frame. She stopped in front of the green machine by the window and stood very still.
'That's a Hermes,' she said quietly. 'I learnt on one just like it. Nineteen fifty-eight. Miss Pratt's secretarial college, Brisbane.'
Ivy pulled out the chair. The woman sat and rested her fingertips lightly on the middle row of keys without looking down. For a moment nothing happened. Then her fingers began to move, faster than Ivy had seen anyone type all day, a steady, rapid rattle like rain on a roof. She did not look at the keys once.
When she finished, she pulled out the sheet with a soft zip and read it over. 'Seventy words a minute, I used to do,' she said. 'Miss Pratt would say I'd slipped.' She smiled, but her eyes were bright and wet.
She folded the letter and slid it into an envelope. Ivy saw the name on the front: Margaret. 'My sister,' the woman explained. 'We used to type each other notes at college, for practice. She lives in a nursing home now. I think she'll know what this is.'
After she had gone, Ivy sat at the Hermes. She placed her fingers where the woman's had been and typed one slow line. The bell rang at the end of it. For some reason, she did not mind the noise at all.
Question: In the first sentence, the word 'occupied' means . . .
Option A: owned
Option B: took up
Option C: decorated
Option D: visited

The Mower That Went Walkabout
The robot mower arrived in a box the size of a suitcase, and Dad named it Clive. 'Clive will give us our Saturdays back,' he announced. He spent a whole weekend pegging a thin green wire around the edges of the lawn, just under the grass. The instructions explained that the wire carried a weak signal. Whenever Clive sensed it, he would turn around and head back into the yard. Inside the wire was lawn; outside was the rest of the world.
For three weeks, Clive was perfect. He hummed across the grass at night, bumped gently off the clothesline pole and returned to his charging station by dawn. The lawn looked like a bowling green, and Dad spent his Saturdays reading the paper.
Then, one Tuesday morning, Mrs Petrakis from next door knocked on the front door holding Clive in her arms like a lost puppy. 'He was in my vegie patch,' she said. 'He's eaten all my parsley.'
Dad apologised, checked the settings and put Clive back. Two nights later, Clive was found halfway down the driveway, blinking a red light, his blades tangled in a garden hose.
'Faulty,' said Dad. 'I'll send him back.'
Priya wasn't so sure. Clive had worked flawlessly for three weeks. Machines didn't usually forget what they knew. Something must have changed, and she suspected it wasn't inside the robot.
After school, she walked slowly around the edge of the lawn, eyes on the ground. Along the back fence, near Mrs Petrakis's side, she found a patch where the soil had been freshly scratched up. A shallow hole led under the palings, and the earth around it was loose and crumbly. Poking out of the dirt was a short piece of green wire, its end snapped and frayed.
That night, Priya waited by the kitchen window with a torch. At about nine o'clock, a round grey shape trundled out of the shadows, squeezed under the fence and began digging in the same spot, sending soil flying in all directions.
'A wombat?' said Dad, peering over her shoulder. 'In the suburbs?'
'We back onto the reserve,' Priya reminded him. 'And look at those claws.'
The next weekend, Dad and Priya joined the broken ends with a little connector from the hardware shop. Then they pulled up the whole back section and pegged it down again a metre inside the fence, curving it around the clothesline.
Clive hasn't left the yard since. Mrs Petrakis has new parsley. And every night at nine, the wombat squeezes under the fence, digs a while near the palings and wanders off again, entirely unbothered by the small machine humming on the far side of the lawn.
Question: Why did Mrs Petrakis knock on the front door?
Option A: A wombat had dug a hole under her side of the fence.
Option B: Clive had tangled his blades in her garden hose.
Option C: Clive had got into her vegie patch and eaten her parsley.
Option D: She wanted to borrow the robot mower for her own lawn.

The Other Half of the Warning
Most people know the ending of the story of Icarus. A boy flies too close to the sun, the wax holding his feathered wings melts, and he falls into the sea. For centuries, the tale has been used as a warning against ambition. Aim too high, it seems to say, and you will come crashing down. I believe this reading misses the most important part of the myth, and that we should stop telling it as a lesson about dreaming too big.
Go back to the version told by the Roman poet Ovid about two thousand years ago. Daedalus, a brilliant inventor, is trapped with his son Icarus on the island of Crete. He builds two pairs of wings from feathers held together with thread and wax. Before they take off, he gives Icarus careful instructions. Do not fly too high, he says, or the sun's heat will soften the wax. But do not fly too low either, or the spray from the sea will weigh down the feathers. Stay in the middle, he tells him, and follow me. Icarus, thrilled by the rush of the wind, soon forgets this advice and climbs higher and higher.
That second instruction is almost always left out when the story is retold in picture books, cartoons and speeches. Yet it changes everything. If Daedalus had warned only against flying high, the myth really would be about the dangers of ambition. Instead, he warns against two opposite mistakes. Flying too low is just as deadly as flying too high. The lesson is not 'never reach for the sky' but 'find the path between recklessness and fear'.
This matters, because the way we tell stories shapes the way we think. A child who hears only the shortened version may conclude that it is safer never to try anything bold. A child who hears the full version learns something wiser: that playing it too safe can sink you too. Hanging back out of fear has its own costs, even if they are quieter and slower to arrive.
Some will argue that it is Icarus's disobedience, not his height, that the story punishes. That is a fair point, and it supports my argument rather than weakening it. The advice Icarus ignores is advice about balance, not advice about staying small.
It is also worth noticing what happens to the other flyer. Daedalus, the man who dreamt up the whole daring plan, flies on and reaches land safely. He soared just as boldly as his son, but he held to the middle course.
So the next time someone mentions Icarus, ask them about the sea. The forgotten half of the warning may be the half we need most.

The Spare Key
Aunt Fen's van smelt of machine oil and peppermints. Rows of tiny drawers lined the back, each labelled in her neat capitals: BLANKS, SPRINGS, PINS, CYLINDERS, and one marked simply ODDS. On the first day of the school holidays, Tilly climbed into the passenger seat with a notebook and a promise to touch nothing without asking.
'Being a locksmith is only half about locks,' Aunt Fen said as they pulled away from the kerb. 'The other half is people. Nobody calls me on their best day.'
The morning's jobs were quick. A café owner had snapped a key in the back door, and Aunt Fen slid two slender tools into the lock and drew out the broken half as neatly as a splinter. Then she cut a new key on the grinder in the van, which whined and threw up a fine glitter of brass dust. Tilly wrote everything down, including the names of the tools.
The last call came just after lunch, as rain began to drum on the roof. An elderly man stood on the porch of a weatherboard cottage, his cardigan soaked through. Inside, a tabby cat watched him from the windowsill.
'Gerald Abernethy,' he said, shaking Aunt Fen's hand. 'I've been out here an hour. My wife always looked after the spare key. She passed away in March, and I've no idea where she put it.'
Aunt Fen crouched by the door and worked slowly, her head tilted, as if the lock were whispering to her. Tilly watched the rain dripping off Mr Abernethy's nose. Without being asked, she ran back to the van, fetched the big umbrella and held it over him. After a few minutes, there was a small, satisfying click, and the door swung open. The cat strolled out, sniffed Mr Abernethy's shoes and strolled back in again.
Before leaving, Aunt Fen cut two spare keys. 'Don't put one under the mat or in a flowerpot,' she said. 'That's the first place anyone looks. Best to give one to someone you trust who lives close by.'
Mr Abernethy turned the keys over in his palm. 'My wife knew all the neighbours,' he said slowly. 'Had them over for tea. I've let that slide.' He looked across the street. On the porch opposite, a woman was carrying shopping bags inside while a small boy in gumboots stamped in a puddle. The boy saw them and waved.
Mr Abernethy hesitated. Then he raised his hand and waved back, and slipped one of the keys into his cardigan pocket, apart from the other.
In the van, Aunt Fen handed Tilly a peppermint. 'You fetched that umbrella,' she said. 'That's the half that isn't about locks.'

Option A: thin
Option B: sharp
Option C: heavy
Option D: shiny

Off the Buddy Box
For six Saturdays in a row, Kai had flown the little yellow trainer plane with an invisible safety net. The net was a cable. It ran from his radio controller to the one in Mr Delaney's hands, and it was called a buddy box. As long as Mr Delaney held down a spring-loaded switch, Kai was in control. The moment anything went wrong, Mr Delaney let go of the switch, and the plane obeyed him instead.
It had happened plenty of times. On the second Saturday, Kai had turned too steeply and the plane had begun to spiral towards the long grass. On the fourth, he had forgotten which way to move the stick when the plane flew towards him, because everything felt backwards. Each time, the plane had wobbled, steadied and climbed away, rescued by Mr Delaney's thumb. Kai had gone home each time feeling as if he had not really flown at all, as if he had only been holding the controls while someone else did the real work.
'Today,' Mr Delaney said, coiling the cable over his arm, 'you're on your own.'
Kai's mouth went dry. The club's airfield was a mown strip between two paddocks at the edge of town, with a windsock on a pole and a shed where members drank tea from a flask. Usually the other members chatted while they fiddled with their planes. Today, Kai noticed, they had all gone quiet. Even old Mrs Pham, who usually never stopped talking about her balsa-wood biplane, had put down her screwdriver to watch.
He checked the controls the way he had been taught: elevator up, elevator down, rudder left, rudder right. He faced the plane into the breeze and pushed the throttle forward. The motor rose to a buzzing whine, the wheels bounced along the strip, and then, without fuss, the plane was in the air.
For the first few minutes he flew wide, careful circles, keeping the plane high so he would have room to recover from a mistake. His thumbs were shaking. Then, slowly, he realised that the plane was flying exactly as it always had. Nothing felt different. The buddy box had never done the flying for him. It had only been there in case.
The landing was the hard part. He lined up too fast, bounced once, twice, and rolled to a stop at the very edge of the strip, nose in the clover, one wheel spinning slowly in the air. It was not pretty. But the plane was in one piece, and so, he discovered, was he.
The members by the shed clapped. Mr Delaney walked over, grinning, and held out the coiled cable.
'What's this for?' asked Kai.
'A girl called Ruby starts next month,' said Mr Delaney. 'She'll need someone on the other end.'
Question: In the first paragraph, the word 'obeyed' means . . .
Option A: followed the commands of
Option B: flew away from
Option C: broke free from
Option D: struggled against

Waiting for the Steps
2 November
We have been in Longyearbyen, on the Norwegian islands of Svalbard, for six weeks, and the sun has stopped coming up. It will not rise again until February. Mum says this is called the polar night. Her research job at the university here lasts a year, so we will see the whole thing. Outside, the snow squeaks and crunches under my boots, and the street lights stay on all day. It feels like living inside a fridge with the door shut.
14 December
I have stopped noticing what time it is. We wear head torches for the walk home from school, and we are not allowed to wander past the edge of town, because polar bears sometimes come close. Last week the sky turned green. Ribbons of light rippled over the mountains, swirling and shimmering, and our whole class stood in the playground with our mouths open. I forgot to feel cold. Our teacher said it was the aurora, and that it happens when tiny particles from the sun crash into the air high above the Earth.
20 January
'It's not really dark, Hana,' my friend Ingrid says. At noon there is a deep blue glow in the south, as if someone has left a lamp on in the next room. She showed me how the snow catches the moonlight, so that you can see the whole valley. I have started to like the blue hours. I still miss the sun, though, and I miss Mum's garden back home in Hobart.
16 February
The sun is officially back, but we still cannot see it! Ingrid laughed when I complained. The town sits in a valley with mountains all around, she explained, so even though the sun now rises above the horizon, it stays hidden behind the peaks. It will not reach the town until early March. Everyone here knows the exact place where it first appears: the steps of the old hospital. On that day there is a festival, and people gather on the steps to wait.
8 March
Today the whole town crowded around the old hospital steps in our thickest jackets, stamping our feet. Ingrid's little brother held a paper sun on a stick. For a long time, nothing happened. Then a thin line of gold slid over the ridge, crept down the slope and touched the top step. Everyone cheered. I felt it on my face, faint and pale, like a hand from very far away. I cried a bit, and I was not the only one.
On the walk home I realised something. I had spent four months waiting for the light to come back, but I will remember the dark just as much: the green sky, the blue noons, Ingrid and the moonlit valley. I think I might even miss it.

Option B: rhyme

Option D: onomatopoeia

The Tablet House
The sun had barely climbed above the walls of Ur when Ludu hurried through the narrow lanes towards the tablet house. He was late again. He could already picture the face of Abba Ningal, the teacher everyone called the school father, and the slow, disappointed way he would lift one eyebrow.
The tablet house was a courtyard with low mud-brick benches along each wall. Twenty boys sat cross-legged, each holding a lump of damp clay in one hand and a sharpened reed in the other. Ludu slipped into his place beside Ennam, who had been there since dawn and had already filled one side of his tablet with neat, wedge-shaped marks.
'You're late,' whispered Ennam, without looking up.
'I know,' Ludu whispered back. 'The donkey ate my sandals.'
'It did not.'
'It tried.'
Today's lesson was the list of signs for animals. The school father pressed each sign into a model tablet, and the boys copied it, pushing the corner of the reed into the clay to make the wedges. Ox. Sheep. Goat. Donkey. Ludu's donkey looked rather like a goat. He smoothed it away with his thumb, which was the beauty of wet clay, and tried again.
Then came the part Ludu dreaded. Bel-ibni, an older student whom the boys called Big Brother, walked along the benches checking each tablet. When he reached Ludu, he held the tablet up to the light and squinted at it for a long time.
'Your sheep,' he said at last, 'has five legs.'
A few boys giggled. Ludu felt his ears burn. But Bel-ibni crouched beside him and showed him, stroke by stroke, how to angle the reed so that each wedge sat cleanly beside the last. 'I drew sheep with six legs when I started,' he said quietly. 'Everyone does.'
By midday the tablets had begun to dry in the heat. Ludu looked at his. The sheep had four legs. The donkey looked like a donkey. It was not as neat as Ennam's, but it was his.
He knew what the school father said about scribes: that a boy who mastered the signs could one day write letters for merchants, keep records of grain for the palace, or even copy the stories of ancient kings. It seemed a very long way off. Today, four correct legs felt like enough.
Thousands of tablets made by students like Ludu have survived, because clay that is baked or buried in dry ground can last for an astonishingly long time. Archaeologists have found them in the ruins of Mesopotamian cities, still covered in wobbly practice signs and the corrections of patient teachers. Some are now displayed in museums around the world.
Question: What did the boys use to make marks in the clay?
Option A: a sharpened reed
Option B: a pointed stone
Option C: a bronze needle
Option D: their fingernails

Letters from the Ger
Dear Nana,
I am writing this by the light of a head torch, sitting cross-legged on a felt rug inside the Batbayar family's ger. A ger, in case you have forgotten my last postcard, is the round tent that herding families in Mongolia live in. It has a wooden lattice wall, a thick felt cover and a little iron stove right in the middle, with a chimney poking out through a hole in the roof. Right now that stove is the most important thing in my life.
Before I came, I imagined the Gobi Desert as a giant sandpit, hot and golden like the deserts in films. I was half right. There are sand dunes here, enormous ones that the family calls the singing sands, but most of the Gobi is gravel and tough little shrubs stretching to the edge of the sky. And it is not hot. This morning the thermometer by the door said minus twenty-two degrees. A desert, Mr Ganbold explained when he saw my face, is about how little rain falls, not how warm it is. The Gobi sits behind tall mountains that block the wet air, so it barely rains at all, and in winter the wind comes straight down from Siberia.
Everyone here has a job, even the youngest. Tuya, who is nine, milks the goats before breakfast without gloves. I tried it with gloves and the goat walked away. The Boards from Corrigan's Store
The old general store on Corrigan Street had been empty for as long as Priya could remember, so when the demolition fence went up she didn't think much about it. Her uncle Dev thought about it a great deal.
'Hundred-year-old hardwood,' he said, peering through the wire on Saturday morning. 'Blackbutt, by the look of the colour. You can't buy timber like that any more.'
By Monday he had spoken to the demolition crew, and by Wednesday Priya was wearing a pair of his gloves, which were far too big, and pulling nails out of floorboards in the back of his workshop.
It was slow work. Each board had to be stacked, checked for rot and cleared of every nail, because a single hidden nail could shatter the blade of his saw. Some boards were splintered at the ends; others had black stains where a stove had once stood. Priya's arms ached by the end of the first afternoon.
'Wouldn't it be quicker to buy new wood?' she asked, dropping another bent nail into the tin.
'Quicker,' Uncle Dev agreed. 'Cheaper too, if you count the hours. But think about where new boards come from. A tree that took eighty years to grow gets cut down, trucked to a mill, dried in a kiln and trucked again. These boards have already paid that price. If nobody saves them, they get crushed and buried in landfill, and somebody somewhere cuts down another tree.'
Priya looked at the pile differently after that. When she ran the plane along a grey, weathered board, curls of shaving fell away, and underneath was a deep reddish-gold, as bright as the day the tree was felled. She gasped.
'Told you,' said Uncle Dev, grinning.
Over the next three weekends the boards became a long dining table. Uncle Dev let Priya choose which ones went into the top, and she chose the ones with stories in them: the board with a row of tiny holes where a shelf had been screwed on, the board with a pencilled sum that someone had added up a century ago, the board worn slightly hollow in the middle by thousands of customers' boots. She sanded around the marks carefully so they would stay.
The table went to a young couple who had just bought a house two streets away. When they came to collect it, the woman ran her fingers along the hollowed board and went quiet.
'My great-grandmother worked in that store,' she said at last. 'She stood behind the counter every day for thirty years.'
Nobody spoke for a while. Then Uncle Dev cleared his throat and helped load the table into the van, and Priya noticed him wipe his eyes on his sleeve.
That night she went back to the workshop and looked at the remaining stack of boards for a long time, wondering what they had been part of, and who might be waiting for them.

In Defence of the Bin Chicken
Few Australian birds are mocked as much as the Australian white ibis. We call it the bin chicken. We share photos of it with its long black beak buried in a rubbish bin or snatching a chip from a toddler's hand. Cafes put up signs warning about it. I used to laugh along with everyone else. But the more I have learned about this bird, the more I think we owe it an apology.
First, the ibis is not an invader. It is a native Australian bird, and until a few decades ago it was rarely seen in cities at all. Its true home is the inland wetlands of the Murray-Darling Basin, where it nests in huge colonies among the reeds and feeds by probing the mud for yabbies, worms and insects. That long curved beak was not designed for bins. It is a precise tool for finding food hidden under mud and water.
Second, it is a refugee rather than a pest. As rivers have been dammed and wetlands drained, and as droughts have dried out its breeding grounds, many ibis have moved to the coast in search of food and water. Our parks, rubbish tips and bins were simply the easiest meals available. In other words, the bird that annoys us at the beach is often a bird whose home we changed.
Third, the ibis does useful work. In paddocks and parks it eats large numbers of grasshoppers, beetle grubs and other insects. Ibis were once known as the farmer's friend because flocks would follow ploughs to gobble up pests. It is hardly fair to praise a bird in the country and scorn it in the city for doing much the same thing: finding food wherever it can.
I will admit that an ibis stealing your sandwich is not a charming experience. But I changed my mind last spring, when I watched a pair of ibis at our local lake building a nest of sticks on a small island. For weeks they took turns sitting on the eggs through wind and rain, and when the chicks hatched, the parents fed them patiently from their own beaks. They did not look like rubbish thieves. They looked like a family doing their best in a place that was never meant for them.
None of this means we should feed them. Human food is bad for ibis, and feeding them only draws more birds to our bins. The better answer is to cover bins, take our rubbish home and support the protection of inland wetlands, so the birds have somewhere better to go.
So the next time an ibis strolls past your picnic rug, try not to sneer. Look at that remarkable beak and remember where it was meant to be: deep in the mud of a wetland, far from here.

Option A: the inland wetlands of the Murray-Darling Basin
Option B: the beaches and headlands along the coast
Option C: the parks and rubbish tips of large cities
Option D: the islands in the middle of city lakes

In Defence of the Bin Chicken
Few Australian birds are mocked as much as the Australian white ibis. We call it the bin chicken. We share photos of it with its long black beak buried in a rubbish bin or snatching a chip from a toddler's hand. Cafes put up signs warning about it. I used to laugh along with everyone else. But the more I have learned about this bird, the more I think we owe it an apology.
First, the ibis is not an invader. It is a native Australian bird, and until a few decades ago it was rarely seen in cities at all. Its true home is the inland wetlands of the Murray-Darling Basin, where it nests in huge colonies among the reeds and feeds by probing the mud for yabbies, worms and insects. That long curved beak was not designed for bins. It is a precise tool for finding food hidden under mud and water.
Second, it is a refugee rather than a pest. As rivers have been dammed and wetlands drained, and as droughts have dried out its breeding grounds, many ibis have moved to the coast in search of food and water. Our parks, rubbish tips and bins were simply the easiest meals available. In other words, the bird that annoys us at the beach is often a bird whose home we changed.
Third, the ibis does useful work. In paddocks and parks it eats large numbers of grasshoppers, beetle grubs and other insects. Ibis were once known as the farmer's friend because flocks would follow ploughs to gobble up pests. It is hardly fair to praise a bird in the country and scorn it in the city for doing much the same thing: finding food wherever it can.
I will admit that an ibis stealing your sandwich is not a charming experience. But I changed my mind last spring, when I watched a pair of ibis at our local lake building a nest of sticks on a small island. For weeks they took turns sitting on the eggs through wind and rain, and when the chicks hatched, the parents fed them patiently from their own beaks. They did not look like rubbish thieves. They looked like a family doing their best in a place that was never meant for them.
None of this means we should feed them. Human food is bad for ibis, and feeding them only draws more birds to our bins. The better answer is to cover bins, take our rubbish home and support the protection of inland wetlands, so the birds have somewhere better to go.
So the next time an ibis strolls past your picnic rug, try not to sneer. Look at that remarkable beak and remember where it was meant to be: deep in the mud of a wetland, far from here.

'Give it a minute,' said Gran from somewhere near the window. 'Your eyes need time to adjust.'

'Gran,' she whispered, 'the sky's on the floor.'
Gran chuckled. 'That's the trick. Light travels in straight lines, you see. Light from the top of the hedge comes down through the hole at an angle and keeps going until it hits the bottom of the wall. Light from the bottom goes up and lands near the top. Everything swaps over.'

Halves, Arms and Mirror Lines
Fold a picture of a butterfly down the middle and the two halves match almost perfectly. Look straight down on a starfish and you can turn it like a wheel, and it looks much the same after every fifth of a turn. These two animals show the two most common kinds of symmetry in the living world, and the difference between them says a lot about how each creature lives.
The butterfly has bilateral symmetry. 'Bilateral' means 'two-sided': only one line divides the body into matching left and right halves. Most animals you know are built this way, including fish, birds, insects, dogs and people. Bilateral animals also have a clear front and back. Their mouth and most of their sense organs, such as eyes, are clustered at the front end, the end that meets the world first as the animal moves forward. Scientists think this body plan suits creatures that travel in one direction, searching for food or escaping danger.
The starfish, on the other hand, has radial symmetry. Its body parts are arranged around a centre, like the spokes of a bicycle wheel, so it can be divided into matching pieces along several lines. Jellyfish, sea anemones and sea urchins are radial too. Many radial animals drift with the current or move very slowly, and their mouths sit in the middle. For them, food and danger might arrive from any direction, so having no particular front is an advantage rather than a weakness.
The starfish holds a surprise, however. Its larvae, the tiny young that swim in the plankton, are bilateral. Only as they settle and grow does the five-part adult shape take over. For this reason, scientists believe starfish are descended from bilateral ancestors and that their wheel-like shape came later.
Nature is rarely perfect, either. Your own face is not truly symmetrical; one eye may sit slightly higher, and one side of your smile may lift further. A fiddler crab takes this to the extreme: the male has one enormous claw and one tiny one. Flatfish such as flounder begin life like any other fish, then one eye gradually travels across the head until both eyes sit on the same side.
These odd ones out are, to many biologists, the most fascinating part of the story. The rule tells you what usually happens. The exceptions show you what is possible.
Next time you are at the beach or in the garden, try a simple test. Look at a creature and ask yourself where its mirror line is, or whether it has several. Then ask the more interesting question: how might that shape help it survive?
Question: Which of these animals has radial symmetry?
Option A: a sea anemone
Option B: a butterfly
Option C: a dog
Option D: a flounder

Setting an Anchor That Holds
Every skipper remembers the first time their anchor dragged. Mine was on a calm-looking evening in a bay near Port Stephens. I woke at midnight to the sound of waves slapping much too close, scrambled on deck and found we had slid a hundred metres towards the rocks. Nothing terrible happened, but I learned that anchoring is a skill, not just a matter of throwing something heavy over the side. These steps will help you get it right.
What you need
an anchor suited to your boat and the type of seabed
enough chain or rope (called the rode) for the depth of water
a chart or a depth sounder
Step 1: Choose your spot. Use the chart to find an area sheltered from the wind and swell. Sand and firm mud hold an anchor well; weed and rock do not. Check the depth, and remember to allow for the tide rising later.
Step 2: Work out how much rode to let out. The length of rode compared with the depth of water is called the scope. As a rule, let out at least five times the depth if you are using chain, and more if you are using rope. In six metres of water, that means at least thirty metres of chain. Too little scope pulls the anchor upwards instead of along the bottom, and it will skip out of the seabed.
Step 3: Approach slowly. Bring the boat to a stop with its bow pointing into the wind or current, the direction it will settle in once anchored.
Step 4: Lower, don't throw. Lower the anchor until you feel it touch the bottom. Then let the boat drift slowly backwards while you feed out the rode, so the chain lies along the seabed rather than piling up on top of the anchor.

If the boat keeps sliding, haul it in and start again. There is no shame in a second attempt. The only shame is in pretending the first one worked.
Step 6: Take bearings and keep checking. Choose two fixed landmarks on shore, such as a headland and a tall tree, and note how they line up. If they shift during the night, your anchor may be dragging. Many boats now also carry an alarm that sounds if the boat moves outside a set circle.
A final word
Beginners often feel embarrassed when they need three tries to anchor while other boats look on. Don't be. The experienced sailors watching have all done the same, and they would much rather see you try again than wake at midnight to find your boat drifting towards theirs. Good anchoring takes patience. The sea is never in a hurry, and neither should you be.

The Windmill on the Hill Paddock
Drive along almost any back road in inland Australia and sooner or later you will see one: a tall steel tower with a wheel of metal blades on top and a tail fin sticking out behind. Below it there is usually a round tank and a long trough, and often a few cattle or sheep standing patiently nearby. For more than a century, the windmill has been one of the most important machines on Australian farms.
The windmill's job is to pump water up from underground. In much of inland Australia, creeks run only after heavy rain and dams can dry up in summer. Yet far below the dry ground, water lies soaking through layers of sand and rock. The Great Artesian Basin, which stretches beneath parts of Queensland, New South Wales, South Australia and the Northern Territory, is one of the largest underground water stores in the world.
To reach this water, a farmer drills a narrow hole called a bore. A long rod runs from the windmill down into the bore, connected to a pump at the bottom. When the wind turns the blades, gears change the spinning movement into an up-and-down movement, and the rod works the pump rather like someone pumping up a bicycle tyre. With each stroke, a little water rises up the pipe and spills into the tank. The tail fin keeps the wheel turned to face the wind, wherever it blows from.
Windmills changed rural life. Before them, stock could only graze within walking distance of a river or waterhole, and huge areas of land could not be used at all. Windmills let farmers spread water across their properties, so animals could feed on pasture that had never been grazed before.
A windmill needs looking after. Someone has to check the troughs, grease the gears and, when the leather seals in the pump wear out, pull up the rods and replace them, often in blazing heat. On large stations, a worker called a windmill runner might spend whole days driving from one mill to the next. If a windmill breaks down in summer and nobody notices, the animals that depend on it can be in serious trouble within a couple of days.
Today, many farms use solar-powered pumps instead. They are cheaper to maintain and keep working on still, sunny days when a windmill would stand idle. Even so, thousands of old windmills still turn across the countryside. Some farmers keep them as a backup. Others simply cannot bring themselves to pull down a machine their grandparents put up, a machine that has creaked faithfully through droughts and floods and has never once sent anyone a power bill.

Option A: the paragraph beginning 'The windmill's job'
Option B: the paragraph beginning 'Windmills changed rural life'
Option C: the paragraph beginning 'A windmill needs looking after'
Option D: the paragraph beginning 'To reach this water'

When the wind turns the blades, gears change the spinning movement into an up-and-down movement, and the rod works the pump rather like someone pumping up a bicycle tyre. With each stroke, a little water rises up the pipe and spills into the tank. The tail fin keeps the wheel turned to face the wind, wherever it blows from.

Strangers on Page Ninety
I bought the book for fifty cents,
a novel, worn and plain,
its corners soft as flannel,
its cover marked by rain.
It waited in a cardboard box
with records, scratched and old,
and jigsaws missing half their sky,
and teapots, chipped, unsold.
But when I opened it that night,
a photo slipped out free
and landed face up on the rug
and smiled straight up at me.
Two girls stood squinting at the sun
beside a garden wall,
one holding up a birthday cake,
the other one quite small.
Their dresses had the faded look
of photos from the past,
and someone's shadow, long and thin,
across the lawn was cast.
And on the back, in pencil script,
a single line was penned:
'To read again on page ninety,
for when you miss me. Fen.'
I turned to page ninety and found
one sentence underlined
in that same pencil, light as breath:
'Love leaves its light behind.'
I read the book from end to end
to see what Fen had seen:
a tale of two girls by the sea
and all the years between.
I studied every clue I had
the way detectives do:
the slanting hand, the fading lead,
the corner bent in two.
I held the photo to the lamp
and searched the garden wall
for house numbers or a street sign,
but found no clue at all.
Inside the cover, someone's stamp
had faded into grey:
a date, the twelfth of something,
the year all worn away.
Now who was Fen, and who was meant
to find that note one day?
Was it the small one, or the tall,
and why'd they give the book away?
I've made a dozen stories up:
a sister sailing far,
a grandmother, a best friend lost,
a wish upon a star.
In one, Fen moved somewhere cold
and wrote that line with care;
in one, the small girl kept the book
for years, then left it there.
I could go back and ask the shop,
I could post it online,
and maybe someone, somewhere, knows
the meaning of this sign.
My brother says I'm being slow,
I ought to crack the case:
'Just post the picture. Someone's sure
to recognise the place.'
But some nights, I confess, I think
I'd rather not be told,
for every story I invent
stays warm, and none grows old.
For once it's solved, the wondering stops,
and all the maybes close;
Fen shrinks into a single name
that only someone knows.
Perhaps one day I'll pass it on
with one more pencilled line,
so someone else can find two notes,
one Fen's, and one of mine.
The photo marks my place each night;
the girls still squint and grin.
A mystery's a door, I've learned,
you needn't hurry in.

Option A: a new bookshop
Option B: a second-hand shop
Option C: a school library
Option D: an online store

Inside the Mountain's Old Pipes
Tuesday, 9 July
We drove four hours inland from Cairns today, and for most of that time my brother Sam complained that we were going all that way to 'look at a hole'. He is fifteen and thinks everything is boring unless it has a screen. I was secretly worried he might be right.
He wasn't.
The Undara Lava Tubes are in Undara Volcanic National Park in north Queensland. Our guide, Leanne, told us that about 190,000 years ago a volcano here erupted and poured out an enormous amount of runny lava. It flowed along old creek beds, some of it for more than 160 kilometres. The top of each lava river cooled in the air and hardened into a crust, like the skin on custard, while the hot lava underneath kept flowing. When the eruption ended, the liquid lava drained away and left long, hollow tunnels behind.
Walking into the first tube felt like walking into the throat of a giant. The roof curved high above us, about ten metres in places, and the walls were rippled where lava had once sloshed past. Leanne pointed out lines along the walls, like the rings a bath leaves, showing the different levels where the lava had flowed for a while.
Sam was quiet for a long time, which for Sam is practically a speech.
Some sections of the tubes have collapsed, and those hollows are now pockets of thick green rainforest, called vine thicket, in the middle of dry, open woodland. Leanne said the hollows trap moisture and shade and are protected from bushfires. From the air, she said, the line of the tubes looks like a string of green beads lying across the brown land. I asked how she knew, and she showed us a photo taken from a plane. It really did.
Bats live in some of the tubes. In the deepest parts of one, the air is so poor, partly because of rotting bat droppings, that only scientists with breathing equipment go in. Sam said that was the best fact of the day.
Leanne said the volcano is long extinct and there is nothing to worry about. I asked her how anyone could be sure. She said scientists study the age of the rocks and there has been no activity for a very long time, but that the Earth is always changing, so 'long extinct' is a scientist's best answer, not a promise. I liked that she was honest.
Driving back, Sam announced that the lava tubes were 'actually all right'. Coming from him, that is a five-star review. I am writing this by torchlight in our cabin, and I keep thinking about all that lava running in the dark, all those years before anyone was here to see it.
Isla

Option B: Isla describes a volcanic eruption she saw in north Queensland
Option C: Isla complains about a boring trip she took with her brother
Option D: Isla describes a visit to ancient lava tubes that impresses her brother

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
The Brown Lump on the Window
The brown lump had been stuck to the classroom window frame since the end of autumn. It was about the size of a walnut, papery and ridged, and most of Class 7B assumed it was an old wasp nest or a blob of dried glue. Only Mr Okafor seemed interested in it. He had stuck a strip of masking tape beside it with a single word written in marker: WAIT.
'It's an ootheca,' he told Noor when she finally asked in July. 'A praying mantis egg case. The mother made it from a foam that hardened, and there could be a hundred eggs inside. They'll hatch when the weather warms up.'
Noor didn't believe him, but she began checking it every morning anyway.
Weeks passed. Nothing happened. The lump just sat there, brown and boring, while winter rain streamed down the glass. Some of the boys drew two columns on the whiteboard, ALIVE and DEAD, and the class voted. Noor wrote her name under ALIVE, mostly because nobody else had.
Then, on a warm Tuesday in October, she walked into the classroom early and stopped dead.
The window was moving.
Tiny pale shapes were wriggling out from the bottom of the ootheca, dangling on fine silky threads like acrobats on ropes. Each one was no bigger than a grain of rice. As she watched, they shook themselves loose and began to climb, their long front legs folded in front of their faces as though they were already praying. Within minutes there were dozens of them, scattered across the glass like spilled punctuation.
'Mr Okafor!' she called, not taking her eyes off the window.
He came in with his coffee, saw the window and smiled so widely that he forgot to drink it.
By the time the bell rang, the whole class was crowded around, whispering as if the hatchlings might hear them. Mr Okafor explained that the babies were called nymphs and looked like tiny adults, with no caterpillar stage, and that they would shed their skins several times as they grew. Then he said they would need to carry the nymphs out to the school garden straight away.
'Why can't we keep them?' asked Jacob, whose name was under DEAD.
'Because they'll eat each other,' said Mr Okafor.
There was a horrified silence.
'Mantises eat whatever is small enough to catch,' he said, 'and right now the smallest things around are their brothers and sisters. Out in the garden they'll spread out and find aphids and tiny flies. In here, crowded together, they'd soon start on each other.'
So 7B spent the first lesson of the day kneeling in the garden, gently tipping nymphs off pieces of card onto leaves. And the masking tape stayed on the window frame until the end of the year, still saying WAIT.
Question: What word did Mr Okafor write on the masking tape?
Option A: WAIT
Option B: ALIVE
Option C: OOTHECA
Option D: HATCH
