The Short Corner
With four minutes left in the grand final, the umpire blew her whistle and pointed to the circle. Penalty corner. The Ridgeview under-fourteens were losing one-nil, and this might be their last real chance.
Kiri jogged to the backline with the ball and tried to slow her breathing. She was the injector, the player who pushes the ball out from the backline to start the corner. It was the least glamorous job on the field. Nobody ever remembered the injector. They remembered whoever put the ball in the net.
At the top of the circle, Hana crouched as the stopper, ready to trap the ball dead. Beside her was Ellie, the hitter, who had the hardest shot in the competition and knew it. The rest of the team spread out around them.
'Plan A?' Ellie called.
Kiri hesitated. All season, Plan A had worked the same way: Kiri pushed the ball out, Hana stopped it and Ellie blasted it at goal. But the other team had watched them do it in every game. Their defenders were already watching Ellie, and the goalkeeper had shuffled slightly to her left.
At training on Thursday, Coach Marsh had made them practise something new. 'Plan Wattle,' she'd called it. Hana would stop the ball, but instead of leaving it for Ellie, she would slip it sideways to Lucy, waiting unmarked near the post. Ellie would pretend to swing anyway, pulling the defenders towards her. They had tried it only four times. It had worked once.
'Wattle,' Kiri said quietly.
Ellie frowned. For a second Kiri thought she would argue. Ellie's whole season had been built on that shot. Then Ellie looked at the defenders and gave the smallest nod. 'Wattle,' she repeated, loudly enough for her own team but not the other.
The whistle blew. Kiri pushed the ball hard and flat along the turf, exactly the way she had practised a thousand times against the back fence at home. It rolled straight to Hana's stick. Hana trapped it, and Ellie wound up for her famous swing, drawing two defenders and the goalkeeper towards her like iron filings to a magnet.
Except the ball wasn't there. Hana had already slipped it sideways.
Lucy didn't even need to hit it hard. She guided it in past the post, and the net shivered.
They didn't win. The other team scored again with a minute left, and the final whistle went at two-one. But in the change rooms afterwards, Ellie found Kiri and sat down beside her.
'That was the best corner we've run all year,' Ellie said. 'And you called it, not me.'
Kiri didn't know what to say, so she just said, 'Hana stopped it perfectly.'
'Yeah,' said Ellie, grinning. 'And Lucy finished it. That's sort of the point, isn't it?'
Question: 'Hana trapped it'. In this sentence, 'trapped' means . . .
Option A: caught in her hands
Option B: hit hard at goal
Option C: lost to a defender
Option D: stopped and controlled

The Pelican at Jetty Four
Every Saturday, Tariq and his uncle Faisal fished from the end of Jetty Four, where the water turned from green to deep blue. Tariq liked the waiting best: the creak of the old boards, the gulls squabbling over scraps, and the pelicans drifting past like stately white ships.
That morning, one pelican was not drifting. It stood hunched on the bottom rung of a ladder, one wing held awkwardly away from its body. As Tariq crept closer, he saw why. A knot of clear fishing line was wrapped around the wing, and a rusty hook had snagged the edge of the bird's enormous pouch.
"Don't grab it," Uncle Faisal warned. "A frightened pelican can hurt you with that beak, and you could hurt it worse." He phoned the wildlife rescue number printed on the sign at the jetty's entrance.
The rescuer, a woman named Bev, arrived forty minutes later with a large towel and a pair of blunt scissors. She moved slowly, talking in a low, steady voice, and in one smooth movement she draped the towel over the pelican's head. The bird stopped struggling at once. "Darkness calms them," she explained. Tariq held Bev's bag of gear while Bev snipped the line, strand by strand, and eased the hook free.
"Is it going to be all right?" he asked.
"This one was lucky," Bev said, examining the wing. "The line hadn't cut too deep. Some I see have lost the use of a wing altogether, or they can't open their pouch to feed." She held up the tangle she had removed. "Somebody cut this off their reel and dropped it, probably without a second thought. Line doesn't rot away. It just waits."
Tariq looked down at his own tackle box. Wedged inside the lid was a nest of old line he had snipped off the week before. He had meant to bin it, but most weeks he simply flicked the scraps over the railing when nobody was watching.
Bev carried the pelican to her van so that a vet could check it. Before she left, she pointed to a tall white tube bolted to the railing, labelled RECYCLE YOUR LINE. "Hardly anyone uses it," she sighed.

The following Saturday, a pelican cruised past the end of the jetty with both wings folded neatly against its sides. Tariq could not tell whether it was the same bird. He fed his own offcuts into the white tube, then pulled a fresh bag from his pocket and started walking.
Question: In the first paragraph, the word 'stately' is closest in meaning to . . .
Option A: speedy
Option B: dignified
Option C: noisy
Option D: tiny

Mochi and the Pretty Pebbles
When my cousin Hana moved to Singapore, she left me two things: a long list of instructions and an axolotl called Mochi. Mochi was pale pink, with feathery gills that fanned out from her head like a crown, and a mouth that always seemed to be smiling.
Hana's list was very clear. Keep the water cool, below twenty degrees. Feed her worms three times a week. Change a quarter of the water every Sunday. And, underlined twice: Never put in anything smaller than her head.
I followed the list carefully for a month. But Mochi's tank looked so bare. Hana had left nothing in it except one large flat rock and a plastic plant. Every time my friends visited, they said it looked like a hospital waiting room. So when I saw a bag of glittering blue and purple aquarium gravel at the pet shop, I bought it with my birthday money. I told myself that Hana's rule was probably about sharp things, and these pebbles were smooth and round.
The tank looked magnificent. Mochi seemed to like it too. She snapped eagerly at her worms, and I noticed that she gulped up a few pebbles along with them.
Four days later, Mochi stopped eating. She floated near the surface, her gills drooping, and refused even her favourite bloodworms. I checked the water temperature: eighteen degrees, perfect. I checked the list again and again. Then I read the underlined line, and my stomach dropped.
Mum drove us to a vet who treated reptiles and amphibians. Dr Okafor examined Mochi gently and held her up to a bright light. "See that shadow?" she said. "Axolotls feed by sucking in whatever is in front of them. Gravel this size is small enough to swallow but too big to pass through easily. It can block the gut completely."
I could hardly speak. "Is she going to die?"
"Not today, I hope," Dr Okafor said. "Take out every pebble, keep the water cool, and we'll give her a few days. Many pass small stones on their own."
That night I scooped out every last speck of glitter. Mochi lay still on the bare floor of her tank, and I sat beside her until midnight.
On the third morning, I found two blue pebbles on the floor of the tank, and Mochi was hovering near the glass, watching me. When I dropped in a worm, she gulped it down.
I rang Hana that evening to confess. She did not shout. She just said, "I should have explained why."
Mochi's tank is still plain. My friends still say it looks boring. Now I tell them that boring is exactly how Mochi likes it.
Question: How often did Hana's list say Mochi should be fed?
Option A: three times a week
Option B: once a day
Option C: every Sunday
Option D: twice a week

Small Shell, Big Rescue
In 1953, a schoolboy near Perth brought an unusual tortoise he had found to a local show. Nobody there could identify it. When scientists examined it, they made a startling discovery. It was a western swamp tortoise, a species known only from a single specimen collected more than a hundred years earlier and never seen alive since.
The western swamp tortoise is Australia's most endangered reptile. It is also one of the smallest freshwater tortoises in the country: a fully grown adult has a shell only about fifteen centimetres long. It lives in a handful of shallow, seasonal swamps on the clay flats north-east of Perth, and nowhere else on Earth.
Its life follows the rhythm of the rain. In winter and spring, when the swamps fill, the tortoise is active, hunting insect larvae, tadpoles and small crustaceans. It can only feed underwater, so the wet season is the only time it can eat and grow. As the swamps dry out in early summer, it buries itself in soil, leaf litter or holes in the ground and enters a resting state called aestivation, which can last six months or more until the rains return.
This way of life has made the species extremely vulnerable. As Perth grew, many swamps were drained or cleared for farms, roads and housing. Introduced foxes dig up and eat the tortoises while they rest underground. By the late 1980s, fewer than fifty western swamp tortoises were thought to survive in the wild.
In response, Perth Zoo began a captive breeding program in 1989. Tortoises hatched and raised at the zoo have since been released into protected nature reserves, and fox-proof fences have been built around important swamps. As a result, the wild population has grown several times over, a remarkable recovery for an animal once down to a few dozen.
However, a new threat is emerging. Rainfall in south-western Australia has declined over recent decades, so the swamps hold water for a shorter time each year. A shorter wet season means fewer weeks of feeding, and young tortoises that cannot grow quickly enough may not survive their long summer rest.
Scientists are now testing a bold idea. In 2016, a small number of young tortoises were released into wetlands near Walpole, about four hundred kilometres to the south, where the climate is cooler and wetter. This is called assisted colonisation: moving a species to a place where it has never lived because its old home may become unsuitable. If the trial succeeds, it could offer a lifeline not only for this small tortoise but for other species whose homes are changing faster than they can adapt.
Question: How long is the shell of a fully grown western swamp tortoise?
Option A: about fifteen centimetres
Option B: about fifty centimetres
Option C: about five centimetres
Option D: about forty centimetres

Guardians of the Flock
When Kate Lindsay walked her paddocks near Cooma one spring morning, she found the remains of three newborn lambs beside the creek. It was the fourth attack in a fortnight. 'I felt sick and, honestly, a bit helpless,' she recalls. 'We'd tried shooting, baiting and lights on poles. The foxes simply learnt our routine and came back.'
Kate's answer now sleeps among her flock. Bella is a Maremma, a large, white guardian dog whose breed was developed centuries ago by shepherds in the hills of central Italy. Unlike a kelpie or a border collie, a Maremma does not round up stock. Its job is to stay with the animals day and night and to frighten off anything that threatens them.
The secret lies in how the dogs are raised. A Maremma pup is placed with livestock when it is only a few weeks old, so it grows up treating the sheep, goats or chickens as its family. Handlers spend enough time with the pup to keep it manageable, but not so much that it would rather be with people. A well-raised guardian will patrol the boundary fence, mark its territory and bark loudly at dusk, when foxes and wild dogs are most active. Most predators decide that a lamb protected by a dog weighing up to 45 kilograms is not worth the risk.
Australian farmers began using guardian dogs in large numbers in the late twentieth century, and the idea has since spread well beyond sheep properties. The best-known example is Middle Island, just off the coast at Warrnambool in Victoria. By 2005, foxes crossing the sand at low tide had reduced the island's colony of little penguins to fewer than ten birds. A local chicken farmer suggested trying his Maremmas, and in 2006 guardian dogs began protecting the island during the breeding season. The colony slowly recovered, and the story was later turned into a feature film.
Guardian dogs are not a magic fix, however. They need a year or more of patient training before they can be trusted alone, and young dogs sometimes play too roughly with lambs. Because they are bred to roam their territory, they can wander onto neighbouring farms or roads if fences are poor. Their night-time barking can also test the patience of people living nearby. A good working dog may cost well over a thousand dollars, plus food and vet bills.
For Kate, the trade-off has been worth it. In Bella's first full lambing season, the farm lost two lambs to foxes, compared with more than thirty the year before. 'I didn't expect to get so attached,' Kate admits. 'She's not a pet. She's a colleague.' Kate has since bought a second pup so that Bella can teach it the job while she is still in her prime.
Researchers say that guardian dogs may also benefit the wider environment. Instead of killing predators, the dogs simply move them on, which reduces the need for poison baits that can harm native animals such as quolls. In this way, a guardian dog offers farmers a means of protecting their income while living more peacefully alongside the bush.

Option A: furious and eager to get revenge
Option B: puzzled about what had killed them
Option C: sick and unable to stop the attacks
Option D: calm, as such losses were rare

When Kate Lindsay walked her paddocks near Cooma one spring morning, she found the remains of three newborn lambs beside the creek. It was the fourth attack in a fortnight. The secret lies in how the dogs are raised. A Maremma pup is placed with livestock when it is only a few weeks old, so it grows up treating the sheep, goats or chickens as its family. Handlers spend enough time with the pup to keep it manageable, but not so much that it would rather be with people. A well-raised guardian will patrol the boundary fence, mark its territory and bark loudly at dusk, when foxes and wild dogs are most active. The Sleep Log
Monday 4 March
Ms Okafor has given us the strangest science assignment ever: keep a sleep diary for a week. We have to record when we go to bed, when we wake up and how we feel during the day. Easy, I thought. Then I actually wrote down last night's numbers. Lights off at 11:40 pm, alarm at 6:15 am. That's about six and a half hours. No wonder I nearly dozed off in maths.
Tuesday 5 March
Looked up how much sleep teenagers need. Most health experts say between eight and ten hours a night, so I'm short by at least an hour and a half every school night. Mum said that when she was my age she was asleep by nine. I pointed out that she didn't have a phone. She pointed out that I do, and that it lives under my pillow. Fair point, but rude.
Wednesday 6 March
Ms Okafor explained something interesting today. Our bodies release a hormone called melatonin that makes us feel sleepy, and during adolescence it starts to be released later in the evening than it is for children or adults. So it isn't just laziness when teenagers can't fall asleep early. Our body clocks really do shift. The bad news is that light from screens can delay melatonin even further. I'm starting to think my phone and I need some time apart.
Thursday 7 March
An experiment within the experiment: phone charging in the kitchen from 9:30. I read a book instead (a paper one, which felt very old-fashioned). Annoyingly, I was asleep by 10:15. I woke up before the alarm for the first time this term and felt clear-headed all morning. I even answered a question in maths without being asked twice.
Friday 8 March
Second phone-free night. Netball training felt easier, too, and my reactions seemed quicker when I was defending. Jaz asked why I hadn't replied to her messages last night, so I told her about the experiment. She laughed, but then she asked if she could try it.
Saturday 9 March
No alarm, so I slept until 10:30. Glorious. Tonight I'm staying up late to watch a film with my cousins, but it doesn't matter because I can sleep in again tomorrow.
Sunday 10 March
Disaster. At 11 pm I was wide awake, staring at the ceiling, even though I'd done nothing tiring all day. I finally fell asleep some time after midnight. Tomorrow is going to be rough.
Monday 11 March
Handed in my diary. When I told Ms Okafor about Sunday night, she nodded and said lots of people have the same problem. Body clocks like routine, she explained, and a big change on the weekend can confuse them, a bit like flying to another time zone. Scientists even have a name for it: social jet lag.
Looking back over my week, the pattern is pretty obvious. My best days came after my earliest nights. I've asked Mum to buy me a proper alarm clock so that the phone can stay in the kitchen for good. Jaz says she has already lost track of time reading in bed, which might be a whole new problem.
Question: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to clear-headed as it is used in the Thursday entry?
Option A: alert
Option B: rested
Option C: muddled
Option D: cheerful

The Bookcase Incident
Dear Nan,
Thank you so much for the bookcase you sent for my birthday. I want you to know that it is now standing proudly in my bedroom, holding all my books, and that nobody was seriously hurt in the making of it.
It arrived on Saturday in a box so heavy that Dad and I had to drag it up the hallway like a pair of removalists. Inside were seven wooden panels, a bag of about four hundred screws and a booklet of instructions with no words at all, only drawings of a smiling cartoon man who never seemed to get tired. Dad flicked through the booklet for roughly four seconds, tossed it onto the bed and announced, 'Instructions are for people with no imagination.' Mum, who was passing in the hallway, said nothing, but I distinctly heard her chuckle.
For the first hour, things went surprisingly well. Dad was in charge of the screwdriver and I was in charge of finding the right screws, which is harder than it sounds when they all look identical and some are only slightly longer than others. Our dog, Biscuit, supervised from the doorway and every so often tried to eat the packaging. By lunchtime we had built something that definitely looked like a bookcase. Unfortunately, it was a bookcase with all the shelves on the outside.
We took it apart. Dad quietly retrieved the instructions from under my pillow, where they had somehow ended up, and we began again. This time the cartoon man was consulted at every step. Dad even started talking to him, saying things like, 'Easy for you, mate. You've got three hands.'
The second attempt was going brilliantly until we reached step fourteen and discovered that one small metal peg was missing. We searched the carpet on our hands and knees. We shook out the box. We emptied the vacuum cleaner. Dad even checked inside Biscuit's water bowl, which shows how desperate we were. Finally my little sister Matilda admitted that she had 'borrowed' it for her doll's house, where it was being used as a lamp post. Negotiations took twenty minutes and cost me two chocolate frogs.
At about four o'clock, the bookcase was finally standing. Dad stepped back, folded his arms and said, 'See? Nothing to it.' That is when we noticed the three screws still sitting on the floor. We decided, after a short family meeting, that they must be spares. The bookcase leans ever so slightly to the left, but Dad says that gives it character, and Mum says that as long as nobody tries to climb it, it will probably be fine.
I have filled every shelf, including a special spot for the book about Antarctic explorers you gave me last Christmas, which I have now read twice and plan to read again. Thank you again, Nan. It is the best present I got this year, and definitely the most memorable.
Lots of love,
Oliver
P.S. Dad would like to know whether the company makes a version that comes already built.

Option A: tore up
Option B: hid away
Option C: read aloud
Option D: got back

One Beat
For most of the season, I was convinced that I was the only person in our dragon boat who was actually trying.
I sat in the third row on the left, and every Saturday at the lake I dug my paddle in as hard and as fast as I could. I could feel the water tearing past the blade. Around me, I could hear everyone else splashing along, always a fraction slower, and I would think, If they'd just keep up with me, we'd fly.
We didn't fly. At the regional heats in March, the Eastside Lorikeets finished fifth out of six, and the boat wobbled so badly in the last hundred metres that our drummer, Grace, nearly slid off her little seat at the front. On the drive home, nobody said much. I stared out of the window and silently blamed everyone but myself.
Afterwards, Coach Lin found me sitting on the jetty with a towel over my head.
'You're the strongest paddler we've got, Ava,' she said.
'Then why are we losing?'
She didn't answer straight away. Instead, she took out her phone and showed me a video someone's dad had filmed from the bank. 'Watch the paddles, not the boat,' she said.
At first I saw only a blur of arms and water. Then I saw it. Nineteen blades rose and fell together, steady as a heartbeat, and one blade, third row on the left, plunged in early on every single stroke. Mine. Each time I rushed, the paddlers around me hesitated, unsure whether to follow me or the front pair. The whole boat lurched.
My face went hot under the towel.
'In a dragon boat, the best paddler isn't the one who pulls hardest,' Coach Lin said. 'It's the one who pulls at exactly the same moment as everyone else.'
For the next six weeks, I stopped watching the water and started watching Hamish, our lead paddler in the front row. The Smallest Find
On the third morning of the dig, Theo had split more than two hundred pieces of rock, and every one of them had been just that: rock.
The site was a flat, grey shelf of stone on the coast near Inverloch, uncovered only when the tide went out. About 125 million years ago, his aunt Ruth had explained on the drive down, this part of Victoria lay much closer to the South Pole. Small dinosaurs had roamed river valleys here through long, dark winters, and when they died, floods sometimes buried their bones in sand and mud that slowly turned to stone.
'So there are dinosaurs under our feet?' Theo had asked.
'Bits of them,' Ruth had said. 'Very small bits, if we're lucky.'
Ruth was a volunteer fossil hunter, and she had arranged for Theo to join the team for a week of his school holidays. He had imagined giant skeletons, or at least a thigh bone as long as his arm. Instead he was handed a hammer, a chisel, a magnifying lens and a bucket of fist-sized chunks of rock. His job was to tap each chunk along its natural cracks until it split, inspect the fresh surfaces, then tap again, until the piece was no bigger than a coin.
By lunchtime on day three, his wrist ached and his enthusiasm had worn as thin as the chips around his knees. Further along the shelf, a university student named Kiri held up something small and dark, and a little cheer went up. Theo went to look. It was a fragment of bone the size of a grain of rice.
'That's it?' he said, before he could stop himself.
Kiri only laughed. 'Most of what we find here is about this size,' she said. 'But every piece tells us something nobody knew yesterday.'
Theo walked back to his bucket feeling slightly ashamed. He picked up the next chunk and, instead of hammering it straight away, turned it slowly in the sunlight, the way he had seen Ruth do. A fine, dark line ran along one edge. He placed the chisel carefully and tapped once.
The rock fell open like a book. Lying in the middle of one page was something shiny, curved and pointed, no longer than his fingernail. Along one edge were tiny ridges, as neat as the teeth of a comb.
For a moment Theo couldn't speak. Then he called, much louder than he meant to, 'Ruth! Ruth, I think it's a tooth!'
Ruth came over, peered through her lens and was silent for so long that Theo began to worry he had made a mistake. Finally she looked up, smiling widely. 'That,' she said, 'is a tooth from a small meat-eating dinosaur. It will need to be checked at the museum, but I'm almost certain.'
That evening, they recorded the find in the logbook: the date, the exact position on the shelf, the layer of rock and a number. Ruth let Theo write his own name in the column marked Found by.
Before he fell asleep, Theo thought about the animal that had lost that tooth so long ago, in a cold, dark forest near the bottom of the world. He realised that he no longer minded that it was small.

Option A: a museum that displays giant dinosaur skeletons
Option B: a student who discovers a new kind of dinosaur
Option C: a family holiday at the beach near Inverloch
Option D: a boy who learns to value a small fossil find

Look Ahead, Not Down
The recycling truck was due at nine, and at eight fifty-two Nell was still sitting on the front step with her arm around a robot.
It was not a handsome robot. Tobb had been built in the days when household machines were all elbows and rivets, and his grey paint had worn through to silver at the knees. One of his eyes flickered whenever he turned his head to the left. When he walked, he made a faint whirr-clunk, whirr-clunk, like a washing machine trying to dance.
Nell's parents had bought him second-hand the year she was born. Her earliest memory was of Tobb's long metal fingers steadying the back of her bike seat as she wobbled down the driveway, his voice crackling, 'Balance, Nell. Look ahead, not down.' He had read her bedtime stories in a different voice for every character, even when his speaker buzzed on the high notes. He had once spent an entire afternoon helping her search the garden for a lost tooth, lifting every leaf with the patience of a surgeon.
But lately things had gone wrong. Tobb had put the cat's food in the dishwasher. He had folded Dad's work shirts into tiny, perfect squares and placed them in the freezer. Last week he had stood in the hallway for forty minutes, calmly greeting the coat rack.
'His memory circuits are wearing out,' Mum had said gently. 'The parts aren't made any more. The new model will be safer, Nell. It can cook, clean and even help with your maths homework.'
The new model had arrived on Monday. It was sleek and white and silent, and it glided across the floor like a cake of soap sliding across a wet bath. It had already learnt the name of everyone in the family and exactly how Dad liked his coffee. It was perfectly polite. Nell couldn't stand it.
Now, on the front step, Tobb turned his head towards her, his left eye stuttering. 'Nell,' he said. 'You are sad. Your face is doing the thing.'
'What thing?'
'The thing it did when you were five and your ice-cream fell on the footpath.'
Nell laughed, though her eyes stung. 'You remember that?'
'I remember all of it,' Tobb said. Then he paused, and a small frown seemed to cross his blank metal face. 'Most of it. Some of it is becoming . . . fuzzy.' His fingers moved slowly to a panel on his chest. With a click, he drew out a small square chip, no bigger than a postage stamp, and pressed it into her hand.
'What's this?'
'My stories,' Tobb said. 'The ones I read to you. The bike. The tooth. The ice-cream. I copied them while I still could. The new model can play them, if you ask it nicely.'
Down the street, the recycling truck rumbled around the corner, its orange lights blinking.
Nell closed her fingers over the chip. It was still warm. 'Thank you,' she whispered.
'Look ahead, not down,' said Tobb, and his voice crackled one last time, exactly as it had on the driveway all those years ago.

Option A: the truck
Option B: Tobb's hand
Option C: the front step
Option D: the chip

The Word That Came from a Play
Robots are so familiar today that it is easy to assume the word has always existed. In fact, it is barely a hundred years old, and it was born not in a laboratory but in a theatre.
In 1920, the Czech writer Karel Čapek was working on a play about a factory that manufactures artificial workers. He had a problem: he could not decide what to call them. His first idea was “labori”, from the Latin word for work, but it struck him as too bookish. According to a story Čapek told years later, he wandered into the studio of his brother Josef, a painter, and explained his difficulty. Josef, holding a brush between his teeth and barely looking up from his canvas, murmured, “Call them robots.” Karel took the suggestion at once.
The word came from the Czech “robota”, which means forced labour or drudgery. It was a clever choice. The name itself told audiences that these beings existed only to work for others.
The play, called R.U.R. (short for Rossum’s Universal Robots), was first performed in 1921. Within a few years it had been staged in New York and London and translated into many languages. Audiences who had never heard of Čapek were soon using his brother’s word.
Modern readers are often surprised by Čapek’s robots. They were not clanking metal machines with flashing lights; they were made from a chemical substance and looked almost exactly like people. In the play, factories turn them out by the thousands to do every job humans dislike. At first this seems wonderful. Gradually, however, people grow idle and the robots grow resentful, until humans lose control of the world they have built. Čapek was less interested in machinery than in a question: what happens to a society that hands all its work to someone else?
Two decades later, another writer added to the vocabulary. In a short story published in 1941, the American author Isaac Asimov used the word “robotics” for the science of building robots. He believed he was using a word that already existed. Asimov also invented his famous “Three Laws”, rules that his fictional robots had to obey to keep humans safe.
Real engineers soon caught up with the writers. In 1961, a robot called Unimate began work on a car assembly line in the United States, lifting and stacking hot pieces of metal. It was nothing like Čapek’s human-shaped workers: it was a heavy arm bolted to the floor. Yet nobody hesitated to call it a robot.
Today, scientists who design self-driving cars and household helpers still discuss the questions that Čapek and Asimov raised. Should machines be given rules? Who is responsible when they make mistakes? What will people do when machines do the work? The words, and many of the worries, began as fiction. Science fiction does not only imagine the future; sometimes it supplies the language we use to talk about that future when it finally arrives.

Reading the Wiggly Lines
Before setting off on an overnight hike, experienced bushwalkers spend time with a map spread across the kitchen table. They are not only looking for the track. They are studying a tangle of thin brown lines that, to a beginner, look like giant fingerprints. These are contour lines, and once you can read them, a flat sheet of paper turns into a three-dimensional landscape.
A contour line joins points that are the same height above sea level. Imagine a hill sliced horizontally, like a loaf of bread, every twenty metres from bottom to top. If you traced the edge of each slice and looked down from above, you would see a set of rings, one inside the other. That is exactly what a contour map shows. The height difference between neighbouring lines is called the contour interval, and it is printed in the map’s margin. On many Australian topographic maps it is ten or twenty metres. Every fifth line is usually drawn thicker and labelled with its height to make counting easier.
The spacing of the lines is the key to the shape of the land. When lines are bunched tightly together, the ground rises a long way in a short distance: a steep slope, or even a cliff. When they are spread far apart, the land is gentle or nearly flat. A small closed loop in the middle of a set of rings marks a summit.
Valleys and ridges are trickier, but there is a handy rule. Where contour lines cross a creek, they bend into a V shape, and the point of the V always aims uphill, towards the creek’s source. On a ridge or spur, the V shapes point the other way, downhill. Learning to tell the two apart lets a walker see where water will collect and where the high, dry ground lies.
Scale matters too. A map with a scale of 1:25 000 shows a lot of detail; one centimetre on the map stands for 25 000 centimetres, or 250 metres, on the ground. A 1:100 000 map covers a much bigger area but leaves out smaller features.
Why does all this matter? Because distance on a map can be deceptive. Two campsites might be only three kilometres apart in a straight line, yet if the route between them crosses tightly packed contours, the walk could take twice as long as a flat stroll of the same length. Many walkers use a rule of thumb: allow about an extra hour for every 600 metres of climbing. Contour lines also warn of danger. A track that looks like a short cut might drop down a slope too steep to descend safely, or lead into a narrow gully that floods after rain.
A GPS device or phone app can show where you are, but batteries go flat and signals drop out in deep valleys. A paper map, and the skill to read it, never runs out of charge. Spending an evening learning the language of those wiggly brown lines may be the best preparation a bushwalker can make.

Option A: points that are the same distance from a track

The Moths That Follow the Stars
Every spring, as the weather warms, millions of brown moths set off on one of the most remarkable journeys made by any insect. Bogong moths, each with a body barely as long as a paperclip, fly up to a thousand kilometres from the plains of southern Queensland, New South Wales and western Victoria to the Australian Alps. There they crowd into cool caves and rock crevices near the mountain tops, sometimes packed so tightly that the walls appear to be covered in brown roof tiles.
The moths travel to escape the heat. Summer on the plains is too hot and dry for them, so instead of feeding and breeding they spend the warm months resting in the cool mountain air, in a state of reduced activity similar to hibernation. When autumn arrives, they fly all the way back to the plains, where they mate, lay their eggs and die. The following spring, a new generation of moths, none of which has ever seen the mountains, makes the same journey to the same caves.
How they find their way has puzzled scientists for decades. The moths fly at night, so they cannot rely on landmarks in the way that many birds do. Research has shown that they can sense the Earth's magnetic field, and recent studies have found that they also use the pattern of stars in the night sky as a compass. When city lights or thick cloud hide the stars, the moths can become confused. In some years, swarms have drifted off course into the bright lights of Canberra and even Sydney.
For such small creatures, Bogong moths punch well above their weight in the alpine ecosystem. Their bodies are rich in fat, so the moths arriving each spring deliver a huge supply of energy to the mountains. Birds, lizards and small mammals feast on them. One animal depends on them more than any other: the endangered mountain pygmy possum, which wakes from its winter hibernation hungry and relies heavily on the moths to rebuild its strength before breeding. For thousands of years, Aboriginal peoples also travelled to the high country in summer to gather the moths, roasting them as a rich and nourishing food.
In recent years, however, the journey has become far less crowded. Between 2017 and 2019, the number of moths reaching the caves dropped dramatically, and some caves that once held huge numbers were almost empty. Scientists believe that severe drought on the plains reduced the plants that the caterpillars feed on, so fewer moths survived to make the trip. During those years, researchers reported that mountain pygmy possums in some areas struggled to raise their young. In 2021, the Bogong moth was listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Researchers now monitor the caves each year, and some communities encourage people to switch off unnecessary outdoor lights during the migration season. The Bogong moth is a reminder that the health of a mountain can depend on events hundreds of kilometres away, and on a creature small enough to sit on your fingertip.

Every spring, as the weather warms, millions of brown moths set off on one of the most remarkable journeys made by any insect. Bogong moths, each with a body barely as long as a paperclip, fly up to a thousand kilometres from the plains of southern Queensland, New South Wales and western Victoria to the Australian Alps. There they crowd into cool caves and rock crevices near the mountain tops, sometimes packed so tightly that the walls appear to be covered in brown roof tiles.
The moths travel to escape the heat. Summer on the plains is too hot and dry for them, so instead of feeding and breeding they spend the warm months resting in the cool mountain air, in a state of reduced activity similar to hibernation. When autumn arrives, they fly all the way back to the plains, where they mate, lay their eggs and die. The following spring, a new generation of moths, none of which has ever seen the mountains, makes the same journey to the same caves.
How they find their way has puzzled scientists for decades. The moths fly at night, so they cannot rely on landmarks in the way that many birds do. Research has shown that they can sense the Earth's magnetic field, and recent studies have found that they also use the pattern of stars in the night sky as a compass. When city lights or thick cloud hide the stars, the moths can become confused. In some years, swarms have drifted off course into the bright lights of Canberra and even Sydney.
For such small creatures, Bogong moths punch well above their weight in the alpine ecosystem. Their bodies are rich in fat, so the moths arriving each spring deliver a huge supply of energy to the mountains. Birds, lizards and small mammals feast on them. One animal depends on them more than any other: the endangered mountain pygmy possum, which wakes from its winter hibernation hungry and relies heavily on the moths to rebuild its strength before breeding. For thousands of years, Aboriginal peoples also travelled to the high country in summer to gather the moths, roasting them as a rich and nourishing food.
In recent years, however, the journey has become far less crowded. Between 2017 and 2019, the number of moths reaching the caves dropped dramatically, and some caves that once held huge numbers were almost empty. Scientists believe that severe drought on the plains reduced the plants that the caterpillars feed on, so fewer moths survived to make the trip. During those years, researchers reported that mountain pygmy possums in some areas struggled to raise their young. In 2021, the Bogong moth was listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Researchers now monitor the caves each year, and some communities encourage people to switch off unnecessary outdoor lights during the migration season. The Bogong moth is a reminder that the health of a mountain can depend on events hundreds of kilometres away, and on a creature small enough to sit on your fingertip.

Option A: build hard shelters on the cave walls
Option B: are heavy and hard like clay tiles
Option C: are very difficult to see in the caves
Option D: rest closely together in great numbers

The Can That Came Back
I began as red rock in a far northern mine,
dug out of the dirt by a growling machine,
then crushed, cooked and smelted until I could shine,
and rolled out as thin as you've ever seen.

At the factory they shaped me and filled me with fizz,
then printed a message in letters of green:
'Please recycle me.' Well, that's what it is,
a small, hopeful plea on a silvery screen.

I waited in rows in a corner-shop fridge
with a hundred twin cans standing stiff in the cold,
till a girl named Lily, on her way to the bridge,
chose me from the crowd for the drink that I'd hold.

By the creek, in the heat, she drank every last drop,
and her brother said, 'Toss it! Who's going to care?'
But Lily said, 'Me. This is where it stops.'
And she tucked me away in her bag with great care.

Her brother just shrugged, and he kicked at a stone,
but he watched as she zipped up the bag on her back,
and later that evening, when walking alone,
he picked up a bottle he'd dropped by the track.

That evening she dropped me, clink, into the bin,
the one with the yellow lid, out by the gate,
where newspapers, bottles and tubs had piled in,
and we rattled together, awaiting our fate.

At dawn came a truck with a long metal arm
that lifted the bin and then tipped us inside;
we tumbled and clattered but came to no harm
and were carried away on a bumpy ride.

At the sorting centre I rode on a belt
through a maze full of clatter and hissing and roar,
where the paper and glass and the steel cans were dealt
to their separate piles on the factory floor.

Then a drum full of magnets, spinning below,
gave me an invisible push through the air,
and I sailed off the end of the belt, just so,
to land with the rest of my kind waiting there.

We were squashed into bales and sent off to be melted
in a furnace that glowed like the heart of the sun;
I was poured, I was cooled, I was rolled and re-shaped,
and in only a few weeks a new life had begun.

I was stretched into sheets that were thinner than leaves,
then punched into circles and pulled into shape,
then washed and then painted and filled, if you please,
and sealed with a lid so the fizz can't escape.

Now I'm back in the fridge in a jacket of blue.
First lemonade, now it is cola I hold.
Who'll pick me this time? I haven't a clue,
but I'm shining as brightly as new-minted gold.

For aluminium never wears out when it's saved;
you can melt me and shape me again and again.
But the cans in the creek, in the weeds and the caves,
just lie where they're dropped through the sun and the rain.

A bottle can lie on a beach for an age,
and a bag can drift out to the turtles at sea,
but a can that is saved can turn page after page,
each chapter as bright as the first used to be.

So next time you finish a drink by the creek,
think of Lily, who carried me home with such care.
It takes only a moment, a choice, not a feat,
and it means I'll come back, and come back, and be there.
Question: In the line 'and we rattled together, awaiting our fate', which word is closest in meaning to awaiting?
Option A: running from
Option B: deciding on
Option C: waiting for
Option D: fighting against

The Can That Came Back
I began as red rock in a far northern mine,
dug out of the dirt by a growling machine,
then crushed, cooked and smelted until I could shine,
and rolled out as thin as you've ever seen.

At the factory they shaped me and filled me with fizz,
then printed a message in letters of green:
'Please recycle me.' Well, that's what it is,
a small, hopeful plea on a silvery screen.

I waited in rows in a corner-shop fridge
with a hundred twin cans standing stiff in the cold,
till a girl named Lily, on her way to the bridge,
chose me from the crowd for the drink that I'd hold.

By the creek, in the heat, she drank every last drop,
and her brother said, 'Toss it! Who's going to care?'
But Lily said, 'Me. This is where it stops.'
And she tucked me away in her bag with great care.

Her brother just shrugged, and he kicked at a stone,
but he watched as she zipped up the bag on her back,
and later that evening, when walking alone,
he picked up a bottle he'd dropped by the track.

That evening she dropped me, clink, into the bin,
the one with the yellow lid, out by the gate,
where newspapers, bottles and tubs had piled in,
and we rattled together, awaiting our fate.

At dawn came a truck with a long metal arm
that lifted the bin and then tipped us inside;
we tumbled and clattered but came to no harm
and were carried away on a bumpy ride.

At the sorting centre I rode on a belt
through a maze full of clatter and hissing and roar,
where the paper and glass and the steel cans were dealt
to their separate piles on the factory floor.

Then a drum full of magnets, spinning below,
gave me an invisible push through the air,
and I sailed off the end of the belt, just so,
to land with the rest of my kind waiting there.

We were squashed into bales and sent off to be melted
in a furnace that glowed like the heart of the sun;
I was poured, I was cooled, I was rolled and re-shaped,
and in only a few weeks a new life had begun.

I was stretched into sheets that were thinner than leaves,
then punched into circles and pulled into shape,
then washed and then painted and filled, if you please,
and sealed with a lid so the fizz can't escape.

Now I'm back in the fridge in a jacket of blue.
First lemonade, now it is cola I hold.
Who'll pick me this time? I haven't a clue,
but I'm shining as brightly as new-minted gold.

For aluminium never wears out when it's saved;
you can melt me and shape me again and again.
But the cans in the creek, in the weeds and the caves,
just lie where they're dropped through the sun and the rain.

A bottle can lie on a beach for an age,
and a bag can drift out to the turtles at sea,
but a can that is saved can turn page after page,
each chapter as bright as the first used to be.

So next time you finish a drink by the creek,
think of Lily, who carried me home with such care.
It takes only a moment, a choice, not a feat,
and it means I'll come back, and come back, and be there.

Ticklish Rats
Pet rats have an unfortunate reputation. Many people picture a sewer-dwelling pest, not a clever companion that can learn its name, come when called and ride happily on its owner’s shoulder. Yet people who keep rats often describe them as among the most affectionate small pets there are. In the late 1990s, an American scientist found evidence that rats may also share something surprising with us: they seem to laugh.
The researcher, Jaak Panksepp, studied emotions in animals. He knew that young rats make high-pitched chirps when they wrestle and play with one another. These calls are pitched at around 50 kilohertz, far too high for human ears, so they can only be heard with a special detector that lowers the sound. Panksepp wondered whether a human hand could trigger the same calls. With his students, he began gently tickling young rats on the back and belly, imitating the rough-and-tumble of play.
The rats chirped enthusiastically. They chirped most when tickled on the nape of the neck, the spot young rats target when they play-fight. They chased the researchers’ hands, and in later experiments they learned to run towards a hand that had tickled them rather than one that had simply been placed in the cage. When a rat was frightened, for example by the smell of a cat, the chirping stopped. Panksepp argued that the sounds were an early form of laughter, a signal of joyful, playful feeling.
Not every scientist was convinced. Some warned that it is easy to read human feelings into animal behaviour, and that a chirp might simply mean excitement. Later studies, however, have tended to support the idea. In one experiment in Germany, researchers found that rats being tickled also leapt into the air, which they called “Freudensprünge”, or joy jumps.
For people who keep rats, this research has practical lessons. First, rats are deeply social. A rat kept alone has no one to play with, which is why experts recommend keeping at least two, ideally of the same sex. Second, gentle, playful handling is not just tolerated but often enjoyed, and it builds trust. Owners report that a rat which is tickled regularly is often eager to come out of its cage.
Rats do have needs that a would-be owner should consider. They are mostly active at dusk and during the night, they need a large cage with places to climb and hide, and their sharp teeth grow continuously, so they need safe things to gnaw. Their lifespan is short, usually only two to three years, which some families find hard.
Still, the image of a rat squeaking with delight, too high for us to hear, is a powerful one. It suggests that the small animal in the cage may experience play much as a child does. Anyone who chooses a rat as a pet is not just caring for an animal, but sharing in its fun.

Option A: looked forward to

Option C: copied exactly
Option D: put up with

The Woman Who Found the Centre
In 1936, a Danish scientist published a research paper with one of the shortest titles in the history of science. It was simply called P′, pronounced 'P prime'. Behind those two characters lay a discovery that changed how we picture the inside of our planet. The scientist was Inge Lehmann, and she had found the Earth's inner core.
Lehmann was born in Copenhagen in 1888. She attended an unusual school for its time, where girls and boys were taught the same subjects and expected to meet the same standards. She later said this experience shaped her belief that she could succeed in any field. She went on to study mathematics in Copenhagen and in Cambridge, England, although illness and other interruptions meant her studies stretched over many years.
Her path to earthquakes was not direct. For a time she worked calculating figures for an insurance company. Then, in the 1920s, she became an assistant to a scientist who was setting up earthquake-recording stations in Denmark and Greenland. Lehmann discovered that she loved the work. In 1928 she was put in charge of the seismology department at Denmark's new national geodetic institute, a post she held until 1953.
Seismology is the study of earthquakes and the waves they send through the Earth. When a large earthquake strikes, instruments called seismographs around the world record its waves. Because these waves change speed and direction as they pass through different materials, they act like messengers, carrying clues about the Earth's hidden layers.
At the time, scientists believed the Earth had a solid mantle surrounding a liquid core. A liquid core should bend certain waves so that they never reached a particular band of places on the far side of the planet, known as the shadow zone. Yet when Lehmann studied records from a powerful 1929 earthquake in New Zealand, she noticed faint waves arriving inside that zone, where none should have been.
Many people might have dismissed these signals as errors. Lehmann did not. She collected and compared readings from stations across the globe, recording them by hand on cardboard cards that she famously stored in old oatmeal boxes. Slowly she built a careful argument: the waves could be explained if there was a solid inner core inside the liquid one, bouncing some waves back towards the surface.
Other leading scientists soon agreed that her explanation fitted the evidence, and decades later, more sensitive instruments and computers confirmed it. Lehmann kept working long after she officially retired, studying the upper mantle and travelling to research centres overseas. In 1971 she became the first woman to receive a major American medal for geophysics.
Inge Lehmann died in 1993, at the age of 104. She never saw the inner core, and no one ever will; it lies more than 5000 kilometres beneath our feet. But by listening patiently to the whispers of distant earthquakes, she revealed a world that had been hidden since the planet formed.

The Boots in Box Fourteen
Mira had agreed to volunteer at the Wattle Creek District Museum for one reason only: her school required twenty hours of community service, and the museum was a five-minute walk from home. On her first morning, she stood inside the old bank building that housed the collection and tried not to sigh. Glass cases lined the walls, crowded with flat irons, faded photographs and farm tools whose purposes she could only guess.
'Everything in here is just old,' she muttered.
Mr Okafor, the volunteer curator, overheard and smiled. 'Old is the easy part,' he said. 'Each of the objects on these shelves has a number, a date and a label. What most of them are missing is a reason for anyone to care.'
He led her to a back room stacked with cardboard boxes. 'These were donated over the years and never properly catalogued. Your job is to record every item: measure it, describe it and write down anything we know.'
Box fourteen held a pair of child's leather boots, cracked across the toes and resoled at least twice. A tag on one lace read only: Boots, child's, c. 1930s. Mira measured them, photographed them and typed the details into the spreadsheet. Then she moved on to a chipped teapot, satisfied that she had done her job.
That afternoon an elderly man came through the front door, leaning on a walking stick. He explained that his late sister had donated some family things years ago and he had always wondered what became of them. Mr Okafor glanced at Mira. 'Box fourteen, I think,' he said quietly.
When Mira carried out the boots, the man went very still. He reached out and touched the patched sole with one finger.
'These were mine,' he said, 'and my brother's before me, and our cousin's before that. Dad fixed them on the kitchen table with leather from an old saddle. I walked three miles to school in these, rain or shine, and I was so proud, because they were the first boots that ever fitted me.' He laughed softly. 'Mum used to say they'd walked further than the mail coach.'
Mira found herself writing furiously on the back of a catalogue sheet. She asked how old he had been, where the school was and what his father did for work. He answered every question and stayed for nearly an hour.
After he left, she sat looking at the boots for a long time. That morning they had been a measurement and a date. Now they seemed to hold an entire family: the hand-me-downs, the long walks, a father working late by lamplight.
'Mr Okafor,' she said, 'can I write a new label for these?'
He handed her a fresh card without a word, though his eyes were bright.
By the end of the holidays Mira had completed far more than twenty hours. She had also started a project of her own: a folder titled Ask Before It's Gone, filled with notes from visitors who recognised something on the shelves.

Option A: recording the details of donated items
Option B: cleaning the glass display cases
Option C: guiding visitors around the museum
Option D: writing new labels for the farm tools

Lines Across the Sky
On a clear day, look up and you may see a thin white line stretching behind a high-flying jet. Sometimes the line fades almost as soon as it appears. At other times it lingers for an hour or more, slowly widening until it looks like a natural wisp of cloud. These lines are called contrails, short for condensation trails, and they are a kind of cloud made by aircraft.
To understand how contrails form, think about your own breath on a cold winter morning. The air you breathe out is warm and contains water vapour. When it meets the cold air outside, the vapour cools rapidly and condenses into tiny droplets, forming a small cloud in front of your face.
A jet engine does something similar on a much larger scale. Burning fuel produces hot exhaust that contains water vapour, along with tiny particles of soot. Passenger jets usually cruise about ten to twelve kilometres above the ground, where the air is often colder than minus 40 degrees Celsius. When the hot, moist exhaust meets this frigid air, the water vapour condenses onto the soot particles and freezes into ice crystals. The result is a trail of ice that can be seen from the ground.
Why do some contrails vanish while others remain? The answer depends on the air the plane is flying through. If that air is dry, the ice crystals soon turn back into invisible vapour, and the trail disappears within seconds or minutes. If the air is already very humid, however, the crystals do not shrink. Instead, they can grow by collecting more moisture from their surroundings, and the contrail may spread across the sky.
For this reason, some people have long treated persistent contrails as a rough weather sign. Because long-lasting trails show that the upper air is moist, they sometimes appear before a change in the weather. This is not a reliable forecast on its own, but it shows that contrails are linked to real conditions high above us.
In recent years, scientists have become interested in contrails for another reason. Spreading contrails behave much like thin, high clouds. During the day they reflect some sunlight back into space, but they also trap heat that would otherwise escape from the Earth, especially at night. Researchers estimate that, overall, these artificial clouds add noticeably to the warming effect of air travel.
The encouraging news is that most long-lasting trails form in fairly small patches of very humid air. If pilots could avoid those patches, perhaps by flying a little higher or lower, many such contrails might never form. Early trials using weather data and computer predictions have produced promising results, although more research is needed to make sure the changes do not cause planes to burn too much extra fuel.
So the next time you spot a white line across the blue, remember that it is more than a pretty pattern. It is a small window into the science of the atmosphere, and a puzzle that scientists and airlines are still working to solve.

Option A: contrast trail
Option B: control rail
Option C: condensation trail
Option D: continuous trail

Silence Made of Sound
Step onto a long-distance flight and you will notice that many passengers are wearing large, cushioned headphones, even when they are not listening to anything. They are using a trick that sounds impossible: they are blocking out noise by adding more sound.
To understand how this works, it helps to remember what sound is. When an engine roars or a person speaks, it pushes and pulls on the air, creating a pattern of high-pressure and low-pressure regions that ripple outwards. Scientists draw this pattern as a wave, with peaks for the high-pressure regions and troughs for the low-pressure ones. When the wave reaches your ear, it makes your eardrum vibrate, and your brain interprets the vibration as sound.
Now imagine two sound waves arriving at the same place at the same moment. If their peaks line up, they combine into a bigger wave and the sound becomes louder. But if the peaks of one wave line up exactly with the troughs of the other, the two cancel each other out. Physicists call this destructive interference. The air pressure stays almost level, and the ear hears very little.
Noise-cancelling headphones put this idea to work. Tiny microphones on each ear cup constantly listen to the noise around you. A small computer chip analyses the sound and, in a tiny fraction of a second, produces a matching wave that is flipped upside down. This “anti-noise” is played through the speakers along with your music. When the anti-noise meets the incoming noise inside the ear cup, much of the noise disappears.
The idea is not new. A German physicist named Paul Lueg patented a method in the 1930s, but the electronics of his day were far too slow and bulky to make it practical. It was not until the late twentieth century that engineers produced headsets for helicopter and aircraft pilots, whose working days were filled with deafening engine drone. Models for the public followed and have since become common.
Yet the technology has limits. It works best on low, steady sounds such as the hum of an engine, the whir of an air conditioner or the rumble of a train. These sounds repeat in a predictable pattern, so the chip has time to match them. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, such as a baby’s cry or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, because they change too quickly. For these, headphones rely on old-fashioned methods: thick padding and a snug seal that physically stop sound from getting in.
Some people also notice a strange feeling of pressure in their ears when they first switch the feature on, a little like being in a plane as it descends, even though nothing has changed in the air around them.
For travellers, the benefit is real. Because the background roar is reduced, listeners do not need to turn their music up as loudly to hear it clearly, which helps protect their hearing over a long journey. A device that fights sound with sound may well be one of the quietest inventions of all.

But if the peaks of one wave line up exactly with the troughs of the other, the two cancel each other out. Physicists call this destructive interference. The air pressure stays almost level, and the ear hears very little.
Noise-cancelling headphones put this idea to work. Tiny microphones on each ear cup constantly listen to the noise around you. A small computer chip analyses the sound and, in a tiny fraction of a second, produces a matching wave that is flipped upside down. This “anti-noise” is played through the speakers along with your music. When the anti-noise meets the incoming noise inside the ear cup, much of the noise disappears.
The idea is not new. A German physicist named Paul Lueg patented a method in the 1930s, but the electronics of his day were far too slow and bulky to make it practical. It was not until the late twentieth century that engineers produced headsets for helicopter and aircraft pilots, whose working days were filled with deafening engine drone. Models for the public followed and have since become common.
Yet the technology has limits. It works best on low, steady sounds such as the hum of an engine, the whir of an air conditioner or the rumble of a train. These sounds repeat in a predictable pattern, so the chip has time to match them. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, such as a baby’s cry or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, because they change too quickly. For these, headphones rely on old-fashioned methods: thick padding and a snug seal that physically stop sound from getting in.
Some people also notice a strange feeling of pressure in their ears when they first switch the feature on, a little like being in a plane as it descends, even though nothing has changed in the air around them.
For travellers, the benefit is real. Because the background roar is reduced, listeners do not need to turn their music up as loudly to hear it clearly, which helps protect their hearing over a long journey. A device that fights sound with sound may well be one of the quietest inventions of all.

Stars Across the River
Wednesday 4 July
Dear Diary,
Three weeks into my exchange and I still can't use chopsticks without dropping half my rice. Mrs Sato, my host mother, just laughs and hands me a spoon, which is kind but slightly humiliating. Tonight at dinner, Yui (my host sister, who is twelve and far more patient than I deserve) told me about a festival on Saturday called Tanabata. She said it comes from a very old legend, and when I asked her to explain, she grabbed a pencil and drew it on a napkin.
Here is the story as best I understood it. Long ago, a princess named Orihime wove beautiful cloth beside the River of Heaven, which is what people here call the Milky Way. Her father, the king of the sky, worried that she was lonely, so he introduced her to Hikoboshi, a young man who herded cattle on the other side of the river. They fell in love at once. The trouble was that they were so happy together that Orihime stopped weaving and Hikoboshi let his cattle wander all over the sky. Furious, the king separated them, one on each bank of the river. Orihime cried so much that he finally agreed they could meet once a year, on the seventh day of the seventh month.
Yui says the two lovers are really stars, Vega and Altair, and that you can see them on either side of the Milky Way in summer. It is summer here now, which still feels completely backwards to me.
Saturday 7 July
Today the whole street was decorated with long paper streamers in every colour imaginable. People write wishes on small strips of paper called tanzaku and tie them to bamboo branches. I wrote mine slowly, checking each character three times with Yui's help: 'I hope my family is well.' It is short, but it took me ten minutes.
In the evening it started to drizzle, and Yui looked genuinely upset. According to the legend, if it rains on Tanabata, the river rises and the lovers cannot cross, so they must wait another whole year. I tried to cheer her up by saying the clouds might clear, though honestly I was just guessing.
Then, around nine o'clock, the rain stopped. Mr Sato switched off the porch light, and the four of us lay on a picnic rug in the back garden, staring up. Yui pointed out Vega, bright and bluish, and then Altair on the other side of a pale, smudgy band of stars. I couldn't quite believe it. People have been looking at those same two stars and telling this story for well over a thousand years.
Lying there, I thought about Mum, Dad and my little brother, Sam, thousands of kilometres away, probably finishing dinner under a winter sky. It is strange, but I didn't feel homesick the way I did in my first week. It felt more as though there was a river between us, wide but crossable, and that soon enough I would reach the other side.
When we went inside, Mrs Sato made hot chocolate. I even managed the mugs without spilling.

Option A: a family holiday spent watching the stars in Australia
Option B: a student learning to cook Japanese food with her host
Option C: an exchange student learning about and celebrating Tanabata
Option D: a girl inventing a new legend about the Milky Way

Her father, the king of the sky, worried that she was lonely, so he introduced her to Hikoboshi, a young man who herded cattle on the other side of the river. They fell in love at once. The trouble was that they were so happy together that Orihime stopped weaving and Hikoboshi let his cattle wander all over the sky. Furious, the king separated them, one on each bank of the river. Orihime cried so much that he finally agreed they could meet once a year, on the seventh day of the seventh month.

The Water Comes to Kalgoorlie
Every morning for as long as Nell could remember, the day in Kalgoorlie had begun with the same sound: the creak of Mr Hasluck’s water cart and the clank of his measuring tin. Water on the goldfields came from condensers that boiled salty ground water and collected the steam, and it was sold by the gallon. Nell’s mother counted the coins for it as carefully as she counted anything. Washing water was used twice, first for clothes and then for the floor, and the little garden behind the boarding house had long since turned to red dust.
But on the morning of 24 January 1903, Nell woke before the cart arrived, because today the water was coming by itself.
For five years, her father had talked of almost nothing else. He had spent two of those years laying pipe in the heat, steel sections as wide as a barrel, joined end to end across scrub and salt lake. Far to the west, in the hills behind Perth, a great dam wall held back a lake, and eight pumping stations along the line would push its water uphill and onward, more than five hundred kilometres to the goldfields.
“Nobody believed it could be done,” he said at breakfast, which was what he said every morning. “They called it madness.”
“And now?” Nell asked, which was what she asked every morning.
“Now we’ll see.”
By ten o’clock the streets were crowded. Miners had come in from the leases still wearing their work boots, women carried parasols against the glare, and children perched on verandah rails. Nell and her younger brother Tom squeezed to the front near the reservoir at Mount Charlotte, where men in dark suits stood on a platform decorated with flags.
The speeches went on for a long time. Tom fidgeted and asked whether the water had got lost. Then Sir John Forrest stepped forward and turned a large valve, and a cheer rolled across the hill like thunder. Nell could not see the water at first, only men waving their hats. Then she heard it: a rushing, gurgling roar.
Afterwards, there were celebrations all over town. Someone opened a standpipe in Hannan Street and the children took turns standing under the spray, gasping and laughing. Nell held out her hands and let the water run between her fingers. It was cool and soft and smelled of nothing at all.
That evening her father was quiet. He sat on the back step looking at the dusty garden. “Mr O’Connor should have been here today,” he said at last. Nell knew the name; the engineer had planned the whole scheme but had not lived to see it finished. She sat beside her father and said nothing.
The next morning, Nell went out with a bucket before breakfast. She did not wait for the creak of the cart. She filled the bucket from the new tap by the gate, carried it to the garden and poured it slowly over the hard ground, watching the red earth turn dark. Then she went back and filled it again.
Question: In “Nell woke before the cart arrived, because today the water was coming by itself”, the word “because” introduces . . .
Option A: a contrast
Option B: a time
Option C: a result
Option D: a reason

The Count at Dawn
The alarm went off at half past four, and Leila seriously considered pretending she hadn't heard it. Instead she dragged on two jumpers and stumbled out to the ute, where Aunt Ros was waiting with a thermos and a clipboard.
'You'll thank me later,' Ros said.
Leila doubted it.
They drove for forty minutes along dirt tracks through the river red gums, the headlights catching the eyes of kangaroos. Leila checked her phone. No signal. She checked it again five minutes later, just in case.
Aunt Ros was a wetland ecologist, and once a month she counted the waterbirds at Boorna Lagoon, a backwater on the Murray River floodplain. For most of Leila's life, Ros explained, the lagoon had been little more than a cracked grey hollow, because the river had not flooded high enough to reach it. Then, last spring, water managers had released a planned flow from upstream dams, and for the first time in almost a decade the lagoon had filled.
'Red gums can survive dry spells,' Ros said, 'but they need a good drink now and then. So do the frogs, the fish, the insects. Floods are how a wetland breathes.'
When they arrived, the sky was turning from black to deep blue. Leila climbed out and was hit by the smell of mud, rotting leaves and something faintly fishy. 'Gross,' she muttered.
Ros simply handed her binoculars and a small metal clicker. 'Every time you see a bird I point to, click once. Don't talk. Just watch.'
At first Leila saw nothing but grey water and grey trees. Then the light grew, and the lagoon seemed to wake up around her. A pair of black swans drifted out from the reeds. A white heron stood so still on one leg that she had mistaken it for a dead branch. Ros murmured names, pelican, darter, spoonbill, and Leila clicked, and clicked again, until her thumb ached.
The frogs were the loudest surprise. Hundreds of them filled the air with a racket like a crowd of tiny engines that never needed to stop.
Near the reeds, something small caught Leila's eye. A neat brown waterbird, no bigger than a teapot, was paddling slowly across the water. On its back, peeking out between the feathers, were three striped chicks.
Leila forgot the rule about talking. 'Aunt Ros. Look.'
Ros raised her binoculars and was silent for a long moment. When she lowered them, Leila was startled to see her blinking hard.
'Australasian grebe,' Ros said quietly. 'With chicks. Nobody has recorded them breeding here since before you started school.'
She wrote something on the clipboard, then hesitated and passed it across. 'You found them. You write it down.'
Leila's handwriting was wobbly from the cold, but she filled in every box carefully: species, number, behaviour, time.
On the drive home, her phone buzzed back to life as they reached the highway. Seventeen notifications. Leila glanced at the screen, then turned it face down on her knee and kept looking out at the trees.

Option A: a scientist who builds new dams along the Murray River
Option B: a girl who comes to appreciate a wetland during a bird survey
Option C: a family camping trip that is spoiled by bad weather
Option D: a girl who loses her phone while visiting a lagoon

She has dyslexia, and reading did not come easily at school. Yet when she was still in primary school, her mother read aloud the story of Jesse Martin, a young Australian who had sailed solo around the globe. Jessica was captivated, and the idea of her own voyage was never far from her mind.
She spent the next few years preparing. She gained her sailing qualifications, sailed offshore with experienced crews and helped refit a second-hand yacht, a sturdy ten-metre boat painted bright pink and named Ella's Pink Lady. After the collision, critics said the accident proved she was not ready. Jessica's response was to repair the boat, study what had gone wrong and keep going.
On 18 October 2009, she sailed out through Sydney Heads. Her plan was to travel non-stop and unassisted, which meant she could not enter a port or accept supplies from anyone. She would cross the Pacific, round Cape Horn at the tip of South America, push across the South Atlantic and the Indian Ocean, and finally sail south of Australia back to Sydney.
Life aboard was a mix of routine and risk. She slept in short bursts, checked the weather constantly and kept in touch with her family by satellite phone. Thousands of followers read her online blog. The Southern Ocean tested her most. In towering seas, the yacht was knocked flat several times, its mast pressed down towards the water. Because of her age, and debate about whether her route covered enough distance, record-keeping bodies did not list the voyage as an official world record. Jessica seemed unbothered. Stepping onto the dock, she told the crowd she did not consider herself a hero, just an ordinary girl who had believed in her dream.

Option D: 18 October 2009

Six Weeks to Opening Night
When the Riverbend Youth Orchestra walks onstage for its winter concert, the audience sees eighty young musicians dressed in black, sitting perfectly still before the first note. What the audience does not see is the six-week process that gets them there. This report follows the orchestra through its preparation and explains the methods its conductor, Daniela Ruiz, uses at each stage.
Weeks one and two: sectionals
At the start, the orchestra rarely plays together. Instead, musicians rehearse in sectionals, small groups made up of a single family of instruments, such as the brass or the woodwinds. Each sectional is led by a senior player, who breaks difficult passages into fragments of two or three bars. 'If you can't play it slowly, you can't play it fast,' says Ms Ruiz. Players use a metronome, a device that clicks a steady beat, starting well below the final tempo and raising it a few beats per minute each session.
Weeks three and four: full rehearsals
Once the sections are secure, the whole orchestra combines. This is often when problems appear. A passage that sounded clean in a small room can turn muddy when eighty instruments play at once. Ms Ruiz uses a technique she calls 'swap and listen'. For ten minutes, players change seats so that, for example, a violinist sits among the trombones. 'Most musicians only ever hear the people beside them,' she explains. 'When they hear the piece from another part of the room, they finally understand how their line fits.'
During this stage, she also records every rehearsal. Players are asked to listen to the recording at home and note one moment where their section was ahead of or behind the beat.
Week five: the run-through
In week five, the orchestra plays the entire program from start to finish without stopping, even if something goes wrong. Thirteen-year-old percussionist Tom Nguyen admits this was hard at first. 'Every instinct tells you to stop and fix it,' he says. 'But in a concert, there's no going back. You have to recover and keep counting.'
Week six: the dress rehearsal
The final rehearsal takes place in the concert hall itself, with lighting, seating and stage positions exactly as they will be on the night. Ms Ruiz invites a small audience of family members. Players also practise walking on and off stage, tuning to the oboe's note and bowing together.
On the night
By opening night, most of the work is done. Ms Ruiz's last instruction is always the same: 'Stop thinking about the notes and start listening to each other.' She believes that if the preparation has been careful, the musicians can trust it.
The orchestra's approach is not unusual among youth ensembles, but it reveals something many audiences overlook. A smooth performance is rarely the result of talent alone. It is built, piece by piece, from slow practice, honest listening and many small corrections.

Option A: as a full orchestra in the concert hall
Option B: alone at home with rehearsal recordings
Option C: in front of a small audience of families
Option D: in small groups of one instrument family
