The Grey Rope
The water of the bay was so flat that morning that Jai could see the reflection of every gull. He and his grandfather had pushed the little aluminium boat off the ramp just after six, the outboard motor puttering, and now they sat a kilometre offshore with their lines in the water, waiting for whiting.
“Glassy,” Grandad said approvingly. “Nothing like an autumn morning.”
Jai agreed, though he would have preferred a fish. For an hour the only thing that moved was the sun, climbing over the headland and turning the water silver. Then, slowly, the light began to change.
It was Grandad who noticed first. He set down his rod and looked out to the south-east, where a line of clouds had been gathering over the open sea. They were not the soft white puffs of earlier; their bases were flat and dark, almost purple, and they seemed to sag towards the water.
“Reel in,” Grandad said.
“But I think I’ve got a—”
“Reel in, Jai.”
Something in his voice made Jai obey without arguing. As he wound in his line, he followed Grandad’s gaze. Beneath the darkest cloud, a thin grey finger was reaching down, wavering like a thread of smoke. Below it, on the surface of the sea, a patch of water had begun to churn, throwing up a ring of spray.
“Is that a—”
“Waterspout,” said Grandad. He was already tugging the cord of the motor. “Probably a fair-weather one. They’re usually weak. But I’m not sitting here to find out.”
The motor coughed, caught, and the boat swung round towards the ramp. Jai twisted in his seat to watch. The finger had become a rope now, joining cloud to sea, and it was moving, though it was hard to tell which way. The ring of spray at its base glittered in the sunlight. It looked almost graceful, like a dancer slowly turning. Jai realised his heart was thumping.
They were halfway to shore when the wind arrived, a sudden cold gust that flicked up whitecaps and sent Grandad’s hat tumbling into the bottom of the boat. Rain followed, hard and stinging, then stopped as quickly as it had started. When Jai looked back again, the rope was thinning. It stretched, bent, and then simply came apart.
By the time they reached the ramp, the sky over the bay was breaking into blue patches. A man launching a jet ski called out, “Did you see that thing?”
“We saw it,” said Grandad. He was smiling now, but Jai noticed that his hands were not quite steady as he winched the boat onto the trailer.
On the drive home, Jai asked why they had left if the waterspout was probably weak.
Grandad kept his eyes on the road. “Probably,” he said, “is a word for people on land.”
That afternoon, Jai looked up waterspouts at the library. He learned that fair-weather spouts often form on calm, warm days beneath growing clouds, and that most last only a few minutes. He also learned that you cannot always tell, from a distance, what kind you are looking at. He thought about the grey rope turning on the silver water, and about his grandfather’s steady voice and unsteady hands.
Question: In which direction did Grandad see clouds gathering?
Option A: to the north-west
Option B: over the headland
Option C: above the boat ramp
Option D: to the south-east

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
Fruit Trees That Grow Flat
Walk through an old walled garden in England or France and you may see something that looks more like a piece of furniture than a tree. Pressed against a sunny brick wall, a pear tree spreads its branches in perfectly straight horizontal lines, like the rungs of a ladder laid on its side. Another tree nearby fans out from a short trunk like the fingers of an open hand. These trees have not grown this way by accident. They are espaliers, plants trained over many years to grow flat.
The word “espalier” comes from French, and it originally referred to the framework or trellis that supports the plant rather than the plant itself. The practice, however, is far older than the word. Ancient Egyptian tomb paintings show fig trees grown in flat shapes, and the Romans trained plants along walls. The technique became especially popular in Europe during the Middle Ages, when monasteries and castles grew fruit within high stone walls.
Gardeners had good reasons for going to so much trouble. Space inside a walled enclosure was precious, and a tree pressed flat against the wall took up only a narrow strip of ground. More importantly, the wall itself changed the climate. In northern Europe, summers are often too short and cool to ripen fruit such as peaches, apricots and pears. A south-facing brick or stone wall soaks up the sun’s heat during the day and slowly releases it at night, keeping the branches pressed against it several degrees warmer. It also shelters them from cold winds. Some later gardens even had hollow walls with fires lit inside them to protect blossoms from frost.
Creating an espalier requires patience. The gardener usually begins with a young, unbranched tree, called a whip, and cuts it back to just above a set of buds. As new shoots grow, the strongest are tied gently to wires or canes in the desired direction, and the rest are removed. Each year the process continues, with summer pruning to control growth and to encourage short, fruit-bearing stems called spurs. A well-formed espalier can take five years or more to reach its full shape, and it needs regular care for the rest of its life.
The patterns have names. A cordon is a single stem, sometimes grown at an angle. A fan spreads out from a low point. A Belgian fence is made of several trees planted in a row, their branches crossing to form a diamond lattice.
Espaliers are now enjoying a revival, particularly in cities. Many people with small courtyards or narrow side passages have discovered that a flat apple or citrus tree can produce a surprising amount of fruit while taking up little more room than a fence. In this way, a method perfected in monastery gardens is helping apartment dwellers grow their own food.
Question: From which language does the word “espalier” come?
Option A: Latin
Option B: Egyptian
Option C: English
Option D: French

A south-facing brick or stone wall soaks up the sun’s heat during the day and slowly releases it at night, keeping the branches pressed against it several degrees warmer. It also shelters them from cold winds. Some later gardens even had hollow walls with fires lit inside them to protect blossoms from frost.
Creating an espalier requires patience. The gardener usually begins with a young, unbranched tree, called a whip, and cuts it back to just above a set of buds. As new shoots grow, the strongest are tied gently to wires or canes in the desired direction, and the rest are removed. Each year the process continues, with summer pruning to control growth and to encourage short, fruit-bearing stems called spurs. A well-formed espalier can take five years or more to reach its full shape, and it needs regular care for the rest of its life.
The patterns have names. A cordon is a single stem, sometimes grown at an angle. A fan spreads out from a low point. A Belgian fence is made of several trees planted in a row, their branches crossing to form a diamond lattice.

Painted by Time
In many of the world’s deserts, travellers notice that rocks seem to come in two colours. Freshly broken stone may be pale grey, cream or orange, while surfaces that have faced the sky for centuries are coated in a glossy layer of dark brown or black. From a distance, whole cliffs look as though someone has poured paint over them. This coating is called desert varnish, or rock varnish, and it is one of the slowest-forming natural materials on Earth.
Desert varnish is astonishingly thin, usually less than the thickness of a human hair. Under a microscope, it turns out to be made mostly of clay minerals, cemented together with oxides of manganese and iron. Iron oxides give it a reddish-brown tint, while manganese makes it black. What is puzzling is the amount of manganese. In the varnish it can be many times more concentrated than in the surrounding dust and soil. Something must be gathering it.
Exactly what that something is has been argued about for more than a century. One group of scientists believes the answer is biological. They point out that certain bacteria and fungi living on rock surfaces can take manganese from their surroundings and deposit it in solid form. Over thousands of years, these tiny organisms might build up a coating, layer by layer. Another group argues that the process is mainly chemical. In their view, dew and occasional rain dissolve minerals from windblown dust and leave them behind as the moisture evaporates, with no living things needed. A newer suggestion is that sunlight triggers chemical reactions on the rock surface. Many researchers now suspect that more than one of these processes may be involved.
Whatever its cause, the varnish grows extremely slowly. Estimates suggest that a layer may thicken by only a few thousandths of a millimetre in a thousand years. For this reason, a dark, glossy surface is a sign that a rock has lain undisturbed for a very long time.
People noticed desert varnish long before scientists did. In places such as the south-west of the United States and Murujuga in Western Australia, artists created images by chipping or scraping through the dark coating to reveal the paler rock beneath. The result is a striking contrast, like a drawing in white chalk on a blackboard. Murujuga holds one of the largest collections of rock engravings in the world, with figures of animals, people and patterns.
Because the varnish slowly creeps back over a scratched surface, the colour of an engraving can offer clues about its age. A freshly made carving appears bright; one made long ago gradually darkens until it almost matches the rock around it. Scientists have tried to use the thickness and chemistry of regrown varnish to date ancient engravings, although the method is still debated.
Desert varnish is a reminder that in the driest places on Earth, change still happens. It simply happens so slowly that a human lifetime is far too short to notice it.

Option A: to reveal the pale rock beneath and make a clear image
Option B: to collect the manganese for making black paint
Option C: to find out how old the rocks really were
Option D: to remove the varnish so the rock would stay clean

Notes in the Margins
The first note was written in pencil, so faintly that Ava almost missed it. It sat in the margin of page forty-seven of a battered mystery novel she had borrowed from the Hollis Street Library: 'Don't trust the gardener.'
Ava frowned. Writing in library books was against the rules; the sign above the returns chute said so in large red letters. Still, she kept reading, and by chapter twelve the gardener had turned out to be the thief.
On the last page, she found a second note in the same spidery handwriting: 'If you liked this, try the blue one on the bottom shelf near the window.'
Ava had not planned to go back to the library so soon. Since moving to the town in January, she had spent most afternoons alone in her room, telling her mother she was fine and telling herself the same thing. But the next Saturday she found herself kneeling by the window, running a finger along the bottom shelf until she reached a faded blue spine. Inside, on the very first page, was the same handwriting: 'Welcome back.'
After that, it became a kind of game. Each book contained a recommendation for the next, and the notes grew longer. Some were jokes. Some were questions: 'Would you have opened the door?' One simply said, 'This chapter made me cry on a bus. Sorry about the tear stain.'
Ava began to answer. She wrote tiny replies beneath the notes in her neatest pencil, always careful to keep them light enough to rub out. 'I would NOT have opened the door.' 'The ending was unfair.' 'Who are you?'
That last question received no answer. The next book contained only a recommendation, as if she had never asked.
Ava decided to find out for herself. She spent a whole Saturday at a table near the window, pretending to read while watching the bottom shelf. People came and went: a teenager with headphones, a mother with twins, an old man who fell asleep over a newspaper. Nobody touched the blue books.
At closing time, the librarian, Mr Osei, came to switch off the lamps. He glanced at the novel in Ava's hands, then at the pencil behind her ear, and smiled.
'You know,' he said, 'writing in library books is strictly against the rules.'
Ava's face went hot. 'I always rub it out,' she began, and then she stopped, because Mr Osei had taken a pencil from his own pocket. It was the short, chewed kind, and as he tapped it absent-mindedly on the desk, Ava noticed the faint grey smudge on the side of his thumb.
He did not explain, and she did not ask. He simply handed her a book from the returns trolley.
'Bottom shelf, near the window,' he said. 'I hear it's good.'
That evening, Ava sat on her bed and opened the cover. On the first page, in spidery pencil, someone had written: 'You found the shelf. Now find the reading club. Thursdays, 4 pm. We could use someone who doesn't open doors.'
Ava laughed out loud. Then she went to tell her mother she would be home late on Thursday.
Question: On which page of the mystery novel did Ava find the first note?
Option A: page forty-seven
Option B: the first page
Option C: the last page
Option D: page twelve

The Long Way Round
When Leo was told he would spend his Year 9 community-service day with Meals on Wheels, he groaned. His friends had scored the animal shelter and the local radio station. He had scored a white van, forty-two foil-covered trays and Mrs Pillay.
Mrs Pillay was seventy-one, wore a bright orange vest and drove like someone who had memorised every pothole in town. 'We deliver to twenty-three people today,' she said, handing him a clipboard. 'Your job is to read me the names and carry the trays. My job is everything else.'
The first few stops went quickly. Leo knocked, handed over a tray, said 'Enjoy your lunch' and jogged back to the van. By the fifth stop he had decided the job was simple, slightly boring and could probably be done by a drone.
Then he noticed that Mrs Pillay was not hurrying.
At every house she lingered. She asked Mr Fraser whether his new glasses were helping. She reminded Mrs Liang that her daughter was visiting on Sunday. At one cottage she stepped inside to check the date on a carton of milk, then quietly poured it down the sink and wrote something on her notepad.
'We're running late,' Leo said as they pulled away from the ninth house.
'We're running exactly on time,' said Mrs Pillay. 'The meal is only part of the delivery.'
Leo didn't understand what she meant until the fourteenth stop, a small brick unit where the curtains were still drawn at midday. Mrs Pillay knocked twice. No answer. She checked the clipboard — Mr Bertram Hale, aged eighty-eight — and knocked again, louder.
Somewhere inside, a faint voice called out.
Mrs Pillay moved faster than Leo had thought possible. She took a key from a small lockbox by the door (it was there, she explained later, for exactly this reason) and found Mr Hale sitting on the bathroom floor. He had slipped that morning and had not been able to stand. He wasn't badly hurt, just cold, embarrassed and very thirsty.
Leo fetched a glass of water while Mrs Pillay phoned for help and wrapped a blanket around Mr Hale's shoulders. When the paramedics arrived, one of them nodded at her like an old colleague. 'Second time this year, Usha,' he said. 'Good catch.'
They finished the round two hours late. Nobody complained. At several houses, people had already heard what had happened and asked after Mr Hale before they asked about lunch.
Back at the depot, Leo handed in the clipboard. Beside each name, Mrs Pillay had written small notes: needs new smoke-alarm battery; lonely — call Friday; daughter visiting Sunday.
'You check on them all,' Leo said slowly. 'Every single one.'
Mrs Pillay unbuttoned her orange vest. 'For some people, we're the only visitor they get all day,' she said. 'That's not a small thing.'
The next week, his friends talked about puppies and microphones. When they asked about his day, Leo surprised himself. He told them he had signed up to go back in the school holidays.
Question: In 'then quietly poured it down the sink', the word quietly is . . .
Option A: an adverb
Option B: an adjective
Option C: a verb
Option D: a noun

The Case for a Shared Room
When families talk about moving house, one question often comes up before any other: will everyone get their own bedroom? For many parents, a separate room for every child has become a sign of success, and for many children it feels like a basic right. I want to argue that something valuable is lost when brothers and sisters never share a room, and that families who have the choice should think twice before giving it up.
Consider first what sharing teaches. A child who shares a room must learn to negotiate. Who gets the bed by the window? How late can the reading light stay on? What happens when one person wants to practise the recorder and the other wants quiet? These are not small questions to a ten-year-old, and working them out — without a parent stepping in every time — is practice for every future flatmate, workmate and partner. Learning to compromise in a space that measures four metres by three may be harder than learning it in a classroom, but it is also more lasting.
Second, a shared room builds closeness. Many adults look back fondly on the late-night conversations they had with a brother or sister after the light was switched off. Fears are confessed, jokes are repeated until they stop being funny, and plans are hatched. Researchers point out that the relationship between siblings is often the longest of a person’s life, outlasting those with parents and, frequently, with friends. Time spent side by side in childhood is an investment in that relationship.
There are practical benefits too. A family that does not need an extra bedroom can live in a smaller, cheaper home, or use a spare room as a study, a play space or a place for visiting grandparents. Smaller homes also cost less to heat and cool.
Of course, sharing is not always easy, and I am not suggesting it suits every family. A teenager studying for exams may need quiet, and children who are very far apart in age may have little in common. Privacy matters, especially as children grow. But these problems can often be solved with thoughtful arrangements: a curtain or bookshelf to divide the room, agreed quiet hours, and a drawer or shelf that belongs to one person alone and is never touched by the other.
In many parts of the world, and for most of history, children sharing a room — or even a bed — has been completely normal. The idea that every child needs a private space is quite recent, and it is worth asking whether it has truly made us happier.
So before your family decides that a separate room for every child is essential, consider what might be gained by sharing. The squabbles over the bed by the window will soon be forgotten. The friendship built in the dark is likely to last a lifetime.

The Eleven-Day Flight
Every year in late September, birdwatchers on the mudflats of northern Australia and New Zealand scan the sky for a long-legged, mottled brown shorebird with a slightly upturned bill. When the first bar-tailed godwits appear, many have just completed one of the most remarkable journeys in the animal kingdom: a non-stop flight across the Pacific Ocean from Alaska.
Godwits breed on the Alaskan tundra during the brief northern summer. There, they nest on the ground and raise their chicks among low shrubs and grasses. As the season ends, adults and young move to coastal estuaries, where they eat almost constantly. They probe the soft mud with their long bills, pulling out worms, clams and tiny crustaceans. Within a few weeks, a godwit can nearly double its body weight, and more than half of that weight may be fat.
At the same time, something surprising happens inside the bird. Its gizzard, liver and intestines shrink, while its heart and flight muscles grow larger. The godwit is preparing for a journey on which it will not eat, drink or land. There is no point carrying a full-sized kitchen on a trip with no meals.
Departure is not random. Godwits wait for weather systems that will give them a strong tailwind for the first part of the trip. Researchers who fit the birds with tiny satellite transmitters have found that most leave within a short window, often just as a storm passes. In 2022, a young godwit tagged in Alaska flew about 13,500 kilometres to Tasmania in roughly eleven days, the longest non-stop bird flight ever recorded. Two Flashes Every Ten
The wind dropped just as the sun slid behind the headland, and the Kittiwake slowed to a lazy drift. Mia watched the sails sag and sighed. They were still six nautical miles from the harbour mouth, and Grandad had promised Mum they would be home before dark.
'No matter,' said Grandad, rolling up the sails. 'We'll motor in.' The little engine coughed into life, and the boat began to push forward again.
Mia settled beside the chartplotter, the glowing screen that showed their boat as a tiny arrow crawling across a map of the bay. She had used it all afternoon. All she had to do was keep the arrow on the dotted line.
Ten minutes later, Grandad ducked below to fetch his jumper. Mia heard him rummaging under the chart table, then a soft click. Moments later, the screen went black.
She tapped it. She pressed every button. Nothing. 'Grandad, it's dead!'
'Is it now?' He didn't sound especially worried. He reached into a locker and handed her a folded paper chart, a pencil and a small compass shaped like a hockey puck. 'Then we'll do it the way I learned.'
The water had turned the colour of slate, and the shore was a smudge of shadows. Mia's stomach tightened. Somewhere out there were the Sisters, a cluster of rocks that had sunk more than one careless boat.
'First, find a light,' said Grandad. 'Not a house light. One that flashes.'
Mia scanned the coast. To the north, a white light winked twice, then waited. She counted under her breath. Two flashes, then darkness, then two flashes again, every ten seconds.
Grandad tapped the chart, where a tiny purple teardrop sat on a point of land. Beside it someone had printed Fl(2) 10s. 'Every lighthouse has its own pattern, so you can tell them apart in the dark. That's Cape Lorne. Now hold the compass to your eye and point it at the light.'
The numbers swam, then steadied. 'Three hundred and forty degrees.'
'Good. Draw a line on the chart from the lighthouse along that bearing. We're somewhere on that line.' He had her repeat it with a red light flickering on the breakwater. Where her two pencil lines crossed, she drew a small, wobbly circle.
'That's us,' she said slowly. 'And the Sisters are... there.' The rocks were well to the south. She let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.
For the next half-hour, Mia took bearings every few minutes, and the Kittiwake slipped steadily through the slap and slosh of the dark swell. When two green lights at the harbour entrance finally lined up, one above the other, Grandad nodded. 'Leads are in line. Steer straight for them.'
As they glided past the breakwater, Grandad leaned under the chart table again. There was a soft click, and the chartplotter flickered back to life, its little arrow sitting exactly inside Mia's wobbly circle.
'Loose wire,' he said, with a perfectly straight face.
Mia looked at him for a long moment. Then she folded the chart carefully and tucked it into her jacket.
Question: Why did the Kittiwake slow down at the start of the story?
Option A: the engine failed
Option B: the screen went black
Option C: the wind dropped
Option D: the tide turned

Let the Main Street Breathe
To the Editor,
Every Sunday morning, Banksia Street is the busiest place in our town, and also the least pleasant. Cars circle the block looking for parks, delivery vans idle outside the cafe, and families with prams squeeze along footpaths barely wider than a bicycle. I believe the council should close Banksia Street to cars every Sunday from 7 am until 1 pm, and I would like to explain why.
First, a car-free street is safer. Last year my younger brother stepped between two parked utes to chase a runaway ball and was nearly hit by a reversing car. He was fine, but the driver was shaking, and so was I. When cars are removed, children can be children without their parents holding their breath at every kerb.
Second, closing the street would be good for business, not bad. I know this sounds backwards. When the idea was first suggested, Mr Kostas, who has run the bakery on the corner for twenty-two years, signed a petition against it. He worried that his regular customers, many of them older people, would stop coming if they could not park outside his door. Then, last March, the council held a four-week trial. Volunteers counted more than twice as many people walking along the street as on a normal Sunday, and most shops reported higher takings. Mr Kostas was baking extra loaves by the second week. By the end, he had put two tables on the road and was handing out free samples of his apricot scrolls. 'People slow down when they aren't dodging traffic,' he told me. 'And when they slow down, they smell the bread.'
Third, a quieter street is a healthier one. Without engines, the air is cleaner and the noise drops to the sound of conversation, buskers and the occasional magpie. People who might never think of walking into town will happily stroll there if the walk itself is enjoyable.
Picture what Banksia Street could become. The library could set up a reading corner outside its doors. Students from the high school could run a stall selling seedlings to raise money for camp. Older residents who no longer drive could meet friends on a bench in the middle of the road without engines drowning out their conversation. During the trial, I watched a toddler draw a chalk sunflower on the very spot where my brother had nearly been hit. It was still there, faded but visible, a week later.
Some residents say they will have nowhere to park. This is a fair concern, and it should not be brushed aside. However, the council car park behind the library sits nearly empty on Sundays, and it is less than three minutes' walk away. A small shuttle bus for people with limited mobility, like the one used during the trial, would solve the problem for those who genuinely cannot walk that far.
Streets are not just pipes for moving cars from one place to another. They are the shared living rooms of a town. For six hours a week, I am asking the council to let Banksia Street be a place for people.
Yours sincerely,
Priya Raman, Year 8

Option A: sit still with their engines running
Option B: sit still with their engines switched off
Option C: park illegally across the footpath
Option D: unload their goods very slowly

The Toll of Merrow Bridge
In the valley town of Merrow, the only way across the river was an old stone bridge, and under the bridge lived a troll whose name nobody knew. Nobody had ever asked.
The troll was not cruel, but he was particular. Every traveller who wished to cross had to pay a toll, and the toll was always the same: 'Give me something you have never given anyone before.'
The merchants of Merrow thought this a fine bargain. The goldsmith handed over a ring he had made that very morning. The weaver gave a scarf woven from thread so fine it floated. The mayor, who liked to make an impression, offered a silver cup polished until it shone like the moon. The troll accepted each gift with a heavy nod and stepped aside.
Yet the troll grew no happier. If anything, he grew greyer and more hunched each season, and his treasures piled up in a damp, gleaming heap that he never looked at. Stranger still, the bridge began to crack. Fine lines crept across the stones, then wider ones. The townsfolk muttered that the troll's sour mood was seeping into the bridge itself, for everyone knew that a troll and his bridge share one heart.
'Pay him more,' said the mayor. 'Something truly magnificent.' So the town collected its finest treasures, and still the cracks grew.
One spring morning, a girl named Edda arrived at the bridge with a basket of eggs to sell at the market on the far side. She was the stonemason's youngest apprentice, and she had nothing of value: no rings, no silver, not even a coin.
'Give me something you have never given anyone before,' rumbled the troll.
Edda thought hard. She looked at the eggs, but she had sold eggs a hundred times. She looked at her hands, rough from carrying stone. Then she looked at the troll himself, really looked, at his drooping ears and the moss growing in the creases of his elbows.
'I have never asked anyone their name,' she said, 'because I already know every name in Merrow. But I don't know yours.'
The troll blinked. For a long moment, the only sound was the river.
'Ormund,' he said at last, in a voice like a small stone rolling. 'My name is Ormund.'
'Good morning, Ormund,' said Edda, and she sat down on the bank beside him. She stayed until the market had closed, asking about the river, the fish and the hundred winters he had spent under the arches. She never did sell her eggs. When she finally stood to leave, she noticed that one of the deepest cracks in the bridge had begun to close, like a wound healing over.
Edda came back the next day, and the day after that, bringing her trowel and a bucket of mortar. As they talked, she patched the smaller cracks, and the larger ones mended on their own.
The goldsmith, watching from his window, could not understand it. 'She paid him nothing,' he complained.
The mayor said nothing at all. But the following week, he walked down to the bridge without his silver cup, stood a little awkwardly in front of the troll, and asked him how he was.
Question: What did the goldsmith give the troll?
Option A: a scarf of very fine thread
Option B: a cup polished like the moon
Option C: a ring he had made that morning
Option D: a basket of fresh eggs

The Teacher Who Went South
When Phillip Law was a young science teacher in country Victoria, nobody would have guessed that he would one day lead Australia's expeditions to Antarctica. Yet for seventeen years he did exactly that, and stations he helped to establish are still in use today.
Law was born in 1912 in Tallangatta, a small town in north-eastern Victoria. His father was a teacher, and Phillip followed him into the profession, teaching in country schools while studying science part-time at the University of Melbourne. It was slow, tiring work, but he was determined. He eventually became a lecturer in physics at the university, where he researched cosmic rays.
He was also adventurous. Law boxed, skied and loved the outdoors, and when the Australian government began planning scientific voyages to the Antarctic region after the Second World War, he jumped at the chance. In the summer of 1947-48 he sailed south as a scientist aboard the small ship Wyatt Earp. In 1949, at the age of 37, he was appointed to lead the Antarctic Division.
At that time, Australia had no permanent base on the Antarctic continent itself. Law was determined to change this. Finding a suitable site was difficult: much of the coastline is lined with ice cliffs, and a station needs bare rock to build on. In 1954, after searching the coast aboard the Danish ship Kista Dan, Law's team found a rocky harbour and built Mawson Station, named after the famous explorer Sir Douglas Mawson. It was the first permanent Australian station south of the Antarctic Circle, and it is the oldest continuously operating station south of the Circle today.
Law did not stop there. Davis Station was established in 1957, and in 1959 Australia took over Wilkes Station from the United States. Each summer, Law sailed with the relief voyages, bringing new teams and supplies and taking home the people who had spent the winter. On these journeys, his teams charted thousands of kilometres of coastline that had never been mapped.
He was known as a demanding leader. He expected hard work and careful science, and he could be blunt. Nevertheless, many expeditioners respected him, because he never asked anyone to face conditions he would not face himself. He shared cramped cabins, endured rough seas and stood on the ice beside his teams.
Law retired as director in 1966, but he remained a passionate supporter of science and education for the rest of his life, helping to guide the growth of colleges in Victoria and speaking widely about Antarctica. When he died in 2010, aged 97, places including an ice dome and a summer research base had already been named in his honour.
Looking back, it is tempting to see Law's life as two separate stories: the country teacher and the polar explorer. In truth, they were the same story. The patience that carried him through years of part-time study was the same patience that kept him searching an icy coast for a single rocky harbour.

Six Dots in the Dark
In 1819, a ten-year-old boy from the French village of Coupvray arrived in Paris to begin school. His name was Louis Braille, and he had been blind since the age of five, after an accident in his father's leather workshop led to an infection that spread to both eyes. His family was determined that he would still receive an education, and he won a place at the Royal Institute for Blind Youth, one of the first schools of its kind in the world.
Life at the Institute was hard. The building was old, damp and cold, and the food was plain. Discipline was strict. Yet for Louis, the greatest frustration was the books. The school's founder, Valentin Hauy, had developed a way of printing ordinary letters in raised form so that students could trace them with their fingers. It was a brilliant idea in theory. In practice, each letter had to be large to be felt clearly, so a single book could weigh several kilograms and hold only a small amount of text. The library contained just a handful of titles. Worse, students could read these books but had no easy way to write in the same system.
In 1821, a visitor named Charles Barbier came to the school. Barbier, a former army captain, had invented a code he called 'night writing', which used patterns of raised dots to represent sounds. His idea had been for soldiers to share messages in the dark without lighting a lamp. The students were excited, Louis most of all. Dots, he realised, were far easier to feel than the curves of letters.
But Barbier's system had problems. Its symbols used up to twelve dots, too many to be felt with a single touch of a fingertip, and because it represented sounds rather than spelling, it had no punctuation and no way to write numbers or music. Louis began to experiment. He worked in the evenings and during holidays at home, pressing dots into paper with a blunt tool. By 1824, when he was just fifteen, he had created a system based on a cell of only six dots, arranged in two columns of three. Each letter fitted neatly under one fingertip.
His classmates adopted the code immediately. They used it to take notes, write letters to one another and copy out books. When Louis became a teacher at the Institute, he continued to improve the system, adding symbols for mathematics and music, and in 1829 he published an explanation of it.
Remarkably, the school did not officially approve Braille's code for many years. Some sighted teachers felt that blind students should use a system that looked like ordinary print. For a time, the code was even banned at the Institute, but students went on using it in secret.
Louis Braille died in 1852, aged 43. Two years later, the Institute finally adopted his system. Today, braille is used in languages all over the world, on everything from library books to lift buttons.
It all began with a schoolboy who was tired of heavy books and decided to do something about it.
Question: Which detail shows that the Institute's raised-letter books were hard to use?
Option A: the building was old, damp and cold
Option B: a single book could weigh several kilograms
Option C: discipline at the school was strict
Option D: the idea was brilliant in theory

The Spread That Almost Wasn't
Few foods are as closely linked with Australia as Vegemite. For some people, a thin scraping on hot buttered toast is the taste of home; for others, it is a salty shock. But this dark, sticky spread had a surprisingly rocky start, and for several years it looked as though it might disappear altogether.
The story begins after the First World War. Before the war, Australians had eaten Marmite, a British spread made from yeast extract. When the war disrupted shipping, imports became unreliable, and a Melbourne businessman named Fred Walker saw an opportunity. If Australians could not easily get Marmite, perhaps they would buy a local product instead.
Walker knew exactly where to find the main ingredient. Breweries produced large amounts of leftover yeast, which was usually thrown away. In 1922, he hired a young chemist named Cyril Callister and gave him a challenging task: turn this waste into a tasty, nutritious spread. Callister spent months experimenting in the laboratory. He broke down the yeast cells, then added salt and vegetable extracts such as celery and onion to improve the flavour. The result was a thick, dark paste with a strong, savoury taste.
Next, the product needed a name. Walker's company ran a national competition, offering a prize for the best suggestion. According to the company's story, Walker's daughter Sheilah pulled the winning entry from a hat: Vegemite. The new spread went on sale in 1923.
Unfortunately, Australians were not convinced. Marmite was familiar, and shoppers saw no reason to switch. Sales were so poor that in 1928 Walker renamed the product Parwill, hoping to make a joke out of the competition: if 'Ma might', then 'Pa will'. The clever slogan fell flat, and a few years later the original name returned.
What eventually saved Vegemite was a combination of good marketing and good science. In the 1930s, Walker's company gave away free jars with other products and ran poetry competitions with imported cars as prizes. Then, in 1939, the British Medical Association recognised Vegemite as a rich source of B vitamins. Doctors and nurses began recommending it for children, and parents took notice. During the Second World War, Vegemite was included in soldiers' rations, and many families had to go without. Rather than hurting sales, the shortage made people want it even more.
By the 1950s, Vegemite had become a household favourite, helped along by a catchy radio jingle about happy little children enjoying it. Today, millions of jars are sold each year, and travellers often pack one in their suitcase to avoid going without overseas.
The history of Vegemite is a reminder that success is rarely instant. A product made from leftovers, renamed in desperation and ignored by shoppers for more than a decade, became a national icon. Not bad for a spread that almost wasn't.
Question: Why did Fred Walker want to make a local spread?
Option A: Marmite had been banned in Australia
Option B: breweries asked him to use their waste
Option C: doctors wanted a food rich in vitamins
Option D: Marmite imports had become unreliable

Few foods are as closely linked with Australia as Vegemite. For some people, a thin scraping on hot buttered toast is the taste of home; for others, it is a salty shock. But this dark, sticky spread had a surprisingly rocky start, and for several years it looked as though it might disappear altogether.
The story begins after the First World War. Before the war, Australians had eaten Marmite, a British spread made from yeast extract. When the war disrupted shipping, imports became unreliable, and a Melbourne businessman named Fred Walker saw an opportunity. If Australians could not easily get Marmite, perhaps they would buy a local product instead.
Walker knew exactly where to find the main ingredient. Breweries produced large amounts of leftover yeast, which was usually thrown away. In 1922, he hired a young chemist named Cyril Callister and gave him a challenging task: turn this waste into a tasty, nutritious spread. Callister spent months experimenting in the laboratory. He broke down the yeast cells, then added salt and vegetable extracts such as celery and onion to improve the flavour. The result was a thick, dark paste with a strong, savoury taste.
Next, the product needed a name. Walker's company ran a national competition, offering a prize for the best suggestion. According to the company's story, Walker's daughter Sheilah pulled the winning entry from a hat: Vegemite. The new spread went on sale in 1923.
Unfortunately, Australians were not convinced. Marmite was familiar, and shoppers saw no reason to switch. Sales were so poor that in 1928 Walker renamed the product Parwill, hoping to make a joke out of the competition: if 'Ma might', then 'Pa will'. The clever slogan fell flat, and a few years later the original name returned.

In the 1930s, Walker's company gave away free jars with other products and ran poetry competitions with imported cars as prizes. How long is the coastline of Australia? It sounds like a simple question with a single answer. Yet depending on which book or website you check, you might find figures that differ by thousands of kilometres. Nobody has made a mistake. The problem lies in the shape of coastlines themselves.
Before his death in 1953, the English scientist Lewis Fry Richardson was puzzled to find that Spain and Portugal reported quite different lengths for the border they shared. Investigating further, he discovered that the measured length of a wiggly line depends on the size of the ruler you use. Measure a coast on a map with a ruler 100 kilometres long, and you will skip straight across bays and headlands. Use a ruler one kilometre long, and you will trace far more of the bends. Walk the beach with a one-metre stick, and you will follow every rock and inlet. Each time the ruler shrinks, the coastline grows.
Most mathematicians treated this as a curiosity. One man, however, saw it as a clue. In 1967, the Polish-born mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot published a paper asking how long the coast of Britain really is. He argued that coastlines share a special property: they look similarly rough whether you view them from a plane, from a clifftop or on your hands and knees. Zoom in, and the same kind of jagged pattern keeps appearing. In 1975, he invented a name for shapes like this. He called them fractals, from the Latin word fractus, meaning 'broken'.
For centuries, geometry had been the study of smooth, tidy shapes such as circles, triangles and cones. Rough shapes were treated as messy exceptions, too untidy to be worth studying. Mandelbrot disagreed strongly. 'Clouds are not spheres, mountains are not cones, coastlines are not circles,' he wrote in 1982, 'and bark is not smooth, nor does lightning travel in a straight line.' He spent much of his career showing that roughness has its own patterns and rules.
Once you know what to look for, fractals appear everywhere. A fern frond is made of smaller fronds, each made of smaller ones again. A head of Romanesco broccoli is a cone of cones, each spiralling floret a miniature copy of the whole. Rivers branch into streams, which branch into creeks, which branch into tiny gullies.
Inside your own body, the airways of your lungs split in two again and again, about twenty-three times, ending in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs. This branching packs an enormous surface for absorbing oxygen, tens of square metres, into a space no bigger than your chest.

Still, the idea has proved remarkably useful. Scientists use it to model forests and weather, and engineers have designed fractal-shaped antennas for mobile phones.
So, how long is Australia's coastline? The honest answer is that it depends on how closely you look.

The Disguise at Point Lowly
Aunt Ros had warned me the water would be cold, but nobody can really warn you about thirteen degrees. When I slid off the rocks at Point Lowly, the sea poured into my wetsuit as if it had been waiting all morning for the chance. I gasped through my snorkel and thought, not for the first time, that I should have stayed in Adelaide and gone to Sam's birthday instead.
Aunt Ros surfaced beside me, her mask pushed up on her forehead. She is a marine biologist, and every winter she helps count the giant Australian cuttlefish that gather here to breed. 'Slate, pencil, eyes open,' she said, tapping the waterproof board clipped to my arm. 'Count every one you see. Males in one column, females in the other.' Then she was gone, flippers flicking.
I put my face in the water and forgot about the cold.
The rocky bottom, only a couple of metres down, was crowded with cuttlefish. Some were as long as my arm. They hovered over the weed, the frilly fins along their sides rippling like the edge of a curtain in a breeze. And they were changing. A big male right below me flickered from mottled brown to bands of white and purple that rolled down his body, over and over, like light moving across a cinema screen. He was showing off, Aunt Ros had told me, to the smaller females nearby and to any rival who came too close.
I counted. Twelve males, nine females. My pencil kept slipping in my numb fingers.
Then I noticed something odd. One 'female' was edging slowly towards the big male's partner. She had the same blotchy pattern as the other females, and she held her arms tucked in just like them. But every time the big male turned away to chase off a rival, she flashed, just for a second, a single stripe of male colour along one side. Then she went blotchy again.
I stared until my mask fogged up. Then I rubbed out the nine in the female column, wrote an eight, and added a thirteen to the male column, with a question mark.
Back on the rocks, Aunt Ros looked at my slate and went very quiet. She stared at the question mark for so long that I thought I had ruined her data. 'Sorry,' I said. 'I can fix it.'
'What made you change it?' she asked.
I told her about the stripe, and the tucked-in arms, and the way it only flashed when the big male wasn't looking.
She pulled a battered notebook out of her bag and flipped to a page covered in sketches. 'We call them sneaker males,' she said. 'Small males that can't win a contest, so they disguise themselves as females to slip past the big ones. I've been coming here for eleven years. It took me three seasons to spot my first one.'
She handed back my slate and didn't say anything else, but on the drive back to the shack she let me choose the music the whole way, which she had never done before.
I didn't think about Sam's party once.

Option A: three degrees
Option B: thirteen degrees
Option C: eleven degrees
Option D: twenty degrees

The Ninth Latch
On the morning the goats were found standing on the bonnet of Aunt Rosa's ute, chewing the windscreen wipers, Nell decided that the farm gate had to be fixed for good.
The problem was simple to describe and maddening to solve. The gate to the goat paddock swung shut on its own, but the old latch only caught if someone slammed it. Visitors never slammed it. Delivery drivers never slammed it. Even Aunt Rosa, who had lived on the farm for twenty years, forgot about half the time. And the goats, who seemed to spend every spare minute studying that gate, always noticed.
Nell was spending the summer holidays on the farm outside Mudgee, and she had a notebook, a toolbox and six weeks. She started by drawing. Her first design used a spring borrowed from an old clothes peg. It worked twice and then snapped. Her second used a magnet from a broken fridge door, but it was too weak to hold against a determined goat called Biscuit, who simply leaned on the gate until it gave way. The third, fourth and fifth designs each solved one problem and created another.
"Most inventors spend their lives being wrong," Aunt Rosa said one evening, watching Nell glare at latch number six. "The trick is to be wrong in a new way each time."
Nell was not comforted. She had pictured herself as the sort of inventor who has one brilliant idea in the bath. Instead she felt like someone trying to untangle a fishing line in the dark, pulling one knot loose only to tighten another.
Then, on a hot, still afternoon, she sat on the fence and simply watched. When the wind pushed the gate closed, it always slowed down at the very end, as if it were tired, and that was exactly when the latch failed. The latch did not need to be stronger. It needed to catch the gate gently, at its slowest moment.
She rebuilt the latch with a sloping metal tongue, shaped like a ramp, so that even a lazy, drifting gate would ride up and over it and drop into place with a soft click. Latch number seven caught the gate. Latch number eight caught the gate even when Nell barely nudged it. Latch number nine, painted bright yellow so that visitors would notice it, survived three days of Biscuit's best efforts.
On her last morning, Nell watched the delivery driver stroll into the paddock, chatting on his phone, and wander out without a backward glance. The gate drifted behind him, slowed, and clicked shut. Biscuit trotted over, sniffed the yellow latch, and walked away in what Nell chose to believe was disgust.
Aunt Rosa did not say anything clever this time. She just handed Nell the notebook, which had grown fat with crossed-out drawings, and said, "Keep that. It's the important part."
Nell had thought the notebook was a record of her mistakes. Riding home in the back seat, flicking slowly through the pages, she began to see it instead as a map of how she had found her way.

Option A: slightly confusing
Option B: quite dangerous
Option C: very expensive
Option D: extremely frustrating

Ahmose Writes Home
This is an imagined letter from a boy training to be a scribe in ancient Egypt, about 3300 years ago.
To my father Senu, at the farm beside the eastern canal, from your son Ahmose, at the scribes' school in Thebes. I hope this finds you well and the fields green.
Father, I have received your message. You say the river rose well this year, that the barley stands thick, and that you want me home for the harvest and home for good after it. I have read your words many times, and now I ask you to read mine.
First, let me tell you how my days pass. We rise early and sit in rows in the courtyard, cross-legged, with our writing boards on our knees. Our teacher, old Paneb, reads a line aloud and we copy it. We do not write on papyrus yet, because papyrus is costly and our mistakes are many. Instead we write on flat chips of limestone and broken pieces of pottery, which are everywhere and cost nothing. When a chip is full, we throw it on the pile behind the wall. That pile is now taller than I am, and I think half of it is mine.
My hand has grown steadier. I mix my own ink now: black from soot, red from ochre, each pressed into a little cake and wetted with water. I chew the end of my reed until it frays into a fine brush. Paneb says my signs are beginning to look like signs and less like ants that have fallen into the ink. From Paneb, who has never praised anyone, this is high praise.
Some days we copy lists: the names of birds, of fish, of towns along the river. Other days we copy old letters and wise sayings, so that we learn good manners as well as good signs. The script we use for everyday writing is quicker than the careful pictures carved on temple walls. Paneb says no granary clerk has time to draw a whole owl for every word.
Now, Father, consider what a scribe can do. A scribe counts the grain in the granaries. A scribe measures the fields after the flood washes away the boundary marks, so that every farmer receives his rightful land. A scribe writes the letters that carry news up and down the river. Who measured our own fields last season? A scribe. Who wrote down how much grain we owed? A scribe. If one of our family could do these things, would anyone ever cheat us again?
I know the harvest is hard and the days are long. I have not forgotten the heat, the dust, the ache in my back after a day with the sickle. I am not running from the work, Father. I am learning a different kind of work, one that can protect the work you do.
Paneb says that if I keep at my lessons for four more years, I may be given a place in the office of the granary. Four years is a long time. But a sycamore is not grown in a single season, and you have told me so yourself.
I will come home for the harvest, as you ask, and I will swing a sickle beside my brothers. But when the barley is in, let me return to my chips of stone and my fraying reed. Send your answer with the boatman who brings this letter.
Your son, who still smells of soot,
Ahmose

Option A: sheets of cheap, rough papyrus
Option B: wooden boards covered in wax
Option C: chips of limestone and broken pottery
Option D: flat tablets of dried river clay

Postcards from the Long Way Round
Dear Earth, I packed a bag and flew
beyond your clouds and out of view.
I promised I would write to you
from every world I travelled through,
so here's the first, still warm to hold.
Wish you were here.
I stopped first at your Moon, so near,
where footprints from a long-past year
still lie in dust no wind can blow,
exactly where they formed long ago.
I tiptoed round them, quiet as a mouse.
Wish you were here.
I waved, but kept a careful space
from the Sun's enormous, blazing face;
a million Earths could fit inside
its fiery ball, so hot and wide.
I wore my darkest glasses twice.
Wish you were here.
On Mercury there is no air
to hold the heat or soften glare.
By noon the rocks could melt a tin;
by night a savage cold creeps in.
The Sun hangs huge, a furnace door.
Wish you were here.
On Venus, clouds of acid lie
in yellow blankets, thick and high.
The ground is hotter, strange to learn,
than Mercury, where sunbeams burn.
The Sun rose in the west today, and slowly.
Wish you were here.
On Mars the soil is rusty red;
two lumpy moons race overhead.
A huge volcano, long asleep,
stands twice as tall as Everest's peak.
I wrote your name in dust with care. A storm rubbed it out.
Wish you were here.
Beyond Mars lies a scattered ring
of rocky lumps, each tumbling thing
a leftover from ancient days
when planets formed in dusty haze.
They're farther apart than you would think. I didn't hit one.
Wish you were here.
There is no ground on Jupiter,
just bands of cloud in swirling blur,
and one red storm, a spinning eye
far wider than you, Earth, rolls by.
It's whirled for over a hundred years. I'm dizzy just watching.
Wish you were here.
Saturn's rings are ice and stone
in countless pieces, each alone.
The planet is so light, I'm told,
a bath that's big enough could hold
it bobbing like a rubber duck. Ridiculous.
Wish you were here.
Uranus rolls around the Sun
tipped on its side, as if, for fun,
it lay down for a long, cold nap
with no one there to wake it up.
Its pale green glow is still and calm.
Wish you were here.
On Neptune, winds go howling by
far faster than a jet can fly
across a dim and freezing sky.
The Sun's a pinprick, small and lone.
I've never felt so far from home.
Wish you were here.
Past Neptune, little Pluto spins,
where icy, heart-shaped plains begin.
It used to be a planet too,
until the experts changed their view.
It didn't seem to mind at all.
Wish you were here.
So then I turned. I'd seen enough
of storms and rings and rusty stuff.
I steered toward a tiny spark,
a speck of blue against the dark,
and every postcard in my pack
seemed to be pulling me back.
Dear Earth, I'm home. I've seen them all,
the scorched, the stormy, huge and small,
and not one had a sky this blue,
or rain, or air to breathe right through,
or a backyard gum where magpies sing.
Wish you were here? I am. I'm here.

Option C: only at noon
Option D: in the west

so here's the first, still warm to hold.
Wish you were here.
I stopped first at your Moon, so near,
where footprints from a long-past year
still lie in dust no wind can blow,
exactly where they formed long ago.
I tiptoed round them, quiet as a mouse.
Wish you were here.
I waved, but kept a careful space
from the Sun's enormous, blazing face;
a million Earths could fit inside
its fiery ball, so hot and wide.
I wore my darkest glasses twice.
Wish you were here.
On Mercury there is no air
to hold the heat or soften glare.
By noon the rocks could melt a tin;
by night a savage cold creeps in.
The Sun hangs huge, a furnace door.
Wish you were here.
On Venus, clouds of acid lie
in yellow blankets, thick and high.
The ground is hotter, strange to learn,
than Mercury, where sunbeams burn.
The Sun rose in the west today, and slowly.
Wish you were here.
On Mars the soil is rusty red;
two lumpy moons race overhead.
A huge volcano, long asleep,
stands twice as tall as Everest's peak.
I wrote your name in dust with care. A storm rubbed it out.
Wish you were here.
Beyond Mars lies a scattered ring
of rocky lumps, each tumbling thing
a leftover from ancient days
when planets formed in dusty haze.
They're farther apart than you would think. I didn't hit one.
Wish you were here.
There is no ground on Jupiter,
just bands of cloud in swirling blur,
and one red storm, a spinning eye
far wider than you, Earth, rolls by.
It's whirled for over a hundred years. I'm dizzy just watching.
Wish you were here.
Saturn's rings are ice and stone
in countless pieces, each alone.
The planet is so light, I'm told,
a bath that's big enough could hold
it bobbing like a rubber duck. Ridiculous.
Wish you were here.
Uranus rolls around the Sun
tipped on its side, as if, for fun,
it lay down for a long, cold nap
with no one there to wake it up.
Its pale green glow is still and calm.
Wish you were here.
On Neptune, winds go howling by
far faster than a jet can fly
across a dim and freezing sky.
The Sun's a pinprick, small and lone.
I've never felt so far from home.
Wish you were here.
Past Neptune, little Pluto spins,
where icy, heart-shaped plains begin.
It used to be a planet too,
until the experts changed their view.
It didn't seem to mind at all.
Wish you were here.
So then I turned. I'd seen enough
of storms and rings and rusty stuff.
I steered toward a tiny spark,
a speck of blue against the dark,
and every postcard in my pack
seemed to be pulling me back.
Dear Earth, I'm home. I've seen them all,
the scorched, the stormy, huge and small,
and not one had a sky this blue,
or rain, or air to breathe right through,
or a backyard gum where magpies sing.
Wish you were here? I am. I'm here.

Option A: to show that the journey has made the speaker glad to be on Earth
Option B: to reveal that the speaker never really left Earth at all
Option C: to show that the speaker was disappointed by every planet
Option D: to suggest that the speaker is already planning another trip

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
The Arithmetic of Friendship
Ask people how a friendship began and most will describe a moment: a shared joke on the first day of school, a conversation at a bus stop, a borrowed pencil that was never returned. Moments matter, but researchers who study friendship have found that the real ingredient is something far less dramatic. It is time.
In 2018, Jeffrey Hall, a communication researcher at the University of Kansas in the United States, set out to measure how long it takes to turn a stranger into a friend. He surveyed adults who had recently moved to a new city and students who had just started university, asking how many hours they had spent with people they had met. His results suggested that it takes roughly 50 hours together to move from acquaintance to casual friend, around 90 hours to become a real friend, and more than 200 hours to become a close friend.
Those numbers come with a catch. Not all hours count equally. Hours spent together at work or in class seemed to do less to build closeness than hours spent hanging out, joking around and catching up on everyday life. In other words, sitting next to someone in maths for a whole year might not make you friends, but talking to them at lunch for a few weeks could.
Distance plays a part, too. In a famous study published in 1950, psychologists looked at students living in a university housing complex in the United States. They found that residents were far more likely to become friends with people who lived next door or near the staircase than with those at the other end of the building, even though the distances involved were only a few metres. Simple, repeated chance meetings, it seemed, gave friendships room to start. The researchers called this "functional distance": what mattered was not only how far apart people lived, but how often their paths happened to cross.
There may also be a limit to how many friendships a person can keep up. The British anthropologist Robin Dunbar has argued that most people can maintain about 150 meaningful relationships at once, arranged in layers. He arrived at this figure partly by comparing the brain sizes of different primates with the sizes of the groups they live in. At the centre are around five very close friends, then about 15 good friends, then wider circles of friends and acquaintances. Because time is limited, moving someone into an inner layer usually means someone else drifts outward.
None of this means that friendship can be reduced to a spreadsheet. A single act of kindness can speed things up, and some friendships survive years of distance, kept alive by regular calls and messages. But the research does carry a useful message. If you want to make a friend, you cannot simply wait for the perfect moment. You need to show up, again and again, and spend that time actually talking.
So the next time you wonder why a new friendship feels slow, do the arithmetic. You may simply not have reached your 50 hours yet.

Option A: residents befriended people next door more than those far away
Option B: casual friendship takes roughly 50 hours spent together
Option C: most people keep about 150 meaningful relationships
Option D: some friendships survive many years of being apart

The Night Puzzler
Monday 8 January
Gran's town has one main street, one bakery and one library, and the library has a puzzle table. Anyone can add pieces. Today it was a 1000-piece picture of a lighthouse, with about a third done. I found six pieces of the rocks before Gran needed me to carry the shopping.
Tuesday 9 January
Something odd. When I came back this morning, the whole lighthouse was finished, and half the sky too. Ms Baptiste, the librarian, said nobody had touched it after I left except the man who comes at four o'clock to read the newspapers, and he "doesn't believe in jigsaws". The library closes at five. So who did it?
Wednesday 10 January
I've decided to investigate properly. Clues so far:
1. The puzzle grows overnight, not during the day.
2. Whoever does it is fast. Nearly 200 pieces in one night.
3. There was a lolly wrapper under the table this morning. Peppermint, the old-fashioned striped kind.
4. Ms Baptiste locks up herself, and she says she goes straight home.
Gran thinks I'm being dramatic. She says maybe the puzzle fairy did it. I'm thirteen, Gran.

Sun on the Roof
At 2.14 on the hottest afternoon of the summer, the fridge stopped humming. Mai noticed that before anything else, the way you notice a clock only when it stops ticking. Then the ceiling fan slowed, wobbled and went still, and the air in the lounge room seemed to thicken.
"Blackout," her brother Tuan announced from the hallway, as if he had personally discovered it.
Mai went to the window. Across the street, every house looked exactly the same as before: brick, quiet, baking. Every house except the Nguyens' place on the corner, where she could see the blue flicker of a television through the front window.
"That's not fair," she said. "Why have they still got power?"
Dad came in, wiping his hands on a tea towel, and peered out. "Battery," he said. "Mr Nguyen put one in last year. Talked about it for months."
Mai frowned and pointed up at their own ceiling. "But we've got solar panels. The sun's practically screaming. Shouldn't we have more power than anyone?"
Dad smiled the patient smile he used when he was about to explain something at length. "You'd think so. But our panels are connected to the grid, and when the grid goes down, the inverter switches them off."
"On purpose?"
"On purpose. Line workers might be out there fixing the fault. If thousands of houses kept pushing electricity back into the wires, someone repairing them could get hurt. So the system shuts itself down until the grid is safe again."
Mai stared at the roof as though it had betrayed her. All those panels, soaking up the brightest sunshine of the year, and not one of them could keep the milk cold.
"So what does a battery do?"
"It stores power from the panels, and during an outage it cuts the house off from the grid so it can keep running safely on its own. Mr Nguyen's house is like a little island right now. Ours is just part of the dark mainland."
The afternoon dragged on. Tuan read comics by the window. Dad filled the laundry tub with cold water so they could take turns soaking their feet. Mai counted the minutes since the fridge had stopped and worried about the ice-cream.
At about four o'clock, Mr Nguyen knocked on the front door holding a heavy-duty extension cord and a grin. "Thought you might like to keep your fridge going," he said. "I've got plenty to share. Sun's doing all the work."
Dad thanked him three times. Mai helped run the cord carefully across the lawn, and when the fridge shuddered back to life she felt ridiculously relieved, as if a friend had woken up.
That evening, when the power finally returned and the street lights blinked on one by one, Mai sat at the kitchen table with Dad's laptop. She was not watching videos. She was looking up the prices of home batteries, adding up numbers on a scrap of paper, and frowning at the totals.
"Saving up?" Dad asked.
"Maybe," Mai said. "Or maybe I'll just make sure we stay friends with Mr Nguyen."
Question: What was the first sign of the blackout that Mai noticed?
Option A: the fridge stopped humming
Option B: the ceiling fan wobbled
Option C: the television went blank
Option D: the street lights went out

The Woman Who Kept the Flock
In 1790, a young Englishwoman stepped ashore at Sydney Cove after a voyage of almost six months. Elizabeth Macarthur was twenty-three, newly married and travelling with her baby son. She had grown up on a farm in Devon, in the south-west of England, but nothing there had prepared her for the dry, unfamiliar land around the tiny settlement.
Her husband, John, was an officer in the New South Wales Corps. In 1793 he was granted land at Parramatta, west of Sydney, and the family named the property Elizabeth Farm. There they built a modest brick cottage, part of which still stands today and is among the oldest surviving European buildings in Australia.
In those early years, Elizabeth was curious about everything. She took lessons in botany and astronomy from William Dawes, a young officer of the First Fleet, and she wrote long letters home describing the plants, the birds and the night sky. Those letters still survive, and they give a vivid picture of daily life in the early colony.
The Macarthurs were among the first in the colony to keep merino sheep, a breed from Spain famous for its fine, soft wool. A small number of merinos had arrived from the Cape of Good Hope in 1797, and John believed that fine wool could become a valuable export to the busy woollen mills of Britain. Wool also had a great advantage over many other farm products: it would not spoil during the long sea voyage to England.
Then, in 1801, John sailed to England. He would be away for four years, and later, from 1809 to 1817, for eight more. During those long absences, it was Elizabeth who ran the family's farms. She managed the workers, kept the accounts, sold produce and, above all, looked after the growing flocks. Letters from her husband could take six months or more to arrive, and by the time his instructions reached her, the season they referred to had often passed. So she made her own decisions: which animals to keep for breeding, when to shear, and which pastures to rest after a dry spell.
It was not easy work. Drought, floods and disease all threatened the flocks, and Elizabeth was raising a large family at the same time. Yet the flocks grew, and the quality of the wool improved. By the time John returned in 1817, the Macarthur merinos were among the most valuable in the colony.
For a long time, history gave most of the credit to John Macarthur, whose name appears in many older textbooks as a founder of the Australian wool industry. More recently, historians reading Elizabeth's letters and the farm's records have argued that her careful, practical management through those long years was just as important.
Elizabeth Macarthur died in 1850 at Elizabeth Farm. Today the house is a museum, and visitors can walk through the rooms where she once added up columns of figures by candlelight, waiting for ships that might bring news from the other side of the world.
Question: From whose point of view is this biography told?
Option A: Elizabeth Macarthur describing her own life
Option B: John Macarthur writing letters from England
Option C: a writer looking back on Elizabeth's life
Option D: a museum visitor touring Elizabeth Farm

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
The Puzzle of Pruney Fingers
Spend long enough in the bath or the pool and something odd happens to your fingers. The smooth pads at their tips crinkle into ridges and valleys, as if they had aged sixty years in half an hour. Your toes do the same. Then, not long after you dry off, the wrinkles quietly disappear.
For a long time, the explanation seemed obvious. The outer layer of skin, people assumed, simply soaked up water and swelled like a sponge, and because it was attached to the layers beneath, it buckled into folds. It was a neat, sensible idea. It was also, as it turned out, mostly wrong.
The first clue came from patients, not from bathtubs. In the 1930s, doctors noticed that fingers in which certain nerves had been damaged did not wrinkle in water at all. If wrinkling were simply a matter of skin absorbing water, nerves should not have made any difference. Something more active had to be going on.
Researchers now understand that wrinkling is controlled by the nervous system. When fingers have been in water for a few minutes, nerves signal the tiny blood vessels beneath the skin to narrow. With less blood flowing through the fingertip, the soft tissue underneath shrinks slightly, and the skin on top is pulled down into wrinkles. The process is automatic, part of the same system that controls things like sweating and heart rate. Doctors even use it as a simple test: if a patient's fingers fail to wrinkle after soaking, it can be a sign that the nerves are not working properly.
This raised a new question. If the body wrinkles our fingers on purpose, what is the purpose?
In 2011, an American scientist named Mark Changizi suggested an answer. He pointed out that the wrinkles look a lot like the tread on a car tyre or a hiking boot, forming channels that might drain water away from the fingertip. That, he argued, could help us grip wet objects, such as rocks in a stream or slippery branches after rain.
Two years later, a team at Newcastle University in England put the idea to the test. Volunteers were asked to move marbles from one container to another, sometimes with smooth fingers and sometimes after soaking their hands. When the marbles were wet, people with wrinkled fingers completed the task faster. When the marbles were dry, the wrinkles made no difference.
That sounds like a tidy ending, but science rarely works that way. A later study in Germany tried a similar experiment and found no clear advantage for wrinkled fingers. Researchers are still debating the results, and the full answer may involve several factors.
What is certain is that pruney fingers are not a simple accident of soggy skin. They are a small, surprising reminder that the body is constantly making adjustments we never notice, even while we are doing nothing more demanding than lying in the bath.

Option A: marbles
Option B: pebbles

Option D: coins

Twenty Paddles, One Boat
Mia Torres had expected dragon boating to be easy. She had been swimming laps since she was six, her shoulders were strong, and when the school team posted a notice saying it needed one more paddler for the regatta, she signed up thinking she would make the boat faster almost by herself.
The boat, it turned out, had other ideas.
It was long and narrow, with a carved dragon's head at the front and twenty paddlers sitting in pairs along its length. At the bow, facing backwards, sat Ellie with the drum. At the stern stood Mr Farouk, the coach, holding the long steering oar. Mia was placed in row six, on the left.
At her first training session she paddled as hard as she could. Her blade tore through the water, again and again, faster than anyone else's. By the end of the first lap she was gasping, and the boat felt heavy and sluggish, as though it were dragging an anchor.
Afterwards Mr Farouk walked over while she was still catching her breath. "You're the strongest paddler I've had in years," he said. "With you in it, the boat should be faster. It isn't."
Mia stared at him.
"Watch the front pair," he went on. "Jai and Priya are the strokes. They set the rhythm. Everyone matches them, and Ellie's drum helps you hear it. When twenty blades go in together, the boat lifts and runs. When one blade goes in early, it hits water that hasn't moved yet and acts like a brake."
For the next three weeks, Mia did something she had never done in a swimming pool. She held back. She kept her eyes on Priya's shoulders, a few rows ahead of her, and tried to make her blade enter the water at exactly the same moment. At first it felt like trying to walk at someone else's pace, all short steps and frustration. Some sessions she was so focused on timing that she barely pulled at all.
Then, one cold Thursday afternoon, it clicked. For a whole length of the lake, she heard only one sound from the blades, a single deep splash, and felt the hull rise and glide beneath her. Ellie whooped from the bow and lost the beat for a moment, and everyone laughed.
At the regatta, their school drew a lane beside the team that had won the previous three years. Over two hundred metres, the boats stayed almost level. Mia never once looked across at the other crew. She watched Priya's shoulders and pulled when Priya pulled. They crossed the line half a second behind, the closest anyone had come to beating that team in years.
On the bank afterwards, Mr Farouk handed out drinks. When he reached Mia he paused. "Priya's finishing school this year," he said. "Next season the boat will need a new stroke, someone who understands rhythm, not just power. You might want to think about it."
Mia looked out at the empty boat rocking by the jetty, its twenty seats waiting. She was already thinking about it.

Option A: in the front pair, on the right
Option B: at the bow, beside the drum
Option C: in row six, on the left
Option D: at the stern, beside the coach

Ginger Stripes and Bandit Masks
For most of the twentieth century, the colour of a dinosaur was a matter of pure guesswork. Museum artists painted them grey, green or muddy brown, often borrowing the dull shades of crocodiles and lizards. Scientists could measure a thigh bone to the millimetre, yet when it came to colour, they shrugged. Skin and feathers rot quickly, and pigments, everyone assumed, could not survive millions of years in rock.
That assumption began to crumble in the hills of Liaoning, in north-eastern China. About 125 million years ago, this region was dotted with lakes surrounded by volcanoes. Fine ash settled over animals that died near the water, burying them so gently and quickly that soft tissues sometimes left traces. In 1996, a farmer there uncovered a small, long-tailed dinosaur, later named Sinosauropteryx, whose body was fringed with a dark halo of fuzzy filaments. It was the first dinosaur outside the bird family found with a feather-like covering, and it raised a tantalising question: if the feathers had survived, might their colour have survived too?
The answer lay in structures far too small to see with the naked eye. In living birds, colour often comes from melanosomes, tiny capsules that hold the pigment melanin. Their shape is a clue to the colour they produce. Long, sausage-shaped melanosomes generally give black or grey, while round, ball-shaped ones give ginger and reddish-brown tones. When researchers examined fossil feathers under electron microscopes, they found exactly these shapes, pressed flat but still recognisable, like seeds scattered across a page.
In 2010, a team of Chinese and British scientists reported that the tail of Sinosauropteryx had been banded in alternating stripes of ginger and white. For palaeontologists who had believed colour was lost forever, the announcement was startling. Some were delighted; others insisted on more evidence, warning that the tiny shapes might be fossilised bacteria rather than pigment capsules. Later studies, which compared fossil structures with those in modern animals, persuaded most of the doubters.
A 2017 study suggested that Sinosauropteryx was darker on its back and paler on its belly, a pattern called countershading. This pattern cancels out shadows cast by sunlight, making an animal look flatter and harder to spot. Because a sharp change from dark to light works best under bright light from directly above, researchers proposed that this little hunter lived in open country rather than dense forest. It even appears to have had a dark stripe across its eyes, like a bandit's mask, a feature that in some modern birds may reduce glare.
Other dinosaurs have since been given colours too. The small, four-winged Microraptor seems to have been glossy black with a shimmering sheen, like a modern crow.
None of this means every dinosaur can now be painted accurately. Most fossils are bones alone, preserved in rocks far coarser than the ash of Liaoning. Still, the old shrug has gone. Colour, once thought to be beyond the reach of science, has become another piece of evidence, telling us not only how dinosaurs looked but where and how they may have lived.

Option A: a verb
Option B: a noun
Option C: an adjective
Option D: an adverb
