Ginger Stripes and Bandit Masks
For most of the twentieth century, the colour of a dinosaur was a matter of pure guesswork. Museum artists painted them grey, green or muddy brown, often borrowing the dull shades of crocodiles and lizards. Scientists could measure a thigh bone to the millimetre, yet when it came to colour, they shrugged. Skin and feathers rot quickly, and pigments, everyone assumed, could not survive millions of years in rock.
That assumption began to crumble in the hills of Liaoning, in north-eastern China. About 125 million years ago, this region was dotted with lakes surrounded by volcanoes. Fine ash settled over animals that died near the water, burying them so gently and quickly that soft tissues sometimes left traces. In 1996, a farmer there uncovered a small, long-tailed dinosaur, later named Sinosauropteryx, whose body was fringed with a dark halo of fuzzy filaments. It was the first dinosaur outside the bird family found with a feather-like covering, and it raised a tantalising question: if the feathers had survived, might their colour have survived too?
The answer lay in structures far too small to see with the naked eye. In living birds, colour often comes from melanosomes, tiny capsules that hold the pigment melanin. Their shape is a clue to the colour they produce. Long, sausage-shaped melanosomes generally give black or grey, while round, ball-shaped ones give ginger and reddish-brown tones. When researchers examined fossil feathers under electron microscopes, they found exactly these shapes, pressed flat but still recognisable, like seeds scattered across a page.
In 2010, a team of Chinese and British scientists reported that the tail of Sinosauropteryx had been banded in alternating stripes of ginger and white. For palaeontologists who had believed colour was lost forever, the announcement was startling. Some were delighted; others insisted on more evidence, warning that the tiny shapes might be fossilised bacteria rather than pigment capsules. Later studies, which compared fossil structures with those in modern animals, persuaded most of the doubters.
A 2017 study suggested that Sinosauropteryx was darker on its back and paler on its belly, a pattern called countershading. This pattern cancels out shadows cast by sunlight, making an animal look flatter and harder to spot. Because a sharp change from dark to light works best under bright light from directly above, researchers proposed that this little hunter lived in open country rather than dense forest. It even appears to have had a dark stripe across its eyes, like a bandit's mask, a feature that in some modern birds may reduce glare.
Other dinosaurs have since been given colours too. The small, four-winged Microraptor seems to have been glossy black with a shimmering sheen, like a modern crow.
None of this means every dinosaur can now be painted accurately. Most fossils are bones alone, preserved in rocks far coarser than the ash of Liaoning. Still, the old shrug has gone. Colour, once thought to be beyond the reach of science, has become another piece of evidence, telling us not only how dinosaurs looked but where and how they may have lived.
Question: The simile “like seeds scattered across a page” helps the reader picture the fossil melanosomes as . . .
Option A: living things that might one day grow again
Option B: small, separate shapes spread over a flat surface
Option C: objects carefully arranged in neat rows
Option D: large structures that were easy to see

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
The Kitchen Voice
The box sat on Nan's kitchen bench for two days before I opened it. Inside was a new smart speaker, white and smooth as a river stone, with a note from Mum taped to the lid: Theo, the old one stops working at the end of the month. Please swap them over while you're at Nan's. She won't do it herself.
The old speaker lived beside the bread bin. It was the size of a tin of tomatoes, its fabric cover stained with what looked like years of gravy. Nan called it Juniper, though that wasn't its real name. When I'd asked why, she'd said that anyone who listened to her that patiently deserved a proper name.
I had come to stay for the first week of the school holidays, and it didn't take me long to notice how much Nan talked to Juniper. She asked it about the weather while standing at a window. She asked it to play the same Dean Martin song every morning while she made porridge. She asked it how many grams were in a cup of flour, even though the answer was printed on the bag. Once, I heard her ask it whether it thought the magpies were back, and when it said, “Sorry, I don't know that one,” she nodded as if it had made a fair point.
On the third night, I sat at the kitchen table with my laptop to start the swap. The company's website said the new speaker could copy the old one's settings, but first I had to download the old activity log. It was a long list of everything Juniper had been asked, with the date and time beside each request.
I expected weather and Dean Martin, and there was plenty of both. But there was something else, too. Night after night, somewhere between two and four in the morning, the same request appeared: Juniper, what time is it? Sometimes it appeared three or four times in one night, a few minutes apart. And every Sunday afternoon there was another: Juniper, remind me to ring Theo.
I sat looking at the screen for a long time. Nan rang me every Sunday. I had always thought she just had a good memory.
In the morning, I didn't unplug Juniper straight away. Instead, I spent an hour setting up the new speaker so that it answered to the same name. I copied across the Sunday reminder and the porridge song. Then I added something new: a video call to my phone every Wednesday evening, with my photo on the speaker's little screen.
“You've made it look like you,” Nan said when she saw it, squinting suspiciously at the speaker.
“It's so you can see me, not just hear me,” I said. “And you can ring me any time. Even at three in the morning.”
She looked at me sharply, and for a moment I thought she was going to be cross. Then she patted my hand and said nothing at all.
That night I heard her shuffle into the kitchen. “Goodnight, Juniper,” she said.
“Goodnight,” replied the new speaker, in a voice a little brighter than the old one.
There was a pause. “Well,” said Nan, “somebody's had a haircut.”
Question: Which detail shows that Nan treats the old speaker almost as if it were a person?
Option A: “It was the size of a tin of tomatoes . . .”
Option B: “. . . she nodded as if it had made a fair point.”
Option C: “The old speaker lived beside the bread bin.”
Option D: “It was a long list of everything Juniper had been asked . . .”

The Novel in the Safe
In 1989, a man named Jean Verne set about opening an old family safe. Everyone believed it was empty, and the key had long been lost, so the safe had to be forced open. Inside lay a handwritten manuscript: a novel his great-grandfather, Jules Verne, had written more than a century before. It was called Paris in the Twentieth Century, and almost nobody alive knew it existed.
Jules Verne was born in 1828 in Nantes, a busy port city in western France. As a boy he watched ships arrive from distant places, and a well-loved family story claims that, at about eleven, he tried to sneak aboard a ship bound for the Indies before his father caught him. Whether or not the story is true, the young Verne certainly longed for adventure. His father, a lawyer, had other plans: Jules was sent to Paris to study law.
In Paris, Verne spent far more time writing plays and visiting libraries than preparing for a legal career. He read everything he could find about geography, engineering and the latest scientific discoveries. In 1862 he met Pierre-Jules Hetzel, a publisher looking for exciting books for young readers. The following year Hetzel published Verne's Five Weeks in a Balloon, the story of an expedition across Africa by hot-air balloon. It was a huge success, and the two men agreed that Verne would write a series of “extraordinary voyages” — journeys to the centre of the Earth, under the sea, around the world and even to the Moon.
Not every manuscript pleased Hetzel. Around 1863, Verne gave him Paris in the Twentieth Century, a novel set in the 1960s. It described a city of tall buildings, electric street lights, cars powered by gas engines and calculating machines in offices. It also imagined a society that valued only money and machines, where a young poet like its hero could find no place. Hetzel rejected it firmly. He told Verne the book was gloomy and unbelievable, and that it would damage his reputation. Verne put the manuscript away and, as far as we know, never tried to publish it again.
Instead, he wrote the adventurous, optimistic novels that made him famous. From the Earth to the Moon (1865) sent three travellers into space from Florida — the same number of astronauts, and the same state, that the real Apollo missions would use about a century later. Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1870) featured the Nautilus, an electric submarine far more advanced than any vessel of its day.
Verne never claimed to be predicting the future. He saw himself as a storyteller who took known science and asked how far it might go. Yet his “gloomy” rejected novel turned out to be surprisingly accurate. When it was finally published in 1994, readers were astonished at how closely his imagined 1960s resembled the real one.
Verne died in 1905, having written dozens of novels. It took another eighty-nine years for the book his publisher had refused to reach readers — and to show that the young writer's darkest vision had been one of his sharpest.

Option A: in a library in Paris
Option B: in a family safe that was thought to be empty
Option C: among Hetzel's old papers
Option D: in a cabin on a ship in Nantes

The Beetles That Cleared the Paddocks
When the Hungarian-born scientist George Bornemissza arrived in Australia in 1951, he noticed something most Australians had stopped seeing. The paddocks were littered with old cow pats: some fresh, some dried into hard grey crusts, many smothering the grass beneath them. In his homeland, dung like this vanished within days. Here, it could sit for months.
Bornemissza soon worked out why. Australia has hundreds of native dung beetle species, but they evolved over millions of years alongside kangaroos, wombats and other marsupials. Marsupial droppings are small, dry pellets. Cattle, brought by European settlers from 1788, produce something very different: large, wet pats, and plenty of them. A single cow may drop around a dozen pats a day. Most native beetles simply could not cope with this unfamiliar food, and so the pats piled up.
The problem was more serious than it looked. Each pat smothered a patch of pasture, and the grass around it grew rank and was avoided by grazing cattle. Nutrients that should have returned to the soil stayed locked on the surface. Worst of all, the pats became nurseries for the native bush fly. A single pat can produce hundreds of flies, and in summer the swarms were so thick that the “Aussie salute”, a wave of the hand in front of the face, became part of the national character.
Bornemissza's solution was simple in theory: bring in dung beetles from places where cattle had lived for thousands of years, such as Africa and southern Europe. In 1965, the CSIRO launched the Australian Dung Beetle Project, which he helped to lead. Its scientists were cautious; the memory of the cane toad, released in 1935 with disastrous results, was still fresh. Every beetle species was tested to make sure it would eat only dung and would not carry diseases. Eggs were cleaned and treated before the young beetles were reared and released.
Between 1968 and 1984, more than forty species were introduced, and about two dozen became established. Each has its own preferences: some suit cooler, wetter regions; others thrive in the tropical north; some are active in spring, others in late summer. They also work in different ways. Tunnellers dig shafts beneath a pat and drag dung down into them; dwellers live inside the pat; rollers shape balls of dung and push them away to bury elsewhere.
The results have been impressive, although they are not complete. Where beetles are active, a pat can be broken up and buried within a day or two. Buried dung feeds the soil, and the tunnels let rainwater soak in rather than running off. Fly numbers in many areas have fallen noticeably. Nevertheless, there are still gaps, particularly in early spring, when few species are active, and researchers continue to search for beetles that can fill them.
Bornemissza died in 2014, but his beetles are still at work. They are a reminder that even the smallest, least glamorous creatures can quietly change a whole landscape.

Option A: neat and orderly

Mend It, Don't End It
Somewhere in your house there is a drawer. In it lie a phone with a cracked screen, a pair of headphones that only works in one ear and a charger whose cable has frayed to the copper. Nobody uses them, nobody throws them out, and nobody fixes them. It is time our schools did something about that drawer. Every high school should run a monthly repair café.
The idea is not new. The first repair café was held in Amsterdam in 2009, when a local woman invited neighbours to bring their broken belongings to a meeting place where volunteers would help mend them. Today there are thousands around the world, including many in Australian towns and suburbs. People arrive with wobbly chairs, torn jackets and silent toasters, and a surprising number leave with them working again.
Imagine that energy in a school hall. Our design and technology rooms already hold soldering irons, sewing machines and screwdrivers. Our teachers already know how to use them. What is missing is the habit of opening something up before giving up on it.
The case begins with waste. Electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing kinds of rubbish on the planet. Australians produce more than twenty kilograms of it per person every year, and worldwide, less than a quarter of it is properly recycled. The rest is dumped, burned or left in drawers like yours. Every gadget that is repaired instead of replaced is one less tangle of plastic and metal in landfill, and one less new device that must be mined, manufactured and shipped.
Then there is the learning. A student who replaces a cracked screen learns more about how a phone works than any textbook diagram could teach. A student who sews on a button or swaps a bicycle chain gains a quiet confidence that carries over to other problems. These are not old-fashioned skills; they are survival skills for a century that must use its resources far more carefully than the last.
Some will object that modern devices are designed to be difficult to open, and that is partly true. Some manufacturers glue batteries in place or use unusual screws. But this is a reason to teach repair, not to abandon it. Students who understand why a product cannot be fixed become adults who ask hard questions before they buy. Others will worry about safety. Fair enough: no student should be poking around inside a microwave. Repair cafés already handle this sensibly, with clear rules about what can and cannot be attempted and an adult supervising every bench.
Finally, a repair café would give the community a reason to visit the school. Grandparents who once darned socks and rewired lamps could share what they know. Parents could bring along the lawnmower that never starts. And students would be the ones holding the screwdriver.
We have become very good at throwing things away. A repair café is a small, practical way to become good at something better. So open the drawer, take out that sad little pile of broken things, and ask your principal a simple question: when can we start fixing them?

The Stationmaster Wore Whiskers
In January 2007, a small country railway station in Wakayama, Japan, welcomed a new stationmaster. She wore a smart navy cap with a gold badge, greeted passengers at the ticket gate and was paid entirely in cat food. Her name was Tama, and she was a calico cat.
Tama was born in 1999 and grew up near Kishi Station, the last stop on a short rural line that carried students, farmers and elderly residents into the city of Wakayama. She was one of several cats looked after by Toshiko Koyama, who ran a small grocery shop beside the station. The cats lived in a shelter near the platform, and regular passengers grew used to seeing them dozing in the sun.
At the time, the line was in serious trouble. Passenger numbers had been falling for years as more people drove cars, and the company running it had been losing money. In 2006, a new company, Wakayama Electric Railway, took over the line to save it from closing. To cut costs, it decided that stations like Kishi would no longer have staff. That decision also meant the cats' shelter, which stood on station land, would have to go.
Mrs Koyama asked the company's president, Mitsunobu Kojima, whether the cats could stay. Kojima met Tama and was struck by how calm and friendly she was with strangers. Instead of simply giving permission, he made her the official stationmaster. The station needed a staff member, he reasoned, and Tama was already there every day.
Kojima knew a good story when he saw one. Newspaper and television crews soon arrived, and before long tourists were travelling from across Japan, and later from overseas, just to see a cat in a cap. In the first year after her appointment, the number of passengers using the line rose noticeably. Local businesses sold Tama postcards, toys and sweets, and one study estimated that she had added more than a billion yen to the local economy.
Tama was promoted several times, eventually earning the title “super stationmaster”. Her first office was a converted ticket booth, but in 2010 Kishi Station was rebuilt in the shape of a cat's face, with two pointed ears on the roof and windows for eyes. Trains decorated with paintings of Tama began running on the line.
Through all the fuss, Tama herself seemed unbothered. Photographs show her sitting patiently on the ticket counter or curled up asleep in her glass-walled office while visitors pressed against the window with their cameras. She was reported to keep regular working hours, with days off each week.
Tama died in June 2015, at the age of sixteen. Thousands of people attended a farewell ceremony at the station. Within two months, another calico cat, Nitama, whose name means “Tama the Second”, had been appointed to carry on her work.
The little line is still running. It was saved, in large part, by a cat who did nothing more than be herself, and by two people who saw that this was enough.
Question: In which paragraph does the reader learn why the cats' shelter had to be removed?
Option A: the second paragraph
Option B: the third paragraph
Option C: the fourth paragraph
Option D: the fifth paragraph

The Morning After the Shake
Grandad's teacups woke me before the earthquake did. At least, that is how it felt. I was lying on the fold-out bed in his front room in Wellington when I heard a fine, high chattering from the dresser, like a crowd of tiny people whispering all at once. Then the floor gave a long, rolling shrug, the window frames creaked, and the chattering became a rattle.
“Ella!” Grandad's voice came from the hallway, calm but loud. “Under the table. Now, love. Hold on to the leg.”
I scrambled out of the blankets and crawled beneath the heavy kitchen table. Grandad arrived a second later, lowering himself stiffly onto his knees beside me, his torch beam swinging across the floor. We held a table leg each. The house swayed like a boat at its mooring. Somewhere a door banged. The teacups rang against each other in a way that set my teeth on edge.
Then, as suddenly as it had begun, it stopped. The silence afterwards was enormous. A dog barked a few streets away, and a car alarm wailed and gave up.
“Well,” said Grandad, after we had waited a full minute to be sure, “that was just the city clearing its throat.” He shone the torch around the kitchen. “Nothing broken. Back to bed, I reckon.”
That wasn't quite true. When he swept the beam across the dresser, I saw that one cup, a pale blue one with a gold rim, had slid off its saucer and lay on its side with a crack through the handle. Grandad looked at it for a moment, then turned the torch away.
The cups had belonged to his mother. There were thirty-one of them, collected over sixty years, and Grandad dusted them every Sunday whether they needed it or not.
I didn't sleep much after that. Every time a truck rumbled past, my heart jumped. Around dawn, I heard small sounds from the kitchen and got up to look.
Grandad was sitting at the dresser in his dressing-gown, a tub of museum putty open beside him. He was pressing a tiny ball of grey putty under each saucer and each cup, fixing them gently to the shelves. On the table behind him, the emergency kit had been unpacked and repacked. I could see new batteries for the radio, a list of phone numbers in his careful handwriting, and the water bottles lined up with their dates facing outwards.
“Couldn't sleep?” I asked.
“Slept like a log,” he said. “Just thought I'd make use of the early start.” He pressed another ball of putty into place. His fingers, I noticed, were not quite steady.
I pulled up a chair beside him and held out my hand. After a moment he dropped a pinch of putty into it, and we worked along the shelf together without saying much. The blue cup he set aside on the windowsill, where the early light caught its gold rim.
“Glue will fix that,” I said.
“It will,” said Grandad. “It'll never be quite the same, mind. But it'll hold.”
Outside, the city was waking up as usual: buses sighing at the stops, a neighbour calling to her cat. It all sounded ordinary. Inside, the cups sat silent on their shelves, each one held firmly in place.

Option A: so that she can help him find the torch
Option B: to keep her warm during the cold night
Option C: to protect her from things that might fall
Option D: because the fold-out bed might collapse

The Last Round
At nine o'clock on a Thursday night, the museum belonged to Nan and me. The last cleaners had gone home, the front doors were bolted, and the great hall, which on weekends echoed with school groups and squeaking pushers, was so quiet that I could hear the hum of the drinks machine at the far end.
“Stay close,” Nan said, clicking on her torch. “And don't touch anything you can't name.”
For thirty-one years, Nan had worked here as a night security officer. Tomorrow she would retire, and after months of asking, her supervisor had agreed that I could come along on her final patrol, provided I signed a form, wore a visitor's lanyard and promised not to wander. I had imagined it would be spooky, the way museums are in films: shadows lurching, glass eyes following you, footsteps behind you that stop when you stop.
It wasn't like that at all.
In the first gallery, the whale skeleton hung from the ceiling on steel cables, each rib as long as a canoe. Nan swept her torch along its spine until the beam reached the enormous jaw. “Evening, Gerald,” she said.
“Gerald?”
“He needed a name. Thirty years is a long time to walk past someone without saying hello.”
We moved through the minerals room, where her torchlight set off tiny explosions of colour: violet amethyst, crusts of green malachite, a lump of fool's gold that winked like a cheeky grin. In the bird gallery, hundreds of stuffed parrots, owls and wrens perched in tall cabinets, frozen mid-glance. In the dark, they looked less like specimens and more like an audience waiting politely for a show to begin. Nan checked every door handle, tugged every lock and peered at the temperature gauges, writing the numbers in a small notebook in neat, upright figures.
“Do you ever get scared?” I asked.
She thought about it. “Once. My first winter, a possum got in through the roof and knocked over a sign in the Egyptian room. I nearly called the police.” She smiled. “After that, I learnt the sounds the building makes. The pipes knock when the heating comes on. The skylights tick as they cool. It's not haunted. It just talks to itself.”
At the end of the dinosaur hall, under the long, arched neck of a sauropod skeleton, there was a wooden bench. Nan sat down and switched off her torch. For a moment the darkness was total. Then my eyes adjusted, and I saw the skeleton outlined faintly against the glow of an exit sign, enormous and patient, like something that had been waiting for us since long before the building was built.
“This is my favourite spot,” Nan said softly. “Every night for thirty-one years, I've had a sit-down here at half past ten. People think the night shift is lonely. It's not. It's just quiet company.”
We sat there until her watch beeped. Then she stood, switched on the torch and finished the round.
Back at the security desk, she opened the logbook and wrote the time and the words “All secure”, as she had thousands of times before. Then, underneath, in smaller letters, she added: Goodnight, everyone. Look after them for me.
She closed the book gently, as though it might wake something.

The Box That Isn't Black
When an aircraft crashes anywhere in the world, investigators immediately begin searching for two devices: the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder. Together they are often called the 'black box', although neither of them is black. Both are painted a vivid orange so that they can be spotted among wreckage, mud or seaweed. Remarkably, the idea behind them came from a young Australian scientist working in a Melbourne laboratory in the 1950s.
David Warren had a personal reason to care about air safety. When he was a boy, his father was among the passengers on the aircraft Miss Hobart, which disappeared over Bass Strait in 1934. No trace of what went wrong was ever found.
In 1953, Warren was a chemist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories when he was asked to help explain a series of crashes involving the Comet, the world's first jet airliner. The investigators had almost nothing to go on. Warren remembered a pocket-sized recorder he had seen at a trade fair and began to wonder. What if every aircraft carried a device that recorded the pilots' voices and the readings of the instruments? Investigators would no longer have to guess.
His superiors were unconvinced. Some officials argued that the device would be of no use to the people actually flying the aircraft, and pilots objected that it would be like having a spy in the cockpit. Warren kept working on the idea, often in his own time, and by 1958 he had built a prototype that stored four hours of speech and instrument readings on a reel of steel wire.
The breakthrough came from overseas. A visiting British aviation official saw the prototype and arranged for Warren to demonstrate it in London, where it attracted enormous interest. Back home, attitudes shifted after a passenger aircraft crashed near Mackay in Queensland in 1960 and investigators could not establish the cause. The inquiry recommended that recorders be fitted to airliners, and Australia later became the first country to make cockpit voice recorders compulsory.
Modern recorders look very different from Warren's wire-reel machine. They store information on memory chips and can track hundreds, sometimes thousands, of measurements, such as altitude, speed and engine temperature. The memory is sealed inside a casing designed to survive a tremendous impact, intense fire and the crushing pressure of deep water. Each recorder also carries a beacon that sends out signals underwater for weeks, helping searchers find it on the sea floor.
The true value of the black box lies less in explaining any single accident than in preventing the next one. When investigators learn that a part failed or a warning was misunderstood, manufacturers can redesign the part and airlines can retrain their crews. Each lesson is shared across the industry, which is one reason flying is now among the safest ways to travel. Warren, who died in 2010, lived to see his invention carried by airliners all over the world. A boy who had lost his father to an unexplained crash had given the world a way to make sure fewer questions went unanswered.
Question: Why are flight recorders painted orange?
Option A: so they can survive the heat of a fire
Option B: so pilots can tell the two recorders apart
Option C: so they can be spotted easily among wreckage
Option D: so they match the colour of airline uniforms

Late Arrivals
I.
This morning, at the dry end of summer, the tank stands empty,
a corrugated drum the colour of old spoons.
I lean in at the inlet and call my own name,
and the tank thinks it over,
then hands it back to me, rounder and slower,
as if it had carried the word down a long hallway
and returned with it wrapped in tin.

Dad says sound is only the air being pushed,
one invisible shoulder nudging the next,
and that inside the tank the push has nowhere to go
but round and round the ribbed walls
until it finds the way out it came in.
I call again. The tank, patient as a cow,
chews my voice and gives it back.

I whisper, and the tank whispers.
I hum, and it hums a little after me,
like a choir that knows only one song
and is always a beat behind the conductor.
For a moment I wonder whether the tank is lonely,
standing out here all summer with nothing inside
but the shapes of the words I lend it.

II.
After lunch Dad is mending the boundary fence,
small as a toy soldier across the home paddock.
I watch the sledgehammer rise and fall,
and the strange thing is
the post is already struck, the hammer already lifting,
before the clang comes wandering over the grass to me.

I try to count the gap the way I count to ten,
but it is far too small for counting,
just a stitch of time between the seeing and the hearing,
a thread pulled tight across the paddock.

Light is the fast one, Dad told me once.
It crosses the paddock before you can blink.
Sound is the old dog that follows behind,
taking its time, sniffing at every tussock.
So I am always watching the present
and listening to the past,
a heartbeat apart, a half-second late.

III.
At dusk the first stars come out over the shed,
and I remember what my teacher said:
that some of that light set off
before anyone I know was born,
so I am seeing those stars the way they were,
not the way they are tonight.

I try to picture a beam of light
leaving a star before the first fence went up on this farm,
crossing all that black, cold distance without stopping,
just to land, tonight, in the eye
of a kid by a shed who happened to look up.

IV.
Then the phone rings in the kitchen.
It is Nan, in Glasgow, where it is morning,
her voice reaching us under oceans
along a cable thinner than my wrist.
When I say hello there is a tiny pause,
a gap where my word is still travelling,
and then she laughs, and the laugh is from a moment ago,
and still it is the warmest thing in the house.

She tells me about the rain on her window
and the robin that visits her bird table.
I tell her about the tank and the hammer,
and every sentence we send each other
takes a small breath before it lands.

Everything I see or hear has already happened:
the tank, the hammer, the stars, the laugh.
But I have decided that late is not the same as lost.
The echo came home. The clang found me.
The starlight finished its enormous journey.
And Nan's voice, from half a world away,
arrived exactly when I needed it.

Option A: a toy soldier
Option B: dry grass
Option C: old spoons
Option D: a ribbed wall

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
Harry Butler's Island
The workers arriving on Barrow Island in the 1960s were often surprised by the checks. Before they stepped ashore, their boots, bags and equipment were searched for seeds, soil, insects and, above all, stowaway rats and mice. The man behind the rules was Harry Butler, a naturalist who believed that a single mouse could do more damage to the island than an entire oilfield.
Butler was born in Perth in 1930. As a boy he spent every spare hour in the bush around the city, turning over logs, watching lizards and learning the calls of birds. The bush was his classroom long before he ever stood in front of one. He trained as a teacher and worked in country schools in Western Australia, but his weekends and holidays belonged to the animals. He became a skilled collector for the Western Australian Museum, travelling to remote places to record creatures that scientists had never studied closely.
Barrow Island, off the Pilbara coast, was one of those places. Because it had been cut off from the mainland for thousands of years, it had escaped the foxes, cats and rabbits that had devastated wildlife elsewhere. Small marsupials that had vanished from much of the mainland still lived there. When oil was discovered on the island and a company began drilling, many conservationists feared the worst.
Butler made a decision that puzzled some of his friends. Instead of campaigning against the company, he agreed to work for it as an environmental adviser. He reasoned that the drilling would go ahead with or without him, and that from the inside he could shape how it was done. He helped design the quarantine system, advised where roads and pipes should go, and taught workers to report any animal they found injured or out of place. Some critics said he had sided with industry. Butler replied that the animals did not care whose side anyone was on, only whether they survived.
Decades later, Barrow Island remains a lifeboat for wildlife, carrying species that have all but sunk on the mainland. It is often held up as an example of industry and conservation working side by side.
In 1976 Butler became a household name when the ABC began screening his television series In the Wild. Viewers watched him wade through swamps, cradle goannas and talk about spiders with the kind of delight most people reserve for a winning football team. He never talked down to his audience. To him, every Australian was a naturalist who simply had not started yet.
In 1979 he was named Australian of the Year. He continued to advise companies and governments for the rest of his life, always arguing that development and nature could share the land if people planned carefully. When he died in 2015, tributes described him as the man who had taught a generation of Australians to look closely at the creatures underfoot.

Option A: is a safe refuge where animals are protected
Option B: is surrounded by deep and dangerous water
Option C: is where animals are taken by boat to be studied
Option D: is slowly sinking further into the sea

Changeover Day
On the morning of Monday the fourteenth of February 1966, my grandfather stood behind the counter of our corner shop, holding a shiny new coin up to the light as if it might be a fake.
'Ten cents,' he said, turning it over. 'Same size as a shilling. Different face.'
I was twelve that summer, and I had been looking forward to Changeover Day for months. The television had been full of a cartoon character called Dollar Bill, who sang cheerful songs about the new money, and at school we had practised with cardboard coins until we could convert in our sleep. Ten shillings made one dollar. One shilling made ten cents. A pound became two dollars. It was simple, I told Pop. Even a child could do it.
'A child, perhaps,' he said. 'It's the rest of us I'm worried about.'
Pop had run the shop for thirty years. He could add up a basket of groceries in pounds, shillings and pence faster than any adding machine, his lips moving silently as the numbers fell into place. Now the bank had sent a cash register that showed only dollars and cents, and a printed chart that hung beside it, listing old prices with their new values.
Our first customer was Mrs Kostas, who wanted bread and milk. She paid with old coins, and I worked out her change in new ones. When she had gone, Pop wrote the sum on the back of a paper bag in his own careful way, just to check.
'Right to the cent,' he said, and I felt about two metres tall.
By mid-morning the shop was full of confusion. The old and new money would be used side by side for a while, so customers paid with florins and expected cents, or paid with dollar notes and asked for pennies. Then Mr Hendry came in for his newspaper, as he had every morning since before I was born. He tipped a handful of mixed coins onto the counter and stared at them through his reading glasses as if they were a train timetable in a foreign language. Finally he pushed some across.
I counted them. 'That's two cents short, Mr Hendry, you need to —'
Pop's hand rested lightly on my arm. 'That's right, Arthur,' he said. 'Spot on.' He folded the paper and passed it over.
I opened my mouth, then closed it again. Pop gave me a look over his glasses that I did not fully understand until many years later, when the shop was mine and Mr Hendry's grandson came in for a paper of his own.
That night, after we pulled down the blind, Pop sat at the kitchen table with the chart and a cup of tea. He was still checking sums on the backs of paper bags, long after the till had balanced.
'You'll get used to it,' I said.
'I expect I will,' he said, without looking up. 'Thirty years is a long time to count one way, love.'
I kissed the top of his head and left him to it. From the hallway I could hear the coins clinking softly as he turned them over, one by one, learning them.

Option A: "Even a child could do it."
Option B: "It's the rest of us I'm worried about."
Option C: "By mid-morning the shop was full of confusion."
Option D: "Thirty years is a long time to count one way . . ."

The Willows Come Down
The willows along Cutter's Creek had been there longer than I had, and longer than my dad. Grandad planted them himself the summer he bought the farm, pushing cuttings into the soft bank with his boot, one every few metres, the way his own father had done in England. By the time I was born they had grown into a long green curtain that trailed its fingers in the water.
So when the woman from the Landcare group came to the kitchen door and said the willows should come out, I expected Grandad to show her the gate.
He didn't. He listened. She explained that willows are not native to Australia and that they cause trouble in creeks like ours. Their roots spread into the channel and trap silt, so the water is pushed sideways and eats into the banks. In autumn they drop all their leaves at once, and the leaves rot in the water and use up the oxygen that fish need. Native trees shed a few leaves at a time, all year round, which a creek can cope with.
'I've watched that creek for fifty years,' Grandad said when she had finished.
'Then you'll have noticed it's getting shallower,' she said gently.
He didn't answer that. He just poured her another cup of tea.
The excavator came in March. I sat on the fence rail beside Grandad and watched the bucket bite into the bank and lift out whole trees, roots and all, dripping mud. Where the curtain had been there was suddenly sky, and a raw brown wound along the water's edge. Grandad's jaw worked as though he were chewing something tough. When the last willow was dragged away, he climbed down from the fence without a word and walked back to the house.
That winter, the Landcare volunteers returned with hundreds of seedlings in plastic tubes: river red gums, bottlebrush and tussocks of spiny-headed mat-rush. Grandad was the first one out in his gumboots. He worked all morning, kneeling in the mud, firming each little plant into the ground with his thumbs. I asked him why he was helping, after everything.
'A man can be wrong for fifty years,' he said, 'and still be useful in the fifty-first.'
The creek did not change overnight. For a while it looked worse, bare and scraped. But by the next spring the banks had stopped crumbling, and the water ran clearer and faster over a bed of stones I had never seen before. One evening Grandad called me down to the bank in a voice I hadn't heard him use. He was crouched beside a still pool, pointing.
A small dark head broke the surface, then a flat bill, then the ripple of a body rolling under.
'Platypus,' he whispered. 'First one I've seen here since your dad was a boy.'
We stayed until it was too dark to see. On the way back, Grandad stopped at the shed and showed me a terracotta pot on the windowsill. In it was a single willow cutting, green and thriving.
'Just the one,' he said. 'Somewhere it can't do any harm.'

Option A: leaves that have fallen into water
Option B: fine soil carried along by water
Option C: small fish that live in creeks
Option D: tangled roots under a riverbank

The Willows Come Down
The willows along Cutter's Creek had been there longer than I had, and longer than my dad. Grandad planted them himself the summer he bought the farm, pushing cuttings into the soft bank with his boot, one every few metres, the way his own father had done in England. By the time I was born they had grown into a long green curtain that trailed its fingers in the water.
So when the woman from the Landcare group came to the kitchen door and said the willows should come out, I expected Grandad to show her the gate.
He didn't. He listened. She explained that willows are not native to Australia and that they cause trouble in creeks like ours. Their roots spread into the channel and trap silt, so the water is pushed sideways and eats into the banks. In autumn they drop all their leaves at once, and the leaves rot in the water and use up the oxygen that fish need. Native trees shed a few leaves at a time, all year round, which a creek can cope with.
'I've watched that creek for fifty years,' Grandad said when she had finished.
'Then you'll have noticed it's getting shallower,' she said gently.
He didn't answer that. He just poured her another cup of tea.
The excavator came in March. I sat on the fence rail beside Grandad and watched the bucket bite into the bank and lift out whole trees, roots and all, dripping mud. Where the curtain had been there was suddenly sky, and a raw brown wound along the water's edge. Grandad's jaw worked as though he were chewing something tough. When the last willow was dragged away, he climbed down from the fence without a word and walked back to the house.
That winter, the Landcare volunteers returned with hundreds of seedlings in plastic tubes: river red gums, bottlebrush and tussocks of spiny-headed mat-rush. Grandad was the first one out in his gumboots. He worked all morning, kneeling in the mud, firming each little plant into the ground with his thumbs. I asked him why he was helping, after everything.
'A man can be wrong for fifty years,' he said, 'and still be useful in the fifty-first.'
The creek did not change overnight. For a while it looked worse, bare and scraped. But by the next spring the banks had stopped crumbling, and the water ran clearer and faster over a bed of stones I had never seen before. One evening Grandad called me down to the bank in a voice I hadn't heard him use. He was crouched beside a still pool, pointing.
A small dark head broke the surface, then a flat bill, then the ripple of a body rolling under.
'Platypus,' he whispered. 'First one I've seen here since your dad was a boy.'
We stayed until it was too dark to see. On the way back, Grandad stopped at the shed and showed me a terracotta pot on the windowsill. In it was a single willow cutting, green and thriving.
'Just the one,' he said. 'Somewhere it can't do any harm.'
Question: What changes in the creek had appeared by the next spring?
Option A: The creek looked bare and scraped and the water was muddy.
Option B: The new seedlings had grown into a long green curtain.
Option C: The water had become deeper and slower over the stones.
Option D: The banks had stopped crumbling and the water ran clearer.

Getting to the Other Bank: Crossing a Creek on Foot
On many Australian bushwalks, the track eventually meets water. Most creek crossings are simple: a few stepping stones and a short wobble. But after heavy rain even a small creek can become fast, cold and powerful. Water flowing at walking pace and only knee deep can push hard enough to knock an adult off their feet. These steps will help your group decide whether to cross and how to do it safely.
Step 1: Stop and assess
Before anyone enters the water, the whole group should stop together on the bank. Look at the colour of the water: if it is brown and carrying sticks or leaves, the creek is probably rising. Throw a stick in and watch how fast it travels. Then ask the most important question of the day: do we need to cross at all? Creeks that flood after storms often drop again within hours. Waiting on the bank, or choosing a different route, is not a failure. Experienced walkers turn back far more often than beginners realise, and this is one reason they have been walking for so long.
Step 2: Choose your crossing point
If the group decides to go ahead, walk along the bank to find the best place. Look for a wide section where the water is shallow and slow, with a gentle exit on the far side. Avoid the outside of bends, where the current is strongest, and never cross just above rapids, a waterfall or a fallen log, where a slip could trap you.
Step 3: Prepare your gear
Unclip the hip belt and chest strap on your pack so that you can slip out of it quickly if you fall. Keep your boots on: bare feet are easily cut on rocks you cannot see, and they grip poorly. Store anything that must stay dry, such as a phone or sleeping bag, in a waterproof bag inside your pack.
Step 4: Cross carefully
Face upstream and move sideways, shuffling your feet rather than lifting them high. Keep at least two points of contact with the bottom at all times; a walking pole planted upstream can act as a third leg. For stronger currents, cross as a group. Two or three walkers can stand one behind the other in a line pointing upstream, each holding the pack of the person in front. The walker at the front, who should be the strongest, breaks the force of the water for those behind. Move only when everyone is ready, and keep talking to each other as you go.
Step 5: Regroup on the far bank
Once everyone is across, count heads. Check that nobody is shivering or injured, and change into dry socks if you have them. Cold, wet feet on a long day can cause blisters and make walkers miserable.
A final word
The safest crossing is the one you plan before you leave home. Check the weather forecast and ask park rangers whether recent rain has affected the creeks on your route. If the answer is uncertain, pack enough food for an unplanned wait. A delay of a few hours is an inconvenience. Rushing into a flooded creek can be far worse.
Question: According to the guide, which sign suggests that a creek is rising?
Option A: brown water carrying sticks or leaves
Option B: clear water flowing over stones
Option C: a stick that floats slowly downstream
Option D: a gentle exit on the far side

Centring the Clay
My grandmother's studio smells of wet earth and cold tea,
and every shelf is crowded with her years:
blue jugs, fat-bellied jars, a teapot with a crooked spout
that she says she will never sell.

On the bench lie tools I have no names for,
a sponge, a wooden rib, a needle on a stick,
and a radio that only ever plays the cricket,
turned down low, in case she wants the score.

She slaps a lump of clay onto the wheel
the way other people close a door,
dips her hands in the bucket, and says,
Before you make anything, you have to centre it.

The wheel begins to hum. The clay begins to turn.
I lean in and push, and the lump lurches sideways,
a lopsided moon trying to escape its orbit,
slapping wet against my palms.
Too hard, she says. You're fighting it.
Clay remembers every argument.

I try again. The wall I raise
rises, thins, wobbles, sags,
and folds into itself like a tired tent.
Gran slices it off the wheel with a wire
and slaps down another lump without a word,
as if failure were just another ingredient
she keeps in a jar beside the sink.

Four times the clay collapses.
Four times she scrapes and slaps and waits.
My arms ache, my jeans are spattered grey,
and I begin to suspect the clay has a grudge
against me in particular.

She shows me how to brace my elbows on my knees,
how to let the spinning do the work,
how to coax the clay instead of commanding it,
pressing steadily, breathing slowly,
until the wobble under my hands grows smaller
and smaller, and then, quite suddenly, is gone.

It feels like a held note,
like the moment a bike stops being a struggle
and becomes a kind of flying.
The clay is still turning, but it seems to stand still.
That's it, Gran says. Now it will listen to you.

By the end of the afternoon I have one small bowl,
thick at the bottom, thin on one side,
with a thumbprint pressed into the rim
where I steadied it too late.
I want to squash it and start again.
Gran takes it from me before I can.

It's ruined, I say. Look at it.
She turns it slowly in the window light,
the way a jeweller studies a stone,
and says only, Leave it to dry.

Weeks later, when it comes out of the kiln
glazed the green of a gum leaf after rain,
she sets it on the top shelf
between the crooked teapot and a jar
she made the year she married Grandpa.
I tell her it isn't good enough to keep.

She runs one finger round the thumbprint.
Nothing up here is perfect, she says.
That's why I keep them. Every single one
is a day I didn't give up.

Gran still says I push too hard.
She is probably right.
But up there, between her teapot and her jar,
a small green bowl with a thumbprint in its rim
reminds me how a wobble can disappear.

Now, when homework tangles or a friend says something sharp
and the whole world seems to lurch on its wheel,
I brace my elbows, and I breathe,
and I wait for the wobble to settle,
pressing steadily, gently, patiently,
until the day begins to listen to me.
Question: What can the reader infer from the line "every shelf is crowded with her years"?
Option A: Gran has been making pottery for a long time.
Option B: Gran's studio is too small for her pottery.
Option C: Gran keeps old calendars on her shelves.
Option D: Gran has only recently started making pottery.

Centring the Clay
My grandmother's studio smells of wet earth and cold tea,
and every shelf is crowded with her years:
blue jugs, fat-bellied jars, a teapot with a crooked spout
that she says she will never sell.

On the bench lie tools I have no names for,
a sponge, a wooden rib, a needle on a stick,
and a radio that only ever plays the cricket,
turned down low, in case she wants the score.

She slaps a lump of clay onto the wheel
the way other people close a door,
dips her hands in the bucket, and says,
Before you make anything, you have to centre it.

The wheel begins to hum. The clay begins to turn.
I lean in and push, and the lump lurches sideways,
a lopsided moon trying to escape its orbit,
slapping wet against my palms.
Too hard, she says. You're fighting it.
Clay remembers every argument.

I try again. The wall I raise
rises, thins, wobbles, sags,
and folds into itself like a tired tent.
Gran slices it off the wheel with a wire
and slaps down another lump without a word,
as if failure were just another ingredient
she keeps in a jar beside the sink.

Four times the clay collapses.
Four times she scrapes and slaps and waits.
My arms ache, my jeans are spattered grey,
and I begin to suspect the clay has a grudge
against me in particular.

She shows me how to brace my elbows on my knees,
how to let the spinning do the work,
how to coax the clay instead of commanding it,
pressing steadily, breathing slowly,
until the wobble under my hands grows smaller
and smaller, and then, quite suddenly, is gone.

It feels like a held note,
like the moment a bike stops being a struggle
and becomes a kind of flying.
The clay is still turning, but it seems to stand still.
That's it, Gran says. Now it will listen to you.

By the end of the afternoon I have one small bowl,
thick at the bottom, thin on one side,
with a thumbprint pressed into the rim
where I steadied it too late.
I want to squash it and start again.
Gran takes it from me before I can.

It's ruined, I say. Look at it.
She turns it slowly in the window light,
the way a jeweller studies a stone,
and says only, Leave it to dry.

Weeks later, when it comes out of the kiln
glazed the green of a gum leaf after rain,
she sets it on the top shelf
between the crooked teapot and a jar
she made the year she married Grandpa.
I tell her it isn't good enough to keep.

She runs one finger round the thumbprint.
Nothing up here is perfect, she says.
That's why I keep them. Every single one
is a day I didn't give up.

Gran still says I push too hard.

a small green bowl with a thumbprint in its rim
reminds me how a wobble can disappear.

and the whole world seems to lurch on its wheel,

pressing steadily, gently, patiently,
until the day begins to listen to me.

The Page Turner
The concert begins at eight o'clock.
The hall holds six hundred velvet seats,
and every one of them is full tonight,
and not one person has come to see me.

I am the page turner.
I sit on a low chair to the left of the pianist,
dressed in black so I can disappear,
a shadow with a pulse and good eyesight.
My whole job fits inside a single sentence:
turn the page at the right moment, and never be noticed.

It sounds easy. It isn't.
I have to read the music half a line ahead of her,
following the black notes like stepping stones across a river,
counting the bars, watching her shoulders,
waiting for the tiny nod she gives
when the bottom of the page is coming.

Too early, and her eyes meet a page she isn't ready for.
Too late, and her hands race on into blank air.
Either way, six hundred people would hear the stumble,
and the stumble would be mine.

Before the concert I washed my hands twice
so that no smudge would ever reach her pages,
and I bent each corner very slightly
so my fingers could find it without looking.
These are small things. Small things are the whole job.

Tonight she plays the sonata she has practised all year:
twenty-two minutes long, eighteen pages, seventeen turns.
It is the most beautiful music ever written.
I have heard it a hundred times in rehearsal
and it still lifts the hair on my arms.

In the second movement there is a page
that has to be turned in the nick of time,
while her left hand is already leaping
and her right is holding a long, trembling note.
I stand, reach, flick the corner,
and slide back down onto my chair
as quietly as a cat settling on a windowsill.
Nobody claps for that. Nobody should.

My heart is going like a drum roll now,
but my face must stay as calm as a lake.
If she glanced across and saw my panic,
it might slip into her fingers and out into the hall.

I have learned that silence is not empty.
It is a room I keep tidy for her,
a space where the music can lean without falling.
If I do my job perfectly,
the audience will leave believing
the pages turned themselves.

At the end the applause comes down like rain on a tin roof,
and she stands, and bows, and bows again,
and someone hands her a bunch of white roses.
I stay seated, as I have been told,
hands folded, eyes on the floor.

People are standing in the aisles to clap,
calling out her name, calling for more,
and she plays one short, bright piece from memory,
with no pages at all, and no need of me.

Still, as the hall empties and the lights go down,
she turns to me before she leaves the stage
and touches the closed music with two fingers,
then touches my shoulder in the same way,
as if to say: we did this together.

At home my mum will ask me how it went,
and I will tell her, Nothing happened.
For a page turner, there is no higher praise.

Nobody will remember my name tomorrow.
Page turners are not printed in the program.
But I was there for every one of those seventeen turns,
and not one of them was late.
Question: Where does the page turner sit during the concert?
Option A: on a low chair to the left of the pianist
Option B: in the front row of the audience
Option C: on a high stool behind the piano
Option D: on a low chair to the right of the pianist

Let the Nature Strip Bloom
Walk down almost any suburban street in Australia and you will see the same thing between the footpath and the road: a narrow strip of lawn, mowed short, watered in summer and mostly ignored. It is time our council changed its rules and encouraged residents to replace these tired rectangles of grass with low native gardens.
At present, the council allows only grass on nature strips, unless a resident applies for a special permit that costs $150 and can take months to approve. This rule made sense decades ago, when lawns were cheap to keep and water seemed endless. It makes far less sense today.
Consider the water. A lawn in our climate can need watering several times a week through summer. Hardy local plants such as kangaroo paw, native grasses and creeping boobialla, once established, survive mostly on rainfall. Every household that switches saves water, and the street looks greener in February rather than brown.
Native plantings also feed wildlife. A strip of flowering shrubs provides nectar for honeyeaters and food for native bees, which a mown lawn simply cannot do. Join several gardens along one street and you create a corridor that small birds can travel along safely, hopping from shrub to shrub instead of crossing open ground where larger birds can chase them.
Then there is heat. On a summer afternoon, bare ground and short grass bake in the sun, while a layer of plants and mulch keeps the soil cooler and holds moisture after rain. Gardens also give children something to notice on the walk to school: a lizard sunning itself, or a bee working along a row of flowers.
Some people worry that gardens will block drivers' views or trip pedestrians. These are fair concerns, but they have simple answers. Councils elsewhere already set sensible limits: plants no taller than half a metre, a clear path at least a metre wide for people getting out of parked cars, and no rocks or hard edges.
I have seen this work. Three years ago, my neighbour Mr Okafor grew tired of dragging his mower out every weekend, especially after his knee operation. First he asked the council for a permit, then he waited five months for an answer. When approval finally arrived, he dug out the couch grass, laid thick mulch and planted twenty small natives from the local nursery, each chosen from a list of species that grew in our area before houses were built. Within a year, eastern spinebills, small honeyeaters with curved beaks, were visiting each morning. Within two, three other families on our street had followed his lead, and they did not bother with permits at all.
That is the real problem. A rule that most people ignore, and that blocks something good, is not doing its job. The council should drop the fee, publish clear height and safety guidelines, and perhaps offer free seedlings to get people started.
Our nature strips are public land, but they are also the first thing anyone sees of our street. Let us make them places that hum with bees rather than lawnmowers.
Question: What does the council currently allow on nature strips without a permit?
Option A: only grass
Option B: only native grasses
Option C: plants under half a metre
Option D: grass and mulch

The Pigeon Lady
At ten minutes to midnight on the nineteenth of March, the whole street went quiet. Above us, the falla rose four storeys high: a laughing sun in spectacles, holding a paintbrush in each of its twelve hands. That morning it had seemed indestructible. Now firefighters were soaking the shopfronts with hoses, and I knew it had about fifteen minutes left.
'Everything we build, we burn,' Grandpa Tomás had told me in October, the first night I went with him to our neighbourhood workshop. I thought he was being dramatic. He was not.
He had been making ninots, the figures that make up a falla, for forty years. His hands knew things mine did not: how to layer wet paper over a clay mould, how to sand a cheek until it caught the light. All winter I swept the floor and mixed paste, some nights staying until eleven, with the radio playing and the whole room smelling of glue and sawdust, and in January he finally let me make a figure of my own. It was only knee-high: an old woman on a bench, scattering crumbs for three pigeons. I gave her Grandma's crooked smile and her habit of wearing odd socks.
'She is too good for the fire,' said Señora Puig, who ran our group. And so my little woman was chosen as our street's entry for the exhibition.
Every year in Valencia, each falla sends one ninot to be displayed in a great hall before the festival. Visitors vote, and the single most popular figure is pardoned. It is carried to the museum and kept forever, while every other ninot meets the flames. For three weeks I imagined my pigeon lady behind museum glass. I visited her twice and stood nearby, pretending to read the labels. I counted the people who stopped to smile at her odd socks.
She did not win. A grinning octopus in a chef's hat won by thousands of votes. When she came back and was fixed to the base of our falla, I would not look at her.
'You are angry with the fire before it has even been lit,' Grandpa said. I did not answer.
Now the streetlights went out. A string of firecrackers snapped across the square like a drum roll, and the first flames licked the bench where my pigeon lady sat. I made myself watch. Her paper cheeks blackened and curled. The pigeons went first, then the odd socks, then the smile.
And something strange happened. The crowd, thousands of people packed shoulder to shoulder, cheered for her. For her, and for the sun in spectacles, and for all the winter nights of paste and sandpaper that had made them. The heat pressed on our faces like an open oven.
Grandpa's hand found my shoulder. 'Next October,' he said, 'you'll make something bigger.'
Walking home through streets thick with smoke and music, a little boy beside us asked his mother why anyone would make something so beautiful just to set it alight.
I answered before she could. 'Everything we build, we burn,' I told him. 'That's how we get to build again.'

Option A: a girl winning a prize for her festival sculpture
Option B: a girl learning to accept the burning of a figure she made
Option C: a grandfather teaching his granddaughter to paint
Option D: a family travelling to Valencia to see a festival

When the Sand Sings
In the thirteenth century, the Venetian traveller Marco Polo described a desert in Central Asia where travellers heard strange sounds: drums, music and voices that seemed to call them away from their companions. Lost travellers, he warned, could be lured off the track and never found. For centuries, stories like his were treated as legends. Today scientists know that at least part of the explanation lies under travellers' feet. Some sand dunes really do sing.
The phenomenon is called booming sand. It has been recorded at only around forty sites in the world, including the Kelso Dunes in California's Mojave Desert, Mingsha Shan, or 'Singing Sand Mountain', in western China, and dunes in Morocco, Oman and Namibia. The sound is a deep, steady drone, often compared to a low-flying propeller plane or a cello note held for a very long time. It can last for several minutes and, on still days, has been heard many kilometres away.
Booming does not happen just anywhere. Most sand on Earth is silent. Booming occurs on the steep downwind face of large dunes, called the slip face, when a layer of sand slides downhill in an avalanche. The grains must be very dry, so booming is rare after rain. They also tend to be well rounded, similar in size and coated in a smooth glaze, which lets them slide past one another easily. If sand from a booming dune is washed or becomes damp, it usually loses its voice.
One of the first scientists to study moving sand seriously was Ralph Bagnold, a British army officer and engineer who explored the Libyan Desert in the 1920s and 1930s. Bagnold was fascinated by how wind shapes dunes, and he described booming sand in his famous book on the subject. His careful measurements of how sand moves are still used by desert scientists today.
Modern researchers have often had to make dunes sing on purpose. Waiting for a natural avalanche could take days, so teams climb to the crest and slide down the slip face on their bottoms, pushing a wave of sand ahead of them while microphones and sensors record the result. It looks like play, but it allows scientists to repeat the same test many times. Other teams have carried booming sand back to laboratories and poured it down narrow chutes to see whether it would sing far from the desert.
Exactly why the sand booms is still debated. One group of researchers argued that when millions of grains tumble together, their collisions fall into step, like a crowd clapping in rhythm, producing a single strong note. Another group suggested that the dune acts like a musical instrument: a loose top layer of dry sand sits over firmer, damper sand, and the sound bounces around within the top layer, which makes it louder.
Whatever the final answer, the desert has turned an old fear into a scientific puzzle. Marco Polo's ghostly voices may simply have been sand, sliding in the quiet of the night.
Question: Where are the Kelso Dunes?
Option A: in western China
Option B: in the Libyan Desert
Option C: in Namibia
Option D: in California's Mojave Desert

'Nobody picks me first,' he said cheerfully as she sat down. 'I'm the book at the back with the boring cover.'
'What were you in the dark for?' Mei asked, because it seemed rude not to.
'Showing people films,' he said. 'I was the projectionist at the Regent Theatre for forty years. Up in a hot little room at the back, behind a square of glass, while everyone below watched the screen.'
Mei sat up. She had watched one film three times last holidays and could recite whole scenes.
He told her how films once arrived in heavy metal cans, with each reel lasting about twenty minutes, so a long film needed several reels and two projectors. Mei returned her slip. On the way out she passed a table with a sheet headed: Student Books Wanted for Next Year. What story could you lend? A few names were already written underneath.
She stopped, uncapped her pen, and wondered what her title might be.

Option A: They had been told to go there first.
Option B: Those books were nearer the door.
Option C: Those books were giving out prizes.
Option D: Their titles sounded more exciting.

Their first customer that morning had been easy, a sleepy old gelding who leaned on Aunt Ros like a fence post. The second was not. Juniper was a young grey mare who had arrived at the property only a month earlier, and she danced sideways the moment the ute door slammed.

Before the Stories Slip Away
Every family has a storyteller: the grandparent who remembers the flood of 1974, the great-aunt who arrived by ship with one suitcase, the uncle who once met a famous cricketer at a petrol station. Their memories are a family treasure, but unlike photographs, they are not stored anywhere safe. Recording an interview is one of the simplest ways to keep them.
Step 1: Ask permission and choose a focus
Explain to your relative why you want to record them and how you will use the recording. Some people are delighted; others feel shy. Never record anyone without their agreement. Then choose a focus, such as their childhood or their first job. A whole life is too much for one sitting.
Step 2: Prepare your questions
Write ten to fifteen open questions, ones that cannot be answered with yes or no. 'Did you like school?' invites a one-word reply. 'What was a normal school day like for you?' invites a story. Start with easy, cheerful questions to break the ice, and save harder topics for later, once your relative feels relaxed.
Step 3: Find a quiet place
Microphones hear everything. The hum of a fridge, the tick of a clock, the clink of a teaspoon, the rustle of a biscuit packet: noises you barely notice in a room can drown out a soft voice on a recording. Choose a carpeted room with the doors closed, switch off the television and put phones on silent.
Step 4: Test your equipment
A phone is perfectly good for recording, but test it first. Record thirty seconds of yourself talking at the distance you plan to sit, then play it back. Check that your phone has enough storage and battery, and keep a charger nearby, because good stories rarely finish when you expect them to. If you are filming as well as recording sound, rest the phone on a small stand or a stack of books so the picture stays steady.
Step 5: Listen more than you speak
Begin the recording by saying the date, the place and both your names. Then let your relative take the lead. If they wander from your question into a different memory, follow them; some of the best stories are detours. Resist the urge to fill silences. A pause often means someone is remembering, not that they have finished. Nod rather than saying 'mm-hmm', which can clutter the recording.
Step 6: Label and store
Afterwards, thank your relative and save the file with a clear name, such as 'Grandad Joe, farm childhood, June 2026'. Keep a copy in a second place. Many families also write a short summary of each interview so that others can find particular stories later.
When my cousin and I interviewed our grandmother, we planned to ask about her wedding. Instead, she spent forty minutes describing the dairy farm she grew up on, including a cow that learned to open the gate with her nose. None of us had ever heard that story. Two years later, the recording was played at her ninetieth birthday, and it is now the most-shared file in our family.

Option A: ten to fifteen
Option B: five to ten
Option C: fifteen to twenty
Option D: about thirty

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
The Clown of the Mountains
High in the Southern Alps of New Zealand lives a bird that seems to treat the whole world as a puzzle to be solved. The kea is the only parrot on Earth that makes its home in alpine country, among snowfields, rocky slopes and stunted beech forest. It is also, according to many scientists, one of the most intelligent birds ever studied.
At first glance a kea looks rather plain: a large, olive-green parrot with a long, curved grey beak. When it spreads its wings, however, it reveals a flash of brilliant orange-red underneath. That beak is a remarkable tool. Kea use it to dig up roots, pry open rotten logs for grubs and tear apart tough plants, which helps them survive in a place where food can be scarce for months at a time.
Living in such a harsh environment may explain why kea are so curious. A bird that will investigate anything new is more likely to discover new sources of food. Visitors to the mountains soon learn that this curiosity has a cost. Kea have been seen peeling rubber seals from car windows, unzipping backpacks and flying off with gloves, hats and other small items left unattended.
Researchers have tested kea in many ways. In one experiment, birds learned that orange tokens earned a food reward while black ones did not. They were then shown two jars holding different mixtures of the two colours. A researcher took one token from each jar without letting the birds see its colour and held out both closed hands. The kea usually chose the hand holding the token from the jar with the higher proportion of orange tokens, even when it held fewer orange tokens overall. This suggested that kea can judge likelihood, a skill once thought to belong mainly to humans and great apes.
Kea are playful too. Young birds toss objects, roll in snow and wrestle with each other. Scientists discovered that kea have a special warbling call used during play. When they played a recording of it to wild kea, the birds that heard it often began to play, rather like people who start laughing when they hear someone else laugh.
Sadly, the kea's boldness has not always served it well. In the past, farmers accused kea of attacking sheep, and for about a century a bounty was paid for dead birds. Around 150,000 were killed before the species was fully protected in 1986. Today kea are endangered. Because they nest in hollows and burrows on the ground, introduced predators such as stoats and possums can easily raid their nests.
People are now finding ways to live alongside these clever birds. When kea kept moving the traffic cones at a mountain road works site, workers built a climbing frame of ropes and pipes nearby, hoping to give the birds something better to do. Rangers ask visitors never to feed kea, since human food can make them sick and teaches them to hang around car parks.
A kea that pulls apart your windscreen wipers may seem a nuisance. Yet that same restless curiosity is exactly what has helped the species survive in one of the toughest places on Earth.
Question: In 'food can be scarce for months at a time', the word 'scarce' means . . .
Option A: easy to reach
Option B: frozen solid
Option C: bad to eat
Option D: hard to find

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
Don't Throw Away the Sextant
On a modern ship's bridge, a navigator can find the vessel's position to within a few metres simply by glancing at a screen. Satellite navigation has made ocean travel safer than ever before, and I would never argue that ships should switch it off. But something important is being lost. Every navigator, from naval officers to weekend sailors, should still learn to find their way by the sun and stars with a sextant.
A sextant is a hand-held instrument that measures the angle between a heavenly body, such as the sun, and the horizon. Combined with an accurate time and a book of tables, that angle allows a navigator to work out the ship's position. Sailors crossed oceans this way for more than two centuries.
The first reason to keep this skill is simple: electronics fail. Satellite signals can be disrupted by severe solar storms. Ships lose power. Antennas are damaged in rough weather. When the screen goes blank in the middle of the Indian Ocean, a crew with no other method is suddenly, frighteningly lost. A sextant needs no batteries, no signal and no subscription.
Navies have taken this seriously. In 2015, the United States Naval Academy brought celestial navigation back into its training after dropping it for nearly twenty years, partly because of concerns that satellite systems could be interfered with. If some of the world's most advanced navies think the old skill is worth teaching, surely the rest of us should listen.
The second reason is less obvious but just as important. Learning to navigate by the sky changes how a sailor thinks. Someone who has taken a sun sight knows roughly where the ship should be, so they are far more likely to notice when a screen shows something that makes no sense. Accident investigators have described cases where crews trusted a faulty position on a display, even when the coastline outside the window disagreed.
Critics say the sextant is a museum piece, that it takes too long to learn and that clouds can hide the sky for days. All of this is partly true. Celestial navigation does demand practice and patience, and it is less precise than satellites. But no one is suggesting it should replace modern tools, only that it should sit beside them, like a spare tyre in the boot of a car. You hope you never need it. You would be foolish to leave home without it.
I learned to use a sextant at sixteen, on a sail-training voyage along the New South Wales coast. Our skipper, a weathered woman named Helen Marsh, made us take a noon sight every day even though the chartplotter worked perfectly. We grumbled. On the fourth day, a power fault blanked every screen for six hours. Helen calmly asked who had that day's figures. We knew exactly where we were.
Satellites are a marvel. Let us keep using them. But let us also keep teaching the quiet art of reading the sky, before the last people who know how to do it put their sextants away for good.

Option A: a simile
Option B: a rhetorical question

Option D: a statistic

A sextant is a hand-held instrument that measures the angle between a heavenly body, such as the sun, and the horizon. Combined with an accurate time and a book of tables, that angle allows a navigator to work out the ship's position. Sailors crossed oceans this way for more than two centuries.
The first reason to keep this skill is simple: electronics fail. Satellite signals can be disrupted by severe solar storms. Ships lose power. Antennas are damaged in rough weather. When the screen goes blank in the middle of the Indian Ocean, a crew with no other method is suddenly, frighteningly lost. A sextant needs no batteries, no signal and no subscription.
Navies have taken this seriously. In 2015, the United States Naval Academy brought celestial navigation back into its training after dropping it for nearly twenty years, partly because of concerns that satellite systems could be interfered with. If some of the world's most advanced navies think the old skill is worth teaching, surely the rest of us should listen.
The second reason is less obvious but just as important. Learning to navigate by the sky changes how a sailor thinks. Someone who has taken a sun sight knows roughly where the ship should be, so they are far more likely to notice when a screen shows something that makes no sense. Accident investigators have described cases where crews trusted a faulty position on a display, even when the coastline outside the window disagreed.
Critics say the sextant is a museum piece, that it takes too long to learn and that clouds can hide the sky for days. All of this is partly true. Celestial navigation does demand practice and patience, and it is less precise than satellites. But no one is suggesting it should replace modern tools, only that it should sit beside them, like a spare tyre in the boot of a car. You hope you never need it. On the fourth day, a power fault blanked every screen for six hours. Helen calmly asked who had that day's figures. We knew exactly where we were.
Satellites are a marvel. Let us keep using them. But let us also keep teaching the quiet art of reading the sky, before the last people who know how to do it put their sextants away for good.
