Gumnuts and Banksia Men
Long before Australian children read about boy wizards, many of them grew up with a very different fantasy world: a bush full of tiny gumnut babies, kindly blossom folk and the wicked, bristly Banksia Men. That world was the creation of May Gibbs, one of the first artists to imagine Australian plants and animals as characters in their own magical stories.
Cecilia May Gibbs was born in England in 1877 and came to Australia with her family as a small child. They settled first in South Australia and later in Perth, where her father, himself a painter, encouraged her drawing. As a girl she roamed the bush near her home, sketching wildflowers, insects and the twisted shapes of trees, and she later said the bush seemed full of hidden life if you looked closely enough.
Determined to become a professional artist, Gibbs travelled to London three times to study and find work. It was not easy. Publishers there wanted fairies with gauzy wings and English bluebells, and a young woman from Western Australia had to compete with established illustrators. She produced book covers and newspaper drawings, but she struggled to earn a steady living, and in 1913 she returned to Australia and settled in Sydney.
It was there that her most famous characters appeared. Gibbs began drawing small figures wearing gumnut caps, first on bookmarks and postcards. Soldiers serving overseas in the First World War were sent the cards from home, and the little bush creatures quickly became popular. In 1916 she published Gumnut Babies, and in 1918 came her best-known book, Snugglepot and Cuddlepie, about two gumnut brothers who set out to see a human. Along the way they meet bush characters with names as playful as their looks, such as Little Ragged Blossom and Mr Lizard.
The villains of that story, the Banksia Men, came from something Gibbs had noticed as a child: the old, dried seed cones of banksia trees, whose gaping seed pods looked like whiskery faces with open mouths. Children who had never looked twice at a banksia cone suddenly saw a scowling face in every one.
Gibbs went on to create the comic strip Bib and Bub, about two gumnut friends, which ran in newspapers for more than forty years. In 1925 she and her husband moved into a house on Sydney Harbour that she named Nutcote, where she worked in her studio until old age. Her stories often carried a gentle message about being kind to bush creatures and leaving wildflowers unpicked.
When May Gibbs died in 1969, she left the rights to her characters to children's charities, so that money earned from her books would continue to help young people. Nutcote is now a museum. More importantly, her stories changed the way many Australians looked at their own landscape. In her hands, the bush was no longer a harsh, strange place to be compared unfavourably with English meadows, but a world with its own magic, waiting under every leaf.

Reading the Leaf Litter
Volunteer Field Guide: Leaf-Litter Survey, Plot 7
Welcome to the team. Most visitors to a tropical rainforest look up, towards the canopy, the orchids and the birds. This survey asks you to look down. The thin layer of fallen leaves on the forest floor is home to beetles, mites, springtails, ants, pseudoscorpions and tiny snails, many of which have never been given scientific names. These animals break dead plant material into nutrients that the trees reuse within weeks. By counting them each season, we can tell whether the forest floor is healthy or under stress.
Before you start
Wear long pants tucked into your socks, and closed shoes. Leeches are common after rain, and although they are harmless, few volunteers enjoy finding one inside a boot. Bring a water bottle, a pencil (ink smudges in the damp) and your plot sheet. Check that your kit contains a metal quadrat frame, a calico bag, a permanent marker and gloves.
Step 1: Choose your sample point
Your team leader will give you a random number. Walk that many paces along the marked line, then stop. Do not choose a spot because it looks interesting. Volunteers naturally drift towards thick, damp patches where they expect to find more animals, and this makes the results look healthier than they really are. The random number keeps everyone honest.
Step 2: Place the frame
Lay the quadrat flat on the ground without stepping inside it. Many litter animals are sensitive to vibration and will burrow downwards at the first heavy footfall, so move slowly and quietly.
Step 3: Collect the litter
Wearing gloves, gather every leaf, twig and seed inside the frame down to the bare soil, and place it all in the calico bag. Work steadily, but don't jump the gun by tipping the bag before it is sealed; a single lost handful can remove a third of the sample's animals. Label the bag with the plot number, sample point and time.
Step 4: Return to the field station
At the station, the litter is spread on a mesh screen above a funnel, with a lamp shining from above. Over two days, the heat and light slowly dry the leaves from the top down. The animals retreat from the drying layer, moving deeper and deeper until they fall through the mesh into a jar of preserving liquid below. This simple device, called a Tullgren funnel, was designed more than a century ago and is still used by scientists around the world.
Step 5: Sort and count
Using a magnifying lamp, sort the animals into groups and record the totals on your sheet. Don't worry if you can't identify everything. A careful 'unknown beetle, brown, 2 mm' is far more useful to us than a confident guess that turns out to be wrong.
A final word
Leaf-litter work can feel slow. You may spend an hour on your knees and collect nothing more exciting than a bag of damp leaves. But this survey has now run for eleven years, and every bag adds to the picture. Last spring, one volunteer's careful sorting turned up a mite never before recorded in Australia. Small things, it turns out, are worth looking at closely.
Question: In Step 4, the word retreat means . . .
Option A: rest quietly in one place
Option B: multiply in large numbers
Option C: dry out completely
Option D: move back away from something

Ahead of the Sledges
In April 1909, a small party of men and dogs stood on the frozen Arctic Ocean, at what they believed was the North Pole. For decades, history books named only one of them: the American naval officer Robert Peary. Yet the man who had driven the lead sledge, broken the trail and spoken with the Inuit guides in their own language was Matthew Henson.
Henson was born in Maryland in 1866, the son of free Black farmers. Both of his parents died while he was still young, and at about twelve he made his way to the port of Baltimore and signed on as a cabin boy aboard a merchant ship. Its captain, a man named Childs, took an interest in the quiet, quick-witted boy. He taught Henson to read and write, and introduced him to the basics of navigation. By the time Henson left the sea, he had sailed to China, Africa and Europe.
In 1887, while working in a hat shop in Washington, he met Peary, who hired him as an assistant for a surveying trip to Central America. It was the start of a partnership that lasted more than twenty years and took Henson to the Arctic seven times.
On these expeditions, Henson became indispensable. He was a skilled carpenter who could build and repair sledges from whatever materials were at hand. More importantly, he took the time to learn from the Inughuit people of north-western Greenland. He became fluent in their language, learned to drive dog teams and build igloos, and earned the trust of the families whose knowledge kept the expeditions alive. In temperatures that could fall below minus forty degrees, such skills were the difference between survival and disaster. Some of them gave him an affectionate name, Miy Paluk, often translated as 'dear little Matthew'.
The 1909 journey was the last and most ambitious. The party set out from Cape Columbia on Ellesmere Island and crossed hundreds of kilometres of shifting sea ice. Support teams turned back one by one, as planned, until only Peary, Henson and four Inuit men, Ootah, Egingwah, Seegloo and Ooqueah, remained. Henson often travelled in front, and by his own account he reached the final camp before Peary did. Whether the party truly stood at the exact Pole is still debated, because their navigation records were incomplete.
When the expedition returned, Peary was celebrated with medals, banquets and lecture tours. Henson received little. Many accounts of the day described him simply as Peary's assistant, if they mentioned him at all. He published an account of his travels in 1912 and then worked for many years as a clerk in a government customs office in New York.
Recognition came slowly. In 1937 he was invited to join the Explorers Club in New York, and in 1944 he was awarded a medal by the United States Congress. He died in 1955. In 1988, his remains were moved to Arlington National Cemetery, near Washington, and buried beside Peary's. Today a United States Navy survey ship carries his name.

Option A: He saw promise in him and wanted to help.
Option B: He found him lazy and hard to manage.
Option C: He paid him little attention on the voyages.
Option D: He was suspicious of his reasons for sailing.

In London at the end of the 1700s, most children from poor families never went to school at all. Lessons cost money, teachers were few, and many children were sent out to work as soon as they could carry a load. Joseph Lancaster, the son of a sieve-maker, believed this was a terrible waste, and he set out to fix it with almost no money at all.
Lancaster was born in 1778 in Southwark, a crowded district south of the River Thames. As a teenager he was restless and full of big ideals. At about fourteen he ran away from home, planning to teach poor children in Jamaica, but he got only as far as Bristol and spent a short time on a navy ship before returning home.
In 1798, when he was about twenty, he opened a small school in a room of his father's house on Borough Road. He charged very little, and children whose parents could not pay were taught for free. Word spread quickly. Soon there were far more pupils than one young teacher could possibly manage, and no money to employ assistants.
Lancaster's solution was to turn the pupils into teachers. He divided the school into small groups according to ability rather than age. In each group, an older or more advanced child, called a monitor, taught the others a lesson that the monitor had learned from Lancaster earlier that day. Other monitors handed out slates, took the roll or checked that books were returned. Lancaster moved about the huge room, keeping an eye on everything.
He was just as inventive about saving money. Paper was expensive, so the youngest children practised their letters by tracing them with a finger in trays of sand, which could be smoothed flat and used again. Older children wrote on slates. Instead of buying a book for every child, Lancaster printed lessons on large cards hung on the walls, so a whole group could read from one card at once. He disliked the canings common at the time and relied mainly on rewards such as badges and small prizes.
By 1805, the Borough Road school had around a thousand pupils. Visitors came to watch a single teacher running a school of that size, and supporters raised money to open similar schools across Britain and beyond. The organisation they formed, later called the British and Foreign School Society, kept training teachers long after Lancaster himself had moved on.
Lancaster was better at inspiring people than at managing money. He spent freely, fell deeply into debt and quarrelled with his supporters. In 1818 he left for America, where he started new schools, but he never again matched the success of Borough Road. He died in New York in 1838.
Historians today see the monitorial system as far from perfect. Children learned mostly by repeating facts, and a monitor of eleven or twelve could pass on only what he or she had been told. Even so, Lancaster showed that schooling could be offered cheaply to thousands of poor children, an idea that helped convince governments that education for everyone was possible.

Forty Onions
The first thing Jaya learned at the Westside Community Kitchen was that Mr Okafor did not say hello. He looked up from the stove when she came through the back door on Saturday morning, glanced at her new apron, and pointed his wooden spoon at a sack in the corner.
'Onions,' he said. 'Forty. Diced.'
Jaya had signed up because her school required twenty hours of community service, and the kitchen was the only place within walking distance of home. Her mother had laughed when she heard. 'You? In a kitchen? You burn toast.' She had imagined serving meals with a friendly smile, not crying over a chopping board while a man with a grey beard ignored her.
By the sixth onion, her eyes were streaming and her pieces were all different sizes. Mr Okafor came over, took one look and swept the whole pile into a bowl.
'Stock,' he said. 'Start again.'
Jaya felt her face go hot. She nearly untied her apron there and then. Instead, she grabbed another onion and attacked it, harder this time, determined not to give him the satisfaction of seeing her quit.
'Stop.' He was beside her again. This time he did not take the board away. He put his large hand over hers and tilted the knife so the tip rested on the board. 'You are chopping like you are angry with it. The onion has done nothing to you. Rock the blade. Let the knife do the work. Curl your fingers, so.' He showed her, his knuckles guiding the side of the blade. 'Cut the root last. The root holds it together, and it holds the tears in too.'
She tried it. The slices came out thin and even. He grunted, which she would later learn was the closest he came to praise, and went back to his pot.
Mr Okafor did not look at her again, but when she reached for the next onion, he slid a bowl of cold water along the bench. 'Wet the knife,' he said. 'Helps.'
By the twentieth onion, she had found a rhythm. By the thirtieth, her eyes had almost stopped stinging. By the fortieth, the smell of onions softening in oil filled the hall, and people had begun to line up outside.
At noon, Jaya stood at the serving table beside a woman named Rosa, who had volunteered every Saturday for nine years. Jaya's arms ached and her apron smelt of onion, but she found she didn't mind.
'He made me do the onions too,' Rosa said, ladling stew into a bowl. 'Everyone does the onions on their first day. Half of them never come back.'
'Why does he do it?'
Rosa shrugged. 'He says if you can't be patient with an onion, you won't be patient with people.' She nodded at the queue, where an elderly man was slowly counting out coins he did not need to pay. 'And people here need patience more than anything.'
Jaya watched the man carry his bowl to a corner table and close his eyes as the steam rose into his face. Somewhere in that stew were her forty onions.
The following Saturday, she arrived ten minutes early. Mr Okafor looked up from the stove, glanced at her apron, and almost smiled.
'Carrots,' he said.

Option A: She wanted to learn to cook for her family.
Option B: Her friend Rosa had asked her to help.
Option C: Her school required community service hours.
Option D: Mr Okafor had offered her a paid job.

In a kitchen? You burn toast.' She had imagined serving meals with a friendly smile, not crying over a chopping board while a man with a grey beard ignored her.
By the sixth onion, her eyes were streaming and her pieces were all different sizes. Mr Okafor came over, took one look and swept the whole pile into a bowl.
'Stock,' he said. 'Start again.'
Jaya felt her face go hot. She nearly untied her apron there and then. Instead, she grabbed another onion and attacked it, harder this time, determined not to give him the satisfaction of seeing her quit.
'Stop.' He was beside her again. This time he did not take the board away. He put his large hand over hers and tilted the knife so the tip rested on the board. 'You are chopping like you are angry with it. The onion has done nothing to you. Rock the blade. Let the knife do the work. Curl your fingers, so.' He showed her, his knuckles guiding the side of the blade. 'Cut the root last. The root holds it together, and it holds the tears in too.'

Jaya watched the man carry his bowl to a corner table and close his eyes as the steam rose into his face. Somewhere in that stew were her forty onions.

The Riddle of the Bare Circles
From the air, parts of the Namib Desert in south-western Africa look as though they have been decorated with polka dots. Thousands upon thousands of bare, round patches, each a few metres across, sit in a sea of grass. Each circle is ringed by taller tufts, and the circles are spread so evenly that they form a pattern rather like the cells of a honeycomb. They are known as fairy circles, and for decades they have puzzled scientists.
For a long time, fairy circles were thought to exist only in Africa. Then, in the mid-2010s, an environmental consultant working in the Pilbara region of Western Australia spotted similar patterns in the spinifex grassland near the mining town of Newman. When researchers studied aerial images, they found the same remarkably regular spacing. Their 2016 report caused great excitement, because circles on opposite sides of the Indian Ocean offered a chance to test competing explanations.
The first explanation blames termites. Supporters of this idea point out that sand termites are often found living beneath the Namibian circles. By eating grass roots, the termites may kill the plants above them, creating a bare patch where rainwater soaks deep into the sand and is stored. The termites then have a reliable underground water supply, and the grass around the edge grows taller because it can reach that stored water.
The second explanation involves no animals at all. According to this idea, the grasses themselves create the pattern. In a very dry landscape, each clump competes with its neighbours for scarce water. Roots spread out to draw moisture from the surrounding soil, leaving gaps where nothing can survive. Computer models based on this kind of competition produce spots spaced almost exactly like real fairy circles. Similar self-organising processes are thought to explain other patterns in dry places, such as the stripes of vegetation seen on gentle slopes in parts of Africa and Australia.
The Australian circles added a new twist. The first researchers reported that the Pilbara circles did not seem to be linked to termites, which appeared to support the grass idea. Other scientists, however, worked with the Martu people, whose Country includes the area. Martu elders explained that the bare patches, which they call linyji, are hard pavements made by termites, and that their people had known and used these surfaces for generations. This knowledge sent scientists back to look much more closely at the ground beneath the circles.
Today, many researchers suspect there may be no single answer. Termites and competing grasses may both play a part, and their importance could vary from place to place. What the debate has made clear is that a striking pattern does not need a designer. Simple rules, repeated across a whole landscape, can produce an order that looks almost planned.

Option A: in short supply
Option B: easy to find
Option C: very salty
Option D: deep underground

The Fin That Flapped
The charter boat Kestrel had been out since dawn, and so far the most exciting thing Nell had seen was her uncle Ray's thermos lid blowing overboard. The fish weren't biting. The other passengers, a family from Melbourne and two retired brothers who argued about everything, had settled into a sleepy silence. Nell sat in the stern with her sketchbook, drawing the gulls that followed the boat.
Then one of the brothers stood up so fast his hat fell off. 'Shark!' he shouted, pointing off the left side.
Everyone rushed to the rail. About thirty metres away, a tall grey fin was poking above the surface. The youngest Melbourne child began to cry. Uncle Ray, who had skippered the Kestrel for fifteen years, reached for the throttle.
Nell watched the fin. Something about it was wrong. A shark's fin, she knew from the documentaries she had watched a hundred times, slid through the water in a straight line, steady as a knife. This fin was flopping lazily from side to side, first leaning one way, then the other, like a tired swimmer's arm.
'Wait,' she said. Nobody heard. She said it again, louder. 'Uncle Ray, wait! Sharks don't move their fins like that.'
Ray paused, his hand still on the throttle. The fin tipped right over, and a broad silver shape rolled at the surface, flat as a dinner plate and nearly as wide as the dinghy tied to the stern. A round eye gazed up at the sky.
'Well, I'll be,' said Ray slowly. 'That's a mola. An ocean sunfish.'
The boat went quiet. The fish lay on its side at the surface, perfectly still, while gulls circled above. Ray explained that sunfish often do this, basking in the warm surface water after diving into the cold depths to feed on jellyfish. Some scientists think the birds help by picking parasites off their skin.
'Is it hurt?' asked the Melbourne boy, who had stopped crying.
'Just sunbathing,' said Ray. 'One of the heaviest bony fish in the world, and it lives mostly on jelly.'
The brothers, for once, had nothing to argue about. They stood shoulder to shoulder, phones forgotten in their hands. Nell flipped to a clean page and sketched as fast as she could: the strange, chopped-off shape of the body, the tall fin above and the matching one below, the way the light caught its skin.
After ten minutes the sunfish righted itself, its fin rose, and it began to flop slowly away. Ray waited until it was well clear before he started the engine.
On the trip back to the harbour, nobody complained about the empty fish box. Ray came and sat beside Nell, looking over her drawing.
'Fifteen years,' he said, 'and that's the closest I've ever been to one. If I'd roared off, we'd have missed the whole thing.' He tapped the page. 'Good eyes. Keep using them.'
Nell smiled and added one more detail: a single gull, perched for a moment on the edge of the fin.

Option A: fishing from the side of the boat
Option B: sketching the gulls following the boat
Option C: watching a documentary on her phone
Option D: chasing her uncle's thermos lid

In Praise of the Steel Box
Ask people to name the greatest invention of the last hundred years and you will hear the usual answers: the computer, the aeroplane, the smartphone, perhaps the internet. These are fine choices. But I want to make the case for an invention that most people never think about, even though it almost certainly carried the device you are reading this on. I mean the shipping container.
At first glance, a container is not much to look at. It is a steel box, usually about six or twelve metres long, with doors at one end. It has no engine, no screen and no moving parts apart from its hinges. That plainness is exactly the point.
Before the 1950s, cargo ships were loaded much as they had been for centuries. Teams of dock workers carried sacks, barrels, crates and bales on board one at a time and packed them into the hold by hand. A single ship could take a week or more to load and unload, and goods were often damaged or went missing. Shipping was so slow and costly that it made little sense to send everyday items across the world.
Then, in 1956, an American trucking businessman named Malcolm McLean tried something new. Frustrated by the hours his drivers spent waiting at ports, he loaded fifty-eight truck-sized metal boxes onto an old tanker called the Ideal X and sailed it from New Jersey to Texas. At the other end, the boxes were lifted straight onto trucks, unopened. McLean later calculated that loading his cargo this way had cost a tiny fraction of the usual price.
Within a few decades, containers of standard sizes were in use around the world. Because every port, ship, train and truck could handle the same boxes, goods could travel from a factory in one country to a shop in another without being unpacked once. Loading a ship now takes hours rather than days. As a result, the cost of moving goods has dropped so far that shipping a pair of sneakers across an ocean may add only a few cents to their price.
Some will argue that a box cannot be a true invention because it is too simple. I disagree. The genius of the container lies not in the box itself but in the system around it: the agreement on standard sizes, the cranes designed to lift them and the ships built to stack them. Even the smartphone could not have become cheap and common without it, since its parts are made in many different countries and must travel between them.
It is true that the container brought painful changes. Many dock workers lost their jobs as machines took over, and some old harbour towns declined. These costs were real and deserve to be remembered. But they do not change the fact that the steel box quietly reshaped the way the whole world lives.
So the next time you see a container on the back of a truck, give it a second look. It may be the most important invention you have never thought about.

The City with No Palace
About 4500 years ago, on the banks of the Indus River in what is now Pakistan, stood one of the largest cities in the world. Today we call it Mohenjo-daro, which means something like 'mound of the dead', a name given much later by local people. Nobody knows what its own residents called it, because no one has yet been able to read their writing.
Mohenjo-daro was part of the Indus civilisation, which spread across a region larger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. At its height, the city may have been home to around 40,000 people. What astonishes archaeologists most, however, is not its size but its organisation.
The streets were laid out in a rough grid, with main roads running north-south and east-west. Houses were built from baked bricks, and those bricks were made to remarkably consistent proportions, roughly 4:2:1 for length, width and thickness, across hundreds of kilometres. Many homes had their own wells, bathing areas and even toilets. Waste water flowed from the houses into covered drains beneath the streets, with openings where workers could reach in to clear blockages. Few cities anywhere would have such a system again for thousands of years. Its builders seem to have cared less about showing off and more about plumbing, paving and planning.
On the city's raised western mound lies a structure known as the Great Bath. The Morning Stones Fell on Murchison
Just before 11 am on Sunday 28 September 1969, residents of the small Victorian town of Murchison heard a series of loud bangs overhead. Some looked up to see a bright fireball streaking across the sky, trailing a cloud of smoke. Moments later, dark stones began dropping into paddocks, gardens and roadsides around the town. One crashed straight through the roof of a hay shed.
Local people soon noticed that the black stones had an odd smell, something like methylated spirits. Many collected pieces as souvenirs. Scientists from Melbourne arrived within days, and they were keen to gather as many fragments as quickly as possible. They knew that rain and handling could contaminate the stones, washing away chemicals or adding new ones that would make them harder to study. Altogether, more than 100 kilograms of meteorite was recovered from an area of about 13 square kilometres. Pieces ranged from tiny crumbs to one weighing around seven kilograms.
The Murchison meteorite turned out to be a rare type known as a carbonaceous chondrite. Only a small fraction of the meteorites seen to fall on Earth belong to this group. Most meteorites are made largely of rock or metal, but this kind also contains carbon-based compounds, the kind of chemicals that living things are built from. It is also very old. Material like this formed around 4.6 billion years ago, from the cloud of gas and dust that gave birth to the Sun and planets, and has changed little since. Studying it is a bit like opening a time capsule from the very beginning of the solar system.
The timing of the fall was fortunate. Only two months earlier, Apollo 11 had returned from the Moon, and laboratories around the world had prepared new equipment for studying lunar samples without contaminating them. These laboratories were ready and waiting. When scientists analysed the Murchison samples, they found amino acids, the chemicals that join together to form proteins in living things. Some of these amino acids are rare or unknown on Earth, which suggests they formed in space rather than seeping into the stones after they landed.
The discoveries did not stop there. In 2020, researchers reported that Murchison contains tiny grains of a mineral called silicon carbide that are older than the solar system itself. By measuring how long the grains had been exposed to cosmic rays in space, they estimated that some were around seven billion years old. These grains had formed in stars that died long before our Sun was born.
None of this means that life came to Earth from space. However, Murchison shows that some of the ingredients for life can form naturally far from any planet, and that they can survive a fiery fall to the ground. Pieces of the meteorite are now held in museums and research collections around the world, and scientists are still studying them more than fifty years later.

'Is that a pram or a hiking trolley?' he said instead.

The Book Nobody Can Read
In 1912, a rare-book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought a collection of old volumes from a college near Rome. Among them was a small, battered book of about 240 vellum pages, crowded with flowing handwriting and strange, colourful drawings. More than a century later, the book still carries his name, and it remains one of the most famous puzzles in the world. Nobody has been able to read a single sentence of it.
The trouble begins with the writing itself. The Voynich manuscript uses an alphabet of roughly twenty to thirty symbols that match no known language. Some look a little like Latin letters; others curl like the numeral 9 or loop like a pretzel. The handwriting is smooth and confident, with very few crossings-out, as though the writer knew exactly what they were putting down.
The pictures only deepen the mystery. One section is filled with plants, but botanists have been unable to identify most of them; some seem to combine the roots of one species with the leaves of another. Another section shows circular charts of stars and signs of the zodiac. A third shows small figures bathing in pools connected by tubes that twist like pipes or veins. Whatever the book was meant to be, it seems to have been a guide to something.
For a long time, many people suspected the manuscript was a clever hoax, perhaps forged by Voynich himself to make money. In 2009, however, scientists carbon-dated the vellum and found that it had been made between 1404 and 1438. Tests on the ink suggested the writing was added not long afterwards. Whoever created the book, it was not a twentieth-century dealer.
Since then, the puzzle has attracted code-breakers, linguists, historians and computer scientists. Some think the text hides a known language inside a cipher. Others believe it records a real language that has since disappeared, or a private language invented by one person. Statistical studies have found that its words repeat in patterns similar to those of real languages, which makes a pure nonsense hoax seem less likely, though not impossible. From Frame to Jar: Harvesting Honey
On many small farms in rural Australia, a few beehives are as much a part of the property as the chook shed or the water tank. The bees pollinate orchards and vegetable patches, and in a good season they produce more honey than they need. Harvesting that surplus is not difficult, but it must be done in the right order and at the right time. The steps below describe how it is done on a typical family property.
Choose the right day
Pick a warm, still, sunny day, ideally late in the morning. At this time many of the older worker bees are out foraging, so fewer bees are at home to defend the hive. Bees become irritable in cold, windy or stormy weather, so avoid harvesting when a change is coming.
Check that the honey is ready
Bees store honey in six-sided wax cells in the top boxes of the hive, called supers. While the honey is still thin and watery, the bees fan it with their wings to dry it out. When it is thick enough, they seal each cell with a thin wax cap. A frame is ready when at least three-quarters of its cells are capped. Honey taken too early holds so much water that it can ferment in the jar.
Calm the bees and remove the frames
Put on a bee suit, veil and gloves. Light a smoker filled with dry grass or hessian, and puff cool smoke gently at the hive entrance and under the lid. The smoke masks the alarm scent that guard bees release, and it prompts the bees to fill up on honey, which makes them calmer. Lift out each ready frame, gently brush the bees back into the hive, and place the frame in a covered box.
Always leave some honey behind. A beekeeper who takes everything forces the colony to survive on sugar syrup, or to go hungry through winter. A good rule is to leave at least one full box of honey for the bees.
Uncap and extract
Indoors, with the doors and windows shut, slice the wax caps off each frame using a heated knife. Place the frames in an extractor, a drum that spins them so fast that the honey is flung out of the cells and runs down the walls. Because the comb is left whole, the frames can go straight back into the hive. This saves the bees an enormous amount of work, since they must eat several kilograms of honey to make one kilogram of wax.
Strain and bottle
Pour the honey through a fine strainer to remove bits of wax and the occasional unlucky bee. Let it settle in a bucket for a day or two so that air bubbles rise to the top, then pour it into clean, dry jars. Unlike most foods, properly stored honey does not spoil. Label each jar with the date and, if you know them, the main flowers the bees were visiting, such as clover, canola or yellow box, since each gives honey its own colour and flavour.
Many beekeepers call honey liquid gold, and after a morning in a hot bee suit, most would agree they have earned it. The bees, of course, did the real work: a single worker makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life.

On many small farms in rural Australia, a few beehives are as much a part of the property as the chook shed or the water tank. Harvesting that surplus is not difficult, but it must be done in the right order and at the right time. The steps below describe how it is done on a typical family property.
Choose the right day
Pick a warm, still, sunny day, ideally late in the morning. At this time many of the older worker bees are out foraging, so fewer bees are at home to defend the hive. Bees become irritable in cold, windy or stormy weather, so avoid harvesting when a change is coming.
Check that the honey is ready
Bees store honey in six-sided wax cells in the top boxes of the hive, called supers. While the honey is still thin and watery, the bees fan it with their wings to dry it out. When it is thick enough, they seal each cell with a thin wax cap. A frame is ready when at least three-quarters of its cells are capped. Honey taken too early holds so much water that it can ferment in the jar.
Calm the bees and remove the frames
Put on a bee suit, veil and gloves. Light a smoker filled with dry grass or hessian, and puff cool smoke gently at the hive entrance and under the lid. The smoke masks the alarm scent that guard bees release, and it prompts the bees to fill up on honey, which makes them calmer. Lift out each ready frame, gently brush the bees back into the hive, and place the frame in a covered box.
Always leave some honey behind. A beekeeper who takes everything forces the colony to survive on sugar syrup, or to go hungry through winter. A good rule is to leave at least one full box of honey for the bees.
Uncap and extract
Indoors, with the doors and windows shut, slice the wax caps off each frame using a heated knife. Place the frames in an extractor, a drum that spins them so fast that the honey is flung out of the cells and runs down the walls. Because the comb is left whole, the frames can go straight back into the hive. This saves the bees an enormous amount of work, since they must eat several kilograms of honey to make one kilogram of wax.
Strain and bottle
Pour the honey through a fine strainer to remove bits of wax and the occasional unlucky bee. Let it settle in a bucket for a day or two so that air bubbles rise to the top, then pour it into clean, dry jars. Unlike most foods, properly stored honey does not spoil. Label each jar with the date and, if you know them, the main flowers the bees were visiting, such as clover, canola or yellow box, since each gives honey its own colour and flavour.

Why We Turn Red
You trip on the stairs in front of the whole class, or a teacher reads out your name for the wrong reason, and within seconds you feel it: a wave of heat rising up your neck and into your cheeks. You are blushing, and there is almost nothing you can do to stop it.
Blushing begins in the sympathetic nervous system, the part of the nervous system that prepares the body for sudden challenges. When you feel embarrassed, this system releases adrenaline. Among its many effects, adrenaline causes the small blood vessels in the skin of the face to widen, or dilate. More blood flows close to the surface, and the skin turns pink or red and feels warm. Your heart may beat faster and your breathing may quicken too, because adrenaline is the same chemical that readies the body to face danger.
Why the face, and not the knees or elbows? The skin of the cheeks contains an unusually large number of tiny blood vessels, and they lie closer to the surface than in many other parts of the body. These vessels also appear to respond more strongly to adrenaline. As a result, a blush usually appears on the cheeks first, and may then spread to the ears, the neck and the upper chest.
What makes blushing so frustrating is that it is involuntary. Unlike a smile, which you can put on whenever you choose, a blush is controlled by systems that work outside conscious thought. Worse still, worrying about blushing can trigger a blush, so people who try hardest not to go red often go redder. For a small number of people, the fear of blushing becomes so strong that it affects their daily lives. This condition even has its own name, erythrophobia, from the Greek word for red.
The naturalist Charles Darwin was fascinated by blushing. In his 1872 book about emotional expressions, he described it as the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions. He gathered reports showing that people from many different cultures blush, and noticed that it is linked with being watched or judged by others. As far as scientists know, no other animal blushes.
So why would humans have developed such an awkward signal? One explanation is that a blush works as a kind of apology that is very hard to fake. In a 2009 study, researchers in the Netherlands showed volunteers pictures of people who had just made a social blunder. When the person in the picture was blushing, volunteers judged them more favourably and felt more inclined to trust them. A red face seemed to say, 'I know I got that wrong, and I care what you think.'
Seen this way, the blush that feels so humiliating may actually be working in our favour. It tells others that we understand the unwritten rules of the group and want to remain part of it. That is unlikely to make the next blush any more comfortable, but it might make it a little easier to forgive yourself.

Option A: widen
Option B: shrink
Option C: harden
Option D: burst

The Wombat Who Couldn't Get Out
Nobody volunteers to be Wally the Wombat. Every year, at the assembly before the Kingsford High athletics carnival, Mr Petrakis holds up the furry brown costume like a fisherman displaying a prize catch, and every year the hall goes quiet in a way that suggests four hundred students have suddenly become fascinated by their shoelaces.
This year, I made the mistake of yawning and stretching. Mr Petrakis took my raised arm as enthusiasm, and that is how I, Priya Nair, came to spend the hottest day of March inside a wombat.
The costume was not designed for comfort. The head was a foam dome with mesh eyes the size of twenty-cent coins, and the body zipped up the back with a zip so stiff it took two Year 7s and a tug-of-war technique to close. Mr Petrakis gave it a final yank, patted the top of my head and said, 'Wally's in safe hands.' I couldn't see his face, but I could hear him grinning.
For the first hour, I was magnificent. I high-fived the little kids from the visiting primary school. I did a slow-motion victory dance at the end of the 100 metres. I even attempted a cartwheel, which went less well; wombats, it turns out, are not built for cartwheels, and neither is anyone wearing one.
By eleven o'clock, though, the sun was blazing, the inside of the head smelled like a decade of other people's sweat, and I had drunk two bottles of water through the mouth hole. That was when I realised I needed the toilet. Urgently.
I waddled to the change rooms and reached behind my back for the zip. Nothing. I reached higher. Still nothing. I tried pulling my arms inside and wriggling out through the neck, but the costume had clearly been built for a much smaller wombat. The zip pull, I discovered later, had snapped off in that final yank, leaving a smooth metal stub that no human fingers could grip. I was sealed in.
What followed was not my finest hour. A small girl from the primary school asked if Wally was crying. Wally was not crying. Wally was concentrating. I tried to find Mr Petrakis, but he was starting the 1500 metres and could not hear a large wombat shouting through foam. I asked a Year 9 boy for help, but he was laughing too hard to stand up straight. Finally, my best friend Leila appeared with a pair of pliers borrowed from the groundsman's shed and, after three attempts and a great deal of advice from onlookers, she de-wombatted me in the middle of the oval, to scattered applause.
I made it to the toilets with seconds to spare.
At the end of the day, Wally was named Best Spirit of the carnival, which meant I had to go back up on stage, in the costume, to accept a certificate. The broken zip had been replaced with three enormous safety pins. Mr Petrakis promised, with his hand on his heart, that next year he would find a different volunteer.
He was speaking to me, but he was looking straight at Leila.

Option A: ran quickly without stopping
Option B: crept quietly so as not to be seen
Option C: skipped happily from side to side
Option D: walked clumsily with short steps

In the months before the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, an eighteen-year-old sprinter from Merrylands, in Sydney's west, bought tickets so that she could watch the athletics from the stands. Betty Cuthbert did not expect to be chosen for the Australian team. Within weeks she was not only on it; she was about to become one of the most celebrated athletes the country had ever produced.
Cuthbert's speed had first been noticed at school by her physical education teacher, June Ferguson, herself a former Olympic sprinter. Ferguson became her coach and mentor, and their partnership lasted for most of Cuthbert's career. Cuthbert had an unusual style, running with her mouth wide open and her knees lifted high, but it worked. In September 1956 she broke the world record for the 200 metres, and the selectors could no longer overlook her.
At the Melbourne Games, the shy teenager won the 100 metres, then the 200 metres. Crowds at the Melbourne Cricket Ground began calling her the Golden Girl. Her third gold medal, however, was one she could never have won alone. In the four-by-100-metres relay she joined Shirley Strickland, Norma Croker and Fleur Mellor. Strickland was already a famous Olympian with several medals; Croker and Mellor were younger and far less experienced. In a relay, raw speed is not enough. Each runner must pass the baton to the next inside a marked zone, at full pace, without looking back. One fumbled change can cost a team more time than any single runner can make up.
The four women spent hours practising their changeovers until each knew exactly when to start running and where to hold out her hand. In the final, the baton moved cleanly around the track, and Cuthbert, running the last leg, carried it across the line first. The team set a world record of 44.5 seconds.

As the crowd rose to its feet, it seemed fitting that the Golden Girl's last Olympic appearance was, once again, part of a relay: a team effort, with another pair of hands helping to carry the flame forward.

Putting a Dinosaur on the Scales
How heavy was a Tyrannosaurus rex? It sounds like a simple question, but no one has ever weighed a living dinosaur. All that remains are bones, and bones alone do not reveal how much muscle, fat, skin and air once surrounded them. Yet body mass matters greatly to palaeontologists. It shapes estimates of how fast an animal moved, how much it ate and how quickly it grew. So scientists have developed several ways to estimate it.
Method one: measure the legs
The first approach relies on a simple principle: the heavier an animal, the thicker the bones that hold it up. Researchers measured the leg bones of hundreds of living mammals and reptiles, from mice to elephants, and found that the distance around the thigh bone and upper arm bone is closely linked to body mass. To estimate a dinosaur's weight, they measure the circumference of its limb bones and apply the same relationship.
This method is quick and needs only a few well-preserved bones, which is useful because complete skeletons are rare. Its weakness is that it assumes dinosaurs followed the same rules as today's animals. Two-legged dinosaurs carried their entire weight on their hind legs, unlike any large living mammal, so researchers must adjust for walking style.
Method two: rebuild the body
The second approach estimates volume and then converts it to mass. In the early twentieth century, scientists sculpted small scale models of dinosaurs, lowered them into water and measured how much water they pushed aside. Today the idea has moved onto computers. A mounted skeleton is scanned with lasers to create a digital copy. Researchers then wrap the skeleton in a virtual body, calculate its volume and multiply that volume by an estimated density.
Every step involves choices. How thick was the tail muscle? How large was the belly? Many dinosaurs, like modern birds, had air sacs connected to their lungs and air spaces inside some bones, which would have made them lighter than a solid animal of the same size. Change any of these assumptions and the final figure changes too.
One team tried to avoid guesswork about flesh by wrapping each digital skeleton in the tightest possible 'skin', like plastic wrap stretched over the bones. They also ran the same process on skeletons of living mammals whose weights were already known. The wrapped models consistently fell short of the true weight by about a fifth, so the team added that amount to their dinosaur results.
Why the answers differ
Because of these choices, published estimates for a large adult Tyrannosaurus rex have ranged from about five tonnes to more than nine. This does not mean the research has failed. When researchers using different methods arrive at similar numbers, they can be more confident. When the numbers disagree, the gap shows exactly which assumptions need more study.
Reading the results
No estimate should be read as a precise measurement. A careful palaeontologist reports a range, explains the method and lists the assumptions behind it. The bones can never step onto a scale, but patient, open reasoning can still tell us a great deal about the giants that left them behind.
Question: In the first method, what do researchers measure on a dinosaur skeleton?
Option A: the distance around its limb bones
Option B: the length of its whole tail
Option C: the size of the air spaces in its bones
Option D: the width of its skull and jaws

A Swarm of a Thousand
On a large white table in a laboratory at Harvard University, a crowd of small robots began to move. Each one was about the size of a coin and stood on three thin metal legs. None had a camera, and none could see the whole group. Yet, over many hours, more than a thousand of them slowly arranged themselves into the shape of a five-pointed star. On later runs, they formed a letter K and the outline of a spanner.
The robots were called Kilobots, and the experiment, published in the journal Science in 2014, was one of the largest demonstrations of swarm robotics ever attempted. Its aim was not to build one clever machine, but to discover what many simple machines could achieve together.
Nature offered the inspiration. A single ant has a tiny brain and very limited senses, yet a colony of ants can find the shortest path to food, build complex nests and move objects far heavier than any one ant. No ant is in charge, and no ant holds a plan of the whole nest. Each one follows simple rules based on what its nearest neighbours are doing, and the overall pattern emerges from countless small interactions. Scientists call this collective behaviour.
The Kilobots worked in a similar way. Each robot was cheap, costing only about fourteen US dollars in parts, and extremely basic. Instead of wheels, it moved by vibrating: two tiny motors shook its body so that it shuffled forwards or turned. To communicate, it bounced infrared light off the table to robots within about ten centimetres. All it could do was measure its distance from its neighbours and pass simple messages along.
To make a shape, the researchers first gave every robot the same picture of the target. Four seed robots were placed together to mark a starting point. The other robots then crept around the edge of the crowd, one at a time, working out their position from the robots they passed. When a robot calculated that it had reached the right place inside the shape, it stopped, and became a reference point for the next robot to arrive. In this way the star grew outwards, layer by layer, like a crystal forming.
The process was not neat. Robots sometimes collided, jammed together or drifted off course, and a single shape could take up to twelve hours to complete. But the swarm coped. Because no single robot was essential, the failure of one did not wreck the whole design; the others simply moved around it.
That ability to keep working despite errors is what makes swarms so attractive to engineers. In the future, swarms of small robots might search disaster zones, monitor coral reefs or help clean up oil spills, covering ground that one large robot could never reach. The Kilobots themselves could do none of these things. Their real achievement was to show that, with the right rules, a thousand simple machines can behave like one intelligent system.
Question: In the sentence 'Because no single robot was essential', the word essential means . . .
Option A: very expensive
Option B: absolutely necessary
Option C: easily damaged
Option D: fully charged

The Day the Overlay Went Dark
In Port Hale, nobody looked at the streets any more. They looked at the overlay.
Every citizen over the age of six had a lens implant that painted helpful information across whatever they saw: glowing arrows along the footpaths, names floating above shopfronts, a soft green line showing the fastest way home. Thirteen-year-old Mira Chen had never once wondered which way was north. The overlay simply knew.
On the morning of the solar storm, she was halfway across the Esplanade Bridge with her little brother, Theo, when the arrows flickered, stuttered and vanished. Around them, hundreds of people stopped mid-step, like toys whose batteries had died. The city was suddenly very plain: grey concrete, grey water, a sky the colour of dishwater. Without their names, the buildings looked like strangers.
'Mira,' Theo whispered, gripping her sleeve. 'Where's home?'
She opened her mouth to answer and realised she had no idea. Home was where the green line ended. It had always been that simple.
Somewhere behind them, a man began shouting at nobody in particular. A delivery drone, its signal lost, settled onto the bridge railing and folded its arms like a tired pigeon. Mira felt panic rising in her chest, cold and fizzing, like a shaken bottle about to burst.
Then she remembered Grandpa Wei's map.
Every Sunday, on visits she had considered boring, her grandfather unfolded a paper map of the city across his kitchen table. It was soft with age, split along its creases and patched with yellowing tape. He would trace the streets with one crooked finger and tell her about places that had once been there: the old fish market, the tram depot, the park where he had learned to ride a bike. 'Machines forget,' he liked to say. 'Paper remembers.' Mira had always nodded politely and waited for afternoon tea.
Now, standing on the bridge, she closed her eyes and pictured that map. The river, a fat blue snake. The bridge, a short black stitch across it. And on the far side, a street that curved like a fish-hook past the park.
'This way,' she said.
She led Theo down off the bridge, past a bakery whose name she had to read from an actual painted sign, past the park, where a small boy was learning to ride a bike while his father ran beside him. Each landmark slotted into place like a puzzle piece. Whenever she was unsure at a corner, she looked for the glitter of the river between buildings and kept it on her left.
By the time they reached their front gate, others had begun to follow: a woman with a pram, two older students, the shouting man, quieter now. Mira pointed each of them in the right direction as best she could.
The overlay returned that evening with a cheerful chime, as though nothing had happened. Theo was asleep on the couch. Mira sat at the kitchen table with a pencil and the back of an old poster, drawing the river, the bridge and the fish-hook street before she could forget them.
On Sunday, she asked Grandpa Wei to show her the map again. This time, she did not wait for afternoon tea.
Question: In the sentence 'He would trace the streets with one crooked finger', the word He refers to . . .
Option A: Grandpa Wei
Option B: Theo
Option C: the shouting man
Option D: the small boy's father

Three Days on the Bibbulmun
Friday 12 April, Mount Cooke campsite
Aunt Jo says keeping a diary will help me 'notice things'. So far I have noticed that my pack weighs eleven kilograms, that my left boot rubs, and that there is no phone reception anywhere in the jarrah forest. The Bibbulmun Track runs for about a thousand kilometres, from the hills outside Perth all the way to Albany, and Jo wants to walk the whole thing next spring. This weekend is her 'practice run'. I am, apparently, her practice companion. She has planned everything: dehydrated meals, a stove the size of a coffee cup, three litres of water each and a paper map in a zip-lock bag in case the markers are hard to find.
We followed the yellow triangle markers all day. At the top of Mount Cooke there were granite slabs warm from the sun, and forest rolled away in every direction like a green ocean. I didn't say anything, but I took a photo. Then I remembered I couldn't send it to anyone.
The campsite has a three-sided timber shelter, a water tank and a toilet, which Jo calls luxury. We wrote our names in the logbook, which every walker is supposed to sign so rangers know who is on the track.
Saturday 13 April, Nerang campsite
I woke at 5.40 because a kookaburra had decided our shelter was a stage. Jo was already boiling water for porridge. She asked if I'd slept well. I said the floor was like sleeping on a chopping board, which was true, but I had actually slept better than I have in weeks.
Today was shorter but hillier. My blister got worse, so Jo showed me how to tape it before it burst. She has a little kit with everything in it: tape, a needle, antiseptic, even a tiny pair of scissors. She told me she once walked on a blister for two days without stopping to fix it and ended up limping for a week. 'The bush doesn't care how tough you are,' she said. 'Fix small problems while they're small.'
In the afternoon we didn't talk for almost an hour. It wasn't awkward. I listened to the wind moving through the treetops and to some birds Jo said were western rosellas. I realised I hadn't thought about the science test once. That night we ate pasta out of the pot and watched the stars come out between the branches.
Sunday 14 April, back at the car
Last entry. My legs ache in places I didn't know had muscles. We walked out this morning through mist so thick the trees looked like grey ghosts, and then the sun burned through and everything sparkled. On the drive home I asked Jo why she had really invited me, since she clearly didn't need any help. She kept her eyes on the road and said that at Christmas I had looked 'like someone who needed more sky'. I didn't know what to say, so I said nothing.
I have already checked the track website. There is a section through the karri forest near Pemberton where the trees are taller than a fifteen-storey building. Jo says that if I keep the blister tape in my pack, I can come.
I told her I'd think about it. I've already thought about it.
Question: When Jo calls the campsite 'luxury', she means it is . . .
Option A: more comfortable than she expected
Option B: too expensive for most walkers
Option C: crowded with other hikers
Option D: far away from the track

Three Days on the Bibbulmun
Friday 12 April, Mount Cooke campsite
Aunt Jo says keeping a diary will help me 'notice things'. So far I have noticed that my pack weighs eleven kilograms, that my left boot rubs, and that there is no phone reception anywhere in the jarrah forest. The Bibbulmun Track runs for about a thousand kilometres, from the hills outside Perth all the way to Albany, and Jo wants to walk the whole thing next spring. This weekend is her 'practice run'. I am, apparently, her practice companion. She has planned everything: dehydrated meals, a stove the size of a coffee cup, three litres of water each and a paper map in a zip-lock bag in case the markers are hard to find.
We followed the yellow triangle markers all day. At the top of Mount Cooke there were granite slabs warm from the sun, and forest rolled away in every direction like a green ocean. I didn't say anything, but I took a photo. Then I remembered I couldn't send it to anyone.
The campsite has a three-sided timber shelter, a water tank and a toilet, which Jo calls luxury. We wrote our names in the logbook, which every walker is supposed to sign so rangers know who is on the track.
Saturday 13 April, Nerang campsite
I woke at 5.40 because a kookaburra had decided our shelter was a stage. Jo was already boiling water for porridge. She asked if I'd slept well. I said the floor was like sleeping on a chopping board, which was true, but I had actually slept better than I have in weeks.
Today was shorter but hillier. My blister got worse, so Jo showed me how to tape it before it burst. She has a little kit with everything in it: tape, a needle, antiseptic, even a tiny pair of scissors. She told me she once walked on a blister for two days without stopping to fix it and ended up limping for a week. 'The bush doesn't care how tough you are,' she said. 'Fix small problems while they're small.'
In the afternoon we didn't talk for almost an hour. It wasn't awkward. I listened to the wind moving through the treetops and to some birds Jo said were western rosellas. I realised I hadn't thought about the science test once. That night we ate pasta out of the pot and watched the stars come out between the branches.
Sunday 14 April, back at the car
Last entry. My legs ache in places I didn't know had muscles. We walked out this morning through mist so thick the trees looked like grey ghosts, and then the sun burned through and everything sparkled. On the drive home I asked Jo why she had really invited me, since she clearly didn't need any help. She kept her eyes on the road and said that at Christmas I had looked 'like someone who needed more sky'. I didn't know what to say, so I said nothing.
I have already checked the track website. There is a section through the karri forest near Pemberton where the trees are taller than a fifteen-storey building. Jo says that if I keep the blister tape in my pack, I can come.
I told her I'd think about it. I've already thought about it.

Crunch Time: Why Insects Belong on Our Plates
Imagine sitting down to a plate of tacos and discovering that the filling is made from crickets. Many Australians would push the plate away in disgust. Yet about two billion people around the world already eat insects as a normal part of their diet, and it is time the rest of us joined them.
The first reason is simple: insects are remarkably good food. Crickets, mealworms and grasshoppers are rich in protein, and many also provide iron, zinc and healthy fats. Dried cricket powder can contain more than sixty per cent protein by weight, which is a higher share than in most cuts of beef.
The second reason is that insects are far kinder to the planet than the animals we usually farm. Because insects are cold-blooded, they do not waste energy keeping their bodies warm, so they turn their feed into body weight very efficiently. Crickets need roughly a twelfth of the feed that cattle require to produce the same amount of protein. Insect farms also use much less water and land, and they release only a tiny fraction of the greenhouse gases produced by cattle. A cricket farm can fit inside an ordinary warehouse, with the insects living in crates stacked from floor to ceiling.
Some people argue that eating insects is unnatural. In fact, the opposite is true. Insects have been on human menus for thousands of years. For First Nations Australians, foods such as witchetty grubs and bogong moths have long been valued sources of nourishment. In Thailand, fried crickets are sold as a snack at markets, and in Mexico, toasted grasshoppers called chapulines are sprinkled over tortillas. Our squeamishness is not a law of nature; it is merely a habit.
Others worry about taste. Here, too, the fears are exaggerated. Roasted crickets have a nutty flavour, a little like toasted sunflower seeds, and cricket flour disappears completely into pasta, biscuits and protein bars. Most people who try a cricket-flour cookie without being told cannot pick the difference. Once the first bite is taken, the 'yuck' factor melts away like ice on a hot footpath.
Of course, insect food is not perfect. People who are allergic to shellfish may also react to insects, because both belong to the same large group of animals with hard outer skeletons. Clear labels must warn shoppers about this risk. Prices are also still higher than for most meat, because the industry is young. However, as more people buy insect products, farms will grow larger and costs will fall, just as they have for other new foods.
Nobody is being asked to give up everything they love. Swapping even one meal a week for an insect-based option would make a real difference. Schools could add cricket-flour muffins to the canteen menu, and supermarkets could stock insect pasta beside the ordinary kind.
The world's population is expected to reach nearly ten billion by 2050, and every one of those people will need to eat. The humble cricket could be part of the answer. All we have to do is be brave enough to take the first crunch.

Option C: about two billion
Option D: about sixty million

The Bin Audit Diary
Monday 3 March
Ms Okafor announced today that our class will run the school's first ever bin audit. On Friday we will tip out every rubbish bin from the canteen area onto tarpaulins and sort through the lot, wearing gloves, of course. The idea is to find out what we are actually throwing away. Jarrah groaned so loudly that the whole class laughed, though I suspect he was secretly pleased to miss maths.
I have to admit I wasn't excited either. Sorting through a week of other people's lunch scraps sounds about as appealing as cleaning out the dog's kennel.
Wednesday 5 March
We spent today planning. Ms Okafor split us into four teams: food scraps, soft plastics, paper and cardboard, and 'everything else'. My team has soft plastics, which means chip packets, cling wrap and the little sleeves that muesli bars come in. Each team will weigh its pile on bathroom scales borrowed from the PE storeroom.
Before we finished, Ms Okafor asked us to guess which pile would be heaviest. Almost everyone guessed soft plastics, because the bins always seem to be overflowing with wrappers. Only Mei guessed food scraps. Nobody took her seriously.
Friday 7 March
Audit day. The smell when we opened the first bin made Jarrah pull his shirt up over his nose, and for once nobody laughed at him.
It took the whole double period to sort everything. By the end, there were four sad-looking piles on the tarps. My team's pile looked enormous, a crinkly mountain of silver and blue. But when we put it on the scales, it weighed only 3.2 kilograms. The food scraps weighed 11.6 kilograms. Mei was right after all.
What shocked me most was not the half-eaten sandwiches but the whole ones. We found eleven sandwiches that had never been unwrapped, plus fourteen apples with no more than a single bite taken out of them. Ms Okafor explained that when food rots in landfill it gives off methane, a gas that traps far more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide does.
Sunday 9 March
I've been thinking about the audit all weekend. Plastic wrappers are easy to notice because they're bright and they take up space, so they fool you into thinking they're the biggest problem. Food is heavier, but it squashes down and hides at the bottom of the bin.
At dinner I asked Mum why she always packs two pieces of fruit when I only ever eat one. She said she worries I'll be hungry. We agreed that from now on I'll pack my own lunch, and that whatever I don't eat comes home again so we can see what's being wasted. Dad has already started sketching a compost bay for the corner of the backyard.
Monday 10 March
Our class presented the results at assembly. Mei explained the scales and the numbers, and I showed photos of the unopened sandwiches. Afterwards, the principal agreed to trial two worm farms beside the canteen. Jarrah has volunteered to look after them. I'm not sure who was more surprised, Ms Okafor or Jarrah himself.

Option A: Ms Okafor had hinted that plastics would win.
Option B: Soft plastics are known to be the heaviest waste.

Teaching Your Budgie to Step Up
Budgerigars, or budgies, are small Australian parrots that have become one of the most popular pets in the world. In the wild they fly in large, chattering flocks across the inland, so a single budgie in a cage can easily become bored and lonely. Training is one of the best ways to keep a pet budgie's mind busy, and the first skill most owners teach is the 'step up', in which the bird hops onto your finger when asked. This guide explains how to teach it safely.
What you will need
- a quiet room with the windows and doors closed and any ceiling fans switched off
- a supply of millet spray, a seed treat most budgies adore
- a short, smooth perch or a clean wooden chopstick
- patience: some birds learn in a week, while others take a month or more
Before you begin
A budgie brought home from a pet shop or breeder needs time to settle. For at least the first week, do not try to handle it. Instead, sit beside the cage each day and talk softly so the bird grows used to your voice and presence. Budgies are prey animals, and in the wild a shape swooping from above could mean a hungry hawk. Rushing this stage can leave a bird nervous of hands for life.
Step 1: Hand in the cage
Rest your hand quietly inside the cage, near but not touching the bird, for a few minutes at a time. Hold a piece of millet between your fingers. At first your budgie may flutter away, but over several sessions it will usually edge closer to nibble the treat. Do not grab at it.
Step 2: Offer a finger
Once your budgie eats calmly from your hand, slide one finger slowly towards it, just above its feet. Approach from the side or below, never from directly overhead. Say 'step up' in a clear, cheerful tone as you press very gently against its lower chest. Most budgies will lift a foot to keep their balance. The moment both feet are on your finger, reward the bird with millet and praise.
Step 3: Practise and progress
Keep sessions short, about five to ten minutes, and finish while your budgie is still keen. A tired or frightened bird will start to puff, pant or flap, which is a sign to stop. Repeat the command using exactly the same words each time. When your budgie steps up reliably inside the cage, you can try carrying it a short distance out of the cage.
Troubleshooting
If your bird bites, do not jerk your hand away, as this teaches it that biting works. Hold still, stay calm and try again later. If your budgie is afraid of fingers, offer the perch or chopstick instead; many birds feel safer stepping onto wood. If your budgie seems uninterested, try a session shortly before its usual feeding time, when a millet reward will seem far more tempting.
A well-trained budgie is a happier, more confident companion. The chirps and chatter you hear at the end of a successful session are your reward for all that patience.

Option A: refuse to eat
Option B: love very much
Option C: find hard to chew
Option D: are allergic to

Teaching Your Budgie to Step Up
Budgerigars, or budgies, are small Australian parrots that have become one of the most popular pets in the world. In the wild they fly in large, chattering flocks across the inland, so a single budgie in a cage can easily become bored and lonely. Training is one of the best ways to keep a pet budgie's mind busy, and the first skill most owners teach is the 'step up', in which the bird hops onto your finger when asked. This guide explains how to teach it safely.
What you will need
- a quiet room with the windows and doors closed and any ceiling fans switched off
- a supply of millet spray, a seed treat most budgies adore
- a short, smooth perch or a clean wooden chopstick
- patience: some birds learn in a week, while others take a month or more
Before you begin
A budgie brought home from a pet shop or breeder needs time to settle. For at least the first week, do not try to handle it. Instead, sit beside the cage each day and talk softly so the bird grows used to your voice and presence. Budgies are prey animals, and in the wild a shape swooping from above could mean a hungry hawk. Rushing this stage can leave a bird nervous of hands for life.
Step 1: Hand in the cage
Rest your hand quietly inside the cage, near but not touching the bird, for a few minutes at a time. Hold a piece of millet between your fingers. At first your budgie may flutter away, but over several sessions it will usually edge closer to nibble the treat. Do not grab at it.
Step 2: Offer a finger
Once your budgie eats calmly from your hand, slide one finger slowly towards it, just above its feet. Approach from the side or below, never from directly overhead. Say 'step up' in a clear, cheerful tone as you press very gently against its lower chest. Most budgies will lift a foot to keep their balance. The moment both feet are on your finger, reward the bird with millet and praise.
Step 3: Practise and progress
Keep sessions short, about five to ten minutes, and finish while your budgie is still keen. A tired or frightened bird will start to puff, pant or flap, which is a sign to stop. Repeat the command using exactly the same words each time. When your budgie steps up reliably inside the cage, you can try carrying it a short distance out of the cage.
Troubleshooting
If your bird bites, do not jerk your hand away, as this teaches it that biting works. Hold still, stay calm and try again later. If your budgie is afraid of fingers, offer the perch or chopstick instead; many birds feel safer stepping onto wood. If your budgie seems uninterested, try a session shortly before its usual feeding time, when a millet reward will seem far more tempting.
A well-trained budgie is a happier, more confident companion. The chirps and chatter you hear at the end of a successful session are your reward for all that patience.

Option A: sit beside the cage and talk softly without handling the bird
Option B: offer millet through the bars of the cage every morning
Option C: practise the 'step up' command for a few minutes each day
Option D: let the bird fly freely around a room with the doors closed

The Volcano That Stopped the Planes
In April 2010, millions of travellers across Europe discovered that a volcano whose name they could not pronounce had cancelled their plans. Eyjafjallajökull, in southern Iceland, is not a particularly large volcano. Yet for about six days its ash closed most of the airspace over northern and western Europe, causing the biggest shutdown of air travel since the Second World War.
Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two of the plates that make up the Earth's crust are slowly pulling apart. Molten rock, or magma, rises to fill the gap, which is why the island has around thirty active volcanic systems. Eyjafjallajökull began to stir in March 2010 with a gentle eruption that sent streams of glowing lava down a mountain slope. Tourists flocked to watch. Then, on 14 April, the eruption shifted to a new vent beneath the ice cap that gives the volcano its name ('jökull' means 'glacier').
This change made all the difference. When the hot magma met the glacier's meltwater, it cooled so suddenly that it shattered into tiny, sharp particles of rock and glass. Steam blasted these particles high into the sky, and a steady wind from the north-west carried the cloud straight towards Britain and mainland Europe.
Volcanic ash is a serious danger to aircraft. A modern jet engine runs at temperatures well above the melting point of volcanic glass. If a plane flies through an ash cloud, the particles can melt inside the engine and then harden again as a glassy coating that blocks the flow of air. In 1982, a passenger jet flying over Indonesia lost power in all four engines after entering ash from the volcano Galunggung. The plane glided silently for several minutes before the crew managed to restart the engines and land safely. Since then, airlines have treated ash clouds with great caution.
As the ash spread in 2010, country after country closed its skies. Around 100,000 flights were cancelled and roughly ten million passengers were affected. Some travellers slept on airport floors for days, growing more exasperated by the hour. Others paid huge sums for taxis, trains and ferries. Yet many people also found themselves gazing up at skies that were, for once, completely empty of vapour trails. Businesses suffered too: flowers from Kenya wilted in storage because they could not be flown to European markets.
Not everyone agreed that the shutdown was necessary. Airlines complained that the rules were too strict, since no one knew exactly how much ash an engine could safely tolerate. Within a week, scientists and engine makers agreed on new limits, and planes were allowed to fly through areas with low levels of ash.
The eruption left a lasting legacy. Today, special centres around the world track ash clouds and advise pilots, and research aircraft measure ash directly. Eyjafjallajökull fell quiet later in 2010, but its larger neighbour, Katla, which has a history of bigger eruptions, is watched closely. Iceland's volcanoes remind us that even in an age of jet travel, the planet still has the final say.
Question: For about how long did the ash close most of the airspace over northern and western Europe?
Option A: two days
Option B: three weeks
Option C: eight months
Option D: six days

Burra, South Australia
Saturday 18 October
Dear Nonna,
You asked me to tell you everything about the field trip, so here it is, all of it, even the part about the snake.
We drove two hours north from Adelaide to a sheep farm near Burra. At first I couldn't see why anyone would bring a bus full of Year 8s here. There were no trees, no creek, nothing but rolling paddocks of pale, wiry grass and a lot of curious sheep. Then Dr Halloran, the researcher we were helping, knelt down, pointed at a hole no wider than a twenty-cent coin and whispered, 'Somebody's home.'
That somebody was a pygmy blue-tongue lizard. It's the smallest kind of blue-tongue, about the length of a pencil, and it is endangered. For more than thirty years, scientists believed it was extinct, because nobody had recorded one since 1959. Then, in 1992, a researcher found one inside the stomach of a dead brown snake on a roadside near here. You can imagine the excitement. If a snake had eaten one, there had to be others nearby.
Here is the strangest part. Pygmy blue-tongues don't dig. They live in old burrows made by wolf spiders and trapdoor spiders, and they hardly ever leave them. A lizard sits at the entrance, basking with just its head poking out, and snaps up any grasshopper or beetle that wanders past. If something dangerous comes near, it slips backwards down the burrow in a flash. So if there are no spider holes, there are no lizards. And the spiders only thrive in native grassland that hasn't been ploughed.
Our job was to help with an experiment. Dr Halloran's team has been testing artificial burrows, short wooden tubes with holes drilled into them, pushed into the ground where real spider holes are scarce. We checked thirty of them with a tiny camera on a long cable. I peered into my eleventh tube expecting nothing as usual, and there, staring patiently back at me, was a lizard with a fat, stumpy tail. I squealed so loudly that Dr Halloran had to remind me that lizards can feel vibrations through the ground.
What surprised me most was the farmer, Mr Pritchard. I'd assumed farmers and endangered animals would be enemies, but he told us that his family had grazed sheep lightly on this paddock for four generations and never ploughed it. He now walks the paddock with Dr Halloran every spring, counting burrows. 'They were here first,' he said, quite simply. 'I'd hate to be the one who lost them.'
On the bus home, I kept thinking about how easily the whole species could have disappeared without anyone noticing. Nobody would have looked twice at that paddock. I certainly didn't.
I've attached a photo of my lizard. Dad says it looks grumpy. I think it looks wise.
Love,
Giulia
P.S. Don't worry about the snake. We didn't see a single one, and believe me, I checked.

Option A: The paddocks looked empty and unremarkable.
Option B: The bus trip from Adelaide had taken too long.
Option C: She was nervous about meeting the farmer's sheep.
Option D: Dr Halloran had not yet explained the experiment.
