We drove two hours north from Adelaide to a sheep farm near Burra. At first I couldn't see why anyone would bring a bus full of Year 8s here. There were no trees, no creek, nothing but rolling paddocks of pale, wiry grass and a lot of curious sheep. Then Dr Halloran, the researcher we were helping, knelt down, pointed at a hole no wider than a twenty-cent coin and whispered, 'Somebody's home.'
That somebody was a pygmy blue-tongue lizard. It's the smallest kind of blue-tongue, about the length of a pencil, and it is endangered. For more than thirty years, scientists believed it was extinct, because nobody had recorded one since 1959. Then, in 1992, a researcher found one inside the stomach of a dead brown snake on a roadside near here. You can imagine the excitement. If a snake had eaten one, there had to be others nearby.
Here is the strangest part. Pygmy blue-tongues don't dig. They live in old burrows made by wolf spiders and trapdoor spiders, and they hardly ever leave them. A lizard sits at the entrance, basking with just its head poking out, and snaps up any grasshopper or beetle that wanders past. If something dangerous comes near, it slips backwards down the burrow in a flash. So if there are no spider holes, there are no lizards. And the spiders only thrive in native grassland that hasn't been ploughed.
Our job was to help with an experiment. Dr Halloran's team has been testing artificial burrows, short wooden tubes with holes drilled into them, pushed into the ground where real spider holes are scarce. We checked thirty of them with a tiny camera on a long cable. I peered into my eleventh tube expecting nothing as usual, and there, staring patiently back at me, was a lizard with a fat, stumpy tail. I squealed so loudly that Dr Halloran had to remind me that lizards can feel vibrations through the ground.
What surprised me most was the farmer, Mr Pritchard. I'd assumed farmers and endangered animals would be enemies, but he told us that his family had grazed sheep lightly on this paddock for four generations and never ploughed it. He now walks the paddock with Dr Halloran every spring, counting burrows. 'They were here first,' he said, quite simply. 'I'd hate to be the one who lost them.'
On the bus home, I kept thinking about how easily the whole species could have disappeared without anyone noticing. Nobody would have looked twice at that paddock. I certainly didn't.
I've attached a photo of my lizard. Dad says it looks grumpy. I think it looks wise.
Love,
Giulia
P.S. Don't worry about the snake. We didn't see a single one, and believe me, I checked.

Crosswind at Ferris Field
The windsock at Ferris Field had hung limp all morning, which was exactly how Lily liked it. She had spent six months building her model plane, a red-and-white trainer she had named Kestrel, from a kit of balsa wood, tissue and glue. Her grandfather had helped with the electrics, but every rib of the wings had passed through her own fingers. Today was the junior precision contest, and Kestrel was ready.
By eleven o'clock, everything had changed. The windsock had filled out and swung sideways across the strip, and the gum trees along the boundary fence were bending and hissing. The contest director, a tall woman in a wide-brimmed hat, called the pilots together.
'The crosswind's picking up,' she said. 'We'll keep flying for now, but if anyone isn't comfortable, there's no shame in sitting it out.'
Nobody moved. Lily glanced at Dev Sharma, who had won the contest the year before. He was already checking the controls on his sleek blue aerobatic plane, which had a carbon-fibre frame and had cost more than Lily's whole kit. Dev caught her eye and grinned. 'Should be fun,' he said.
Lily was fourth to fly. Her take-off was smooth, and as Kestrel climbed she felt the familiar thrill of the controls coming alive under her thumbs. She flew the figure-eight cleanly and then the loop, though she had to fight the wind on the way down. Her score so far put her in second place, just behind Dev.
Only the landing remained. Lily brought Kestrel around and lined it up with the strip. Halfway down, a gust struck from the side. The little plane lurched, one wing dipping towards the grass. Lily corrected and Kestrel steadied, but it was drifting towards the spectators' fence.
'Go around,' her grandfather said quietly beside her.
She knew a go-around would cost points. A perfect landing would win her the contest. She could hear Dev's friends calling for her to bring it in. For a second, her thumbs hovered.
Then she pushed the throttle forward. Kestrel's motor buzzed and the plane climbed away from the fence. Lily circled twice, waiting, watching the windsock. When it sagged for a moment, she brought Kestrel down in a gentle, slightly crooked landing well away from the crowd.
Dev flew last. His plane looked magnificent, rolling and climbing as if the wind did not exist. On his landing, the same gust caught it. Dev didn't go around. The blue plane cartwheeled across the grass, and a wing snapped clean off.
When the scores were added up, the go-around had dropped Lily to third. On the way home she sat with the trophy, a small plastic cup, resting on her knees.
'Disappointed?' her grandfather asked.
Lily thought about the fence, and about Dev kneeling in the grass beside his broken wing, pretending he didn't care.
'No,' she said, and was surprised to find she meant it. 'Kestrel can fly again next month.'
Question: Why did Lily like the windsock hanging limp?
Option A: It meant there was little wind to trouble her plane.
Option B: It meant the contest would be cancelled for the day.
Option C: It meant Dev's plane would not be able to take off.
Option D: It meant the spectators would stay away from the field.

Why the Sky Is Blue (and Sunsets Are Not)
Look up on a clear afternoon and you will see a blue sky. Look again at sunset and the same sky may glow orange, pink or red. You have probably seen this thousands of times without wondering why. The explanation involves sunlight, air and a surprising amount of bouncing around.
Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. You can prove this with a glass prism, which spreads a beam of white light into a band of red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. Light travels as a wave, and each colour has a different wavelength, the distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next. Red light has the longest wavelength we can see; blue and violet have the shortest.
Air may seem empty, but it is crowded with tiny molecules, mostly of nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. When sunlight strikes them, some of the light is scattered, sent off in all directions like balls ricocheting around a pinball machine. Crucially, the molecules do not scatter all colours equally. Short wavelengths are scattered much more strongly than long ones, so blue light bounces around the sky far more than red light does. This effect is called Rayleigh scattering, after the British scientist Lord Rayleigh, who described it in the 1870s.
So when you look at any part of the sky away from the sun, you are seeing blue light that has been scattered towards your eyes from every direction. The sky is, in a sense, lit up by its own scattered light.
But wait: violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? There are three reasons. The sun gives out less violet light than blue in the first place, some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are much more sensitive to blue. Put together, these make the sky look blue to us.
Sunsets follow the same rule, just from a different angle. When the sun is low on the horizon, its light has to travel through a much thicker slice of atmosphere to reach you. Along the way, most of the blue light is scattered out sideways long before it arrives. What is left is mainly the longer wavelengths: yellows, oranges and reds. Dust, smoke or ash in the air can make sunsets even more vivid.
The same process explains why distant hills often look hazy and bluish. It also explains why the sky on the Moon is black even in the middle of the day. The Moon has almost no air, so there is nothing to scatter the sunlight, and astronauts there saw the blazing sun hanging in a dark sky.
Next time you watch a sunset, remember that the blue light missing from your sky has not disappeared. It has been scattered across the sky of someone far to the west of you, where it is still the middle of the afternoon.

Option A: It involves readers by linking the science to what they see themselves.
Option B: It makes the passage sound like a story told by one of its characters.
Option C: It shows that the writer is unsure whether the explanation is correct.
Option D: It suggests that readers already understand why the sky is blue.

Look up on a clear afternoon and you will see a blue sky. Look again at sunset and the same sky may glow orange, pink or red. You have probably seen this thousands of times without wondering why. The explanation involves sunlight, air and a surprising amount of bouncing around.
Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. You can prove this with a glass prism, which spreads a beam of white light into a band of red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. Light travels as a wave, and each colour has a different wavelength, the distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next. Red light has the longest wavelength we can see; blue and violet have the shortest.
Air may seem empty, but it is crowded with tiny molecules, mostly of nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. When sunlight strikes them, some of the light is scattered, sent off in all directions like balls ricocheting around a pinball machine. Crucially, the molecules do not scatter all colours equally. Short wavelengths are scattered much more strongly than long ones, so blue light bounces around the sky far more than red light does. This effect is called Rayleigh scattering, after the British scientist Lord Rayleigh, who described it in the 1870s.
So when you look at any part of the sky away from the sun, you are seeing blue light that has been scattered towards your eyes from every direction. The sky is, in a sense, lit up by its own scattered light.
But wait: violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? There are three reasons. The sun gives out less violet light than blue in the first place, some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are much more sensitive to blue. Put together, these make the sky look blue to us.
Sunsets follow the same rule, just from a different angle. When the sun is low on the horizon, its light has to travel through a much thicker slice of atmosphere to reach you. Along the way, most of the blue light is scattered out sideways long before it arrives. What is left is mainly the longer wavelengths: yellows, oranges and reds. Dust, smoke or ash in the air can make sunsets even more vivid.
The same process explains why distant hills often look hazy and bluish. It also explains why the sky on the Moon is black even in the middle of the day. The Moon has almost no air, so there is nothing to scatter the sunlight, and astronauts there saw the blazing sun hanging in a dark sky.
Next time you watch a sunset, remember that the blue light missing from your sky has not disappeared. It has been scattered across the sky of someone far to the west of you, where it is still the middle of the afternoon.

Option A: Light from a low sun crosses more air, so most blue is scattered away.
Option B: Red light has a shorter wavelength than blue, so it scatters more.
Option C: Dust, smoke or ash in the air can make sunsets even more vivid.
Option D: The sun gives out less violet light than blue in the first place.

Why Wombat Droppings Are Cubes
Of all the strange facts about Australian animals, few make people laugh as much as this one: the bare-nosed wombat produces droppings shaped like cubes. Each night, a single wombat may leave eighty to a hundred of these neat little blocks, each about two centimetres across, scattered around its home range. For years, the cubes were a curiosity that puzzled naturalists and delighted tourists. Then a team of scientists set out to discover how a soft-bodied animal could make something with flat sides and corners.
The wombat itself is a sturdy, burrowing marsupial with short legs, powerful claws and a backward-facing pouch, which stops soil getting in while a mother digs. Wombats are mostly nocturnal and spend their days in burrows that can stretch for many metres underground. They have poor eyesight but an excellent sense of smell, and smell is the key to understanding why the cubes matter.
Wombats use their droppings to communicate. They leave them in prominent places, such as on top of rocks and logs, where the scent can be detected by other wombats. These scent piles mark territory and may help wombats find mates. A round dropping placed on a rock might roll off. A cube stays put.
How the cubes are formed was a question that fascinated Dr Patricia Yang, an American engineer who studies how fluids and other materials move through animal bodies. When she first saw a photo of the droppings, she was astonished. Working with Dr Scott Carver, a wildlife ecologist at the University of Tasmania, she examined the intestines of wombats that had been put down after being hit by cars. By inflating the intestines with a long balloon, the team discovered something unexpected. The walls of the intestine were not equally stretchy all the way around. Some sections were stiff, while others were flexible. As the waste moved along and dried out, the stiff and flexible regions squeezed it unevenly, gradually forming flat faces and sharp edges.
The team's early results, presented in 2018, won an Ig Nobel Prize the following year. These prizes go to research that 'first makes people laugh, and then makes them think'. Behind the humour, there was a serious point. Humans usually make cubes by moulding or cutting material. The wombat produces them using soft tissue alone. Engineers believe that understanding this could one day lead to new ways of manufacturing objects from soft materials. A fuller study was published in 2021.
The research also matters to wildlife scientists. Bare-nosed wombats in some areas suffer from mange, a painful skin disease caused by tiny mites, and Dr Carver's work on the disease depends on understanding wombat bodies as fully as possible.
The humble wombat dropping, it turns out, is not just a joke. It is a reminder that even the most ordinary parts of an animal's life can hold surprises, if someone is curious enough to look.
Question: In 'They leave them in prominent places', the word prominent means . . .
Option A: easily seen
Option B: well hidden
Option C: damp and shady
Option D: far from home

from blooms of metal light.
He touched the pillars of his hall,
the benches and the door;
they blazed like sunrise, every one,
and still he wanted more.
He trailed his fingers through the drapes
of fine and flowing silk;
they rattled stiffly, gold and cold,
no longer soft as milk.
He hurried in and called for bread,
for meat and wine and cheese.
His servants set the table high
and bowed upon their knees.
He lifted bread: it clinked like coin.
He sipped: his lips were lined
with hardened gold that would not pour,
and hunger filled his mind.
He tried again with figs and grapes,
with honey and with cream;
each mouthful rang against his teeth
and glittered like a dream.
His servants watched him, pale with fear,
and edged back from his hand,
for none could guess what he might touch
or what he might command.
He sat among his golden things,
the richest man on earth,
and learned, too late, that bread and drink
had more than gold was worth.
He raised his shining arms and wept,
'O Dionysus, hear!
Take back the gift I begged of you;
I've paid for it too dear.
I asked for gold, and gold I have,
in hall and cup and plate,
but I would trade it all tonight
for one plain crust to break.'
The god, who'd known it all along,
said, 'Go where waters run;
wash in the River Pactolus,
and what is done, undone.'
He knelt beside the river's edge
and plunged his hands below,
and as the cold stream washed him clean
he felt the magic go.
And to this day, the old tales say,
that river's sand is bright:
the gold that washed from Midas' hands
still glitters in the light.
And Midas walked his fields again
and loved the plainer things:
the scent of rain, the taste of bread,
worth more than golden rings.

Its red gum wharf stretched more than a kilometre along the bank, and on a good day the air was thick with steam, shouting and the slap and churn of paddles. Towns such as Goolwa, Mannum, Wentworth and Bourke grew up because the boats stopped there. Remove the paddle-steamers from the story, and you cannot properly explain why many inland towns exist at all.

However, length is not the measure of importance. For roughly seventy years, these boats were the lifeline of a vast region. Should we ignore a chapter simply because it ended?

The PS Adelaide, built in 1866, still operates at Echuca, making it one of the oldest wooden-hulled paddle-steamers working anywhere in the world. Leave Lowry's Swamp Wet
On the edge of our town, behind the showgrounds, lie forty hectares of reeds, mud and shallow water that most people drive past without a second glance. This is Lowry's Swamp, and next month the council will vote on a plan to drain it and build four new sports fields. As a member of the Year 8 science club, which has studied the swamp for two years, I urge councillors to vote no.
Supporters of the plan say the swamp is wasted land. It floods, it smells after summer storms and it breeds mosquitoes. I understand why it looks useless. But a wetland is not empty space waiting to be improved. It is working every single day, even when nobody notices.
First, the swamp acts like a giant sponge. When heavy rain falls in the hills, water rushes down Kelly's Creek towards town. The swamp soaks up much of that water and releases it slowly over weeks. Our club measured the creek after three big storms last year. Below the swamp, the water rose about half as fast as it did above it. Without this sponge, floodwater would reach the shops on Main Street far more quickly.
Second, the swamp cleans the water. Reeds and sedges slow the flow so that mud settles out, and their roots, along with the tiny organisms living on them, take up some of the nutrients washed off farms and gardens. Water leaving the swamp is noticeably clearer than water entering it. Our tests showed it carried far less sediment.
Third, the swamp is home to an astonishing range of life. We have recorded eleven kinds of frogs, including the threatened growling grass frog, and more than sixty species of birds. Every spring, the reeds fill with the chatter of reed warblers that have flown south from northern Australia.
The person who has taught us most about the swamp is Doug Petrie, whose farm lies just downstream. Thirty years ago, Mr Petrie asked the council to let him dig drains through the swamp so he could graze more cattle. The council refused, and he was furious. Then came the flood of 1998. The creek burst its banks upstream, but by the time the water reached his paddocks it had spread out and slowed down in the reeds. 'My neighbours lost fences and stock,' he told us. 'I lost a gate.' Today he is one of the swamp's fiercest defenders, and he brings his grandchildren to count frogs with us.
Nobody is saying our town does not need more sports fields. Junior football numbers have doubled, and teams are crowded onto two worn ovals. But there is an alternative. The old quarry site on Brand Road is flat, already owned by the council and currently unused. Building there would give us the fields and keep the swamp.
Draining a wetland takes a few months. Rebuilding one, if it can be done at all, takes decades. Please, councillors, think beyond the next football season. Leave Lowry's Swamp wet.

Option A: a new showground
Option B: four new sports fields
Option C: a quarry on Brand Road
Option D: shops along Main Street

The Cave with Its Own Jungle
In 1990, a local man named Ho Khanh was searching for agarwood in the rainforest of central Vietnam when a storm forced him to look for shelter. Near the base of a limestone cliff, he found a dark opening. Cold air poured out of it, and from somewhere deep inside came the roar of a river. Uneasy, Ho Khanh did not go in. Later, when he tried to return, he could not find the entrance again. For almost two decades, the hole in the cliff remained a story only he could tell.
The area, now part of Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park, is riddled with caves. Since the early 1990s, a team from the British Cave Research Association had been exploring it with Vietnamese scientists, mapping many kilometres of passages. In 2008, Ho Khanh finally rediscovered his cave, and the following year he led the team to it. They named it Hang Son Doong, which means 'mountain river cave'.
What the explorers found astonished even these experienced cavers. The main passage runs for several kilometres and in places is more than 200 metres high and 150 metres wide, large enough to hold a city block of skyscrapers. Son Doong is now regarded as the largest known cave passage on Earth by volume.
The team's progress was not easy. In their first season, they were stopped by an enormous wall of calcite, slick with mud and rising about 90 metres. They nicknamed it the Great Wall of Vietnam. Only on a later expedition did they climb it and confirm that the passage continued beyond it to an exit.
Size alone does not explain Son Doong's fame. In two places, parts of the ceiling collapsed long ago, creating huge openings called dolines. Sunlight streams through these skylights, and beneath them a forest has grown inside the cave, with some trees reaching 30 metres tall. Monkeys, birds and insects live there. The cavers gave one doline a playful name: 'Watch Out for Dinosaurs'. The cave is so vast that it even has its own weather. Warm air from outside meets the cooler air within, and wisps of cloud drift beneath the roof.
Elsewhere, the floor is scattered with cave pearls. These form when drops of mineral-rich water fall into shallow pools and layers of calcite slowly build up around grains of sand. In most caves, pearls are the size of peas. Some in Son Doong are as large as baseballs.
Since 2013, small groups of visitors have been able to join guided expeditions into the cave, but numbers are strictly limited to roughly a thousand people a year. A trip takes several days and involves jungle trekking, river crossings and abseiling, and visitors camp underground. Many guides and porters are local people, and Ho Khanh himself has worked with expeditions.
Scientists continue to study the cave's rock, water and wildlife. Some believe other giant passages may still be waiting in the region's limestone hills. Somewhere out there, perhaps, cold air is flowing from an opening that nobody has noticed yet.

Option A: A storm had broken over the rainforest.
Option B: He had become lost in the national park.
Option C: Night was falling over the limestone hills.
Option D: Cold air was pouring from the cliff.

Many Hands Behind the Wave
It is one of the most recognisable images in the world. A huge wave curls over three narrow boats, its foaming crest breaking into claw-like fingers, while far in the distance the snowy peak of Mount Fuji looks small enough to be swallowed. Under the Wave off Kanagawa, usually called The Great Wave, was created in Japan in about 1831 by the artist Katsushika Hokusai, who was then around seventy years old. Yet the picture most people know is not a single painting. It is a woodblock print, and it was the work of many hands.
In Hokusai's time, colour prints were produced by a team. A publisher chose the subject, paid for the project and sold the finished prints. The artist drew the design in ink on thin paper. A skilled carver then pasted this drawing face down onto a block of cherry wood and cut away everything except the lines, destroying the original drawing in the process. Further blocks were carved, one for each colour. Finally, a printer brushed water-based ink onto each block in turn, laid damp paper on top and rubbed the back with a flat pad called a baren. Small notches cut into the corner of each block made sure the paper lined up perfectly every time.
Because the blocks could be inked again and again, a single design could produce thousands of copies. Prints were sold cheaply, for roughly the price of a bowl of noodles, and ordinary townspeople bought them the way people today might buy a poster. Many prints were worn out, thrown away or used to wrap other goods.
The Great Wave belonged to a series called Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. Part of its appeal came from a new colour. Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment first made in Europe, had recently become affordable in Japan. Unlike older plant-based blues, it was bright and deep and did not fade quickly. Hokusai and his publisher used it boldly, and the series was so popular that ten extra designs were added, bringing the total to forty-six.
As the blocks were used, they wore down. Lines became softer and fine details began to disappear. For this reason, collectors today prize early impressions, in which the edges of the wave are crisp and the sky shows a delicate pink tint. Experts compare surviving copies closely, looking for cracks in the wood and fading lines that reveal when each was printed.
Decades later, when Japan opened to trade with the West, prints like The Great Wave reached Europe in large numbers. Artists such as Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh collected them eagerly. Their flat areas of colour, bold outlines and unusual viewpoints helped inspire new ways of painting.
Today, early impressions of The Great Wave are held by major museums around the world. A picture once sold for the price of a meal is now displayed behind protective glass, in low light and only for short periods, to protect its fragile paper and colours.

Option A: They sold for roughly the price of a bowl of noodles.
Option B: They were printed on thin paper with water-based ink.
Option C: They were made using blocks of cherry wood.
Option D: They were collected by Claude Monet and Van Gogh.

Bottling the Smell of Rain
After weeks of dry, dusty heat, the first fat drops of a summer storm begin to fall. They darken the footpath, patter on the leaves and tap on tin roofs. Then, almost at once, a rich, earthy scent rises from the ground. Many people find it deeply comforting. Some say it smells like relief.
For a long time, nobody could explain exactly what that smell was. In 1964, two Australian scientists working for the CSIRO in Melbourne, Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, set out to investigate. They steam-distilled rocks and clay that had been exposed to warm, dry conditions and collected a yellowish oil. They named the scent petrichor, combining two Greek words: petra, meaning 'stone', and ichor, the golden fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods in ancient myths. The name suggests something precious hidden in ordinary rock.
Bear and Thomas found that during dry spells, plants release oils that collect on rocks and in soil. One of the most important ingredients of the smell, however, comes from tiny soil bacteria. As they grow, these bacteria produce a chemical called geosmin, a name meaning 'earth smell'. Geosmin is the same compound that gives beetroot its earthy taste. Humans are astonishingly sensitive to it. Some studies suggest we can detect it at just a few parts per trillion, which is a little like noticing a single drop of liquid in an Olympic swimming pool.
But how does the smell reach our noses? In 2015, researchers in the United States used high-speed cameras to film raindrops landing on different surfaces. When a drop hits porous ground such as dry soil, it traps tiny pockets of air. These bubbles shoot upward through the drop and burst, flinging a fine spray of particles into the air, like the fizz rising from a glass of soft drink. The particles carry the scent along on the breeze. Light, steady rain produces more of this spray than a heavy downpour does, which helps explain why a gentle shower often smells strongest.
Sometimes people notice a different, sharper smell just before a storm arrives. This is often ozone, a form of oxygen that can be produced by lightning. Downdrafts from the storm can carry it ahead of the rain, giving an early warning on the wind.
Some scientists think our love of petrichor may have helped our ancestors survive, since in dry lands the smell of rain meant water, and water meant food. Whatever the reason, the scent is so loved that people have tried to capture it. In the town of Kannauj in northern India, perfume makers have for generations produced mitti attar, which means 'earth perfume'. They bake discs of local clay, then heat them in copper pots and collect the scented vapour in sandalwood oil.
So, the next time a storm breaks a long, dry spell, pause and breathe in. You are smelling plants, rocks, bacteria and physics all working together.

After weeks of dry, dusty heat, the first fat drops of a summer storm begin to fall. They darken the footpath, patter on the leaves and tap on tin roofs. Then, almost at once, a rich, earthy scent rises from the ground. Many people find it deeply comforting. Some say it smells like relief.
For a long time, nobody could explain exactly what that smell was. In 1964, two Australian scientists working for the CSIRO in Melbourne, Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, set out to investigate. They steam-distilled rocks and clay that had been exposed to warm, dry conditions and collected a yellowish oil. They named the scent petrichor, combining two Greek words: petra, meaning 'stone', and ichor, the golden fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods in ancient myths. The name suggests something precious hidden in ordinary rock.
Bear and Thomas found that during dry spells, plants release oils that collect on rocks and in soil. One of the most important ingredients of the smell, however, comes from tiny soil bacteria. As they grow, these bacteria produce a chemical called geosmin, a name meaning 'earth smell'. Geosmin is the same compound that gives beetroot its earthy taste. Humans are astonishingly sensitive to it. Some studies suggest we can detect it at just a few parts per trillion, which is a little like noticing a single drop of liquid in an Olympic swimming pool.
But how does the smell reach our noses? In 2015, researchers in the United States used high-speed cameras to film raindrops landing on different surfaces. When a drop hits porous ground such as dry soil, it traps tiny pockets of air. These bubbles shoot upward through the drop and burst, flinging a fine spray of particles into the air, like the fizz rising from a glass of soft drink. The particles carry the scent along on the breeze. Light, steady rain produces more of this spray than a heavy downpour does, which helps explain why a gentle shower often smells strongest.
Sometimes people notice a different, sharper smell just before a storm arrives. This is often ozone, a form of oxygen that can be produced by lightning. Downdrafts from the storm can carry it ahead of the rain, giving an early warning on the wind.
Some scientists think our love of petrichor may have helped our ancestors survive, since in dry lands the smell of rain meant water, and water meant food. Whatever the reason, the scent is so loved that people have tried to capture it. In the town of Kannauj in northern India, perfume makers have for generations produced mitti attar, which means 'earth perfume'. They bake discs of local clay, then heat them in copper pots and collect the scented vapour in sandalwood oil.
So, the next time a storm breaks a long, dry spell, pause and breathe in. You are smelling plants, rocks, bacteria and physics all working together.
Question: Who gave petrichor its name?
Option A: researchers using high-speed cameras
Option B: perfume makers in the town of Kannauj
Option C: two scientists working for the CSIRO
Option D: ancient Greek writers of myths

Forty Years in a Pot
The third leaf fell on a Tuesday. Kenji found it lying on the windowsill beside the little fig, curled and yellow, and his stomach dropped with it.
'No,' he whispered. 'No, no, no.'
The tree was barely taller than his ruler. Its trunk twisted like a wrung-out cloth, and its roots gripped a rock as if they were afraid of falling. His grandmother, Obaachan, had planted it the year she arrived in Australia, more than forty years ago. Now she was living in a unit with no balcony and no sunny windows, and the fig had come to live with Kenji.
Three weeks earlier, she had carried it into his room herself, refusing his help.
'It is not difficult,' she had said, setting it down. 'Water when the soil is dry, not before. Turn it every week so it grows evenly. And do not fuss.'
'What if I kill it?'
She had laughed. 'Trees are tougher than boys think. But they are honest. If you do something wrong, they will tell you. You only have to listen.'
At first, Kenji had been careful. Then he started to worry. What if the soil was dry underneath? What if the tree was thirsty? He watered it on Saturday. He watered it again on Monday, just in case. He moved it to the kitchen, where it was warmer, then back to his room, where it was brighter. On Sunday, he gave it some plant food from the shed.
Now leaves were falling.
He sat on his bed and stared at the tree. He thought about calling Obaachan, but he could already imagine the quiet on the other end of the phone, and that was worse than any scolding. Instead, he searched the internet. Too much water, one website said. Roots need air as well as moisture. Leaves drop when a plant is stressed by sudden changes.
Kenji looked at the soil. It was dark and soggy. He touched it, and water oozed around his fingertip.
They will tell you. You only have to listen.
That afternoon, he did something difficult. He did nothing. He put the fig back on the windowsill in his room, in the morning sun, and he left it there. He pushed a chopstick into the soil, the way he had seen Obaachan do, and checked it every evening. For six days, it came out dark and damp. On the seventh, it came out clean and dry, and only then did he water.
Two more leaves dropped. Kenji swept them into his palm and did not panic.
On a Saturday morning in late spring, he noticed something at the tip of a branch: a tiny point of red-green, tightly furled, no bigger than a grain of rice. By Wednesday there were five.
That weekend, he and his father drove to Obaachan's unit. Kenji had a photo of the buds on his phone, but he had decided that was not enough. On the way, he asked his father to stop at a nursery, where he spent his pocket money on a small pot and a fig cutting, its single leaf as glossy as a new coin.
Obaachan opened the door, saw what he was holding and said nothing for a moment.
'For your kitchen bench,' Kenji said. 'It doesn't need much sun. I checked.'
She took it in both hands. 'You listened,' she said.
Question: Which of these events happened first in the story?
Option A: Kenji gave the fig plant food from the shed.
Option B: Obaachan carried the fig into Kenji's room.
Option C: Kenji noticed tiny buds at the tip of a branch.
Option D: Kenji bought a fig cutting at a nursery.

Nobody Invited Them
In August 1947, a grand new arts festival opened in Edinburgh, Scotland. Its organisers had invited orchestras, opera companies and famous theatre groups from across Europe. But eight small theatre companies that had not been invited turned up anyway. Rather than going home, they found whatever spaces they could and put on their shows around the edges of the official program. A local writer described their efforts as happening on the 'fringe' of the festival, and the name stuck.
Those uninvited performers started something remarkable. Today, the Edinburgh Festival Fringe is one of the largest arts festivals on the planet, with thousands of shows each August staged in theatres, school halls, cafes, lecture rooms and even a double-decker bus. Its central rule is simple: there is no selection panel. If you can find a venue and pay the registration fee, you can perform.
Australia has embraced the idea. The Adelaide Fringe began in 1960 and is now the largest arts festival in the Southern Hemisphere. During February and March, the city is transformed. Comedians perform in shipping containers, jugglers fill the parks, and a magician might share a laneway with a string quartet.
I believe the open-door model is the best way to run a festival, and our school's annual arts night should adopt it.
At the moment, a committee of teachers chooses which acts will perform. The committee does a careful job, but the result is predictable. The same confident students, usually those who already take music or drama lessons, appear every year. Plenty of talented people never audition because they assume they will not be picked.
A fringe removes that barrier. Without a panel deciding who is good enough, performers take risks. Some shows will be brilliant, some will be odd and a few may fall flat. That is part of the fun. Edinburgh has launched the careers of countless comedians, writers and actors who were unknown when they first arrived. Nobody would have chosen them in advance, but audiences discovered them.
An open festival also builds its audience in a different way. At a fringe, people do not simply sit through one long program. They wander from show to show, take a chance on something unfamiliar and tell their friends what they found. Imagine our school grounds with a poetry reading in the library, a band on the basketball court and a science magic show in Lab 3, all running at once.
Critics may worry that some acts will not be polished. They are right; some will not. But a festival is not an exam. Its purpose is to celebrate creativity, and creativity is often messy before it is marvellous. The organisers can still set sensible rules about safety, time limits and suitable content without judging talent.
In 1947, eight groups refused to wait for an invitation. Our school does not have to make its performers wait either. Let's open the doors, hand out a map of venues and see who turns up.
Question: What can be inferred about the eight theatre companies in 1947?
Option A: They had been chosen by the festival's organisers.
Option B: They were too nervous to perform in large theatres.
Option C: They were determined to perform without an invitation.
Option D: They came to Edinburgh only to watch the orchestras.

The Fourth Climb
The dune rose ahead of them like a wave of rust frozen in the moment before it broke. Mia gripped the dashboard as her father revved the engine. The four-wheel drive surged forward, climbed halfway up the slope and then slowed, its wheels spinning and spraying red sand behind them. With a final groan, it stopped and began to slide gently backwards.
'Third time unlucky,' Dad said cheerfully.
Mia didn't laugh. They were four days into their crossing of the Simpson Desert, and she had counted the dunes on the map: more than a thousand of them, lined up across their path like the ribs of a giant animal. This one was the biggest so far. Beyond it, the track ran east for hundreds of kilometres, with no shops, no phone signal and no other cars in sight.
'Can't we just go back the way we came?' she asked.
'We could,' Dad said. 'But that's even further.' He switched off the engine and climbed out into the heat.
Mia followed reluctantly. The air was so dry it seemed to suck the moisture from her lips. Above them, the sky was an enormous, cloudless blue, and the only sound was the tick of the cooling engine.
Dad crouched beside a front tyre and unscrewed the valve cap. 'Here's the trick,' he said. 'Softer tyres spread out. More rubber on the sand means the car floats instead of digging in.' He handed her a pressure gauge. 'Let them down to fourteen. I'll check the others.'
Mia pressed the gauge to the valve. Air hissed out in a long, weary sigh. She watched the needle sink, slowly, slowly, until it reached fourteen. The tyre looked flat and sad, bulging at the bottom like a tired cushion.
'Are you sure about this?' she called.
'Positive.'
While her father finished the last tyre, Mia climbed the dune on foot. It was harder than she expected. Each step slid backwards in the loose sand, and by the time she reached the crest her legs burned and her heart thudded. But the view stopped her. To the east, red ridges rolled away in endless parallel lines, each dotted with grey-green spinifex and the occasional stubborn shrub. A small lizard watched her from the shade of a bush, unbothered, as though it climbed dunes like this every day. It probably did.
She raised her arm and waved. Dad waved back and started the engine.
This time, the car climbed differently. It did not roar or race. It rolled up the slope steadily, almost calmly, the soft tyres gripping the sand. Near the top it lurched, and Mia held her breath, but it kept going and crested the dune beside her with sand pouring from its wheels.
Dad leaned out of the window, grinning. 'Well? Who's driving the next one?'
'I'm thirteen!'
'Then you can be in charge of the tyres.'
Mia climbed in, brushing sand from her knees. Ahead, the next dune was already waiting. She looked at it, then at the gauge in her hand.
'Only nine hundred and ninety-nine to go,' she said.

Option A: slowly
Option B: unhappily
Option C: willingly
Option D: carefully

Walk into almost any school or public library and look at the bottom of a non-fiction book's spine. You will see a short label carrying a number and a few letters, something like 599.75 HAR. This is a call number, and it tells you exactly where the book lives. Learning to read it is the first step to becoming a library volunteer, and it is easier than it looks.
Most school libraries use the Dewey Decimal Classification, created in 1876 by an American librarian named Melvil Dewey. Dewey was obsessed with efficiency. He shortened his first name from Melville to Melvil to avoid wasting letters, and for a time even signed his surname 'Dui'. His system divides knowledge into ten main classes, numbered from 000 to 900. For example, 500 covers science, 600 technology, 700 the arts and sport, 800 literature and 900 history and geography. Each class is split again and again into narrower topics, so the longer the number, the more specific the subject. Books about animals sit in the 590s, books about mammals in the 599s, and books about wild cats at 599.75.
Step 1: Read the whole number before the decimal point. Books are shelved from lowest to highest, left to right along each shelf and then down to the next shelf. A book labelled 549 comes before one labelled 551.

Fiction is usually shelved separately, in alphabetical order by the author's surname, and picture books and graphic novels may have their own sections. Some libraries also add a letter, such as R for reference, to show that a book cannot be borrowed.

The Key Cutter's Week
On Monday morning, Priya arrived at Holt's Locks and Keys expecting to spend her week of work experience sweeping up metal shavings. The shop was narrow and smelled of oil, and every wall was hung with rows of blank keys that chimed faintly whenever a truck passed outside.
Mr Holt was a large, slow-moving man with reading glasses pushed up into his grey hair. He showed her how to clamp a blank into the cutting machine, how to trace the original key with the guide, and how to file away the tiny burrs that the blade left behind. 'A key is a promise,' he said, holding one up to the light. 'If it sticks, somebody is standing on their doorstep in the rain, cursing my name.'
By Wednesday Priya could cut a house key in under two minutes. She was proud of her speed, and a little bored. She had imagined locksmiths cracking safes, not copying keys for the real estate agent next door.
Then, on Thursday afternoon, the phone rang. An elderly woman named Mrs Kostas had locked herself out, and her medication was inside. Mr Holt grabbed a canvas bag and nodded at Priya to follow.
Mrs Kostas was waiting on her front step in a cardigan, clutching her handbag with both hands. She apologised four times before they reached the gate. Priya expected Mr Holt to get straight to work, but instead he sat down on the step beside her and asked about the roses along her fence. He listened to the story of how her late husband had planted them, nodding as though he had all the time in the world.
Only when her hands had stopped trembling did he open his bag. He slid two thin metal tools into the lock, one to hold gentle pressure and one to lift the pins inside, and worked with his eyes half closed, as if he were listening to the door. Within a minute, the lock gave a soft click.
Mrs Kostas laughed with relief and insisted on making them both a cup of tea. Mr Holt accepted, even though Priya knew three customers were due back at the shop.
On the drive back, Priya asked why he had spent ten minutes talking about roses when he could have opened the door straight away.
Mr Holt kept his eyes on the road. 'Picking the lock was the easy part,' he said. 'When people are locked out, they feel foolish and frightened. If I'd rushed in, she'd have spent the whole time apologising. Now she'll remember an afternoon tea, not a mistake.'
On Friday, a young man came in looking flustered, holding a snapped key in two pieces. Before reaching for the cutting machine, Priya asked him how his morning had gone. He blinked, then laughed and told her about the gate that had jammed and the bus he had missed.
When he left, his new key slid smoothly into the lock he had brought to test it. Mr Holt, who had been watching from behind the counter, said nothing at all. He simply handed Priya the shop's spare apron, with her name freshly written on the pocket in black marker.

Option A: her reading glasses
Option B: her spare key
Option C: her medication
Option D: her husband's photograph

The Hundred-Hour Logbook
On the morning of my sister's driving test, the logbook sat on the kitchen bench like a trophy. One hundred and twenty hours, every line filled in Dad's cramped handwriting. Maya picked it up, put it down, and picked it up again.
'You'll be fine,' I said, which was the wrong thing, because she glared at me as if I had personally invented parallel parking.
I had been in the back seat for at least forty of those hours. Mum worked Saturdays, so whenever Dad took Maya out, I had to come along. I was supposed to be a calming presence. Mostly I was luggage.
The first drive, last summer, had been in the empty car park behind the hardware store. Maya gripped the wheel so tightly that her knuckles turned white, and when she pressed the accelerator the car leapt forward like a startled kangaroo. Dad's hand shot out towards the handbrake. Nobody spoke for a full minute. Afterwards, Dad wrote 'car park, 20 minutes' in the logbook as if it had been perfectly ordinary.
It did not improve quickly. Maya stalled at roundabouts. She drifted towards parked cars. Dad, who was normally the calmest person I knew, developed a habit of sucking air through his teeth that made Maya furious. Some Saturdays they barely spoke on the way home, and I sat in the back pretending to read, feeling the silence press against the windows.
The worst drive was in June, on the highway in the rain. A truck overtook us, throwing a wall of spray across the windscreen, and Maya braked hard. When we finally pulled into a service station, she burst into tears and said she was never driving again. Dad switched off the engine. I expected a lecture. Instead, he told her about failing his own test twice, once for running over a witch's hat in front of the examiner. Maya laughed in spite of herself, a wet, hiccupping laugh. Then she drove us home, slowly, with both hands steady on the wheel.
After that, something changed. Dad stopped sucking air through his teeth and started saying 'nice' when she merged well. Maya began asking to go out on weeknights. Once, on a long country road at dusk, they argued cheerfully about music for twenty kilometres while I fell asleep against the window. She learned to reverse into our narrow driveway without touching the letterbox, which Dad admitted was more than he could manage.
Now, in the kitchen, Dad picked up the logbook and handed it to her. 'You've already done the hard part,' he said. 'Today is just someone watching.' Mum hugged her at the door and slipped a muesli bar into her pocket, as if she were setting off on a long journey.
She came home three hours later and didn't say anything. She just held up a small plastic card and grinned.
That evening, she offered to drive me to the shops for ice-cream. Just the two of us. Dad stood on the verandah and watched us reverse down the driveway, one hand raised, the other pressed against his mouth as though he were holding something in. I sat in the front seat for the first time, and I didn't bring a book.
Question: How many hours of driving were recorded in Maya's logbook?
Option A: one hundred
Option B: forty
Option C: twenty
Option D: one hundred and twenty

Not Just a Bin Chicken
Every lunchtime at the Riverside shopping centre, the ibises came. They stalked between the outdoor tables on long black legs, poking their curved beaks into bins and, if anyone looked away for a second, into chip packets. Kofi hated them. Everyone did. His friends called them bin chickens and flapped their arms to scare them off, and Kofi flapped hardest of all.
So when his science teacher, Ms Okonjo, announced that the class would spend a Saturday helping with a bird survey at Mullet Creek wetland, and that the survey was mainly about ibises, Kofi groaned loudly enough for the whole room to hear.
The wetland was twenty minutes from the shopping centre, but it felt like another country. Reeds whispered along the water's edge. A heron stood motionless in the shallows. Ms Okonjo handed out binoculars and clipboards and introduced the class to Dr Lim, a researcher with mud up to her knees.
'You know these birds as pests,' Dr Lim said, pointing to a group of ibises wading through the shallows. 'Most of them would rather be out here.' She explained that Australian white ibises had once lived mainly in the inland wetlands of the Murray-Darling Basin. When drought and changes to the rivers dried out many of those wetlands, large numbers moved to the coast, where cities offered water, parks and, of course, rubbish. 'They're not dirty birds,' she added. 'They're survivors of a drought.'
Kofi watched through his binoculars. Out here, the ibises did not look scruffy or sneaky. They moved with a patient, rocking rhythm, sweeping their beaks through the mud. One pulled out a small yabby and swallowed it whole. Kofi realised he had never actually watched an ibis before. He had only ever chased them.
'Their beaks are like tweezers,' Dr Lim said. 'They can feel prey buried in the mud without seeing it.'
For three hours the class counted birds, recorded the coloured bands on their legs and noted which nests had chicks. Kofi found himself holding his breath as an adult landed beside a nest of untidy sticks and two fluffy grey chicks stretched up, squawking. The parent wore a yellow band. Dr Lim checked her notes and said that this bird had been banded at the wetland eleven years earlier.
'So it came back,' Kofi said slowly. 'Even though there's food at the shops.'
'It came back to breed,' said Dr Lim. 'The city feeds them. The wetland is home.'
On Monday, Kofi sat at the usual table with his friends. An ibis edged towards a bin, and Jayden started to stand up, arms already lifting.
Kofi did not move. He kept eating his sandwich, watching the bird's beak probe carefully along the rim of the bin, testing and feeling, the way it had in the mud.
'What?' said Jayden.
'Nothing,' said Kofi. Then, after a moment: 'Did you know they can feel food without seeing it?'
Jayden stared at him. The ibis pulled out a crust and stalked away, unhurried, as though it had somewhere better to be.
Question: 'Reeds whispered along the water's edge.' Here, 'whispered' means the reeds . . .
Option A: spoke quietly to each other
Option B: grew very thickly together
Option C: bent down towards the water
Option D: made a soft rustling sound

One Hand for the Ship
On the fourth morning of the voyage, the bosun looked up at the main topsail yard, then looked at me. 'Your turn, Elliot,' she said. 'Harness on.'
I was one of twenty trainees on the sail-training ship Kestrel Bay, spending ten days learning to sail her along the coast. I had imagined sunsets and dolphins. I had not imagined climbing twenty-five metres up a swaying mast.
The bosun, Grace Tuhiwai, was in charge of everything above the deck. She was short and weathered, with a voice that could cut through any wind, and in four days I had not once seen her smile. She made us clip and unclip our harnesses until we could do it with our eyes shut. She shouted if anyone stepped over a coiled rope instead of around it. Privately, I had decided that she did not much like teenagers, and liked me least of all.
The wind had been rising since dawn, and the captain wanted the topsail furled before it grew any stronger. Two trainees were already climbing on the other side of the mast. I put my foot on the first rung of the rope ladder and started up.
For the first ten metres, it was almost fun. Then the ship rolled. The whole mast swung out over the grey water, paused, and swung back, and my legs simply stopped working. I clung to the ropes with my cheek pressed against the tarred line, staring at the deck far below. I could hear my own breathing, loud and fast, like a dog that had been running.
Something tugged at my harness. Grace had climbed up beside me, so quickly and quietly that I had not noticed.
'Look at your hands,' she said. Her voice was not loud now. 'Not the deck. Your hands. Three points on the ropes at all times. Move one thing, then the next.'
I looked at my hands. They were white at the knuckles, but they were holding on.
'Old sailors had a saying,' she said. 'One hand for yourself and one for the ship. You've got the first part right. Let's do the second.'
We climbed together, one rung at a time. On the yard, she showed me how to lean over the spar with my feet on the footrope, gathering the heavy canvas in armfuls, tucking it in and passing the ties around. My fingers were clumsy, but the sail grew smaller and tighter until it lay neatly along the yard. Below us, the ship steadied as if she were grateful.

Two days later, a girl named Sunny froze on the same ladder. I climbed up beside her before I had even thought about it. 'Look at your hands,' I heard myself say. 'Not the deck.'
When we came down, Grace was standing at the foot of the mast. She did not smile. But she nodded at me, once, and that was enough.
Question: Which detail best shows that Elliot was frightened during the climb?
Option A: For the first ten metres, it was almost fun.
Option B: I put my foot on the first rung of the rope ladder
Option C: my legs simply stopped working
Option D: I had imagined sunsets and dolphins.

I was one of twenty trainees on the sail-training ship Kestrel Bay, spending ten days learning to sail her along the coast. I had imagined sunsets and dolphins. I had not imagined climbing twenty-five metres up a swaying mast.
The bosun, Grace Tuhiwai, was in charge of everything above the deck. She was short and weathered, with a voice that could cut through any wind, and in four days I had not once seen her smile. She made us clip and unclip our harnesses until we could do it with our eyes shut. She shouted if anyone stepped over a coiled rope instead of around it. Privately, I had decided that she did not much like teenagers, and liked me least of all.
The wind had been rising since dawn, and the captain wanted the topsail furled before it grew any stronger. Two trainees were already climbing on the other side of the mast. I put my foot on the first rung of the rope ladder and started up.
For the first ten metres, it was almost fun. Then the ship rolled. The whole mast swung out over the grey water, paused, and swung back, and my legs simply stopped working. I clung to the ropes with my cheek pressed against the tarred line, staring at the deck far below. I could hear my own breathing, loud and fast, like a dog that had been running.
Something tugged at my harness. Grace had climbed up beside me, so quickly and quietly that I had not noticed.
'Look at your hands,' she said. Her voice was not loud now. 'Not the deck. Your hands. Three points on the ropes at all times. Move one thing, then the next.'
I looked at my hands. They were white at the knuckles, but they were holding on.
'Old sailors had a saying,' she said. 'One hand for yourself and one for the ship. You've got the first part right. Let's do the second.'
We climbed together, one rung at a time. On the yard, she showed me how to lean over the spar with my feet on the footrope, gathering the heavy canvas in armfuls, tucking it in and passing the ties around. My fingers were clumsy, but the sail grew smaller and tighter until it lay neatly along the yard. Below us, the ship steadied as if she were grateful.
Back on deck, Grace inspected my ties, retied one, and walked off without a word. Then I noticed how she watched every trainee on the rigging, her eyes moving from one to the next, never resting. I still don't know whether she liked teenagers. But I know now what all that shouting was for.
Two days later, a girl named Sunny froze on the same ladder. I climbed up beside her before I had even thought about it. 'Look at your hands,' I heard myself say. 'Not the deck.'
When we came down, Grace was standing at the foot of the mast. She did not smile. But she nodded at me, once, and that was enough.

The Bumps Beneath Your Feet
Stand on almost any railway platform in an Australian city and look down. Near the edge, you will see a strip of yellow or contrasting tiles covered in small raised dots. At the top of many staircases and at kerb ramps you will find the same pattern. These bumps are not decoration. They are tactile ground surface indicators, and they are one of the quietest pieces of safety equipment in the modern city.
Where they came from
Tactile paving was invented in Japan by an engineer named Seiichi Miyake, who wanted to help a friend who was losing his sight. The first tiles were laid in 1967 on a street near a school for the blind in Okayama. The idea spread across Japan's busy rail network and, over the following decades, to cities around the world. Today Australia has a national standard that sets out how the indicators must be designed and where they should be placed.
Two kinds of message
There are two main types of tactile indicator, and each sends a different message through the soles of the feet or the tip of a long cane.
Warning indicators are covered in rows of round, flat-topped domes. They mean 'stop and check': there is a hazard ahead, such as a platform edge, a staircase or a road crossing. They are usually laid across the full width of the path so that nobody can walk past them by accident. Most people with good sight barely notice them, but a person using a cane can feel the change in surface instantly.
Directional indicators have long, raised bars running in the direction of travel. They act like a path drawn on the ground, guiding people through large, open spaces such as station concourses, where there may be no wall or kerb to follow. Where a directional path reaches a decision point, such as a turn or a lift, it usually meets a patch of warning domes.
How to share them
If you are sighted, the indicators still ask something of you:
1. Keep directional paths clear. Do not stand, park scooters or leave luggage on them.
2. If you see someone using a cane along the bars, step aside rather than expecting them to go around you.
3. On a platform, wait behind the warning strip, not on it. The strip marks the edge of safety, not a place to stand.
4. Report damaged or missing tiles to the station or council. A gap in the pattern is like a missing word in a sentence: the message no longer makes sense.
Not just for one group
Although tactile paving was designed for people who are blind or have low vision, it helps far more people than that. The bright colour contrast warns anyone who is distracted by a phone. Parents with prams use the kerb ramps it marks. Visitors who are unfamiliar with a busy station can follow the bars towards the exits. Even in a crowd, the bumps underfoot are a gentle tap on the shoulder, reminding everyone that the edge is close.
The next time you feel those small domes through your shoes, remember that the ground is speaking. For thousands of travellers every day, it is saying exactly where it is safe to go.

The Weighing Stone
In the market town of Ollery, where three roads met beneath a crooked clock tower, there stood a set of scales that no one owned. Their bowls were carved from grey river stone, smooth as eggs, and they rested on a plinth in the middle of the square. People said the river spirit had left them there long ago, in the time of the first market.
The scales did not weigh flour or apples. They weighed bargains. When two people made a deal, each placed a hand in a bowl and spoke their terms aloud. If the bargain was fair, the bowls hung level. If one side was cheating, that bowl sank like a stone dropped in a well, and everyone in the square would see.
Because of the scales, the market of Ollery was the most honest for a hundred miles. Travellers came from far away to trade there, knowing they would not be tricked.
Not everyone was pleased. A merchant named Corvin Pell sold cloth that was thinner than he claimed and dyed with colours that faded in the first rain. Customers who bargained with him at the scales watched his bowl plunge again and again, and soon nobody would trade with him at all.
One moonless night, Corvin crept into the square with a wheelbarrow and a crowbar. He levered the scales from their plinth, wrapped them in sacking and hid them beneath the floor of his shop. 'Now,' he thought, 'Ollery will have to trust its own eyes, and eyes can be fooled.'
For a while, his plan worked. Without the scales, the market grew noisy with argument. Prices crept upwards. People checked their change twice and looked at each other sideways. Corvin's cloth sold well, and he grew fat on other people's doubt.
But a girl named Tamsin, who swept the square each morning, noticed something odd. Every night, a thin line of water trickled from beneath the door of Corvin's shop, though it had not rained for weeks. One evening she knelt and pressed her ear to the boards. From below came the faint sound of a river.
Tamsin did not run for the town guard. Instead, she knocked on Corvin's door and asked him, politely, whether he had ever weighed his own bargain with the town.
Corvin laughed at her. But that night he could not sleep for the sound of water. By midnight his floor was soaked, and the trickle had become a stream that ran out of his door, across the street and straight to the empty plinth.
At sunrise the townspeople found the scales back in their place, water still dripping from the stone bowls. Nobody could say who had returned them. Only Tamsin noticed Corvin at the edge of the crowd, his boots soaked, his face grey from lack of sleep.
Later, she led him to the scales. 'Shall we make a bargain?' she said quietly, placing her hand in a bowl. 'You will sell honest cloth, and I will never tell who took the scales.'
Corvin hesitated. Then he placed his hand in the other bowl. Slowly, the bowls swung, steadied and hung perfectly level.

Option A: flour and apples
Option B: how fair a bargain was
Option C: gold and silver coins

Their bowls were carved from grey river stone, smooth as eggs, and they rested on a plinth in the middle of the square. People said the river spirit had left them there long ago, in the time of the first market.
The scales did not weigh flour or apples. They weighed bargains. When two people made a deal, each placed a hand in a bowl and spoke their terms aloud. If the bargain was fair, the bowls hung level. If one side was cheating, that bowl sank like a stone dropped in a well, and everyone in the square would see.
Because of the scales, the market of Ollery was the most honest for a hundred miles. Travellers came from far away to trade there, knowing they would not be tricked.
Not everyone was pleased. A merchant named Corvin Pell sold cloth that was thinner than he claimed and dyed with colours that faded in the first rain. Customers who bargained with him at the scales watched his bowl plunge again and again, and soon nobody would trade with him at all.
One moonless night, Corvin crept into the square with a wheelbarrow and a crowbar. He levered the scales from their plinth, wrapped them in sacking and hid them beneath the floor of his shop. 'Now,' he thought, 'Ollery will have to trust its own eyes, and eyes can be fooled.'
For a while, his plan worked. Without the scales, the market grew noisy with argument. Prices crept upwards. People checked their change twice and looked at each other sideways. Corvin's cloth sold well, and he grew fat on other people's doubt.
But a girl named Tamsin, who swept the square each morning, noticed something odd. Every night, a thin line of water trickled from beneath the door of Corvin's shop, though it had not rained for weeks. One evening she knelt and pressed her ear to the boards. From below came the faint sound of a river.
Tamsin did not run for the town guard. Instead, she knocked on Corvin's door and asked him, politely, whether he had ever weighed his own bargain with the town.
Corvin laughed at her. But that night he could not sleep for the sound of water. By midnight his floor was soaked, and the trickle had become a stream that ran out of his door, across the street and straight to the empty plinth.
At sunrise the townspeople found the scales back in their place, water still dripping from the stone bowls. Nobody could say who had returned them. Only Tamsin noticed Corvin at the edge of the crowd, his boots soaked, his face grey from lack of sleep.
Later, she led him to the scales. 'Shall we make a bargain?' she said quietly, placing her hand in a bowl. 'You will sell honest cloth, and I will never tell who took the scales.'
Corvin hesitated. Then he placed his hand in the other bowl. Slowly, the bowls swung, steadied and hung perfectly level.
Question: Where did Corvin hide the scales?
Option A: under the crooked clock tower
Option B: at the bottom of the river
Option C: in a wheelbarrow in the square
Option D: beneath the floor of his shop

Farmers Under the Leaves
Walk along a trail in a Central or South American rainforest and you may see a strange parade: a line of green fragments, each the size of a fingernail, apparently marching across the forest floor by themselves. Crouch down and the mystery is solved. Each fragment is held high in the jaws of a leaf-cutter ant, and the line may stretch for a hundred metres or more.
A meal they never eat
For a long time, people assumed that leaf-cutter ants ate the leaves they carried. In fact, they cannot digest them. Instead, the ants are farmers. Back in the nest, smaller workers chew the leaf pieces into a soft pulp and spread it through underground chambers. On this pulp grows a special fungus, and it is the fungus, not the leaf, that the colony eats. Some scientists describe this as one of the oldest forms of agriculture on the planet, far older than human farming.
The fungus feeds the ants, and the ants feed, weed and protect the fungus. This particular fungus is not found living wild; it survives only in the gardens the ants tend. Scientists believe the ants and their crop have depended on each other for millions of years.
A city of specialists
A large colony can contain several million ants, all daughters of a single queen. Workers come in very different sizes, and each size has its own job. Large workers with powerful jaws cut leaves and defend the nest. Medium workers carry the pieces home, often holding loads many times their own weight. The tiniest workers, called minims, are too small to cut or carry. They stay in the gardens, tending the fungus and picking out any mould that might spoil it.
Danger on the trail
The trail is a risky place. Tiny parasitic flies hover above the column, looking for an ant whose jaws are full. Some of these flies are smaller than an ant's head. If a fly manages to land, it lays an egg on the ant, and the larva that hatches eventually kills its host. A worker carrying a leaf has no free jaws to fight back.
Watch the parade closely and you will notice something curious. Here and there, a minim is perched on top of a moving leaf. It has left the gardens, it is too small to carry anything, and yet it rides all the way along the trail. When a fly swoops low, the little rider rears up with its jaws open.
Starting again
When a young queen leaves her home colony to begin her own, she carries something precious: a small piece of the fungus, tucked in a pouch inside her mouth. After mating, she digs a chamber, spits out the fungus and starts a new garden before she lays a single egg.
Shaping the forest
Leaf-cutter ants are among the most important plant-eaters in the American tropics. That might sound destructive, but by carrying leaves underground, they move nutrients into the soil and help recycle the forest's plant material. Their tunnels let air and water reach deep below the surface. In their small way, these farmers help keep the whole rainforest growing.
Question: What do leaf-cutter ants actually eat?
Option A: the leaves they carry
Option B: the flies on the trail
Option C: the fungus they grow
Option D: the soil in their tunnels

The Vault in the Frozen Mountain
On the island of Spitsbergen, in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, a narrow concrete wedge juts out of a snowy mountainside. In winter, when the sun does not rise for months, a light artwork on its roof glows in the darkness. Behind its steel doors lies one of the most unusual storerooms on Earth: the Svalbard Global Seed Vault.
Why store seeds?
Every crop we eat, from wheat and rice to beans and barley, exists in thousands of varieties. Some resist drought; others survive pests or salty soil. Plant breeders need this variety to develop crops that can cope with new diseases and changing weather. Around the world, more than a thousand seed banks keep collections of these varieties. But seed banks can be damaged by floods, fires, power failures or simple accidents. When a collection is lost, varieties that took farmers centuries to develop may disappear for ever.
The Svalbard vault, opened in 2008, was built as a backup for those seed banks. It does not replace them. Instead, it holds spare copies of their seeds, so that if anything goes wrong, the originals can be replaced.
Why the Arctic?
The vault is cut into a mountain, at the end of a tunnel more than a hundred metres long. The surrounding ground is permafrost, soil and rock that stay frozen all year. Inside, cooling machines keep the seeds at about minus 18 degrees Celsius, a temperature at which many seeds can survive for decades. If the power failed, the frozen mountain itself would keep the chambers below freezing for a long time. The site is also well above sea level, so it would stay dry even if polar ice melted.
How it works
The vault works rather like a bank's safe-deposit boxes. Countries and organisations send their seeds in sealed boxes, and those boxes remain their property. Only the depositor can open them or ask for them back. The vault can hold about four and a half million seed samples and already contains more than a million.
Tested by events
For its first few years, the vault simply waited. Then, in 2015, a research centre that had lost access to its own collection asked for its seeds back. Using those copies, it rebuilt its stores in a new location and later sent fresh duplicates back to Svalbard. The backup had worked exactly as planned.
The vault has faced challenges of its own. In 2016, unusually warm weather thawed permafrost near the entrance, and meltwater seeped into the start of the access tunnel. The seeds were never in danger, but Norway spent several years upgrading the entrance with a new waterproof tunnel and moving heat-producing equipment away from the passage.
There is an irony in this. A vault built to protect crops from a changing world must now be protected from that change itself. Yet the people who run it remain hopeful. Every new box that arrives is a small act of planning for a future that no one can predict.

Option A: the beauty and isolation of Arctic landscapes
Option B: protecting crop variety as insurance against future loss
Option C: the long history of farming in Norway
Option D: the dangers faced by polar explorers

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
Carry a Poem in Your Pocket
In Year 5, my teacher asked every student to learn a poem by heart and recite it to the class. I chose the shortest one I could find. I practised it in the shower, mumbled it on the bus and, on the day, stood at the front of the room with my knees shaking so hard I was sure everyone could hear them. Here is what I said:
The tide goes out and leaves the sand
all wrinkled like an old man's hand;
it comes back in at close of day
and smooths the creases all away.
I got to the end. Nobody laughed. And four years later, I still know every word. That is more than I can say for almost anything else I learned that year.
Somewhere along the way, learning poems by heart went out of fashion. Many people now see it as old-fashioned rote learning, the kind of thing students did in the days of slates and inkwells. Why memorise anything, they ask, when every poem ever written is a quick search away? I believe that view is mistaken, and that every secondary school should ask students to memorise and recite at least one poem each term.
First, memorising a poem trains the memory itself. It is not about storing facts we could look up; it is about exercising the part of us that does the storing. Like a muscle, memory grows stronger the more we use it. Students who practise holding lines in their heads may find it easier to remember formulas in maths, dates in history and lines in the school play.
Second, recitation builds confidence. Speaking in front of others is one of the most common fears there is, and it does not disappear by being avoided. A short poem is the perfect first step: it is brief, it is already written, and its rhythm carries the speaker along when nerves threaten to take over. I know, because it carried me. By the third line, my voice had stopped wobbling.
Third, and most importantly, a poem you know by heart becomes yours in a way that a poem on a screen never can. You start to notice how the sounds work and why one word was chosen over another, and how a line can turn in the middle. A memorised poem keeps you company. It surfaces at odd moments: waiting at a bus stop, lying awake before an exam, walking along a beach at low tide.
Some will argue that students already have too much to learn, and that memorising poems wastes precious class time. But reciting one poem a term would take only a single lesson, and the practice can happen anywhere, at no cost. Others worry that shy students will suffer. Yet schools could allow students to recite to a small group or to their teacher first, building up gradually to a larger audience.
We carry phones everywhere, full of information we never really learn. Surely there is room in our pockets, and in our heads, for a few lines worth keeping. I did not choose that poem in Year 5 because I loved it. I chose it because it was short. But somewhere along the way, it became one of the things I would least like to lose.
Question: How often does the writer think students should memorise and recite a poem?
Option A: at least once each week
Option B: once every school year
Option C: only once, in Year 5
Option D: at least once each term

The Geometry of Drying
Next time you walk past a dried-up puddle, a cracked creek bed or a farm dam shrunk by summer, I urge you to stop. Most people step around cracked mud as if it were nothing more than mess. They are missing one of the best free science lessons on Earth, and it is time we started paying attention.
Consider what is happening beneath your feet. Wet mud is packed with water. As the sun and wind draw that water out, the mud shrinks, but the ground below holds it in place. Something has to give, so the surface splits. The first crack runs wherever the mud is weakest. Each crack that follows tends to stop when it reaches an earlier one, meeting it at close to a right angle, like the letter T. Look carefully at fresh cracks and you can actually read the order in which they formed: the long, unbroken lines came first, and the short ones that butt into them came later.
Now comes the part that should convince even the doubters. Scientists who study cracking have found that when the same mud is wetted and dried again and again, the cracks reopen and shift a little each time. Over many cycles, the T-shaped joins slowly bend into Y-shaped ones, where three cracks meet at roughly equal angles, and the pattern drifts towards hexagons. A patch of ordinary mud, in other words, keeps a record of how many times it has been soaked and dried. If a puddle can hold a history like that, surely it deserves more than a passing glance.
The same rule works on a giant scale. When a thick flow of lava cools, it contracts just as drying mud does, and cracks spread down into the rock as it hardens. The result can be tall, many-sided columns packed together like pencils in a box. Visitors travel across the world to see the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland, yet Australians need not go so far. At Organ Pipes National Park, on the edge of Melbourne, basalt columns formed this way stand beside Jacksons Creek. The forces that built them are the same forces at work in your driveway after a storm.
Some people argue that patterns like these are only interesting to geologists. I disagree. Engineers deliberately cut grooves into concrete footpaths so that, when the concrete shrinks, it cracks neatly along the lines instead of randomly across the slab. Furniture restorers study the fine cracks in old varnish to help judge an object's age. Understanding how materials split is useful to anyone who builds, repairs or simply wants to know how the world works.
So I am asking for something small. Teachers, take your classes outside after the next dry spell and let students map the cracks in a garden bed. Parents, point them out on weekend walks. Everyone else, photograph the same patch of mud through a whole season. You will never look at a cracked creek bed the same way again, and you will discover that the most ordinary ground is quietly doing geometry.
