Option A: dried puddles should be cleared away before they become messy
Option B: students should study geology instead of other sciences
Option C: lava columns are far more impressive than cracks in mud
Option D: cracked mud is worth noticing because it reveals interesting science

The Corkscrew in the Wrack Line
The storm had blown itself out overnight, and by eight o'clock the beach at Shoreham looked as if someone had emptied a giant's pockets across it. Ropes of kelp lay in tangled heaps along the high-tide mark. There were cuttlebones, crab shells, a single orange thong and, half buried under the weed, something Ellie had never seen before.
She crouched and tugged it free. It was the length of her hand, dark brown and leathery, and wound around itself in a tight spiral, like a screw made for a giant's toolbox. Two thin flanges twisted along its sides.
'Aunt Rosa!' she called. 'Is this a plant?'
Her aunt, who worked as a ranger on the Mornington Peninsula, came crunching across the sand with her coffee. She took one look and smiled. 'That,' she said, 'is a Port Jackson shark egg case. People call them mermaid's purses, though I've never met a mermaid who'd carry something that shape.'
Ellie nearly dropped it. 'There's a shark in here?'
'Probably not any more. Most of the ones that wash up are empty. The pup hatches after about ten or eleven months and swims away, and eventually the old case comes loose.' Rosa turned it gently. 'The mothers lay them on shallow reefs in late winter. Then, and this is the clever part, a mother will often pick the case up in her mouth and wedge it into a crack in the rocks so the waves can't drag it away. The spiral helps hold it in place.'
Ellie examined the twisting edges with new respect. Then she frowned and held the case up towards the low morning sun. The leathery wall was thinner than it looked, and through it, faintly, she could see a pale shape curled against one end. As she watched, the shape gave a small, unmistakable flick.
'It moved,' she whispered.
Rosa put her coffee down in the sand. She took the case and tilted it to the light, and for a long moment neither of them spoke. 'Well,' she said at last, quietly. 'The storm must have torn this one loose before it was finished. There's still a pup inside, and some yolk left, by the look of it.'
'Can we take it home? We could put it in a tank.'
'It needs cold, moving sea water and the right reef, not a bucket on the kitchen bench.' Rosa was already pulling off her shoes. 'Tide's going out. If we're quick, we can get it back where it belongs.'
They waded out to the rock platform at the southern end of the bay, where the reef lay just below the surface in pools fringed with weed. Rosa searched until she found a narrow crevice, deep enough to stay underwater even at low tide. She handed the case back to Ellie.
'You found it,' she said. 'You do the honours. Pointy end first, and twist it the same way as the spiral.'
Ellie knelt on the cold rock and fed the case into the crack, turning it slowly. It bit into the gap, and when she let go, it stayed.
For the rest of that winter, she checked the tide charts every weekend.

Option A: a ranger teaching a group of children about sharks on a beach
Option B: a girl who raises a baby shark in a tank at her aunt's house
Option C: a girl and her aunt returning a living shark egg case to the reef
Option D: a storm that badly damages the reef at the end of a bay

A Rolled Paper Tube
Paris, 14 March 1817
My dear Marie,
Thank you for your letter and for the wool socks, which have made winter in my lodgings almost bearable. You asked whether I am still certain that I want to be a doctor. After this week, I am more certain than ever, and I must tell you why.
You will remember that I now follow Dr Laennec on his rounds at the Necker Hospital. He is a small, thin man with a cough of his own, but his mind is sharper than anyone's I have met. For months the other students have whispered about a strange habit of his, and on Tuesday I saw it for myself.
Until now, a doctor who wishes to hear a patient's heart or lungs has had only one method: he presses his ear directly against the chest. You can imagine how unsatisfactory this is. If the patient is large, the sounds are muffled. If the patient is a lady, the business is embarrassing for everyone. Dr Laennec told us that last year he faced exactly this difficulty with a young woman whose heart troubled him. Rather than press his ear to her, he remembered something he had once seen: children playing with a long wooden beam, one scratching at one end while another, ear to the other end, heard the scratches clearly.
So he rolled a few sheets of paper into a tight tube, placed one end on her chest and put his ear to the other. He says he was astonished. The heartbeat came through louder and clearer than it ever had with his bare ear. The next day he tried it on other patients, half expecting the effect to vanish, but it did not.
Since then he has abandoned paper. He turns his own tubes of wood on a lathe, for he is as handy with tools as he is with his flute, and he has tried cedar, ebony and other timbers to find which carries sound best. The one he uses now is a plain cylinder about as long as my forearm, which comes apart in the middle to fit in his pocket. He has named it the stethoscope, from the Greek words for 'chest' and 'to examine'.
On Tuesday he let me listen to an old sailor with a wet cough. At first I heard only a rushing noise, like the sea in a shell. Then, slowly, I began to tell the sounds apart: a crackle here, a whistle there. I confess I was clumsy at first. I pressed the tube so hard that I heard only my own pulse thumping, until Dr Laennec showed me how to hold it lightly, as one holds a pen. Dr Laennec writes down every sound he hears, and when a patient dies, he compares his notes with what is found in the body. In this way he is building a kind of dictionary, linking each noise to a particular illness.
Not everyone approves. Old Dr Boucher declared at dinner that a real physician needs no toy to do his job. Yet I noticed that he asked to borrow the toy the very next morning.
I have saved enough to have a cylinder made for myself. Do not tell Father yet; I want to surprise him when I come home in the summer.
Your loving brother,
Antoine

Option A: a long wooden beam
Option B: a hollow piece of cedar
Option C: a few sheets of rolled paper
Option D: a seashell from a sailor

Water in the Rose-Red City
In the dry mountains of southern Jordan lies one of the most astonishing cities of the ancient world. Its grandest buildings were not built from blocks at all. They were carved directly into cliffs of pink and red sandstone, which is why a nineteenth-century poet called Petra a 'rose-red city half as old as time'. Most visitors remember the towering carved fronts. Many archaeologists, however, argue that Petra's real masterpiece is something far less obvious: its water system.
Petra was the capital of the Nabataeans, an Arab people who grew wealthy over several centuries by controlling trade routes across the desert. Camel caravans carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia, along with spices and other goods, towards ports on the Mediterranean. Travellers needed food, shelter and above all water, and the Nabataeans were able to supply all three.
That was no simple task. The region receives very little rain, and much of what does fall arrives in a few violent winter storms. Water rushing off bare rock can turn a dry gorge into a deadly torrent within minutes. The main entrance to Petra is just such a gorge: the Siq, a narrow, winding passage over a kilometre long, with walls up to eighty metres high.
The Nabataeans tackled both problems at once. Near the entrance of the Siq they built a dam to block floodwaters and cut a tunnel through the rock to send the flow around the city instead of through it. Along the walls of the Siq itself, they carved channels and laid clay pipes that carried water from a spring outside the city. Small basins along the way allowed sediment to settle, so cleaner water reached the people. Throughout Petra, hundreds of cisterns, many cut deep into the rock, stored rain for the long dry months.
With water under control, the city flourished. Researchers estimate that tens of thousands of people may have lived in and around Petra at its height. Excavations have even uncovered the remains of a large pool with an island pavilion at its centre, surrounded by gardens. In a desert, nothing could have announced wealth and power more clearly than open water that people could simply sit and admire.
Petra's fortunes eventually changed. In 106 CE the Romans took over the Nabataean kingdom, and over the following centuries trade increasingly shifted to sea routes and other cities. A powerful earthquake in 363 CE damaged buildings and water systems alike. With fewer people and less money for constant repairs, the channels and cisterns gradually stopped working, and the population dwindled further. By the time a Swiss traveller, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, reached the site in 1812, Petra was known mostly to local people.
Today, engineers searching for ways to manage scarce water in dry regions still study what the Nabataeans achieved. Their city reminds us that the most important part of a civilisation is not always the part that looks most impressive.

Shoulder to Shoulder
Picture two pairs of friends. One pair sits across a café table, talking about their worries, their families and their plans. The other spends Saturday afternoons fixing an old bike in a garage, barely saying a word beyond 'pass the spanner'. Which pair has the closer friendship? Many people would choose the first. People who study friendship suggest the answer is not so simple.
Some psychologists describe two broad styles of friendship. In face-to-face friendships, closeness grows mainly through conversation: sharing feelings, swapping stories and offering advice. Diary of the Desk Lid
Monday 4 March
Mr Okafor made us carry the old wooden desks out of the storeroom today so it can become a robotics lab. Most of them were covered in initials and ancient chewing gum, but one lid had something different scratched into the inside, in neat capital letters:
COUNT THE WINDOWS. ADD THE STEPS. WALK THAT MANY FROM THE FIG. M.K. 1963.
Mr Okafor said it was probably a joke. Maybe. But nobody carves that carefully for a joke. I asked if I could keep the lid until Friday. It is now leaning against my bedroom wall, and Mum keeps asking why there is half a desk in my room.
Tuesday 5 March
The fig must be the huge Moreton Bay fig beside the Old Block, the only building old enough to have been here in 1963. Jas and I counted at lunch. The Old Block has twelve windows facing the fig and seven sandstone steps up to the door. Twelve plus seven is nineteen. We paced out nineteen big steps from the trunk towards the building and ended up in the middle of the downball court, which is solid concrete. Jas said, 'Well, that's that.' I don't think it is.
Wednesday 6 March
Couldn't sleep, so I made a list of things that might have changed since 1963. Buildings get renovated. Courts get laid. Sixty years is a long time for anything to stay the same, even a building.
Thursday 7 March
I asked Mrs Hartley in the library whether the school kept any old photographs. She took me into the archive room, which smells of dust and pencil shavings, a room where time has been folded up and filed away. She found a box marked 1960-1965, and halfway down was a photo of a class lined up on the steps of the Old Block. I counted the windows behind them three times to be sure. Fourteen. Two have since been bricked up; you can still see the outlines if you know where to look. Mrs Hartley also found a class list with a Margaret Kowalski on it.
Fourteen plus seven is twenty-one.
Friday 8 March
Jas and I paced twenty-one steps at recess. This time we missed the court completely and landed in the garden bed beside it. We weren't allowed to dig, of course, so I showed Mr Okafor the photo and my working. He went very quiet, then fetched a trowel. Ten centimetres down, something clinked.
It was a small, rusted toffee tin. Inside, wrapped in waxed paper, were six glass marbles and a note: 'If you found this, you are cleverer than Peter Baines, who said nobody ever would.'
Saturday 9 March
Mrs Hartley tracked down Margaret Kowalski, who is now Mrs Margaret Hale and lives in Toowoomba. She rang her this morning and passed me the phone. Mrs Hale laughed so hard she had to put the receiver down. She said Peter Baines had bet her a week of lunches that nobody would ever solve her puzzle. 'Sixty-one years,' she said. 'I suppose that means I've won.'
She would like the marbles back. I said I'd post them on Monday, along with a photo of the lid.
Question: What was inside the toffee tin?
Option A: six glass marbles and a note
Option B: an old class photo and a list
Option C: toffees wrapped in waxed paper
Option D: a key to the school archive room

The Last Night of the Diesel
For thirty-one years, my Uncle Bram has kept the lights on at Wreck Bay.
Our island is too far from the mainland for a power cable, so every house, the shop, the school and the fish co-op have always run on electricity from three diesel generators in a tin shed behind the jetty. Uncle Bram knows them the way some people know horses. He can tell from the pitch of their roar whether one needs an oil change, and he once fixed a broken fuel pump at two in the morning with a torch held in his teeth.
Tomorrow, the shed goes mostly quiet. On the ridge above town stand four new wind turbines, and beside the school is a field of solar panels and a container of batteries the size of a small truck. From tomorrow, the wind and sun will do most of the work, and the batteries will store what they make for still nights. The generators will only start if everything else runs low.
'Mostly,' Uncle Bram said at dinner, stabbing a potato. 'That's the word they keep using. Mostly. You watch. First big blow off the Southern Ocean and those windmills will shut themselves down to stop their blades spinning too fast, and who'll be down at the shed then?'
'You will,' said Mum.
'Exactly.' He seemed pleased about this.
I asked whether it was true that the island burned nearly a million litres of diesel a year, which is what the engineer had told our class. He grunted. 'Sounds about right. Every litre comes over on the barge, and when the barge can't get through, we ration.' He paused. 'Mind you, that's not the generators' fault.'
After dinner he asked if I wanted to come down to the shed for the last full night. I said yes, mostly because I'd never been allowed in after dark.
The noise hit me before the door was fully open: a deep, steady hammering that I felt in my ribs. The shed smelled of hot metal and oil. Uncle Bram walked along the three engines, resting a hand on each one as he passed. Then he showed me the logbook, a stack of fat exercise books going back to 1993, every page filled with his square handwriting: dates, hours, litres, faults, repairs.
'Who reads all that?' I asked.
'Nobody,' he said. 'That's not why you write it.'
At midnight we sat on upturned crates outside and looked up at the ridge. The turbines were turning slowly against the stars, perfectly silent from where we sat. Behind us, the generators thundered on.
'They're quiet, I'll give them that,' he said eventually. 'Your mum won't have to shut the windows in summer.'
'And the barge won't matter as much,' I said.
He didn't answer for a while. Then he stood, stretched and went back inside. Through the doorway I watched him take a new exercise book off the shelf, write tomorrow's date at the top of the first page and, underneath it, in his square handwriting, a single word: Turbines.
Question: The story is told by . . .
Option A: Uncle Bram, looking back on his long career
Option B: a narrator outside the story who knows everyone's thoughts
Option C: the engineer who spoke to the island's school class
Option D: Uncle Bram's niece or nephew, in the first person

Throwing the Fleece
The shearing shed at Wilga Downs woke at seven-thirty sharp, when the overhead gear began to whine and four shearers bent over their first sheep of the day. By seven thirty-two, Jess Hartigan was already behind.
It was her first year as a rouseabout, and her job had sounded simple when Dad explained it. As each fleece came off a sheep in one piece, she had to gather it up from the board, carry it to the wool table and throw it so that it spread out flat, outside facing up, like a tablecloth flicked across a kitchen table. Then she and the other rousie, a quiet woman named Dot, would pick off the dirty edges, called skirtings, before the wool classer looked it over.
That was the theory. In practice, Jess's fleeces landed in lumpy heaps, folded over on themselves, or slid off the far side of the slatted table onto the floor. Each time, she had to drag the whole greasy mass back and try again, while behind her the shearers kept peeling off fleeces and the pile at her feet grew.
'Don't fight it,' said Col, the oldest shearer, as she passed his stand for the fourth time with her cheeks burning. He didn't look up from the ewe between his knees. 'Gather it right and it'll throw itself.'
Jess had no idea what that meant. She wasn't even sure Col meant to be helpful. He had shorn in this shed since before she was born, and he was famous across the district for two things: his speed and his silence. People said he had once gone a whole week of shearing without speaking a complete sentence.
At smoko, Jess sat on an upturned bucket with her tea going cold, feeling sorry for herself. Dot sat down beside her.
'Watch me after the break,' Dot said. 'Not my arms. My hands, when I pick it up.'
So Jess watched. Dot didn't grab the fleece in a bundle. She folded the two sides in towards the middle, rolled it loosely from the tail end towards the neck, and lifted it with the neck end held in her hands. At the table, she let go of the outer edge while keeping hold of the inner, and the fleece unrolled through the air and dropped flat as a sheet.
Jess's first attempt after smoko was ugly. Her second was a little better. By her tenth, the fleece opened in the air and settled across the table, almost perfectly spread. Dot gave her a single nod.
Late in the afternoon, Jess threw a merino fleece so cleanly that it landed with every edge squared to the table. She turned to go back for the next one and found Col standing at the end of his pen, straightening his aching back. He was looking at the table.
'Told you,' he said, and went back to his stand.
That evening, Dad asked how her first day had gone. Jess thought about the burning cheeks, the cold tea and the long, clumsy morning. Then she thought about the fleece floating down across the table like a sail.
'Not bad,' she said. 'Col talked to me twice.'

Option A: the boards along the shed walls
Option B: the dirty edges picked off a fleece
Option C: the shearers' separate work areas
Option D: the bales packed at the day's end

Cross-Country, Seven a.m.
The oval is white with frost at the start,
and forty of us stand in a ragged line,
breathing out ghosts. Each puff of warm breath
meets the cold and turns to cloud,
the water in it caught and made visible,
as if our bodies were writing on the air.

The whistle. Forty pairs of shoes
crunch the white grass back to green.
For the first hundred metres I feel fine,
light and quick and a little smug,
and I wonder why I dreaded this all week.

By the gum trees at the far fence, I know.
Beneath my ribs a sheet of muscle,
the diaphragm, is pulling down, down, down,
flattening itself to make more room,
and my lungs rush to fill the space
the way water fills a footprint in wet sand.

Inside them, out of sight, are millions
of tiny sacs, as thin as soap bubbles,
wrapped in a net of narrow vessels.
There, oxygen slips across into my blood,
and the waste my working muscles make,
carbon dioxide, slips the other way
to ride out on my next breath.

My heart, which idled through breakfast,
has stopped politely knocking.
It is pounding on the door now,
sending blood around and around
to legs that want more, and more, and more,
the way a crowd at the tuckshop window
wants everything at once.

Deep in my thighs, the muscles burn
the fuel I ate at breakfast,
the toast and honey, the bowl of oats,
turning it into movement
with every breath I bring them.
Starved of oxygen, the fire dims;
that is why my lungs keep heaving
and my heart keeps up its drumming.

Halfway. The hill behind the science block.
Someone overtakes me, then someone else.
My skin is wet now, even in the cold,
but the sweat is not a failure.
It is a cooling system, switched on,
each drop lifting heat away as it dries.

Past the canteen, a knot of parents
stamp their feet and clap their gloves.
Somebody's little brother yells
a name that isn't mine.
I pretend it is. It helps.
Strange, how a single shout
can travel down into the legs
and push them on a little further.

I want to stop. My body has a vote,
and it is voting loudly. But I've learned
that the first wish to quit comes early,
long before the real limit,
like a smoke alarm that shrieks at toast.
So I keep my feet moving, left and right.

Down the track beside the creek,
where the mud sucks at my shoes,
I find a rhythm I can hold:
two steps in, two steps out,
my breathing and my feet in time,
like a drummer and a band
who have stopped arguing at last
and agreed to play one song.

The last bend. The finish flags.
I am not first, or tenth, or even twentieth,
but I pass two runners on the straight,
my breath a rough saw going back and forth,
and cross the line with nothing left.

Afterwards, on the frosty grass,
I lie and watch my breath go up,
slower now, and slower still,
as my heart eases back to a knock,
small clouds drifting towards a sky
that has turned, while I wasn't looking,
from grey to a clean and early blue.
Question: Which stanza describes the runner sweating?
Option A: the stanza beginning "Halfway."
Option B: the stanza beginning "The whistle."
Option C: the stanza beginning "By the gum trees"
Option D: the stanza beginning "The last bend."

carbon dioxide, slips the other way
to ride out on my next breath.

My heart, which idled through breakfast,
has stopped politely knocking.
It is pounding on the door now,
sending blood around and around
to legs that want more, and more, and more,
the way a crowd at the tuckshop window
wants everything at once.

Deep in my thighs, the muscles burn
the fuel I ate at breakfast,
the toast and honey, the bowl of oats,
turning it into movement
with every breath I bring them.
Starved of oxygen, the fire dims;
that is why my lungs keep heaving
and my heart keeps up its drumming.

Halfway. The hill behind the science block.
Someone overtakes me, then someone else.
My skin is wet now, even in the cold,
but the sweat is not a failure.
It is a cooling system, switched on,
each drop lifting heat away as it dries.

Past the canteen, a knot of parents
stamp their feet and clap their gloves.
Somebody's little brother yells
a name that isn't mine.
I pretend it is. It helps.
Strange, how a single shout
can travel down into the legs
and push them on a little further.

I want to stop. My body has a vote,
and it is voting loudly. But I've learned
that the first wish to quit comes early,
long before the real limit,
like a smoke alarm that shrieks at toast.
So I keep my feet moving, left and right.

Down the track beside the creek,
where the mud sucks at my shoes,
I find a rhythm I can hold:
two steps in, two steps out,
my breathing and my feet in time,
like a drummer and a band
who have stopped arguing at last
and agreed to play one song.

The last bend. The finish flags.
I am not first, or tenth, or even twentieth,
but I pass two runners on the straight,
my breath a rough saw going back and forth,
and cross the line with nothing left.

Afterwards, on the frosty grass,
I lie and watch my breath go up,
slower now, and slower still,
as my heart eases back to a knock,
small clouds drifting towards a sky
that has turned, while I wasn't looking,
from grey to a clean and early blue.

The family group chat was called 'Hendersons Unite!', and it had been created by Gran, who used it mainly for photographs of her tomatoes and for reminding everyone whose birthday was coming up. Josh had muted it in March. This turned out to be important.

One sleeve was noticeably longer than the other.
Josh put it on, took a photo in the bathroom mirror and sent it to his best friend, Kai, with the message: 'Gran has outdone herself. I look like a confused banana. Where do I even wear this??'

The photo was not in his chat with Kai. It was in 'Hendersons Unite!', directly beneath a picture of Gran's tomatoes.
Josh made a sound like a kettle. He knew there was a way to delete messages, but in his panic he pressed the wrong thing and sent a thumbs-up instead. Uncle Rob replied first with a crying-laughing face. His cousin Bella wrote 'CONFUSED BANANA' in capitals, which did not help. Mum, who was in the next room, called out, 'Josh? Have you looked at your phone?' in the tone usually reserved for broken windows.
Gran did not reply at all.
Josh sat on the edge of the bath for a long time. He imagined Gran in her armchair, needles on her lap, reading the words 'confused banana' under a jumper that must have taken her weeks. He considered deleting the chat, or the whole family, or possibly moving to another country. In the end, he did the only thing he could think of. His thumb hovered over her name for nearly a minute. Then he rang her.
She answered on the second ring. 'Hello, darling,' she said, and her voice sounded perfectly normal, which was somehow worse.
'Gran, I'm really sorry about the message. It wasn't meant for... I mean, it was meant for... I love the jumper.'
There was a pause. Then a noise came down the line that Josh did not recognise at first. Gran was laughing: wheezing, helpless, delighted laughter.
'Josh,' she said finally, 'I ran out of yellow wool halfway through that sleeve and had to buy a different batch. And the reindeer was knitted for your grandfather's jumper in 1987. Option A: to thank Gran for sending the birthday parcel
Option B: to show the family that the jumper fitted well
Option C: to share a joke about it with his best friend
Option D: to ask Mum where he could wear it in May

The Third Control
In orienteering, speed is only useful if it is pointed in the right direction. Coach Harland said this at every training session, and at every session Mia nodded and privately believed she was the exception.
She was the fastest runner in the Year 8 squad by a long way. On a track she could leave anyone behind. The problem was that orienteering does not happen on a track. It happens in the bush, with a map, a compass and a string of checkpoints, called controls, that each runner must find in order. Miss one and the whole team is disqualified.
At the state schools relay, Mia was running the second of three legs. Jarrah ran first. He was steady rather than quick, and he did something that drove Mia mad: he stopped at the edge of every clearing, turned the map until it matched the land, and only then moved on. 'You lose ten seconds every time,' she told him once. 'And I never lose ten minutes,' he answered. Priya, who would run the final leg, only laughed and said that between the two of them they might make one decent orienteer.
Jarrah came in from his leg sixth out of twenty teams, red-faced and grinning, and slapped her hand. Mia took off up the first slope as if fired from a cannon. Control one, a boulder beside a dry creek, came easily. Control two, a fence corner, she found by luck as much as skill. She was overtaking people. Fifth. Fourth.
Control three was a small pit in a patch of low scrub. Mia ran to where it should have been. There was no pit. The scrub all looked the same: grey-green bushes, waist high, every gap identical to the last. She ran in a wider circle, then a wider one, her breath loud in her ears. Two runners she had passed jogged by, calmly checked their compasses and headed off to the left. She followed them, then doubted herself and doubled back. By the time she found the orange-and-white flag, hidden exactly where the map said it would be, she had lost almost four minutes.
She looked at the rest of her course. Then she did something she had never done in a race. She stopped. Her heart was still pounding, but her head, for the first time all morning, felt clear. She turned the map until the track on the paper lay along the track at her feet. She picked out a hill and a gully to aim for. Then she ran, not as fast as she could, but as fast as she could think.
She handed over to Priya in ninth place, which felt like a disaster. Priya, the team's best navigator, ran a beautiful final leg and brought them home fifth. Nobody on the team mentioned control three. On the bus, Mia sat down next to Jarrah.
'Ten seconds,' she said.
He looked at her, waiting, the way he waited at the edge of a clearing.
'At every clearing,' she said. 'Show me how you decide where to stop.'
He pulled a crumpled map out of his bag, and for the rest of the trip home they bent over it together, tracing the route with their fingers, while the bush slid past the windows in the dusk.

Option A: the runner loses ten minutes
Option B: the runner must restart the leg
Option C: the whole team is disqualified

Windows of Golden Resin
Walk along certain beaches of the Baltic Sea after a winter storm and you may find small, honey-coloured lumps among the seaweed. Pick one up and it feels surprisingly warm and light, almost like plastic. It is amber, and some pieces hold a secret: a tiny creature, frozen mid-step, that has not moved for tens of millions of years.
Amber begins as resin, the thick, sticky liquid that many trees release when their bark is damaged. Resin seals the wound and helps keep out insects and fungi. Sometimes, however, it traps the very creatures it is meant to stop. An ant crossing the bark, a gnat landing for a moment, a spider spinning nearby: once caught in the ooze, they cannot escape, and more resin may flow over them.
If the resin is then buried in sediment, a slow change begins. Over millions of years, the lighter chemicals in it escape and the remaining molecules link together into long, tough chains. The young, partly hardened stage is called copal. Only after a much longer time does it become true amber. Most Baltic amber formed roughly 40 to 45 million years ago.
What makes amber so valuable to scientists is the detail it keeps. Most fossils form when minerals slowly replace bone or shell, so soft parts are usually lost. Amber works differently. It seals a creature away from air and water almost at once, so the fine hairs on a fly's legs, the veins in a wing or the threads of a web can survive. Scientists call these trapped objects inclusions, and they include not only animals but pollen, feathers, seeds and even tiny drops of ancient water.
In 2016, researchers described one of the most famous inclusions ever found: part of the feathered tail of a small dinosaur, sealed inside a piece of amber about 99 million years old from Myanmar. Because the tail was enclosed, scientists could see how the feathers were arranged along it, something bones alone could never show.
It is tempting to imagine going further. A popular film once suggested that dinosaur DNA could be drawn from the blood inside a mosquito trapped in amber. Sadly, the science does not hold up. DNA is a fragile molecule that breaks apart over time, and studies suggest that even in ideal conditions it would not last anywhere near this long. In the 1990s, some scientists claimed to have extracted ancient DNA from amber insects, but other laboratories could not repeat the results, and the samples were most likely contaminated with modern DNA.
Amber also gives a lopsided view of the past. It mostly captures small creatures that lived on or near tree trunks. A large animal, or one that lived in open grassland, would almost never end up inside. Scientists must remember that what they find in amber is a keyhole view, not the whole room.
Even so, each clear piece is a kind of window. Hold it up to the light and you are looking straight into a forest that vanished long before the first humans walked the Earth.

Option A: buried deep beneath the sand
Option B: inside the trunks of living trees
Option C: in rock pools during low tide
Option D: after storms have washed it ashore

My granddaughter tugs me past the steam engines.
She's nine, and walks the way she reads, too fast,
skipping the boring bits to reach the end,
past the cases of valves and coiled copper wire,
to a corner where an orange arm stands bolted to the floor,
its elbow bent, its wrist cocked like a question.
'Look, Nanna,' she says. 'A robot.' The sign reads
WELDING ARM, 1984. GIFT OF KESTREL MOTOR WORKS.
I know, I tell her. I used to work beside it.

It came the winter I turned thirty,
crated like a piano, unpacked like a prince.
The foreman called us round to watch it move.
It swung, it dipped, it touched the seam with light,
and where its fingertip had kissed the steel
a weld ran neat as stitching on a Sunday shirt.
Nobody clapped. We knew what it could count.

For eleven years we shared the line, that arm and I.
It never asked for smoko, never hummed,
never brought a thermos or a photo of its kids.
It did four hundred welds an hour, each one the same,
while I did fewer, and each one was mine:
a little thick here, a little proud there,
the way a signature is never quite repeated.

At smoko we would sit along the wall
with sandwiches and crosswords and the radio,
and watch it working on right through our break,
not tired, not bored, not anything at all.
Big Col would raise his mug to it and say,
'Cheers, mate, have one on us,' and we would laugh
the way you laugh at weather you can't change.

People ask me now if I hated it.
I tell them hate is for things that can choose.
It didn't choose to come. It didn't take my job;
somebody signed a paper in an office far away,
and the arm just went on welding, innocent as rain,
the same week they handed us our envelopes,
a handshake and a clock with a brass plate.

Still, I'll admit, on bad nights I would dream it
swinging toward me down an empty line,
its single eye of light gone cold and searching,
and I would wake and hear the fridge, and think
of all the hands that used to make that sound,
the clink and hiss and shout of forty people
turned into one long, perfect, patient hum.

My granddaughter presses the button on the rail.
The arm lifts, turns and slowly bows to her,
a little stiff, the way my knees are now.
She laughs and waves. She builds robots at school,
small ones, from kits, that follow a black line
across the classroom floor and win her ribbons.
She tells me how the sensors read the floor,
how every move begins as lines of code
that she can change whenever something's wrong.
She wants to make one that can help old people walk.

And here's the thing I never thought I'd feel:
I'm proud of her, and not one bit afraid.
The arm and I are both museum pieces now,
both pensioned off, both slower than we were.
Maybe the question never was the arm,
but whose hands plan the work, and what it's for.
And hers, I think, are good hands for the job.
Question: In the second stanza, the word crated means . . .
Option A: lifted into place by a crane
Option B: painted in bright factory colours
Option C: checked carefully by experts
Option D: packed in a large wooden box

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
Designing an Alien That Makes Sense
Science fiction is full of aliens that are really just people in rubber masks: two arms, two legs, a lumpy forehead and a bad attitude. If you want readers to believe in your creature, you need to think like a scientist before you think like an artist. This guide shows you how to build an alien from the ground up, starting not with the creature but with its world.
What you will need
A notebook, a pencil, some basic knowledge of how living things on Earth survive, and a willingness to throw away your first idea.
Step 1: Choose the planet first
Every living thing is shaped by its surroundings, so begin there. Decide how big your planet is, because size affects gravity. On a large, heavy world, gravity pulls harder, so tall, spindly creatures would struggle; short, broad bodies with thick legs make more sense. On a small world with weak gravity, tall and delicate shapes become possible. Write down whether the planet is hot or cold, wet or dry, and whether it has seasons.
Step 2: Look at the light
Next, think about the star your planet orbits. Many stars are smaller, cooler and redder than our Sun. Under a dim red sun, plants might be dark, even black, to soak up as much light as possible, and animals might have huge eyes, or senses that do not rely on sight at all. On a world wrapped in thick cloud, hearing or smell could matter far more than vision.
Step 3: Decide what it eats and what eats it
A creature's body is a record of how it gets food and avoids becoming food. Hunters on Earth often have eyes facing forward to judge distance, while hunted animals often have eyes on the sides of their heads to watch for danger. Ask the same questions about your alien. Does it chase, graze, filter or trap? What is it afraid of?
Step 4: Give every feature a reason
Now sketch the body, but justify each part. If it has six legs, why? If it is covered in plates, what are they protecting it from? A useful rule is that if you cannot explain a feature, cut it. The best alien designs feel strange at first and then, a moment later, feel inevitable.
Step 5: Test it with a story
Finally, drop your creature into a short scene. Have it hunt, hide, raise young or survive a storm. Problems will appear quickly. Perhaps its delicate wings would be shredded by the planet's fierce winds, or it has no way to stay cool in the long summer. Go back and adjust. Designers of films and games often go through dozens of versions before they settle on one.
Common mistakes
The most common mistake is making an alien too human. Another is giving it features simply because they look frightening, such as rows of teeth on a creature that eats only moss. Readers notice these things, even if they cannot say why.
Remember, an alien is not a monster with a costume on. It is the answer to a question your planet has asked. Get the question right, and the answer will almost design itself.

Option A: Step 2
Option B: Step 1
Option C: Step 4
Option D: Step 5

Bearing Two-Seventy
When Callum's mum married Russ, Callum decided three things about him: he talked too little, he wore socks with sandals, and he owned a compass, an actual plastic compass on a cord, as if the twenty-first century had never happened.
So when Russ suggested an overnight hike to Mount Garnet Hut, just the two of them, Callum agreed mainly because saying no would have meant a conversation. He loaded the track onto his phone, packed a charger cable he would later discover was the wrong type, and spent the drive with his earbuds in.
The first day was easy. The track climbed steadily through stringybark and then out onto a bare granite ridge, where the whole valley spread beneath them like a crumpled green blanket. Russ stopped every so often to check a paper map, folding it carefully back into its plastic sleeve. Callum checked his phone. It showed a blue dot moving along a red line, which seemed to him a far more sensible system.
The hut was a tin shed with six bunks and a water tank. They ate noodles and watched the light drain out of the sky. Russ said perhaps twenty words all evening, three of which were 'Pass the salt'.
In the morning, the world had disappeared.
Fog had rolled up from the valley overnight, so thick that Callum could barely see the toilet block twenty metres away. It beaded on his jacket and dripped from the brim of his cap. The cairns that marked the route across the granite vanished after two or three steps. That was when Callum looked at his phone and saw the battery icon, red and nearly empty, blink once and go dark.
He felt something cold settle in his stomach that had nothing to do with the weather.
Russ didn't say 'I told you so'. He didn't say anything. He unfolded the map on a flat rock, laid the compass on it, turned the little dial and studied it for a long minute. Then he handed the compass to Callum.
'Bearing two-seventy,' he said. 'Due west, near enough. Hold it flat and keep the needle lined up. Pick something ahead of you, a rock or a bush, and walk to it. Then do it again.'
'Why me?' Callum asked.
'Because you've got younger eyes,' said Russ, 'and because next time you might be on your own.'
So Callum led. He chose a lichen-spotted boulder and walked to it, then a twisted shrub, and walked to that. Russ followed a few steps behind, silent, occasionally saying 'Good' in a way that made Callum stand a little straighter. After forty minutes a cairn loomed out of the grey exactly where it should have been. Then the track dropped off the ridge into the trees, and the fog thinned to a soft white glow among the trunks.
At the car, Callum held out the compass. Russ shook his head.
'Keep it,' he said.
Callum looked at it for a moment. Then he hung it around his neck, where it bumped against his chest the whole way home. He left his earbuds in his pocket.

Option A: painted signs nailed to trees
Option B: piles of stones that mark a route
Option C: small wooden shelters for hikers
Option D: patches of thick, low fog

Eye to Eye: Photographing Insects Up Close
Most people walk past thousands of insects every day without noticing them. A close-up photograph changes that. Suddenly a fly has jewelled eyes made of hundreds of tiny lenses, a beetle's shell gleams like polished metal, and a moth's wing turns out to be covered in overlapping scales, like tiles on a roof. You do not need expensive equipment to take pictures like these, but you do need the right approach.
Equipment
A phone camera can work well, especially with a clip-on macro lens, which costs little and lets you focus much closer than normal. A sheet of white paper to bounce light is also useful. Most important of all is a field notebook to record where and when you found each subject.
Step 1: Pick your time
Early morning is the best time to start. Insects are cold-blooded, which means their body temperature rises and falls with their surroundings. On a cool morning they move slowly, and a butterfly that would dart away at noon may sit still long enough for several shots. Dew on wings and spider webs adds sparkle, too.
Step 2: Find your subject
Look where insects feed and rest: flowers, the undersides of leaves, fence posts, the edges of puddles. Move slowly and avoid casting your shadow over the insect, since a sudden shadow often signals danger and it will fly off.
Step 3: Get close and get level
Approach in small steps, pausing often. Once you are near, lower the camera until it is level with the insect's eyes. A photo taken from above usually looks like a specimen in a museum drawer; one taken at eye level feels like a portrait. Focus on the eyes, because if they are sharp, viewers will forgive a blurry leg.
Step 4: Control the light
Harsh midday sun creates dark shadows and bright glare. Soft light is kinder. On a sunny day, hold the white paper to one side so that it reflects light onto the shadowed side of the insect. Avoid using your phone's flash directly, which tends to flatten the shape and can startle your subject.
Step 5: Respect your subject
Never pin, chill or trap an insect to make it easier to photograph. A good wildlife photographer leaves an animal exactly as they found it. If an insect flies away, let it go. Another will come along, and patience is part of the craft. Still, it helps to know that many insects return to the same perch again and again. Wait quietly nearby and you may get a second chance.

The Month Without Wrappers
It was Mum's idea, which was the first warning sign. 'For the whole of July,' she announced at dinner, 'this family is going plastic-free.'
Dad said, 'Right,' in the voice he used for things he planned to forget. My brother Sami, who is nine, asked whether that included Lego. I said nothing, because I was fourteen and had learned that the best way to survive Mum's projects was to wait for them to collapse on their own.
The first week was chaos. You don't realise how much plastic there is until you try to avoid it. Bread came in plastic bags. Cheese came in plastic. Even the bamboo toothbrushes Mum ordered online arrived in a plastic sleeve, which she held up at breakfast like evidence in a court case. Sami's lunch box, normally a cheerful pile of little packets, became a stern arrangement of apple slices and a cheese sandwich in a beeswax wrap that smelled faintly of candles. He swapped it for a muesli bar on the first day and got caught.
I started keeping a list of every failure so I could read it out at the end, like a reporter. Then Nana came to stay.
Nana grew up on a dairy farm near Bega in the 1950s, and she watched our battle with the bread bags for about two days before she quietly took over. She showed Mum how to ask the bakery to drop loaves straight into a cotton bag. She made yoghurt in a glass jar wrapped in a tea towel on the bench. She taught Sami to bake crackers, which he decided were better than the packet ones, mostly because he was allowed to cut them into dinosaur shapes. She remembered milk in glass bottles with foil caps that birds pecked through, and a grocer who wrapped everything in newspaper. 'We weren't trying to save the planet,' she said. 'We just didn't have the other stuff yet.'
She took me with her to the bulk-food shop on Saturday, where you fill your own containers from big bins of oats, lentils and nuts. I expected it to be boring. Instead it was oddly satisfying, like a cross between a library and a lolly shop. Nana weighed the empty jars first so the cashier could subtract them, and the man behind the counter knew her name by the second visit.
By the end of July, we were not plastic-free. Not even close. Medicine still came in blister packs, Dad never found a shampoo he liked, and Sami's Lego remained a protected species. But our yellow recycling bin, which used to overflow every fortnight, was only half full, and the red bin was lighter too.
At the final dinner, Mum asked what we had learned. I had my failure list in my pocket, three pages long. I didn't read it out. Instead I said we should keep the bulk-shop trips going, and maybe the yoghurt.
Nana smiled into her cup of tea. Later I found the list still folded in my pocket, and on the back I started a different one: things we could actually keep doing. It was shorter. But it was the kind of list you can stick on a fridge.
Question: Why did the narrator say nothing when Mum announced her plan?
Option A: the narrator expected the project to fall apart on its own
Option B: the narrator was too excited about the plan to speak
Option C: the narrator did not understand what plastic-free meant
Option D: the narrator was waiting for Nana to arrive and decide

A Pet for Life, and Then Some
Most people who buy a puppy expect to share ten or fifteen years with it. Someone who buys a cockatoo may be making a promise that lasts far longer than that. Large parrots are among the longest-lived animals people keep as pets, and their lifespans raise questions that dog and cat owners rarely have to consider.
Sulphur-crested cockatoos, the noisy white birds with yellow crests seen across eastern Australia, can live for decades in the wild. In captivity, with good food and veterinary care, some live even longer. One of the most famous long-lived parrots was Cookie, a Major Mitchell's cockatoo at Brookfield Zoo near Chicago. He arrived at the zoo in 1934 as a young bird and lived there until 2016, when he died at an estimated age of 83. He had outlived many of the keepers who first cared for him.
A long life is not the only challenge. Cockatoos are highly intelligent and intensely social. In the wild, they spend their days in flocks, travelling, feeding and squabbling together, and they keep in touch with loud calls. A pet cockatoo often treats its human family as its flock. It may want company for most of the day, and if it does not get it, it lets everyone know. A cockatoo's scream can be heard several houses away, which neighbours do not always appreciate, especially at six o'clock in the morning or late on a summer evening.
Boredom is a serious problem. A wild cockatoo spends hours stripping bark, digging for roots and cracking seeds. In a cage with nothing to do, that energy has to go somewhere. Some birds begin to pull out their own feathers, a habit called feather plucking that can be very hard to stop once it starts. Experienced owners provide branches to shred, puzzle feeders that make the bird work for its food, and several hours a day outside the cage. Many say that a cockatoo is less like a pet and more like a toddler who never grows up, and who has a beak strong enough to snap a pencil.
Because the birds live so long, responsible owners plan ahead. Some include their parrot in their will, naming a friend or relative who has agreed to care for it. Others arrange for a bird rescue group to take it in. Without a plan, an elderly cockatoo may pass from home to home, and each move can be stressful for an animal that bonds so closely with its people.
None of this means cockatoos make bad pets. People who understand their needs often describe them as affectionate, funny and endlessly curious. Many cockatoos learn to mimic words, bob along to music and greet their owners at the door. But experts suggest that anyone thinking of buying one should first spend time with an adult bird, ideally at a rescue centre, and ask a simple question: who will look after this bird when I no longer can?
For a cockatoo, that is not a distant problem. It is almost certain to happen.
Question: About how old was Cookie when he died?

Earthquake Milne
In March 1876, a young English geologist named John Milne arrived in Tokyo after one of the strangest journeys any new teacher has ever made. Offered a job at the Imperial College of Engineering, he chose to travel most of the way overland, across Europe, Russia and the frozen expanse of Siberia, partly because he dreaded seasickness. The trip took him around eleven months. On his first night in Japan, the ground shook beneath him. It was only a small earthquake, but it set the direction of the rest of his life.
Milne had been born in Liverpool in 1850 and trained in mining and geology. In Japan, earthquakes were frequent, yet almost nothing was understood about them scientifically. People recorded how much damage they caused, but there was no reliable way to measure the shaking itself, to tell where it had begun, or to compare one quake with another. Milne found this gap irresistible.
In 1880, a strong earthquake struck near Yokohama. It damaged buildings, and it shook Milne into action. Within weeks he helped found the Seismological Society of Japan, the first organisation of its kind in the world. Working with fellow British scientists James Ewing and Thomas Gray, he helped develop instruments that could record the motion of the ground. One of the most successful was the horizontal pendulum seismograph, which traced the side-to-side movements of an earthquake as a line on a moving surface. For the first time, shaking could be captured, measured and studied afterwards.
Milne was tireless. He organised a network of observers across Japan who reported every tremor they felt, gathering information on thousands of earthquakes. He studied how different buildings behaved during shaking and argued that structures should be designed with earthquakes in mind, an idea that seems obvious now but was new at the time. He also married a Japanese woman, Tone Horikawa, and came to regard Japan as his home.
Then, in 1895, disaster struck of a different kind. A fire destroyed his house, his library and much of his observatory, along with years of records. Soon afterwards, Milne and Tone left Japan for England. Many people might have retired. Milne instead set up a new observatory in a house at Shide, on the Isle of Wight.
From that quiet village, he did something remarkable. He had realised that the waves from a large earthquake travel right through and around the planet, so a sensitive seismograph could detect a quake on the other side of the world. He persuaded scientists in many countries to install matching instruments and send him their records. Eventually dozens of stations, from Canada to New Zealand, were part of his network. By comparing when the waves reached each station, scientists could locate distant earthquakes and begin to learn about the Earth's hidden interior.
Milne died at Shide in 1913. Today, thousands of seismographs around the world share data within minutes. They are descendants of the idea he pursued for nearly forty years: that the trembling ground has a story to tell, if someone is patient enough to listen.

Museums Without Walls
When most people imagine a museum, they picture glass cases, quiet halls and labels on the wall. But some of the world's most popular museums have no halls at all. They are open-air museums: villages, farms and streets where whole buildings are the exhibits, and visitors walk among them as though they had stepped back in time.
The idea began in Sweden. In the late 1800s, a teacher and collector named Artur Hazelius noticed that his country was changing fast. Railways and factories were drawing people from the countryside into cities, and the traditional farmhouses, crafts and customs of rural Sweden were disappearing. Hazelius had already gathered thousands of everyday objects, such as tools, clothes and furniture, for a museum in Stockholm. Yet he felt that a spinning wheel in a glass case told only part of the story. To understand how people had lived, visitors needed to see the spinning wheel in the room where it was used, beside the fire, under the low wooden roof.
So in 1891 he opened Skansen, on a hill overlooking Stockholm. Over the following years, more than a hundred buildings were taken apart in their original locations, carried to the site piece by piece and rebuilt: farmhouses, barns, a schoolhouse, workshops and windmills. Staff dressed in traditional clothing baked bread, wove cloth and played folk music. Skansen was an immediate success, and its name became the word for an open-air museum in several European languages.
The idea soon spread around the world. In Australia, one of the best-known examples is Sovereign Hill in Ballarat, which opened in 1970. It recreates a gold-mining town of the 1850s, with a main street of shops, a blacksmith, a school and a creek where visitors can pan for gold. Many of its buildings are reconstructions based on old photographs and drawings rather than originals.
Supporters argue that open-air museums bring history to life in ways that indoor galleries cannot. Visitors can smell wood smoke, hear the clang of a forge and feel how cramped a miner's hut really was. These museums also focus on ordinary people, such as farmers, miners and shopkeepers, whose lives are often left out of history books.
Critics, however, point out some problems. A building moved from its original village loses its connection to the landscape and community around it. Reconstructions may contain guesses, and visitors cannot always tell which parts are original. There is also a risk that the past appears cleaner and happier than it was. A tidy street with friendly guides may not show the hunger, disease and hard labour that many people actually faced.
The best open-air museums try to meet these challenges. They label what is original and what has been rebuilt, and they use careful research to show daily life honestly, including its hardships. Handled well, a museum without walls can do what Hazelius hoped: help visitors understand not just what people owned, but how they lived.

When most people imagine a museum, they picture glass cases, quiet halls and labels on the wall. But some of the world's most popular museums have no halls at all. They are open-air museums: villages, farms and streets where whole buildings are the exhibits, and visitors walk among them as though they had stepped back in time.
The idea began in Sweden. In the late 1800s, a teacher and collector named Artur Hazelius noticed that his country was changing fast. Railways and factories were drawing people from the countryside into cities, and the traditional farmhouses, crafts and customs of rural Sweden were disappearing. Hazelius had already gathered thousands of everyday objects, such as tools, clothes and furniture, for a museum in Stockholm. Yet he felt that a spinning wheel in a glass case told only part of the story. To understand how people had lived, visitors needed to see the spinning wheel in the room where it was used, beside the fire, under the low wooden roof.
So in 1891 he opened Skansen, on a hill overlooking Stockholm. Over the following years, more than a hundred buildings were taken apart in their original locations, carried to the site piece by piece and rebuilt: farmhouses, barns, a schoolhouse, workshops and windmills. Staff dressed in traditional clothing baked bread, wove cloth and played folk music. Skansen was an immediate success, and its name became the word for an open-air museum in several European languages.
The idea soon spread around the world. In Australia, one of the best-known examples is Sovereign Hill in Ballarat, which opened in 1970. It recreates a gold-mining town of the 1850s, with a main street of shops, a blacksmith, a school and a creek where visitors can pan for gold. Many of its buildings are reconstructions based on old photographs and drawings rather than originals.
Supporters argue that open-air museums bring history to life in ways that indoor galleries cannot. Visitors can smell wood smoke, hear the clang of a forge and feel how cramped a miner's hut really was. These museums also focus on ordinary people, such as farmers, miners and shopkeepers, whose lives are often left out of history books.
Critics, however, point out some problems. A building moved from its original village loses its connection to the landscape and community around it. Reconstructions may contain guesses, and visitors cannot always tell which parts are original. There is also a risk that the past appears cleaner and happier than it was. A tidy street with friendly guides may not show the hunger, disease and hard labour that many people actually faced.
The best open-air museums try to meet these challenges. They label what is original and what has been rebuilt, and they use careful research to show daily life honestly, including its hardships. Handled well, a museum without walls can do what Hazelius hoped: help visitors understand not just what people owned, but how they lived.

Tuesday Plane
Out here the week has a hinge,
and the hinge is Tuesday,
when the whole station listens past the windmill's creak
for a sound smaller than a blowfly
working its way across the enormous blue.
My brother hears it first. He always does.
He drops the bucket by the chook pen
and runs to the airstrip, graded flat as a table,
where Dad has already driven the ute
to chase the kangaroos off the red dirt runway.
Then it appears: a white speck, a cross, a plane,
tilting its wings as if to wave,
lowering itself the way Nan lowers into her chair,
careful, a little stiff, glad to be down.
The wheels touch, bounce once, and dust rolls out behind
like a long brown scarf that the wind unwinds.
The pilot's name is Jo. She has a sunburnt nose
and a clipboard, and she knows everybody's business
in the kindest possible way.
She hands down the canvas sack of letters,
a carton of medicine for the Wilsons' baby,
a new fan belt for the generator,
a library book I ordered six weeks ago
from a city I have only seen on television.
Then she takes things back the other way:
the mailbag heavy with our news,
a blood sample in a cold box for the doctor in town,
Mum's order for seeds and school paper,
and the drawing my brother made of the plane,
folded in four, addressed to Jo herself.
Twenty minutes, that's all she has.
There are four more stations on her run,
four more dusty strips with four more families
standing in the heat with their hands over their eyes.
Dad signs the forms. Mum gives her a slab of fruitcake
wrapped in a tea towel. Jo laughs and says
we'll make her too heavy to take off.
I stand by the wing and touch the metal.
It is warm as a lizard's back,
and it hums faintly, as if it remembers the sky.
I ask Jo what it looks like from up there,
and she thinks for a moment, then says,
'Small. Everything you worry about looks small.'
Then the propeller coughs and blurs,
the engine climbs from a mutter to a roar,
and the plane runs, runs, runs down the strip
until the ground lets go of it.
We watch it shrink to a cross, a speck, a nothing,
and the silence comes back and settles like dust.
For six days the letters will be read and reread,
the medicine measured out by the spoonful,
the fan belt fitted while Dad mutters at the spanners.
And I will lie on the hot tin of the shed roof
reading my library book,
watching the empty sky to the east.
Some nights, when the generator is off
and the stars come down close enough to touch,
I hear a far-off drone, a real plane, high and secret,
blinking red and green across the dark,
full of people asleep on their way
to places with names I practise saying.
One day I will be the speck that someone waits for.
I will tilt my wings above a windmill
and see a child with her hand over her eyes,
and I will remember being small
on a big red page of land,
waiting for Tuesday to come down out of the blue.

Option A: marked with a score
Option B: sorted into groups
Option C: painted with lines
Option D: levelled and smoothed

like a long brown scarf that the wind unwinds.

and a clipboard, and she knows everybody's business
in the kindest possible way.

a carton of medicine for the Wilsons' baby,
a new fan belt for the generator,
a library book I ordered six weeks ago
from a city I have only seen on television.

a blood sample in a cold box for the doctor in town,
Mum's order for seeds and school paper,
and the drawing my brother made of the plane,

The Upside-Down Garden
Since her hip operation, Gran had not been further than the bathroom. The physio said six weeks, maybe eight, and Gran said that was fine, but Tess noticed that she kept asking about the garden. Were the camellias out yet? Had the magpies come back to the birdbath? Was the old plum in blossom?
'Go and look for me,' she would say, and Tess would go and look, and come back and describe it, and Gran would nod. But Tess could tell that words were not the same as seeing.
The idea arrived during a science lesson. Mr Okafor was explaining that light travels in straight lines, and he drew a diagram on the board: a tree, a tiny hole and a screen, with lines crossing over at the hole. 'Make a room completely dark and let light in through one small opening,' he said, 'and the scene outside appears on the opposite wall, upside down. It's called a camera obscura. That's Latin for dark room.'
Tess stopped copying the diagram. Gran's bedroom faced the garden.
That Saturday she spent the morning on a ladder. She covered Gran's window with black cardboard, taping every edge until not a crack of light showed. Gran watched from the bed, eyebrows raised. 'Are you turning me into a mushroom?'
'Wait,' said Tess. With a skewer, she poked a hole in the middle of the cardboard, about the width of a pencil. Nothing happened. The room just stayed dark, and Tess felt her face go hot. She had promised a miracle and produced a cupboard.
Then her eyes began to adjust. On the white wall opposite the window, something was forming: a smudge of pink, a darker shape, a pale strip that might be the path. Slowly the smudges sharpened. There was the plum tree, its blossom faint and soft, hanging from the ceiling with its roots in the sky. There was the birdbath, upside down, and on its rim a magpie, also upside down, dipping its beak.
Gran gave a small gasp. 'Oh,' she said. 'Oh, look at him.'
The image was dim, so Tess widened the hole. The picture grew brighter but fuzzier, and she remembered Mr Okafor saying that a larger hole lets in more light but spreads out each point of the image. She taped a scrap of cardboard over it, made a new, smaller hole and found the best balance she could.
They sat together in the dark for almost an hour. A cloud passed and the whole garden dimmed, then brightened again. When the magpie flew off, it fell upwards out of the picture, and Gran laughed so much she had to hold her side.
'It's back to front as well,' Gran said. 'The plum's on the wrong side.'
'That's because the light crosses over at the hole,' Tess explained. 'Left goes right and top goes bottom.'
Gran was quiet for a while. 'Your grandfather would have loved this,' she said at last. 'He was always pulling things apart to see how they worked.'
When Mum came home and found them sitting in the dark, she reached for the light switch.
'Don't!' they both said at once.

Option A: a girl who learns about light in a science lesson at school
Option B: a grandmother who recovers from a hip operation in hospital
Option C: a girl who uses a camera obscura to show her grandmother the garden
Option D: a girl who builds a camera to photograph magpies in the garden

Old Man of the Jetty
He comes in low across the inlet
at the hour the boats come home,
a great white ship with folded sails,
not flapping, barely moving,
riding a cushion of air a hand's width above the water
as though the bay had agreed to carry him.
He lands the way a suitcase lands,
feet first, all skid and splash and fuss,
then settles, smooths his feathers,
and becomes, at once, a dignified old man
who has never in his life done anything clumsy
and would thank you not to mention it.
He chooses the post beside the cleaning table.
He always chooses that post.
From there he can watch the fishers' hands,
the flash of the knife, the silver of the bream,
the bucket where the heads and tails are thrown.
He pretends to be looking at the horizon.
His beak is longer than my forearm,
pink as the inside of a shell,
and under it hangs a pouch of skin
that could hold more than his stomach can,
a net he carries everywhere,
folded like an umbrella waiting for rain.
Up close he is not so white.
There is a grey smudge on his chest, a black edge to his wings,
a yellow ring around a pale and staring eye,
and his feet, flat and grey as old inner tubes,
grip the post as if they did not quite trust it.
He smells, to be honest, of yesterday's bait.
The sign on the jetty says DO NOT FEED THE BIRDS.
He cannot read, or chooses not to.
When a careless fisher turns his back
the pelican shuffles one step closer,
then another, eyes half-closed, innocent,
the way my little brother edges towards the biscuit tin.
But when the boy in the red cap drops a fishing line,
tangled and spiky with hooks,
the old man flinches back, remembers something,
and will not come near that end of the jetty
for the rest of the afternoon,
though the best scraps are lying there in the sun.
Out on the sandbar, others of his kind
are working the way pelicans were meant to work,
a line of them swimming slowly side by side,
driving the small fish into the shallows,
dipping their great pouches all together
like a team of fishermen hauling a single net.
He could join them. Some days he does.
But mostly he stays on his post,
a little apart, a little proud,
having worked out long ago
that patience near the cleaning table
pays better than effort on the bar.
At sunset the fishers pack their eskies and go.
The gulls drift off. The jetty lights flicker on.
The boards cool, and the water turns from blue to pewter.
He stays until the last bucket is rinsed,
then lifts, heavy at first, a slow run across the water,
his feet slapping, slapping,
until the air takes him and he is all at once
light, enormous, gliding,
as graceful in the sky as he was awkward on the boards.
I watch him climb the evening, turning on the warm air,
and I think how strange it is
that the same bird can be a clown at noon
and a kite of white silk at dusk,
and how none of us, perhaps,
are only what we look like on the jetty.
Question: Where does the pelican choose to stand on the jetty?
Option A: next to the sign about feeding birds
Option B: at the end where the boy is fishing
Option C: on the post beside the cleaning table
Option D: beside the fishers' eskies

The Ironmaster's Wife and the Welsh Legends
In the 1830s, some of the oldest stories in Britain were locked away in a medieval manuscript in Oxford. Written in Middle Welsh hundreds of years earlier, the Red Book of Hergest contained tales of shape-shifting magicians, a giant king who waded across the sea, a woman made from flowers and an early version of King Arthur. Few people outside a small circle of scholars could read them. The woman who changed that was not Welsh, had no university training and was raising a large family at the time.
Charlotte Bertie was born in Lincolnshire, England, in 1812. Her father died when she was six, and she grew up in an unhappy household where she often felt ignored. She escaped into books. Listening in on her brother's lessons and studying on her own, she taught herself French, Italian, Latin and Greek, and even made a start on Arabic and Persian. Girls of her class were expected to learn music and manners, not ancient languages, so much of this study was done quietly.
In 1833, at the age of twenty-one, she married John Guest, the owner of the Dowlais Ironworks in south Wales, then one of the largest ironworks in the world. Moving to Wales, Lady Charlotte Guest found herself surrounded by a language she could not understand. Rather than ignore it, she learned it. Within a few years she could read Welsh well, and she became friends with local scholars who were proud of their country's literature and worried that it was being forgotten.
They told her about the old tales in the Red Book. No complete English translation existed, so Lady Charlotte decided to make one. With the help of a Welsh clergyman who copied out the medieval text for her, she began translating, working early in the morning and late at night around her other duties. Over the next twelve years she gave birth to ten children, helped with the business of the ironworks and set up schools for workers' families. Her translation appeared in parts between 1838 and 1845, with notes explaining the places, customs and history behind each tale.
She called the collection the Mabinogion, and the name has been used ever since. Her English was clear and graceful, and readers who had never heard of Welsh legend suddenly had access to it. The poet Alfred Tennyson based part of his famous retelling of the Arthurian stories on one of her translations. In Wales, the work gave many people fresh pride in a literature that some had dismissed as old-fashioned.
Later scholars found mistakes in her version, and she had softened some passages she thought unsuitable for Victorian readers. Modern translations are more exact. Yet hers was the first, and for decades it was the only way most English speakers could meet these stories.
Her energy did not stop there. After her husband died in 1852, she ran the ironworks herself for a time, and in later life she became a famous collector of china, fans and playing cards, which she gave to museums in London. But it is the Mabinogion for which she is best remembered: the work of an outsider who learned a language out of curiosity and gave its stories to the world.

Option B: She was born in Wales and wanted to read its old manuscripts.
Option C: Her husband required all his workers' families to speak Welsh.
Option D: She moved to Wales after her marriage and could not understand the language.

In 1892, prospectors found gold at Coolgardie, in the dry country more than five hundred kilometres east of Perth. Into the Drowned Forest
Ivy had planned her argument for three days, and she delivered it at breakfast while Dad was still half asleep over his toast.
'First,' she said, counting on her fingers, 'the environmental water only reaches the forest every few years, and the ranger said this is the biggest flow since I was born. Second, the egrets and spoonbills are nesting right now, and in a month the chicks will be gone. Third, I've done the canoe course, so I'm not just a passenger anymore. And fourth, you've been saying "one day" for ages. Today is a day.'
Dad looked at her over his mug. 'Is that the whole speech?'
'Yes. Well, nearly. I'll carry the canoe.'
He laughed, and she knew she had won.
They put in at dawn where the track disappeared under brown water. The river had spread out across the flats, and the red gums stood up to their knees in it, their trunks reflected so perfectly that each tree seemed to grow both up and down. Ivy pushed off, and the canoe slid forward without a sound. Behind them, the ute, the track and the ordinary world disappeared.
It was not like paddling on a river. There was no current, no bank and no clear direction, only an endless maze of trunks and silver water and patches of sky. Dad steered from the back, reading the gaps between the trees. Frogs called from everywhere at once, a rattling, clicking, bonking chorus that stopped when the canoe drifted near and started again behind them. Somewhere a bird boomed, low and hollow, like someone blowing across the top of a bottle.
'Listen,' Dad whispered. 'Five kinds, at least. The last time it was this wet, I was younger than you.'
Ivy rested her paddle across her knees. A cormorant surfaced beside them with a fish, swallowed it in one gulp and stared at her, offended. Further in, the water was dotted with tiny black ducklings that zipped behind their mother like beads on a string.
Then they heard the colony before they saw it: a harsh, croaking racket, like a hundred rusty gates. Dad backed the canoe into the shelter of a fallen limb, and they peered through the branches. Ahead, a stand of dead trees was crowded with nests, and every nest seemed to hold a white shape. Egrets balanced on the branches with their long plumes lifting in the breeze. Spoonbills swept their strange flat bills from side to side in the shallows. Chicks, all neck and appetite, squawked for food.
Ivy did not take a photo. She had meant to, but somehow it seemed rude, like talking during a concert. They stayed for a long time without moving, and the birds forgot they were there.
On the way back, the sun had risen higher and the water had turned from silver to gold. Neither of them said much. When they reached the track, Dad lifted the canoe onto his shoulders before Ivy could reach for it.
'You said you'd carry it,' he said, 'but I reckon you've earned a rest. Same time in three years?'
'Two,' said Ivy. 'If it rains.'

Here Be Nothing
On the oldest maps, where the known world ended,
the mapmakers drew sea serpents and storms,
or simply left the parchment bare,
a pale silence at the edge of everything,
as if to say: we don't know, come and see.
Sailors stared at those blank spaces
the way I stare at the last page of a book I haven't read.
They packed salt beef and rope and courage,
and sailed off the edges,
and came back, some of them, with coastlines.
Little by little the blankness filled.
Rivers were traced to their beginnings,
deserts were crossed and named,
mountains climbed and measured to the metre,
until the serpents had nowhere left to swim
and the parchment was crowded with ink.
Satellites took over where the sailors stopped.
They circle the planet a few hundred kilometres up,
counting trees, tracing rivers, watching ice sheets shrink,
until there is hardly a square metre of land
that has not been photographed from above,
named, numbered and filed away.
Now my phone can show me any street on Earth.
I can drop a little yellow figure
on a road in Mongolia or a beach in Chile,
spin around, and see the houses, the cars,
a dog asleep in a doorway,
all photographed and stitched together by a camera on a pole.
Some days that makes the world feel finished,
like a jigsaw with every piece pressed in,
nothing left for me but to admire it.
My grandfather says that's rubbish.
He says the map is not the place,
and a photograph of a mountain never made anyone's legs ache.
He points out that the deep ocean floor
is still less known than the face of the Moon,
that new kinds of beetle and frog and fungus
are found every year in forests we thought we knew,
that caves still breathe cold air
from passages no torch has entered.
But that is not really his point.
His point is that every person's map starts blank.
The streets two suburbs over are a white space to me.
So is the creek past the end of the bus line,
the hill behind the school I have never climbed,
the language my neighbour speaks on the phone.
So on Saturday I take no phone.
I walk until the streets stop being familiar,
until I don't know which way the creek bends
or where the track behind the reservoir leads,
until I am, for an hour or so, a little lost,
which is another word for exploring.
I find a footbridge I never knew existed,
a stand of old pines that hums in the wind,
a man selling lemons from a bucket on his fence,
a view of the city looking small and far away.
None of it is new to the world.
All of it is new to me.
I talk to the lemon man. He tells me
the creek used to flood the whole valley,
that platypus lived under the footbridge once,
and might again, if you're patient at dusk.
That night I draw it on a sheet of paper,
my own crooked map, with the footbridge and the pines,
and at the edges, where my knowledge stops,
I leave the paper bare, a pale silence,
not empty, but waiting,
the way the old mapmakers did.
Question: What did the old mapmakers draw where the known world ended?
Option A: mountains and rivers
Option B: sea serpents and storms
Option C: ships and sailors
Option D: coastlines and deserts
