Here Be Nothing
On the oldest maps, where the known world ended,
the mapmakers drew sea serpents and storms,
or simply left the parchment bare,
a pale silence at the edge of everything,
as if to say: we don't know, come and see.
Sailors stared at those blank spaces
the way I stare at the last page of a book I haven't read.
They packed salt beef and rope and courage,
and sailed off the edges,
and came back, some of them, with coastlines.
Little by little the blankness filled.
Rivers were traced to their beginnings,
deserts were crossed and named,
mountains climbed and measured to the metre,
until the serpents had nowhere left to swim
and the parchment was crowded with ink.
Satellites took over where the sailors stopped.
They circle the planet a few hundred kilometres up,
counting trees, tracing rivers, watching ice sheets shrink,
until there is hardly a square metre of land
that has not been photographed from above,
named, numbered and filed away.
Now my phone can show me any street on Earth.
I can drop a little yellow figure
on a road in Mongolia or a beach in Chile,
spin around, and see the houses, the cars,
a dog asleep in a doorway,
all photographed and stitched together by a camera on a pole.
Some days that makes the world feel finished,
like a jigsaw with every piece pressed in,
nothing left for me but to admire it.
My grandfather says that's rubbish.
He says the map is not the place,
and a photograph of a mountain never made anyone's legs ache.
He points out that the deep ocean floor
is still less known than the face of the Moon,
that new kinds of beetle and frog and fungus
are found every year in forests we thought we knew,
that caves still breathe cold air
from passages no torch has entered.
But that is not really his point.
His point is that every person's map starts blank.
The streets two suburbs over are a white space to me.
So is the creek past the end of the bus line,
the hill behind the school I have never climbed,
the language my neighbour speaks on the phone.
So on Saturday I take no phone.
I walk until the streets stop being familiar,
until I don't know which way the creek bends
or where the track behind the reservoir leads,
until I am, for an hour or so, a little lost,
which is another word for exploring.
I find a footbridge I never knew existed,
a stand of old pines that hums in the wind,
a man selling lemons from a bucket on his fence,
a view of the city looking small and far away.
None of it is new to the world.
All of it is new to me.
I talk to the lemon man. He tells me
the creek used to flood the whole valley,
that platypus lived under the footbridge once,
and might again, if you're patient at dusk.
That night I draw it on a sheet of paper,
my own crooked map, with the footbridge and the pines,
and at the edges, where my knowledge stops,
I leave the paper bare, a pale silence,
not empty, but waiting,
the way the old mapmakers did.
Question: Which line best shows that the speaker sometimes feels there is nothing left to discover?
Option A: 'like a jigsaw with every piece pressed in'
Option B: 'and the parchment was crowded with ink'
Option C: 'Now my phone can show me any street on Earth'
Option D: 'None of it is new to the world'

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
Treasure from the Roadside
Most artists build their careers in their twenties and thirties. Rosalie Gascoigne held her first solo exhibition at the age of fifty-seven, using materials that most people would have driven straight past: weathered road signs, broken soft-drink crates, rusty iron and the feathers of swans. Within a few years, she was one of the most admired artists in Australia.
Gascoigne was born in Auckland, New Zealand, in 1917. In 1943 she married an astronomer, Ben Gascoigne, and moved with him to Mount Stromlo Observatory, on a hilltop outside Canberra. It was a lonely place for a young mother. The observatory was isolated, the community was small, and the dry, windswept paddocks looked nothing like the green hills of her childhood. For years she felt like a stranger in the landscape.
Her way of coming to terms with it was to walk. While her husband studied the stars, she explored the grasslands of the Monaro and the roadsides around Canberra, bringing home things that caught her eye: smooth stones, sheep bones, dried thistles, sheets of rusted corrugated iron. She began arranging them, at first simply to decorate the house. In the 1960s she studied ikebana, the Japanese art of flower arranging, which taught her to think carefully about line, space and balance.
Gradually her arrangements became something more. She started to create assemblages, works made by combining found objects. She never painted the landscape directly. Instead she tried to capture how it felt: the glare of the light on dry grass, the rhythm of fence posts, the way a paddock looks from a moving car. In one well-known work, she pushed hundreds of swan feathers into a wire fence frame, so that it seemed to shimmer like a flock in flight.
Her most famous works used old road signs. Gascoigne collected them from tips and roadsides, cut them into strips and squares, then rearranged the pieces in grids. Letters were broken up so the words no longer made sense, and what remained were patterns of bright yellow, black and white. Viewers often say these works suggest sunlight flickering across fields or the endless repetition of a country road.
Recognition came quickly once it began. Galleries bought her work, and in 1982 she was chosen to represent Australia at the Venice Biennale, one of the world's most important art events. Yet she never stopped scavenging. Friends remembered her roaming the tips with a sharp eye, delighted by a faded plank or a sun-bleached sign that nobody else wanted.
Gascoigne died in 1999, but her work remains in major galleries across Australia. Her story is often told as one of a late beginning, and it is that. It is also a story about looking. She spent decades in a landscape that at first seemed empty and harsh to her, and by paying close attention to it, and to the things others had thrown away, she found beauty that had been there all along.
Question: What is the passage mainly about?
Option A: an astronomer who studied the stars at Mount Stromlo Observatory
Option B: the history of the Venice Biennale and the artists who exhibit there
Option C: an artist who began late and made admired art from discarded materials
Option D: the Japanese art of ikebana and how it spread to Australia

Watch It Once, Live
Last month I went to see my favourite band play at a theatre in the city. I had saved for the ticket since February. When the lights dropped and the first chord rang out, I stood on my toes, ready for the moment I had imagined for months. What I saw instead was a sea of glowing rectangles. Hundreds of people in front of me had raised their phones, and the band had shrunk to a row of tiny figures on other people's screens.
I want to make a simple case: when you go to a live performance, put your phone away. Not for the whole night, perhaps, but for almost all of it.
My first reason is that filming steals the very thing you paid for. A concert, a play or a dance recital is not just sound and light. It is the feeling of being in a room where something is happening only once, never to be repeated in exactly the same way. When you watch through a screen, you are not really there; you are working as an unpaid camera operator. Researchers who study memory have found that people who photograph an experience often remember fewer details of it than people who simply pay attention. In other words, the recording you make may replace the memory you would have kept. You can buy a T-shirt as a souvenir; you cannot buy back a moment you were too busy filming.
My second reason is that phones spoil the show for everyone else. A raised phone blocks the view of the person behind it, and a bright screen in a dark theatre pulls eyes away from the stage. Some performers now ask audiences to lock their phones in small pouches at the door. One comedian I admire explained that he cannot test new jokes when he fears every word will be online by morning. Performers are human. They take risks when they feel the room is with them, and they hold back when they feel they are being watched by strangers who aren't even present.
Third, be honest: how often do you watch those videos again? Last year I filmed an entire song at a festival, holding my arm up until it ached, and I have watched the clip exactly once. My videos sit in a folder, shaky and muffled, the bass crackling like a broken speaker. The official recording, made with proper microphones, sounds far better, and it is usually free to stream.
Some people argue that filming lets them share the night with friends who could not come. I understand that. Others say it is their ticket, so it is their choice. That is true too, but a ticket buys you a seat, not the right to ruin someone else's view. If you must, take one photo before the show begins, then switch the phone to silent and slide it into your pocket.
At the end of that concert, the band played a slow song with the house lights down. The singer asked us to put our phones away just this once, and to my surprise, almost everyone did. For four minutes, the room was dark and still and full of voices singing together. I have no video of it. I don't need one. I remember every second.
Question: According to the writer, what often happens when people photograph an experience?
Option A: they remember it more clearly later
Option B: they remember fewer details of it
Option C: they notice more about the performers
Option D: they enjoy the music a great deal more

The Trap on the Windowsill
Leo bought the Venus flytrap with his birthday money from a stall at the Sunday market. It sat in a plastic pot no bigger than a teacup, a cluster of green jaws edged with fine bristles, each one blushing red inside like an open mouth.
'They eat insects,' the stallholder said. 'Don't overdo it.'
Leo didn't hear the second part. He was already imagining it.
At home he put the pot on his bedroom windowsill and touched one of the traps with the end of a pencil. Nothing happened. He touched it again, brushing two of the tiny hairs inside, and the trap snapped shut in less than a second. Leo laughed out loud.
For the rest of the week, the flytrap was the best thing he owned. He showed it to his sister, his friends, the boy next door. Snap. Snap. Snap. When there were no flies about, he fed it tiny pinches of mince from the fridge and watched the jaws seal tight around them. He watered it from the kitchen tap every morning, just to be sure.
By the second week, something had changed. Three of the traps stayed closed and turned black. Others opened slowly and lay limp, like tired hands. A sour smell rose from the pot. Leo poked one, then another, waiting for the snap. It didn't come.
On Sunday he carried the pot back to the market, holding it out in front of him as if it were something broken.
The stallholder, a tall woman with soil under her fingernails, looked at it for a long time without speaking. Then she lifted one of the black traps between her finger and thumb.
'How many times did you set them off?' she asked.
Leo felt his face grow hot. 'A few,' he said. Then, more honestly, 'A lot.'
She nodded slowly. 'Every time a trap closes, it costs the plant energy. Closing on nothing wears it out. A trap can only do it a handful of times before it dies.' She pointed to the dark ones. 'And these tried to digest mince. Too rich. It rotted inside them.' She sniffed the soil. 'Tap water too, I'd guess. They need rainwater. And sun. Lots of sun.'
'So I killed it,' said Leo.
'Not yet,' she said. She snipped off the dead traps with a small pair of scissors until only four green ones were left, tucked low against the soil. 'Put it outside where the sun hits it. Stand it in a saucer of rainwater. Then leave it alone. Let it catch its own dinner.'
Leo did what she said. He set the pot on the back step, filled the saucer from the rainwater tank, and made himself walk past without touching it. It was harder than he expected. His fingers itched every time he saw the green jaws.
For a month, nothing much happened. Then new traps began to unfurl from the centre, small at first, then larger and redder than before. One warm afternoon in December, Leo was sitting on the step when a blowfly buzzed down and landed on the newest trap.
It crawled once, twice, across the bristles.
Snap.
Leo didn't laugh this time. He just sat very still, watching, and felt something that was much better than laughing.
Question: Which word from the story is an example of onomatopoeia?
Option A: blushing
Option B: snap
Option C: limp
Option D: unfurl

The Night of the Radishes
On the evening of 23 December each year, thousands of people queue for hours in the main square of Oaxaca, a city in southern Mexico. They are not waiting for a concert or a parade. They are waiting to look at vegetables. This is the Noche de Rabanos, or Night of the Radishes, one of the most unusual festivals in the world.
The radishes on display are nothing like the small red ones found in Australian salad bowls. They are grown specially for the event and can reach half a metre in length and weigh several kilograms. Their shapes are twisted and knobbly, with long tangled roots. Carvers use these odd forms as part of their designs, so a bulging root might become a dancer's skirt, a horse's leg or the back of a crocodile. Using small knives, they cut into the white flesh beneath the red skin to create detailed scenes: market stalls, village weddings, musicians, animals and figures from local history. The finished pieces are arranged on tables in the square, and visitors shuffle slowly past behind ropes.
The festival's history begins with farming. Radishes were brought to Mexico by Spanish colonists in the 1500s, and farmers around Oaxaca grew them alongside other vegetables. By the 1800s, market sellers had begun carving their radishes into figures to catch the eye of shoppers at the busy Christmas market. The idea proved so popular that in 1897 the city's mayor declared an official competition. It has been held every year since.
Today the city government sets aside land where competitors can grow their radishes, and planting is timed carefully so that the vegetables are ready in late December. Some families have entered for generations, passing down techniques from grandparents to grandchildren. There are separate sections for adults and children, as well as categories for two other traditional materials: dried corn husks and a dried flower known as flor inmortal, or 'immortal flower'. Prize money is awarded, but many carvers say the honour of winning matters more.
The festival has one great challenge: the radishes do not last. Once a radish is harvested and cut, it begins to dry out and wilt within hours. Carvers usually work through the day before the display, spraying their pieces with water to keep them fresh. By the next morning, many sculptures have already begun to droop and shrivel. That is why the display lasts only a single evening. If visitors miss it, they must wait another year.
In recent decades the Night of the Radishes has drawn visitors from across Mexico and around the world, and the queue can stretch for several city blocks. Yet at its heart the festival remains local: a celebration of farmers, of patient handwork, and of the idea that even an ordinary vegetable, in the right hands, can become a work of art.

When the Sahara Was Green
Stand in the middle of the Sahara today and you could walk for days without seeing a blade of grass. The desert covers about nine million square kilometres of northern Africa, an area larger than mainland Australia, and parts of it receive almost no rain for years at a time. Yet scattered across this dry land are clues that tell a startling story. Not very long ago, in geological terms, the Sahara was green.
The clues come in many forms. In a rock shelter in south-western Egypt, now known as the Cave of Swimmers, ancient painters left images of small human figures that appear to be swimming. When the explorer Laszlo Almasy saw them in 1933, he suggested that the climate must once have been far wetter. Many experts were doubtful at first. Since then, however, scientists have found the fossilised bones of hippopotamuses, crocodiles and fish in places now hundreds of kilometres from any river. Layers of mud at the bottom of dried-up lakes contain pollen from grasses and trees that could never survive there now.
Together, this evidence points to a period that scientists call the African Humid Period, which lasted from roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago. During this time, much of the Sahara was savanna, a landscape of grassland dotted with trees, and it held enormous lakes. The largest, Lake Mega-Chad, may have covered more than 350,000 square kilometres. Today's Lake Chad, its shrunken remnant, is a tiny fraction of that size.
What turned the desert green? The main cause was a slow wobble in the direction that Earth's axis points. Over a cycle of about 23,000 years, this wobble changes how much sunlight different parts of the planet receive in each season. Around 10,000 years ago, northern Africa received stronger summer sunshine than it does today. The land heated up, drawing moist air in from the ocean and pushing the summer monsoon rains much further north.
Once plants began to spread, they seem to have helped the rains along. Vegetation is darker than bare sand, so it absorbs more heat, and plants release moisture into the air. Both effects may have encouraged more rain to fall, which in turn allowed more plants to grow.
As the wobble continued, the summer sunshine weakened and the rains retreated south. Exactly how quickly the green Sahara disappeared is still debated. Some lake records suggest the change happened within a few centuries; others point to a slower decline over a thousand years or more. The answer matters, because it helps scientists understand how suddenly other regions might change in a warming world.
The Sahara's story is not finished. Its dust still blows across the Atlantic each year, carrying minerals that help fertilise the Amazon rainforest. And if the planet's wobble continues as expected, the rains will one day return, though not for many thousands of years.

Option A: small human figures swimming

Rope, Saddle and Saw
On a cold morning in a suburban street, a woman in a bright orange helmet stands at the base of a towering river red gum, flicking a small weighted bag on a thin line up into its branches. On her third throw, the bag sails over a limb nearly twenty metres above the footpath. Within minutes she has pulled a climbing rope into place, clipped it to the harness, or saddle, around her waist, and begun to inch her way up into the canopy. She is an arborist, and the tree is her workplace for the day.
Arborists are specialists in the care of individual trees, especially those growing in cities and towns. While foresters manage whole forests, arborists look after the street trees, park trees and backyard giants that most of us walk past without a second glance. Their work includes pruning branches away from power lines, removing dead or dangerous limbs, planting young trees and deciding whether a tree is healthy enough to keep.
That last task is more complex than it sounds. A tree can look perfectly green and still be rotting from the inside. To check, some arborists tap the trunk with a mallet and listen: solid wood gives a sharp knock, while a hollow trunk returns a dull, deep thud. Others use instruments that send sound waves through the wood, or a thin drill that measures resistance as it bores in. The arborist then has to weigh up the risk. Removing a tree that is still sound means losing years of shade, habitat and beauty; keeping one that is failing could put people and property in danger.
Much of the job takes place high above the ground. Climbing arborists move through the canopy on ropes, which lets them reach the outer branches without damaging the bark. Once in position, they cut with a small chainsaw, lowering heavy pieces slowly on separate ropes controlled by a teammate below. On the street, the snarl of the saw, the creak of the ropes and the grinding roar of the woodchipper can make a work site sound like a battle, but every move is carefully planned. Climber and ground crew talk constantly, often through radios fitted inside their helmets.
In Australia, people usually enter the career through a Certificate III in Arboriculture, which combines classroom study with practical training. Those who want to assess trees professionally or advise councils often go on to a Diploma of Arboriculture. Arborists need a head for heights and physical fitness, but they also need patience, a knowledge of plant biology and the ability to explain their decisions to worried residents.
Many arborists say the best part of the work is the view. From the top of a gum tree, a suburb looks like a forest with houses scattered through it, and that is exactly the point. Every street tree cools the air in summer, soaks up stormwater and gives birds a place to nest. The people who keep those trees standing safely play a quiet but essential role in the life of a city.

Option A: a weighted bag on a thin line
Option B: a long extension ladder
Option C: a thin drill and a mallet
Option D: a crane on the back of a truck

Bringing the Whole Clan Together: How to Plan a Family Reunion
Families today are often scattered across suburbs, states and even continents. Cousins may know each other only through photos, and the stories older relatives carry can fade without anyone noticing. A family reunion gathers everyone in one place, but a good one does not happen by accident. The following steps will help you plan a day that people remember for the right reasons.
Step 1: Form a small team. Planning a reunion alone is exhausting. Ask two or three relatives from different branches of the family to help. A mix of ages works best: an older relative will know who should be invited, while a younger one may be quicker at setting up a group chat or an online invitation.
Step 2: Build the guest list. Start with the oldest living generation and work downwards, branch by branch. It is easy to forget second cousins, new partners or relatives who have moved overseas, so ask each branch to check its own section. A shared spreadsheet with names, contact details and ages will save confusion later.
Step 3: Choose a date and place. Give people at least six months' notice, especially if some must travel long distances. School holidays or long weekends usually suit the most people. When choosing a venue, think about who is coming. A park with shelter, toilets and wheelchair access may suit a crowd of toddlers and elderly relatives better than a restaurant, and it is usually cheaper.
Step 4: Share the costs and the food. A 'bring a plate' lunch spreads the work and lets each household contribute a dish it is proud of. If you need to hire a venue or buy supplies, divide the cost fairly and be open about where the money goes. Arguments about money can sour a reunion before it even begins.
Step 5: Plan activities for every generation. Not everyone will want to sit and chat all day. Organise games that mix ages, such as a trivia quiz about family history with teams that include a grandparent, a parent and a child. A 'memory wall' also works well: invite people to pin up old photographs and label who is in them. Some of the best conversations start when a teenager points at a faded picture and asks, 'Who is that?'
Step 6: Record the day. Ask someone to take photos, and consider setting up a quiet corner where older relatives can be recorded telling stories about their childhood. These recordings often become the most treasured part of the reunion, especially in years to come.
Step 7: Follow up. Within a week, send everyone the photos and a thank-you message. Update the guest list with any new contacts. Then ask the big question: when shall we do it again?
A reunion takes effort, but the reward is more than a pleasant afternoon. When three or four generations share a meal and a laugh, children discover that they belong to a story much larger than themselves.
Question: How much notice does the writer suggest giving people?
Option A: at least three months
Option B: at least one year
Option C: at least six months
Option D: at least six weeks

Zara had been fishing off Jetty Four with her dad since she was seven, and she had never once seen a pelican hurry.
The pelicans of the inlet were not hurriers. They drifted on the green water like small white boats, or stood along the railings with their great bills tucked against their chests, looking down their noses at the fishermen as if they had been appointed to inspect the catch. When someone cleaned a fish at the tap, they gathered in a hopeful, shuffling crowd, but even then they moved with a kind of lazy dignity.
So when Zara saw one flapping and lurching across the planks on Saturday morning, she knew at once that something was wrong.
'Dad,' she said. 'Look at its wing.'
A length of clear fishing line was wrapped around the bird's left wing and trailed behind it, ending in a hook caught near the top of its leg. Every time the pelican tried to fold the wing, the line pulled tight and it jerked sideways, clacking its bill in alarm. A boy further along the jetty laughed. Zara wanted to throw his bait bucket into the water.
Her dad was already on his phone to a wildlife rescue group. The woman who answered told them not to grab the bird, because a frightened pelican could strike with its bill and they might make the injury worse. She asked them to keep people back and watch where it went.
Zara stood at the end of the jetty with her arms spread, turning away anyone who came too close. It felt like the longest forty minutes of her life. The pelican eventually settled on the boat ramp, panting, its throat pouch trembling.
The rescuer was nothing like Zara had pictured. She was small and grey-haired, wearing gumboots and carrying an old beach towel. She walked towards the pelican slowly, talking to it in a low, ordinary voice, as if she were discussing the weather. Then, in one smooth movement, she dropped the towel over its head, folded the wings against its body and held the long bill closed with a gentle hand.
'Covering their eyes calms them,' she explained. 'Now, would you like to hold the bill while I work?'
Zara's hands shook, but she held on. The bill was cool and smooth, like the inside of a shell. The rescuer snipped the line away loop by loop, then eased the hook free with pliers.
'He'll do,' she said at last, and stepped back.
For a moment the pelican didn't move. Then it shook off the towel, stretched both wings wide and walked to the edge of the ramp with enormous, careless dignity, as though nothing at all had happened. It slid into the water and paddled away without looking back.
That afternoon, Zara walked the length of the jetty with a plastic bag, collecting every scrap of tangled line she could find. She filled the bag twice. The boy who had laughed watched her for a while. On her second trip, without saying anything, he started picking up line too.

Option A: the boy frightened it by laughing
Option B: its foot was caught in the railing
Option C: the fishing line pulled tight
Option D: the rescuer threw a towel over it

Riding the Hillside Stairs
Monday, 8 July
Aunty Grace warned me that Hong Kong would be steep, but I thought she meant a bit hilly, like the streets near our house in Brisbane. She did not. Her flat is halfway up the side of a mountain, and the footpaths outside tilt so sharply that my calves were burning before we had even found the lift. Tonight, from her balcony, I counted eleven towers between me and the harbour, every window lit like a page in an advent calendar.
Tuesday, 9 July
Today Aunty Grace introduced me to what she calls "the hill that carries you". It is a chain of covered outdoor escalators, about 800 metres long, that climbs from the business district near the harbour up through the Mid-Levels, where she lives. It opened in 1993, and people here say it is the longest outdoor covered escalator system in the world. Between the moving sections are short walkways and staircases, so you can step off wherever you like and disappear into a side street.
The strangest part is that it only goes one way at a time. Early in the morning it runs downhill, carrying office workers towards their jobs. Around ten o'clock the whole thing stops for a while and then starts again in the opposite direction, running uphill until late at night. We arrived at 9.55, so we had to climb the stairs beside the stopped escalator. Aunty Grace laughed at my face. "Timing is everything," she said.
Wednesday, 10 July
I rode it on my own this afternoon, from bottom to top, and tried to notice everything. The escalator passes so close to the buildings that you can look straight into first-floor windows: a tailor pinning a jacket, a man asleep over a newspaper, a room full of children practising violin. Cafes and little restaurants line the route, and Aunty Grace says the street below barely had a shop on it before the escalator came. Now the smell of coffee and fried dough follows you the whole way up.
It took me about twenty minutes, and I was not even slightly out of breath. I kept thinking about Dad, who complains whenever the escalator at our local station is broken. He would think this was paradise.
Thursday, 11 July
Not everything is perfect, apparently. At dinner, Aunty Grace's neighbour, Mr Leung, told me that when the escalator was built, planners hoped it would mean fewer cars on the narrow roads. He shrugged and said the traffic is still terrible. Instead, so many people wanted to live near the escalator that rents in the area went up. "It solved one problem," he said, "and made a different one." I had not thought of it like that. I had only thought of how much fun it was.
Friday, 12 July
Last ride. I went down this morning, squeezed between office workers in suits, and realised I had started to think like a local: I knew which exits led to the bakery, which steps were slippery and exactly when the escalator would turn around. At the bottom I looked back up at the long, glinting line of it, threading between the towers like a zip. I will miss it more than I expected. Brisbane suddenly feels very flat.
Question: According to the diary, when does the escalator run downhill?
Option A: late at night
Option B: in the afternoon
Option C: around lunchtime
Option D: early in the morning

Letters from the Restless Map
Dear Tam,
I have been in Thistlemoor for nine days, and I have already ruined fourteen maps. You will remember that everyone in our village said I was lucky to be chosen as Mistress Odile's apprentice. Nobody mentioned that the roads here do not stay still.
It is true. Every night, while the town sleeps, the lanes of Thistlemoor shuffle about like restless cattle. The baker's alley that ran east on Monday ran north on Tuesday, and by Wednesday it had wandered off behind the clock tower altogether. I spend each day measuring streets with my chain and copying them carefully onto parchment, and each morning my work is useless.
Mistress Odile only smiles when I complain. She has not drawn a single line since I arrived. She sits by the window, drinking nettle tea and watching people walk past. If this is mapmaking, I could have stayed home and watched the goats.
Your grumpy sister, Wren
Dear Tam,
Something odd has happened, and I want to tell you before I forget the details.
Last Thursday, old Mr Hobb, who sells lamp oil, broke his ankle. For a week he could not walk to the market, so his customers had to carry their empty jars all the way to his cottage at the edge of town. By Saturday, the oil-sellers' lane had moved. It had curled right around, so that it now ends at Mr Hobb's front gate.
Then I noticed other things. The lane past the school grows shorter during term and longer in the holidays. The road to the river widens on washing days. When the Fennick sisters stopped speaking to each other, the path between their houses simply vanished, and when they made up, it returned overnight, a little crooked, as if it were embarrassed.
I asked Mistress Odile whether the roads follow people. She raised one eyebrow and asked me what I thought. I said I did not know. "Then watch until you do," she said, and went back to her tea.
Your puzzled sister, Wren
Dear Tam,
I understand now, and I am almost cross that it took me so long.
The roads of Thistlemoor are not wandering at random. They go where people need to go, and they fade where nobody does. A map of Thistlemoor that shows only streets will always be wrong by morning. But a map that shows the people - who visits whom, who is ill, who has quarrelled, who has a new baby - will tell you where the roads are going to be.
Yesterday I showed Mistress Odile my first true map. It has hardly any streets on it, only names, joined by soft pencil lines that I rub out and redraw each evening. She studied it for a long time. Then she opened a drawer I had never seen her open, took out a map of her own, covered in names and smudged pencil, and laid it next to mine.
"I could have told you on your first day," she said. "But you would have drawn what I told you, not what you saw."
I think I will be staying a while longer.
Your proud sister, Wren
P.S. Please ask Mother to write. I would like the road between our two houses to stay wide.

Option B: valuable

Option D: careless

The Kangaroo in the Canopy
Tessa had expected the rainforest to be loud. In films, jungles screeched and chattered from every branch. But the forest on the Atherton Tableland, where Aunt Jo worked as a wildlife carer, was mostly quiet: a drip of water somewhere, the creak of a trunk, and now and then a whipbird's call cracking across the gully like a flicked tea towel.
"We're looking for Kiri," Aunt Jo said, handing her a pair of binoculars. "She's a Lumholtz's tree-kangaroo. I raised her from a joey after her mother was hit by a car, and we released her here in March. I just want to see that she's doing well."
Tessa nodded politely, but secretly she thought the whole idea was ridiculous. Kangaroos lived in paddocks. They did not live up trees.
For the first hour she kept checking her phone, though there was no signal, and she sighed loudly whenever Aunt Jo stopped to examine the leaves. Aunt Jo didn't seem to notice. She would stand for minutes at a time with her head tipped back, scanning the canopy. Now and then she crouched to pick up a chewed leaf and turn it over in her fingers.
"Fresh," she said once, holding one up. "Something's been feeding around here."
"How do you know it's her?"
"I don't, for certain. But tree-kangaroos are quiet animals that spend much of the day asleep, high in the branches. You don't find them by chasing them. You find them by paying attention."
Tessa rolled her eyes when her aunt turned away. Then, because there was nothing else to do, she lifted the binoculars.
At first everything was simply green. Gradually, though, the green separated into layers: glossy leaves near the ground, vines twisting up the trunks, ferns sprouting from the forks of branches, and far above, the crowns of the tallest trees spreading against slices of white sky. A blue butterfly as big as her hand drifted through a sunbeam. A plump fruit-dove with a purple chest shuffled along a branch. Tessa realised she had stopped thinking about her phone.
It was nearly midday when she saw it: a dark, rounded shape wedged into the fork of a tree, twenty metres up. She took it for a clump of dead leaves. Then a long tail, much too long for a clump of leaves, swung gently beneath it.
"Aunt Jo," she whispered, and her voice came out strange and tight. "Is that . . . ?"
Aunt Jo raised her binoculars. For a long moment she said nothing. Then Tessa heard her let out a slow breath.
"That's her," she said softly. "See the pale patch on her chest? That's Kiri." She lowered the binoculars, and Tessa was surprised to see her blinking rapidly. "She looks healthy. Heavier, even."
They stood together without speaking while, high above them, Kiri opened one eye, scratched her ear with a curved claw and went back to sleep.
On the walk back to the car, Tessa kept stopping every few metres to look up.
"You're slowing us down," Aunt Jo teased.
"I'm paying attention," Tessa said.
Question: Why did Aunt Jo raise Kiri from a joey?
Option A: Kiri had been found injured in a paddock.
Option B: Kiri's mother had been hit by a car.
Option C: Kiri's mother had left her alone in a tree.
Option D: Kiri had been born in a wildlife park.

The Bear in Odori Park
Mia had imagined Japan in February as a postcard: quiet temples, steaming bowls of ramen, a polite dusting of snow. She had not imagined standing in a Sapporo park at seven in the morning, shovel in hand, while her cousin Hana shouted instructions in rapid Japanese to a dozen strangers in matching blue jackets.
'You're on the left paw,' Hana said, switching to English and pointing at a mound of packed snow taller than Mia herself. 'Smooth it. Don't carve it yet.'
Every year the Sapporo Snow Festival filled the city's long central park with sculptures, some as tall as buildings, others small enough to be finished by a family in an afternoon. Hana's neighbourhood group entered the community section, and this year they were building a brown bear rearing up to catch a salmon. They had been working for four days. Mia, who had arrived on the second day still dizzy from the flight from Brisbane, had spent most of that time feeling like an extra pair of hands that nobody quite knew what to do with.
The group was friendly enough. Mr Takeda, a retired bus driver who led the team, bowed to her each morning and offered her hot barley tea from a battered thermos. But the jokes flew past her, and when the others laughed she smiled a beat too late. At home she was the one who organised things. Here she was a visitor holding a shovel.
On the fourth afternoon the weather turned. The forecast had promised minus five degrees; instead a warm wind blew hard across the park, and by three o'clock the bear's raised paw had begun to sag. Water dripped from the salmon's tail. Mr Takeda walked around the sculpture twice, frowning, and then spoke quietly to Hana.
'He says if the paw falls tonight, we won't have time to rebuild before judging,' Hana translated. 'Nobody knows how to hold it up.'
Mia looked at the paw. Last year, for a science project, she had built a bridge out of paddle-pop sticks and learnt more than she ever wanted to know about load and support. The problem with the paw was that all its weight hung out over nothing.
'What if the salmon held it up?' she said slowly. 'If we made the fish longer, so it curved up from the base and touched the paw, it would work like a prop. It'd look like the bear had just caught it.'
Hana stared at her, then turned and explained. For a moment nobody spoke. Then Mr Takeda laughed, a sudden bark of delight, and clapped his gloved hands together.
They worked into the evening under the park's floodlights, packing fresh snow into a wooden frame to stretch the salmon into a long, twisting arc. Mia's fingers went numb inside her gloves. Someone handed her a hot bun filled with sweet bean paste, and someone else showed her how to spray a fine mist of water over the surface so that it froze into a hard, glassy skin. By the time the temperature dropped again, near midnight, the paw rested firmly on the leaping fish.
The festival opened two days later. Mia watched crowds of tourists stop in front of the bear and point at the salmon, which seemed to burst upward from the snow. The group did not win a prize; a giant snow octopus took the community award. But on the final evening, Mr Takeda presented each member with a small enamel badge shaped like a bear. When he reached Mia, he said something that made everyone laugh, and she laughed too, not because she understood the words but because, for once, she knew the joke was meant to include her.
'What did he say?' she asked Hana afterwards.
'He said the fish was the best idea the bear ever had.'
Question: What was Hana's neighbourhood group building for the festival?
Option A: a giant octopus reaching upward
Option B: a salmon leaping from a river
Option C: a bear sleeping beside a fish
Option D: a brown bear catching a salmon

Counting the Storm
On a summer evening, a flash splits the sky over the hills. You start counting: one, two, three, four, five, six. Then the thunder arrives, a long, grumbling roll that rattles the windows. Without realising it, you have just measured the distance to the storm, and you have done it by using one of the most striking differences in physics: light is fast, but sound is slow.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe. In empty space it travels at almost 300,000 kilometres per second, quick enough to circle the Earth more than seven times in a single second. Over the few kilometres between you and a storm, its journey is effectively instant. Sound is a different matter. Sound is a vibration that must be passed from particle to particle, and in air at about 20 degrees Celsius it moves at roughly 343 metres per second. That is close to a million times slower than light.
This gap explains the counting trick. Because sound takes about three seconds to cover one kilometre, you can divide the number of seconds between the flash and the thunder by three to estimate the distance in kilometres. Six seconds means the lightning struck about two kilometres away. Saying 'one thousand, two thousand' between the numbers can help you keep a steady pace. The method is not precise, since temperature and wind affect the speed of sound slightly, but it is accurate enough to be useful.
But what actually is thunder? A bolt of lightning heats the narrow channel of air around it to around 30,000 degrees Celsius, several times hotter than the surface of the Sun, in a fraction of a second. The air expands so violently that it creates a shock wave, which quickly becomes the sound wave we hear. The rumble comes from the length of the lightning bolt itself. A bolt may be several kilometres long, so sound from the nearest part reaches you first, while sound from the far end arrives seconds later. Each of these waves travels a slightly different distance, and together they blend into a roll rather than a single crack.
The same delay appears in everyday life, once you start looking for it. At a fireworks display you see the burst of colour before you hear the bang. Sitting high in the stands at a large cricket ground, you may see the batter hit the ball a fraction of a second before the crack of the bat reaches you. Sound is not always slow, however. It travels more than four times faster through water and around seventeen times faster through steel, because the particles in liquids and solids are closer together and more tightly linked. In the vacuum of space, where there are almost no particles at all, sound cannot travel. Despite what science-fiction films suggest, an explosion in space would make no sound at all.
Perhaps the most important lesson of the flash-and-count method, though, is about safety. Thunder can usually be heard up to about 15 kilometres away, and lightning can strike at similar distances from the storm that produced it. In other words, if you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Weather experts advise heading indoors as soon as thunder is heard and waiting 30 minutes after the last rumble before going back outside. It is a rule worth remembering. Counting the seconds may be fun, but a storm that sounds distant may be much closer than it seems.

Option A: brilliant
Option B: distant
Option C: immediate
Option D: constant

Counting the Storm
On a summer evening, a flash splits the sky over the hills. You start counting: one, two, three, four, five, six. Then the thunder arrives, a long, grumbling roll that rattles the windows. Without realising it, you have just measured the distance to the storm, and you have done it by using one of the most striking differences in physics: light is fast, but sound is slow.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe. In empty space it travels at almost 300,000 kilometres per second, quick enough to circle the Earth more than seven times in a single second. Over the few kilometres between you and a storm, its journey is effectively instant. Sound is a different matter. Sound is a vibration that must be passed from particle to particle, and in air at about 20 degrees Celsius it moves at roughly 343 metres per second. That is close to a million times slower than light.
This gap explains the counting trick. Because sound takes about three seconds to cover one kilometre, you can divide the number of seconds between the flash and the thunder by three to estimate the distance in kilometres. Six seconds means the lightning struck about two kilometres away. Saying 'one thousand, two thousand' between the numbers can help you keep a steady pace. The method is not precise, since temperature and wind affect the speed of sound slightly, but it is accurate enough to be useful.
But what actually is thunder? A bolt of lightning heats the narrow channel of air around it to around 30,000 degrees Celsius, several times hotter than the surface of the Sun, in a fraction of a second. The air expands so violently that it creates a shock wave, which quickly becomes the sound wave we hear. The rumble comes from the length of the lightning bolt itself. A bolt may be several kilometres long, so sound from the nearest part reaches you first, while sound from the far end arrives seconds later. Each of these waves travels a slightly different distance, and together they blend into a roll rather than a single crack.
The same delay appears in everyday life, once you start looking for it. At a fireworks display you see the burst of colour before you hear the bang. Sitting high in the stands at a large cricket ground, you may see the batter hit the ball a fraction of a second before the crack of the bat reaches you. Sound is not always slow, however. It travels more than four times faster through water and around seventeen times faster through steel, because the particles in liquids and solids are closer together and more tightly linked. In the vacuum of space, where there are almost no particles at all, sound cannot travel. Despite what science-fiction films suggest, an explosion in space would make no sound at all.
Perhaps the most important lesson of the flash-and-count method, though, is about safety. Thunder can usually be heard up to about 15 kilometres away, and lightning can strike at similar distances from the storm that produced it. In other words, if you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Weather experts advise heading indoors as soon as thunder is heard and waiting 30 minutes after the last rumble before going back outside. It is a rule worth remembering. Counting the seconds may be fun, but a storm that sounds distant may be much closer than it seems.

'Plants don't know any maths, of course. But when each new seed grows at the same small angle from the last one, the seeds pack together as tightly as possible, with no gaps and no wasted space. Everywhere she looked, something was quietly following a rule.

Option D: untrustworthy and sly

Why Your Body Clock Runs Late
If you have ever lain in bed at eleven o'clock at night feeling wide awake, then struggled to drag yourself out of bed at seven the next morning, you are not simply being lazy. You may be experiencing one of the most predictable changes of adolescence: a shift in the body's internal clock.
Deep inside the brain, a tiny cluster of cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus acts as a master timekeeper. It runs on a cycle of roughly 24 hours, known as the circadian rhythm, and it uses light entering the eyes to stay in step with day and night. As evening falls and light fades, this clock signals a small gland in the brain, the pineal gland, to release a hormone called melatonin. Melatonin does not knock you out, but it tells the body that night has arrived, lowering body temperature slightly and making sleep easier.
During the teenage years, this whole system shifts later. Research suggests that melatonin may be released up to two hours later in teenagers than in children or adults. At the same time, the 'sleep pressure' that builds up the longer a person stays awake seems to grow more slowly in adolescents. The result is that many teenagers genuinely do not feel sleepy until late at night, even when they are tired.
This would not matter much if teenagers could simply sleep later in the morning. Health experts recommend that people aged 14 to 17 get between eight and ten hours of sleep each night. But school, sport, part-time jobs and early buses rarely allow it. A student who falls asleep at midnight and wakes at 6.30 a.m. gets only six and a half hours, and over a week the missing hours add up to a 'sleep debt'.
Sleep is far from wasted time. During deep sleep the body releases growth hormone and repairs tissue, while during the dreaming stage known as REM sleep, the brain sorts and stores the day's memories. Studies have linked too little sleep in teenagers with poorer concentration, lower marks, more frequent illness and a greater risk of accidents, including on the road. Lack of sleep also affects mood, making it harder to manage stress and frustration.
Modern habits can make matters worse. Phones, tablets and computers give off blue-toned light, which is especially good at telling the brain's clock that it is still daytime. Scrolling in bed can therefore delay melatonin even further, while messages and games keep the mind alert. Caffeine from energy drinks, cola and coffee can stay active in the body for many hours, so an afternoon drink may still be affecting sleep at bedtime.
The good news is that the body clock responds to routine. Sleep researchers suggest going to bed and getting up at similar times every day, including weekends, since long weekend sleep-ins can push the clock even later. Getting bright light early in the morning, ideally outdoors, helps reset the clock, while dimming the lights and putting screens away an hour before bed allows melatonin to rise. Some schools overseas have even experimented with later start times, and several have reported that students arrive more alert.
Understanding your body clock will not make early alarms disappear. But it does show that the struggle to fall asleep is real, and that a few small changes can help a teenage brain get the rest it needs.

It runs on a cycle of roughly 24 hours, known as the circadian rhythm, and it uses light entering the eyes to stay in step with day and night. As evening falls and light fades, this clock signals a small gland in the brain, the pineal gland, to release a hormone called melatonin. Melatonin does not knock you out, but it tells the body that night has arrived, lowering body temperature slightly and making sleep easier.
During the teenage years, this whole system shifts later. Research suggests that melatonin may be released up to two hours later in teenagers than in children or adults. At the same time, the 'sleep pressure' that builds up the longer a person stays awake seems to grow more slowly in adolescents. The result is that many teenagers genuinely do not feel sleepy until late at night, even when they are tired.
This would not matter much if teenagers could simply sleep later in the morning. Health experts recommend that people aged 14 to 17 get between eight and ten hours of sleep each night. But school, sport, part-time jobs and early buses rarely allow it. A student who falls asleep at midnight and wakes at 6.30 a.m. gets only six and a half hours, and over a week the missing hours add up to a 'sleep debt'.
Sleep is far from wasted time. During deep sleep the body releases growth hormone and repairs tissue, while during the dreaming stage known as REM sleep, the brain sorts and stores the day's memories. Studies have linked too little sleep in teenagers with poorer concentration, lower marks, more frequent illness and a greater risk of accidents, including on the road. Lack of sleep also affects mood, making it harder to manage stress and frustration.

Scrolling in bed can therefore delay melatonin even further, while messages and games keep the mind alert. Caffeine from energy drinks, cola and coffee can stay active in the body for many hours, so an afternoon drink may still be affecting sleep at bedtime.

Getting bright light early in the morning, ideally outdoors, helps reset the clock, while dimming the lights and putting screens away an hour before bed allows melatonin to rise. The Patience of Dry Country
Roughly seventy per cent of mainland Australia is classed as arid or semi-arid, making it one of the driest inhabited continents on Earth. To a visitor, the deserts of the centre can seem empty: red sand, grey-green hummocks of spinifex and a sky that rarely offers a cloud. Yet scientists who study these landscapes describe them very differently. They see a place crowded with life that has mastered a single difficult skill: waiting.
The challenge in a desert is not only that rain is scarce, but that it is unpredictable. A region might average 150 millimetres a year, but that figure hides the truth. Several years may pass with almost nothing, and then a single storm may drop more than the yearly average in a few days. Living things cannot rely on a regular season, so they must be ready to survive long droughts and to act quickly when water finally arrives.
Many desert plants solve this problem by spending most of their lives as seeds. The seeds of some wildflowers can lie in the soil for years, protected by tough coats. Some are also coated with chemicals that stop them from sprouting. A light shower is not enough to wash these chemicals away, which prevents the seeds from germinating after rain too small to support a plant until it flowers. Only a heavy soaking removes the coating. When it does, the desert can be carpeted in paper daisies within weeks, and the plants race to flower and set new seed before the ground dries out again.
Spinifex takes a different approach. Rather than disappearing, it stays put and endures. Its narrow leaves roll inward, reducing the surface exposed to the sun and wind, so less water escapes. The prickly hummocks also provide shade and shelter for lizards, insects and small mammals that would otherwise be exposed on open sand.
Animals have developed equally clever strategies. The water-holding frog burrows deep into the ground as a drought begins and surrounds itself with layers of shed skin that form a waterproof cocoon. Inside, it can remain inactive for months or even years until rain softens the soil above. The thorny devil, a small spiky lizard, has a network of fine grooves between its scales. When it stands on damp sand or touches dew, water is drawn along these grooves to the corners of its mouth, where it can be swallowed.
Some animals avoid drought by moving. Flocks of budgerigars travel huge distances in search of areas where rain has fallen and grasses are seeding. When Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre, normally a vast crust of salt, fills after floods further north, Australian pelicans arrive from hundreds of kilometres away to breed on its islands. How they know the lake has filled is still not fully understood.
Even reproduction can be timed to the weather. A female red kangaroo can carry an embryo that pauses its development, resuming growth only when conditions improve. In a severe drought, breeding may stop altogether, sparing the mother the cost of raising a joey that could not survive.
What links all of these examples is economy. Desert life does not waste water, energy or opportunity. The bare red ground that looks lifeless to a passing traveller is, in reality, full of seeds, sleeping frogs and patient roots. The desert is not empty. It is simply holding its breath, waiting for the next storm.

Good Intentions, Wrong Bin
We have all done it. Standing over the kerbside bins, holding a greasy pizza box or a crumpled chip packet, we hesitate for a moment and then drop it into the recycling bin, hoping for the best. It feels like the responsible choice. Surely it is better to give something a chance at a second life than to condemn it to landfill? Unfortunately, this habit, which some waste experts call 'wishcycling', is doing real harm, and it is time we stopped.
To understand why, picture what happens after the truck collects your bin. Its contents travel to a materials recovery facility, where a combination of machines and workers separates paper, cardboard, glass, metal and certain plastics. These facilities are designed for specific items. When the wrong things arrive, the whole system suffers. Soft plastics such as bread bags and cling wrap are a notorious example. In most Australian council areas they do not belong in the yellow bin, because they wrap around the spinning shafts of sorting machines, forcing staff to stop the line and cut them free by hand. Every stoppage costs time and money.
Food waste causes a different problem. A jar still half full of pasta sauce or a pizza box soaked in oil can spoil clean paper and cardboard. Paper fibres that have absorbed grease are much harder to turn into new products, and a contaminated load may be worth far less, or nothing at all. In the worst cases, an entire truckload is sent to landfill because it is too dirty to sort. In other words, one hopeful gesture can undo the careful efforts of a whole street.
Some people argue that sorting is the facility's job, not ours. It is a tempting view, but it ignores reality. No sorting system is perfect, and the more rubbish that arrives mixed with recyclables, the more good material slips through the cracks. Recycling is a partnership. Householders are the first and most important link in the chain, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
The good news is that recycling correctly is not difficult. First, learn what your own council accepts, because the rules vary from place to place. Most councils publish a simple guide online or on a sticker for the bin lid. Second, empty containers and give them a quick rinse; they do not need to sparkle, but they should be free of food scraps. Third, place items in the bin loose rather than tied inside a plastic bag, which sorting machines cannot easily open. Finally, when in doubt, leave it out. An uncertain item placed in the general waste bin does far less damage than one that contaminates a load of clean recyclables.
There are also better options for the troublesome items themselves. Soft plastics can be avoided by choosing reusable bags and containers, and some communities run special collections for them. Old phones and batteries should never go in either kerbside bin; they can be taken to dedicated drop-off points, where valuable metals are recovered safely.
None of this requires heroic effort. It simply requires us to replace hopeful guessing with a few seconds of thought. The recycling bin is not a magic portal that transforms whatever we throw into it. It is the starting point of an industry that depends on us getting the basics right. Next time you stand at the bin with something in your hand, pause and check. Our good intentions deserve to be matched by good information.

Option B: they wrap around the spinning shafts of machines

Option D: they are too light for the trucks to collect

The Clock That Found the Sea
For most of history, a sailor far from land faced a puzzle that could cost lives. Working out how far north or south a ship had travelled, its latitude, was fairly straightforward. By measuring the height of the sun at noon, or of certain stars at night, a skilled navigator could calculate it with reasonable accuracy. Finding longitude, a ship's position east or west, was another matter entirely. There was no fixed point in the sky to measure it against, and without it a captain could only guess.
Those guesses were often wrong. Navigators relied on 'dead reckoning', estimating their position from their speed, direction and time travelled. But currents and winds pushed ships off course in ways that were hard to measure, and small errors added up over weeks at sea. Ships ran aground on coasts their crews believed were still hundreds of kilometres away, while others sailed back and forth hunting for islands where they hoped to take on fresh water. Long voyages became even longer, and sailors suffered from scurvy as fresh food ran out.
In 1714, the British Parliament offered a prize of up to 20,000 pounds, a fortune at the time, for a practical way to find longitude at sea. Many of the leading scientists of the day believed the answer lay in astronomy. They hoped to use the moon's position against the background of stars as a kind of heavenly clock, but the method required detailed tables and long, complicated calculations.
The key to the problem, however, was time itself. The Earth turns a full 360 degrees every 24 hours, or 15 degrees each hour. If a navigator knew the exact time at his home port at the very moment it was noon on board ship, the difference between the two times would reveal how far east or west he had travelled. Each hour of difference equalled 15 degrees of longitude. The theory was simple; the difficulty was building a clock that could keep accurate time on a rolling, pitching ship, through heat, cold and damp. The pendulum clocks of the day were useless at sea.
The man who solved this was not a famous scientist but John Harrison, a carpenter and self-taught clockmaker from the north of England. Over several decades he built a series of timekeepers. His first sea clock was a large machine weighing more than thirty kilograms. Each new version improved on the last, until his fourth, now known as H4, which looked like an oversized pocket watch about 13 centimetres across. On a trial voyage to Jamaica in 1761 and 1762, it lost only a few seconds over more than two months at sea.
Harrison's success did not bring him instant reward. The Board of Longitude, the committee responsible for the prize, demanded further tests and asked him to explain his methods in detail. Some members still preferred the astronomical solution. Harrison spent years arguing for what he believed he was owed, and he received substantial payments only late in his life.
Meanwhile, his invention proved itself in the hardest possible way. Captain James Cook carried a copy of H4 on his second great voyage across the Pacific in the 1770s. He praised it in his journal as a trusted guide, and his charts of the region were remarkably accurate. Within decades, marine chronometers had become standard equipment on ocean-going ships.
Today, satellites can fix a vessel's position within metres. Yet satellite navigation still depends on extremely precise clocks. In a sense, every phone that shows a moving blue dot on a map owes something to a carpenter who refused to give up.

A Speck in a Sunbeam
On 14 February 1990, a spacecraft about six billion kilometres from home turned around and looked back. The spacecraft was Voyager 1, and the photograph it took that day has become one of the most famous images in the history of space exploration. Strangely, it showed almost nothing at all.
Background
Voyager 1 was launched in September 1977, a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2. Its main mission was to study the giant outer planets. It flew past Jupiter in 1979, sending back detailed images of the planet's swirling storms and its volcanic moon Io, and reached Saturn in 1980. That encounter bent its path up and out of the flat plane in which the planets orbit, sending it towards the outer edge of the solar system. There were no more planets for it to visit.
The proposal
The astronomer Carl Sagan, a member of the Voyager imaging team, had suggested years earlier that the spacecraft should take one final picture of Earth before leaving. Many colleagues were unenthusiastic. From such a distance, they pointed out, Earth would appear far too small to show any detail, so the image would have little scientific value. There was also a practical concern. Earth would appear close to the Sun in the sky, and engineers worried that pointing the cameras in that direction could damage them. Sagan argued that the picture's value would not be measured in data. It would give humanity a perspective it had never had before. After lengthy discussion, and with the support of NASA's leaders, the plan was approved.
The method
In the end, the photograph was taken as part of a larger sequence. Voyager's cameras captured 60 frames, which were later combined into a mosaic known as the 'Family Portrait' of the solar system. Six planets appeared in it. Mercury was too close to the Sun to be seen, Mars was too dimly lit and Pluto was too small and faint. Shortly after the last frame was taken, the cameras were switched off for good to save power and memory for the long journey ahead. Because the spacecraft could only transmit information slowly, the stored images were sent back to Earth over the following months.
The result
In the frame showing Earth, the planet occupies less than a single pixel, a tiny pale dot sitting inside a streak of light. The streak is not a real object in space; it was created when sunlight scattered inside the camera because it was pointed so close to the Sun. Scientists learned very little from the picture. The public, however, found it unforgettable.
Sagan later wrote about the image in a book titled Pale Blue Dot. He reflected that everyone who had ever lived had lived on that small speck, and that seeing Earth so small should encourage people to treat one another more kindly and to care for the only home they have known.
Legacy
Voyager 1 is still travelling. In 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space, the region beyond the bubble of particles blown out by the Sun. Its power supply is slowly running down, and engineers have switched off instruments one by one to keep it working. Eventually it will fall silent. The photograph it took looking back, however, is likely to be remembered long after that. It remains a reminder that sometimes the most valuable observation is not the one that reveals the most detail, but the one that changes how we see ourselves.

Option C: the picture was part of a 60-frame mosaic
Option D: Voyager 1 is still travelling through space

In the end, the photograph was taken as part of a larger sequence. Voyager's cameras captured 60 frames, which were later combined into a mosaic known as the 'Family Portrait' of the solar system. In the frame showing Earth, the planet occupies less than a single pixel, a tiny pale dot sitting inside a streak of light. Voyager 1 is still travelling. In 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space, the region beyond the bubble of particles blown out by the Sun. Its power supply is slowly running down, and engineers have switched off instruments one by one to keep it working. Eventually it will fall silent. 'Good,' said Sam. 'You're terrible at it.'

Measurements by Feel
'How much flour?' Zara asked, pencil hovering over her notebook.
Her grandfather, whom everyone called Nana Ji, considered the question as though it were deeply philosophical. 'Enough,' he said.
'Enough isn't a measurement.'
'It is the only measurement that matters.' He lifted his bandaged right wrist, which he had sprained a week earlier stepping off a tram, and waved it vaguely towards the bag of atta on the bench. 'You will know.'
Zara did not know. That was the whole problem. On Sunday, twenty-two relatives were coming for lunch to celebrate her cousin's engagement, and Nana Ji had made the parathas for every family celebration for forty years. Nobody else had ever made them. Nobody else had ever been allowed to. Now, with his wrist strapped and his doctor's warning ringing in his ears, he had appointed Zara, aged fourteen, as his hands.
She had tried to prepare. The night before, she had searched online and found a recipe that listed everything precisely: three cups of wholemeal flour, one teaspoon of salt, one cup of warm water, two tablespoons of oil. She had copied it neatly into her notebook and underlined the quantities twice. When she showed it to Nana Ji, he read it carefully, nodded politely and said, 'Very nice. Put it away.'
So now she stood at the bench, pouring flour into the steel bowl while he watched from a kitchen chair.
'Stop,' he said, before she had reached the third cup. 'Now water. Slowly. Slowly! You are making a dough, not a swimming pool.'
She mixed with her fingers. The dough was sticky and clung to her hands like wet sand. She reached for more flour, but Nana Ji shook his head.
'Wait. Knead first. Let the flour drink.'
She kneaded. Gradually the stickiness faded. The dough became smooth and springy, and when she pressed it with a finger, the dent slowly filled itself back in.
'There,' said Nana Ji quietly. 'Feel that? Remember it.'
She rolled the first paratha too thick and the second too thin. The third tore when she folded the butter-brushed dough into layers. Nana Ji did not criticise. He simply said, 'Again,' each time, in the same calm voice, until the word stopped sounding like a judgement and started sounding like encouragement.
By the tenth paratha, something had changed. Zara stopped looking at the notebook. Her hands seemed to know how hard to press, how far to stretch, and when the pan was hot enough, because a drop of water danced and vanished. When she flipped a paratha and saw golden-brown blisters rising across its surface, she let out a whoop, and Nana Ji laughed so hard he had to steady himself on the chair.
On Sunday, the parathas disappeared within minutes. Her aunt asked who had made them, and when Zara admitted it was her, the room went briefly silent. Then her cousin raised a buttery hand and said, 'Same as always,' which was the highest compliment anyone in the family could give.
That evening, Zara opened her notebook to the neatly copied recipe. She looked at it for a long moment. Then, beneath the precise quantities, she wrote in pencil: Enough flour. Water slowly. Let the flour drink. Knead until it springs back. Again, again, again.
She closed the notebook and smiled. It was, she thought, the first recipe she had ever truly understood.

Option A: an adjective
Option B: a noun
Option C: a verb
Option D: an adverb

The Night Shift
The web appeared on the first warm evening of spring, stretched across the narrow path between the back door and the clothesline. Theo walked straight into it while carrying out the rubbish. For the next thirty seconds he performed a frantic dance on the lawn, slapping at his hair and neck, convinced that something with eight legs was crawling down his collar.
Nothing was. The spider, a plump brown creature with a body like a hazelnut, had dropped to the edge of the ruined web and hung there, perfectly still.
'Garden orb-weaver,' said his grandmother from the kitchen window, where she had watched the entire performance. 'Harmless, really. She's more scared of you than you are of her.'
'I doubt that,' muttered Theo.
The next morning the path was clear. But the following evening, the web was back, strung between the same branch of the lemon tree and the same corner of the shed. Theo fetched the broom and swept it away. The spider scuttled into the leaves.
The evening after that, the web was back again.
This went on for a week. Each evening the spider rebuilt; each evening Theo destroyed. He began to think of it as a contest, one he was clearly winning, since he had a broom and the spider had only silk. Yet every morning when he checked, the web was gone, even on nights he had not touched it.
'Where does it go?' he asked his grandmother eventually, irritated by the mystery.
'She eats it,' she said. 'Rolls it up at dawn and eats it, so she can use the silk again. Then she hides in the lemon tree all day and builds a fresh web at dusk. You've been knocking down something she was going to take down herself.'
Theo frowned. 'So I'm not winning?'
'I don't think she knows there's a competition.'
That night, instead of fetching the broom, Theo sat on the back step with a torch and watched. He did not mean to stay long. But the spider was already at work, and what she was doing was so precise that he forgot to leave.
First she let a single thread drift on the breeze until it caught on the shed. She crossed it, tightened it and dropped a second line, making a Y-shape. From the centre she laid down spokes, one after another, measuring each gap with her legs. Then she began to spiral outward, round and round, so evenly that Theo found himself holding his breath every time she turned a corner. The whole web took less than an hour. When it was finished, she settled at its centre, head down, and waited.
At about ten o'clock a moth blundered into the lower edge. The spider was there in an instant, turning the struggling insect in her legs and wrapping it in silk until it was a neat white parcel.
Theo realised his mouth was open. He closed it. He thought about the broom leaning against the shed, and about how many of these webs he had swept into a grey tangle without ever looking at one properly.
The next evening he went outside at dusk, torch in hand, and found the spider had not yet begun. He waited. Then, carefully, he moved the laundry basket to the other side of the yard, so that he could reach the clothesline without passing between the lemon tree and the shed.
His grandmother saw him from the window. She didn't say anything, but a few minutes later she carried two cups of tea out to the back step and sat down beside him to watch.

Option A: moved clumsily without seeing where it was going
Option B: flew in carefully and completely on purpose
Option C: was carried along gently by the evening wind
Option D: landed softly and gracefully in one place

Saturday Log: Operation Bookcase
Dear Diary,
9.15 am. Today Dad and I are assembling the new bookcase for my room. It arrived yesterday in a flat cardboard box that weighed roughly the same as a small car. Dad says it will take 'forty minutes, tops'. He said the same thing about the barbecue last summer, which we eventually finished in March, but I am trying to be positive.
9.40 am. We have opened the box. Inside are eleven wooden panels, a bag of what Dad calls 'the little bits', and an instruction booklet with no words in it, only drawings of a smiling cartoon person who never seems to be in any difficulty. Dad has put the booklet aside. 'It's basically common sense,' he says. I have quietly rescued the booklet from under the couch.
10.25 am. Progress report: the base and two sides are attached. There is a small problem, which is that the sides are attached upside down, so the holes for the shelves face outward like the portholes of a very confused ship. Dad says this is 'a design choice'. I have consulted the cartoon person. The cartoon person disagrees.
11.10 am. We have taken everything apart and started again. Dad has stopped saying 'forty minutes'. He has started saying 'nearly there', which, in my experience, is a phrase that means the opposite.
12.30 pm. Lunch break. Dad is eating a sandwich with the dark, steady stare of a man who has been personally betrayed by a cam lock. A cam lock is a small metal disc that is supposed to tighten when you turn it. Ours spins forever, like a tiny planet orbiting nothing. Mum walked past, looked at the half-built bookcase, looked at us, and said, 'I'll be in the garden,' in the voice she normally saves for when the dog has eaten something it shouldn't.
2.05 pm. Breakthrough! I discovered that the cam locks would not tighten because we had used the long screws in the short holes and the short screws in the long holes. The cartoon person had shown this clearly on page four. I pointed this out to Dad as gently as possible. He was silent for a while and then said, 'Well, it's good that one of us checks the details,' which I am counting as a compliment.
3.30 pm. Shelves in. Back panel nailed on, mostly straight. We stood the bookcase up together, very slowly, like explorers raising a flag on a mountain summit. It did not fall over. Dad shook my hand.
4.00 pm. Small issue. We have six leftover pieces: four screws, a wooden peg and a mysterious plastic thing shaped like a tiny boomerang. The cartoon person shows no leftover pieces. Dad says manufacturers always include spares. I have placed the leftover pieces in a jar labelled EVIDENCE.
6.45 pm. I have put my books on the shelves. The bookcase leans very slightly to the left, as if it is trying to hear a conversation in the next room. If you put the heavy atlas on the right-hand end, it straightens up beautifully. I have decided this is a feature.
9.00 pm. Dad has just come in to admire our work. He said, 'Seven hours. Not bad,' and then, after a pause, 'Next time we'll read the instructions first.' I said I had read them. He said, 'Exactly. Teamwork.'
Lessons learned: forty minutes is not a real unit of time, the cartoon person is always right, and a little quiet support from the right-hand side can keep almost anything standing straight.
Signing off, slightly bruised but victorious,
Jess

Option A: seven hours
Option B: forty minutes
Option C: nearly an hour
Option D: until March

9.40 am. We have opened the box. 10.25 am. Progress report: the base and two sides are attached. There is a small problem, which is that the sides are attached upside down, so the holes for the shelves face outward like the portholes of a very confused ship. Dad says this is 'a design choice'. I have consulted the cartoon person. The cartoon person disagrees.
11.10 am. We have taken everything apart and started again. Dad has stopped saying 'forty minutes'. He has started saying 'nearly there', which, in my experience, is a phrase that means the opposite.
12.30 pm. Lunch break. Dad is eating a sandwich with the dark, steady stare of a man who has been personally betrayed by a cam lock. A cam lock is a small metal disc that is supposed to tighten when you turn it. Ours spins forever, like a tiny planet orbiting nothing.
