Write Me a Future Worth Wanting
Walk into the young adult section of any bookshop and count the ruined cities on the covers. Flooded coastlines, cracked domes, teenagers in grey uniforms sprinting away from drones. Somewhere along the way, science fiction for young readers decided that the future is a disaster to be survived rather than a place worth building. I think it is time we asked our writers for something braver: stories in which tomorrow is better than today.
Let me be clear about what I am not saying. Dystopian fiction has earned its place. A good cautionary tale works like a smoke alarm, warning us about dangers while there is still time to act. Some of the most important novels ever written imagined societies gone wrong, and readers have been grateful for the warnings. The problem is not that these stories exist. The problem is that, for many young people, they are now almost the only stories about the future they ever read.
That matters because stories do more than entertain; they rehearse. When we read, we practise imagining. If every future we picture is one of collapse, we become very skilled at imagining collapse and strangely clumsy at imagining anything else. Ask a class of fifteen-year-olds to describe the world in 2080 and see how many reach for the word 'apocalypse' before the word 'garden'. A generation that cannot picture a good future will find it very hard to work towards one.
Science fiction also has a long record of shaping what inventors chose to build. Igor Sikorsky, who designed some of the first practical helicopters, said that as a boy he was captivated by a Jules Verne novel describing a flying machine lifted by spinning propellers. Hermann Oberth, one of the founders of modern rocket science, traced his interest in space travel to reading Verne's From the Earth to the Moon as a child. Neither man was inspired by a story about everything falling apart. Both were drawn towards machines that worked and journeys that succeeded.
Some critics argue that hopeful fiction is naive, that it ignores real problems such as climate change. But hope is not the same as pretending. The best optimistic stories begin with hard problems and imagine how people might solve them: cities cooled by rooftop forests, villages powered by the sun, communities that repair rather than replace. Such stories are not easier to write than dystopias; they are harder, because the author has to think through a solution instead of simply describing a catastrophe. Imagining a workable answer demands real knowledge of science, of people and of how change actually happens.
There are encouraging signs. A small but growing movement of writers, sometimes called 'solarpunk', sets its stories in worlds where technology and nature work together. Their books, however, are still rare on school reading lists, and rarer still in the displays that greet young customers. Publishers often say they are simply giving readers what sells, but readers can only choose from what they are offered.
So here is my request to authors, publishers and teachers. Keep the warnings, but give us the blueprints too. Put a story on the shelf in which a teenager fixes something instead of fleeing from it. Let us finish a novel feeling not relieved that we survived, but impatient to begin. The future will be shaped by today's young readers. The least we can do is show them a version worth building.

Option A: a blueprint.
Option B: a rehearsal.
Option C: a rooftop forest.
Option D: a smoke alarm.

The Doctor Who Stitched a Nation's Songs
In 1828, a young medical student set off on foot from the Finnish town of Turku with a notebook, a knapsack and very little money. His name was Elias Lönnrot, and the journey he began that year would eventually give Finland its national epic, the Kalevala. Lönnrot is often described as a mere collector of old poems, but that label does him a serious injustice. He was a collector, certainly, but he was also an editor, a scholar and, in a very real sense, an author.
Lönnrot was born in 1802 in the village of Sammatti, the son of a poor tailor. Lack of money interrupted his schooling again and again, yet he reached university and qualified as a doctor in 1832. A year later he accepted the post of district medical officer in Kajaani, a small, remote town in the east of the country. The work was exhausting and poorly paid, and a man of his talents might easily have found a more comfortable position in the south. He stayed in Kajaani for some twenty years.
In the forests and lake country of eastern Finland and Karelia, an ancient tradition of sung poetry still survived. Singers, often farmers or fishermen, could chant thousands of lines from memory. They told of the wise old singer Väinämöinen, of the smith Ilmarinen, who forged a magical object called the Sampo, and of the reckless adventurer Lemminkäinen. Yet no one had ever written these songs down as a whole. They were scattered like seeds across hundreds of villages, and each singer knew only some of them.
From Kajaani, Lönnrot made journey after journey into this country, eleven in all, covering thousands of kilometres, mostly on foot or on skis. He slept in farmhouses, treated the sick as he went, and listened. One famous singer, Arhippa Perttunen, sang to him for days on end.
Some critics have complained that the Kalevala is not a 'genuine' folk epic, because Lönnrot arranged the poems himself, linked episodes that no singer had ever linked, and even composed lines of his own to join them. Yet this is exactly why he deserves more credit, not less. No single singer held the whole story; it existed only in pieces. It took Lönnrot's judgement to decide which version of each episode was strongest, how the pieces fitted together and where gaps needed filling. A cathedral built from salvaged stones is still the work of its architect.
The first Kalevala appeared in 1835. Its preface was dated 28 February, a day Finns still celebrate as Kalevala Day. Lönnrot was not satisfied, however. He kept collecting, and in 1849 he published a far larger edition of fifty poems and nearly 23,000 lines. At the time, most books in Finland were written in Swedish, the language of the educated classes. The Kalevala showed that Finnish, the everyday language of farmers and fishermen, could carry great literature. Its stories later inspired the composer Jean Sibelius, and the writer J.R.R. Tolkien admired it deeply.
Lönnrot himself remained modest. He became professor of Finnish at the University of Helsinki in 1853 and spent many of his later years compiling an enormous Finnish–Swedish dictionary. He died in 1884 in Sammatti, the village where he was born.
We should remember him not as someone who simply wrote down what he heard, but as someone who listened, chose and built. Without the singers there would be no Kalevala. Without Lönnrot, there would be none either.

Ward Six and the Robot Called Pip
Trial Report: Autonomous Delivery Robot, Kestrel Bay District Hospital
Purpose
This report describes a twelve-week trial of an autonomous delivery robot at Kestrel Bay District Hospital. The aim was to find out whether the robot could reduce the time nurses spend fetching medicines, linen and samples, so that they could spend more time with patients.
Background
Before the trial, a survey found that nurses on the busiest wards walked, on average, more than eight kilometres per shift. Much of this walking involved trips to the pharmacy and pathology laboratory on the ground floor. The hospital leased one robot, which staff soon nicknamed Pip. Pip is about the size of a small refrigerator. It finds its way using cameras, laser sensors and a stored map of the building, and it can call lifts using a wireless signal. Its storage drawers open only when a staff member enters a personal code.
Method
Pip was assigned to Ward Six, a 30-bed medical ward, and made deliveries between 7 am and 9 pm every day. Staff recorded each trip, any problems, and the time they would otherwise have spent walking. At the end of weeks two, six and twelve, nurses completed a short survey.
Findings
Weeks 1–3: Early results were disappointing. Pip took an average of 19 minutes per round trip, compared with 12 minutes for a nurse on foot. The main cause was what one engineer called the robot's 'politeness'. Pip was programmed to stop whenever a person came within a metre of it and to wait until the path was completely clear. At visiting hours, when corridors were crowded, it could sit motionless for minutes at a time. Several visitors even stood in front of it to take photographs. 'Honestly, I wanted to push it down the corridor myself,' admitted nurse unit manager Grace Tupou. 'We were losing more time than we were saving.'
Weeks 4–8: Two changes were made. Engineers reduced the stopping distance to half a metre and allowed Pip to steer slowly around people instead of waiting. Staff also agreed to schedule non-urgent deliveries outside visiting hours, and a small sign was attached to Pip asking visitors to let it pass. Average trip time fell to 11 minutes.
Weeks 9–12: Pip completed 1,146 deliveries over the full trial with no lost items. In the final four weeks, nurses on Ward Six walked about two kilometres less per shift than before the trial. In the week-twelve survey, 81 per cent of nurses said they would like the robot to continue, compared with 35 per cent in week two. 'I didn't expect to miss it on the weekend it went in for servicing,' said Tupou. 'We'd built our whole routine around it.'
Some problems remained. Pip cannot open doors that lack automatic sensors, and on two occasions it waited more than ten minutes for a lift because the lift was full. It also cannot judge urgency: a bag of urgent blood samples travels no faster than a stack of clean towels.
Conclusions and Recommendations
The trial suggests that a delivery robot can save nursing time on a busy ward. It is recommended that the hospital lease two further robots for Wards Four and Seven, that urgent deliveries continue to be carried by staff, and that each new ward be given a four-week adjustment period before results are measured.

Option B: Background

Option D: Conclusions and Recommendations

The Case for the Crackle
Last summer, at a caravan park on the south coast, I watched a family of five arrive in a gleaming four-wheel drive. Within twenty minutes they had unfolded an awning, switched on a television and connected every device they owned to the park's wi-fi. By nightfall the only light on their faces came from screens. They had travelled three hours to sit in the bush and do exactly what they did at home.
I want to argue for something simpler and, to many people, less appealing: the basic campsite. No powered sites, no wi-fi, no camp kitchen with a microwave. Just a patch of flat ground, a fire pit if the season allows, a drop toilet and, if you are lucky, a tap. Families who choose this kind of camping, I believe, get far more from the outdoors than those who bring the comforts of home with them.
The most obvious objection is that basic camping is uncomfortable, and I will not pretend otherwise. The ground is hard. Mornings are cold. Without a fridge, you plan meals carefully and eat the fresh food first. But discomfort is not the opposite of enjoyment. Ask anyone about their most memorable holiday and you will rarely hear about a soft mattress. You will hear about the night the tent leaked, or the morning the kookaburras woke everyone at dawn. Small hardships, shared, become the stories a family tells for years.
Then there is boredom, which parents seem to fear more than snakes. On a basic site, children will almost certainly announce, sometime on the first afternoon, that there is nothing to do. This is the moment to hold your nerve. Researchers who study play have long argued that unstructured time is when children invent games, explore and learn to solve problems for themselves. In my experience, the complaint lasts about an hour. After that, someone discovers that the creek has tadpoles, or that a fallen branch makes an excellent bridge, and the afternoon disappears.
Basic camping also teaches skills that are hard to learn anywhere else. Pitching a tent in a rising wind, reading the sky for rain, rationing water when the nearest tap is a long walk away: these are small lessons in planning and patience. They also teach respect for the environment. When you must carry out every scrap of rubbish yourself, you quickly notice how much of it you create.
Finally, there is the night. Away from the glow of town lights and screens, the sky fills with more stars than most city children have ever seen. The fire hisses and pops. Somewhere a boobook owl repeats its soft, two-note call, and possums thump across the roof of the car. Who Really Wrote Aesop's Fables?
Almost everyone knows a few of Aesop's fables. The tortoise beats the overconfident hare; the boy who cries 'wolf!' too often is not believed when a real wolf comes; the fox who cannot reach a bunch of grapes decides they must be sour anyway. These tiny stories, usually featuring talking animals and ending with a lesson, have been retold for more than two thousand years. Yet the question of who actually wrote them has a surprisingly slippery answer.
According to ancient tradition, Aesop was a slave who lived in Greece in the sixth century BCE and won fame for his wit. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing about a century later, mentions him briefly, and many colourful stories about his life circulated afterwards. Most of these – including tales that he was ugly, that he outwitted his master again and again, and that he advised kings – appeared centuries after his death and are probably legends. Some historians doubt that Aesop existed at all. Others think a real storyteller of that name may have lived, but that his reputation grew so large that almost any clever animal story came to be credited to him.
What is clear is that the fables were not first written as a book. They were told aloud, at dinners, in law courts and in everyday conversation, where a speaker might use a well-chosen fable to make a point without stating it directly. The first known written collection was made around 300 BCE by an Athenian statesman, Demetrius of Phalerum. Sadly, his collection has been lost. In the first century CE, a freed slave named Phaedrus retold many fables in Latin verse, and later a poet called Babrius did the same in Greek. Each writer added, changed and polished the stories to suit his own audience.
Even the famous morals were not always part of the original tales. In many early versions, the lesson was placed at the beginning, to show the speaker how the fable could be used. Over time, editors moved the moral to the end and sometimes wrote new morals that did not quite match the story. As a result, the same fable might teach slightly different lessons in different collections.
The fables also travelled. Similar stories appear in the Panchatantra, a collection of animal tales from ancient India, though scholars debate whether one tradition borrowed from the other or whether both drew on even older sources. In 1484, the English printer William Caxton published one of the first books of Aesop's fables in English. Nearly two centuries later, the French poet Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695) rewrote many of them as witty, elegant poems that French students still learn by heart.
Today, the collection known as 'Aesop's Fables' contains several hundred stories. Some are certainly ancient; others were added much later; a few may even have been written in the Middle Ages and given Aesop's name because it lent them authority. The word 'Aesop' now works less like a name and more like a label – a sign that tells readers what kind of story to expect.
Perhaps this is a fitting fate for a storyteller whose life is lost in legend. Fables were always meant to be borrowed, adapted and passed on, and each generation has reshaped them for its own needs. In a sense, Aesop's fables have had thousands of authors, and they are still being written.

Five Days on the Book Bus
When Ms Pham handed out work experience placements, I had asked for the vet clinic. I got the mobile library instead.
'It's a bus full of books,' I complained to Mum that night. 'I'll be shelving. In a bus.'
On Monday the bus was waiting at the council depot, a long white vehicle with a faded kookaburra painted on its side. Lorna, the librarian who drove it, was sixty-two, wore a fleece vest covered in badges and had been doing the job for nineteen years. She gave me a lanyard and told me to sit up front. 'You can navigate,' she said, 'though I could do this route asleep.'
The route wound through four small towns and a scatter of farms in the hills, places where the nearest proper library was an hour's drive away. The paddocks lay still and brown under a flat grey sky. I counted the minutes until lunch.
At our first stop, the hall at Wirrin Creek, five people were already waiting, though we were ten minutes early. An old man handed back three westerns and asked after Lorna's knee. A woman named Mrs Ferreira returned a large-print mystery and spent fifteen minutes describing her new great-granddaughter. Lorna listened to every word, then reached without looking for the next book in the series, which she had set aside the week before.
By the end of the day we had issued forty-one books. I said, not very kindly, that the town library probably issued that many in an hour.
Lorna considered this. 'Probably,' she said. 'How many people did we talk to?'
I hadn't counted.
On Tuesday we stopped at a tiny primary school, where twenty barefoot children swarmed the bus at once. Lorna knew which of them were halfway through a dragon series and which boy had been banned by his mum from anything with sharks in it. I spent most of the morning reshelving picture books that had been pulled out, admired and abandoned on the floor, and wondering how anyone could do this for nineteen years.
On Wednesday, a farmer named Doug came aboard to print a form for his licence because his internet had been down for a week. A boy about my age borrowed a book on electric guitars, then asked, very quietly, whether we had anything on anxiety. Lorna found two, slid them into a plain paper bag without comment and stamped them as if they were cookbooks. On Thursday, Mr Bui was not at his usual stop. Lorna waited five minutes, then drove to his house, where we found him in the garden, perfectly well but muddled about the days. She wrote THURSDAY on a card in thick black marker and stuck it to his fridge.
Still, I counted the minutes until lunch. I won't pretend I was transformed overnight. The bus smelled of diesel and old paper, the seat was hard, and I never learned to like westerns.
But on Friday, at the last stop, Mrs Ferreira climbed aboard with a photo of the baby and showed it to me, not Lorna. She asked whether I would be back next week. When I said no, she looked genuinely sorry.
On the drive back, I checked Lorna's records: 187 books issued that week. There was no record of the rest, but I tried to add it up anyway: Doug's form, the card on Mr Bui's fridge, the plain paper bag, the photo of the baby. I lost count long before I reached the end.
'So,' said Lorna as she parked. 'Still think it's just a bus full of books?'
I didn't answer. I think she knew I didn't need to.

Option A: the vet clinic
Option B: the town library
Option C: the council depot
Option D: the school office

The Man Who Counted His Steps
In the middle of the nineteenth century, the Survey of India was carrying out one of the most ambitious mapping projects ever attempted. Its surveyors had measured vast areas of the subcontinent with chains, telescopes and careful triangles. Yet one great blank remained on their maps: the high plateau of Tibet, a land that, at the time, did not welcome foreign visitors. British surveyors could not simply walk in with their instruments. The solution was to train local men who could travel without attracting attention. These secret surveyors became known as the 'pundits', and the most celebrated of them was Nain Singh Rawat.
Nain Singh came from a village in the Himalayan foothills of Kumaon. He had worked as a schoolteacher and had travelled in Tibet as a young man, so he spoke the language and understood local customs. In the early 1860s, he and his cousin were trained at the Survey's headquarters in Dehradun. There they learned to use a compass and a sextant, to read the positions of stars and to keep their records in code.
The most remarkable part of their training involved walking. Nain Singh practised until every pace he took was the same length, uphill or down, so that two thousand of his paces equalled very close to one mile. To keep count without writing anything down, he carried a string of beads. A typical string of this kind had 108 beads, but his had exactly 100. Every hundred paces, he slipped one bead through his fingers, so a full circuit of the string meant ten thousand paces, or about five miles. Day after day, across freezing passes and windswept plains, he kept counting.
Recording his results was just as challenging. Nain Singh hid his notes inside a hollow hand-held cylinder of a kind that travellers in the region commonly carried and spun. He stored mercury, needed for taking readings of the stars, in a shell. To estimate how high he had climbed, he boiled water and measured its temperature. Water boils at a lower temperature as altitude increases, so the reading allowed him to calculate his height above sea level. The thermometer he used was concealed in the hollow top of his walking staff.
In 1865 he set out from Kathmandu, travelling with a group of traders, and reached Lhasa early the following year. He stayed for several months, quietly taking readings that allowed him to fix the city's position far more precisely than before. On the return journey he followed a great river for hundreds of kilometres, mapping its course as he went. All the while he had to keep his instruments out of sight and his counting steady, even while chatting with fellow travellers. By the time he reached India again, he had covered well over a thousand kilometres, much of it on foot, and every step had been counted.
His later journeys added thousands of square kilometres to the map. In 1877 the Royal Geographical Society in London awarded him one of its gold medals. Yet for years his name appeared in official reports only as a code, 'the Pundit', because his work depended on secrecy.
Today, Nain Singh is remembered in India as a national hero, and a postage stamp was issued in his honour in 2004. His story is a reminder that exploration is not always about planting flags. Sometimes it is about patience, discipline and the quiet courage to keep counting when no one is watching.

Option A: Kathmandu
Option B: Lhasa
Option C: London
Option D: Dehradun

The Squire Who Drew the Aeroplane
More than a century before the Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk, an English landowner engraved a small silver disc with a design that would change the way people thought about flight. On one side, Sir George Cayley sketched a craft with a fixed wing, a tail and a seat for a pilot. On the other, he drew a simple diagram of the forces acting on a wing as it moves through the air. The year was 1799, and Cayley was still in his twenties.
For centuries, would-be aviators had tried to copy birds. They strapped feathered or flapping wings to their arms and leapt from towers, usually with painful results. Their reasoning seemed obvious: birds fly by flapping, so people should flap too. Cayley's great insight was that this approach mixed up two separate problems. A flapping wing had to do two jobs at once: hold the craft up and push it forward. Cayley argued that these jobs should be divided. A fixed wing, angled slightly into the airflow, could provide lift, while a separate mechanism provided thrust. Almost every aeroplane since has followed this principle.
Cayley lived at Brompton Hall in Yorkshire and pursued an astonishing range of interests. He designed a lightweight wheel with wire spokes held in tension, sketched early ideas for caterpillar tracks and proposed safety devices for railways. But flight remained his lifelong passion. He tested curved wing shapes on a whirling arm, a long rotating rod that swept models through the air so that he could measure the forces on them. In 1804 he flew a model glider about a metre and a half long, often described as the first modern aircraft. Between 1809 and 1810 he published his findings in a three-part paper, 'On Aerial Navigation', setting out the science that later inventors would build on.
What Cayley lacked was an engine. The steam engines of his day were far too heavy for their power, and although he experimented with alternatives, including an engine driven by hot air, none was light enough to keep a craft in the air. He therefore concentrated on gliders, which needed no engine at all. It would take the light petrol engine, developed decades after his death, to solve the problem he had identified.
In 1849 one of his gliders carried a ten-year-old boy a short distance down a hillside. Then, in 1853, when Cayley was almost eighty, a larger glider carried an adult across a small valley near Brompton Hall. According to a story later told by his granddaughter, the passenger was Cayley's coachman, who climbed out shaken but unhurt and announced that he wished to resign, as he had been hired to drive and not to fly. Whether every detail of the story is true is uncertain, but the flight is often described as the first recorded flight by an adult in a winged aircraft.
Cayley died in 1857, decades before powered flight became possible. Yet his ideas did not disappear. The Wright brothers studied his work closely, and Wilbur Wright later credited him with carrying the science of flight further than anyone before him. Modern engineers have built replicas of the coachman glider, and they have flown.
It is tempting to remember inventors only for the machines that finally worked. Cayley's story suggests a different measure of success: the person who asks the right question may matter as much as the person who builds the final answer.

Locked In: Designing a Classroom Escape Room
An escape room is a game in which a team must solve a series of puzzles to 'escape' a room, or open a final locked box, before time runs out. Commercial escape rooms can cost thousands of dollars to build, but a classroom version needs little more than a few padlocks, some envelopes and plenty of imagination. The following steps will help you design one that is challenging without being frustrating.
Step 1: Choose a story
Every good escape room begins with a story that explains why the players are trying to escape. Perhaps they are scientists who must find an antidote before a laboratory seals itself, or detectives who must recover a stolen painting. Two or three sentences read aloud at the start are enough. The story's job is to give the puzzles a purpose, so that players feel they are uncovering something rather than completing a worksheet.
Step 2: Work backwards
Experienced designers usually start with the ending. Decide what the final 'treasure' will be, such as a box containing the antidote, and what will open it. Then ask: what clue will give players the code for that last lock? What puzzle will reveal that clue? Working backwards creates a chain in which each solution leads to the next problem. It also helps you avoid the most common design mistake: a puzzle whose answer does not lead anywhere.
Step 3: Vary the puzzles
Players have different strengths, so include a mix of puzzle types. A coded message might appeal to someone who enjoys patterns; a jigsaw to someone who thinks visually; a riddle to someone who loves words. Hidden objects, such as a key taped under a chair, reward careful observation. Aim for five to eight puzzles for a 45-minute game. Fewer can make the game feel thin, while more can leave teams rushed and confused.
Step 4: Allow for teamwork
Design some puzzles that can be worked on at the same time, rather than one long single chain. If only one puzzle is available at a time, a confident player can easily take over while everyone else watches. Parallel puzzles give every team member something meaningful to do. Some designers deliberately split the pieces of one puzzle between different parts of the room, so that players must talk to each other to combine them.
Step 5: Test it
Before running the game for real, ask two or three people who were not involved in designing it to play through it. Watch closely but say nothing. You will almost certainly find that a clue you thought obvious is baffling, or that a puzzle you were proud of can be solved in seconds by guessing. Note where players get stuck and adjust the clues. Designers often find this step humbling.
Step 6: Plan your hints
Even well-tested rooms can leave a team stalled. Decide in advance how players can ask for help, for example by allowing three hint cards per game. A good hint nudges rather than tells: 'Have you looked at the clock?' is better than 'The code is 1045.' Players should finish feeling that they solved the room themselves.
Step 7: Debrief
When the game ends, whether or not the team has escaped, take five minutes to talk about it. Ask which puzzle was most satisfying and which was hardest. Players often enjoy explaining how they cracked a code, and their answers will help you improve your next design.
A final tip: resist the urge to make your room as difficult as possible. The aim is not to defeat the players but to give them the pleasure of working something out together. A room that no team can escape is not a clever room. It is a badly designed one.

Option B: very confusing
Option C: easy to see
Option D: well hidden

An escape room is a game in which a team must solve a series of puzzles to 'escape' a room, or open a final locked box, before time runs out. Commercial escape rooms can cost thousands of dollars to build, but a classroom version needs little more than a few padlocks, some envelopes and plenty of imagination. The following steps will help you design one that is challenging without being frustrating.
Step 1: Choose a story
Every good escape room begins with a story that explains why the players are trying to escape. Perhaps they are scientists who must find an antidote before a laboratory seals itself, or detectives who must recover a stolen painting. Two or three sentences read aloud at the start are enough. The story's job is to give the puzzles a purpose, so that players feel they are uncovering something rather than completing a worksheet.
Step 2: Work backwards
Experienced designers usually start with the ending. Decide what the final 'treasure' will be, such as a box containing the antidote, and what will open it. Then ask: what clue will give players the code for that last lock? What puzzle will reveal that clue? Working backwards creates a chain in which each solution leads to the next problem. It also helps you avoid the most common design mistake: a puzzle whose answer does not lead anywhere.
Step 3: Vary the puzzles
Players have different strengths, so include a mix of puzzle types. A coded message might appeal to someone who enjoys patterns; a jigsaw to someone who thinks visually; a riddle to someone who loves words. Hidden objects, such as a key taped under a chair, reward careful observation. Aim for five to eight puzzles for a 45-minute game. Design some puzzles that can be worked on at the same time, rather than one long single chain. The Inventor's Logbook: A Guide for Young Designers
Many of history's best-known inventors were also tireless note-takers. Thomas Edison and his team filled around 3,500 notebooks with sketches, measurements and ideas. Leonardo da Vinci's surviving notebooks run to thousands of pages. You do not need to be a genius to keep a logbook, but if you are entering a design competition or working on a school invention project, a good one can make the difference between a vague idea and a working product. Follow these steps to set one up and use it well.
1. Choose the right book
Use a bound notebook with numbered pages rather than loose sheets or a ring binder. Pages in a bound book cannot be removed or reordered without leaving obvious signs. This matters more than you might think: a logbook is a record of how your idea developed, and its value depends on being trustworthy. If you prefer to work digitally, use a program that automatically records the date of every change.
2. Date every entry
Begin each session with the date, and write in pen, not pencil. If you make a mistake, draw a single line through it so that it can still be read. Never tear out a page or use correction fluid. A crossed-out error tells a story; a missing page raises suspicions.
3. Record everything, especially failures
This is the step most beginners skip. It is natural to want your logbook to look impressive, filled only with clever ideas and successful tests. Resist that temptation. Write down what you tried, what you expected to happen and what actually happened, even when the result was disappointing. A prototype that collapses tells you something important about your materials or design. Competition judges often say that the most convincing logbooks are the ones with the most crossings-out, because they show genuine thinking. An inventor who records only successes has, in effect, thrown away half of their evidence.
4. Sketch, label and measure
A quick labelled sketch often explains an idea faster than a paragraph. Include measurements wherever possible and note the materials you used. Tape in photographs of prototypes, and date them too. If you borrowed an idea from a book, a website or a classmate, say so and record where it came from.
5. Reflect regularly
At the end of each week, read back over your entries and write a short reflection. What have you learned? Which problem is now most urgent? What will you try next? These reflections turn a collection of notes into a plan.
6. Have entries witnessed
In the past, inventors often asked a trusted person to sign and date important pages, confirming that they had seen the work on that day. This could help prove who had an idea first if a dispute arose. For a school project, ask a teacher or parent to initial your logbook every few weeks. It takes only a moment and adds weight to your record.
Common mistakes to avoid
• Writing up the logbook at the end of the project from memory
• Leaving gaps of several weeks without explanation
• Recording results without saying how they were measured
• Copying neat versions of messy pages and throwing the originals away
A logbook is not a work of art, and nobody expects it to be tidy. Its worth lies in its honesty. Years from now, you may look back at a page covered in scribbles and crossings-out and see the exact moment a stubborn problem began to give way. That page will be worth more than any polished final report.

Tunnels Under the Savanna
Walk across the grassy woodland of Undara Volcanic National Park, about 275 kilometres south-west of Cairns, and you might notice something odd. Here and there, winding through the dry, open country, are long strips of thick green forest. From the air they look like ribbons dropped across the landscape. These ribbons mark the roofs of collapsed tunnels, and they are the visible clues to one of the longest lava flows on Earth.
About 190,000 years ago, a volcano in this part of north Queensland erupted. It did not explode in a towering cloud of ash. Instead, an enormous volume of runny, red-hot lava poured out of the crater and spread across the land, following the paths of old creek beds and valleys. One flow travelled more than 160 kilometres from its source, a remarkable distance for lava, which usually cools and stops long before then.
The secret of its long journey lay on the surface. As the outside of each river of lava met the cooler air, it hardened into a crust of rock. That crust acted like insulation, keeping the molten lava beneath it hot and flowing. The lava kept moving downhill inside its own stone pipe. When the eruption finally ended, the remaining lava drained away, leaving behind long, hollow tubes. Some are wide enough to drive a bus through.
Over thousands of years, parts of the tube roofs caved in. The collapses created deep, sheltered hollows where moisture and rich soil collected. Seeds blown in or dropped by birds sprouted, and today these hollows support patches of dry rainforest, with vines and tall trees that could never survive in the surrounding grassland. In other places the roofs held, leaving dark caves that stretch underground for hundreds of metres.
These caves are home to colonies of small insect-eating bats. At dusk, thousands of them pour out of the entrances to hunt. Snakes sometimes wait among the rocks and roots near the openings, snatching bats from the air as they fly past. Deeper inside the tubes, scientists have found tiny animals, including insects that spend their entire lives in darkness.
The Ewamian people, whose Country includes the area, have known these features for many thousands of years. The name Undara is often said to come from an Aboriginal word meaning "long way", a fitting description of the flow.
For many decades, the land above the tubes was part of a cattle property. Rather than keep visitors out completely, the family who had run cattle there helped set up a tourism business, working alongside park rangers, and today the caves can only be entered with a trained guide. Walkways and lighting have been placed carefully so that visitors do not trample the fragile cave floors or disturb the bat colonies. Some tubes are closed altogether, partly to protect wildlife and partly because carbon dioxide can collect in their deepest sections, making the air unsafe to breathe.
Standing in the cool shadow of a lava tube, with roots dangling from the ceiling, it is hard to picture the glowing river that once rushed through. Yet the smooth, curved walls still carry its marks: ridges where the lava level paused, and shiny glazes where the rock briefly melted. The volcano has been quiet for a very long time, but its handiwork is still there for anyone willing to take a closer look.

Option A: The volcano erupted about 190,000 years ago.
Option B: Seeds were blown in or dropped by birds.
Option C: Thousands of bats pour out of the caves at dusk.

The Lagoon at Bell's Bend
Uncle Ray had both kayaks off the trailer before Jonah had even taken out his earbuds.
"Hat," Ray called over his shoulder. "And leave the phone in the ute. There's no signal down there anyway."
Jonah slid the phone into his pocket instead. He had agreed to spend the holidays on his uncle's farm beside the Murray because his parents were both working, not because he cared about rivers. Last summer the lagoon behind the farm had been a cracked plate of grey mud, ringed by red gums with bare, pale branches. Ray had stood at its edge for a long time without saying a word, and Jonah, bored, had wandered back to the house.
This year would be different, Ray had promised on the phone. Water had been released from the dams upstream on purpose, as an environmental flow, and part of it had been steered down an old channel into the lagoon. Jonah had pictured a large puddle.
They carried the kayaks down through the paddock. Jonah heard the lagoon before he saw it: a thick, rising chorus of croaks and clicks, as if a thousand tiny motors were idling in the reeds.
"Frogs," said Ray, grinning. "Six kinds at least. They've been waiting in the mud for years for this."
Then the trees opened, and Jonah stopped walking. The water stretched away among the trunks, flat and brown and shining, holding a perfect copy of the sky. Along the grey bark of the red gums, clusters of soft new leaves had burst out, bright green, as though someone had stuck them on with glue. A flock of ibis lifted from the shallows and wheeled overhead, their long beaks curved like sickles.
"They're alive," Jonah said. "I thought those trees were dead."
"So did half the district," Ray replied. "Red gums are tough. They can hang on through a long dry, but they can't wait forever. Floods used to come through here every few years. Since the river's been dammed and its water shared out, the big floods hardly happen. This lagoon needs a drink, not a drowning, but it does need one."
They pushed off. Jonah's first strokes sent the kayak spinning in a slow circle, and Ray laughed so loudly that a pair of spoonbills took off in protest. By the time Jonah had worked out how to paddle in a straight line, they had reached a white post standing in the water, marked in centimetres. Ray read the level aloud and wrote it in a battered notebook.
"For the Landcare group," he explained. "They want to know how long the water stays. My grandfather used to swim here every summer, you know. He'd jump off that branch over there." He pointed his paddle at a thick limb hanging low over the water. "I used to think I'd never see it full again."
Jonah looked at the branch, then at his uncle's face, and suddenly understood the silence of the summer before.
Late in the afternoon, the light turned gold and the frog chorus grew louder. A heron stood motionless on a log, watching them pass as if it had been waiting all day for company. Jonah drifted, letting the kayak turn as it wished. He felt the phone in his pocket and thought about taking a photo. Instead, he left it where it was. Some things, he decided, were better kept in your head, where no one could swipe them away.
When they finally hauled the kayaks up the bank, he turned for one last look. The lagoon lay among the trees like an open hand, holding everything it had been given.
"Same time tomorrow?" he asked.
Ray only smiled.
Question: What did the lagoon look like the summer before?
Option A: a shallow pool full of reeds
Option B: a cracked plate of grey mud
Option C: a large puddle full of frogs
Option D: a muddy channel to the river

Yellow Stripes in the Moss
The tub on Tali's lap was no bigger than an ice-cream container, but she held it as if it contained the crown jewels. Inside, nestled in damp moss, were forty-two eggs, each a pale bead with a tiny dark shape curled inside.
"Don't grip it so hard," said her aunt Meg, steering the four-wheel drive around another pothole. "They're tougher than they look. It's the next three years that will be hard on them."
Tali had begged for this week of work experience at the frog facility where Meg worked. Her friends had chosen vet clinics and cafes. Tali had chosen a windowless room full of humming tanks, where she had spent four days rinsing containers, feeding tiny crickets to tiny frogs and writing numbers on a clipboard. She had loved it, though she found it hard to explain why.
The frogs themselves were the reason. Southern corroboree frogs are barely the length of a thumb, glossy black with stripes of electric yellow, as if someone had decorated them with a highlighter. They once lived in their thousands in the sphagnum bogs of the Snowy Mountains. Then a disease caused by the chytrid fungus spread through Australia's frogs, and the corroborees began to vanish. By the early 2000s, only a few dozen were thought to remain in the wild.
"Without the breeding program," Meg had told her on Monday, "you'd be writing about them in the past tense."
Now they parked at the end of a gravel track and walked uphill through snow gums. The air was thin and cold, even in February. Meg carried a backpack of equipment; Tali carried the tub, stepping carefully over roots. At last they reached the bog: a soggy, spongy carpet of moss and low shrubs, threaded with trickles of water. Somewhere nearby, water gurgled beneath the moss like a slow, hidden stream.
Meg knelt beside a shallow pool lined with fresh sphagnum. "Here. This is where the males would call from in summer, if there were enough of them. The female lays her eggs in a little nest in the moss. The tadpoles develop inside the eggs, then wait until autumn rain or melting snow floods the nest. That's when they hatch."
"They just wait?" Tali asked.
"They're patient. They have to be."
Tali thought of the three years Meg had mentioned, and wondered whether she could have waited that long for anything.
Tali eased the eggs into the moss, one cluster at a time, while Meg recorded the location on a GPS. Her fingers grew numb, but she barely noticed. When she had finished, she sat back on her heels and looked at the bog, which seemed far too large and wild for forty-two specks.
"How many will make it?" she asked.
Meg was quiet for a moment. "Honestly? Not many. The fungus is still out here. But every year we put more back, and every year a few more survive long enough to breed. Some of the frogs in these bogs now were eggs in a tub like yours."
They walked back down in the late afternoon. Behind them, a currawong called, a long ringing note that echoed across the valley. Tali kept looking over her shoulder, as though she could still see the pool, small and bright as a coin dropped in the grass.
On Friday, her last day, she wrote her work experience report. Under "What did you learn?" she paused for a long time. Then she wrote: Saving something takes longer than one week. She crossed it out and wrote: Saving something takes more than one person. Then she looked at both lines, left them there, and handed it in.
Question: Why had Tali chosen to do her work experience at the frog facility?
Option A: her friends had all chosen the same place
Option B: she was planning to become a vet one day
Option C: she was fascinated by the corroboree frogs
Option D: her aunt had insisted that she go there

Let Us Out in the Rain
A letter to the editor of the Kingfisher College newsletter
Every time the sky turns grey at our school, the same thing happens. Before a single drop has fallen, the bell rings three times, an announcement crackles over the speakers, and seven hundred students are sent to "wet weather areas". In practice, that means the library, the hall and a handful of classrooms, packed so tightly that you cannot hear yourself think. I am writing to argue that this rule should change. Unless there is lightning, strong wind or flooding, students should be allowed outside when it rains.
My first reason is simple: light rain is not dangerous. A shower will not hurt anyone. People in Melbourne, Hobart and much of the world walk to work, play sport and hang out washing in drizzle every day. We happily stand in the rain waiting for the bus at three o'clock. It makes little sense that the same rain becomes a hazard at lunchtime.
Second, staying indoors has real costs. On wet days, students spend almost seven hours sitting down with no chance to run, stretch or even talk loudly. Some of us struggle to concentrate at the best of times; without a break outdoors, it becomes almost impossible. Teachers often say that afternoon classes after a wet lunch are the hardest to manage, and it is easy to see why. Energy that would have been used on the oval ends up bouncing off the classroom walls. Health guidelines recommend that young people be active for at least an hour every day. A wet-weather routine that keeps us seated all day works against that advice.
Third, I believe we are missing out on something valuable. Some of my best memories from primary school are of splashing through puddles, watching water race along the gutters and noticing how the whole oval smelled different after a storm. Rain changes the world in interesting ways, but we only ever see it through a window. When our science class studied the water cycle last term, we watched a video of rain instead of walking twenty metres outside to look at the real thing. Learning about weather from a screen while real weather is happening just outside seems a strange way to teach.
Some people will argue that wet students mean wet carpets, muddy shoes and complaints from parents about soggy uniforms. These are fair points, but they can be solved. The school could set up a boot rack and towel station near the canteen. Students who want to go outside could bring a spare pair of socks or a raincoat. Those who prefer to stay dry would still have the library. Nobody is asking for everyone to be marched into a downpour; we are asking for a choice.
Others worry about slipping. Again, the answer is not to ban the outdoors but to manage it. The asphalt near the science block floods quickly and could be closed in heavy rain, while the covered walkways and grassed areas stay open. Teachers on duty would still supervise, just as they do on any sunny day.
At the last assembly, our principal told us that she grew up on a farm where "nobody stopped work just because of a bit of weather". I would simply ask the school to give us the same chance she had to learn that rain is part of life, not something to hide from.
We spend years at school learning to cope with uncomfortable things: tests, new classes, difficult conversations. Surely a little rain can be one of them. Let us out.
Mia Tran, Year 9
Question: Where are students sent on wet days at present?
Option A: the covered walkways and the canteen
Option B: the oval and the grassed areas
Option C: the science block and the gym
Option D: the library, the hall and some classrooms

The Winter Gathering at Point Lowly
Slip into the chilly water off Point Lowly, near Whyalla in South Australia, on a calm morning in June, and you may find yourself surrounded. Hovering over the rocky reef below are dozens of strange animals with rippling fins, eight arms, two long tentacles and large, watchful eyes. Their skin flickers with stripes and spots, changing from moment to moment like a screen. These are Australian giant cuttlefish, and every winter they gather here in their thousands to breed.
Giant cuttlefish are the largest cuttlefish in the world. Big males can grow to about half a metre in body length and weigh more than five kilograms. Despite their name, cuttlefish are not fish at all. They are molluscs, closely related to squid and octopuses, and they carry a light, chalky internal shell called a cuttlebone, which helps them control how they float. If you have ever found a white, oval cuttlebone washed up on a beach, it once belonged to one of these animals.
For most of the year, giant cuttlefish live alone, scattered along the southern coast of Australia. But between about May and August, huge numbers travel to a short stretch of rocky coast in upper Spencer Gulf. No other gathering of cuttlefish this large is known anywhere on Earth. Scientists believe the area is attractive because its rocky ledges provide safe places to attach eggs, and its water is especially salty and stable.
Once the cuttlefish arrive, the competition begins. Males greatly outnumber females, sometimes by several to one. To win a mate, a large male puts on a dazzling show, spreading his arms and sending waves of colour pulsing along his body. Rival males face each other in displays that can end in chases or brief wrestling matches. Remarkably, cuttlefish are thought to be colourblind, so their displays probably rely on contrast, pattern and the way light reflects, rather than on colour itself.
Smaller males have another trick. Unable to win a contest of strength, some of them hide their longer arms and change their skin to the mottled pattern of a female. In this disguise, they can slip past a large male guarding his partner and try to mate with her while he is not paying attention. Scientists call these imitators "sneaker" males, and they are often surprisingly successful.
After mating, a female lays her eggs one at a time, tucking each one into a crevice or under a ledge. The young hatch several months later as tiny copies of their parents. The adults never see them. Giant cuttlefish live for only one or two years, and most die soon after breeding.
In the early 2010s, the number of cuttlefish at Point Lowly fell sharply, from well over one hundred thousand in the late 1990s to only about thirteen thousand in 2013. Fishing for cuttlefish in the area was banned, and researchers began counting the animals each winter. Since then, numbers have recovered strongly, although scientists are still not certain what caused the decline.
Today, the gathering draws divers and snorkellers from around the world, along with local families who simply wade in from the shore. Visitors are asked not to touch the animals or disturb the eggs. Watching a giant cuttlefish shift from deep red to pale cream in a single breath, it is easy to see why so many people return year after year.

The Ghost Sign
The letters were still there if you knew where to look. High on the brick wall above the laundromat on Albert Street, beneath a century of soot and sunlight, a pale ghost of words could just be made out: MORRIS & SONS - FINE TEAS. Nell had walked past it every day for three years and never noticed it until her grandfather pointed it out.
"I painted that," he said. "Well, I touched it up. Nineteen sixty-eight. The original was older than me."
That was in March. By June, the owner of the laundromat had asked whether the old sign could be restored, and Grandad, who had retired from signwriting long before Nell was born, had said yes before anyone could suggest that a man of eighty-one should not be climbing scaffolding.
He did not climb it, in the end. Nell did.
The first weekend, she was not allowed to paint at all. She spent two days on a plank three storeys up, gently washing the bricks with a soft brush while Grandad called instructions from a folding chair on the footpath. The second weekend, he taped huge sheets of brown paper to the wall, and she traced every faded letter in pencil, including the curling tail of the ampersand. Back in his shed, he laid the paper flat and pricked tiny holes along every line with a spiked wheel.
"Why can't we just print a vinyl copy and stick it on?" Nell asked, rubbing her sore shoulders. "Mr Lam said a company could do it in a day."
Grandad set down the wheel. "Three reasons," he said, holding up a paint-stained finger. "One: a sticker sits on top of the wall. Paint soaks in and becomes part of the brick. Two: vinyl peels in this sun within ten years. Good enamel lasts fifty. Three," and here he smiled, "a machine can copy the letters, but it can't copy the hand that made them. Somebody stood up there in 1920 and decided exactly how fat to make that M. I'd like to keep his decision, not just his outline."
Nell did not have an answer to that.
On the third weekend, they returned to the wall. Nell held the pricked paper against the bricks while Grandad, now persuaded onto the lowest level of scaffolding, patted a cloth bag of chalk dust along the holes. When she peeled the paper away, the outline of every letter hung on the wall in dotted white lines, like a constellation waiting to be joined.
Then came the painting. Grandad showed her how to load the long, thin brush, how to rest her wrist on a padded stick so her hand would not shake, and how to pull each stroke in one smooth movement instead of dabbing. Her first E looked as though it had been written during an earthquake. Her tenth was nearly straight. By late afternoon her letters were steady, and she had stopped noticing how high up she was.
Grandad painted the M himself. He took nearly an hour over it, working in silence while the traffic hummed below. When he finished, he leaned back and studied it for a long time.
"He was left-handed," he said quietly. "The fellow who painted the first one. You can tell from the way the strokes finish. I never noticed that in sixty-eight."
Nell looked at the wall, then at her grandfather's hands, then at her own, blue with enamel to the wrist.
The sign was finished in August. People stopped on the footpath to take photographs, and Mr Lam put a small plaque by the door. Nell walks past it every day now, and she always looks up. Somewhere in the long tail of the ampersand is a stroke she painted herself, and in a hundred years, she hopes, someone will be able to tell.

Option A: a map of the streets far below the wall
Option B: stars that could be linked to form a picture
Option C: a long row of tiny lit-up windows
Option D: a trail of chalk dust falling to the ground

The Pharaoh Who Was Chiselled Away
When nineteenth-century scholars began reading the inscriptions on the temples of ancient Egypt, they came across a puzzle. Some walls showed a powerful king who had ruled for about twenty years, built magnificent monuments and sent ships to distant lands. Yet the king's name had often been hacked out of the stone, and the carvings sometimes used female word endings for a ruler who was dressed as a man. It took decades for historians to piece together the story of Hatshepsut, one of the most remarkable rulers of the ancient world.
Hatshepsut was born around 1500 BCE, the daughter of the pharaoh Thutmose I. Following royal custom, she married her half-brother, who became Thutmose II. When he died after a fairly short reign, the heir to the throne, his son Thutmose III by another wife, was still a small child. Hatshepsut was appointed to rule on his behalf as regent, a common arrangement when a king was too young.
What happened next was not common at all. Within about seven years, Hatshepsut had taken the full title of pharaoh. She did not push the boy aside entirely; he remained co-ruler. But it was Hatshepsut who held the power. In official statues and carvings, she appeared with the traditional symbols of kingship, including the royal headdress and even the long false beard that male pharaohs wore. To many modern readers this looks like a disguise. Historians now think it was more like a uniform. Egyptians expected a pharaoh to look a certain way, and Hatshepsut presented herself as the office required.
Her reign was largely peaceful and prosperous. She ordered building projects across Egypt, including a pair of towering obelisks at the temple of Karnak. Her greatest monument is her temple at Deir el-Bahari, near modern Luxor, which rises in three wide terraces against a wall of golden cliffs. Its walls record her proudest achievement: a trading expedition to a land the Egyptians called Punt, probably near the southern coast of the Red Sea. The carvings show ships returning loaded with ebony, gold, animal skins and living myrrh trees, their roots carefully packed in baskets so they could be replanted in Egypt.
Hatshepsut died around 1458 BCE, and Thutmose III went on to rule alone for about thirty years. Then, late in his reign, many of her images were destroyed. Her name was chiselled from monuments, her statues were smashed and dumped in a quarry, and she was left off later lists of kings. For a long time, historians assumed this was an act of revenge by a stepson who had resented her. However, the destruction seems to have begun some twenty years after her death, which hardly fits a burst of anger. Many experts now suggest a more practical reason: by removing evidence of a female king, Thutmose III may have been protecting his own son's claim to the throne and restoring what Egyptians saw as the proper order.
If the aim was to erase her, it did not succeed. Archaeologists later gathered the broken statues from the quarry and pieced them back together. In 2007, a mummy that had lain unidentified for about a century was linked to Hatshepsut, partly because a tooth found in a box bearing her name fitted a gap in its jaw.
Today, visitors to Deir el-Bahari can still see the scenes of Punt on the temple walls. The ruler who was meant to be forgotten has become one of the best known of all the pharaohs.

The Pharaoh Who Was Chiselled Away
When nineteenth-century scholars began reading the inscriptions on the temples of ancient Egypt, they came across a puzzle. Some walls showed a powerful king who had ruled for about twenty years, built magnificent monuments and sent ships to distant lands. Yet the king's name had often been hacked out of the stone, and the carvings sometimes used female word endings for a ruler who was dressed as a man. It took decades for historians to piece together the story of Hatshepsut, one of the most remarkable rulers of the ancient world.
Hatshepsut was born around 1500 BCE, the daughter of the pharaoh Thutmose I. Following royal custom, she married her half-brother, who became Thutmose II. When he died after a fairly short reign, the heir to the throne, his son Thutmose III by another wife, was still a small child. Hatshepsut was appointed to rule on his behalf as regent, a common arrangement when a king was too young.
What happened next was not common at all. Within about seven years, Hatshepsut had taken the full title of pharaoh. She did not push the boy aside entirely; he remained co-ruler. But it was Hatshepsut who held the power. In official statues and carvings, she appeared with the traditional symbols of kingship, including the royal headdress and even the long false beard that male pharaohs wore. To many modern readers this looks like a disguise. Historians now think it was more like a uniform. Egyptians expected a pharaoh to look a certain way, and Hatshepsut presented herself as the office required.
Her reign was largely peaceful and prosperous. She ordered building projects across Egypt, including a pair of towering obelisks at the temple of Karnak. Her greatest monument is her temple at Deir el-Bahari, near modern Luxor, which rises in three wide terraces against a wall of golden cliffs. Its walls record her proudest achievement: a trading expedition to a land the Egyptians called Punt, probably near the southern coast of the Red Sea. The carvings show ships returning loaded with ebony, gold, animal skins and living myrrh trees, their roots carefully packed in baskets so they could be replanted in Egypt.
Hatshepsut died around 1458 BCE, and Thutmose III went on to rule alone for about thirty years. Then, late in his reign, many of her images were destroyed. Her name was chiselled from monuments, her statues were smashed and dumped in a quarry, and she was left off later lists of kings. For a long time, historians assumed this was an act of revenge by a stepson who had resented her. However, the destruction seems to have begun some twenty years after her death, which hardly fits a burst of anger. Many experts now suggest a more practical reason: by removing evidence of a female king, Thutmose III may have been protecting his own son's claim to the throne and restoring what Egyptians saw as the proper order.
If the aim was to erase her, it did not succeed. Archaeologists later gathered the broken statues from the quarry and pieced them back together. In 2007, a mummy that had lain unidentified for about a century was linked to Hatshepsut, partly because a tooth found in a box bearing her name fitted a gap in its jaw.

Thirty-One Stamps
At the back of the book, on a slip gone yellow,
a column of dates runs down the page,
inked in purple, then blue, then black,
each one pressed by a hand I will never shake.

The first is 1979, faint as a whisper.
The last is 2009, crisp as a cracker.
Between them, thirty-one borrowers
carried this same story home.

I found it on the bottom shelf in the corner,
where the carpet is worn to its threads
and the light from the window arrives
already tired from crossing the room.

It is not a famous book.
Its cover shows a lighthouse and a girl
in a raincoat the colour of mustard,
and the title has rubbed off the spine.

Nobody has borrowed it for years.
The pages have the smell old books keep,
part dust, part rain, part kitchen cupboard,
like a house you visited once as a child.

But the old slip holds its ground.
I run my thumb down the column
and the dates rise up like stepping stones
across a river I cannot see the bottom of.

Who took it out in the winter of '83,
three times in a row, renewing and renewing,
as if they could not bear to let it go?
Who kept it four weeks overdue in '91
and paid the fine in coins, I imagine,
counted out slowly on the wooden desk?

Someone read it in a hospital bed, perhaps.
Someone read it on a bus and missed their stop.
Someone read it aloud to a sleepy child
who drifted off before the storm arrived.

Someone, I hope, took it camping
and read it by a fire with sparks going up,
and someone else, on a hot afternoon,
fell asleep with it open across their face.

There are crumbs in the spine,
a coffee ring on page ninety,
and a pencilled line under one sentence
that somebody, once, could not let pass:
"Nothing truly read is ever really lost."

I do not know whose pencil it was.
I do not know if they were twelve or seventy,
if they laughed or cried at the final chapter,
if they ever came back for another.

I like not knowing.
It means they could be anyone:
the man who sweeps the station platform,
the woman with the green umbrella at the bus stop,
my own teacher, before she was a teacher.

At the desk, the librarian tells me
nobody stamps books any more.
A red beam reads the barcode, a beep agrees,
and a receipt curls out of the machine
like a tongue that has nothing to say.
My name goes somewhere I will never see.

She turns the book over in her hands.
'I haven't seen this one go out in years,' she says,
and for a moment she holds it the way
you might hold a letter from an old friend.

I read it in three nights under the blanket,
the torch fading on the final page,
and when I closed it I understood
why someone had renewed it three times.

I wanted to tell somebody,
but the only ones who would understand
were thirty-one people with no names,
only dates, pressed in purple, blue and black.

So here we are, the thirty-one and me,
a queue that stretches over forty years,
each of us waiting our turn
at the same small door of paper.

When I bring it back on Monday,
I borrow the librarian's pencil
and, very small, beneath 2009,
write the date I took it home:
one more stone across the river
for whoever comes next to find.

Then I slide it back onto the bottom shelf,
into the corner where the tired light falls,
and leave it there to wait, as it has always waited,
patient as a lighthouse, for the next one.

At the back of the book, on a slip gone yellow,
a column of dates runs down the page,
inked in purple, then blue, then black,
each one pressed by a hand I will never shake.

The first is 1979, faint as a whisper.
The last is 2009, crisp as a cracker.
Between them, thirty-one borrowers
carried this same story home.

I found it on the bottom shelf in the corner,
where the carpet is worn to its threads
and the light from the window arrives
already tired from crossing the room.

It is not a famous book.
Its cover shows a lighthouse and a girl
in a raincoat the colour of mustard,
and the title has rubbed off the spine.

Nobody has borrowed it for years.
The pages have the smell old books keep,
part dust, part rain, part kitchen cupboard,
like a house you visited once as a child.

But the old slip holds its ground.
I run my thumb down the column
and the dates rise up like stepping stones
across a river I cannot see the bottom of.

Who took it out in the winter of '83,
three times in a row, renewing and renewing,
as if they could not bear to let it go?
Who kept it four weeks overdue in '91
and paid the fine in coins, I imagine,
counted out slowly on the wooden desk?

Someone read it in a hospital bed, perhaps.
Someone read it on a bus and missed their stop.
Someone read it aloud to a sleepy child
who drifted off before the storm arrived.

Someone, I hope, took it camping
and read it by a fire with sparks going up,
and someone else, on a hot afternoon,
fell asleep with it open across their face.

There are crumbs in the spine,
a coffee ring on page ninety,
and a pencilled line under one sentence
that somebody, once, could not let pass:
"Nothing truly read is ever really lost."

I do not know whose pencil it was.
I do not know if they were twelve or seventy,
if they laughed or cried at the final chapter,
if they ever came back for another.

I like not knowing.

the man who sweeps the station platform,
the woman with the green umbrella at the bus stop,
my own teacher, before she was a teacher.

At the desk, the librarian tells me
nobody stamps books any more.
A red beam reads the barcode, a beep agrees,
and a receipt curls out of the machine
like a tongue that has nothing to say.
My name goes somewhere I will never see.

and for a moment she holds it the way
you might hold a letter from an old friend.

the torch fading on the final page,
and when I closed it I understood
why someone had renewed it three times.

but the only ones who would understand
were thirty-one people with no names,
only dates, pressed in purple, blue and black.

a queue that stretches over forty years,
each of us waiting our turn
at the same small door of paper.

one more stone across the river
for whoever comes next to find.

into the corner where the tired light falls,
and leave it there to wait, as it has always waited,

Monday
We arrived at the station after nine hours in the car, and the first thing I noticed was how flat it is. Dry grass, a few gidgee trees and a sky so big it almost hurts to look at. It is hard to believe that this paddock was once the bottom of a sea. Dr Hollis, who runs the dig, says that about a hundred million years ago a shallow inland sea covered much of Queensland. Giant marine reptiles swam where the cattle now graze. When they died, some sank into the soft mud on the seabed, and over millions of years the mud turned to rock.
There are eleven volunteers, and I am the youngest by about twenty years. A retired dentist called Pat showed me how to use a geologist's pick. I think she felt sorry for me.
Tuesday
Nothing. Eight hours of nothing. We walked slowly in lines across the paddock, heads down, looking for pieces of bone weathering out of the ground. Every pale stone looked like a fossil to me until I picked it up. Dr Hollis says this is normal, and that most days on a dig are like this. "Patience is the main tool," she said. I was not in the mood for wise sayings. My neck is sunburnt in a perfect stripe above my collar.
Wednesday
Pat found a shark tooth before morning tea, and then I found something too! It was a grey lump about the size of a loaf of bread, sticking out of a gully bank, with a curved, honeycombed edge showing on one side. Dr Hollis said the edge was probably part of a vertebra, a piece of backbone, and possibly from an ichthyosaur. Ichthyosaurs looked a bit like dolphins, though they were reptiles, not mammals. She photographed it, recorded its exact position with GPS and drew a quick sketch in her notebook before anyone was allowed to touch it.
"A bone without its location is just a souvenir," she said. "With its location, it's evidence."
Thursday
We spent the whole day digging around my lump with small tools and brushes. It turned out to be a hard ball of limestone called a concretion. These form around a bone or shell as minerals collect, and they protect the fossil, but they also make it very hard to see. In the afternoon, Dr Hollis wrapped the concretion in a jacket of hessian and plaster, like a cast for a broken arm, so it could be lifted without cracking. It took four of us to carry it to the ute.
Friday
Today we visited the laboratory in town where the fossils are prepared. A technician showed us a concretion sitting in a tub of weak acid. The acid slowly dissolves the limestone but not the bone, so the fossil appears little by little over weeks or months. Afterwards, each exposed bone is hardened with special glue. She said a large skeleton can take years to finish. I asked how long my vertebra would take, and she laughed and said it would be on the waiting list behind about forty other jackets.
Saturday
Our last morning. I walked out to the gully one more time on my own. The paddock looked exactly the same as it did on Monday: flat, dry, enormous. But I could not see it the same way. Now, when I look at it, I imagine the water above me, green and deep, and something long and sleek passing overhead.
Pat gave me her spare pick as a goodbye present. Dr Hollis said there would be a place for me next season if I wanted it. I said yes before she had finished the sentence.

Option A: a young volunteer's week on a fossil dig in outback Queensland
Option B: how ichthyosaurs lived and hunted in the ancient inland sea
Option C: a retired dentist who learns to become a fossil expert
Option D: the history of a cattle station in outback Queensland

The Iron That Fell
On Saturdays, beyond the dinosaur hall,
where school groups thin and footsteps start to fade,
a table used to stand against the wall
beneath a sign: PLEASE TOUCH. DON'T BE AFRAID.

An old man sat behind it on a chair,
his knuckles thick as knots in mallee wood,
his cardigan done up on the wrong buttons,
his voice like gravel, rolling, low and good.

I'd come with Mum, who left me for an hour
while she researched old maps up on the stairs.
I'd seen the dinosaurs a dozen times,
and drifted, bored, towards the old man's chairs.

Around us every glass case hummed and gleamed.
Each spearhead, shell and fossil had its name
typed neatly on a card, so that it seemed
the whole of history was locked and tame.

No one could touch. A guard walked by each hour.
The air smelled faintly of floor wax and dust.
You looked, you read the card, you shuffled on,
the way a quiet museum says you must.

But on his cloth there sat a lump of dark,
no bigger than a pear and twice as rough,
pitted like toast left burning in the pan,
as plain as any rock, and plain enough.

"Go on," he said, the first time that I came.
"It's older than the Earth. It doesn't bite."
I laughed, because I thought it was a game,
then felt it drag my wrist down with its weight.

It was cold the way a winter tap is cold,
and heavier than anything that small
had any right to be. "It's iron," I was told,
"and nickel. Came from space. Survived the fall."

He showed me where its skin had turned to glass,
the crust it grew while blazing through the air,
and how a farmer, walking through his wheat,
had kicked it, cursed, then knelt and found it there.

He kept it on his mantelpiece for years
to prop the door, or crack a walnut shell,
until a visiting teacher saw it, gasped,
and wrote to the museum. Just as well.

"I mined for iron forty years," he said,
"so far down you'd forget there was a sun.
I never once looked up, or asked myself
where all that metal came from. Not once. None.

"Then my grandson read me something from a book:
the iron in my blood was made in stars.
I caught the train here the next Saturday,
and held this rock, and felt how near they are."

He set the meteorite back in my palm.
"So that's my job," he said. "That's why I sit.
I hand the sky to anyone who'll hold it,
and watch them when they feel the weight of it."

I came back every Saturday that year,
and every year until I'd nearly grown.
He taught me how to read the crust and pits,
and how to tell a meteorite from stone.

I'd stand beside him, watching people's faces:
the toddler's frown, the teenager's surprise,
the grandmother who cried a little, laughing,
the man who held it up against the skies.

He let me mind the table while he rested,
then let me run it while he watched the clock,
then one day, when his knees had had enough,
he gave me his old lanyard and the rock.

He moved up north to live beside his daughter
and sends me postcards: beaches, boats and sun.
Below his name, in shaky capitals,
the same three words: KEEP LOOKING UP. Each one.

Last week a girl came by, perhaps eight years old.
"Go on," I said. "It's older than the Earth."
She laughed, as if I'd made the whole thing up,
then gasped, and held it tight for all her worth.

where school groups thin and footsteps start to fade,
I keep a table there against the wall
beneath his sign: PLEASE TOUCH. DON'T BE AFRAID.

Somewhere in your laundry there may be a machine that eats electricity like few others in the house. It roars, it tumbles, it heats up the whole room, and at the end of an hour it hands you a load of warm, slightly shrunken clothes crackling with static. Meanwhile, out in the backyard, a perfectly good clothesline stands empty, its wires glinting in the sunshine. It is time we gave it its job back.
The electric clothes dryer is one of the hungriest appliances a household can own. Unlike a fridge, which sips power steadily, a dryer gulps it, because turning the water in wet fabric into vapour takes an enormous amount of heat. A typical older-style dryer can use several kilowatt-hours to dry a single load, which is roughly as much electricity as a modern fridge uses in a couple of days. Families who run one every day may find it quietly adding hundreds of dollars a year to their power bills.
The clothesline, by contrast, runs on two things Australia has in abundance: sunshine and wind. Neither sends a bill. Neither breaks down. In most parts of the country, for most of the year, a load of washing hung out in the morning will be dry by lunchtime. Even on a cool, overcast winter's day, a steady breeze can do most of the work.
The benefits go beyond money. Sunlight has a mild bleaching effect that helps fade stains and keeps white shirts white. Clothes dried on a line also tend to last longer. That fluffy grey lint you scrape from a dryer's filter is not dirt from nowhere; it is made of fibres torn from your clothes, a little more of your favourite T-shirt lost with every cycle. The heat of a dryer can also shrink woollen jumpers and loosen elastic.
Then there is the question of where our electricity comes from. Although solar and wind farms are growing quickly, a large share of Australia's power is still generated by burning coal and gas. Every load that dries in the sun instead of in a machine means a little less fuel needs to be burnt.
Critics say the clothesline belongs to the past. They call it old-fashioned, slow and inconvenient. Yet Australians once took great pride in it. The famous rotary Hills Hoist, invented in an Adelaide backyard in 1945, became a symbol of suburban life, spinning above lawns from Perth to Brisbane. Rejecting something simply because our grandparents used it is not progress. Sometimes the old way was the clever way all along.
Others raise practical problems, and some of them are fair. Not everyone has a backyard, and some apartment buildings ban washing on balconies. Rain does not respect laundry schedules. For these situations, a folding clothes horse beside a sunny window or under a covered verandah works remarkably well. Where a dryer truly is needed, a heat-pump model uses far less energy than the older vented kind. The aim is not to ban dryers but to stop using them out of habit on days when the sun is shining for free.
Hanging out a load of washing takes perhaps ten minutes. That is ten minutes outside in the fresh air, with a peg basket and your own thoughts. It is hardly a great sacrifice.
So next time you reach for the dryer's dial on a bright, breezy morning, stop. Pick up the basket instead. The sun has been waiting all day to help.

She waited until the music swelled at the end of a phrase, then slid a finger beneath the extra leaf and eased it back onto the correct page without a sound. She sat down. Ferreira's glance went to the score and stayed there, and the next turn came exactly where she had pencilled it.
