The Lost Property Cupboard
The lost property cupboard at Ridgeview High smelled of old oranges and damp socks. Theo Marsh had been sentenced to it for three weeks.
"Seven late arrivals in one term," Ms Brandt had said, sliding a clipboard across her desk. "You can spend your Wednesday lunchtimes doing something useful. Sort it, label it, and anything unclaimed by Friday week goes to the op shop."
So on Wednesday Theo dragged open the sliding door and stared. There were drink bottles furred with mould, a single football boot, eleven hats, a calculator with its battery cover missing and a tangle of blazers that seemed to have bred in the dark. He began making piles and writing a list, mostly so that he would look busy if anyone walked past.
At the bottom of the heap, under a crushed lunchbox, was a jumper. It was not a school jumper. It was hand-knitted, deep maroon, with cables twisting down the front and sleeves of slightly different lengths, as though whoever had made it had run short of wool and patience at about the same time. Inside the collar, sewn with careful, wobbly stitches, was a fabric label: R. OKAFOR.
Theo checked the student list in the office. There was one Okafor in the school: Rafael, Year 7.
He found Rafael the next day near the canteen, standing with three other boys. Theo held up the jumper. "This yours? It's got your name in it."
The other boys looked at the jumper, then at each other. One of them snorted. Rafael's ears went red. His eyes dropped for a moment to the bag at his feet, and then he shook his head.
"Nah," he said. "Never seen it."
"It says Okafor."
"Must be someone else's." He turned back to his friends, and after a moment of silence they all began talking loudly about a video game.
Theo walked away with the jumper over his arm, feeling oddly heavy. He thought about the label. Nobody bought a jumper with a name stitched in by hand like that. Somebody had sat with it for weeks, probably in the evenings, counting stitches and unpicking rows when they went wrong. He thought about his own grandmother, who had sent him a scarf every winter until her hands grew too stiff to knit, and about how he had stopped wearing the scarves at twelve because a boy on the bus had laughed at them.
Friday week arrived. The op shop box sat by the door, half full. Theo held the maroon jumper for a long time, then put it in his own bag instead.
After the last bell, he waited near the Year 7 lockers until the corridor had emptied. Rafael came round the corner alone, saw him, and stopped.
Theo held out the jumper. "Nobody's watching," he said. "It was going to the op shop today. Seemed a waste, after somebody went to all that trouble."
For a second Rafael didn't move. Then he took it, folded it quickly and pushed it deep into his bag. "My grandma made it," he said quietly. "She lives with us. She keeps asking where it is."
"Tell her it was in lost property," said Theo. "Tell her it's warm."
The following Wednesday was cold and grey, the first real day of winter. Theo was on his way to the cupboard when he passed a group of Year 7s in the quad. Rafael was among them, laughing at something, his blazer buttoned up to the neck. Only at his wrists, where his sleeves had ridden up, could Theo see a narrow band of maroon wool.

The lost property cupboard at Ridgeview High smelled of old oranges and damp socks. Theo Marsh had been sentenced to it for three weeks.
"Seven late arrivals in one term," Ms Brandt had said, sliding a clipboard across her desk. "You can spend your Wednesday lunchtimes doing something useful. Sort it, label it, and anything unclaimed by Friday week goes to the op shop."
So on Wednesday Theo dragged open the sliding door and stared. There were drink bottles furred with mould, a single football boot, eleven hats, a calculator with its battery cover missing and a tangle of blazers that seemed to have bred in the dark. He began making piles and writing a list, mostly so that he would look busy if anyone walked past.
At the bottom of the heap, under a crushed lunchbox, was a jumper. It was not a school jumper. It was hand-knitted, deep maroon, with cables twisting down the front and sleeves of slightly different lengths, as though whoever had made it had run short of wool and patience at about the same time. Inside the collar, sewn with careful, wobbly stitches, was a fabric label: R. OKAFOR.
Theo checked the student list in the office. There was one Okafor in the school: Rafael, Year 7.
He found Rafael the next day near the canteen, standing with three other boys. Theo held up the jumper. "This yours? It's got your name in it."
The other boys looked at the jumper, then at each other. One of them snorted. Rafael's ears went red. His eyes dropped for a moment to the bag at his feet, and then he shook his head.
"Nah," he said. "Never seen it."
"It says Okafor."
"Must be someone else's." He turned back to his friends, and after a moment of silence they all began talking loudly about a video game.
Theo walked away with the jumper over his arm, feeling oddly heavy. He thought about the label. Nobody bought a jumper with a name stitched in by hand like that. Somebody had sat with it for weeks, probably in the evenings, counting stitches and unpicking rows when they went wrong. He thought about his own grandmother, who had sent him a scarf every winter until her hands grew too stiff to knit, and about how he had stopped wearing the scarves at twelve because a boy on the bus had laughed at them.
Friday week arrived. The op shop box sat by the door, half full. Theo held the maroon jumper for a long time, then put it in his own bag instead.
After the last bell, he waited near the Year 7 lockers until the corridor had emptied. Rafael came round the corner alone, saw him, and stopped.
Theo held out the jumper. "Nobody's watching," he said. "It was going to the op shop today. Seemed a waste, after somebody went to all that trouble."
For a second Rafael didn't move. Then he took it, folded it quickly and pushed it deep into his bag. "My grandma made it," he said quietly. "She lives with us. She keeps asking where it is."
"Tell her it was in lost property," said Theo. "Tell her it's warm."
The following Wednesday was cold and grey, the first real day of winter. Theo was on his way to the cupboard when he passed a group of Year 7s in the quad. Rafael was among them, laughing at something, his blazer buttoned up to the neck. Only at his wrists, where his sleeves had ridden up, could Theo see a narrow band of maroon wool.
Question: According to Ms Brandt, what would happen to unclaimed items?
Option A: They would go to the op shop.
Option B: They would be thrown in the bin.
Option C: They would be given to Year 7s.
Option D: They would stay in the cupboard.

Still as Bark
Grandad used to be the one who spotted things. On every holiday at the cabin near Mossman, he would stop dead on the track, raise one finger and point at a patch of forest that looked to Ana exactly like every other patch of forest. Then, slowly, something would separate itself from the green: a musky rat-kangaroo nosing through the leaf litter, a tree frog folded on a leaf, a cassowary's blue neck sliding between the palms.
"You have to let your eyes go soft," he would say. "Stop looking for an animal. Look for something that doesn't belong."
This year he walked behind her. The eye doctor had a long word for what was happening to his sight, but Grandad called it "the smudge". The middle of everything he looked at had gone blurry, as if someone had smeared a thumb across a photograph. He could still see the edges of things. He just couldn't see what was right in front of him.
"Your turn to be the eyes," he said on the first morning, handing her his old binoculars. The strap was cracked and smelled of insect repellent. "I want a Boyd's forest dragon before we go home. Thirty years I've been coming here and I've never found one. Not once."
Ana had read about them in his battered field guide. Boyd's forest dragons lived in the rainforests of far north Queensland, clinging to tree trunks at about head height. They had a spiky crest running down the neck and pale, enlarged scales on their cheeks, and their survival depended on keeping perfectly still. When a person came too close, a dragon would simply edge around to the far side of the trunk and wait.
For three days they walked the creek track. Ana looked until her eyes ached. She saw a hundred lumps of bark that might have been lizards and a hundred lizards that turned out to be lumps of bark. Grandad never complained. He walked behind her with one hand resting lightly on her backpack, and when she stopped, he stopped.
"Don't beat yourself up," he said on the third afternoon, when she kicked a stone into the creek. "If it were easy, I'd have one by now."
On the last morning it rained, a fine silver drizzle that dripped from the fern fronds and made the whole forest smell of wet soil. They almost didn't go. But Grandad pulled on his hat and said that rain was good luck for dragons, although Ana suspected he had invented that rule on the spot.
They had been walking for twenty minutes when she remembered what he used to tell her. Stop looking for an animal. She let her eyes go soft, the way he had taught her, and let the trunks blur into one long wall of brown and green.
Then something didn't belong. It was a line, too sharp and regular to be bark, running down the side of a trunk just above her shoulder. The line became a crest. The crest became a neck. A single dark eye regarded her without the slightest interest.
Ana didn't breathe. She reached back, found Grandad's sleeve and guided him forward, step by step, until he stood beside her.
"Where?" he whispered.
"Straight ahead. A hand's width above my head." She lifted his hand and pointed his finger at the spot. "You won't see it in the middle. Look just to the side of it."
Grandad turned his head a little, the way a person does when they are listening rather than looking. For a long moment nothing happened. Then his breath went out of him in a soft rush.
"There you are," he said. "There you are, you beauty."
They stood in the rain until the dragon, with great dignity, edged around to the other side of the tree.
Question: What is the story mainly about?
Option A: a girl helping her grandfather see a lizard he has long hoped to find
Option B: a family holiday spoiled by three days of heavy rain
Option C: a grandfather teaching his granddaughter to use binoculars
Option D: a girl reading a field guide about Queensland rainforests

Bay Fourteen
The new timetable had started on Monday, and by Wednesday afternoon the Halden Street interchange was still full of people staring up at the screens as though they had been personally betrayed.
Priya had worked it out on the first day. Her bus, the 412, no longer left from Bay 3 beside the coffee kiosk. It had been moved to Bay 9, at the far end of the concourse, and it now departed at 3:52 instead of 4:05. If she came off the train, took the escalator two steps at a time and didn't stop for anything, she could make it with a minute to spare. If she missed it, the next one wasn't until 4:30.
At 3:47 she was halfway along the concourse, weaving through the after-school crowd, when she saw the old man.
He was standing beneath the departure board in a tweed jacket buttoned to the top, holding a folded sheet of paper close to his face. People flowed around him the way water flows around a rock. A man with a briefcase clipped his shoulder and didn't look back. The old man swayed, steadied himself and went back to studying the paper. Even from a distance, Priya could see it was a printed timetable, the kind nobody used any more. The kind that had become useless on Monday.
She slowed. She looked at the clock. 3:48.
Somebody else will help him, she thought. Then she watched four more people walk past, and nobody did.
"Excuse me," she said. "Are you looking for a bus?"
He turned, and she saw relief and embarrassment arrive in his face at the same moment. "The 207," he said. "To Fairmont. It goes from Bay 6. It always goes from Bay 6. But Bay 6 says it goes to the airport now." He held out the paper as if to prove it. "My daughter printed this for me. Last month."
"They changed everything on Monday," Priya said. She pulled out her phone, opened the transport app and scrolled. "The 207 goes from Bay 14 now. Next one's at 4:10."
"Fourteen," he repeated. "Where is fourteen?"
Over his shoulder, through the glass doors at the end of the concourse, Priya watched the 412 pull into Bay 9. She watched the doors open and the queue shuffle aboard.
"I'll show you," she said.
Bay 14 was down a ramp and around a corner, past a construction fence covered in posters announcing the improvements. The old man walked slowly, one hand on the rail. On the way he told her his name was Mr Vukovic and that he was going to his grandson's eighth birthday.
"I drove trams in this city for thirty-one years," he said as they reached the shelter. "The 19, the 6, the old 11 before they pulled up the line. I knew every stop. People used to ask me for directions." He gave a short laugh and looked down at his sheet of paper. "Now I need a schoolgirl and a telephone."
"Everyone needs a telephone this week," said Priya. "Even the drivers. I heard one asking for directions yesterday."
That made him laugh properly.
The 207 arrived at 4:10 exactly. Mr Vukovic climbed aboard, then turned on the top step and pressed something into her hand. It was the old timetable, folded into a small square.
"A souvenir," he said. "Of the way things were."
Priya caught the 4:30. She was forty minutes late home, and her mother wanted to know why. Priya considered several explanations and settled on the simplest.
"Someone needed directions," she said.
Later, unpacking her bag, she found the folded timetable and smoothed it out on her desk. On the back, in neat blue biro, someone had written: Bay 6. Stay on until the big church. Ring Lena when you get there. She looked at it for a long time before she pinned it to her noticeboard.
Question: From which bay does the 207 leave under the new timetable?
Option A: Bay 3
Option B: Bay 6
Option C: Bay 9
Option D: Bay 14

Taking Turns at the Front
From the grandstand, a team pursuit can look almost peaceful. Four riders in matching skinsuits circle the steeply banked velodrome in a tight line, their wheels only centimetres apart, their bodies bent so low that their backs are nearly flat. They move like the carriages of a single train. Yet each rider is working at the very edge of what a human body can do, and the smallest mistake by any one of them can cost the whole team the race.
The rules are simple. Two teams of four start on opposite sides of a 250-metre track and race over 4 kilometres, or 16 laps. The clock does not stop when the first rider crosses the finish. Instead, a team's time is taken when the front wheel of its third rider crosses the line. In other words, a team is only as fast as its third rider at the end, and this rule shapes nearly every decision the riders make.
The reason the riders cluster so tightly is air. At racing speed, most of a cyclist's effort goes into pushing air out of the way, and the rider at the front of the line does this hardest work. The riders behind sit in the pocket of calmer air, or draft, created by the rider ahead, and research suggests they may use around a quarter to a third less energy than the leader at the same speed. No single rider could hold the front for 4 kilometres at that pace, so the team shares the burden.
This sharing happens through a manoeuvre called a change. After a turn at the front, usually lasting a lap or half a lap, the leading rider swings up the banking, lets the line pass beneath, and drops back down to rejoin at the rear, where the draft offers a chance to recover. The new leader must hold the pace exactly, neither surging nor fading. A change done well takes only a moment; done badly, it opens gaps that waste precious energy as riders chase to close them. Teams practise changes for hundreds of hours, because at such speeds even a brief touch of wheels can bring the whole line down.
Because only three riders need to finish together, teams plan carefully how the effort is shared. Some riders are especially powerful starters and are given the job of hauling the team from a standstill up to full speed. Some teams arrange for one rider to take a very long, punishing turn at the front late in the race and then peel away, leaving the other three to finish on fresher legs. That rider will not cross the line with the team, yet may have done more than anyone to win the race.
The results of this cooperation are remarkable. The fastest men's teams now cover the distance in well under four minutes, averaging more than 60 kilometres per hour, and the leading women's teams are not far behind. A lone rider could not hold such speeds over the same distance.
For this reason, coaches often describe the team pursuit as less a race between cyclists than a race between systems. Raw strength matters, but it is worthless without trust. Each rider must believe that the person in front will hold a steady line and that the person behind will be there when the change comes. In my view, that is what makes the event so compelling to watch: it rewards not the strongest individual but the group that has learned to share the load most generously.

Option A: shows which single rider is the strongest
Option B: is the fastest race held in a velodrome
Option C: rewards the group that shares the work best
Option D: lets the fourth rider finish ahead of the team

The Kingfisher Shot
The competition rules were pinned above Jas's desk, and by the second week of the school holidays she knew them by heart. Open to photographers aged twelve to seventeen. One image per entry. Entries close Friday 5 pm. And then, at the bottom, in smaller print she had barely noticed: The welfare of the subject must always come before the photograph.
She had found the kingfishers on her first day at her uncle's farm. A pair of sacred kingfishers had dug a nest into a termite mound high on the trunk of a dead red gum beside the creek. One bird would perch on a fence post nearby, its back flashing turquoise in the sun, its chest the colour of weak tea, while the other disappeared into the dark hole in the mound. Jas could hear the chicks inside, a thin, impatient wheezing that grew louder whenever a parent came near.
On the first morning she photographed them from the far side of the creek, lying on her stomach in the dry grass with her uncle's long lens. The pictures were sharp enough, but the birds were small in the frame, two bright commas against a wide grey trunk.
"Get closer," said her cousin Liam, scrolling through them. "Winners always fill the frame."
So the next day she crossed the creek and set up behind a fallen log, twenty metres from the tree. The day after that she moved to fifteen. The parents still came and went, though Jas noticed that they now landed on the fence post first and sat there for a while before flying to the nest, bobbing their heads and calling a sharp, repeated kek-kek-kek.
On Thursday she crept to ten metres. She had just rested the camera on the log when one of the parents landed on a branch right in front of her, a skink dangling from its beak. It was so close she could see every scale on the little lizard's tail. The kingfisher raised the feathers on its head, opened its beak wide and screeched at her. The shutter clattered. Jas held her breath.
The bird did not fly to the nest. It flew to the fence post, then to a tree further along the creek, then back to the post, the skink still in its beak. Inside the mound, the wheezing grew more frantic. One minute passed, then five, then fifteen. The bird sat on the post and called and called.
Jas looked down at the screen. The photograph was extraordinary: the raised crest, the open beak, the skink caught perfectly in focus, a gleam of light in the bird's dark eye. It was the kind of picture that won competitions.
She looked up at the bird on the post, still holding the food it had caught for its chicks. Very slowly, keeping low, she packed up the camera and backed away through the grass until she was on the far side of the creek again. Almost at once the kingfisher left the post, flew straight to the mound and vanished inside. The wheezing stopped.
That night she sat at her desk for a long time, the two pictures side by side on her laptop. The close one glowed. The distant one showed a small bird on a fence post, feathers sleek and smooth, gazing calmly out over the water.
At 4:52 on Friday afternoon, Liam leaned over her shoulder as she pressed submit.
"That's the boring one," he said. "Why would you send the boring one?"
Jas glanced up at the sheet pinned above the desk, at the line in small print near the bottom.
"Because in that one," she said, "he wasn't scared of me."
Question: Where had the kingfishers made their nest?
Option A: in a hollow inside a fallen log
Option B: in a termite mound on a dead red gum
Option C: in a burrow dug into the creek bank
Option D: on top of a fence post near the creek

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
One Trunk, Forty Fruits
In early spring, in a handful of gardens, museum grounds and university campuses across the United States, a very strange tree comes into flower. Its blossoms are not one colour but many: pale white on one branch, soft pink on the next, deep crimson further up. A few months later, the same tree bears peaches, plums, apricots, nectarines and cherries. It is known as the Tree of 40 Fruit, and it is the work of an artist named Sam Van Aken.
The tree is not a genetic experiment or a trick of photography. It is the result of grafting, a technique gardeners have used for thousands of years. In grafting, a small piece of one plant, such as a bud or a short length of stem, is cut and fitted into a slit on another plant. If the thin layer of growing tissue just under the bark lines up on both pieces, the two grow together and share water and nutrients. The new branch keeps its own identity: a plum bud grafted onto a peach tree will grow into a branch that produces plums.
Grafting only works between closely related plants. Every fruit on Van Aken's trees belongs to one plant group, the genus Prunus, which includes all the common stone fruits as well as almonds. An apple or a lemon could not be added, however skilled the gardener.
Van Aken grew up on a family farm in Pennsylvania, where he learned to graft as a boy. He later became an artist and a university professor, but the idea of a tree covered in many kinds of blossom stayed with him. In 2008 he heard that an experimental orchard in New York State was going to be removed because of funding cuts. The orchard held hundreds of varieties of stone fruit, including old and rare types, some more than a century old, that were no longer grown commercially. Many of them existed almost nowhere else.
This mattered because most fruit varieties cannot be saved simply by planting seeds. A seed from a delicious old plum will usually grow into a tree with quite different fruit, so the only reliable way to keep a variety alive is to take cuttings and graft them. Van Aken took over the orchard and began collecting from it. His trees became a way of keeping these varieties alive while also creating something beautiful.
Building one tree takes years of patience. Van Aken starts with a young tree and grafts new varieties onto it in stages, carefully planning which branch will hold which fruit so that the tree stays balanced and its flowering looks pleasing. Each spring he checks which grafts have taken and which have failed, and replaces the failures. It may be many years before a single tree carries its full collection.
Today his trees grow in public places, where people can wander underneath and look up at a century or more of fruit history growing side by side. Van Aken has said he hopes they will make people curious about where their food comes from and how much variety has been lost. A supermarket might offer three or four kinds of plum. A single one of his trees can hold dozens of varieties.
At a time when much of our food comes from a small number of varieties grown in enormous quantities, there is something quietly hopeful about a tree that insists on diversity. It is a sculpture, a living library and an orchard all at once, and it is still growing.

Option A: the history of growing stone fruit on farms in Pennsylvania
Option B: a grafted tree that is both an artwork and a way of saving rare fruit
Option C: a genetic experiment that created a new kind of fruit tree
Option D: the best way to plant fruit trees from seeds in a garden

The Case for the Grey Muzzle
Walk into any animal shelter and you will notice where the crowds gather. Families cluster around the puppy pens, laughing at the tumbling, chewing, yapping balls of fluff, and most of those puppies will be in new homes within days. Further along, in the quieter runs, older dogs lie with their chins on their paws and watch the visitors walk past. Some of them will wait for months. Some will still be waiting at Christmas. If you are thinking about bringing a dog into your family, I want to persuade you to walk to the end of that row.
I did not always think this way. When our family went to the shelter four years ago, my younger brother and I had our hearts set on a puppy. We wanted to choose its name, teach it tricks and watch it grow up with us. Then a volunteer asked whether we would meet just one more dog. His name was Major, he was nine years old, and his owner had moved into an aged-care home that did not allow pets. He walked over, leaned his whole weight against my leg and sighed. We took him home that afternoon.
The first argument for an older dog is that what you see is what you get. A puppy is a mystery. No one can tell you exactly how big it will grow, how much energy it will have or what kind of temperament it will develop. A senior dog's personality is already formed. Shelter staff can tell you honestly whether it likes children, gets along with cats or panics during thunderstorms. You are choosing a companion you already know, not gambling on one you don't.
The second argument is that older dogs are usually far easier to live with. Most are already house-trained. Many know basic commands such as sit and stay. They have long since grown out of chewing shoes, digging up gardens and howling all night. Major arrived knowing how to walk politely on a lead, and on his first night he curled up on his bed and slept until morning. Our neighbours, who had just bought a puppy, were not so lucky.
Then there is the matter of energy. Puppies need a great deal of exercise, training and supervision, often far more than busy families expect. Many older dogs are content with a gentle walk or two each day and a long afternoon nap. Major's idea of a perfect Sunday was a slow stroll to the corner shop followed by a sunny patch of carpet. For households with full-time jobs, small apartments or elderly members, that calmer pace can be a perfect match.
Critics point out, fairly, that senior dogs may have health problems and that families will have less time with them. Both things can be true. An older dog may need a special diet, regular check-ups or medicine for stiff joints, and some shelters help by reducing adoption fees for senior animals. As for time, Major was with us for three and a half years. They were not fewer years than we deserved; they were the best years he could have had.
Adopting an older dog is not an act of charity. It is a practical, sensible choice that suits many families better than a puppy ever could, and it gives a dog that has done nothing wrong a comfortable place to spend the rest of its life.
So when you visit the shelter, by all means say hello to the puppies. Then keep walking. Somewhere near the end of the row, a grey-muzzled dog is waiting to lean against your leg.
Question: How old was Major when the family first met him?
Option A: nine years old
Option B: four years old
Option C: three and a half years old
Option D: a few months old

The sign went up on a Saturday morning: a square of cardboard taped inside the rear window, the words FOR SALE written in Dad's careful capitals, with a phone number underneath. Tess saw it from her bedroom and pulled the curtain closed again, as though that might undo it.
The car was a green 1998 station wagon that Kip, her little brother, had named the Gherkin when he was four. It had a dent in the back door from a shopping trolley, a radio that found only two stations, and a smell, deep in the seats, of sunscreen and old oranges. It had carried the family to every holiday Tess could remember.
"We need something that starts on cold mornings," Dad said at breakfast, not looking at her. "And something with airbags that actually work."
"It starts," said Tess.
"On the third go," said Mum. "If you talk to it nicely."
Tess pushed her cereal around the bowl. She knew the arguments. She had heard them for months, in low voices after she had gone to bed. Knowing them did not make them easier to agree with.
That afternoon, while Dad was out buying a new battery so the car would behave for the buyers, Tess climbed into the passenger seat and opened the glovebox. Under the tyre gauge and a fan of old parking tickets was the logbook: a fat exercise book, its cover soft as cloth, in which every member of the family had written something on every trip. Dates, distances, who got carsick, what they saw.
She was still reading when Dad came back. He slid into the driver's seat and held out his hand. She gave him the book without a word, and he flipped to a page near the middle and began to read aloud.
"Twelfth of January. Kip wrote, 'Saw a cow that looked exactly like Grandma's dog,' and then he drew it, so we would believe him." Dad laughed, and the laugh caught somewhere in his throat. "You were seven. You told him it looked more like a sofa."
"It did look like a sofa."
They sat for a while with the windows down. A magpie walked along the fence. Dad turned the key, and the Gherkin started first time, as if it were trying to change his mind.
"Show-off," he said quietly.
The buyers came on Sunday: a young couple with a baby asleep in a capsule and a toddler who wanted to press every button on the dashboard. The woman asked about the dent. The man asked about the kilometres. Dad answered every question honestly, even the ones about the radio, and Tess, watching from the verandah, realised he was almost hoping they would say no.
They did not say no. They said it was exactly what they needed, big enough for a pram and cheap enough to leave a little money over, and the man shook Dad's hand twice.
While the adults talked about paperwork, Tess fetched the logbook. She sat in the Gherkin one last time, turned to the first empty page and wrote the date. Under it she wrote: Last trip with us: nowhere. Distance: zero kilometres. Saw: a family who needs a big green car. Then, after a moment, she added two more words, closed the book, and put it back in the glovebox under the parking tickets.
"Aren't you keeping that?" Mum asked when the car had gone.
Tess shook her head. "I wrote down everything I needed to."
The new owners would find her last two words the first time they went looking for the tyre gauge: Your turn.

Option A: The morning sun is shining into her room.
Option B: She does not want the car to be sold.
Option C: She wants to go back to sleep.
Option D: She is embarrassed by the handwriting.

then behind them, croaking about small frogs
who have no ears and no tails.

and pretend to be very interested in my phone.

It was the hottest part of a February afternoon, and Leo had been sent outside to water Mum's tomatoes. His sister Ana, who was eight and allergic to being left out, followed him with a bucket she had no intention of filling.

Ana dropped the bucket. "A rainbow! Leo, keep it there!"
She ran straight at it, arms out, and the rainbow slid politely away from her, keeping exactly the same distance however fast she went. She stopped, frowning, among the tomato stakes.
"It moved."
"It always moves," Leo said. "You can't catch it. It isn't a thing sitting there."
"It's right there."
"Come back and I'll show you."
He remembered being her age and asking the same question on a beach at Inverloch, while Dad held a hose borrowed from the caravan park. Dad had not simply told him the answer. He had made him find it.
So Leo did the same. "Stand with your back to the sun. Now imagine a line running from the sun, through the back of your head, out past your eyes and into the garden. See where it hits the grass?"
Ana squinted at the lawn and pointed.
"The middle of the rainbow is always right there, exactly opposite the sun from your eyes. The colours make a circle around that spot. Sunlight goes into each drop of water, bends, bounces off the back of the drop and bends again on the way out. Every colour bends by a slightly different amount, so they spread apart, like a fan opening." He drew an arc in the air. "Red ends up on the outside, violet on the inside."
"So why can't I touch it?"
"Because the coloured light only reaches your eyes from drops at one particular angle from that line, a bit over forty degrees. When you move, the line moves with you, so different drops make the colours. You were chasing a pattern, not an object."
Ana considered this with the seriousness she usually saved for choosing ice-cream. Then she stepped sideways and stood right next to him, so close their elbows touched.
"Is it the same rainbow for both of us now?"
Leo had asked exactly that, years ago. He grinned. "Nope. Your eyes are in a different place from mine, even if it's only a few centimetres. So the light that makes your rainbow comes from different drops than the light that makes mine. We're each seeing our own."
"So nobody ever sees anybody else's rainbow?"
"Not ever. Not even twins."
She was quiet, watching the colours hang in the spray. Water pattered on the tomato leaves. Somewhere down the street a lawnmower started and stopped again.
"Then this one's mine," she said finally, with great satisfaction. "Nobody else has ever had it."
Leo moved the hose a fraction, and the rainbow brightened. A fainter second band had appeared above the first, its colours the other way round, but he decided to leave that for another afternoon. Dad had saved it for another afternoon too.
By the time Mum came out to see why her tomatoes were drowning, Ana was explaining to her, very slowly and with many hand movements, that the rainbow was not in the garden at all. It was in a circle around her head, it belonged to her, and if Mum wanted one she would have to stand in exactly the right place and make her own.
Question: What had Leo been sent outside to do?
Option A: mow the lawn
Option B: water Mum's tomatoes
Option C: fill a bucket for Ana
Option D: look after the caravan

In the steamy lowland rainforests of far north Queensland lives a bird that looks as though it has wandered out of prehistory. The southern cassowary stands up to 1.8 metres tall, can weigh more than 60 kilograms, and is Australia's heaviest bird. Its coarse black feathers hang like hair; its neck is a vivid blue, with red wattles dangling at the throat; and on its head sits a tall, helmet-like crest called a casque. Not the Same Girl
At the airport my aunt holds me at arm's length,
the way you hold a photo up to the light,
and says, 'Look at you! You haven't changed a bit!'
Her perfume is the same. Her laugh is the same.
I smile, because that is what you do.
But on the long drive home I start to argue with her
inside my head, the way I argue with everyone,
and by the time we reach the freeway
I have built my case.

Aunty, the skin you kissed on my cheek
is not the skin you kissed two years ago.
The outer layer of me wears away all the time,
flake by invisible flake,
and every month or so a whole new surface
has pushed up from below to take its place.
You have never touched the same me twice.

The blood that rushed to my face when you hugged me
is not the blood I carried last time you visited.
Each red cell lives about four months,
squeezing through vessels thinner than a hair,
until it wears out and is broken down,
and the marrow inside my bones makes millions more
every second, to keep the river running.

The lining of my stomach, which must survive
its own acid every day, is replaced every few days.
My taste buds are new every couple of weeks,
which may explain why I suddenly like olives
when you still remember me spitting them into a napkin.

My fingernails, which you once painted
pink with silver stars before my first school concert,
have grown out and been clipped away
a dozen times since then.
A whole nail takes about six months to replace itself,
creeping forward a few millimetres every month,
so not one sliver of that pink is left.

And my hair, which you plaited so tightly
I could feel my eyebrows lifting,
grows about a centimetre every month
and has been trimmed and swept off salon floors,
so the plaits you remember
were thrown away long ago.

Even my skeleton, Aunty, the hard frame of me,
the part you would think was fixed like a building's steel,
is being taken apart and put back together
by tiny cells that dissolve old bone and lay down new.
Slowly, quietly, over roughly ten years,
the whole thing is rebuilt,
like a house renovated room by room
while the family goes on living inside it.
So you see, I am not the girl you remember.
Hardly a piece of her is left.
I rehearsed it twice under my breath
while my aunt talked about the traffic.

That was my argument, and I was pleased with it,
until I looked up one more fact
on my phone in the back seat, and it spoiled everything.
Most of the nerve cells in the thinking part of my brain
are never replaced at all.
They are the same cells I was born with,
or very nearly, and they will stay with me
for the rest of my life,
holding on to everything they have been given.

So somewhere in my head, in cells that have not changed,
is the morning you taught me to float at Rosebud,
your hand flat beneath my back, saying, I've got you.
Somewhere is the smell of your kitchen,
the song you sang badly in the car,
the olives in the napkin,
the jigsaw of the Opera House we never finished,
the pink nails with silver stars.
New skin, new blood, new bones,
but the same keepers of memory,
looking out from the same place.

When we pull into the driveway
my aunt turns around in her seat and asks,
'What have you been thinking about all this time?'
and I tell her that she was right after all,
and also completely wrong,
and that it will take the whole holiday to explain.

When the Atacama Blooms
For all fourteen years of his life, Mateo had known the desert as one colour. From the edge of town the land ran brown and grey to the mountains, crusted with salt in the low places, so dry that the tracks of trucks stayed sharp for months. Teachers liked to tell visitors that some weather stations in the Atacama had gone years without recording a useful shower. Mateo liked to tell visitors that if they wanted green, they should go to Santiago.
His grandmother, Abuela Rosa, did not agree. Whenever the conversation turned to the desert, she would set down her coffee and say, 'You have never seen it wake up.'
She had seen it twice. Once as a girl, riding in the back of her father's truck, when the hills outside Vallenar turned purple 'as if someone had spilled wine across the whole world'. Once as a young mother, with Mateo's own mother asleep against her shoulder. Mateo had heard both stories so often that he could have told them himself, and privately he suspected the details had grown brighter with every telling.
Then, that winter, it rained. Not the thin, apologetic drizzle that sometimes drifted in from the coast and was gone by lunchtime, but real rain, for three days, drumming on the tin roofs and running in muddy streams down streets that had no gutters because nobody had ever needed them. The radio talked about warm water in the Pacific and unusual weather. Abuela Rosa stood at the window and said nothing at all, which was more unsettling than anything she might have said.
In science, Señora Paz explained what might happen next. The desert soil, she said, was full of seeds and bulbs that had been lying dormant, some of them for many years, sealed in tough coats that let them survive heat and drought. They were not dead. They were waiting. When enough water soaked down to reach them, and the spring days grew warm, they would sprout, flower and scatter new seeds as fast as they could, before the ground dried out again.
'How long do they get?' someone asked.
'A few weeks,' said Señora Paz. 'Then they wait again. Maybe five years. Maybe ten.'
By September, a green fuzz had appeared along the roadsides. By October, Abuela Rosa announced that they were going for a drive.
Mateo brought his phone, fully charged, intending to post enough photos to silence everyone at school who had ever laughed at his grandmother's stories. For the first few kilometres there was little to see. Then the road crested a rise, and his father slowed the car without being asked.
The hills were purple. Not dotted, not patched, but purple from the road to the horizon, a soft sheet of colour that rippled when the wind passed over it. Closer to the car he could see separate flowers, and between them smaller blooms in yellow and white, and he could hear the low hum of insects that seemed to have arrived from nowhere.
Mateo got out and stood on the gravel shoulder. He raised his phone, looked at the screen, and lowered it again. The little rectangle made it look like a postcard. It did not look like this.
Abuela Rosa came and stood beside him. She did not say 'I told you so', although she had every right to.
'Like spilled wine,' Mateo said at last.
She took his arm. 'Now,' she said, 'you have a story too.'
Question: The seeds had been 'lying dormant'. 'Dormant' means . . .
Option A: dead and decaying
Option B: growing very slowly
Option C: buried too deeply to sprout
Option D: alive but not active

The Nurdle Count
Dear Editor,
Last Thursday, twelve students from my Year 9 science class spent an hour on our hands and knees at Garland Beach. We were not looking for shells or sea glass. We were looking for nurdles, and I am writing because we found far more than any of us expected.
If you have never heard of a nurdle, you are not alone. Until a month ago, neither had I. Nurdles are plastic pellets, most about the size of a lentil, and they are the raw material from which almost every plastic product is made. They are melted down and moulded into everything from drink bottles to car parts. Because they are so small and are moved around in enormous quantities, they are easily spilled when they are loaded, transported or stored. Once spilled, they can be washed into stormwater drains, and from there into creeks and the sea.
While nurdles are tiny, the problem they cause is not. Scientists have found that they soak up harmful chemicals from the water around them, and seabirds and fish often mistake them for food. A nurdle in the stomach of a young bird does not break down. It simply takes up space where real food should be.
Our class followed the method used by citizen-science surveys around the world. We marked out three stretches of beach, each fifty metres long, and searched the strandline, where the tide leaves seaweed and rubbish, for exactly twenty minutes at each site. We found 1,214 nurdles near the mouth of Coopers Creek, 397 in the middle of the beach, and 61 at the southern end, near the rocks. Most were clear or white, but some were blue, green and even pink. Counting them back in the classroom took longer than collecting them.
Our teacher reminded us that one count on one day is not proof of anything. Even so, the pattern is hard to ignore. The closer we searched to the creek, the more nurdles we found, which suggests that many are arriving from upstream rather than floating in from the open ocean. Coopers Creek collects stormwater from the industrial estate on Bay Road, and although I am not accusing any particular business, it seems sensible to start looking there.
I would like to make three suggestions. First, the council could fit filters to the stormwater drains that empty into the creek, as some other councils have already done. Second, businesses that handle plastic pellets could join the voluntary industry program that trains staff to prevent and clean up spills, which costs very little and stops valuable material from being wasted. Third, residents could join our class when we repeat the count next term, because the more data we collect, the clearer the picture will become.
Some people have told me that a few plastic pellets hardly matter when the ocean is so big. I understand why they think so. But the ocean is not something far away; it is the water we swim in at the end of our street. If we cannot fix a problem we can see with our own eyes on our own beach, I do not know which problem we expect to fix.
Our full results, including photographs and a map of each site, are on the school website. I would be happy to show them to anyone who is interested, especially the council.
Yours sincerely,
Imogen Hartley
Year 9, Garland Bay Secondary College

Option A: to explain what nurdles are and how they reach the sea
Option B: to describe the method the class used
Option C: to list Imogen's suggestions for the council
Option D: to describe the colours of the nurdles found

Local Noon
On the second morning out from Port Macquarie, the chartplotter died. One moment its screen showed a neat line of dots creeping east across a blue emptiness towards Lord Howe Island; the next it was black, and no amount of switching off and on would wake it. Somewhere behind the panel, seawater had found its way into a connection.
'There's the handheld,' said Maya, who was fourteen and had expected the trip to be mostly sunbathing.
Her mother, Jo, found the handheld GPS in the chart-table drawer, pressed the button, and watched the screen flicker once and fade. The spare batteries, when she found them, had leaked white crust all over their packet.
For a long minute neither of them spoke. The yacht, Kestrel, went on lifting and sliding over the long swell, perfectly indifferent. Then Jo laughed, a short, surprised laugh, and climbed down into the cabin. She came back with a battered wooden box.
Maya groaned. She knew that box. Her mother had bought the sextant second-hand years ago for a navigation course and had been teased by the whole family for refusing to sell it. Before this trip she had made Maya practise with it on the back lawn until Maya could bring the sun down to the horizon in her sleep, and Maya had complained about it in every message to her friends.
'Lord Howe is a speck,' Jo said. 'If we miss it, the next stop is New Zealand. So. Local noon.'
The idea was simple, she explained, even if the arithmetic was not. Each day the sun climbs to its highest point and then begins to fall. That moment is local noon, and if you measure exactly how high the sun stands above the horizon right then, tables in the nautical almanac let you work out how far north or south you are: your latitude. Longitude, how far east or west you are, was a much harder problem without an accurate clock or a working radio, and Jo did not trust the cheap watch on her wrist.
At half past eleven Maya braced herself against the backstay and lifted the sextant. It was heavier than she remembered. The brass arc along its base covered only sixty degrees of the three hundred and sixty in a full circle, yet, thanks to its mirrors, it could measure angles twice that size. Through the eyepiece she swung the reflected sun down until its lower edge just kissed the line of the sea, and called out the reading. Jo wrote it down. A few minutes later Maya did it again. The angle grew, then grew more slowly, then for several readings did not grow at all. Then it began to shrink.
'That's it,' said Jo. 'That's the top.'
She worked at the chart table for twenty minutes, muttering, checking and rechecking. Finally she drew a pencil line across the chart.
'Thirty-one degrees, fifty-one minutes south. The island's at thirty-one thirty-three.' She tapped the gap between the lines. 'Each minute of latitude is one nautical mile. We're about eighteen miles too far south.'
She did not point the boat straight at the island. Instead she steered north-east until the next day's noon sight put them exactly on the island's latitude, then swung Kestrel due east and held her there, mile after mile.
Maya took the sights. Jo did the sums. Neither of them mentioned the back lawn.
At dawn on the fourth day Maya was at the helm when two grey shapes lifted out of the haze dead ahead, the twin mountains at the southern end of Lord Howe, solid as a promise.
She did not shout. She reached for her phone, which had no signal at all, and typed a message to send her friends the moment it did: Ok. The sextant was worth it.
Question: What caused the chartplotter to stop working?
Option A: Seawater got into one of its connections.
Option B: Its batteries leaked white crust.
Option C: Jo switched it off and on too often.
Option D: It was knocked over by the swell.

The Planet That Rolls
On the night of 13 March 1781, in a garden in Bath, England, a musician named William Herschel pointed a home-made telescope at the sky and noticed something odd. Among the pinpoint stars was a small, greenish disc. Over the following nights it shifted slightly against the background stars. Herschel assumed he had found a comet and reported it as one.
Other astronomers soon calculated its path, however, and found that it did not behave like a comet at all. It travelled in an almost circular orbit far beyond Saturn, which until then had been the most distant planet known. Herschel had discovered a new planet, the first ever found with a telescope, and in doing so had roughly doubled the known size of the solar system.
A planet without a name
The discovery made Herschel famous, but the new world still needed a name. Herschel suggested Georgium Sidus, Latin for 'George's Star', in honour of King George III. The choice was not entirely unselfish. Herschel, who had been born in Germany and earned his living teaching and performing music, hoped for royal support, and the King soon granted him a yearly salary that allowed him to give up music and study the sky full-time.
Astronomers outside Britain were less enthusiastic about naming a planet after an English king. The German astronomer Johann Bode proposed Uranus, after the Greek god of the sky, who in mythology was the father of Saturn. Since Saturn was the father of Jupiter, the name continued a neat family line through the outer planets. Bode's suggestion gradually won out, although Britain's official nautical almanac kept using the Georgian name until 1850.
Knocked on its side
Uranus is strange in many ways, but its most remarkable feature is its tilt. Most planets spin roughly upright as they travel around the Sun, like tops. Uranus is tipped over by about 98 degrees, so that it spins almost on its side, rolling along its orbit like a ball. Many scientists believe that early in its history it was struck by an object several times the size of Earth, and the impact knocked it over.
This tilt gives Uranus the most extreme seasons in the solar system. The planet takes about 84 Earth years to orbit the Sun, and each pole receives roughly 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by roughly 42 years of darkness.
An ice giant
Uranus is about four times as wide as Earth. Unlike Jupiter and Saturn, which are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, Uranus has a thick interior of water, ammonia and methane, which is why astronomers call it an ice giant. Methane in its upper atmosphere absorbs red light and reflects blue and green, giving the planet its pale cyan colour. Temperatures in its atmosphere have been measured as low as about minus 224 degrees Celsius, colder than any other planet, even though Neptune is further from the Sun.
Uranus also has a set of thin, dark rings, discovered in 1977, and more than two dozen known moons. Breaking with the tradition of naming moons after figures from mythology, most are named after characters in the plays of William Shakespeare, among them Miranda, Ariel and Puck.
The forgotten planet
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus. Voyager 2 flew past in January 1986 on its way to Neptune, sending back the first close-up images and discovering ten new moons. Since then, no mission has returned. Many planetary scientists now argue that a dedicated spacecraft to orbit Uranus should be a priority. After all, more than two centuries after a musician spotted it from his garden, this tilted, frozen world still has many secrets to give up.

Option A: a moon
Option B: a star
Option C: a comet
Option D: a planet

The Seat Next to You
Ask people how they met their closest friends and you will hear many different stories, but a surprising number share one plain ingredient: distance, or rather the lack of it. Psychologists call this the proximity effect. Put simply, we tend to become friends with the people we happen to be near.
One of the best-known studies of this idea took place in the late 1940s at Westgate, a housing estate for married students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Researchers Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back asked residents to name the people they saw most often socially. The results were striking. Residents were far more likely to name next-door neighbours than people who lived only a few doors further along. Those whose front doors faced the street rather than the courtyard were named less often, while people who lived beside a staircase or the letterboxes, where others passed every day, were among the most popular in the estate. The students had not chosen their flats. Their friendships, it seemed, had partly been chosen for them by the architects.
Why should a few metres matter so much? One explanation is the mere exposure effect: the more often we see something, the more we tend to like it, whether it is a song, a face or a stranger at the bus stop. Repeated small meetings also give people low-risk chances to talk. Nobody needs courage to comment on the weather to someone they see every morning. Over weeks, those tiny conversations add up to trust.
Consider Mira, who started Year 8 at a new school. For the first fortnight she ate lunch in the library, telling herself that she preferred the quiet. In science she was placed alphabetically beside a boy named Tomas, who spent the first lessons drawing comic strips in the margins of his workbook. Mira said nothing for a week. Then, during an experiment, their beaker cracked, and both of them burst out laughing as vinegar crept across the bench. By the end of term they were swapping comics, and Mira had stopped visiting the library at lunchtime. She later admitted that she had been 'pretending to be busy so nobody would see me alone'.
Mira's story shows both the power and the limits of proximity. Sitting beside Tomas gave her the opportunity, but it was the shared laugh, and the courage to keep talking afterwards, that turned a seating plan into a friendship. Researchers point out that closeness can magnify dislike as well as liking; a neighbour whose habits annoy you becomes more annoying the more often you meet.
The research also carries a quieter message. Many people who feel lonely assume there is something wrong with them, when the real problem may simply be that their daily routine rarely places them near the same people twice. Joining a club, catching the same bus, or volunteering at the same place each week can create the repeated contact that friendships need to take root.
None of this means friendship is merely an accident of floor plans. We still choose whom we trust and whom we confide in. But it does suggest that the next time you wonder how to make a friend, the answer may be less about saying something brilliant and more about simply turning up, again and again, in the same place.

Option A: at a high school for students new to the area
Option B: in a university science laboratory for volunteers
Option C: at a housing estate for married university students
Option D: at a holiday camp for first-year university students

Change Day at Pettigrew's
On the morning of Monday 14 February 1966, the bell above the door of Pettigrew's General Store rang for the first time at half past seven, and Judy Pettigrew, thirteen and still yawning, braced herself behind the counter.
For weeks the wireless had played a cheerful jingle about dollars and cents, and a cartoon man called Dollar Bill had smiled from posters in the post office window. Australia was leaving behind pounds, shillings and pence. From today, ten shillings would become one dollar, and a single shilling would be ten cents. Simple, said the government pamphlets. Judy was not so sure.
Her father had not gone to bed at all. When she came downstairs at six, she found him hunched over the old brass cash register with a screwdriver, a mug of cold tea and a man from the conversion company who had driven out from Goulburn the night before. The keys that had once said 'pence' and 'shillings' now said 'cents' and 'dollars'. 'Every till in the state has to be done,' the man had explained, 'and there aren't enough of us to go round, so it's nights or nothing.'
Pinned above the counter was a long card covered in tiny print: the conversion chart. One penny, one cent. Twopence, two cents. Sixpence, five cents. Judy had spent Sunday afternoon memorising it while her grandmother sat on the verandah shelling peas and muttering.
Nan did not approve. She had kept the store's books for forty years, and she believed that money, like weather, should not be fiddled with. 'A penny's a penny,' she said at breakfast. 'You can't call it something else and expect it to behave.' Then she carried her biscuit tin of coins upstairs, as if someone might try to decimalise it while she wasn't looking.
The first customer was Mr Costa from the orchard, who wanted a tin of tobacco, a box of matches and a pound of sugar. He paid with a ten-shilling note. Judy rang it up, checked the chart twice, and handed him his change in shiny new coins. Mr Costa turned a five-cent piece over in his palm and studied the little echidna on the back. 'Like a toy,' he said, but he was smiling.
By lunchtime the store was full of people who had come mostly to complain and stayed mostly to gossip. Old notes and new coins lay side by side in the till, because the two kinds of money would be used together for a while. Mrs Hollis insisted she had been cheated out of a fraction of a penny. Judy patiently showed her on the chart that the difference was so small it could not be paid in any coin at all, and Mrs Hollis left with a bag of humbugs 'on the house' to settle the matter.
In the late afternoon, when the light slanted gold through the front window, Nan came downstairs. She stood at the counter for a long time, watching. Then she held out her hand.
'Show me one of those shilling ones,' she said.
Judy gave her a ten-cent coin. Nan weighed it in her palm, then took an old shilling from her apron pocket and laid the two side by side. They were exactly the same size.
'Well,' Nan said at last. 'At least they had the sense to keep it honest.'
That evening Judy saw her grandmother at the kitchen table with the biscuit tin open, sorting coins into two piles. One pile was going to the bank. The other, much smaller, was a single penny with the old king's head on it, which Nan wrapped carefully in a handkerchief and tucked away.

Option A: leaned on the counter for support

Option C: prepared herself for something difficult
Option D: hurried nervously to her position

On the morning of Monday 14 February 1966, the bell above the door of Pettigrew's General Store rang for the first time at half past seven, and Judy Pettigrew, thirteen and still yawning, braced herself behind the counter.
For weeks the wireless had played a cheerful jingle about dollars and cents, and a cartoon man called Dollar Bill had smiled from posters in the post office window. Australia was leaving behind pounds, shillings and pence. From today, ten shillings would become one dollar, and a single shilling would be ten cents. Simple, said the government pamphlets. Judy was not so sure.
Her father had not gone to bed at all. When she came downstairs at six, she found him hunched over the old brass cash register with a screwdriver, a mug of cold tea and a man from the conversion company who had driven out from Goulburn the night before. The keys that had once said 'pence' and 'shillings' now said 'cents' and 'dollars'. 'Every till in the state has to be done,' the man had explained, 'and there aren't enough of us to go round, so it's nights or nothing.'
Pinned above the counter was a long card covered in tiny print: the conversion chart. One penny, one cent. Twopence, two cents. Sixpence, five cents. Judy had spent Sunday afternoon memorising it while her grandmother sat on the verandah shelling peas and muttering.
Nan did not approve. She had kept the store's books for forty years, and she believed that money, like weather, should not be fiddled with. 'A penny's a penny,' she said at breakfast. 'You can't call it something else and expect it to behave.' Then she carried her biscuit tin of coins upstairs, as if someone might try to decimalise it while she wasn't looking.
The first customer was Mr Costa from the orchard, who wanted a tin of tobacco, a box of matches and a pound of sugar. He paid with a ten-shilling note. Judy rang it up, checked the chart twice, and handed him his change in shiny new coins. Mr Costa turned a five-cent piece over in his palm and studied the little echidna on the back. 'Like a toy,' he said, but he was smiling.
By lunchtime the store was full of people who had come mostly to complain and stayed mostly to gossip. Old notes and new coins lay side by side in the till, because the two kinds of money would be used together for a while. Mrs Hollis insisted she had been cheated out of a fraction of a penny. Judy patiently showed her on the chart that the difference was so small it could not be paid in any coin at all, and Mrs Hollis left with a bag of humbugs 'on the house' to settle the matter.
In the late afternoon, when the light slanted gold through the front window, Nan came downstairs. She stood at the counter for a long time, watching. Then she held out her hand.
'Show me one of those shilling ones,' she said.
Judy gave her a ten-cent coin. Nan weighed it in her palm, then took an old shilling from her apron pocket and laid the two side by side. They were exactly the same size.
'Well,' Nan said at last. 'At least they had the sense to keep it honest.'

The Browning Code
Why does toast taste so much better than bread? Why does a seared steak smell irresistible while a boiled one seems dull and grey? The answer lies in a set of chemical reactions named after the French scientist Louis-Camille Maillard, who first described them in 1912. Maillard was not interested in cooking at all; he was investigating chemistry connected with the human body. Yet his discovery now sits at the heart of almost every kitchen in the world.
The Maillard reaction happens when amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, react with certain sugars under heat. Rather than one tidy change, it is a tangled cascade of reactions that produces hundreds of new compounds. Some of these give food its brown colour; others create the rich, roasted, nutty flavours we associate with crusty bread, fried onions, roasted coffee and grilled meat.
Temperature is crucial. The reaction does occur slowly at lower temperatures, but it only becomes rapid at roughly 140 degrees Celsius and above. This explains a frustrating kitchen mystery. Water boils at 100 degrees, and while a food's surface is wet, it cannot get much hotter than that. So a damp piece of chicken placed in a pan will first steam rather than sizzle, and it will not brown until the surface moisture has evaporated. Experienced cooks therefore pat meat dry with paper towel before cooking it.
The same principle explains a common beginner's mistake: overcrowding the pan. When too many pieces of food are squeezed in together, the moisture they release has nowhere to escape. The pan temperature drops, the food stews in its own juices, and the result is pale and limp. Cooking in smaller batches takes longer, but it leaves room for steam to escape and for the surface to reach browning temperature.
Chemistry also offers a few clever shortcuts. The reaction speeds up in alkaline conditions, which is why traditional German pretzels are dipped in an alkaline solution before baking, giving them their deep, glossy, mahogany crust. Some cooks add a tiny pinch of bicarbonate of soda to onions to make them brown faster, although too much leaves a soapy taste.
It is worth distinguishing Maillard browning from caramelisation, which is often confused with it. Caramelisation involves sugar alone breaking down under heat and requires higher temperatures, generally above 160 degrees. Melting sugar into toffee is caramelisation; browning a sausage is mostly Maillard. Many foods, such as roasted carrots, experience both at once.
Like many good things, browning has a downside when taken too far. Push the reactions past golden-brown and they begin to produce bitter, burnt compounds. Food scientists have also found that very dark browning of starchy foods, such as burnt toast and overcooked chips, can form a substance called acrylamide, which health authorities recommend keeping to a minimum. Their advice is simple and easy to remember: aim for golden, not charcoal.
Understanding the Maillard reaction will not instantly make anyone a great cook. However, it does turn a few mysterious kitchen rules into common sense. Dry the surface, give food space, use enough heat, and stop before it burns. Behind every perfect golden crust is a century-old piece of chemistry that its discoverer never expected to end up on a dinner plate.

Option D: a slow and gentle process that rarely changes

Sugarbag Summer
Saturday 3 December
Dad came home today with a wooden box the size of a shoebox and announced that we now own about five thousand bees. Mum went pale. I went straight to my room. I am fourteen, I have been stung twice in my life, both times on the foot, and I do not need five thousand more chances. Dad kept repeating the magic words 'they don't sting' as if that settled everything.
Sunday 4 December
Fine. I have done some research, mostly so that I can prove Dad wrong. The bees are Tetragonula carbonaria, one of Australia's native stingless bees. They really do not have a working sting. The worst they can do, apparently, is crawl into your hair and nip. They are tiny, black and about four millimetres long, so small that the first time I saw one land on the box I thought it was a fly.
Wednesday 7 December
Dad put the hive on a post under the eaves on the eastern side of the house, so it gets morning sun but stays out of the afternoon heat. According to his book, these bees struggle in extreme heat, but they also stop flying when it gets cold. Before school I watched them pour out of the little entrance like grains of pepper shaken from a jar. I was not scared. I would not admit that to Dad, however.
Saturday 10 December
Mr Nguyen from next door came over to look. He keeps European honey bees and says his hives give him buckets of honey, while ours will produce only about a kilogram a year, if that. Dad didn't seem to mind. He said we didn't get them for the honey; we got them for the garden. Mr Nguyen nodded slowly and said that native bees were excellent pollinators for macadamias, mangoes and many other plants. Then he admitted, a little sheepishly, that he had always wanted a hive of them himself, and asked whether he could come back next week.
Thursday 15 December
I opened the observation window on the side of the box for the first time, and I could not believe what I saw. Inside, the bees have built a spiral of brood cells, like a tiny staircase winding upwards, made of a dark waxy mixture called cerumen. The Doorway Ate My Thought
You stand up from the couch with a clear purpose. You walk briskly down the hallway, step into the kitchen, and stop. You stare at the fridge. You stare at the bench. You have absolutely no idea why you are there. Eventually you trudge back to the couch, and the moment you sit down, you remember: scissors. You needed scissors.
If this has happened to you, take comfort. You are not losing your mind, and you are certainly not alone. Psychologists have studied this maddening little mishap, and they have a name for it: the doorway effect.
The best-known research comes from Gabriel Radvansky and his colleagues at the University of Notre Dame in the United States. In one series of experiments, volunteers moved through a virtual building on a computer screen, picking up an object in one room and carrying it to another. Every so often, the researchers asked them what they were carrying. The results were clear. People who had just walked through a doorway forgot more often than people who had travelled the same distance within a single room. Later experiments in real rooms, with real objects hidden in boxes, produced similar results.
Radvansky's explanation is that the brain does not record life as one endless video. Instead, it chops experience into chunks, or episodes, rather like scenes in a film. A doorway acts as what researchers call an event boundary. When you cross it, your brain files away the previous scene and opens a fresh one for the new room. Your intention, unfortunately, was packed into the old scene. It has not vanished; it has simply been put in a filing cabinet you are no longer looking at. That is also why returning to the couch so often brings the memory flooding back: you have stepped back into the scene where the thought was formed.
In fairness to our brains, this system is usually rather clever. Dividing experience into episodes helps us remember what happened where, and it stops the details of one situation from cluttering up the next. A student who carried every thought from the classroom into the canteen, the bus and the dinner table would find life exhausting. The doorway effect is simply what happens when an excellent filing system occasionally files something too early.
There are some practical tricks for outwitting it. Saying the purpose out loud as you walk, such as 'scissors, scissors, scissors', keeps it active in your working memory. Picturing the object vividly before you leave can help too. Some people swear by carrying a related item with them, such as the paper they intend to cut, as a physical reminder that cannot be accidentally filed away.
Of course, none of these tricks will help with the other classic household mishap: walking into a room, remembering exactly what you came for, and discovering that someone else has borrowed it. For that, science has no answer at all, although a family meeting may help.
So the next time you find yourself standing blankly in the laundry, holding nothing and staring at the washing machine as though it might explain itself, do not panic. Your brain has not failed you. It has simply turned the page a little too quickly. Wander back to where you started, and the missing thought will usually be waiting there for you.

Option A: why people forget their purpose after walking through doorways
Option B: how homes can be designed so that their rooms connect better
Option C: why some people naturally have poorer memories than others
Option D: how virtual buildings are used to train young psychologists

A Cable to the Stars
Every rocket launch is, in a sense, an act of brute force. To lift even a small satellite into orbit, a rocket must burn enormous quantities of fuel, much of it simply to lift the rest of the fuel. For more than a century, dreamers have wondered whether there might be a gentler way to leave the Earth. Their answer is one of the strangest ideas in science or fiction: the space elevator.
The concept is usually traced to the Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky. In 1895, after seeing the newly built Eiffel Tower in Paris, he imagined a tower stretching tens of thousands of kilometres upward. In 1960, the engineer Yuri Artsutanov proposed a cleverer version. Rather than building upward from the ground, he suggested lowering a cable downward from a satellite while extending another cable outward into space to balance it.
The key to the idea is a special height called geostationary orbit, about 35,786 kilometres above the equator. A satellite at this height circles the Earth exactly once a day, so it appears to hang motionless above one spot. If a cable ran from the equator past that height to a heavy counterweight further out, the spin of the Earth would keep the whole cable taut, rather like a stone whirled on the end of a string. Electric vehicles called climbers could then crawl up the cable, carrying cargo into space for a fraction of the cost of a rocket launch.
For decades, the idea lived mainly in novels. In 1979, Arthur C. Clarke made a space elevator the centrepiece of his novel The Fountains of Paradise, and he later joked that such a structure would be built about fifty years after people stopped laughing at it. Other writers followed, and the elevator became a familiar part of the imagined future, rising from tropical islands into the clouds.
The trouble is a matter of materials. A cable that long would have to support its own enormous weight. Steel, the strongest material in most buildings, would snap under its own weight long before reaching orbit. Engineers estimate that the cable would need to be many times stronger than steel for its weight. In the 1990s, hopes rose with the discovery of carbon nanotubes, microscopic tubes of carbon atoms that are extraordinarily strong. Yet so far, scientists can only make them in very short lengths, and even tiny flaws dramatically weaken them. Other obstacles remain too: lightning storms, space junk and the challenge of powering climbers over thousands of kilometres.
So is the space elevator merely science fiction? Not entirely. Engineering teams in Japan and elsewhere continue to study the problem, and small experiments have tested climbers and tethers. Even if no full elevator is ever built, the research may produce stronger materials that are useful on Earth.
Perhaps the space elevator's greatest value lies in the way it changes how we think. Science fiction often works as a kind of rehearsal for the future, allowing writers and readers to explore an idea long before anyone can build it. Some of those rehearsals, such as earlier visions of communication satellites, eventually became everyday reality. Others remain on the stage. Whether the space elevator joins the first group or the second, it reminds us that the path to the stars may not always need a rocket.

Option A: seeing the Eiffel Tower in Paris
Option B: reading a novel by Arthur C. Clarke
Option C: watching an early rocket launch
Option D: studying satellites in high orbit

The Contests at Utgard
Thor, the thunder god, had never been beaten at anything, and he did not intend to begin now. So when he, the trickster Loki and a swift young farm boy named Thialfi arrived at the towering gates of Utgard, the stronghold of the giants, Thor strode straight into the great hall as if he owned it.
The giant king, Utgard-Loki, looked down from his high seat and smiled in a way Thor did not like. 'So this little fellow is the mighty Thor?' he said. 'No one stays in my hall unless he is skilled in some contest. What can you and your companions do?'
Loki, who was always hungry, spoke first. 'No one can eat faster than I can.' The king called forward a servant named Logi. A long trough of meat was set between them, and the two began eating from opposite ends. They met exactly in the middle, but while Loki had eaten only the meat, Logi had devoured the meat, the bones and the wooden trough itself. Loki was declared the loser.
Thialfi offered to run. He was the fastest boy in all his valley, but the king's champion, a slender youth called Hugi, beat him so easily in three races that Hugi had turned around and was strolling back before Thialfi reached the finish.
Then it was Thor's turn. A drinking horn was brought to him. 'A strong drinker empties this in one swallow,' said the king. Thor drank until his chest ached, three enormous draughts, yet the level in the horn had sunk only a little. Next the king challenged him to lift his grey cat from the floor. Thor heaved with all his might, but the cat merely arched its back, and Thor managed to raise only one of its paws. Furious now, Thor demanded someone to wrestle. The king sent for his old nurse, Elli, a bent and wrinkled woman. The harder Thor struggled, the firmer she stood, until at last she forced the god down onto one knee.
The travellers spent a gloomy night in the hall, eating little and speaking less. Thor lay awake for hours, staring at the rafters and wondering how he would ever explain such defeats at home. In the morning, Utgard-Loki himself walked them beyond the gates. There he turned to Thor, and his voice was no longer mocking.
'Now that you are outside my walls, I will tell you the truth, and you will never enter them again. I deceived you with illusions from the start. Loki's opponent was Logi, which is wildfire itself, and fire consumes everything, bones and wood alike. Thialfi raced against Hugi, my own thought, and no runner alive can match the speed of thought.'
Thor stared. The king went on.
'The end of your horn was dipped in the sea. When you reach the shore, you will see how far the ocean has fallen because of your drinking. The cat was the great serpent that circles the whole world, and when you lifted its paw, it was nearly dragged from the deep. And Elli, my nurse, is old age. No one has ever wrestled her without being brought down, yet you fell only to one knee. In truth, we giants were terrified of your strength.'
Thor reached angrily for his hammer, but Utgard-Loki and his entire stronghold had vanished, leaving only an empty, windswept plain. Thor returned home with nothing to show for his journey. Yet the Norse storytellers said that the ebb of the tide, when the sea draws back from the shore, began on the day that Thor drank from the horn.
Question: In the third paragraph, the word devoured means . . .
Option A: refused to eat
Option B: ate up completely
Option C: shared out fairly
Option D: tasted carefully
