Loki, who was always hungry, spoke first. 'No one can eat faster than I can.' The king called forward a servant named Logi. A long trough of meat was set between them, and the two began eating from opposite ends. They met exactly in the middle, but while Loki had eaten only the meat, Logi had devoured the meat, the bones and the wooden trough itself. Loki was declared the loser.
Thialfi offered to run. He was the fastest boy in all his valley, but the king's champion, a slender youth called Hugi, beat him so easily in three races that Hugi had turned around and was strolling back before Thialfi reached the finish.
Then it was Thor's turn. A drinking horn was brought to him. 'A strong drinker empties this in one swallow,' said the king. Thor drank until his chest ached, three enormous draughts, yet the level in the horn had sunk only a little. Next the king challenged him to lift his grey cat from the floor. Thor heaved with all his might, but the cat merely arched its back, and Thor managed to raise only one of its paws. Furious now, Thor demanded someone to wrestle. The king sent for his old nurse, Elli, a bent and wrinkled woman. The harder Thor struggled, the firmer she stood, until at last she forced the god down onto one knee.
The travellers spent a gloomy night in the hall, eating little and speaking less. Thor lay awake for hours, staring at the rafters and wondering how he would ever explain such defeats at home. In the morning, Utgard-Loki himself walked them beyond the gates. There he turned to Thor, and his voice was no longer mocking.
'Now that you are outside my walls, I will tell you the truth, and you will never enter them again. I deceived you with illusions from the start. Loki's opponent was Logi, which is wildfire itself, and fire consumes everything, bones and wood alike. Thialfi raced against Hugi, my own thought, and no runner alive can match the speed of thought.'
Thor stared. The king went on.

Option D: so each separate contest can teach its own moral lesson in turn

Last Call for Marlow
Every school morning for six years, Jas had caught the 7.40 ferry from Harrow Wharf, and every school morning for six years, Marlow had announced it.
Marlow was the terminal robot, a squat, barrel-shaped machine with a dented aluminium shell and a single round screen that served as a face. It rolled slowly between the benches, reminding passengers to keep their tickets ready and to stand behind the yellow line. Its voice was slightly too loud and slightly too cheerful, and its screen showed a smiling face that had faded to the colour of weak tea. Tourists photographed it. Regulars ignored it. Jas had always found it oddly comforting, like a clock that never stopped ticking.
Then, one Monday in March, a laminated notice appeared on the ticket office window: From 1 April, Harrow Wharf will be served by our new automated information system. We thank Unit M-04 for its years of service. Beneath the notice, someone had already stuck a sticker of a sad face.
'They're replacing it with screens,' said Mr Delaney, who sold coffee from a cart by the gate. 'Cheaper to run, apparently. Old Marlow's off to the recyclers.'
Jas told herself it did not matter. Marlow was a machine, a collection of wires and motors and outdated software. It did not know her name. It probably did not know anything.
Yet over the following weeks she began to notice things. Marlow always paused for a moment before announcing the 7.40, a tiny hesitation that never happened with the other ferries. When an elderly man dropped his walking stick, Marlow rolled over and waited beside him until he had picked it up, its screen glowing a slow, patient blue. On windy days it parked itself at the end of the queue, where the rain blew sideways, as though it had decided to take the worst spot so that nobody else had to.
'It's just programming,' her brother said when she told him at dinner. 'Someone wrote a line of code that says: if a person drops something, go and wait.'
'Someone also wrote the pause,' Jas said. 'Why would anyone write a pause?'
He didn't have an answer.
On the last morning, a small crowd gathered at the wharf. Mr Delaney handed out free coffee. A girl from the primary school had made a card with a crayon drawing of Marlow wearing a captain's hat. Jas had brought nothing; she had not known what you were supposed to bring to a robot's farewell.
At 7.38, Marlow rolled to its usual position by the gangway. Its screen flickered. For a moment Jas thought it might not work at all. Then came the familiar, slightly too loud voice.
'The seven-forty ferry to Gannet Point is now boarding. Please have your tickets ready. Thank you for travelling with us.'
And then, after the pause, something it had never said before.
'Have a good day, everyone.'
Nobody moved. The ferry's engine rumbled patiently at the wharf. Mr Delaney cleared his throat and looked hard at his coffee cart. Jas felt something tighten in her chest, as though a rope had been pulled taut between her and the dented little machine.
Later, she would learn that a technician had added the farewell line the night before as a joke. Or perhaps not as a joke. He never quite explained, and she never quite asked.
By the following week, Harrow Wharf had two bright new screens, which displayed departure times in crisp white letters. They were accurate, efficient and perfectly silent. Jas still found herself pausing before she stepped onto the 7.40.
Question: In the second paragraph, the word squat means . . .
Option A: crouching low
Option B: short and wide
Option C: tall and narrow
Option D: badly damaged

Behind the Skirting Table
At half past seven on a winter morning, the shearing shed on our property already smells of lanolin, diesel and sweat. Six shearers are bent over their sheep on the board, the handpieces buzzing like angry insects. I stand at the far end of the shed beside a slatted wooden table, waiting for the first fleece. My job, for the next three weeks, is to decide what every one of those fleeces is worth.
I am a wool classer, and I have been one for twenty-two years. People who have never been inside a shearing shed often imagine that wool is simply wool. It is not. A single shed may produce several distinct grades, and mixing them carelessly can cost a farmer thousands of dollars at sale.
The process begins with the rouseabouts. As each sheep is shorn, a rouseabout gathers the fleece and throws it onto the skirting table in one smooth, practised motion so that it spreads out flat like a blanket, cut side down. It is a skill that looks easy and is not; a badly thrown fleece lands in a tangled heap. The slats let short pieces and dirt fall through. Then the skirters move in quickly, pulling away the edges: the stained patches, the burrs, the short, dirty wool from the legs and belly. These skirtings are not wasted; they are sold separately, at a lower price.
What is left comes to me. I look at it, I feel it and, in a sense, I listen to it. The most important quality is fineness, measured in microns, where one micron is a thousandth of a millimetre. A human hair is often somewhere between fifty and a hundred microns thick; good merino wool is commonly below twenty. The finer the fibre, the softer the cloth it makes and, usually, the higher the price. I also check the staple length, which is the length of a natural lock of wool, and its strength. I take a staple between my fingers and give it a flick. If it snaps in the middle, the sheep was probably stressed at some point during the year, perhaps by drought or illness, and the fibre grew thin and weak at that moment.
Once I have made my decision, the fleece goes into one of several bins, each holding a particular line of wool. When a bin is full, the wool is pressed into a bale weighing around two hundred kilograms. Each bale is stencilled with the farm's brand, the line and a number, and those details travel with it all the way to the auction floor. A buyer in a city office, or even overseas, will judge the whole farm by what is inside it, so a bale is a kind of promise that must be kept.
These days, samples from every bale are tested in a laboratory, so buyers know the exact micron and yield before they bid. Some young people ask me whether that makes my job pointless. I understand the question; the machines are remarkably accurate. However, the laboratory tests the bale, not the fleece. If I put the wrong fleece into a bin, the whole bale is dragged down with it, and no test can separate it again afterwards.
That is why I still trust my hands. By the end of a long day, my fingertips are soft with lanolin and my back aches from bending over the table. But when a buyer later tells the farmer that the clip was even and well prepared, I know that each of those thousands of small decisions mattered.

Option A: Machines have made traditional skills useless.
Option B: Careful skill adds real value to a farm's wool.
Option C: Shearing is the hardest job on any sheep farm.
Option D: Farm life in winter is lonely and exhausting.

Six shearers are bent over their sheep on the board, the handpieces buzzing like angry insects. I stand at the far end of the shed beside a slatted wooden table, waiting for the first fleece. My job, for the next three weeks, is to decide what every one of those fleeces is worth.
I am a wool classer, and I have been one for twenty-two years. People who have never been inside a shearing shed often imagine that wool is simply wool. It is not. A single shed may produce several distinct grades, and mixing them carelessly can cost a farmer thousands of dollars at sale.
The process begins with the rouseabouts. As each sheep is shorn, a rouseabout gathers the fleece and throws it onto the skirting table in one smooth, practised motion so that it spreads out flat like a blanket, cut side down. It is a skill that looks easy and is not; a badly thrown fleece lands in a tangled heap. The slats let short pieces and dirt fall through. Then the skirters move in quickly, pulling away the edges: the stained patches, the burrs, the short, dirty wool from the legs and belly. These skirtings are not wasted; they are sold separately, at a lower price.
What is left comes to me. I look at it, I feel it and, in a sense, I listen to it. The most important quality is fineness, measured in microns, where one micron is a thousandth of a millimetre. A human hair is often somewhere between fifty and a hundred microns thick; good merino wool is commonly below twenty. The finer the fibre, the softer the cloth it makes and, usually, the higher the price. I also check the staple length, which is the length of a natural lock of wool, and its strength. I take a staple between my fingers and give it a flick. If it snaps in the middle, the sheep was probably stressed at some point during the year, perhaps by drought or illness, and the fibre grew thin and weak at that moment.
Once I have made my decision, the fleece goes into one of several bins, each holding a particular line of wool. When a bin is full, the wool is pressed into a bale weighing around two hundred kilograms. Each bale is stencilled with the farm's brand, the line and a number, and those details travel with it all the way to the auction floor. A buyer in a city office, or even overseas, will judge the whole farm by what is inside it, so a bale is a kind of promise that must be kept.
These days, samples from every bale are tested in a laboratory, so buyers know the exact micron and yield before they bid. Some young people ask me whether that makes my job pointless. I understand the question; the machines are remarkably accurate. However, the laboratory tests the bale, not the fleece. If I put the wrong fleece into a bin, the whole bale is dragged down with it, and no test can separate it again afterwards.
That is why I still trust my hands. By the end of a long day, my fingertips are soft with lanolin and my back aches from bending over the table. But when a buyer later tells the farmer that the clip was even and well prepared, I know that each of those thousands of small decisions mattered.

Shelter Above the Snowline
High in the Australian Alps, scattered across the plains and valleys of Kosciuszko National Park and the Victorian high country, stand dozens of small, weathered huts. Some are built of slab timber, some of corrugated iron and a few of stone. Many have a stone fireplace, a rough table and a sleeping platform, and almost none have electricity. To a passing bushwalker on a fine summer afternoon they may look like quaint relics. To a walker caught in a sudden blizzard, they can look like the most beautiful buildings in the world.
Most of the huts were never intended for recreation. Many were built from the late nineteenth century onwards by graziers, who drove cattle and sheep up to the high plains each summer to fatten on the alpine grass and needed somewhere to sleep and shelter. Others were built by miners searching for gold, by workers on the Snowy Mountains Scheme, or by early ski clubs. Each hut tells a story about the people who once worked in these mountains, and some still carry the carved initials of stockmen who passed through decades ago.
Over time, grazing in the high country was gradually phased out of the national parks, and the original builders no longer needed the huts. Without regular care, timber rotted, roofs blew away and some huts collapsed. In 1971, a group of bushwalkers and skiers who had sheltered in these huts formed the Kosciuszko Huts Association to look after them. Today its volunteers spend weekends hauling timber, replacing roof iron and repairing chimneys, often walking for hours to reach a site with tools on their backs. Their work is entirely unpaid. Many of them simply say that they are repaying a debt to the huts that once kept them safe.
The huts face natural dangers as well as neglect. In the bushfires of 2003, several historic huts were destroyed. Some have since been painstakingly rebuilt, often using traditional methods and materials so that the new building looks as much like the original as possible.
For modern visitors, the most important thing to understand is that the huts are not hotels. They cannot be booked, and walkers are strongly advised never to plan a trip on the assumption that a hut will have space. In a storm, a hut built for four people may end up sheltering fifteen. For this reason, park authorities urge everyone to carry a tent, a warm sleeping bag and enough food, treating a hut as a welcome bonus rather than a guaranteed bed.
There is also an unwritten code of hut etiquette. Visitors should leave the hut cleaner than they found it, replace any firewood they use, and carry out all their rubbish. Many huts contain a logbook, where walkers record their names, the weather and their route. These logbooks are more than souvenirs; in an emergency, rescuers have used entries to work out where a missing walker was last seen. Leaving the door firmly closed matters too, because a hut left open can quickly fill with snow or become a home for wildlife.
The alpine huts belong to everyone and to no one. They survive because strangers who will never meet each other keep choosing to look after them. Each time a walker restocks the woodpile for whoever arrives next, the old spirit of the high country is quietly carried forward.

Option C: Rangers move all walkers into huts each night.
Option D: Walkers prefer huts to tents in fine summer weather.

Cut the Last Line
At the end of almost every fable in the books I grew up with sat a single sentence in italics, like a teacher standing at the door to make sure nobody left with the wrong idea. 'Slow and steady wins the race.' 'Look before you leap.' 'Pride goes before a fall.' I would like to propose something that may sound like vandalism: we should cut that last line and let the story speak for itself.
Consider the fable of the fox and the grapes. A hungry fox leaps again and again at a bunch of grapes hanging from a vine, fails to reach them, and finally stalks away muttering that they were probably sour anyway. It is a perfect little scene. Any reader over the age of eight recognises that fox, because we have all been that fox. We have all decided that the team we didn't make was boring, or that the party we weren't invited to would have been dull. The pleasure of the story lies in that flash of recognition. When the book then adds, 'It is easy to despise what you cannot get,' the flash is replaced by a lecture. The reader is no longer discovering; they are being told.
Many scholars believe that the neat morals were not part of the oldest versions at all. The tales were passed on by word of mouth for centuries, and many of the tidy summaries seem to have been attached later by collectors who wanted the stories to be useful in schoolrooms. The moral, in other words, is often a sticky note pressed onto a painting by someone worried that we might not understand it.
There is a further problem: the stated moral is frequently narrower than the story. The tortoise and the hare is usually summed up as 'slow and steady wins the race', yet a thoughtful reader might conclude something quite different: that overconfidence is more dangerous than slowness, or that a race is only lost when you stop running. The hare, after all, is not beaten by the tortoise's speed but by his own nap. A single printed sentence shuts every one of those doors except one.
Some will object that young readers need the moral spelled out or they will miss the point. I disagree. Children are expert judges of fairness and foolishness; they spot a cheat in a playground game long before an adult does. The Dispensary Window
On the first morning of work experience, Aunt Leila handed me a white coat that reached almost to my knees and said, 'Rule one: you don't touch the medicines. Rule two: you watch everything.'
Her pharmacy sat on the main street of Wirrega, between the bakery and the newsagent, and I had expected the week to be dull. I imagined myself stacking shampoo bottles and pricing packets of throat lozenges. Instead, Aunt Leila stood me beside her at the dispensary window, the raised counter at the back where prescriptions were handed over, and for three days I watched the town pass through. She checked every prescription twice, once when she typed the label and again when she handed the bag across, and she never seemed to hurry, even when the queue stretched back to the sunscreen stand.
By Wednesday I knew the regulars. Mrs Abara came in each Monday for her blood pressure tablets and always brought a scone from the bakery for whoever served her. A young farmer named Tom collected cream for his hands, which were cracked like a dry creek bed. Children arrived clutching notes from their parents, and Aunt Leila spoke to each of them as if they were the only customer in the world.
Then, on Thursday, Mr Doyle came in.
He was a tall, stooped man with his cardigan buttoned into the wrong holes, and he placed a plastic shopping bag on the counter. Inside were nine or ten boxes of tablets, some half empty, some unopened. 'I've got myself muddled,' he said quietly. 'My daughter usually sorts them, but she's moved to Adelaide.'
I expected Aunt Leila to sigh, or at least to glance at the clock. The shop was busy, the phone was ringing, and two people were already waiting behind him. Instead she lifted the flap in the counter, came out to his side, and pulled up two chairs at the little table near the window.
'Let's sort it out together,' she said. 'Ruby, could you ask Dimitri to look after the counter?'
For forty minutes she worked through the bag box by box. She checked each label against his records on the computer, set aside two boxes that had expired, and explained every remaining medicine in plain words: this one is for your heart, this one is for your sore knee, this one you take only with food. Although Mr Doyle asked the same question three times, her voice never changed. She drew a chart on a piece of card with a sun for morning and a moon for night, and she promised to pack his tablets into a weekly blister pack so that each day's dose sat in its own little window.
When he finally stood up, he shook her hand, then mine, as though I had done something. 'You've taken a weight off me,' he said.
After he left, I asked Aunt Leila why she hadn't simply printed him a list. She was quiet for a moment as she wiped down the counter.
'A list tells someone what to do,' she said. 'Sitting with them tells them they're not a nuisance. People who feel like a nuisance stop asking questions, and people who stop asking questions make mistakes with their medicine.'
On Friday afternoon Mr Doyle came back for his first blister pack. He had combed his hair and buttoned his cardigan properly, and he had brought two scones from the bakery.
I had arrived at that pharmacy thinking the job was about tablets and labels. I left knowing that the most important thing behind the dispensary window was not on any shelf at all.

Option A: printed him a list of all his medicines from the computer
Option B: came out from behind the counter and pulled up two chairs
Option C: drew him a chart with a sun for morning and a moon for night
Option D: set aside the two boxes of tablets that had expired

In Praise of Turning Back
We tell the stories of explorers as if there is only one ending worth celebrating: the flag on the summit, the footprint at the Pole, the first boat through the strait. Schoolbooks are crowded with people who reached the place they set out for. I would argue that we have been celebrating only half of what makes an explorer great. Some of the bravest decisions in the history of exploration were made by people who stopped, looked at the horizon, and turned around.
The finest example came on the ninth of January, 1909. Ernest Shackleton and three companions had dragged their sledges across the Ross Ice Shelf, up a vast glacier and onto the high, freezing polar plateau. No human had ever been so far south. The South Pole lay just 97 nautical miles ahead, a few more days of marching. Yet their food was running out, their bodies were weakening in the thin, cold air, and every step forward was a step further from the depots that would keep them alive on the way back. Shackleton stood with his companions in the bitter wind, looking south across the endless white. Then he planted a flag, took a photograph and gave the order to go home.
It is hard to imagine what that cost him. He had spent years raising money and planning for this moment. The glory of being first was almost within touching distance, and he knew that if he turned back, someone else would probably claim the prize. They did, less than three years later. But all four men survived the starving march north. Writing to his wife afterwards, Shackleton explained his choice with a wry phrase: he thought she would prefer 'a live donkey' to 'a dead lion'.
Some will argue that turning back is simply failure dressed up in noble language. If everyone turned around when things became difficult, they say, no mountain would ever be climbed and no ocean crossed. This misses the point. Shackleton did not turn back because the journey became hard; every day of it had been hard. He turned back because he calculated, honestly and in terrible conditions, that going on would almost certainly kill the men who trusted him. That is not a lack of courage. It is courage of a rarer and quieter kind: the courage to disappoint yourself.
Modern adventurers have learnt this lesson. Many high-altitude climbing teams agree on a fixed 'turnaround time' before they leave camp on summit day. If they have not reached the top by, say, two o'clock in the afternoon, they turn around, however close the summit appears. The rule exists because the mind becomes a poor judge near the goal. Exhausted and short of oxygen, climbers can talk themselves into one more hour, then another, until there is no longer enough daylight or strength to get down safely. Deciding in advance takes the choice away from the tired, hopeful self on the mountain.
We should teach young people about these decisions as proudly as we teach them about summits. A student who learns only about those who pressed on may come to believe that stopping is always shameful. A student who also learns about Shackleton at 88 degrees south learns something more useful: that the goal is not the only thing that matters, and that knowing when to stop is a skill, not a weakness.
The summit will still be there next year. The explorer who turns back lives to try again.

Option A: he discovered that a rival had already reached it
Option B: he believed going on would cost his men their lives
Option C: his sledges had been badly damaged on the glacier
Option D: he had promised his wife he would be home by January

Circuit Number One
The instructor's door clunked shut, and for the first time in her life Mei was alone in an aeroplane.
Through the side window she watched Gareth walk back across the apron, past the parked planes and the fuel bowser, his hands in his pockets, as casually as if he were leaving a cafe. He did not look back. That, she decided, was either a very good sign or a very bad one.
The little Cessna ticked and shivered around her. She had flown it forty times with Gareth in the right-hand seat, his big hands resting on his knees, ready. Today that seat was empty except for a clipboard and a bottle of water, and the cockpit felt suddenly enormous.
There had been no warning. They had flown three circuits together that morning, and after the third landing Gareth had asked her to stop on the taxiway. He had unbuckled his harness without a word, then leant back in. 'Do one on your own,' he said. 'Exactly the same as you've been doing. I'll be watching from the clubhouse.'
She pressed the radio button. 'Corella traffic, Cessna Kilo Delta Romeo, taxiing for runway two-seven, circuits.' Her voice came out higher than she expected, a stranger's voice. She cleared her throat and tried to look like someone who did this every day.
At the end of the runway she ran through her checks, touching each switch and gauge the way Gareth had drilled into her: fuel on, mixture rich, flaps set, harness tight. The windsock hung limp as a wet towel. No crosswind. No excuses.
She lined up on the centreline, pushed the throttle smoothly forward, and the engine rose from a mutter to a roar. The runway markings blurred beneath the nose. At fifty-five knots she eased back on the control column, and the rumble of the wheels simply stopped.
That was the strangest part. Without Gareth's weight, the aeroplane leapt off the ground sooner than she expected, climbing like a kite let off its string. She laughed aloud, and the sound was swallowed by the engine.
Then the work began. At five hundred feet she turned left onto the crosswind leg, then left again onto downwind, the runway now a grey ribbon sliding past her shoulder. Below, the wheat paddocks were stitched together in squares of gold and green, and a road ran to the horizon as straight as if someone had ruled it with a pencil. She made her radio call, checked her height, checked her speed, checked her height again. Once, she glanced at the empty seat beside her and felt a flutter of panic rise in her chest. Then she heard Gareth's voice in her head, calm and dry as always: fly the aeroplane, Mei, one thing at a time. She breathed out slowly and did exactly that.
Turning onto final approach, she saw the runway ahead, wide and patient, waiting for her. Power back. Flaps down. Hold the nose steady. The ground swelled, the hangars grew, the white numbers on the runway slid beneath her. Hold it, hold it, hold it, she told herself, and the wheels kissed the bitumen with a squeak, then another, and she was rolling, the nose settling gently, the engine sinking back to a mutter.
She did not remember taxiing back. She remembered only Gareth standing at the edge of the apron, no longer casual, his hands out of his pockets now and clapping above his head.
'Well?' he called as she climbed down on legs that felt borrowed.
Mei looked back at the runway and the empty sky above it, already ordinary again.
'Can I go again?' she said.
Question: At what speed did Mei ease back on the control column?
Option A: forty knots
Option B: fifty-five knots
Option C: five hundred knots
Option D: seventy-five knots

The Extra Coin
The honesty box in the Kurrajong High library was a dented biscuit tin with a slot cut into its lid. It sat on a small table near the returns desk, beside a basket of secondhand paperbacks and a hand-lettered sign: ALL BOOKS $1. As library monitor, it was my job to empty the tin each afternoon and record the takings in a spiral notebook.
For most of the term, the sums were boring. Three books gone, three dollars in the tin. Then, one Tuesday in May, I tipped out the coins and found something that did not belong: a small brass-coloured coin with a neat round hole through its centre. The writing on it was not in English. And the basket was one book short.
'Probably someone's idea of a joke,' said Ms Ferreira, the librarian, turning the coin over in her palm. She dropped it into her desk drawer and forgot about it.
I didn't forget. The next Tuesday there was another holed coin and another book missing, and the Tuesday after that, too. Each coin joined the first in Ms Ferreira's drawer. By the fourth week I had started a new page in the notebook headed THE CASE OF THE EXTRA COIN, which my friend Priya said was the most library-monitor thing she had ever heard.
Still, she helped. We listed what we knew. The coins only ever appeared on Tuesdays. Only one book vanished each time, never more. And the missing books were not random. I had kept a list of the basket's contents, and when I checked, the gaps were always the same kind of book: a picture dictionary, a graphic novel about a soccer team, a thin chapter book with large print and drawings on every page.
'Someone who doesn't want a hard read,' Priya said.
'Or someone who can't manage one yet,' I said slowly.
That was when I remembered the timetable pinned up behind the desk. Every Tuesday at lunch, the library was booked for Mr Okafor's English language group, the students who had recently arrived in Australia and were still learning the language. There were six of them. One, a quiet Year 8 boy named Kenji, had started at our school at the beginning of May.
Priya looked up the coin on her phone, scrolling through pictures of foreign money until she found an exact match. It was a fifty-yen piece from Japan, worth well under a dollar.
We could have marched straight to Ms Ferreira with our answer. Priya wanted to; she said a mystery wasn't solved until you announced it. But I kept thinking about that coin. Kenji hadn't stolen anything. He had paid with the only money he had, probably embarrassed that it was the wrong kind and too shy to ask anyone what to do. Announcing the answer would only make him feel worse, and he might stop coming to the library altogether. A mystery, I decided, could be solved without being shouted about.
So instead, the next Monday, I asked Ms Ferreira if we could add something to the sign. She listened, smiled, opened her drawer, and looked at the four coins lying there in a row.
On Tuesday afternoon, the tin held no coin with a hole in it. But tucked under the lid was a folded piece of paper. In careful pencil, someone had written: THANK YOU FOR THE BOOKS. I WILL PAY WHEN I HAVE DOLLARS.
Above the basket, beneath ALL BOOKS $1, a new line in Ms Ferreira's neat handwriting read: NEW STUDENTS: YOUR FIRST TERM'S BOOKS ARE FREE.
Question: On which day of the week did the holed coins appear?
Option A: Monday
Option B: Wednesday
Option C: Friday
Option D: Tuesday

Reading Comprehension Text/Essay/Article:
Paint Over the Mistake
In the early 1950s, a typing error was a small disaster. Offices ran on typewriters, and every letter, report and contract had to be typed perfectly. A single wrong key could mean pulling the page out and starting again. For Bette Nesmith Graham, a single mother working as a secretary at a bank in Dallas, Texas, those mistakes were more than an annoyance. Her job, and the wage that supported her young son, depended on producing clean, error-free pages.
The problem had recently become worse. Offices were switching to new electric typewriters, which used a carbon-film ribbon. The letters they produced were sharp and dark, but they smudged badly when typists tried to rub them out with an eraser. A correction that once took seconds now left a grey smear across the page. Bosses expected perfect work, and a typist who handed in a smudged letter could be told to retype the whole thing.
Graham had an unusual advantage: she was also an artist. To earn extra money, she painted festive designs on the bank's windows each holiday season. As she worked, she noticed that sign painters never tried to scrape off their mistakes. They simply painted over them. Why, she wondered, couldn't a typist do the same?
She went home, mixed some white water-based paint in her kitchen and poured it into a small bottle. At work the next day she used a fine watercolour brush to dab it over her errors. Once it had dried, she could type the correct letter on top. The first mixture was far from perfect: it was lumpy, slow to dry and not quite the right shade of white. But on the page it did its job.
For about five years she used her mixture quietly, almost secretly. But other secretaries noticed, and soon they were asking for bottles of their own. Graham began making it in her kitchen and garage, experimenting with help from a chemistry teacher at her son's school to make the fluid dry faster and cover more neatly. In 1956 she began selling it under the name Mistake Out. Her teenage son, Michael, and his friends earned pocket money filling the bottles.
Growth was slow at first. For years Graham ran the business at night and on weekends while still working at the bank. In 1958 she renamed the product Liquid Paper. Secretaries recommended it to one another, and gradually it spread from desk to desk, then from office to office, and eventually around the world. By the late 1960s the company was selling more than a million bottles a year, and in 1979 Graham sold it to the Gillette company for $47.5 million.
Graham was proud of what she had built, but she was equally interested in how people were treated. When the company built a new headquarters in Dallas in the 1970s, she made sure it included a library and a childcare centre for the children of employees. Later she set up foundations that gave money to help women build careers and businesses of their own.
Graham died in 1980, only months after selling her company. Correction fluid has since been largely replaced by computers and delete keys, but her story remains a reminder that good ideas can come from unexpected places, and that sometimes the cleverest solution to a problem is not to erase it but to cover it up and keep going.
Question: Why did corrections become harder when offices switched to electric typewriters?
Option A: the keys were much harder to press than before
Option B: the paper used in them was too thin to erase
Option C: the carbon-film ribbon smudged when it was rubbed out
Option D: the letters were printed too faintly to fix

She said it was the chance of a lifetime. I said it was the summer holidays, and that my friends were all going to the beach.
Then, on the third morning, I climbed up on deck and stopped complaining.
The ship was sliding through water as flat and dark as oil. On either side, mountains rose straight out of the sea, draped in snow so white it hurt to look at. And everywhere, drifting slowly like a fleet of abandoned ships, were icebergs: some no bigger than a car, others as large as our block of flats, carved into arches, towers and fins.
That afternoon we went out in an inflatable boat with six other passengers and a guide named Tomas, who steered with one hand and talked with the other. Before we left, he gave us a warning. 'We keep our distance from the big ones,' he said. 'An iceberg melts faster underwater than above it. When enough of the bottom has gone, it becomes top-heavy, and it can roll over without any warning at all.'
I nodded as if I were listening, but I was busy photographing a leopard seal asleep on a floe.
We had been out for about twenty minutes when it happened. Across the bay, perhaps three hundred metres away, a tall iceberg gave a crack so loud that several passengers ducked. Then, almost lazily, it began to tilt. Its peak leant further and further, until the whole mountain of ice toppled sideways and rolled, sending a wave racing across the bay that lifted our little boat and set it down again like a toy.

It was blue: a deep, glassy, impossible blue, smooth as polished stone and streaked with pale ribbons where old snow had been pressed into ice.

I realised I had never once asked her why she had spent half my life studying creatures smaller than my little finger, or what it was about this place that kept pulling her back.
On the ride back to the ship, I asked.
She talked the whole way: about krill swarms so vast they tint the sea, about the first time she had seen the ice twenty years ago, about how small and lucky it made her feel. I listened, and for once I didn't look at my phone.

Option B: krill
Option C: penguins
Option D: icebergs

A Flood in the Dry Season
Imagine a place in southern Africa where no rain has fallen for months. The grass has turned brown, the waterholes have shrunk to cracked mud, and dust hangs in the air. Then, in the middle of this dry season, the water begins to rise. Channels fill, lagoons spread, and a vast green wetland swells across the sand. The flood comes from the Okavango River, which travels for more than a thousand kilometres and then, instead of reaching the ocean, simply spreads out and vanishes.
The river begins in the highlands of Angola, where heavy summer rains fall between about November and March. From there it travels south-east, crossing a narrow strip of Namibia before entering Botswana. There, instead of finding a path to the coast, it reaches a vast, almost flat basin of sand on the edge of the Kalahari. Long ago, movements in the Earth's crust created faults that act like low walls, trapping the water in this basin. The river fans out into a maze of channels, lagoons, swamps and islands known as the Okavango Delta.
Most deltas form where a river meets the ocean. The Okavango is called an inland delta because it never reaches the ocean at all. About ninety-five per cent of its water or more is lost to the air, either evaporating under the fierce sun or being drawn up by plants and released through their leaves. Only a tiny fraction trickles out the far side. The delta's size changes with the seasons, too: when the flood is at its peak, the area under water can be more than double what it is at its lowest.
One of the delta's greatest surprises is its timing. The rain that feeds it falls in Angola in the first months of the year, but the water moves slowly across the flat land, pushing through reeds and papyrus. It can take months for the flood to reach the lower parts of the delta. As a result, the floodwaters are usually at their highest between about June and August, during Botswana's dry winter, when the surrounding land has not seen rain for months. Just as the bush becomes parched, the delta swells.
This strange calendar makes the Okavango a lifeline. As waterholes elsewhere dry up, huge numbers of animals move towards the delta. Elephants, buffalo, zebras and hippos gather along its channels, and more than four hundred species of birds have been recorded there. Hippos even help to shape the delta, pushing paths through the reeds that later become open channels. The red lechwe, an antelope with long, splayed hooves, is so well suited to the wet ground that it can bound through shallow water faster than the lions and wild dogs that hunt it.
Even the islands have an unusual origin. Many began as termite mounds. When the floods arrive, the mounds stay just above the water; seeds land on them, trees take root, and over many years the patch of dry ground grows. Some of the delta's thousands of islands are tiny; others stretch for kilometres.
People have lived alongside the Okavango for centuries. Fishing families have long travelled its channels in a mokoro, a narrow canoe pushed along with a long pole and traditionally carved from a single tree trunk, and today guides use the same craft to take visitors quietly past grazing elephants.
In 2014 the Okavango Delta was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. It was the thousandth site to be included, a fitting honour for a river that never reaches the coast, yet carries a flood of life to the edge of a desert.

Option A: on the edge of the Kalahari
Option B: in a narrow strip of Namibia
Option C: in the highlands of Angola
Option D: in the lowlands of Botswana

The Swamp in July
The tortoise in my hands weighed about as much as a mandarin, and it was trying very hard to leave.
'Hold the edges of the shell, not the legs,' Mum said. 'And keep him low. If you drop him from that height, you'll do more damage than any fox.'
I lowered my hands until they were almost brushing the reeds. The tortoise's flat brown shell was no bigger than my palm, and his long neck reached out sideways, his small dark eyes fixed on the water a few metres away. Painted on the back of his shell in white was the number 214.
It was a grey morning in July, and we were standing in a swamp north-east of Perth with six other people, two plastic tubs and a clipboard. Mum had worked on the zoo's breeding program for western swamp tortoises since before I was born. For most of my childhood, these tortoises had been something she talked about at dinner: the hatchlings no bigger than a ten-cent coin, the long, hot summers when the swamps dried and the wild tortoises dug down to wait underground, sometimes for months. I had heard the numbers so often they were like a song. In the 1980s, fewer than fifty were thought to be left in the wild. Australia's rarest reptile, she always said, as if it were a family nickname.
Today was the first time I had been allowed to come. I had begged for three years, and Mum had finally agreed on the condition that I listened, stayed out of the way and did exactly as I was told.
'Why July?' I asked, while the others checked the water depth with a measuring stick.
'Because the swamp's full,' Mum said. 'They can only feed in the water. If we released them in summer, there'd be nothing here but cracked clay. This way they get the whole winter and spring to eat and grow before the dry comes.'
'And then they go underground.'
'And then they go underground, and we hope.'
That word bothered me. I had pictured release day as an ending, the moment the story turned out well. But standing there, watching Mum scan the edge of the swamp, I noticed things I had walked straight past: the tall fence around the reserve, its wire buried deep in the ground to stop foxes digging under it; the stakes marking where earlier tortoises, fitted with tiny transmitters glued to their shells, had last been tracked; a woman with an antenna, walking slowly along the bank, listening.
'Do they all make it?' I asked.
Mum didn't answer straight away. 'Not all,' she said finally. 'But more than before. Every one that does is a tortoise that wouldn't exist otherwise.'
When it was my turn, I crouched at the edge of the water. I set number 214 down on the wet mud and took my hands away.
For a moment he did nothing. I thought perhaps he was frightened, or confused, or simply too used to the tanks at the zoo. Then he pushed forward, slid into the brown water with barely a ripple, and was gone among the tall green reeds.
I stayed crouched there longer than I needed to. The water closed over the place where he had been as if nothing had happened at all.
On the drive home, Mum asked what I thought.
'I thought it would feel like finishing something,' I said. 'It feels more like starting.'
She smiled at the road ahead. 'That,' she said, 'is exactly what it is.'

Option A: a stake that marks the place where a tortoise was released
Option B: a measuring stick used to check the depth of the water
Option C: a small device that sends signals so an animal can be tracked
Option D: a painted number that identifies each tortoise's shell

Valley Fog, Mid-May
Last night the sky was clear and still,
without a breath of wind or cloud,
and stars hung low above the hill,
so sharp they almost seemed too loud.
While Riverton lay fast asleep,
the cold air trickled down the rise
and settled on the river flats
the way a tired dog sinks and lies.

Now morning comes, and Riverton
has vanished in a sea of white.
I step outside at ten to seven:
no street, no shops, no hills in sight,
just our front gate, our letterbox,
the first grey post along the fence,
and after that, a soft blank wall
that swallows every shape and sense.

I breathe, and my own breath joins in,
a little cloud that drifts away;
the air tastes cold and wet as stone,
the colour of a rainy day.
Our neighbour's car creeps past the gate,
its yellow fog-lamps blurred and wide,
and then the sound of it goes too,
as if the white had pulled it inside.

The wire is threaded thick with beads,
each strand a string of tiny glass;
my school shoes darken as I walk
through spiderwebs slung low in grass.
Somewhere the Hendersons' old dog
is barking at a thing unseen,
and somewhere cows are breathing smoke
across a paddock once called green.

The clock tower bells ring seven times
from nowhere I can point towards;
the sound comes muffled, wrapped in wool,
like voices underneath floorboards.
A magpie on the bus-stop sign
looks just as lost as me, and shakes
the wet from off its folded wings
with every jerky hop it makes.

The bus arrives as two pale moons
that swell to headlights, then a door.
Mr Pappas grips the wheel
and creeps along at twenty-four;
he says that on a day like this
the valley road is worse than ice,
that fog has fooled a hundred drivers
and never needed asking twice.

Inside, the windows weep and cloud;
we write our names with fingertips,
and Mai, beside me, swears she saw
a lantern swinging on a ship's
tall mast near Miller's poplars, though
it's just the dairy's light, still on.
The bus groans low in second gear;
the town behind us is long gone.

We climb the switchbacks to the school
that sits up high on Wattle Ridge,
and halfway up, the white thins out,
then tears like paper near the bridge,
and all at once the sun breaks through,
so bright it makes the windows glare.
I turn and see the fog below
as if the valley wasn't there:

a white lake lying flat and calm,
with only treetops poking through,
and somewhere on its silent floor
my house, still waiting for its view.
All morning, from the science lab,
I watch the sun get down to work:
it nibbles at the lake's white rim
and thins the middle into murk.

At recess, kids from down the hill
come stamping in with beaded hair
and say the flats are colder still,
that you can't see your hand down there.
Ms Carter says the sun must work
from top to bottom, day by day,
through layers thick as cotton wool
before it burns the grey away.

The highest paddocks surface first,
then rooftops, then the clock tower's face,
and last of all the river gums,
still holding mist in their embrace.
By lunch the valley's back again,
as ordinary as bread and tea,
and no one down in Riverton
would know just how it looked, but me.

Tonight, if skies stay clear and still,
the fog, Dad says, will creep back in;
I'll leave my curtains open wide
to watch the slow white tide begin.
Question: In the fifth stanza, the word 'muffled' means . . .
Option A: made louder and sharper
Option B: repeated over and over
Option C: rung at the wrong time
Option D: made softer and less clear

The Spiral on the Tideline
The storm had blown itself out by Sunday morning, leaving Shelly Beach strewn with kelp, cuttlebones and the odd thong that had lost its partner. Lena walked the tideline with her younger brother, Theo, who was collecting anything that looked like treasure in a plastic bucket.
'Look at this one,' he called, holding up something dark and twisted. 'It's a screw from a pirate ship.'
Lena took it from him. It was about the length of her hand, brown and leathery, with two thin ridges winding around it like the thread on a corkscrew. It was heavier than it looked, and one end was still tightly sealed.
'It's not a screw,' she said slowly. 'I think it's an egg.'
Theo stared at her as if she had said it was a spaceship. 'Eggs are round.'
'Not shark eggs.' She remembered a poster at the marine centre on the esplanade: a row of strange cases with labels underneath. Some were flat purses with curling tendrils at each corner. One was a spiral, exactly like this.
Theo wanted to put it on the windowsill at home, next to his sea-urchin shells. Lena turned it over in her palm. The surface was cool and slightly slippery, and when she tilted it towards the sun she thought, though she could not be sure, that something shifted inside.
'We're taking it to the marine centre,' she said.
'But I found it.'
'And if it's alive, a windowsill will kill it.'
The marine centre was a squat building that smelled of salt water and disinfectant. A volunteer named Ruth, whose grey plait reached halfway down her back, examined the case under a lamp.
'Port Jackson shark,' she said, smiling. 'The mothers lay these in late winter and wedge them into cracks between rocks with their mouths. The spiral shape helps them stay put. But a big swell can wrench them free.' She ran a thumbnail along the sealed end. 'Most of the ones people bring us are empty. The pup has hatched and swum off, so the end's open and the case is as light as paper. This one's still closed.'
'So there's a baby in there?' Theo asked, suddenly interested.
'Possibly. They take ten or eleven months to hatch, so it may have a long way to go.' Ruth lowered the case into a tank where cold water bubbled over a bed of rocks. 'We'll keep it here and check on it. If it hatches, it'll be about as long as your forearm. Then it goes back to the reef.'
For weeks after that, Lena called in at the centre on her way home from school. Usually there was nothing to see but the brown spiral lying still among the rocks, as patient as a seed in winter soil. Theo lost interest by the second week. Lena did not. She learned that Port Jackson sharks crunch sea urchins with flat back teeth, and that they return to the same reefs year after year to breed.
It was a warm Thursday in October when Ruth met her at the door, grinning. In the tank, nosing along the gravel, was a small shark with a harness-like pattern of dark bands across its back. The empty case lay beside it, its end split open like a seam.
Lena crouched by the glass for a long time. She thought of the windowsill, and of how close the little shark had come to being an ornament.
The following Saturday, she and Ruth carried it in a bucket to the rocks at the northern end of the beach. When it slid out into the clear water, it hesitated, then flicked its tail and vanished into the weed.
Theo, who had come along at the last minute, watched the spot where it had disappeared. 'Next storm,' he said, 'I'm checking every screw.'
Question: Which detail made Ruth think the case might not be empty?
Option A: It had a spiral shape.
Option B: It was brown and leathery.
Option C: It washed up after a storm.
Option D: Its end was still closed.

Leading Lines: A Work-Experience Diary
Monday 15 June
I thought work experience at a stained-glass studio would mean a week of colouring in with glass. I was wrong. Mrs Okafor, who has run Okafor Glass for thirty-one years, handed me safety glasses, a broom and a lecture on glass dust before I'd even put my bag down. Then she showed me the job that will fill the studio for the next month: a window from the old Mechanics' Institute hall, cracked by a falling branch during a storm in March. Six of its forty panels are broken, and one, a blue-and-amber panel showing a sailing ship, is missing a third of its glass.
My job today was sweeping. I swept a lot.
Tuesday 16 June
Today I learned that the dark lines in a stained-glass window aren't painted on. They're strips of lead called cames, shaped like the letter H when you look at them end-on, so a piece of glass can slot into each side. The lead holds the whole picture together, like mortar between bricks. Mrs Okafor says a good glass artist plans the lead lines as part of the design, because your eye follows them before it notices the colours.
She let me practise cutting on scrap. You don't really cut glass; you score a line with a little wheel and then snap it. My first eleven attempts shattered into shards. My twelfth broke almost where I wanted. I've never been so proud of a piece of rubbish.
Wednesday 17 June
We took the ship panel apart. First Mrs Okafor photographed it and made a rubbing, pressing paper over the panel and rubbing with a crayon so the lead lines came through like a map. 'Once you pull the lead out, the original is gone,' she said. 'The rubbing is the only memory you have.'
The missing glass is the problem. The sky behind the ship was a streaky blue that isn't made any more. Mrs Okafor keeps a crate of salvaged glass from demolished houses and shops, and we spent two hours holding pieces up to the window, looking for a match. Nothing was right. Some blues looked fine until the sun came out, then turned purple or grey.
Thursday 18 June
I asked why we didn't just use a modern blue that was close enough. Surely nobody would notice. Mrs Okafor didn't answer. Instead she drove me to the hall, where the undamaged panels are still in place, and pointed at a small panel near the bottom. Decades ago, someone had replaced a cracked piece of green with a slightly yellower green. Once she'd shown me, I couldn't stop seeing it. It looked like a patch on a good shirt.
'Repairs should be honest,' she said, 'but they shouldn't shout.' She told me that restorers often scratch a tiny date along the edge of each replaced piece, hidden under the lead, so future restorers know what's original.
That afternoon she found the blue. It was in the very last box, wrapped in newspaper from 1974: a sheet saved from the same hall when one of its side windows was removed during renovations. It was exactly right.
Friday 19 June
My last day. Mrs Okafor let me score and snap the first new piece of sky. I held my breath, and it broke cleanly, right on the line. She ground the edges smooth and fitted it into the new lead herself, but first she handed me the scriber and pointed to the edge. I scratched '2026' into the glass, small enough that no one will see it once the lead is in place.
That's the strange thing about this work. If we've done it well, nobody who walks past the hall will know we were there. I thought that would bother me. It doesn't. Somewhere in that window, hidden under a strip of lead, is a number I wrote, and in fifty years someone will find it and know exactly what we did.
Question: What damaged the window from the Mechanics' Institute hall?
Option A: a branch that fell during a storm
Option B: a ball thrown during a game
Option C: workers renovating the hall
Option D: a fire in the hall's kitchen

Wedges in Wet Clay
Before the sun climbs off the river,
I pack my lunch of bread and dates
and walk the lane past sleeping doorways
to where the tablet house awaits.
My mother tugs my cloak around me
and tells me, as she always does,
to mind the school father, learn my signs
and be the scribe my grandfather was.

The courtyard smells of reeds and water
and grey clay dug from the river's bed;
the big brother, oldest of the pupils,
has patted it to shapes like bread.
He hands us each a tablet, yielding
the way ripe fruit gives to a thumb,
and checks the reeds we cut for styluses
and trimmed to points the night we come.

I copy what the big brother writes,
pressing each wedge, then pressing twice:
the sign for barley, sign for sheep,
the signs for 'silver' and for 'price'.
My lines must march across the tablet
as straight as furrows in a field,
for clumsy marks, the school father says,
leave every reader's meaning sealed.

The big brother lays his tablet by mine
and runs a finger down each row;
where my wedges lean like reeds in wind,
he taps the clay and murmurs, 'No.'
Where they stand neat, he only nods
and moves along the bench to see
the next boy's work, and I let out
the breath I'd held inside of me.

Mistakes are easy while it's damp:
I smooth them over with my thumb
and start again, the way the river
wipes out our footprints when floods come.
But leave the tablet in the sunlight
and by the afternoon it's set;
the errors harden there for good,
and what is dry, clay won't forget.

At noon we chant the lists together,
the names of every fish and tree,
of every pot and tool and measure
a palace storehouse needs to see.
I know two hundred signs by heart now.
The school father says four hundred more,
and then, perhaps, in seven summers,
I'll keep the tallies at a storehouse door.

The lists are long and dull to learn:
a hundred kinds of wood, of stone,
of birds that wade along the marshes,
of every fish the nets have known.
But when I write the sign for 'river',
I see the river where it bends,
and when I write the sign for 'sheep',
I hear them bleating as day ends.

My father counts the grain in baskets
and cannot read a single line;
he marks the tablets other men write
with a little seal, a carved design.
He says that men who hold the stylus
are trusted when the harvest's in,
and never sent to dig the ditches
where other boys like me begin.

Each dawn I pass the palace storehouse,
where tablets stand in rows on shelves,
the counts of barley, oil and wool
that only scribes can read themselves,
each one a promise someone made
and pressed in clay for all to see,
so no one later can pretend
the count was less than it should be.

Today, when all the rest had hurried
home through the dust to their evening meal,
I took a pinch of leftover clay
and flattened it with my palm's heel.
I wrote my name, my father's name,
and 'Today I learned the sign for sun',
then pressed the date, the way the scribes do
when any useful work is done.

They say a fire that takes a storehouse
will turn its tablets hard as stone,
so words that should have dried and crumbled
last on when all their writers have gone.
I pushed my little tablet deep
into a crack beside the door.
Perhaps a stranger, not yet born,
will read my name when I'm no more.

Option B: A young pupil describes learning to write on clay and hopes his words will last.
Option C: A school father explains to his pupils how to make tablets from river clay.
Option D: A boy describes a fire that destroyed the storehouse where his tablets were kept.

Before the sun climbs off the river,
I pack my lunch of bread and dates
and walk the lane past sleeping doorways
to where the tablet house awaits.
My mother tugs my cloak around me
and tells me, as she always does,
to mind the school father, learn my signs
and be the scribe my grandfather was.

The courtyard smells of reeds and water
and grey clay dug from the river's bed;
the big brother, oldest of the pupils,
has patted it to shapes like bread.
He hands us each a tablet, yielding
the way ripe fruit gives to a thumb,
and checks the reeds we cut for styluses
and trimmed to points the night we come.

I copy what the big brother writes,
pressing each wedge, then pressing twice:
the sign for barley, sign for sheep,
the signs for 'silver' and for 'price'.
My lines must march across the tablet
as straight as furrows in a field,
for clumsy marks, the school father says,
leave every reader's meaning sealed.

The big brother lays his tablet by mine
and runs a finger down each row;
where my wedges lean like reeds in wind,
he taps the clay and murmurs, 'No.'
Where they stand neat, he only nods
and moves along the bench to see
the next boy's work, and I let out
the breath I'd held inside of me.

Mistakes are easy while it's damp:
I smooth them over with my thumb
and start again, the way the river
wipes out our footprints when floods come.
But leave the tablet in the sunlight
and by the afternoon it's set;
the errors harden there for good,
and what is dry, clay won't forget.

At noon we chant the lists together,
the names of every fish and tree,
of every pot and tool and measure
a palace storehouse needs to see.
I know two hundred signs by heart now.
The school father says four hundred more,
and then, perhaps, in seven summers,
I'll keep the tallies at a storehouse door.

The lists are long and dull to learn:
a hundred kinds of wood, of stone,
of birds that wade along the marshes,
of every fish the nets have known.
But when I write the sign for 'river',
I see the river where it bends,
and when I write the sign for 'sheep',
I hear them bleating as day ends.

My father counts the grain in baskets
and cannot read a single line;
he marks the tablets other men write
with a little seal, a carved design.
He says that men who hold the stylus
are trusted when the harvest's in,
and never sent to dig the ditches
where other boys like me begin.

Each dawn I pass the palace storehouse,
where tablets stand in rows on shelves,
the counts of barley, oil and wool
that only scribes can read themselves,
each one a promise someone made
and pressed in clay for all to see,
so no one later can pretend
the count was less than it should be.

Today, when all the rest had hurried
home through the dust to their evening meal,
I took a pinch of leftover clay
and flattened it with my palm's heel.
I wrote my name, my father's name,
and 'Today I learned the sign for sun',
then pressed the date, the way the scribes do
when any useful work is done.

They say a fire that takes a storehouse
will turn its tablets hard as stone,
so words that should have dried and crumbled
last on when all their writers have gone.
I pushed my little tablet deep
into a crack beside the door.
Perhaps a stranger, not yet born,
will read my name when I'm no more.

Option A: He smooths it with his thumb while the clay is still damp.
Option B: He scrapes it off with his reed once the clay has dried.
Option C: He leaves the tablet in the sun so the error hardens.
Option D: He asks the big brother to rewrite the sign for him.

Books on a Chain
Walk into the chained library at Hereford Cathedral in England and you will see something that looks, at first, like a mistake. Hundreds of old books stand on wooden shelves with their spines facing the wall. From the front edge of each one hangs a slim iron chain, and the chains run down to a metal rod along the shelf. The books are not being punished. They are being protected, and the way they are arranged tells a story about how precious books once were.
Before the printing press reached Europe in the fifteenth century, every book was copied by hand. A single volume could take a scribe months, sometimes years, to complete. The pages were usually made of parchment, prepared from animal skin, and a large book might need the skins of dozens of animals. Bindings were often wooden boards covered in leather and fitted with brass clasps. Such a book could be worth as much as a farm. Leaving it on an open shelf, where anyone might tuck it under a cloak, would have been foolish.
Libraries solved the problem with chains. A short chain was riveted to the edge of the front cover rather than the spine, because the spine had to flex each time the book was opened. The other end of the chain finished in a ring that slid along a rod. A reader could lift the book down onto a sloping desk or a reading shelf attached to the bookcase and read it there, but could carry it no further than the chain allowed. When a librarian needed to remove a book, he unlocked the rod and slid the ring off.
Because the chain was fixed to the front edge, books had to be shelved the 'wrong' way round, with that edge facing outward so the chain would not twist or tangle. This created a new difficulty: with no visible spines, how could readers find what they wanted? Some libraries wrote titles on the page edges in ink. Others pinned a handwritten list to the end of each bookcase, recording which books sat on which shelf.
Chains were not the only defence. Some owners wrote warnings inside their books, and many of these took the form of short rhymes. A typical example, written in the spirit of those found in old volumes, might run:
This book is mine, and mine alone;
Return it, friend, unto its home.
If you should take it, mark it well:
Its owner's name the page will tell.
Verses like this had a practical purpose. A short verse with a steady beat and matching end sounds sticks in the memory far better than a plain sentence, so a reader was more likely to remember the warning.
Chained libraries were common across Europe for several centuries, but as printing made books cheaper and more plentiful, the chains gradually came off. By the eighteenth century most libraries had abandoned them, and the iron was often sold for scrap. That makes the few survivors especially valuable to historians. Hereford's collection, with around 1,500 chained books on bookcases built in the early 1600s, is often described as the largest surviving example. In the Dutch town of Zutphen, a small library founded in the 1560s still keeps its chained books on sloping desks, much as they were.
Today, of course, libraries guard their collections differently, with barcodes, security gates and digital catalogues. Yet the problem they are solving is the old one. A library must let people use its books while making sure the books are still there for the next reader. The chains of Hereford were simply a heavier answer to a question every librarian still asks.

Option A: an adjective

Option D: a noun

Reading Fossil Dung
When most people picture a fossil, they imagine a skull, a claw or a long line of backbones. Bones are thrilling, but they can tell scientists only so much. A skeleton shows what an animal looked like; it rarely shows what the animal did. For that, palaeontologists often turn to a humbler kind of evidence: fossilised droppings, known as coprolites.
The name comes from two Greek words meaning 'dung' and 'stone', and it was introduced in 1829 by the English geologist William Buckland. Buckland had been puzzling over strange stony lumps found inside the skeletons of ichthyosaurs, the dolphin-shaped marine reptiles collected along the Dorset coast by the fossil hunter Mary Anning. Anning had noticed that when the lumps were broken open, they contained fish bones and scales. Buckland concluded that they were the remains of the reptiles' last meals, preserved where the gut had been, and that similar lumps on the old sea floor were their droppings.
Coprolites form only under unusual conditions. Most dung is quickly eaten by beetles, broken down by bacteria or washed away by rain. To become a fossil, a dropping must be buried rapidly, often in fine mud or volcanic ash, and then slowly hardened as minerals seep into it. Droppings from meat-eaters have an advantage here. Because they contain crushed bone, they are rich in phosphate, a mineral that helps them harden before they rot. This is one reason coprolites from predators are far more common than those from plant-eaters.
Once found, a coprolite can be sliced into thin sections, polished and examined under a microscope. Inside, scientists have discovered fragments of bone, fish scales, insect parts, pollen, seeds and even the remains of tiny parasites. Each item is a clue to an ancient food web, showing not just who ate whom, but what grew nearby and which pests troubled the animals.
One of the most famous examples was discovered in Saskatchewan, Canada, in the 1990s. Longer than a school ruler and packed with splintered bone, it could only have come from a very large meat-eater, and the age and location of the rock pointed to Tyrannosaurus rex. Palaeontologist Karen Chin found that between a third and a half of the specimen was made of bone fragments from a young dinosaur. The finding confirmed what tooth marks on other fossils had suggested: T. rex did not merely slice flesh but crunched through bone with tremendous force.
Plant-eaters have their surprises, too. In Montana, Chin examined coprolites thought to belong to large duck-billed dinosaurs and found that they contained chunks of rotting wood. Since rotting wood is not especially nourishing, she suggested the dinosaurs may have been eating it for the fungi and small creatures living inside, a little like a snack hidden in a log.
There is one awkward problem with coprolites: it is very hard to know exactly who left them. Unless a dropping is found inside a skeleton, scientists must work like detectives, comparing its size, shape and contents with the animals known from the same rock layer. A coprolite is rarely signed.
Even so, these unglamorous fossils are prized. A skeleton is a portrait of an animal; a coprolite is a page from its diary, recording a single meal eaten on a single day millions of years ago.

Option A: plainer
Option B: older
Option C: rarer
Option D: stranger

The Herbarium Sheets
Monday 5 January
Mum says the summer holidays are 'too long to waste', which is how I ended up spending them in a basement that smells of old paper and mothballs. I need twenty hours of community service for the Year 9 Service Award, and the Wimmera Regional Herbarium was the only place that would take a fourteen-year-old. Dr Mehta, the curator, showed me round. There are rows of grey metal cabinets, and inside them about 60,000 sheets of stiff card, each with a dried plant glued or stitched onto it and a label in the bottom corner. Some date back to the 1850s.
My job is to photograph each sheet, then type the label details into the online database: plant name, collector, date and place. Today I did forty-two. That leaves roughly 59,958.
Tuesday 6 January
The labels are the hard part. Half of them are written in faded ink by people whose handwriting looks as if a spider fell in an inkwell. I asked Dr Mehta if I could fix the obvious spelling mistakes, and she said absolutely not. 'Type exactly what's there,' she said, 'and put your best guess in square brackets afterwards. If you correct it silently, nobody will ever know what the collector actually wrote, and you might be wrong.' She told me about a researcher who spent a month hunting for a creek that had been 'corrected' to the wrong name in an old catalogue.
Fifty-one sheets today.
Wednesday 7 January
Dr Mehta caught me yawning and asked whether I knew why we were bothering. I said, honestly, not really. So she pulled out two sheets of the same wattle, one collected in 1902 and one in 2011, both from near Horsham and both in full flower. The first was picked on 28 August; the second on 3 August. She said scientists have compared thousands of sheets like these, and some plants now flower weeks earlier than they did a century ago, probably because of warmer winters. Nobody in 1902 was thinking about that. They just pressed a flower and wrote down the date.
'Every sheet is a witness,' she said. 'It saw something we can't see any more.'
Sixty-three sheets today. I read every label properly.
Thursday 8 January
Something strange. I found a sheet of a tiny orchid, about the height of my finger, collected on 14 October 1893 by 'Miss E. Harcourt' at 'Merrin, in the grassland by the railway'. I looked Merrin up. It's a locality about forty minutes from here, and on satellite maps it's nothing but wheat paddocks and a grain silo. I searched the database: no record of that orchid anywhere near Merrin since 1893.
When I showed Dr Mehta, she went very quiet, then said, 'This is why herbaria matter. Sometimes a sheet like this is the only proof a plant grew somewhere before the ploughs arrived.'
I also found out that Miss Harcourt collected more than 300 sheets in this herbarium. There's no biography of her anywhere, not even a first name.
Friday 9 January
I've finished my twenty hours. I've done 286 sheets, and I could stop now and collect my award.
I'm not stopping. Dr Mehta says the orchid sometimes survives along old roadsides and railway lines, where the ground was never ploughed, and the railway at Merrin still runs past the silo. She's applying for permission to survey the strip next October, when the orchid would flower, and she says I can come if I'm still volunteering.
I'll be here every Tuesday next term. Somebody has to find out what the E stands for.
Question: What is the writer's job at the herbarium?
Option A: photographing sheets and typing their label details
Option B: pressing new plants and gluing them to card
Option C: cleaning the metal cabinets in the basement
Option D: correcting spelling mistakes on old labels

The Quiet Spin Above Your Head
On a sticky January night, millions of Australians reach for the same remote control. The air-conditioner beeps, the unit outside rumbles into life and, a few minutes later, cool air pours into the room. It feels like a miracle, and on the worst nights it can be one. It is also, very often, an expensive way to solve a problem that a cheaper, quieter machine could handle. That machine is probably already hanging from your ceiling, and it is time we started using it.
A ceiling fan does not actually cool the air at all. Instead, it moves air across your skin, carrying heat away from your body and speeding up the evaporation of sweat. The result is a breeze that can make a room feel two or three degrees cooler than it really is. That may not sound like much, but on a warm evening it is often the difference between restless tossing and a comfortable night's sleep.
The real argument for the fan, however, is the power bill. A typical ceiling fan uses somewhere between 30 and 80 watts, about the same as an old-fashioned light globe. A split-system air-conditioner cooling a bedroom typically draws ten to twenty times as much. Run for eight hours a night across a long summer, that gap can easily add up to well over a hundred dollars. Multiply it by every home on a hot street and you begin to see why electricity networks strain during heatwaves, when air-conditioners all switch on at once.
Some will say that fans are useless in a real heatwave, and on the very hottest days that is partly true. When the air is above body temperature, blowing it around offers little relief, and the elderly and the unwell need proper cooling for their health. But these days are the exception. For most of an Australian summer, nights sit in the low to mid twenties, exactly the range where a fan can do the job alone.
Even when the air-conditioner is necessary, the fan can help. Government energy advice suggests that every degree you raise the air-conditioner's thermostat can cut its running costs by up to ten per cent. Set the air-conditioner to 25 degrees instead of 21, switch on the fan, and the room will feel almost as cool for a fraction of the cost. The two machines are not rivals; they are teammates.
Others complain that fans are noisy or old-fashioned. Anyone who has slept under a rattling fan from the 1980s will understand. But modern fans with efficient motors are close to silent, and many come with remote controls and several speeds. Some even run in reverse in winter, gently pushing warm air that has gathered near the ceiling back down into the room.
Fans have another quiet advantage. They are cheap to buy, simple to repair and, unlike air-conditioners, they contain no refrigerant gases that can harm the atmosphere if they leak. A good fan can spin faithfully for twenty years, asking for nothing more than a wipe of dust from its blades each spring.
So when the next warm night arrives, try a small experiment before you reach for the remote. Open a window if the air outside is cooler, switch on the fan and give it ten minutes. You may find that the cheapest, gentlest cooling in the house has been circling patiently above your head all along.

Option A: angry and scornful
Option B: sad and nostalgic
Option C: enthusiastic and practical
Option D: cautious and doubtful

The Gap Where the Old Tree Fell
The cyclone had passed two nights earlier, but the rainforest was still dripping when Dad and I set off along the track behind the field station. He walked quickly, the way he does when he is worried, his camera bag thumping against his hip. For eleven years he had photographed the same red cedar on the first day of every month. Forty-two metres tall, he liked to tell visitors, and older than any building in Cairns. He called it the Old Man. On my first visit, when I was six, I had tried to hug its trunk and needed four other children to reach all the way around.
I knew before we reached the bend what we would find. The track was littered with snapped branches, and the light was wrong: too bright, too white, falling in places it had never reached before.
The Old Man lay across the creek like a bridge nobody had asked for. Its roots stood up in a muddy wall taller than Dad, still clutching stones the size of footballs. Where its crown had been, there was simply sky.
Dad didn't say anything. He lifted the camera, lowered it, then lifted it again, as if he couldn't decide whether this counted as one of the photographs. I wanted to say something useful, but everything I thought of sounded like a sympathy card. So I stood beside him and listened to the forest drip.
After a while he sat down on a buttress root and I wandered into the clearing. Mud sucked at my boots. The air in the gap was warmer than the air under the canopy, and already it smelled different: sharp and green, like cut stems. Somewhere above us a catbird was making its strange, wailing call. Beetles were tracking across the fallen bark. A pair of Ulysses butterflies tumbled through the sunlight, flashing electric blue, then vanished into the shade as though someone had switched them off.
Then I crouched and saw them. Seedlings, dozens of them, were pushing up through the leaf litter, some no taller than my thumb. A few had only two leaves, pale and creased like tiny paper fans. Others were knee-high saplings, thin as pencils, that I must have walked past a hundred times without noticing.
"Dad," I called. "Come and look at this."
He came slowly. When I showed him, he knelt in the mud and was quiet for a long time. Then he explained, in his lecturing voice, which I have never been so glad to hear, that rainforest seedlings can survive for years in the deep shade of the forest floor, barely growing, until a tree falls and opens a hole in the canopy. Then they race. Whichever sapling reaches the light first wins the gap; the others are shaded out.
"So the Old Man's not finished," I said.
"Not exactly." He picked a fleck of bark from his knee. "He's just changed jobs."
He took a photograph of the seedlings, then one of the empty sky, then one of me. On the walk back he talked about starting a new series: the same patch of ground on the first day of every month until one of the saplings closed the gap. That might take twenty years, he said. I'd be thirty-four.
"You'll have to carry the tripod," he said.
"I'll be carrying you by then," I told him, and he laughed for the first time in two days.
That evening the rain came back, heavy and warm, drumming on the tin roof of the field station. Dad sat at the table sorting eleven years of photographs into a single folder. I lay awake thinking about the seedlings out there in the dark, drinking.
