Option A: once a week since he arrived
Option B: on the first day of every month
Option C: once each year after the wet season
Option D: on the first day of each new season

The Mayor Who Built a Subway Above Ground
On a Friday evening in 1972, construction crews in Curitiba, a city in southern Brazil, began tearing up the road surface of Rua XV de Novembro, one of the busiest streets in the city centre. They worked through the night and all weekend. By Monday morning the cars were gone. In their place were paving stones, lamps and flower beds. Shopkeepers who had threatened to take the city to court were soon asking for the walking zone to be extended past their own doors.
The man behind this overnight change was Jaime Lerner, the city's new mayor. He had moved quickly on purpose. He knew that if the plan were debated for months, it might never happen; once people had seen a street full of walkers instead of traffic, he believed, they would not want the cars back.
Lerner was born in Curitiba in 1937, the son of immigrants from Poland who ran a fabric shop near the railway station. As a boy he watched the circus that camped near his home, and he later said that a city should be a kind of stage where people meet. He trained as an architect and urban planner and, in 1971, at the age of thirty-three, was appointed mayor.
Curitiba was growing fast, and many planners insisted that the answer was an underground railway. Lerner disagreed. A subway would cost a fortune and take years to dig. Why not, he asked, make buses behave like trains? In 1974 the city opened its first dedicated bus lanes, where buses ran in their own corridors, separated from cars, so that they no longer crawled through traffic. Over the following years the network grew into a web of express, feeder and cross-town routes, colour-coded so that passengers could tell at a glance which bus to catch. New buses could be bought far more cheaply than new tunnels could be dug.
His most memorable invention came in 1991: the tube station. These glass cylinders, raised to the height of the bus floor, allowed passengers to pay before boarding and then step straight on, with no stairs and no fumbling for coins. A bus could load in seconds, and drivers no longer had to handle money. Wheelchair users rode a small lift into the tube and rolled onto the bus at the same level. Lerner liked to call the system a surface subway: the speed of a metro at a fraction of the price.
Lerner's ideas were not only about transport. When rubbish piled up in hillside neighbourhoods that garbage trucks could not reach, the city offered bus tokens and food in exchange for bags of sorted waste. Parks were built on flood-prone land so that rivers had somewhere to spread instead of swamping homes.
He also had a gift for the small, cheerful gesture. Soon after the walking street opened, a group of drivers announced that they would reclaim it with their cars. When they arrived, they found the street covered in long rolls of paper and hundreds of children sitting on it, painting. The cars turned back.
Lerner served three terms as mayor and later became governor of the state of Parana. He described his approach as urban acupuncture: small, quick, precise actions that could relieve pressure on a whole city, just as a needle placed at the right point is said to ease pain in the body. Today, bus rapid transit systems inspired by Curitiba carry passengers in cities from Bogota to Guangzhou. Lerner died in 2021, aged eighty-three, but the bright tubes, buses and boulevards of his home city still bear his mark.

Option B: to explain how the tube stations worked
Option C: to describe the problems caused by rubbish
Option D: to list the cities that copied Curitiba's buses

The Second Touch
When Coach Ferris read out the positions at the first training session of the season, Lani Tuilagi heard her own name followed by the word she had been dreading: setter.
She had spent the whole summer practising her jump. She had imagined herself rising above the net, arm drawn back, slamming the ball into the floor on the other side while the crowd in the Westvale gym roared. Setters didn't do that. Setters took the second touch, the soft one, and pushed the ball up for somebody else to hit.
"You see the whole court," Coach Ferris told her afterwards, when Lani asked why. "Hitters see the ball. You see everyone."
It did not feel like a compliment.
For most of the season Lani did the job the simplest way she knew. Whenever the ball came to her, she set it high to Jada Okafor on the left side. Jada was the tallest girl in the under-sixteen competition and could hit the ball so hard that opposing players flinched. Westvale won eight games in a row. Lani's sets were neat and reliable, and her name almost never appeared in the match reports. Nobody complained, least of all Jada.
Ruby Chen had joined the team halfway through the season after moving from Perth. She was quiet and, in matches, nervous; twice she had served straight into the net and spent the rest of the game on the bench. But after training on Thursdays, while the others packed up, Ruby stayed back to practise hitting, and Lani stayed too, partly because someone had to set for her and partly because she secretly enjoyed it. Ruby, Lani discovered, had a fast, flat swing that seemed to come from nowhere. The ball barely touched her palm before it hit the floor.
In the semi-final against Kingsley, everything went wrong. Kingsley had studied them. Every time Lani set to Jada, two blockers were already waiting, their hands a wall above the net. Jada was blocked once, then twice, then a third time in a row, and Westvale fell behind 18-21 in the deciding set. Coach Ferris called a time-out. Somewhere behind the bench, a parent's air horn blared and fell silent.
In the huddle, Jada was red-faced and breathing hard. "They know where it's going," she said. "Every single time."
Coach Ferris didn't look at Jada. She looked at Lani. "Then the setter decides where it goes."
Lani glanced across at Ruby, who had come on as a substitute only a few points earlier and was staring at her shoes.
On the next rally the pass came to Lani cleanly. She could see both Kingsley blockers drifting left, towards Jada. Lani pushed the ball the other way, low and quick, to Ruby on the right.
Ruby swung and hit it straight into the net.
A groan rose from the Westvale parents. Ruby's face crumpled. Lani walked over and said only, "Same again. I'm not changing it."
The next pass was rougher, but Lani got under it and sent the same set to the same place. This time Ruby's flat, fast swing caught the Kingsley blockers still leaning towards Jada. The ball smacked into the floor before anyone moved.
After that, Kingsley did not know where to look. When their blockers shifted right, Lani set Jada; when they stayed left, she set Ruby. Westvale won the next seven points and the match.
In the change room, Jada dropped her bag next to Lani's. "That was the best you've played all year," she said.
"I didn't hit a single ball," Lani said.
"I know," said Jada. "That's what I mean."
Question: Which of these events happened first?
Option A: Coach Ferris named Lani as the team's setter.
Option B: Ruby joined the team after moving from Perth.
Option C: Westvale won eight games in a row.
Option D: Jada was blocked three times in a row.

The Bird That Leads the Way to Honey
In the dry woodlands of northern Mozambique, a honey hunter walks between the trees making a strange sound: a loud trill followed by a grunt, "brrr-hm". Within minutes, a small brownish bird lands on a branch nearby and begins to chatter. When the hunter follows, the bird flies ahead from tree to tree, pausing so that he can keep up, until it reaches a tree with a wild bees' nest hidden inside. The hunter calms the bees with smoke, chops open the trunk and takes the honeycomb. The bird waits. When the people leave, it flies down to feast on what remains.
This bird is the greater honeyguide (Indicator indicator), and the partnership described above is one of the few known cases in which humans and a wild animal cooperate so that both sides benefit. (Another famous example involves dolphins that help fishers in southern Brazil.)
Each partner supplies what the other lacks. Honeyguides are among the very few birds able to digest beeswax, and they also eat the bee larvae inside the comb. However, they cannot break into a nest buried deep inside a tree trunk, and an angry swarm can be deadly to a small bird. People, on the other hand, have axes and smoke, but wild nests are hard to find, often tucked inside hollow trunks where a person could walk past a hundred times without noticing. The bird knows where the nests are, whereas the humans know how to open them.
For a long time, scientists wondered whether the birds were really responding to people's calls or were simply following anyone who happened to be walking in the forest. In 2016, Claire Spottiswoode of the University of Cambridge tested this with Yao honey hunters in Mozambique's Niassa Reserve. She played recordings of the "brrr-hm" call, of ordinary spoken words and of another bird's song. The special call roughly doubled the chance of a honeyguide leading the way, and it raised the chance of finding a nest from about 17 per cent to 54 per cent. In other words, the birds were not just following people; they were listening to them.
Not every community uses the same signal. About 1,500 kilometres to the north, Hadza honey hunters in Tanzania call the birds with a melodious whistle. A 2023 study found that honeyguides in each region responded far more strongly to their own local call than to the call from the other country. In both places, the calls are passed down from older hunters to younger ones.
The honeyguide has a less charming side. It is a brood parasite: instead of raising its own young, the female lays her eggs in the nests of other birds, such as bee-eaters. The honeyguide chick hatches with a sharp hook on the tip of its bill, which it uses to kill the host's chicks, so that it receives all the food. Because honeyguides are raised by other species, scientists are still working out how young birds learn to guide people at all.
The tradition faces an uncertain future. In many places, sugar has become cheap, so fewer people hunt for wild honey; where people stop answering the birds, the birds eventually stop guiding. In some areas, hunters bury or burn the leftover wax rather than leaving it behind. Researchers are now recording the calls and stories of honey hunters, hoping to understand this ancient partnership before it fades. It may have lasted for many thousands of years, but it survives only as long as both partners keep their side of the bargain.

Option A: a loud trill followed by a grunt
Option B: a melodious whistle
Option C: a sharp clap of the hands
Option D: a soft chattering call

The Flower That Reads the Soil
Two gardeners buy identical hydrangeas from the same nursery on the same day. Each plant is covered in soft pink flower heads. A year later, one gardener's plant is still pink, but the other's has turned a deep, cool blue. Neither gardener has done anything special. What happened?
The answer lies beneath their feet. The bigleaf hydrangea, the kind with round heads like crumpled pom-poms, is one of the few garden plants whose flower colour depends on the soil it grows in. In a sense it is a living chemistry test, quietly reporting on the ground below. Bigleaf hydrangeas originally came from Japan, where they have been grown in gardens for centuries.
The colour comes from a pigment in the flowers called delphinidin, which on its own produces pink or red. When this pigment combines with aluminium, it turns blue. Almost all soils contain aluminium, but whether a plant can absorb it depends on the soil's pH, a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is. In acidic soil, with a pH below about 5.5, aluminium dissolves easily in the water around the roots, and the plant draws it up into its flowers. In neutral or alkaline soil, with a pH above about 6.5, the aluminium stays locked up in forms the roots cannot take in, and the flowers stay pink. In between, the result is often a muddle of mauve and purple.
This explains why hydrangeas in some regions are famous for their blues. In much of the Blue Mountains west of Sydney, the soil is naturally acidic, and hedges of hydrangeas glow sapphire and violet each summer. In parts of Adelaide, where many soils are alkaline, the same varieties more often bloom in shades of pink. It even explains the odd bush that flowers blue on one side and pink on the other: its roots have spread into two patches of soil with different chemistry, perhaps where old concrete or builders' rubble has made one corner more alkaline.
Gardeners can use this knowledge to choose their colour. To encourage blue, they can make the soil more acidic and add aluminium sulfate, which supplies aluminium directly. To encourage pink, they can dig in garden lime, which raises the pH. The change is not instant. Because the colour depends on what the roots absorb over many months, it may take a full season, or even two, before the flowers respond. Plants in pots change more quickly, since there is less soil to adjust. Gardeners in areas with hard, alkaline tap water may notice their blue potted hydrangeas slowly drifting towards pink unless they water with rainwater.
Not every hydrangea plays along. White varieties lack the pigment and stay white whatever the soil. Folk remedies, such as burying rusty nails beside the roots, do little, because iron is not the metal that matters.
There is one more surprise. The colourful parts most people call petals are actually sepals, the leaf-like structures that usually protect a flower bud. In many hydrangeas, these showy sepals surround tiny fertile flowers that are easy to overlook. In lacecap hydrangeas the effect is easy to see: a flat cluster of tiny flowers is ringed by a halo of larger, showy ones. The bright display acts like a signboard, drawing bees and other insects to the small flowers that produce the seeds.
So the next time you walk past a hedge of hydrangeas, look closely at the colour. Each flower head is a small report on the ground below, written in shades of pink and blue.

Option D: take in

Two gardeners buy identical hydrangeas from the same nursery on the same day. Each plant is covered in soft pink flower heads. A year later, one gardener's plant is still pink, but the other's has turned a deep, cool blue. Neither gardener has done anything special. What happened?
The answer lies beneath their feet. The bigleaf hydrangea, the kind with round heads like crumpled pom-poms, is one of the few garden plants whose flower colour depends on the soil it grows in. In a sense it is a living chemistry test, quietly reporting on the ground below. Bigleaf hydrangeas originally came from Japan, where they have been grown in gardens for centuries.
The colour comes from a pigment in the flowers called delphinidin, which on its own produces pink or red. When this pigment combines with aluminium, it turns blue. Almost all soils contain aluminium, but whether a plant can absorb it depends on the soil's pH, a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is. In acidic soil, with a pH below about 5.5, aluminium dissolves easily in the water around the roots, and the plant draws it up into its flowers. In neutral or alkaline soil, with a pH above about 6.5, the aluminium stays locked up in forms the roots cannot take in, and the flowers stay pink. In between, the result is often a muddle of mauve and purple.
This explains why hydrangeas in some regions are famous for their blues. In much of the Blue Mountains west of Sydney, the soil is naturally acidic, and hedges of hydrangeas glow sapphire and violet each summer. In parts of Adelaide, where many soils are alkaline, the same varieties more often bloom in shades of pink. It even explains the odd bush that flowers blue on one side and pink on the other: its roots have spread into two patches of soil with different chemistry, perhaps where old concrete or builders' rubble has made one corner more alkaline.
Gardeners can use this knowledge to choose their colour. To encourage blue, they can make the soil more acidic and add aluminium sulfate, which supplies aluminium directly. To encourage pink, they can dig in garden lime, which raises the pH. The change is not instant. Because the colour depends on what the roots absorb over many months, it may take a full season, or even two, before the flowers respond. Plants in pots change more quickly, since there is less soil to adjust. Gardeners in areas with hard, alkaline tap water may notice their blue potted hydrangeas slowly drifting towards pink unless they water with rainwater.
Not every hydrangea plays along. White varieties lack the pigment and stay white whatever the soil. Folk remedies, such as burying rusty nails beside the roots, do little, because iron is not the metal that matters.
There is one more surprise. The colourful parts most people call petals are actually sepals, the leaf-like structures that usually protect a flower bud. In many hydrangeas, these showy sepals surround tiny fertile flowers that are easy to overlook. In lacecap hydrangeas the effect is easy to see: a flat cluster of tiny flowers is ringed by a halo of larger, showy ones. The bright display acts like a signboard, drawing bees and other insects to the small flowers that produce the seeds.
So the next time you walk past a hedge of hydrangeas, look closely at the colour. Each flower head is a small report on the ground below, written in shades of pink and blue.

Slow Inheritance
When Great-Gran moved into the home on Elder Street,
there were things that could not follow her:
the lemon tree, the piano with its yellowed keys,
the garden she had dug for sixty years.
The roses went to the neighbours. The piano went to Mum.
And the tortoise, in a fruit box lined with straw,
came to me.

"Her name is Agatha," Great-Gran said,
pressing a list into my hand: dandelions, not lettuce;
a warm brick in the sun each morning;
a bowl of water shallow enough to stand in.
"She was a present from my father
the summer I turned eight. Look after her.
She's looked after me."

I could not see how a tortoise looked after anyone.
For a week Agatha did nothing I could name.
She sat beneath the fern. She chewed one leaf
for what felt like a whole afternoon.
I tapped her shell. I told her she was boring.
She blinked at me as if I were a kind of weather
she had seen before and would see again.

At night I heard her scraping in the box,
a slow, dry sound like someone sanding wood.
I worried she was lonely, or cold, or sad,
then worried I was silly to have worried.
I typed Do tortoises get bored? into my laptop
and closed it again, none the wiser.

What do you do with a pet that will not fetch,
that will not purr, that will not learn its name?
I asked my friends. They laughed. I asked my mum,
who shrugged and said, "Then go and ask Great-Gran.
She's had her longer than she's had any of us."

So on Sunday, with the fruit box on my knees,
I caught the bus to Elder Street.
Great-Gran was in the sunroom by the window.
When she saw the box, her whole face changed.
She lifted Agatha out with careful hands
and set her on the blanket on her lap,
and Agatha, who'd never once come out for me,
stretched her leathery neck as far as it would go
and turned her ancient head towards the light.

"She knows you," I said. Great-Gran only laughed.
"She knows the sun. She knows the way I hold her.
She's heard my voice since nineteen fifty-two.
She heard me practise scales she never liked;
she watched my children learning how to walk;
she slept through every winter, every move,
and woke each spring as if no time had passed."

I thought of all the things she had outlasted:
three dogs, two houses, half a dozen fences,
a flood, a drought, a hundred kitchen radios.
And here she was, still blinking at the sun,
as if the whole of it had been one long
and pleasant afternoon.

Then she told me what the list had left out:
that Agatha is not slow, but patient;
that a creature who can live a hundred years
has no reason to hurry through an afternoon;
that I should sit with her, and wait, and watch,
and let her come to me in her own time.

On the bus home, Agatha put her head out
and watched the suburbs sliding past the window,
and I watched her, and neither of us hurried.

Now each morning I set the brick out in the sun
and sit beside it with my toast, and wait.
Some days she comes. Some days she keeps to the fern.
I have learnt to read her by the smallest things:
the stretch of neck, the slow blink, the eager walk
whenever she hears a dandelion picked.

Last week I counted forward on my fingers.
If Agatha lives as long as tortoises can,
she'll still be grazing when my hair is grey,
and one day I'll be handing down this box
to someone young who thinks she's very dull.
What will I tell them? Only this: look after her.
She'll look after you.
Question: According to Great-Gran's list, what should Agatha be fed?
Option A: lettuce, not dandelions
Option B: fern leaves and straw
Option C: lemons from the garden
Option D: dandelions, not lettuce

Hush: Why Every Family Sings
Every night, in kitchens, bedrooms and hospital wards around the world, someone is singing a baby to sleep. It might be a mother or a father, a grandmother, an uncle or a big sister standing by the cot. The words change from place to place, but the lullaby itself seems to be one of the oldest and most widespread family traditions on Earth.
Lullabies sound remarkably alike, even across very different cultures. In a 2018 experiment, researchers at Harvard University played recordings of songs from 86 small communities around the world to hundreds of listeners in about 60 countries. The listeners did not understand the words, yet they could usually tell which songs were lullabies. The researchers concluded that lullabies share a recognisable shape: they tend to be slow, soft and simple, with melodies that drift gently downwards and a swaying rhythm that matches the rocking of a parent's arms.
Repetition is another common feature. Many lullabies repeat a soothing word or phrase at the start of each line, and many end where they began. Here is a short example of the kind of lullaby a family might make up for itself:
Hush now, the possums are out on the wire,
hush now, the kettle's asleep by the fire,
the moon's on the roof and the stars are all near,
hush now, my darling, for Nana is here.
Notice how each pair of lines rhymes, how "hush now" returns again and again, and how the final line turns from the outside world to the singer and the child.
Do lullabies actually work? A 2021 study suggests that they do. Babies who heard lullabies, even ones from cultures they had never encountered, became more relaxed than babies who heard other kinds of songs. Their heart rates slowed, their pupils became smaller and their skin showed fewer signs of stress. In other words, the calming effect does not depend on knowing the words or the tune. The researchers suggested that babies may be born ready to respond to these sounds, which could help explain why lullabies are found almost everywhere.
Lullabies help the singer, too. Parents of newborns are often exhausted and anxious, and singing slowly forces them to breathe slowly. Many parents say that the songs calm them as much as they calm the baby. Singing also gives fathers, grandparents and siblings a simple, gentle way to share in the care of a new family member. A few minutes of quiet singing can also become part of a bedtime routine, a signal that tells a baby the busy day is ending.
Perhaps the most precious thing about lullabies, however, is the way they travel down the generations. A grandmother who grew up speaking Greek or Vietnamese may sing to her grandchild in that language, passing on sounds and words the child may never hear anywhere else. Families also change the words to fit their own lives, adding a child's name, the family dog or the creek behind the house. A lullaby sung today may contain lines from a great-grandmother's childhood alongside lines invented last week. Some families even record grandparents singing, so that the songs survive when relatives live far apart.
You do not need a good voice to sing one. Babies are not music critics; they respond to the closeness, the rhythm and the familiar voice, not to perfect notes. So if there is a baby in your family, it may be worth learning the songs your parents or grandparents sang to you, or making up a new one. Some day, someone may sing it to a child you will never meet.

Option A: difficult to sing
Option B: pleasant to hear
Option C: easy to identify
Option D: newly invented

The Farmer Who Lent His Fields to Music
On 19 September 1970, about 1,500 people walked through the gates of a dairy farm near the village of Pilton, in Somerset, England. They had each paid one pound for a ticket, and the price included free milk from the farm's own cows. On a small stage in the corner of a field, bands played into the evening, finishing with T. Rex, a late replacement for another group. The festival lost money, and few people that weekend could have guessed that it would grow into one of the largest music festivals on the planet. Its organiser was a thirty-four-year-old dairy farmer named Michael Eavis.
Eavis was born in 1935 and grew up on Worthy Farm, the land his family had worked for generations. As a teenager he trained for a life at sea and joined the merchant navy, but when he was nineteen his father died, and he came home to run the farm. For the next fifteen years his days were ruled by milking times, weather and the price of feed. He learnt to rise before dawn, a habit he never lost.
Then, in the summer of 1970, he went to an open-air blues festival at a showground not far from his farm. Standing in the crowd, he was struck by the atmosphere: thousands of people gathered peacefully in the open air, listening to music together. He went home convinced that his own fields could host something similar. Within three months he had booked the bands and printed the tickets. It was a bold step for a man with no experience of the music business.
From these humble beginnings, the Glastonbury Festival grew steadily. In 1971 a striking pyramid-shaped stage was built, and a version of the Pyramid Stage still stands at the heart of the festival today. Over the years, the line-ups grew to include many of the world's most famous musicians, as well as theatre, circus, comedy and dance. From the early 1980s, Eavis began giving a large share of the profits to charities, and the festival now donates millions of pounds every year to groups that work on causes such as clean water and the environment.
Success brought problems. In very wet years the fields turned into a sea of mud, and festival-goers waded between the stages in gumboots. As crowds grew, so did the number of gatecrashers who climbed over fences to get in without tickets. By 2000 the site was so overcrowded that local authorities threatened to stop the festival altogether. Eavis took a year off to rethink, then returned in 2002 with a huge new fence and stricter ticket checks. Neighbours who had complained about traffic and noise were offered help and a say in the planning.
One of Eavis's best decisions was to let the farm rest. Every five years or so, the festival takes a fallow year, a break that allows the grass to recover, the cows to graze in peace and the villagers to enjoy a quiet summer. Even in festival years, the cows return to the fields once the stages have been packed away and the last of the litter has been collected.
Today the festival welcomes more than 200,000 people, and its organisation has largely passed to Eavis's daughter, Emily. Yet Eavis has always described himself as a farmer first. For decades he was often seen on the site before dawn, checking on his herd before the music started. The milk that was handed out free in 1970 still comes from Worthy Farm, where the cows have always been part of the story.

Cushions at Midnight
In 1895, Harvard University in the United States had an embarrassing problem. The lecture hall in its brand-new art museum was almost impossible to use. When a lecturer spoke, each word lingered and blurred into the next, until the audience heard only a booming jumble. Speakers complained, and audiences gave up trying to follow. The university turned to a young physics instructor, Wallace Clement Sabine, and asked him to fix it. Sabine was twenty-seven and had never studied the science of sound.
The trouble was reverberation. When sound is made in a room, it travels out in every direction and bounces off the walls, floor and ceiling. Each time it strikes a surface, some of the sound is absorbed and the rest is reflected. In a room full of hard, bare surfaces, the reflections keep going long after the sound itself has stopped, because there is little soft material to soak it up. A little reverberation makes music sound rich and full, but too much turns speech into mud, because each new syllable overlaps the echoes of the ones before. In the museum's lecture hall, a single spoken word could still be heard about five and a half seconds later.
Sabine realised that he could not fix what he could not measure. He had no electronic equipment, so he used an organ pipe, a stopwatch and his own ears. He would sound the pipe, stop it suddenly, and time how long it took for the sound to fade until he could no longer hear it. He repeated each measurement many times, because his ears, like anyone's, could be tired or distracted. To keep out the clatter of carts and trams, he worked late at night, usually between midnight and five in the morning.
To test how soft materials changed the result, he borrowed hundreds of seat cushions from a nearby theatre that was famous for its clear sound. Night after night, Sabine and his assistants carried the cushions in, laid them along the benches, took their measurements and then hurried the cushions back before dawn, so that the theatre would be ready for its next audience.
Slowly a pattern appeared. Every cushion added to the room shortened the reverberation by a predictable amount. Sabine discovered that reverberation time depends on two things: the volume of the room and the total amount of absorbing material inside it. Large rooms ring for longer; carpets, curtains, cushions and even the audience's clothing soak up sound. He turned this relationship into a simple formula that architects still use today. Fittingly, a unit of sound absorption is now called the "sabin".
The museum's lecture hall was never perfect, but with felt panels added to its walls it became usable. Sabine's greatest test came in 1898, when he was asked to advise on a new concert hall for the Boston Symphony Orchestra. For the first time, a hall was designed using calculations about sound before a single brick was laid. Sabine chose the shape, size and materials of the room so that music would linger for just under two seconds when the seats were full. The wooden panels, the plaster and even the shallow niches along the upper walls were all chosen with sound in mind.
Boston's Symphony Hall opened in 1900. More than a century later, musicians and listeners still rank it among the finest concert halls in the world. The young man who had started with borrowed cushions and a stopwatch had turned the guesswork of building for sound into a science.
